pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Use a fresh experiment directory outside original stores; do not overwrite original PDFs.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on PatClArC and removal of Clever Hans and backdoor behavior. V2 reframes the central contribution around directional precision versus concept separability and adds a main claim about improving TCAV sensitivity testing. The claim that pattern-based vectors better estimate concept directions remains, while the specific backdoor-removal contribution disappears.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive applicability qualifications: filter-CAVs may be preferable for concept detection and bottleneck models, estimated artifact masks can distort evaluation, and correlated signals may explain the Bone Age exception. It also interprets ResNet18's spatially diffuse TCAV maps. V1 instead emphasizes MNIST backdoor failures and the limitation of representing artifacts with one linear direction.

D1.justification: V1 documents MNIST colors, a small CNN, and its AdaDelta schedule. V2 provides substantially fuller information for its experiments: dataset counts and splits, FunnyBirds class construction, pretrained-weight provenance, optimizer/learning-rate/epoch schedules, and the RR-ClArC penalty search and selected values (Appendices B and C.4; Tables 2–5). It also identifies the attribution software and configuration.

E1.justification: V2 removes the MNIST/CIFAR10 experiments, explicit backdoor scenarios, and ILSVRC2012 artifact evaluations. It adds Bone Age brightness artifacts, controlled ISIC2019 timestamps, and FunnyBirds concept tasks. Real ISIC2019 band-aid evaluation remains and expands to rulers and skin markers. ImageNet remains a pretraining source rather than an artifact-evaluation benchmark.

E2.justification: V1 primarily compares pattern-CAVs with SVM-derived CAVs and baseline models. V2 systematically evaluates lasso, logistic regression, ridge regression, and SVM CAVs alongside pattern-CAVs, retaining a vanilla model control for correction. Its TCAV comparison additionally includes sample-specific ground-truth directions (Figure 6).

E3.justification: V2 replaces the small-CNN controlled experiments with VGG16, ResNet18, and EfficientNet-B0 evaluations and examines many more layers. It introduces paired-sample cosine alignment, AUC, TCAV, and artifact-relevance metrics, plus mask-based insertion of real artifacts into test images. Its correction experiments use ten-epoch RR-ClArC training and validation-selected penalty weights, unlike v1's five-epoch augmentation or training-free projection.

E4.justification: V2 extends the distractor demonstration with feature-scaling, noise-magnitude, and random-seed experiments, and adds preprocessing sensitivity, layerwise correction, neuron-visualization, and TCAV-localization analyses. V1's predicted-versus-ground-truth artifact-label study (Appendix C), fine-tuning trajectories, and ImageNet nearest-neighbor case studies are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: V1 provides averaged results and shaded curves in Figure 4 without defining their uncertainty calculation. V2 explicitly reports standard errors for alignment/AUC and correction results, specifies Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney-based AUC error estimation, and adds seed-varying toy examples. These additions establish expanded uncertainty reporting, not an increase in repeated model-training runs.

E6.justification: Most result sets are replaced or newly introduced. For example, v1 Table 1 reports poisoned CIFAR10-box input accuracy of 0.730 versus 0.625 for pattern versus filter A-ClArC; v2 Table 1 reports 0.69 versus 0.36 for pattern versus SVM RR-ClArC on controlled ISIC2019 with VGG16. These are different settings, not cross-version performance gains. V2 additionally reports alignment, separability, and TCAV outcomes.

M1.justification: The CAV estimator remains covariance divided by label variance (v1 Equation 1; v2 Equation 3). However, its model-correction integration changes substantially: v1 uses A-ClArC augmentation or P-ClArC projection, whereas v2 adopts the cited RR-ClArC procedure with a squared directional-gradient training penalty (Section 4.3.2). This changes the correction objective and procedure without introducing a different pattern estimator.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. PCAV/PatClArC terminology gives way to pattern-CAV terminology, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around directional accuracy and downstream applications. The appendices are rebuilt around methods/proofs, experimental details, and additional results.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout and substantially redesigns the visual presentation. New introductory concept illustrations, alignment plots, sensitivity maps, and grouped multi-metric tables replace much of v1's correction tables and nearest-neighbor galleries. Attribution-difference displays also change their organization and color conventions; this exceeds renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 retains the foundational Haufe, Kindermans, TCAV, and ClArC references but substantially redirects related work from broad explainability and backdoor defenses toward concept representations and applications. Added positioning includes superposition, CRAFT, concept activation regions, post-hoc concept bottlenecks, and RR-ClArC, rather than merely updated bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: V1 supplies the covariance estimator, correction equations, and a toy signal/distractor construction. V2 adds substantial mathematical analysis in Appendix A: the binary-label difference-of-means derivation, coordinate-scaling behavior, expected robustness to independent zero-mean noise, and logistic/SVM divergence arguments, including Theorems A.1–A.3.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central concept-direction claim by replacing largely indirect validation with paired-sample alignment measurements, broader comparisons, and explicit mathematical analysis. Fuller protocol documentation and uncertainty reporting also improve assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of earlier backdoor and predicted-label studies, although v2 introduces reporting problems: some band-aid values disagree between Tables 1 and 7, and Section 4.3.1 equates zero sensitivity with TCAV 0.5 despite Equation 6's strict-positive definition.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pattern-based concept activation vector research despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original concept-alignment, TCAV, and model-correction experiments on Bone Age, ISIC2019, and FunnyBirds, including extensive appendix results.

before.justification: V1 reports original toy experiments, MNIST/CIFAR10 model-correction results, and ImageNet/ISIC2019 artifact analyses, with additional experiments in Appendices C and D.

results.title: Navigating Neural Space: Revisiting Concept Activation Vectors to Overcome Directional Divergence

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain unchanged. The abstract and introduction modestly broaden the explicitly claimed demonstration of benefits to ReXNet and Vision Transformers, beyond the VGG, ResNet, and EfficientNet architectures named in v2.

C2.justification: V3 explains that unsupervised discovery requires manual concept selection and may miss the desired concept (D.3), and interprets high classifier test accuracy as evidence that directional errors are not simply classification failures (D.5). It removes v2's warning about error-prone estimated artifact masks. The limitation favoring filter-CAVs for concept detection is retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds an explicit code-access pointer, exact pretrained checkpoint identifiers in Table 4, GPU specifications and training/correction times in C.3, and asset licensing information in C.4. It also expands architecture-specific training and correction settings. V2 provides optimizer schedules and correction weights but lacks these important access, checkpoint, and resource disclosures.

E1.justification: V3 adds ImageNet timestamp/backdoor evaluation and CelebA hair-color prediction with a natural tie-related bias (Appendix D.9). It also adds artificial timestamps and naturally occurring L-marker artifacts in Bone Age (D.8). These extend the original coverage to additional domains and shortcut conditions; ImageNet previously served only as a pretraining source.

E2.justification: The lasso, logistic, ridge, SVM, and Vanilla comparisons are retained. V3 additionally evaluates CRAFT's unsupervised concept directions against pattern-CAV and SVM-CAV for the ISIC2019 timestamp experiment (D.3.1, Figure 28). CRAFT was cited but not experimentally compared in v2. This is a limited comparator addition.

E3.justification: V3 adds ResNet50, ResNeXt50, ReXNet100, EfficientNetV2, ViT, and Swin experimental configurations. Table 4 also revises existing settings: controlled-ISIC2019 VGG16 changes from learning rate 0.05 and 150 epochs to 0.005 and 300 epochs, while ResNet18 changes from SGD to Adam. Correction layers and the regularization search grid change, and transformer attribution uses SHAP. These are reported protocol revisions; they do not establish which retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds a 1024-dimensional distractor simulation (B.5), reduced-data and mislabeled-concept tests (D.3), held-out filter-classifier accuracy diagnostics (D.5), and variance/PCA analyses connecting activation noise to directional divergence (D.6). Conversely, v2's correction-layer sensitivity sweeps in Figures 8 and 28 are absent from v3.

E5.justification: V2 already reports standard errors. V3 additionally documents 500 randomly subsampled CAV fits and two-sided TCAV t-tests with Bonferroni correction (D.5, Table 5), ten-seed averaging for the new robustness experiments (Figure 29), and z-test significance markers in correction tables. The 500-fit count is newly reported, not an established increase over a stated v2 count.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results for new architectures, datasets, artifacts, and robustness analyses, and replaces numerous ResNet18 and EfficientNet-B0 entries. For example, EfficientNet-B0's Bone Age biased accuracies for pattern-CAV/SVM change from 0.61/0.50 in v2 Table 6 to 0.75/0.75 in v3 Table 8. Because stated settings also change, these are revised results rather than demonstrated same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The proposed pattern-CAV estimator remains activation-label covariance divided by label variance, reducing to a difference of means for binary labels. TCAV and the RR-ClArC gradient penalty are retained. Clarified mathematical exposition and additional tested architectures do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. V3 refines explanations and terminology, updates author/affiliation/header text, moves limitations from Section 4.3.3 to the conclusion, and reorganizes the appendices around additional analyses. Most retained prose is recognizably preserved rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V3 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column conference format and substantially rearranges displays. V2 Figures 3 and 4 merge into v3 Figure 3, and Figures 6 and 7 merge into Figure 5. Tables gain checkpoint columns, architecture groups, and significance markers; new robustness and noise-analysis displays are added, while correction-layer plots are removed.

R1.justification: The main research positioning remains stable. V3 adds Zhang et al. on unsupervised concept explanations and references supporting new architectures, datasets, attribution tools, and checkpoints. Its CRAFT discussion adds a limited comparison with unsupervised discovery. The revised Dreyer RR-ClArC citation represents publication of the same work, not a new method.

T1.justification: V3 corrects the matrix regression specification in Equation (2), replacing the 2-norm with an explicitly defined Frobenius norm and expressing the feature-wise bias as 1b^T. The covariance estimator, difference-of-means result, scaling/noise assumptions, and three divergence theorems and proofs remain substantively intact.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v2's limited architecture and domain coverage. Tests of scarce or incorrect concept labels, an evaluated unsupervised alternative, and additional natural biases address important questions about robustness and applicability. Statistical analyses and concrete reproducibility disclosures improve auditability. These gains outweigh losing the correction-layer sweep, although reporting inconsistencies remain, including selected weights in Table 7 outside the search grid stated in D.7.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pattern-CAV study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support matching retained, revised, added, and removed material.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments involving further architectures, robustness conditions, ImageNet, CelebA, and additional Bone Age artifacts.

before.justification: V2 reports original simulations and experiments on ISIC2019, Pediatric Bone Age, and FunnyBirds, including concept alignment, TCAV, and model correction results.

results.title: Navigating Neural Space: Revisiting Concept Activation Vectors to Overcome Directional Divergence

C1.justification: v2's abstract and contribution statement add identification with right censoring and truncation by death, alternative sufficient assumptions, and a nonparametric-framework claim. Censoring was explicitly future work in v1, which lacked the corresponding observed-data restriction result. The central g-computation, IPW, and double-robustness claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and limitations. Section 3.9 qualifies nonparametric generality through Assumption 9 and leaves broader generality conjectural. Section 5.1 discusses discrete observation, measurement error, irregular sampling grids, and unresolved smoothing choices, while the discussion develops positivity limitations.

D1.justification: New Section 5.1 documents a tentative estimation workflow using increasingly fine partitions and suggests pre-smoothing discretely observed curves. This adds limited practical guidance, but no implemented algorithm, tuning parameters, software, or new data-access instructions.

E1.justification: Figure 1 retains the same three illustrative process scenarios. The expanded medical examples describe possible applications; no additional dataset or task is actually analyzed.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. v2 Table 1 classifies related literature and introduces no evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: No experimental evaluation protocol is added or revised. The censoring framework is theoretical, and Section 5.1's partitioning and smoothing suggestions are prospective estimation ideas.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness experiments, or applied case-study results. v2's numbered clinical examples remain illustrative, and sensitivity analysis remains future work.

E5.justification: Neither version reports simulation seeds, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 adds no uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: The simulated paths displayed in Figure 1 are unchanged. No empirical estimates, performance comparisons, or additional observed findings are reported; the new mathematical results are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: v1 develops identification for an uncensored terminal outcome. v2 Section 4 adapts the intervention measure, weighting processes, and estimating equations to outcome histories and time-to-event outcomes with right censoring. This substantially extends the inference procedure while retaining its g-computation, IPW, and doubly robust foundations.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and literature narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 moves preliminaries before the technical review, adds a more detailed section hierarchy, and collects major proofs in Appendix A. Terminology changes include regular/irregular/functional longitudinal data and 'intervenable' replacing 'achievable'.

P2.justification: v2 adds the literature-summary Table 1. Figure 1 moves from page 2 to page 3 and receives a revised caption, while retaining its paths, axes, and panel arrangement. The overall single-column presentation remains similar.

R1.justification: Sections 1.1 and 2.4 substantially expand positioning around estimand-based versus model-based approaches. Added discussion includes Singer, Commenges and Gégout-Petit, Sun and Crawford, and functional-treatment/covariate research. Table 1 organizes this distinction across regular, irregular, and functional longitudinal data.

T1.justification: v2 replaces v1's ancillary-treatment sufficient condition with coarsening-at-random and strong-consistency conditions in Section 3.8, adds continuity Assumption 9 and Theorem 7 with an appendix proof, and introduces censoring assumptions and primed identification theorems in Section 4. Theorems 3–4 also now require Assumptions 1, 2, and 5 instead of 1–5. These changes go beyond relocating existing proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important limitation explicitly deferred in v1 by developing identification with death and right censoring. The alternative sufficient conditions, explicit connections to earlier frameworks, and clearer separation of exposition from proofs substantially improve theoretical completeness and accessibility. These gains are qualified: estimation remains heuristic, and the abstract's broad nonparametric claim requires the continuity qualification acknowledged in Section 3.9.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same continuous-time causal identification framework despite the changed title and expanded scope. All pages, equations, displays, and v2 Appendix A support comparison; v1 presents its proofs in the main text.

after.justification: Figure 1 retains the illustrative simulated realizations from v1. The additional clinical examples and sample-level estimation discussion do not report further empirical analyses.

before.justification: Limited to illustrative simulation output: Figure 1 presents simulated covariate-process realizations for fixed visits, irregular visits, and continuous monitoring. No estimator-performance experiment or original real-data analysis is reported.

results.title: Causal Identification for Complex Functional Longitudinal Studies

C1.justification: Both versions claim two central contributions: propagating epistemic uncertainty through MCTS and using it for optimistic deep exploration. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claim of improved Deep Sea exploration relative to non-planning exploration baselines. V3 adds supporting evidence without materially redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds Section 3.1's distinction between epistemic and non-epistemic uncertainty sources and explains how partially learned models fit the framework. Section 3.4 expands the existing representation-collapse discussion with auxiliary-model and ensemble-target alternatives. New interpretations connect beta robustness to separate exploration episodes and explain why cited UBE criticisms are argued not to apply to E-MCTS's UCB-style exploration.

D1.justification: V3 adds explicit E-MCTS pseudocode, the RND/UBE maximum prescription, BDQN implementation-source and configuration information, and an A-40 GPU to the compute description. Most implementation appendices and architecture/hyperparameter tables are retained. The new BDQN batch-size disclosure is internally inconsistent: Appendix C.3 writes '5 × 256 = 1230,' leaving the actual setting uncertain.

E1.justification: V2 evaluates only 40-by-40 Deep Sea. V3 Figure 2 adds sizes 10, 20, 30, and 50, extending coverage to different exploration horizons and environment sizes; its sensitivity experiment uses 30-by-30 Deep Sea. The domain and underlying task remain unchanged.

E2.justification: V3 adds Bootstrapped DQN with ensemble size 10 as an evaluated model-free reference in Figure 1 and the scaling comparison in Figure 2. The existing UBE and uninformed comparators remain; 'Only UBE' becoming 'UBE' is a rename, and its action-selection equation is retained in Appendix B.7.

E3.justification: V3 adds protocols measuring episodes until average regret falls below 90% for scaling, and average regret over 1,000 episodes for a beta sweep. The existing architecture and hyperparameter tables remain unchanged. An unresolved inconsistency limits interpretation of the main experiment's budget: v3 Figure 1 plots the abstracted model through 40,000 steps, while Table 4 still specifies 35,000.

E4.justification: V2 has no comparable sensitivity or diagnostic studies. V3 adds exploration-cost scaling with environment size, a beta-sensitivity analysis, and single-run heat maps comparing root uncertainty with inverse visitation counts over training. These substantially expand evidence about scalability, parameter dependence, and uncertainty behavior.

E5.justification: Figure 1's reported replication increases from five seeds generally, and ten for anchored E-MCTS/UBE in v2, to twenty seeds in v3. Table 1 newly specifies method-dependent totals of 20–35 seeds, while Figure 2 reports five seeds for scaling and three for sensitivity. Standard deviations and standard errors remain the reporting conventions; the substantial change is replication and explicit run-count reporting.

E6.justification: Main results are extensively replaced and supplemented. Table 1's true-model E-MCTS result changes from 7,279 ± 2,430 steps and 100% discovery to 10,539 ± 9,006 and 94% of 35 seeds; abstracted-model UBE discovery changes from 80% to 57%. V3 also adds BDQN, scaling, sensitivity, and heat-map findings. These are revised aggregates with changed reported replication, not controlled before-and-after performance gains.

M1.justification: The core propagation equations, optimistic search objective, and training losses are retained. However, v3 Appendix B.3 explicitly sets the RND-based value-uncertainty estimate to the maximum of an RND error and a UBE prediction, whereas v2 describes using UBE at leaves without this maximum. The PDFs do not establish whether this is a procedural revision or a previously undocumented implementation detail.

P1.justification: V3 adds a dedicated uncertainty-sources subsection, substantially rewrites the limitations, related-work, and experimental narratives, and reorganizes the background. The UBE baseline equation moves into Appendix B.7, while exploration/exploitation implementation discussion is consolidated in Appendix B.5. These are substantial explanatory and structural revisions beyond added results.

P2.justification: V3 adds the two-panel scaling/sensitivity Figure 2, the multi-panel uncertainty heat maps in Figure 3, and a color-highlighted Algorithm 1. Figure 1 gains BDQN curves and revised legends and axes; Table 1 gains explicit seed-count and successful-run labels. Appendix Tables 3 and 4 are also consolidated onto one page.

R1.justification: Section 4 substantially broadens positioning beyond v2's detailed Plan2Explore and stochastic/POMDP-planning discussion. V3 adds several model-based exploration works, ensemble-based uncertainty methods, Bootstrapped DQN, Wasserstein temporal-difference learning, and discussion of Janz et al.'s UBE critique. This changes the breadth and substance of the comparison with prior research.

T1.justification: The Taylor approximations, total-variance derivation, independence assumption, and uncertainty-backup equations retain their mathematical substance. Appendix A's proof and Appendices B.1–B.2's targets and losses are unchanged. Simplified notation, conceptual explanations, and the new pseudocode do not add a theorem or revise the theoretical derivation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v2's narrow empirical validation through an established model-free comparator, larger reported replication, scaling tests, beta sensitivity, and direct uncertainty diagnostics. These additions better substantiate the claimed exploration advantage and its robustness, while pseudocode and expanded explanations improve assessability. Evaluation remains confined to Deep Sea, and the batch-size arithmetic, training-horizon discrepancy, and uncertain status of the RND/UBE rule limit reproducibility, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same E-MCTS research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, Tables 1–4, and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V3 reports revised Deep Sea results and additional Bootstrapped DQN comparisons, environment-size scaling, exploration-parameter sensitivity, and uncertainty visualizations in Figures 1–3.

before.justification: V2 reports original Deep Sea experiments comparing E-MCTS, UBE-only exploration, and uninformed exploration under three transition-model variants, with numerical results in Table 1 and learning curves in Figure 1.

results.title: Epistemic Monte Carlo Tree Search

C1.justification: The central uncertainty-propagation and deep-exploration claims remain, but v4 expands the contributions to a theoretically motivated UCB framework and a parallel JAX agent/environment implementation. Its abstract and conclusion add substantive claims about programming-task sample efficiency and exploration with stochastic rewards, extending v3's Deep Sea-focused empirical scope.

C2.justification: V4 adds substantive qualifications about neural-network prediction dependence and the UCB theorem's lack of automatic applicability to learned transitions. It also interprets input-output hashing through task-relevant novelty and proposes more reliable exploratory action sequences as an explanation for faster learning despite similar state coverage. These extend v3's emphasis on latent-state collapse and sufficient exploration strength.

D1.justification: Appendices C and E add Subleq semantics, example programs, JAX implementation provenance, hashing details, network activations and training/evaluation hyperparameters. Appendix D.6 additionally documents an optimistic floor for UBE predictions. Conversely, v3 Appendix B.8's GPU specifications, per-run resource allocations and 12–65-hour training-time disclosure are removed.

E1.justification: V3 evaluates deterministic-reward Deep Sea. V4 adds the Subleq programming domain with Negate Positives and Identity Function tasks, plus a stochastic-reward Deep Sea scenario requiring repeated exploration to distinguish rewarding and misleading terminal transitions. The original deterministic coverage remains.

E2.justification: The principal comparator families remain baseline Alpha/MuZero, UBE-based exploration and BDQN. However, Figure 2's scaling comparison replaces the anchored-model UBE comparator with AZ+UBE using RND and MZ+UBE using counts. The anchored-model comparison remains elsewhere, in v4 Figure 4; its removal is specific to the scaling experiment.

E3.justification: The new Subleq protocol uses program-correctness tests, Gumbel/Sequential Halving search, 32 search simulations, 128 parallel episodes and batch size 4096 (Sections 5.1 and E.4). The scaling experiment also changes its learned-model configuration from anchored reconstruction to abstracted/count-based models. The retained Deep Sea architecture and hyperparameter tables are unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds an ablation comparing full-observation and input-output hashing, tests exploration under stochastic rewards, and adds direct UBE-head predictions to the uncertainty heat maps. These examine estimator choice, reward-noise robustness and the benefit of propagating uncertainty through search. The existing beta sensitivity analysis and transition-model comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: V4 reports the new Subleq experiments over 15 seeds with two standard errors, introducing a different uncertainty-display convention, and reports 10 seeds for stochastic Deep Sea. Existing Deep Sea run counts and standard-error reporting, and Table 1's standard deviations, remain unchanged. This does not establish increased replication of retained experiments.

E6.justification: V4 adds Subleq results showing faster Identity Function learning with EMCTS, particularly with input-output hashing, and stochastic Deep Sea results favoring E-AZ. Revised scaling results include MZ+UBE solving size 40 in only two of five seeds and size 50 in none. Table 1's goal-discovery values and success percentages are unchanged; these are not new performance gains.

M1.justification: The equations and Algorithm 1 change the exploration bonus from the square root of averaged backup variances to averaged backup standard deviations, with a corresponding variance bound in v4 Equation 13. V4 also introduces a separately trained exploration-prior policy for its Subleq agent. These change the procedure beyond renaming E-MCTS to EMCTS.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much of the background and method narrative are rewritten. Section 3 is reorganized around learned reward models, epistemic search policies and uncertainty propagation; experiments are split into Subleq and Deep Sea. The appendices are extensively reorganized, with retained material moved alongside new theory, experiments and environment documentation.

P2.justification: V4 adds the Subleq learning-curve figure, expands Figure 2 from two to three panels, and adds a UBE row to Figure 3's heat maps. V3 Figure 1 becomes appendix Figure 4 with revised styling, and Table 1 moves to the appendix. Typography, headers and table placement also change throughout.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning around UCB-based RL theory and algorithm discovery, citing works such as Azar, Jin, Fawzi and Mankowitz. Related work adds Bayesian MCTS by Tesauro and model-based uncertainty by Luis, while dropping the discussion of Moerland's second type of MCTS uncertainty. This exceeds bibliographic updates to retained references.

T1.justification: V4 introduces Theorem 1's probabilistic UCB statement, a Chebyshev-based proof and a covariance-based bound for correlated backups. V3's Taylor/Jacobian uncertainty propagation and law-of-total-variance derivation are removed. V4 Appendix A.3 instead develops a maximal-uncertainty approximation for learned transitions and explains restrictions on extending the theorem.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially addresses v3's narrow empirical basis through programming tasks, stochastic-reward tests and direct EMCTS-versus-UBE uncertainty diagnostics. These test practical applicability and the proposed mechanism beyond deterministic Deep Sea. The revised covariance treatment and explicit theoretical qualifications also improve assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of hardware/runtime documentation, although the theoretical scope remains restricted and the unchanged Table 1 supplies no additional performance evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same epistemic MCTS research. All 18 pages of v3 and 27 pages of v4, including their appendices, support comparison. Methods, experiments and tables can be matched despite extensive renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains original Deep Sea results and adds original Subleq programming experiments, stochastic-reward Deep Sea results and uncertainty-estimator comparisons.

before.justification: V3 reports original Deep Sea experiments, including learning curves, goal-discovery statistics, environment-size scaling, exploration-parameter sensitivity and uncertainty visualizations.

results.title: Epistemic Monte Carlo Tree Search

C1.justification: v1 principally claims empirical exploration benefits and complementarity with parameter sharing. v2 additionally claims an unbiased off-policy framework that preserves convergence and is at least as sample efficient as its underlying algorithm. Its abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden complementarity claims to data sharing and multiple MTRL frameworks.

C2.justification: v2 explains gains through bridging SAC's policy-improvement gap and discusses Q-estimation errors. It adds substantive qualifications concerning available shared behavior, imperfect policy selection, the absence of guarantees for H-step sharing, and cases where sharing provides little benefit or hurts, including data sharing with QMP in Kitchen.

D1.justification: v2 documents mean-action scoring and omitted entropy, online UDS batch filtering and relabeling, additional environment hyperparameters, the MT10 sharing rule, and batching/runtime details (G–H). The video access address changes. Conversely, v1's explicit standalone QMP warmup search is omitted, although multihead warmup settings remain.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original three task sets, renaming Meta-World Manipulation as Meta-World CDS. It adds MT10, MT50, four-task Walker2D locomotion, ten-task Franka Kitchen manipulation and the illustrative 2D point-reaching experiment, substantially broadening evaluated task and environment coverage.

E2.justification: The independent/shared SAC and DnC variants are retained. v2 additionally evaluates online UDS and CDS, PCGrad, two MCAL variants and DECAF (Sections 7.1 and E.2–E.5). UDS also joins the retained Reacher per-task comparison. These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled protocols varying policy duration, softmax temperature, expected-Q estimation and SAC target entropy, plus three-versus-ten-task Maze comparisons. The point-reaching experiment uses fixed candidate policies with one trainable policy. Reported Meta-World CDS curves extend to 10M steps versus 8M in v1; original benchmark hyperparameters otherwise largely match.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained uniform/domain-knowledge ablations and mixture heatmap, v2 tests temporal sharing, probabilistic switching, mean-action approximation, single-task exploration and task-count scaling. It adds sharing trajectories over training, a Drawer Open rollout case study and computational-overhead analysis (Sections E–G), substantially expanding mechanism and sensitivity evidence.

E5.justification: The central practice remains reporting means and standard deviations over five seeds, with ten evaluation episodes per task (v1 Figure 4; v2 Figure 7). Additional plots and tabulated uncertainties do not document increased run counts or a new statistical estimation or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: v2 updates or extends retained learning curves and adds extensive benchmark, comparator, diagnostic and runtime results. For example, Table 2 newly reports Maze success of 72.9 for one-step QMP versus 99.9 at H=25, while MT10 falls from 89.0 to 82.0 at H=10. These are new within-v2 comparisons, not matched-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The core Q-switch data collection and task-specific SAC training remain. v2 adds limited procedural variants: selecting the current task policy 70% of the time on MT10 (H.5), and executing a selected policy for H steps (E.6). The new formal derivation and mean-action implementation disclosure alone do not establish a changed core implementation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and approach are extensively rewritten around off-policy data collection and formal policy improvement. Complementarity results move ahead of behavior-sharing comparisons. The compact original appendix is reorganized into Appendices A–H with a contents page, substantially changing the narrative and navigation.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. The introductory illustration is replaced, the method diagram is redrawn, and v1 Figure 5's panels are redistributed. New theory, trajectory, rollout and diagnostic figures, algorithm pseudocode, and result/runtime tables substantially expand the displays. Some appendix figure numbers duplicate main-text numbers.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around unbiased data collection, selective regularization, policy reuse and temporally extended exploration. Added discussions include Vuong et al., critic-guided policy reuse, Xu et al. (2024), and option-learning work; MCAL and DECAF also receive substantive comparisons. This exceeds bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: v1 contains the MDP formulation and mixture weights but no convergence proofs. v2 adds an entropy-regularized mixture derivation and soft policy improvement/iteration theorems with proofs (Sections 4–5 and Appendices B–C). It also permits task-specific transitions. The tabular proof introduces an additional assumption concerning differences in state coverage.

improvement.justification: v1's generality and complementarity claims rested on three task sets and one parameter-sharing study. v2 substantially strengthens their evidence through broader benchmarks, additional MTRL comparisons, targeted mechanism controls and runtime/implementation details. These resolve important validation gaps. The gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including duplicated figure numbering and sample-efficiency claims that extend beyond what the tabular analysis, with its additional state-coverage assumption, establishes for the implemented approximation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QMP research, with matching authors, core algorithm and original task sets despite the changed title. The main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across seven multi-task designs, a point-reaching example, additional comparator studies, ablations, behavior analyses and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on Multistage Reacher, Maze Navigation and Meta-World Manipulation, including baseline comparisons, ablations and per-task appendix results.

results.title: QMP: Q-switch Mixture of Policies for Multi-Task Behavior Sharing

C1.justification: The central claims of combating forgetting without task labels and approaching offline-oracle performance remain. V2 drops the three-solver contribution, adds an explicit small-buffer effectiveness claim and extends its comparative claim to model-based methods.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of MBPO's sampling bias and online EWC's adaptation–retention tradeoff, plus limitations concerning network capacity and more complex contexts requiring larger buffers. V1's explanations for surpassing offline policies and LCPO-P's weaker performance disappear. The exploration limitation is retained and expanded.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code URL, hardware and runtime information, tuning procedures, OOD sampling details and new-baseline hyperparameters. Software documentation changes from OpenAI Gym 0.26.2 to Gymnasium 0.29.1 and MuJoCo 3.1.1. Some earlier straggler specifications, including the full observation and reward description, are omitted.

E1.justification: V2 adds wind-driven InvertedPendulum-v4, InvertedDoublePendulum-v4, Hopper-v4 and Reacher-v4 evaluations. These substantially broaden the control tasks beyond v1's Pendulum-v1 and straggler mitigation. The grid-world example, four synthetic wind traces and two real workloads are retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with MBCD, MBPO and online EWC alongside the retained A2C, TRPO, DDQN, SAC and offline-oracle comparisons. Appendix A.2 also compares against Ideal MBPO using ground-truth dynamics. MBPO is additionally included in the wind-free Pendulum validation.

E3.justification: V2 introduces normalized-return aggregation, limited-buffer settings, buffer-size sweeps, EWC tuning protocols and a ground-truth-model MBPO control. It also revises the stated straggler OOD thresholds from -5/-6/-7 to 5/6/7, with corresponding interpretation changes. This reported correction does not establish that the underlying implementation changed.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of buffer-size sensitivity, EWC hyperparameter sensitivity, change-point detector sensitivity and whether model error explains MBPO's weakness. It removes v1's LCPO-S/D/P comparison while retaining the OOD-threshold sensitivity analysis. These changes substantially alter the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: The stated seed counts rise from five to ten for straggler mitigation and the wind-free Pendulum validation; the main wind-driven control experiments remain at five. V2 explicitly reports 95% confidence bounds or ranges and latency uncertainty bands, whereas v1's result tables provide point estimates without confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive MuJoCo and diagnostic results and revises retained-task estimates. For example, Pendulum trace 3 changes from LCPO-S -194 in v1 Table 1 to LCPO -237 in v2 Table 2; revised settings prevent interpreting this as a controlled performance decline. The new Reacher results show DDQN and online EWC outperforming LCPO on all four traces.

M1.justification: V2 retains v1's LCPO-S procedure as LCPO, but removes the doubly constrained LCPO-D and proximal LCPO-P alternatives. It adds bounded reservoir sampling to the accumulating experience archive described in v1. Automatic entropy regularization was already used in v1; its explicit inclusion in v2's objective is not a new component.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title and replaces input terminology with context terminology throughout. It substantially rewrites the introduction and methodology, swaps Preliminaries and Related Work, reorganizes evaluation around comparisons and sensitivities, and adds separate Discussion and Limitations and Broader Impact sections. The appendices are also extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the grid-world illustration into two modes and combines its two performance plots. It adds change-point, normalized-return, EWC and buffer-size figures; removes the Pendulum learning-curve figure; relocates trace and systems illustrations to the appendices; and substantially expands result tables and uncertainty displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated latent-context literature discussion and substantially expands positioning within observed exogenous-context RL, citing works such as Zintgraf, Caccia, Chen, Feng and Sinclair. It also develops comparisons with model-based learning and online EWC. The LCPO-P relationship to editable neural networks and its Sinitsin citation disappear.

T1.justification: V1 Appendix A.1's dual/KKT derivation for the doubly constrained optimization problem, including Equations 5–12, is removed entirely. V2 retains the former LCPO-S trust-region formulation and explicitly states the existing policy-gradient and entropy objectives, but supplies no replacement derivation for the removed solver.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical coverage and limited diagnostic and uncertainty reporting. Additional control tasks, relevant baselines, memory and model-error controls, confidence ranges and reproducibility disclosures make the evidence much more informative. These gains outweigh the narrower solver coverage and some lost environment detail. The broad superiority wording nevertheless needs qualification given the Reacher exceptions in Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LCPO research, with matching core formulations and retained experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original results across six evaluation environments, the grid-world illustration, and additional sensitivity and diagnostic experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original grid-world, wind-driven Pendulum and straggler-mitigation experiments, plus action-space validation in Appendix B.

results.title: Online Reinforcement Learning in Non-Stationary Context-Driven Environments

C1.justification: The central contribution remains OOD-based policy anchoring to mitigate forgetting without task labels in observed exogenous-context environments. Both versions claim strong aggregate performance relative to online baselines and proximity to offline-trained policies. Expanded supporting evidence and oracle-to-prescient terminology do not redefine that contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations for Sliding OGD, CLEAR, and PT-DQN failures and for LCPO-P's sensitivity to its penalty coefficient. It develops the causal-versus-prescient performance distinction, discusses OOD tuning requirements, and proposes forgetting sufficiently old contexts when network capacity becomes limiting.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds reservoir and OOD-sampling pseudocode and implementation detail. v3 also supplies new baseline/LCPO-P hyperparameters, warm-up details, software versions/licenses, and runtime information, and changes the code-access pointer. It newly discloses that the straggler environment and dataset are nonpublic and proprietary.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same grid-world example, five Gymnasium environments under four wind traces, and straggler mitigation on two production workloads. The added OOD and LCPO-P studies vary detector or optimizer configurations within this coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Tables 5–6 add evaluated Sliding OGD, CLEAR, BFDQN, and PT-DQN comparators. Appendix E.1 also compares LCPO-P. The buffer-size table replaces individually listed baseline columns with the best baseline per condition; the oracle-to-prescient renaming does not introduce a new comparator.

E3.justification: The grid-world diagnostic changes from up-action probability for one context to total-variation distance for both contexts. Added experiments specify OOD metric/threshold configurations and PPO settings for LCPO-P. Existing action discretization and main LCPO hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: OOD sensitivity testing expands beyond the retained straggler thresholds to Gymnasium threshold sweeps and a detector using joint state-context inputs without their separation. New analyses compare constrained anchoring with LCPO-P and examine forgetting in both grid-world modes. Existing buffer-size and ideal-model MBPO checks remain.

E5.justification: v3 reports 25 seeds for most main Gymnasium comparisons instead of five, retaining five for MBPO/MBCD and ten for straggler experiments. CDFs gain 95% confidence bands, and table captions explicitly define boldface through 95%-confidence superiority. Confidence intervals already existed in v2's tables.

E6.justification: Many Gymnasium estimates change alongside revised seed counts: LCPO on Pendulum trace 2 changes from -357 ±6.38 to -355 ±2.57. New comparator, OOD, LCPO-P, and runtime results substantially expand the evidence. Straggler Table 1 remains numerically unchanged; updated estimates do not establish an algorithmic performance gain.

M1.justification: The principal constrained LCPO algorithm is retained. Appendix E.1 introduces LCPO-P, an alternative that uses a cross-entropy anchoring penalty and repeated PPO updates instead of LCPO's hard anchoring constraint.

P1.justification: v3 reorganizes the illustration and methodology into subsections, moves detailed baseline explanations into Appendix D, rewrites the related-work narrative, and reverses the ordering of the two sensitivity sections. It adopts prescient terminology, adds reproducibility and acknowledgement sections, and removes the generic broader-impact section.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. v3 merges and expands the grid-world figures, adds an LCPO architecture diagram and new analysis tables, splits the main benchmark table, and rearranges existing context and latency panels. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 3 and new Appendix A substantially expand positioning against latent-context inference, meta-learning, multitask RL, stationary interference, and limited-buffer methods. New citations include Woo et al. (2022) and Anand and Precup (2023), with detailed discussion of how their approaches differ from LCPO.

T1.justification: v3 adds formal lifelong-average-return definitions, Lemma B.1 and Theorem B.2 with a tabular Q-learning convergence proof under restricted context assumptions, and binomial OOD-sampling analysis. These are absent from v2. The theorem's printed reward and learning-rate inequalities contain apparent sign errors.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's limited continual-learning comparator coverage and evidence for the anchoring design through additional baselines, Gymnasium OOD tests, and the LCPO-P comparison. More reported seeds, computational measurements, and implementation details strengthen empirical reliability and transparency. The new theorem's erroneous printed inequalities require correction, but this localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial validation and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LCPO research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds comparator results, OOD experiments, an LCPO-P comparison, and computational measurements in Section 5 and the appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original grid-world, wind-driven Gymnasium, and straggler-mitigation experiments, including comparative results and ablations in Section 6 and Appendices A–B.

results.title: Online Reinforcement Learning in Non-Stationary Context-Driven Environments

C1.justification: v5 narrows v4's broad claim of being the first generative-model data-valuation work to being the first model-agnostic, training-free approach, acknowledging existing model-specific methods. It also elevates image-quality calibration and four evaluation criteria into explicit contributions in the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive explanations of equal-credit bias for poor generated images, accumulated contributions from distant samples, and the accuracy/runtime tradeoff of DreamSim. It attributes VAE-TracIn's weak CIFAR-10 results to possible underfitting and identifies other modalities as future validation. v4 mainly interprets training-set proximity and qualitative facial resemblance; its applications discussion survives in Appendix F.

D1.justification: v5 newly provides hardware specifications in Table I, expanded dataset and model information in Appendix E, and layer/latent specifications in Table VII, substantially extending v4's sparse implementation documentation. Reliability is limited by reversed CPU/GPU labels and apparently swapped BigGAN/beta-VAE headings. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: Beyond v4's MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA scope, v5 evaluates high-resolution animal faces through AFHQ and human faces through FFHQ. It also introduces a Gaussian-corrupted MNIST data-cleansing scenario, expanding both represented domains and evaluation conditions.

E2.justification: v4 evaluates no external data-valuation baseline. v5 adds VAE-TracIn to the identical-class and runtime comparisons in Tables II and IV, and IF4GAN to noisy-data ranking and runtime comparisons in Figure 5 and Table IV.

E3.justification: v5 introduces quantitative class agreement using 100 generated samples and k=30, 50, 100, attribute agreement at k=5, 10, 15, corruption-ranking evaluation using 10,000 generated images, and timing protocols. It adds beta-VAE evaluations and changes the reported CelebA generator from StyleGAN2 to Diffusion-StyleGAN. The retained training/non-training experiment's Xv1/Xv2 swap is a relabeling.

E4.justification: v5 adds comparisons with and without re-ranking and across distance metrics, noisy-data ranking analysis, and generated-sample-size sensitivity testing in Appendix C. Figure 3 also examines the equal-credit problem using normal versus uniform latent sampling. These substantially extend v4's proximity tests and qualitative high/low-value face examples.

E5.justification: Appendix C newly specifies ten repetitions with resampled generated sets and adds variability plots; its prose describes mean and standard deviation, although Figure 7 displays boxplots. Appendix A revises the inherited test hypotheses and corrects the p-value wording while retaining the original test statistics. Repeated-run uncertainty remains limited to the supplementary sensitivity study.

E6.justification: v5 adds extensive class, attribute, cleansing, runtime, and sensitivity results. For example, Table II reports CIFAR-10 class agreement of 77.94% for DreamSim versus 6.28% for VAE-TracIn at k=30; Table IV reports noisy-MNIST valuation times of 17,086 seconds for DreamSim versus 14,543 for IF4GAN. These are new comparisons. The earlier statistical means, p-values, and t-statistics are retained after matching the swapped subset labels.

M1.justification: v5 retains PQ-based matching but adds perceptual re-ranking with LPIPS or DreamSim and MANIQA-based generated-image quality assessment. Its contribution function multiplies normalized similarity scores by image quality before aggregation, substantively changing valuation beyond v4's distance-based credits.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, formulation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. v5 organizes the method around explicit challenges and modules, replaces the research-assumption experiment structure with four criteria, and moves retained statistical and applications material into Appendices A and F. The title and author line also change.

P2.justification: v5 redraws the pipeline and distribution visualization, replaces the earlier high/low-value face displays with contributor grids, and adds quality examples, a violin plot, sensitivity boxplots, and structured experimental tables. The original statistical table is relocated to Appendix A, while typography, captions, and table organization are substantially revised.

R1.justification: v5 substantially revises positioning by acknowledging and discussing IF4GAN and VAE-TracIn, distinguishing concurrent LAVA, and organizing valuation methods into metric-based, influence-based, and data-driven approaches. New references supporting DreamSim, MANIQA, and evaluation criteria further expand the discussion beyond v4's largely discriminative-model literature.

T1.justification: v5 removes the explicit Wasserstein/coupling formulation, specifies deduplicated training data, extends the contribution definition with quality weighting, and adds a brief O(mnC)-to-O(mQD) recall-complexity argument. These are limited formal revisions around the retained similarity-score aggregation; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4's validation relied mainly on proximity assumptions, one statistical comparison, and qualitative face matches, without evaluated valuation baselines. v5 substantially addresses that weakness through baseline comparisons, quantitative attribution tests, cleansing and runtime evaluation, and repeated-sample sensitivity analysis, while narrowing its novelty claim. Contradictory wording in Table V, mislabeled technical tables, and inconsistent sample-size labels limit reliability, but the stronger comparative evidence and more accurate positioning provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GMValuator and retain identifiable methodological and experimental content. All nine pages of v4 and thirteen pages of v5, including Appendices A–F, support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent matching the material.

after.justification: v5 reports original class and attribute comparisons, noisy-data rankings, runtime measurements, and supplementary sensitivity experiments in its main text and appendices.

before.justification: v4 reports original CIFAR-10 distribution visualizations and statistical comparisons, plus qualitative CelebA attribution results in Figures 2–4 and Table 1.

results.title: GMValuator: Similarity-based Data Valuation for Generative Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand from multi-state recovery gains to claims of superior single-state recovery and speed over Rosetta, support for partial design, and zero-shot mutant prioritization. Partial/masked design, previously presented as future work, becomes an advertised capability. The original multi-state representation-learning contribution remains.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations of benefits in flexible/exposed nucleotides and of autoregressive decoding improving self-consistency. It discusses limitations of recovery and secondary-structure proxies, increased multi-state memory costs, and fitness-ranking advantages restricted to low screening budgets. New applicability limits include interacting RNA chains, ligand interactions, negative design and control of conformational propensities. Wet-lab validation remains future work.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's basic hyperparameters and encoder pseudocode, v4 documents cross-entropy training, teacher forcing, label smoothing, coordinate noise, dropout, sampling temperature and parameter count. It supplies the RNASolo snapshot date, A100 hardware, training time and state-dependent memory costs. These substantially expand reproducibility information; newly disclosed settings alone do not establish procedural changes.

E1.justification: v4 expands beyond inverse-folding recovery to zero-shot fitness ranking on 74,943 RNA polymerase ribozyme variants, adding experimental fitness data and a distinct prediction task (Section 4.3). The dedicated ensemble-size evaluation and theophylline case study from v1 are no longer reported. RNASolo remains the inverse-design data source.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares multi-state gRNAde with its single-state variant. v4 adds Rosetta and FARNA comparisons using published recovery values, plus fitness-ranking baselines that randomly select from all variants, single mutants, or single and double mutants. Appendix Table 2 additionally compares autoregressive and one-shot decoders.

E3.justification: v4 replaces the three original splits with structurally clustered single-/multi-state splits using TM-score >0.45, and changes validation/test sizes from 200 to 100 each. Resolution filtering changes from 3 to 4 Å, and sampled designs from 100 to 16 per example. It adds MCC/perplexity metrics and screening-budget evaluation, while changing encoder/decoder depth from 3 to 4 layers, training from 100 to at most 50 epochs, and initial learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0001.

E4.justification: State-count comparisons continue, but v4 adds decoder-type and maximum-training-length ablations (Appendix Table 2), recovery analyses by nucleotide pairing, solvent accessibility and RMSD (Figure 6), and a perplexity–recovery analysis (Figure 4). The detailed theophylline case study in v1 Table 2 is removed.

E5.justification: Three-seed model evaluation is retained, with v4 explicitly identifying standard deviations. The new fitness study extends uncertainty reporting through 10,000 simulations per randomized strategy and screening budget. Figure 7 specifies medians and interquartile ranges, although the surrounding text calls the intervals confidence intervals. This does not establish an increase in training runs.

E6.justification: The original splitwise and theophylline results are replaced by new benchmark, ablation and fitness-ranking findings. v4 Appendix Table 1 reports recovery of 0.5682 for gRNAde versus 0.45 for Rosetta and 0.32 for FARNA. In its multi-state split, one-to-five-state mean recovery rises from 0.4549 to 0.4722, while mean MCC falls from 0.5689 to 0.5488 (Appendix Table 2). Changed protocols prevent interpreting these as performance changes relative to v1.

M1.justification: The multi-state GVP encoder, conformer averaging and autoregressive decoder remain. Graph construction changes from C4' coordinates with 10 neighbors to three-bead centroids with 32 neighbors, and edge encodings increase from 16 to 32 channels. v4 also describes distance/angle/torsion features and evaluates a one-shot MLP decoder variant. These refine the retained architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The method becomes a structured exposition of the problem, representation, architecture and metrics; results are organized into three application sections. Separate related-work and usage-FAQ appendices substantially reorganize and expand the narrative around retained technical material.

P2.justification: v4 changes the main layout from two columns to one, redraws the pipeline and adds feature, architecture, evaluation and tensor-symmetry diagrams. New benchmark, nucleotide-analysis and fitness plots accompany redesigned result tables. The dataset-statistics display is retained and updated as Figure 9; the theophylline structure/sequence-logo table is removed.

R1.justification: v4 adds a substantial related-work appendix covering energy-based inverse folding, backbone generation, structure prediction and RNA language models, including RNA FM, RiNaLMo and CodonBERT. It develops comparisons with Rosetta and positions gRNAde as a structure-conditioned language model, substantially extending v1's shorter RNA-versus-protein motivation.

T1.justification: v4 adds an explicit distinction between the SO(3)-equivariant encoder with dihedral inputs and its O(3)-equivariant GVP layers. Section 4.2 also introduces a numerical probability-averaging counterexample; it does not establish the accompanying criticism of logit averaging because it averages probabilities. The main pooling mathematics remains, without substantial new theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence previously centered on recovery against its own single-state baseline. Structural-cluster holdouts, comparisons with published Rosetta/FARNA results, controlled ablations and retrospective fitness analysis improve assessment of generalization and practical utility. Expanded technical details and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: Rosetta runtime superiority is not established by controlled timing, and Figure 5's single-seed self-consistency benefit does not persist in the three-seed means in Appendix Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde multi-state RNA design framework. Their main texts, appendices, equations, figures and tables are readable and support reliable comparison despite the changed title and expanded scope.

after.justification: v4 reports original gRNAde evaluations, ablations, nucleotide-level analyses and retrospective fitness-ranking simulations. Rosetta and FARNA results are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations across three data splits and a theophylline aptamer case study, including numerical sequence-recovery results in Tables 1–2.

results.title: gRNAde: Geometric Deep Learning for 3D RNA inverse design

C1.justification: The abstract and central design, speed, and multi-state claims remain stable. V5's conclusion adds the claim that perplexity correlates with structural recovery. The introduction stops foregrounding partial design as a contribution, although that capability remains described in Section 2.3.

C2.justification: V5 adds substantive interpretations of 3D designability, native-sequence predictions as a reference ceiling, transfer from ribosomal training data, and autoregressive modeling of paired nucleotide constraints. It expands guidance on predictor-dependent sequence selection. It also removes explicit statements about inability to modulate conformational propensities and random selection outperforming gRNAde at larger screening budgets; the latter behavior remains visible in revised Figure 7.

D1.justification: V5 specifies a 3,000-node minibatch limit for the reported GPU-memory figures and eight encoder layers for non-autoregressive models. It also supplies designed sequences with structural examples. These improve implementation and reproduction detail without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments; code access remains unchanged.

E1.justification: V5 extends fitness-ranking evaluation from catalytic subunit 5TU to scaffolding subunit t1, covering 47,504 mutants in Figure 12. RNASolo coverage and the 14-RNA benchmark remain unchanged; the three structural case studies use RNAs already represented in v4.

E2.justification: V5 adds ViennaRNA to the 14-RNA comparison and both aggregate test splits, plus ground-truth-sequence and random-sequence controls in Table 1. These substantially broaden comparison beyond the retained Rosetta/FARNA results and model variants.

E3.justification: V5 adds RhoFold-based C4' RMSD, TM-score, GDT_TS, and designability-threshold percentages. Appendix A introduces evaluations using 100 designs per RNA at temperature 0.5, alongside the retained standard 16-design, temperature-0.1 protocol. Figure 7 revises screening budgets and extends them from 2,000 to 10,493. The stated 'All data' evaluation changes from the multi-state to single-state test set, and one training-length ablation changes from 2,000 to 2,500 nucleotides; these disclosures do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: V5 adds invariant-versus-equivariant GNN ablations, extends autoregressive/non-autoregressive comparisons to the single-state split, and evaluates existing ablations using 3D metrics. Figures 8–11 add structural case studies and perplexity-versus-structural-consistency analysis. Conversely, v4's three-state and five-state non-autoregressive ablation rows are absent from v5 Table 1.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations across three consistent random seeds and summarize stochastic fitness-ranking strategies using medians and interquartile ranges from 10,000 simulations. Added results retain these practices; changed numerical uncertainties do not establish a change in statistical procedure.

E6.justification: V5 adds extensive 3D scores, baseline results, structural examples, and t1 fitness-ranking outcomes. Some retained aggregate values change beyond rounding: single-state, one-state AR recovery changes from 0.5271 to 0.530, and secondary-structure MCC from 0.5706 to 0.585 (v4 Table 2; v5 Table 1). The original 14-RNA gRNAde, Rosetta, and FARNA entries remain unchanged, with ViennaRNA added at 0.27 overall recovery. 'All data' results accompany a changed stated test split and cannot establish same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The proposed backbone featurization, multi-state GVP-GNN encoder, conformer pooling, autoregressive decoder, loss, and sampling procedure remain unchanged in Section 2 and Listing 1. The added invariant-GNN configurations are evaluated as ablations.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section order are retained. V5 makes local language corrections, adds an author and affiliation, expands metric and FAQ explanations, and organizes appendix material into dedicated visualization, ablation, results, and figure sections.

P2.justification: V5 adds structural overlays, structural-score plots, and the t1 ranking figure; expands the aggregate table substantially; and adds ViennaRNA to Figure 4. It redraws and promotes the evaluation schematic, relocates the architecture diagram to the appendix, and merges existing multi-state recovery plots while dropping the separate secondary-consistency panel. These materially revise visual presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V5 adds Shen et al. (2022) for its structure-prediction evaluation and Vicens and Kieft (2022) for RNA structural interactions, while removing Maron et al. (2020). The related-work discussion and principal novelty positioning remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, symmetry statements, and Equations 1–3 are retained. The illustrative argument against averaging single-state predictions moves into the FAQ. New empirical metrics and interpretive discussion introduce no formal derivations, proofs, or revised mathematical results.

improvement.justification: V4 evaluates a 3D design method mainly through sequence recovery and secondary structure. V5 addresses this important evidential gap with systematic 3D self-consistency measurements, native/random controls, and structural examples, while expanded ablations and a second fitness landscape strengthen assessment of applicability. Predictor limitations and selected examples constrain biological conclusions, and removing the explicit high-budget caveat weakens balance somewhat. Nevertheless, the added evidence substantially improves the paper's ability to demonstrate and expose limits of design fidelity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V5 retains these original results and adds structural evaluations, expanded ablations, and retrospective fitness ranking for the t1 ribozyme subunit.

before.justification: V4 reports original gRNAde evaluations on single-state and multi-state RNA design, ablations, and retrospective simulations of ribozyme mutant selection.

results.title: gRNAde: Geometric Deep Learning for 3D RNA inverse design

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit wet lab validation contribution, specifying ten backbones and approximately 50% success versus 35% for Rosetta. The broader superiority, multi-state novelty, and zero-shot ranking claims remain; v6's conclusion already asserted an advantage in experimental performance.

C2.justification: v7 adds interpretations of experimental scores as evidence of target folding, including the qualification that scores below 80 need not indicate failure. It also adds DSS expressivity/cost tradeoffs, a GPU-versus-CPU timing caveat, and substantial arguments about RDesign's sampling limitations and possible overfitting. The existing limitations concerning interacting chains and negative design remain.

D1.justification: v7 newly explains DSS update steps and discloses approximately 200,000 additional parameters and training iteration times of four versus eight minutes. It also explicitly identifies training/inference code, checkpoints, Colab notebooks, and tutorials. These expand documentation; the retained hyperparameters and pseudocode do not establish an implementation change.

E1.justification: Section 5 adds experimental validation on ten OpenKnot targets, including the SARS-CoV-2 frameshift element, HCV IRES, and synthetic kissing-loop RNA, using partial and full redesign tasks. The existing RNASolo benchmarks and ribozyme fitness datasets remain.

E2.justification: Figure 5a newly includes RDesign in the multi-state benchmark. The new wet lab comparison evaluates Rosetta HiRes and LoRes variants alongside wildtype controls. The original single-state comparator membership is unchanged, including RDesign despite its omission from v7 Table 2's caption.

E3.justification: v7 introduces SHAPE-based evaluation using a 0–100 OpenKnot score and a success threshold above 80, with ten partial and ten full gRNAde designs per target. Existing computational splits and training settings remain unchanged. The separate 100-design, temperature-0.5 RhoFold case-study protocol in v6 Appendix D is removed.

E4.justification: v6 Appendix D's dedicated analysis relating perplexity to 3D designability across three RNAs, together with nine illustrated designs, is removed entirely. Aggregate structural metrics and the architectural ablations remain. v7 additionally reports training-fit and computational-cost diagnostics for the already evaluated DS/DSS pooling variants.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations across three consistent seeds and retain the 10,000-simulation uncertainty reporting for retrospective fitness ranking. The new wet lab figures report score distributions and success proportions without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or a new stated uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New wet lab results report 52% success for partial designs and 49% for full designs, versus 35% and 31% for Rosetta HiRes and LoRes. Figure 5a adds RDesign recovery of 0.385 on the multi-state test set. DSS training-loss diagnostics are newly reported, while the standalone 3D case-study results disappear. Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: The backbone representation, multi-state GVP-GNN, pooling, autoregressive decoding, and training objective are retained. DSS pooling receives additional explanation, but DSS variants already appear in v6 Table 1. Partial redesign was also already described in v6.

P1.justification: Localized wording edits and expanded explanations accompany the new wet lab section and RDesign appendix. The visualization appendix is removed and later appendices are relabeled, but most existing prose, the main methodological sequence, and the FAQs remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v7 adds aggregate and per-target wet lab plots, adds a RDesign comparison scatterplot, and redraws Figure 5a to include RDesign. It removes v6 Figures 8–11 containing structural analyses and overlays. Retained architecture diagrams, dataset plots, and pseudocode are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: New Appendix F expands RDesign from a briefly described contemporary baseline into a detailed discussion of publication priority, architectural differences, evaluation choices, and claimed reproducibility problems. Related work also expands its Rosetta explanation and adds references on RNAInvbench, DSS pooling, and cryo-EM.

T1.justification: The mathematical representations, equivariance statements, Equations 1–3, and the FAQ counterexample are retained. The expanded DSS description and assay-score explanation introduce no new formal result, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: Independent SHAPE validation of 200 generated sequences addresses v6's reliance on computational design metrics and retrospective mutant ranking, substantially strengthening experimental support for practical RNA design. Success remains assay-score based rather than direct determination of 3D structures. The gain outweighs the removed structural case studies and a new overstatement in Appendix F: its claim of beating RDesign on all 14 targets conflicts with Table 2's 354D values, 0.4410 versus 0.4458.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite additions, removals, and renumbering.

after.justification: v7 retains those original computational results and adds independent SHAPE assay results for 200 gRNAde-designed sequences across ten RNA backbones.

before.justification: v6 reports original single-state and multi-state design experiments, architectural ablations, and retrospective simulations evaluating ribozyme mutant ranking.

results.title: gRNAde: Geometric Deep Learning for 3D RNA inverse design

C1.justification: The central contribution broadens from improving Llama-2 to improving multiple backbone families, with new claims about data efficiency and the importance of instruction evolution and process supervision. V1 acknowledges trailing GPT-4 and Claude 2; v2 claims superiority over early GPT-4 and other proprietary models and emphasizes strong performance from a 7B Mistral model.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations concerning complementary evolution directions, instruction-quality control, PRM's advantages on longer reasoning problems, and generalization across backbones and datasets. It attributes gains to evolved-data quality rather than contamination and discusses the accuracy-cost tradeoff of replacing GPT-4 with an open teacher. Appendix A.7 also explains DART-Math's advantage at small data scales.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendices A.1–A.5 add model-version information, learning rates, epoch counts, batch size, sequence length, data-construction details, and evolution, ranking, labeling and filtering prompts. Minimum-over-steps PRM reward aggregation is newly documented. V1's literal training/evaluation templates and explicit Hugging Face access pointer are omitted; this does not establish that resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: GSM8k and MATH remain, while v2 adds seven out-of-domain benchmarks: College Math, TAL, Math23k, Ape210k, GaokaoBench Math, AGIEval Gaokao Math and AGIEval SAT Math. Tables 7 and 18 extend evaluation to additional school, college and examination settings beyond v1's coverage.

E2.justification: The GSM8k/MATH comparisons drop older comparators such as Falcon, MPT and Vicuna and add MetaMath, DART-Math, Xwin-Math, MathScale, Skywork-Math and newer proprietary models. V2 also introduces reward and verification comparisons against ORM, PRM800k, Math-Shepherd and self-consistency in Tables 4–5 and Figure 3.

E3.justification: V1 reports eight evolution turns producing a 96k instruction corpus; v2 describes five-round evolution, 418k SFT examples and a separate 90k reward-training instruction set. V2 adds test-overlap filtering, multiple backbone families and scales from 0.1B to 70B, controlled data-size sweeps, and verification using 1–256 candidate solutions. Headline greedy CoT pass@1 evaluation is retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's subtopic breakdown and selected solution cases, v2 adds PRM/IRM ablations, upward/downward evolution ablations, data-scaling studies, reward-source comparisons, verifier sensitivity, out-of-domain testing and contamination checks. Appendix Tables 15–18 further examine synthesis methods and transfer of reward training to other SFT models. The original six solution-comparison cases are replaced with evolution and error-labeling examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's multiple sampled solutions are inference budgets, not repeated experimental runs or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces WizardMath-Llama2-70B's GSM8k/MATH results of 81.6/22.7 with 92.8/58.6 under revised training conditions.
