V2 adds many backbone, ablation and generalization results, including Mistral-7B scores of 90.7/55.4 and PRM verification scores of 95.2/64.7 with 256 candidates in Table 5. These are not controlled same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: V1 describes SFT on regenerated seed solutions followed by active evolution and PPO; v2 uses GPT-4-evolved problems for SFT. IRM ranking criteria change from definition, precision and integrity to difficulty and definition. V2 also introduces PRM-weighted answer aggregation at inference in Section 3.4. These substantially revise the training and inference procedures.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and results narrative, moves related work before the method, and reorganizes method and experimental sections. The two-part solution-case appendix becomes a ten-part prompt and analysis appendix. Citation style, authorship and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, the original GSM8k leaderboard bar chart disappears, and new scaling, verification and similarity plots appear. Table 1 gains a backbone column and extensive grouping. Compact ablation tables and color-coded annotation cases replace the original long solution tables, with substantial changes to figure/table placement and surrounding layout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially updates positioning around mathematical data synthesis, modern math-specialized models and process supervision, adding discussion of MetaMath, DART-Math, Xwin-Math, Llemma and other newer work. It explicitly distinguishes its approach from Python-assisted reasoning and human-labeled supervision. V1's broad instruction-fine-tuning survey is removed.

T1.justification: V2 adds explicit mathematical definitions for IRM ranking loss, PRM step-label loss and PRM-weighted answer aggregation in Equations 1, 2 and 4. V1 specifies only the combined reward product. This is a limited addition of formal methodological definitions; no theoretical guarantees or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: V1 mainly supports its method through benchmark scores and selected solutions. V2 adds direct component ablations, stronger comparative evidence, seven-benchmark generalization tests, contamination checks and detailed training and annotation instructions. These substantially address attribution and reproducibility gaps. Numerical inconsistencies, such as Table 6 versus its discussion, and the unexplained binary-versus-ternary PRM labels in Equation 2 and Appendix A.3 weaken precision, but the stronger empirical support and documentation provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WizardMath and RLEIF, with identifiable correspondences in the methods and GSM8k/MATH experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original WizardMath benchmark results, component ablations, verifier experiments, out-of-domain evaluations and contamination analyses, including substantial appendix results.

before.justification: V1 reports original WizardMath benchmark results for 7B, 13B and 70B models, MATH subtopic scores, and generated solution cases in Appendix A.

results.title: WizardMath: Empowering Mathematical Reasoning for Large Language Models via Reinforced Evol-Instruct

C1.justification: The central claims that surface-only methods underperform and that graph/surface integration improves the tested Atom3d results remain. v2 extends the abstract and conclusion's state-of-the-art claim explicitly to ligand-binding pocket classification, without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantial explanation attributing training instability to protein-scale variation, and explains hybrid design choices through complementary local/global processing and parameter allocation to message passing. v1 offered a briefer long-range-diffusion hypothesis. The conclusion also makes memory requirements an explicit limitation.

D1.justification: Sections 2.3–2.5 and Appendix A add task-specific depths and widths, encoder internals, BatchNorm placement, the 8-angstrom bipartite cutoff and implementation-library links. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to every disclosed setting. Conversely, v1's explicit Gaussian projection of atom features onto surface vertices is omitted; the project code/data link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds MaSIF-ligand binding-site classification, predicting one of seven co-factors from a binding site. This introduces a distinct ligand-preference task and dataset beyond the retained protein interaction, mutation stability and structure-ranking tasks.

E2.justification: MaSIF and HMR, previously cited without scored comparisons, become evaluated comparators in the new binding-site experiment, Figure 3. This adds direct comparisons against specialist surface-learning methods. The existing Atom3d comparator sets and adapted HoloProt baseline remain.

E3.justification: The binding-site experiment introduces 1,634/202/418 training/validation/test instances, balanced accuracy, chemical and geometric features comparable to the baselines, and parameter-count matching to HMR. Existing Atom3d splits and metrics remain unchanged. The reported surface-model depth changes from 'three or four' blocks to consistently three; this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds a PSR validation-convergence comparison between original and modified DiffusionNet, testing the combined adaptations' optimization benefit. The existing architecture, message-passing and depth ablations, together with the PIP qualitative examples, are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or other uncertainty estimates. The new convergence curves and binding-site scores likewise provide no stated run aggregation or uncertainty.

E6.justification: Figure 3 newly reports binding-site balanced accuracy of 0.88 for AtomSurf, 0.81 for HMR and 0.74 for MaSIF; Figure 5 adds PSR convergence results. Existing tables also contain substantive revisions, including surface PSR local R from 0.32 to 0.330 and three-block attention PIP AuROC from 0.791 to 0.792. The principal Atom3d rankings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 introduces protein-scale-informed diffusion-time initialization using absolute samples from N(2,2). The core graph/surface architecture and residual bipartite GAT combination remain intact. Batching and BatchNorm were already described in v1 and are not new components.

P1.justification: The introduction and methods are extensively rewritten. The original two method subsections become five, separating graph modeling, surface modeling, scale adaptation, hybrid representation and architecture. The conclusion is rewritten around conclusions and limitations, and implementation/proof appendices create a substantially different explanatory structure.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws the representation overview and architecture schematic, and removes the separate v1 Figure 2 graph/surface illustration. It adds binding-site and convergence charts. Existing tables and qualitative predictions are resized or relocated, with the qualitative content preserved.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on geometric GNNs, sequence models, over-smoothing and heat/surface geometry, including Duval, Rao, Li, Bronstein–Kokkinos, Meyer and Sun, while removing Méndez-Lucio et al. The central positioning around Atom3d, DiffusionNet and hybrid representations remains, with more specific discussion of graph-based limitations.

T1.justification: v1 contains architectural equations but no scale proposition or proof. v2 introduces Proposition 2.1 on expected Brownian geodesic distance under uniform scaling, with an Appendix B derivation using eigenvalue, eigenfunction, heat-kernel and area scaling. This is substantive new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v1's validation and reproducibility: Section 3.4 directly compares specialist surface methods under stated feature and parameter controls, while Appendix A supplies concrete architecture settings. The scale analysis and convergence evidence also make the adaptation rationale more assessable. These gains outweigh the omitted Gaussian-projection detail. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and the convergence comparison does not isolate individual modifications.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AtomSurf, with matching authors, core architecture and Atom3d experiments. The supplied text, figures, tables and equations support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 adds readable Appendices A and B.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds binding-site classification results in Figure 3 and a DiffusionNet convergence comparison in Appendix B, Figure 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original surface and hybrid-model experiments on PIP, MSP and PSR, including quantitative comparisons, architectural ablations and qualitative predictions.

results.title: AtomSurf: Surface Representation for Learning on Protein Structures

C1.justification: v3 retains the central claim that integrating graph and surface representations improves protein learning, but expands the claimed contributions to antibody–antigen binding-site detection, richer sequence-informed representations and competitive computational throughput. Its conclusion claims state-of-the-art results across several benchmark tasks, whereas v2 claimed them across all benchmark tasks.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of computational applicability: coarsening shifts the runtime bottleneck toward graph encoding, while variable mesh sizes cause memory spikes and restrict batching. It also attributes stronger competing PSR performance to explicit geometric priors and revises the explanation of sequential fusion's weakness from optimization difficulty toward inadequate simultaneous multiscale communication. The high-memory limitation remains.

D1.justification: v3 documents additional feature construction, mesh cleaning, neighborhood construction, a 0.1 coarsening rate and dynamic batching. Appendix D.3 newly reports hardware, training durations and aggregate training expenditure. The stated repository changes from atom2D to atomsurf, and pip-package availability is mentioned. Existing block widths and depths mostly move from Appendix A to Appendix C rather than becoming newly disclosed settings.

E1.justification: The three protein-only Atom3D tasks and MaSIF-ligand are retained. v3 additionally evaluates functional segmentation of 5S ribosomal RNA surfaces and antibody–antigen binding-site detection. These introduce a new molecular domain and distinct residue-level prediction requirements.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds ProNet, GVP, GVP-ESM and GearNet-ESM comparisons on retained Atom3D tasks, and Table 3 adds ProNet to MaSIF-ligand. New evaluations compare against DGCNN, DeltaConv and GEP. The parallel fusion comparator disappears from the architectural ablation; HoloProt is the renamed v2 holo comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds a richer 600k-parameter evaluation setting alongside the restricted benchmark model, plus antibody–antigen evaluation with a 186/49 train/test split, antibody scoring restricted to CDRs, and MCC reporting. Reported minimum mesh size changes from 128 to 256 vertices, and diffusion initialization changes from N(2,2) to N(10,5). Original dataset splits are retained in Appendix E. For MaSIF-ligand, the prose still specifies balanced accuracy while Table 3 says AuROC, so an actual metric switch cannot be established.

E4.justification: v3 adds RNA training-stability comparisons, diffusion-scale visualizations, learned-time distributions, memory profiling and distance-threshold sensitivity including out-of-memory failures. The existing PSR stabilization analysis is retained and supplemented with a results table. Qualitative protein examples are replaced, while the parallel-fusion and separate depth comparisons in v2 Table 3 are removed from v3 Table 4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, replicated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3's approximately 100 model trainings describe aggregate computational expenditure across settings and failed experiments, not repeated-run statistical estimation.

E6.justification: The original hybrid benchmark scores are retained as AtomSurf-bench. New AtomSurf results include PIP 0.907, MSP 0.715 and PSR local/global correlations 0.613/0.861 under the richer configuration, rather than demonstrating same-setting gains over v2. New results include RNA accuracy of 84.1% versus original DiffusionNet's 80.9%, and antibody MCC of 0.47 versus GEP's 0.28. Additional baseline, sensitivity and computational results appear, while ablation entries are revised or removed.

M1.justification: Beyond naming the original benchmark hybrid AtomSurf-bench, v3 introduces a distinct AtomSurf variant using residue graphs, pretrained ESM features, ProNet graph encoding and GVP messages between representations. Reported bipartite connectivity changes from an 8-angstrom cutoff to 16 nearest neighbors, and dynamic batching is introduced. These are procedural additions and revisions, not merely expanded descriptions.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial introductory and methodological passages are rewritten. v3 introduces a dedicated Motivation and Contribution section, reorganizes the method presentation, distinguishes Surface Diff, AtomSurf-bench and AtomSurf, and moves detailed dataset descriptions and architectural alternatives into expanded appendices. These changes substantially reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from two columns to one, redraws the architecture diagrams, consolidates and transposes the original benchmark tables, and replaces the ligand-classification bar chart with a table. It also replaces the qualitative prediction panels and adds binding-detection, diffusion-scale, memory and supplementary-result displays. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around multimodal protein learning, discussing Lee et al., Pegoraro et al. and Xu et al. and contrasting their fusion or pretraining approaches with communication across intermediate layers. It also incorporates protein-language-model integration and newer geometric encoders. This extends the scientific comparison beyond v2's narrower treatment of surface methods and HoloProt.

T1.justification: The Brownian-motion scaling proposition and its proof are retained with renumbering. v3 corrects an eigenfunction index in the initial heat-kernel formula, although inconsistent indices remain later in the derivation. Appendix D.1 adds an auxiliary asymptotic runtime analysis of diffusion, graph encoding and bipartite message passing.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's limited validation through contemporary competing methods, independent RNA and antibody–antigen tasks, and targeted diffusion, threshold and memory analyses. Separating restricted benchmarking from the richer model also makes the comparisons more informative, while computational disclosures improve practical assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of depth and parallel-fusion ablations and new reporting inconsistencies, notably Table 3's AuROC label despite balanced-accuracy prose and inconsistent model naming in the binding-detection discussion.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AtomSurf, with matching core benchmarks, hybrid representation framework and scaling proposition. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds evaluations of another model configuration, RNA segmentation, antibody–antigen binding-site detection, and computational and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original surface and hybrid-model experiments on PIP, MSP, PSR and MaSIF-ligand, architectural ablations, qualitative predictions and a PSR learning-curve comparison.

results.title: AtomSurf: Surface Representation for Learning on Protein Structures

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapting a surface encoder, benchmarking representations, integrating surface and graph features across layers, and achieving strong performance with computational efficiencies. Additional validation does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation of generalization and feature dependence. It interprets PINDER results as evidence of robustness and tentatively links small ESM benefits under stricter splits to sequence memorization versus structural generalization. Appendix F.5 discusses optimization as a possible explanation for MSP failure without ESM, and the conclusion newly acknowledges the need for real-world validation.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly documents random RNA splitting, sequence-identity criteria for retained datasets, chronological PSR splitting, and unbound PIP test structures. PINDER composition and the unchanged-hyperparameter ESM ablation are also documented. Existing construction details are largely relocated, while architecture sizes, hardware, training-time information, and repository access remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 adds the clustered PINDER dataset, containing approximately 42,000 structures, while retaining the earlier datasets. It introduces paired-residue interaction prediction and single-protein binding-site prediction evaluated on bound, unbound, and AlphaFold2-predicted structures, substantially expanding coverage.

E2.justification: Relative to v3 Table 2, v4 Table 3 adds explicit pretrained GVP and pretrained GearNet-ESM comparator rows. The existing comparator families remain; using ProNet on the new PINDER benchmark does not itself introduce another baseline method.

E3.justification: The added PINDER experiments introduce interface-similarity-based splitting and AUROC/accuracy evaluation across structural conditions. Appendix E specifies 1,955 test clusters, with 342 corresponding unbound and 1,747 predicted structures. The ESM ablation also introduces a control holding hyperparameters fixed. Newly documented split rules for retained datasets do not establish changes to their existing protocols.

E4.justification: v4 adds extensive ESM-removal analyses across the existing tasks and PINDER, testing dependence on pretrained sequence features. PINDER comparisons across bound, unbound, and predicted structures add robustness evidence. Earlier architecture, diffusion-stability, and distance-threshold analyses remain, although several are relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix F.2 and Supplementary Table 2 newly report means and standard errors over three replicates for Atom3D, AbAg, and MaSIF-ligand results. v3 provides no explicit per-result repeat counts or corresponding standard errors. This establishes new uncertainty reporting, not an increase from a previously specified run count; baseline replicates remain unavailable for formal significance tests.

E6.justification: New PINDER, ESM-ablation, and pretrained-comparator results substantially expand the evidence. Existing AtomSurf estimates also change: PIP AUROC is revised from 0.907 to 0.909 and PSR global correlation from 0.861 to 0.857 in the main comparison tables. AbAg antibody AUROC/MCC changes from 0.86/0.47 to 0.88/0.53, while antigen scores change from 0.73/0.18 to 0.673/0.143, below GEP's 0.72/0.18. The later AbAg values are explicitly reported as replicate means.

M1.justification: The modified DiffusionNet, layerwise surface–graph communication, AtomSurf-bench, and residue-based AtomSurf architecture remain unchanged. Representation-construction details move to Appendix C.1; the ESM-free variants are experimental ablations rather than revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The organization changes substantially: representation-construction passages move into Appendix C.1; ligand classification and antibody prediction are reordered and grouped in Section 4.3; detailed architectural ablations move from the main text to Appendix F.4; and the supplementary-results section is reorganized. Conference headers, acknowledgements, funding, and a broader-impact statement are also added, although much scientific prose is retained.

P2.justification: v4 moves the representation illustration to the appendix, promotes the RNA learning curve and results table to the main text, and relocates the architectural-ablation table. It adds PINDER, uncertainty, and ESM-ablation tables and restructures the main comparison table to distinguish PLM use and additional pretraining. The MaSIF-ligand header is corrected to balanced accuracy, and Figure 3's display is updated.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to structure-informed protein language models by Bepler and Berger, Heinzinger and colleagues, and Su and colleagues, plus PINDER and structural-robustness references. The central positioning against surface-only approaches and early/late representation fusion remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The heat-equation formulation, scaling proposition and Appendix B proof, and computational-complexity derivation remain substantively unchanged. Renaming the appendix heading from 'Proposition' to 'Theorem' introduces no new mathematical result.

improvement.justification: PINDER evaluation under stricter splitting and varied structural conditions, ESM-removal controls, and three-replicate uncertainty estimates address important gaps in generalization, attribution of gains, and reliability present in v3. Some reporting weaknesses remain: MSP is 71.6 in Table 3 versus 71.5 in Supplementary Table 2, antigen performance is still described optimistically despite lower scores, and baseline uncertainty is unavailable. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AtomSurf and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–F. Corresponding content can be matched despite substantial relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds PINDER evaluations, ESM-feature ablations, and performance estimates over three replicates.

before.justification: v3 reports original experiments on RNA segmentation, Atom3D tasks, antibody–antigen binding-site prediction, and MaSIF-ligand, together with architectural and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: AtomSurf: Surface Representation for Learning on Protein Structures

C1.justification: The central IPSD, appearance-control, and high-quality generation claims remain. v3 extends the stated applicability to guidance by arbitrary complex images and makes limitations of existing single-image-to-3D methods an explicit central motivation, broadening v2's predominantly text-to-3D framing.

C2.justification: v2 stresses dependence on initial NeRF quality and warns that IPSD alone cannot fully preserve reference identity. v3 instead emphasizes that a basic coarse NeRF suffices and presents IPSD as improving existing single-image methods, omitting that explicit identity warning. Appendix D newly documents hours-long optimization and incomplete style control, supported by the failure in Figure D.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository link and substantial implementation documentation in Appendix C: A100 hardware, 5k/10k/15k optimization steps, timestep schedules, batch size 1, rendering resolution 512, memory requirements, and attention/joint-loss details. It also supplies a prompt list. These are newly disclosed settings, not evidence that retained experiments changed their training budgets.

E1.justification: The same text-to-3D, image-guided editing, and single-image-to-3D tasks remain. v3 modestly extends tested input conditions through deliberately extreme reference/coarse-object mismatches in Figure 5 and the failed doll example in Figure D. Complex-image guidance itself was already demonstrated in v2.

E2.justification: DreamFusion, Magic3D, Fantasia3D, and ProlificDreamer remain the text-to-3D baselines; Zero-1-to-3 and SyncDreamer remain single-image comparators. v3 additionally evaluates Zero-1-to-3 against IPDreamer in the text-to-3D comparison of Section 4.4/Figure 7, where v2 showed IPDreamer examples without that comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds FID against Stable Diffusion images and text-image CLIP evaluation over 20 prompts. It introduces an 80-volunteer, 16-prompt, 1,280-pair preference study with image prompts generated without scribble guidance, plus image-image CLIP evaluation of the geometry prompt difference. These substantially expand v2's visual evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: The visual geometry-prompt-difference ablation in v2 Figure 8 is replaced by an aggregate alignment ablation in v3 Table 3, while the normal-map ablation is retained. v3 also adds a stagewise optimization example, a joint-loss comparison in Figure C, and a failed style-transfer case in Figure D, substantially expanding component and failure analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v3's new scores and preference percentages remain point estimates; its volunteer and comparison counts describe evaluation sample sizes rather than repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: v3 adds numerical results absent from v2: IPDreamer obtains FID 257.17 and CLIP score 0.2859 in Table 1, 58.35% preference against ProlificDreamer in Table 2, and image-alignment scores of 0.8228 without versus 0.8389 with the geometry prompt difference in Table 3. Additional qualitative comparisons and failure outcomes also appear. These are newly reported results, not measured improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The NeRF-to-mesh pipeline, IPSD geometry and texture optimization, geometry prompt difference, and main Equations (1)–(10) are retained. Combining IPSD with Zero-1-to-3 for single-image generation was already described in v2 Section 4.4; v3 supplies further documentation rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: Selected passages in the abstract, introduction, method overview, NeRF discussion, and conclusion are rewritten around complex-image guidance. Experimental subsections are reorganized and 'embeddings' often becomes 'features'. The main section hierarchy and much of the related-work and technical exposition remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The two-column layout becomes single-column, the pipeline illustration is simplified, and several figure panels are substantially rearranged, including v2 Figure 3 becoming v3 Figure 4. New quantitative tables and appendix displays expand the presentation. Portions of v2 Figure 4 reappear in v3 Figure 7 and Figure B rather than being wholly removed.

R1.justification: v3 adds InstantID, SSR-Encoder, ConsistNet, and references supporting CLIP evaluation, FID, and optimization. Most related-work discussion remains intact, with additional positioning around image-prompt adaptation and existing single-image methods' difficulty handling complex images.

T1.justification: Main Equations (1)–(10) remain unchanged. Appendix C adds explicit decoupled-attention and weighted joint IPSD/Zero-1-to-3 gradient definitions in Equations (A.1)–(A.4), providing a limited expansion of the mathematical specification without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's qualitative-only validation through quantitative baseline comparisons, human preferences, and an aggregate ablation, while providing essential training details and explicit failure limitations. These additions address important evidential and reproducibility gaps. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 2's Fantasia3D percentages sum to 98%, and Table A lists 20 prompts under a user-study caption although Section 4.3 specifies 16. These inconsistencies limit confidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of IPDreamer with matching methods and experiments. The supplied v2 ends after its references; v3 includes Appendices A–E, which are assessed as newly supplied content.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and adds quantitative comparisons, a user study, quantitative ablation results, and appendix experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original generated 3D objects, qualitative baseline comparisons, and geometry and texture ablations in Section 4.

results.title: IPDreamer: Appearance-Controllable 3D Object Generation with Complex Image Prompts

C1.justification: v4 adds LEPI as an explicit principal contribution, claiming successful editing when image prompts differ substantially from the initial NeRF. This extends the contribution beyond v3's IPSD framework and general controllable-generation claims. The central claims concerning high-quality, appearance-controllable 3D synthesis remain.

C2.justification: v4 explains complex-image guidance through attention-based spatial alignment and attributes severe-mismatch failures to inadequate localization. LEPI is presented as addressing that mechanism. The limitations discussion changes from v3's demonstrated doll-editing failure and incomplete style control to residual appearance/color inconsistency and deployment speed.

D1.justification: Appendix F.3 adds a substantial implementation workflow: GPT-4v analysis, SAM segmentation, user-adjustable partial prompts, ControlNet enhancement with a specified checkpoint, and local followed by global optimization. Existing hardware, iteration counts, timestep schedules, memory requirements, and code access remain unchanged. However, v3's explicit several-hours-per-model runtime description disappears.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate text-to-3D generation, single-image-to-3D generation, and complex-image-guided texture editing. Severe prompt–NeRF mismatch was already tested in v3's failed doll example. The additional LEPI examples and single-image example extend results within this coverage without introducing a distinct task or dataset.

E2.justification: The new LEPI comparisons explicitly use IPDreamer without LEPI as an internal comparator, including Table 5 and Figures 3, 7, and 10. External comparator membership remains unchanged: DreamFusion, Magic3D, Fantasia3D, and ProlificDreamer for text-to-3D, and Zero-1-to-3 and SyncDreamer for the corresponding image-based comparisons.

E3.justification: v4 adds a paired with/without-LEPI evaluation using image prompts from Figures 3, 7, 10, and 11, assessed through CLIP scores and user preferences. The original 20-prompt benchmark, 80-volunteer study with 1,280 comparisons, and stated optimization budgets remain unchanged. LEPI-specific participant and trial counts are not separately specified.

E4.justification: v4 adds substantial evidence testing whether LEPI preserves object semantics under strong appearance mismatch: the revisited doll failure, bird and cottage ablations, additional controlled examples, quantitative comparisons, and localization-mask visualization. The existing geometry-loss, geometry-prompt-difference, and combined-supervision analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed evaluations, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. v4's additional CLIP scores and preference percentages follow the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v4 adds a substantial block of LEPI findings. Table 5 reports CLIP scores of 0.2041 without LEPI and 0.2189 with LEPI, with preference rates of 24.363% and 75.637%, respectively. New qualitative comparisons demonstrate improved semantic preservation, and Figure 14 adds a single-image example. The original benchmark, baseline-preference, and geometry-prompt ablation numbers are unchanged.

M1.justification: v4 introduces optional Local Editing with Partial Images (LEPI). It uses partial image prompts and localization words to construct spatially masked attention, followed by global texture optimization using combined prompt features. This substantially extends the procedure beyond v3's global image-prompt guidance; the original NeRF and IPSD components remain.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized around LEPI. The original user study, single-image generation, and Zero-1-to-3 comparison move into expanded appendices; attention explanation enters the main method section, and VSD preliminaries are shortened. The introduction, contribution list, limitations, title, and author block are also revised.

P2.justification: v4 changes the page format and extensively rearranges displays. It redraws the teaser and pipeline, transposes Table 1, adds LEPI comparison figures, a mask visualization, and Table 5, and relocates several retained figures. The original standalone optimization illustration and teaser's dragon panels are omitted; the doll failure is reused within a new controlled comparison.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Prompt-to-Prompt, Segment Anything, DreamGaussian, LucidDreamer, and newer image/video diffusion work. Related work expands to Gaussian-based 3D optimization and additional editing methods, while the main positioning against text-to-3D and single-image-to-3D approaches remains.

T1.justification: v4 substantially extends the mathematical formulation with localization-mask and masked-attention definitions in Equations 10–11 and local/global LEPI supervision in Equations 15–21. Core IPSD and combined Zero-1-to-3 supervision equations are retained. v3's preliminary VSD optimization equations are removed. Neither version provides formal guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 materially addresses a demonstrated weakness in the paper's central controllability goal: v3's failed doll edit becomes a controlled LEPI comparison in Figure 3, supported by further ablations and Table 5. The added mechanism explanation and implementation workflow strengthen this evidence. LEPI-specific study details and uncertainty reporting remain limited, and runtime disclosure is weakened, but the demonstrated mitigation of an important failure makes the overall improvement substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IPDreamer. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and equations, support reliable comparison despite changes in title, organization, and layout.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds qualitative comparisons, CLIP scores, and user preferences evaluating LEPI.

before.justification: v3 reports original 3D-generation experiments, FID and CLIP scores, an 80-person preference study, and geometry and texture ablations.

results.title: IPDreamer: Appearance-Controllable 3D Object Generation with Complex Image Prompts

C1.justification: The principal empirical claim shifts from accurate SR predictions and faster TD learning in Pinball to online SF-based navigation and adaptation relative to LSTM and CSCG. V2 drops the advertised HMM-version-of-RNN contribution and adds claims about long-horizon belief propagation and neuromorphic implementation. The core contribution of local Hebbian temporal memory remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantial discussion of fast learning versus weak trajectory generalization, correlated-buffer overfitting, and encoder non-stationarity as a possible explanation for AnimalAI baseline failures. It qualifies that LSTM/CSCG are not inherently incapable of solving the tasks and proposes a future fast/slow hierarchy. These interpretations and limitations extend well beyond v1's encoder caveats.

D1.justification: V1 mainly documents the encoder and a brief experimental setup. V2 adds explicit Hebbian update formulas, baseline architectures and training regimes, buffer sizes, validation rules, DHTM dimensions, initialization, learning rates, pruning and planning thresholds (Appendix D). It also details preprocessing and environment interaction and supplies a source-code access link; the link's availability was not independently verified.

E1.justification: The Pinball environment and its force-field scenarios are removed. V2 evaluates fully observable coordinate-based Gridworld, partially observable colour-based Gridworld, and first-person visual navigation in AnimalAI. These change the observation conditions, dynamics and navigation requirements.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates LSTM, RWKV and factorial CHMM against DHTM. V2 removes RWKV from experimental comparisons and introduces Q-table and SR-table agents in fully observable Gridworld (Figure 3). LSTM remains in partially observable Gridworld (Figure 4), and the clone-HMM comparison lineage continues through CSCG, with a differently described implementation.

E3.justification: V1 measures prediction surprise and reward using short Pinball episodes and one-/five-step TD predictions. V2 measures steps to the goal and introduces trajectory-buffer refresh and change-oracle protocols. Planning uses ten steps in fully observable Gridworld and adaptive horizons up to 50 elsewhere, with respective discounts of 0.99 and 0.8 (Appendix D). These are replacement experimental protocols.

E4.justification: V1's explicit one-versus-five prediction-step ablation is removed. V2 instead compares CSCG with and without an environmental-change oracle in both Gridworld settings, testing whether renewed random-policy data collection restores adaptation (Figures 3–4). This changes the central diagnostic question from prediction horizon to training-data refresh.

E5.justification: V1 reports averaging three trials and displays shaded bands without identifying their statistical meaning. V2 explicitly reports at least five differently seeded runs per setup and identifies the displayed variation as standard deviation. This describes the new evaluations, not additional runs of the earlier Pinball experiments.

E6.justification: The Pinball surprise and adaptation results are replaced by navigation results. V2 reports faster Gridworld adaptation than CSCG, approximately 13 steps versus a nine-step optimum after the partially observable maze changes, and stable AnimalAI goal reaching after about 150 episodes. AnimalAI baseline training failures are also reported. These findings cannot establish same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: V1's agent explicitly learns SR through n-step TD and uses log reward priors for valuation. V2 specifies direct SF rollouts under a uniform future policy, adaptive stopping and linear feature-reward Q estimates (Section 3.3). The segment-likelihood computation also changes through an added mean-synaptic-efficacy multiplier (v1 Equation 11; v2 Equation 8), while the underlying Hebbian factor-graph memory remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, agent explanation and conclusion are substantially rewritten around SF-based planning. Methods is reorganized into factor-graph, neural-implementation and agent subsections. The single encoder appendix becomes part of an A–F appendix structure with dedicated explanations and a glossary; the original encoder discussion is largely retained.

P2.justification: V1's compact three-panel method figure is replaced by separate, expanded factor-graph and neural-implementation diagrams, plus a new biological illustration. Pinball screenshots and plots disappear, replaced by larger Gridworld/AnimalAI learning curves and new environment illustrations (v2 Figures 3–9). This substantially revises the visual organization.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted references and connections concerning successor features, episodic memory, cortical layers, AnimalAI and baseline implementations, including Gershman, Touati et al., and Staiger and Petersen. Godot and several earlier cortical-model references disappear. The principal positioning around Factorial HMMs, world models and local Hebbian learning is retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical revisions are localized: Section 2.3 changes SR from finite-horizon observation occupancy to infinite-horizon future-state occupancy; Appendix B adds a feature-additive reward approximation and value decomposition. V2 Equation 8 also revises the segment-likelihood interpolation. The underlying factor-graph formulation remains, without a new theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves assessability and reproducibility through explicit learning rules, baseline training details, uncertainty definitions and implementation information. Its comparative Gridworld navigation tests and oracle controls address adaptability more directly than v1's prediction comparison and DHTM-only horizon ablation, while new limitations constrain interpretation. Losing the predictive-surprise and horizon analyses, and lacking successful AnimalAI baseline curves, narrows some evidence, but the methodological transparency and more direct validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DHTM research, despite the title changing from Successor Representations to Successor Features. The complete text, equations, figures and appendices support comparison; the experiments are substantially revised.

after.justification: V2 reports original navigation experiments in fully and partially observable Gridworld and in AnimalAI, with learning curves in Figures 3–5.

before.justification: V1 reports original Pinball experiments measuring prediction surprise and adaptation after environmental changes, including a prediction-horizon comparison (Figures 3–4).

results.title: Learning Successor Features with Distributed Hebbian Temporal Memory

C1.justification: Although the abstract is essentially unchanged, the introduction and conclusion redefine the contribution around episodic memory that matches table episodic control while supporting distributed representations and their dependencies. v3 also introduces an order-of-magnitude sample-efficiency claim against Dreamer V3. v2 primarily emphasized an online Factorial-HMM-like memory outperforming LSTM and CSCG.

C2.justification: v3 argues that episodic trajectory recall explains much of DHTM's performance and interprets the new ablation as evidence for cross-feature dependencies. It proposes DHTM as an adaptive trajectory buffer for a slower generalizing model, replacing v2's emphasis on a two-layer DHTM hierarchy. New qualifications address uniform-policy nonoptimality, evaluation limited to basic RL setups, and excessive segment growth in noisy environments.

D1.justification: v3 documents encoder datasets, 64x64 image inputs, VAE epochs and batch size, EC pseudocode, softmax temperatures, factor configurations and a segment-count limit. These replace extensive spatial-pooler implementation details in v2. Some earlier disclosures, including synapse initialization and pruning thresholds, are no longer stated. The anonymous source-code resource identifier also changes; its availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v3 removes the fully observable 5x5 Gridworld scenario reported in v2 Section 4.1 and Figure 3. Partially observable Gridworld with a blocked path and the AnimalAI room-navigation task remain. The new encoders and factor configurations concern retained tasks, rather than additional environments or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds an episodic-control dictionary comparator in both environments, Dreamer V3 in AnimalAI, and an explicitly plotted LSTM-oracle comparator in Gridworld. Q-table and SR-table comparisons disappear with the fully observable experiment. AnimalAI now includes plotted CSCG and LSTM comparisons using K-Means; v2 described their unsuccessful training with its spatial-pooler encoder.

E3.justification: Appendix D substantially revises training protocols: LSTM's buffer changes from 100 to 1000 trajectories, with a new learning rate and update schedule; CSCG's buffer changes from 2500 to 500 steps and its smoothing coefficient from 0.9 to 0.05. Oracle handling changes to memory reinitialization and buffer clearing. DHTM initialization, learning rates and AnimalAI discounting also change. v3 introduces encoder pretraining, total-step metrics and a Dreamer evaluation without the other agents' frame skipping.

E4.justification: v3 adds a substantive test of distributed prediction: Figure 3B varies context factor size from 1 to 5 and includes the factor 1* control with additional hidden-variable copies to investigate state collisions. The new EC comparison also tests whether simple trajectory storage explains DHTM's performance. v2 lacked these analyses; its changing-maze adaptation test is retained.

E5.justification: Section 4 changes the replication statement from 'at least five' experiments with different seeds to five. Both versions report standard deviations. This makes the reported run count more specific without establishing that the number of runs actually increased or decreased.

E6.justification: v3 replaces the experimental curves, removes the MDP results, and adds EC parity and factor-size findings. Its revised oracle CSCG results show sustained post-change recovery, unlike v2's earlier oracle procedure. Appendix F newly reports Dreamer solving AnimalAI after about 105,000 raw steps, converted by the authors to 35,000 versus DHTM's 3,500. These results involve changed or unequal protocols and do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core DHTM factor graph, belief propagation and Hebbian updates are retained. The AnimalAI encoder component changes substantially within that retained architecture: v2's event preprocessing and online spatial pooler are replaced by pretrained K-Means or categorical VAE encoding. The VAE adds a linear reward-prediction loss and deterministic latent-state selection (v3 Appendix C).

P1.justification: v3 extensively edits retained introductory and methodological prose, rewrites the experimental narrative and conclusion, and reorganizes the background around SR, HMM and episodic control. Learning receives a separate subsection, and the value-decomposition, biological-interpretation and encoding appendices are reordered. The impact statement is removed and the glossary is revised.

P2.justification: v3 redraws and combines v2 Figures 1–2 into a two-panel Figure 1. Experimental displays become paired learning-curve and total-step plots, while the fully observable Gridworld plot and map are removed. New appendix displays show factor-graph configurations and Dreamer learning. The retained biological illustration and environment images are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 substantially positions DHTM within episodic memory and control, adding literature on model-free, neural and successor-feature episodic control and integrating it into Sections 2.4 and 3.5. It adds explicit HTM-neuron attribution and encoder-related references while removing spatial-pooler-related works. Dreamer was already cited in v2, but becomes an evaluated comparator and a prominent positioning reference.

T1.justification: v2's explicit bootstrapped SR updates in Equations 3–4 are removed. The relocated value-function decomposition removes an extra feature multiplier from the reward formula and changes successor-feature probability conditioning from an individual hidden component to the full hidden vector (v2 Appendix B; v3 Appendix A). Core DHTM mathematical updates remain, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central distributed-memory contribution: v2's AnimalAI implementation used one encoded feature, whereas v3 tests multiple features, cross-feature factor sizes and a collision control. Shared-encoder baseline comparisons and the EC control also make the mechanism and comparative benefits much clearer (Figures 2–3). Removing fully observable Gridworld narrows coverage, and the tenfold Dreamer claim remains inadequately controlled because encoder pretraining and action protocols differ. Nevertheless, the direct validation and clearer explanation of the central contribution represent a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DHTM research work. All 20 pages of each version, including equations, figures, references and appendices, are readable and support comparison after matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 reports original Gridworld and AnimalAI experiments, including baseline comparisons, a factor-size ablation and the Dreamer V3 experiment in Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original navigation experiments in fully and partially observable Gridworld and AnimalAI, with learning curves in Figures 3–5.

results.title: Learning Successor Features with Distributed Hebbian Temporal Memory

C1.justification: The central contributions—online Hebbian episodic memory, successor-feature planning, and distributed representations—remain unchanged. V4 extends the abstract and introduction's comparative claim to RWKV and adds a qualified novelty claim concerning episodic control in partially observable environments. The conclusion's principal claims remain stable.

C2.justification: V4 adds substantive explanations of why factorization tolerates noisy features and why including all variables loses that advantage. Appendix H.2 discusses exploration-dependent memory growth, unstable policies in larger grids, linear computational costs, and planning-horizon limitations requiring pruning or alternative planning approaches. These considerably sharpen v3's broader limitations discussion.

D1.justification: V4 documents segment-creation conditions, KL-based stopping, RWKV implementation and training, EC's VAE mapping, and parameters for the scalability and noise experiments. It replaces the anonymous code reference with a named GitHub repository and iclr25 branch. Conversely, it removes the explicit statement that the oracle-CSCG buffer continuously grows, without specifying a replacement behavior.

E1.justification: The two navigation domains remain Gridworld and AnimalAI. V4 expands their test scenarios with empty 5x5, 7x7, and 10x10 grids with opposite-corner goals, and AnimalAI observations containing an additional noisy feature (Appendices H.2–H.3). This broadens conditions within the existing task coverage.

E2.justification: RWKV becomes an evaluated baseline in both main experiments, having only been discussed in v3. Figure 2 also adds oracle-reset EC, while Figure 3 adds EC using VAE codes mapped through a dictionary. These materially strengthen the comparator set beyond the retained LSTM, CSCG, EC, and Dreamer comparisons.

E3.justification: V4 adds controlled evaluations of grid size, memory use after 300 episodes, episode length under 100 episodes of uniform exploration, and noisy features with varying factor sizes. Appendix E specifies different planning horizons, temperatures, discounts, and reward thresholds for these tests. Figure 3 also replaces the displayed LSTM K-Means condition with VAE, and Figure 2 adds an EC reset control.

E4.justification: Appendices H.2–H.3 introduce substantial analyses of scalability, memory growth with experience, and robustness to an irrelevant noisy variable. Figures 10–12 test these questions directly. The original clean-input factor-size analysis and Dreamer experiment remain; their relocation is not an additional analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five experiments with different seeds. V4 clarifies that one standard deviation is shown except for boxplots, qualifying v3's blanket standard-deviation statement. This is a limited reporting clarification, without evidence of increased repeated-run counts or new statistical tests.

E6.justification: V4 adds RWKV, oracle-EC, and EC-VAE outcomes. New Figures 10–11 show fewer DHTM memory units during goal-directed learning but more than EC under uniform exploration, with approximately linear growth versus episode length. Figure 12 shows noise tolerance for smaller DHTM factors and failure for EC and factor-6 DHTM. The original factor-size and Dreamer findings are retained.

M1.justification: The proposed factor graph, segment excitation, Hebbian updates, and successor-feature planning procedure are retained. Much of v3 Section 3.2 moves to v4 Appendix B. Expanded explanations of segment creation and stopping criteria document the existing procedure; experiment-specific parameter choices do not establish a redesigned DHTM.

P1.justification: V4 substantially rewrites background and neural-implementation explanations, moves the detailed neuronal derivation into Appendix B, and incorporates the former episodic-control background into Section 3.5. The introduction's narrative is expanded and reorganized. These structural and explanatory revisions go beyond the accompanying new scientific content.

P2.justification: V4 adopts ICLR formatting, revises Figures 2–3 and their legends, labels the Gridworld maps more explicitly, and adds Figures 7 and 10–12 for scaling environments, memory growth, and noise tolerance. Existing biological diagrams and the Dreamer plot are retained or relocated, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning around cognitive maps versus episodic memory and compares DHTM conceptually with asymmetric Hopfield networks, temporal predictive coding, and HTM. It adds corresponding literature and a probabilistic-HTM interpretation, replaces the earlier Hawkins framework citation with Hawkins and Ahmad (2016), and removes the Blundell episodic-control citation. These exceed bibliographic or citation-style changes.

T1.justification: New Appendix G assumes uniformly sampled categorical features, derives a collision-based capacity expression in Equation 18, and argues for linear scaling with neuron count using a Taylor expansion. This adds a substantive theoretical argument absent from v3. Existing DHTM and value-decomposition derivations are retained or relocated; Section 2.1 also corrects the Q-function discount exponent.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens evidence for DHTM's advantages and limits relative to episodic control. V3's AnimalAI EC comparison used K-Means; v4 adds EC with VAE encoding, a noisy-feature test, and controlled scalability and memory-growth analyses. Together with RWKV comparisons and clearer implementation details, these address important gaps in comparative validity and reproducibility. The new analyses also expose instability and resource costs instead of presenting uniformly favorable results. Simple navigation environments and the simplifying assumptions of the capacity argument still limit generality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DHTM and successor-features research. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including content moved or renumbered in v4.

after.justification: V4 retains original navigation results and adds RWKV comparisons, scalability experiments, and noise-tolerance results in Appendix H.

before.justification: V3 reports original Gridworld and AnimalAI experiments, including agent comparisons, factor-size experiments, and the Dreamer evaluation in Appendix F.

results.title: Learning Successor Features with Distributed Hebbian Temporal Memory

C1.justification: The central contribution remains efficient, similarity-conditioned Mixup improving performance and calibration across classification and regression. v2 adds an explicit main claim linking mixing distance to manifold-intrusion risk and extends efficiency claims to reaching the best validation performance faster, while emphasizing the accuracy–calibration trade-off.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantive interpretation connecting distant mixing, non-convex manifolds, label noise, and calibration (Section 3.1). It replaces v1's dataset-dependent joint-hyperparameter explanation with a tau_std-dominated tuning account. Appendices B, I, and J add limitations concerning calibration theory after temperature scaling, hyperparameter selection, and explanations of warping and similarity choices.

D1.justification: Appendices G–I add GPU sampling and lookup-table implementation details, baseline hyperparameters and C-Mixup bandwidths, explicit stratified 90/10 cross-validation, and settings for the new datasets. The code reference changes from torch-uncertainty to a dedicated sim_kernel_mixup repository. Conversely, v1's averaging over the last ten classification epochs is no longer specified.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet classification evaluations and Moons/Circles toy classification experiments. CIFAR10/100, Airfoil, Exchange-Rate, and Electricity remain. Coverage therefore expands substantially into larger-scale image classification and explicit non-convex toy problems.

E2.justification: v2 adds reproduced classification comparisons with RankMixup and Manifold Mixup, plus attributed calibration baselines including MMCE, ECP, LS, FL, FLSD, CRL, CPC, and MbLS (Table 2). Regression adds RegMixup (Table 4). MIT-L disappears, and v1's ResNet34 RegMixup/MIT comparisons are absent from the corresponding v2 Table 1.

E3.justification: The stated CIFAR learning-rate decay epochs change from 100/150 to 80/120. v2 adds ResNet101 comparisons, AECE, and distinct Tiny-ImageNet/ImageNet training protocols. New analyses introduce distance-quantile controls, before/after temperature-scaling measurements, and validation-selected best-epoch timing. These establish reported protocol changes without establishing which retained numerical results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's hyperparameter heatmaps and similarity ablation, v2 adds manifold-intrusion cases, controlled distance-quantile mixing, direct versus lookup-table sampling comparisons, and Airfoil warping-function and similarity-space analyses (Section 3.1; Appendices D, G, J). Hyperparameter sensitivity is revised, while v1's classification-weight and asymmetric input/target similarity comparisons disappear.

E5.justification: v2 reports ten runs for all regression datasets, versus five for Exchange-Rate/Electricity and ten for Airfoil in v1. Classification retains four runs and standard deviations. v2 additionally specifies averaging cross-validation over four splits and reports uncertainty for implementation timing in Table 7, whereas v1's timing table contains single values.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark, ablation, and timing results; ImageNet results include 76.2±0.26 accuracy and 1.46±0.09 ECE (Table 3). v1's Airfoil Beta-CDF MAPE of 1.694±0.176 reappears in v2 Table 9 alongside the inverse-CDF variant's 1.609±0.137. Earlier ResNet50 CIFAR benchmark results and most RMSE baseline entries disappear. Revised methods and settings preclude treating these additions as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The central coefficient-generation procedure changes: v1 uses Beta-CDF warping with a kernel increasing exponentially with distance; v2 uses inverse-Beta-CDF warping with a distance-decreasing Gaussian kernel (Sections 3.2–3.3). v2 also fixes initial coefficients to uniform/Beta(1,1), removing tunable alpha. Separate input/target warping remains available in Appendix G.

P1.justification: The title and method name change, and the abstract, contributions, related work, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. The method narrative is reorganized around manifold intrusion; detailed settings and input/target disentangling move into appendices. Existing appendix material is reorganized alongside dedicated proof, implementation, sensitivity, and limitations sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds toy decision-boundary plots and distance-comparison boxplots, combines revised warp curves and density visualization in Figure 4, and replaces cross-validation heatmaps with tabulated sensitivity results. Classification and regression tables use reorganized dataset columns, timing expands into a multipart display, and the title, headings, typography, and page layout are redesigned.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands calibration-focused positioning through a dedicated calibration-driven Mixup discussion, RankMixup and calibration-regularization references, and detailed distinctions from AdaMixUp and Local Mixup. The offline oversampling subsection and references such as Borderline-SMOTE and ADASYN are removed. These are substantive positioning changes beyond bibliographic reformatting.

T1.justification: v2 revises the central mathematical definitions of the warp and similarity kernel and adds Proposition 3.1 with its Appendix F proof: inverse-CDF warping transforms a uniform coefficient into an exact Beta(tau,tau) variable. v1 instead illustrates approximately Beta-shaped outputs without this formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 replaces v1's approximate distribution argument with an exact sampling construction and proof. Controlled distance and warping analyses directly test previously weakly supported design assumptions, while broader calibration comparisons and detailed implementation settings substantially strengthen evaluation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of some earlier ResNet50 and RMSE comparisons. Calibration itself remains unproved, but Appendix B now explicitly acknowledges that limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' similarity-conditioned Mixup research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–E in v1 and A–J in v2 are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and renaming.

after.justification: v2 reports original repeated-run classification and regression experiments, toy-data demonstrations, ablations, and timing measurements. These are distinguishable from the externally attributed baseline scores in Table 2.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR classification, Airfoil and time-series regression, similarity ablation, cross-validation, and training-time results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Tailoring Mixup to Data for Calibration

C1.justification: The central contributions remain normal-structure regularisation, reduced overfitting to seen anomalies, improved unseen-anomaly detection and integration into other supervised detectors. The rewritten abstract and introduction preserve these claims; the six-dataset statement describes expanded supporting evidence.

C2.justification: Appendix C.2 explicitly interprets lower seen-anomaly average AUC-PR than BCE (0.710 versus 0.743) as a fitting–generalisation trade-off. Sections 4.8 and C.3 add explanations involving gradient-scale compatibility and redundant normal–anomaly relations. These qualify and extend the retained normality-based explanation.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B newly provide training/evaluation pseudocode, dataset statistics, anomaly-class selection rules, Yelp graph-view and clustering details, weighted sampling, dependency versions, neighbour-sampling counts, scoring-network dimensions and baseline training settings. These substantially expand reproducibility information; they do not establish that previously reported implementations changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-proteins while retaining all four original datasets. These extend coverage to substantially larger citation and protein graphs, including a biological network domain absent from v1.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds DOMINANT, GGAN, CoLA, TAM and AMNet to the six retained baselines. AMNet also enters data-efficiency and runtime comparisons. The ablation comparisons additionally evaluate supervised and unsupervised contrastive regularisers, expanding the alternatives tested against NSR.

E3.justification: The original main-text settings and AUC-ROC/AUC-PR metrics are retained. The added large-graph experiments use 100 labelled anomalies, 1% labelled normal nodes and 400 training epochs at learning rate 0.001. Appendix C.2 additionally evaluates the seen-anomaly subset. Newly disclosed preprocessing details do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds contrastive-regularisation controls, a normal–anomaly relation ablation, seen-only performance analysis, representation/score-contour case studies and sensitivity to lambda. The earlier hypersphere and two-relation ablations remain, with the latter renamed NSR (dual). Appendix C.5 also supplies AUC-ROC data-efficiency curves absent from the supplied v1.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five random runs and mean-plus-standard-deviation table reporting. However, the vertical error bars in v1's alpha-sensitivity Figure 3 are omitted from the corresponding v2 Figures 5–6. Changed average-column standard deviations do not, by themselves, establish a changed statistical procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new baselines, large graphs, regularisers and appendix analyses. Original per-dataset means in Table 1 remain unchanged, but average-column standard deviations are revised. SAD ablation scores also change: Photo all-anomaly AUC-PR moves from 0.127 in v1 Table 3 to 0.269 in v2 Tables 3 and 7, without an explanation of the revision.

M1.justification: v2 introduces an adjustable weight lambda into the previously unweighted combination of detection and regularisation losses (Equations 2 and 6). It uses lambda=2 for ogbn-proteins and 1 otherwise. The three relation types, representation architecture and inference procedure remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Parts of the abstract and introduction are rewritten, relation-prediction terminology becomes relation modelling, and authorship/header text changes. New appendix sections organise implementation details and additional results. The main section sequence and much of the existing exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redraws the architecture diagram, adds representation visualisations, expands comparison tables and reorganises the earlier ablation tables into Tables 3 and 7. Data-efficiency and sensitivity displays are split or relocated across the main text and appendix. The document also adopts a different conference layout with author blocks and running headers.

R1.justification: v2 expands citations within the existing related-work categories, including additional semi-supervised graph/fraud detectors, graph augmentation and imbalanced-learning work, plus references supporting new baselines and datasets. Its positioning around unseen-anomaly generalisation and its distinction from PReNet remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The open-set assumptions and relation-label definitions are retained, and neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs. v2's added GraphSAGE update equation explains the encoder already specified in v1 rather than introducing new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central mechanism through alternative regularisers, broader baseline comparisons, large-graph tests and an explicit seen-anomaly trade-off analysis. Appendix B supplies important dataset-construction and implementation information missing from the supplied v1. These gains outweigh reporting defects: Algorithm 2 misdefines the unseen set relative to the prose, Tables 3 and 7 swap contrastive-method labels, and sensitivity error bars disappear. Those defects still limit reproducibility and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NSReg research and are readable throughout, including equations, figures and tables. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–C. References to supplementary material in v1 do not establish content outside the supplied PDF.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds large-graph evaluations, further baselines and regulariser comparisons, representation visualisations and appendix analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original anomaly-detection experiments on Photo, Computers, CS and Yelp, including baseline comparisons, ablations, sensitivity studies and runtime measurements.

results.title: Open-Set Graph Anomaly Detection via Normal Structure Regularisation

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes the first generative binary LLMs, two optimization-related pretraining tasks, and superiority across three downstream tasks. v3 centers its contributions on hierarchical attention, contrastive learning, and representation analyses, with two-task performance claims headlined as improvements up to 146.54% for decompilation and 6.17% for similarity detection.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking functionality clustering, optimization-distance ordering, attention entropy, and instruction-summary attention to its mechanisms. Its limitations emphasize X86-only coverage and untested larger models. v1's explicit inability to capture global dependencies and discussion of restoring normalized addresses and calls are removed, changing the stated applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 Appendices A.1–A.3 document contrastive-data filtering, 1,024/2,048-token limits, loss weighting, revised batch sizes and learning rates, and eight 40GB A100 GPUs. v1 instead specifies its normalization pipeline, cross-compilation environment, and A5000/A10 infrastructure. The new truncation and filtering disclosures provide substantial additional implementation information without establishing that equivalent settings existed in v1.

E1.justification: v3 adds AnghaBench pretraining and evaluates HumanEval-Decompile plus Binutils, Curl, ImageMagick, SQLite, OpenSSL, and Putty. Generated/Codeflaws and BinaryCorp testing disappear; BinaryCorp remains BCSD fine-tuning data. ARM64 coverage and cross-architecture translation are removed. Binary recovery continues as decompilation, so that terminology change does not itself introduce a new task.

E2.justification: For BCSD, v3 retains jTrans and adds evaluated comparisons with DiEmph and CodeArt. For recovery/decompilation, GPT-3.5 remains, GPT-4 and LLM4Decompile are added, and v1's published-score comparisons with Coda and Neutron disappear (v1 Tables 2–7; v3 Tables 2–8).

E3.justification: BCSD changes from twelve optimization directions at pool sizes 32 and 10,000 to O0-to-O3 retrieval at sizes 50, 100, 200, and 500, with Recall@1 replacing MRR-focused reporting. Decompilation uses executable Pass@1/10 evaluation instead of lexical recovery metrics. Model scales, preprocessing, and fine-tuning budgets also change; v3 specifies one fine-tuning epoch rather than v1's two.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's Nova/Nova+ comparisons and illustrative cases, v3 introduces component ablations removing contrastive learning and hierarchical attention on both retained tasks. Section 4.3 and Appendices A.4–A.7 add decompilation cases, PCA/t-SNE visualizations, embedding-distance analyses, and layer/head attention analyses addressing how the proposed components affect representations.

E5.justification: v3 newly presents embedding-distance distributions as boxplots (Figure 13) and specifies 20 sampled decompilations per assembly for Nova and LLM4Decompile (Section 3.2). These add distribution and sampling information, but neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's BinaryCorp, Generated, and Codeflaws results are replaced by new benchmark and ablation results. For example, v1 reports Nova+ MRR 0.727 at pool size 10,000, whereas v3 reports Nova-6B average decompilation Pass@1 of 29.42% and average Recall@1 of 0.67 at pool size 500. These are different-condition results, not directly comparable performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: v1's StarCoder-based Nova/Nova+ uses language modeling followed by optimization generation and optimization-level prediction. v3 replaces these auxiliary tasks with functionality and optimization contrastive learning, introduces instruction-summary tokens and hierarchical attention, and uses DeepSeek-Coder as its backbone (Sections 2–3). These change the architecture and training procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and explanatory narrative are extensively rewritten around security applications, low information density, and optimization diversity. Related work moves after the results, training details move into an expanded appendix, and the conclusion/limitations order changes. The appendices are reorganized from task examples into implementation details and analyses.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the motivation and overview figures and introduces attention-mask diagrams, contrastive-learning illustrations, embedding projections, boxplots, and attention heatmaps. Tables are redesigned around decompilation optimization levels, individual BCSD projects, and ablations. These substantially replace v1's three-task schematics, architecture-by-metric tables, and large code-example displays.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning around recent assembly models, discussing CodeArt, SLaDe, and LLM4Decompile and adding DeepSeek-Coder, SimCSE, and attention-analysis literature. It replaces v1's broad first-generative-binary-LLM positioning with distinctions concerning architecture and assembly-specific training, and removes the separate disassembler discussion.

T1.justification: v3 Section 2.3 introduces quantified constraints separating same-function and different-function embeddings, an ordering constraint across optimization levels, and corresponding contrastive losses and a combined objective. Its BCSD loss also differs from v1's cosine-similarity softmax formulation. These are substantive mathematical changes, although neither version contains theorem-and-proof developments.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through executable decompilation tests, contemporary baselines, component ablations, and appendix representation analyses. This addresses v1's reliance on similarity metrics that can reward incorrect recovery: Figure 8 gives incorrect code 100% token accuracy. Coverage narrows, and reporting defects weaken exact claims: v3 Table 4 repeats a Pass@10 baseline row under Pass@1, while Table 2's Nova-1B scores average 20.695%, not 22.09%. Despite these defects, the improvement in assessing functional correctness and explaining component effects is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Nova assembly-language-model research by the same authors, despite extensive redesign. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original executable decompilation and binary similarity results, component ablations, and embedding and attention analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original binary similarity, cross-architecture translation, and source-code recovery experiments, including model-generated examples and appendix embedding comparisons.

results.title: Nova: Generative Language Models for Assembly Code with Hierarchical Attention and Contrastive Learning

C1.justification: The original claims about joint Gaussian diffusion and adaptive schedules remain. V2 broadens the central contribution to initialization and data-type homogenization, and makes scalability a prominent claim: faster training, improved handling of high-cardinality features and accommodation of arbitrary category counts. These extend the paper's claimed contribution beyond v1's emphasis on sample quality and competitive sampling speed.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for emphasizing low noise levels, slower convergence with feature-specific schedules, and TabDDPM's apparent preference for categorical fidelity. It discusses mixed effects in the component ablation and explicitly acknowledges ARF's categorical-marginal advantage. New limitations address schedule-selection cost, embedding-initialization sensitivity, privacy-sensitive applications and possible disadvantages on specialized data such as time series.

D1.justification: Appendices F–J substantially expand implementation information with baseline package versions and sources, licenses, RTX 4090 hardware, PyTorch 2.2.2, architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, EMA decay and warmup. Appendix P supplies detailed runtime measurements. However, v1's quantile-transformation and dequantization instructions disappear; this establishes lost documentation, not that preprocessing actually stopped.

E1.justification: V2 retains all six original datasets and adds acsincome, covertype, diabetes, lending and news. This expands evaluation into additional income, forest-cover, hospital-readmission, lending and news settings, including high-cardinality categorical features. Appendix E specifies binary task conversions for covertype and diabetes.

E2.justification: The four evaluated baselines—ARF, CTGAN, TVAE and TabDDPM—are retained. CoDi, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator, including on the original datasets. Its results are omitted for diabetes and lending because of estimated training cost. STaSy and Diffusion Forest remain discussed rather than evaluated.

E3.justification: V1's 25-trial generator tuning with 10,000–20,000 training steps is replaced by fixed architectures calibrated to approximately three million parameters on adult and 30,000 training steps. V2 also changes diffusion sampling settings, increases detector tuning from 25 to 50 trials, introduces a 50,000-sample evaluation cap, revises downstream learners and metrics, and replaces signed DCR differences with absolute differences. Rank aggregation introduces explicit penalties for unavailable baseline results.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained comparison of three schedule granularities, v2 adds a five-configuration ablation across four datasets, testing grouped homogenization components, schedule functional form, type-specific schedules and initialization (Table 2 and Appendix O). Appendices K–M add learned-schedule fit diagnostics, univariate and bivariate distribution comparisons, and feature-level correlation-error visualizations.

E5.justification: Both versions already report five generation seeds and ten downstream-model seeds. V2's predictive-result captions explicitly incorporate these seeds into the uncertainty description, whereas v1 describes standard deviations across model averages. V2 also adds plus/minus quantities to average ranks. Some ambiguity remains because its captions mention four downstream models while Section 4.1 and Appendix I list three.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded with new datasets, CoDi, AUC, ablations and timing measurements.
