For example, adult CDTD per-type correlation error changes from 0.094 to 0.125 (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 7), under revised models and settings rather than a controlled performance comparison. V2 also resolves v1 Table 1's apparent JSD/Wasserstein label swap relative to its appendix averages.

M1.justification: V2 replaces v1's Diffusion Transformer with a TabDDPM-style MLP using five fully connected layers and 16-dimensional categorical embeddings. It adds learned time-dependent normalization of the joint loss and changes noise-schedule initialization from approximately uniform to emphasizing low noise levels, with mu changing from 0.5 to 0.25. These substantially revise the architecture and training procedure while retaining the joint Gaussian diffusion framework.

P1.justification: The introduction, method explanation and discussion are extensively rewritten. V2 adds an explicit contribution list, reorganizes the method into framework, homogenization, noise schedules and customization subsections, and introduces a dedicated limitations section. The appendices are substantially reorganized while retaining and expanding earlier calibration and timewarping material.

P2.justification: The framework diagram is redrawn, and v2 adds architecture, noise-schedule, runtime, density and correlation-heatmap figures. The main results table changes from mean metric values to ranks, with updated mean results in Appendix N. Detailed tables gain comparator and real-data columns, while new ablation and runtime tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of Diffusion Forest's scalability and cites Karras et al. (2023) and Kingma and Gao (2023) for adaptive loss normalization, alongside additional dataset and software references. References connecting v1 to non-uniform diffusion, Diffusion Transformers and numerical-feature embeddings disappear. The principal positioning around score interpolation and mixed-type diffusion remains intact.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix B adds an analytical derivation showing how output initialization yields expected unit loss across timesteps for both data types, extending v1's terminal-time calibration argument. Appendix A explicitly incorporates EDM weighting and preconditioning. Sections 2.1 and 3.3 correct diffusion coefficients to include the noise-schedule derivative. The existing logistic CDF, inverse and density derivations are retained in Appendix D.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for its design choices through component ablations, broader benchmarks, explicit architecture and training-budget controls, and an initialization derivation. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility, and the JSD/Wasserstein summary inconsistency is corrected. Fixed baseline configurations replace per-dataset tuning, preprocessing documentation is lost, and learner-count captions remain inconsistent. Nevertheless, the gains in experimental scrutiny, mathematical explanation and transparency are substantial; the judgment does not depend on treating revised scores as performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CDTD research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on eleven datasets, component ablations, learned-schedule diagnostics, qualitative analyses and timing results in Section 4 and Appendices K–P.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data experiments on six datasets, comparing four baselines and three CDTD noise-schedule variants in Section 4 and Appendix H.

results.title: Continuous Diffusion for Mixed-Type Tabular Data

C1.justification: The original domain-agnostic, interpretable FWD contribution remains. v3 adds computational efficiency and FD-DINOv2's residual domain bias and high computational cost as explicit introduction contributions. The abstract and conclusion extend the critique to FD-DINOv2, and the conclusion adds environmental-cost and complementary-use claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving DINOv2 training-data overlap, SWD random-projection variability and StableDiffusion-2.1 image artifacts. It removes v2's explicit limitations concerning FWD's limited added utility on ImageNet, its frequency/spatial rather than semantic emphasis, and possible joint optimization of FWD and FID. These qualifications are not relocated to an appendix.

D1.justification: v3 supplies an explicit FWD implementation link and identifies the FD-DINOv2 code source. It documents the Sentinel winter subset, its 31,825 images, format conversion and generator-training settings, and identifies the StableDiffusion versions evaluated. Appendix compute information changes from A40 GPUs to A100 GPUs and ties the resources to sample generation. These materially expand or revise reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v3 adds Sentinel remote-sensing imagery and Conceptual Captions text-to-image evaluation, while removing CIFAR-10 coverage entirely. It also adds human realism judgments. The DNDD description changes from sugar beet to winter wheat and rye, but retained sample counts and scores leave unclear whether this corrects documentation or reflects different underlying data.

E2.justification: FD-DINOv2 becomes a central evaluated comparator. Tables 8–9 add FID-infinity, IS, IS-infinity, Clean-FID and SWD, and introduce KID into the domain-bias comparison. PSNR and SSIM disappear, while FD-DINOv2 replaces KID in the reweighting and corruption comparisons. Some cross-domain retrained-Inception comparisons from v2 Table 2 are removed.

E3.justification: New protocols include real-versus-generated image choices with over 1,000 responses from 50 volunteers, Conceptual Captions evaluation against external user ratings, and feature-extraction GFLOPs and throughput measurements over 50,000 images. The reported Proj. FastGAN learning rate on CelebA-HQ and DNDD changes from 2e-4 to 1e-4; the PDFs do not establish whether those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds human-perception validation, an SWD-versus-FWD reproducibility analysis in Table 9, and a CelebA-HQ class-histogram comparison for DDGAN and Proj. FastGAN in Figure 5a. It extends the existing corruption and FID-optimization analyses to FD-DINOv2. The packet-interpretability analysis is retained, while some cross-domain retrained-backbone checks disappear.

E5.justification: Table 9 newly reports minimum, mean and standard deviation across five independent metric computations. Conversely, the retained reweighting results lose v2 Table 3's explicit five-run caption in v3 Table 6, although their uncertainty values remain. This does not establish a change in the underlying run count.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical evidence for FD-DINOv2, Sentinel, EDM, human perception, efficiency and additional metrics. Existing ImageNet values also change: Improved Diffusion VLB has FID 42.257 and FWD 2.221 in v2 Table 1, versus 33.522 and 2.182 in v3 Table 4. With unchanged reweighting means, the reported FID change is corrected from -47% to -52.53%, and FWD from +2.5% to +17.75%. CIFAR-10 and several comparison entries are removed.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same Haar wavelet-packet decomposition, pixel normalization, per-packet means and covariances, Fréchet distances and averaging procedure. The resolution-dependent transformation-depth rule is also retained. New evaluated generators and comparison metrics do not alter FWD.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: domain bias leads, the broad generator comparison moves later, and a user-study section is introduced. Related-work material moves into Appendix B, appendices are reorganized into A–C, and the limitations section disappears. The introduction, results interpretation and conclusion are extensively revised, alongside language and author-information edits.

P2.justification: v3 restructures the benchmark and retrained-backbone tables, adds efficiency, perception and additional-metric tables, and introduces extensive sample grids in Appendix C. The corruption plot moves to the appendix with a changed comparator legend; the DNDD histogram moves into a combined main-text figure. Sample panels, captions, figure placement and the conference-template layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The positioning expands beyond Inception-based and traditional pairwise metrics to address FD-DINOv2 and SWD as important alternatives. New discussion cites Stein et al., Oquab et al. and Nguyen et al. to motivate training-domain, computational and reproducibility concerns. Additional generator and dataset references support the expanded evaluation; moving the spectral-method discussion to Appendix B is separately a structural change.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same wavelet construction, statistical definitions and Fréchet-distance formulation. The appendix explanation of forward and inverse wavelet transforms is preserved. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or removed.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical grounding of the unchanged metric through relevant FD-DINOv2 and other comparisons, measured computational cost, broader domains and an original human-realism study. These address important gaps in v2's perceptual validation and practical comparison. The implementation link and corrected percentages also help. Removing explicit limitations weakens balance, and Table 7 uses external ratings whose comparability to the evaluated samples is undocumented. Nevertheless, the direct comparisons and original human evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fréchet Wavelet Distance work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds computational measurements, Sentinel results and an original 50-volunteer perception study. The externally sourced ratings in Table 7 are distinct from these original results.

before.justification: v2 reports original generator evaluations, retrained-Inception comparisons, sample-reweighting experiments and corruption tests in Tables 1–3 and Figure 6.

results.title: Fréchet Wavelet Distance: A Domain-Agnostic Metric for Image Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution lists retain the same principal claims: an MIO formulation of SPNs, SPN likelihood as a plausibility measure, and LiCE for producing plausible, close and sparse counterfactuals satisfying common desiderata. Causality receives less main-text emphasis but its formulation and claimed support remain in the appendices.

C2.justification: v4 substantially qualifies reliance on SPN likelihood. F.4 discusses lost statistical superiority under successful-factual comparisons and poor win95pts rankings; G.4 suggests insufficient training coverage as an explanation for weaker andes density estimates. It also expands explanations of threshold tradeoffs and infeasible Credit cases, beyond v3's emphasis on computational overhead and possible numerical failures.

D1.justification: v4 specifies the sum-node big-M constant as 100 and documents the bnlearn software, target variables and sampling procedures for the new synthetic experiments. The rough total compute estimate rises from 15,000 to 20,000 CPU hours. Most original hyperparameters and hardware details remain; the repository was already linked in v3.

E1.justification: The three real-world datasets are retained. v4 adds synthetic distributions from eight Bayesian networks for density-estimation evaluation (G.4), including counterfactual-generation tasks on asia, alarm and win95pts (F.4). These introduce substantial coverage of scenarios with known generating probabilities.

E2.justification: The external baseline roster remains DiCE, VAE, C-CHVAE, both FACE variants and PROPLACE; PlaCE and DACE remain unevaluated. Within the matched variant comparison, LiCE (sample) is added (v3 Table 9 versus v4 Table 10). The runtime comparison also gains quartile and sample variants (v3 Table 10 versus v4 Table 12).

E3.justification: The original preprocessing, neural-network architecture and five-fold design are retained. v4 adds comparisons on common successful factuals, synthetic CE experiments using 10,000 training samples and 100 fresh factuals, and density evaluation using 1,000 test samples. New metrics include true generating probabilities and density-fit measures. Synthetic optimizing LiCE uses alpha = 1, whereas the real-data experiments retain 0.1.

E4.justification: Beyond v3's variant and runtime comparisons, v4 tests MIO approximation accuracy against the actual SPN output (Table 2), compares methods on common factuals (F.2), evaluates CEs against known probabilities (F.4), and assesses SPN distribution fidelity (G.4). The sample-threshold variant also extends the sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: v3 already reports standard deviations and five-fold experiments. v4 adds five-seed synthetic experiments, Friedman and Nemenyi significance tests with critical-difference diagrams, and significance tests for density correlations. F.4 aggregates synthetic runs, while G.4 explicitly selects the best-performing SPN from five fits.

E6.justification: Many retained benchmark and runtime values are revised. For example, LiCE (optimize) Credit NLL changes from 30.3 ± 3.8 to 28.8 ± 3.3, and LiCE (median) GMSC success changes from 53.6% to 60.0%. v4 also adds approximation, synthetic-probability, ranking and correlation results. These are revised and additional reports, rather than demonstrated controlled performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: Appendix F.1 introduces LiCE (sample), which sets the likelihood threshold to the minimum of the factual's likelihood and the training median. This adds an adaptive threshold rule to the retained SPN/MIO method; its main architecture, distance-likelihood objective and desiderata constraints remain.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition and results discussion are extensively revised. Prerequisites become separate from related work, and v3's single nested Appendix A becomes thematic Appendices A–G. Existing causality, diversity and encoding material is redistributed, and unfinished editorial notes in v3's supplementary discussion are removed.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a substantially different conference layout, transposes and revises Table 1, and redraws Figure 1 with a different example and explicit likelihood clipping. It adds approximation and common-factual tables, synthetic evaluation tables, critical-difference diagrams and an eight-panel density-fit figure. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands research positioning through comparisons with adversarial-random-forest and GAN approaches, CeFlow, PPCEF and diffeomorphic counterfactuals. Section 3 and G.3 develop the distinctions between SPNs, GMMs, flows, autoregressive models and autoencoders, particularly categorical-data support and compatibility with linear MIO formulations.

T1.justification: v4 supplies explicit binary/big-M inequalities for sum-node maximization and an argument for tightness under likelihood maximization (Section 4), replacing v3's solver-level max expression. It removes the assertion that hard-EM training makes the approximation exact and adds formulation-size reasoning in F.3. The existing log-sum-exp bound and most other mathematics remain.

improvement.justification: v3 evaluates plausibility primarily through the same SPN used by LiCE and acknowledges that methods succeed on different factuals. v4 substantially addresses these weaknesses through known-probability synthetic evaluations, common-factual comparisons, direct approximation checks and statistical analyses. It also reports unfavorable findings that clarify dependence on SPN quality. Best-of-five selection in the density study and weak win95pts results limit generality, but the added validation and more explicit limitations substantially improve the paper's evidential quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LiCE research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v4 retains original real-data experiments and adds SPN approximation measurements, synthetic counterfactual experiments and distribution-estimation evaluations.

before.justification: v3 reports original counterfactual-generation experiments on GMSC, Adult and German Credit, including validity, plausibility, similarity, sparsity and runtime results.

results.title: Generating Likely Counterfactuals Using Sum-Product Networks

C1.justification: V3's introduction explicitly frames the contribution as explaining the model's decision-making rather than discovering true causal relationships in the data. This qualifies the contribution's scope while retaining the central claims about answering three query types, comparable prediction, and benefits of joint training.

C2.justification: V3 explains why omitting input reconstruction simplifies optimization and why added latent components preserve concept-level interpretability. Appendix C.3 interprets competing loss-weight effects, while Appendix E attributes some implausible baseline outputs to soft concept values. The existing limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: V3 documents the new encoders, 143 CIFAR10 and 19 SIIM concepts, and benchmark-specific hyperparameters. It newly describes validation on a training subset and optional staged or warm-up training. The repository link, software versions, hardware, and original hyperparameter entries remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V3 adds ten-class object classification on CIFAR10 and binary pneumothorax classification on chest X-rays from SIIM, retaining the original three datasets. These substantially broaden domain coverage and evaluate settings without supplied concept annotations.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Black Box, CBM, and CEM for predictive performance and BayCon, C-CHVAE, VAE-CF, and VCNet for counterfactual generation. V3 extends these comparator sets to new datasets without adding or removing comparison methods.

E3.justification: The added benchmarks introduce automatic concept extraction, CLIP ViT-B/16 and CXR-CLIP encoders, and training budgets of 30 and 100 epochs, respectively. Table 7 adds controlled loss-weight variations on MNIST addition. Previously stated settings for the original datasets remain unchanged; the newly described validation-based selection is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: New Table 7 tests how loss-weight emphasis affects validity, sparsity, and proximity. New Appendix E examines generated examples across all five datasets, exposing infeasible concept combinations and unnecessary changes. These add sensitivity and qualitative failure analyses beyond the retained confounder and concept-noise experiments.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and standard errors over five runs with different initializations and retain the Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Mann–Whitney tests in Section 5.2. Additional results follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds predictive, counterfactual, timing, sensitivity, and qualitative results. Table 3 reports CF-CBM validity of 100.0% on CIFAR10 and 99.9% on SIIM; its revised averages cover five datasets. Original tabulated benchmark scores are retained, but Figure 5 roughly doubles intervention-proximity values for retained datasets, such as VCNet on dSprites from about 24% to 48%, without explaining the revision.

M1.justification: The two-latent-variable architecture, shared predictors, training objectives, and inference procedures remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendices A–B. V3's benchmark-specific encoders and discussion of optional training schedules do not establish a revision to the core CF-CBM procedure.

P1.justification: V3 makes localized abstract and introduction revisions, replaces the arthritis illustration with pneumothorax throughout the explanatory examples, and expands architectural and hyperparameter explanations. It adds acknowledgments and Appendix E and moves the efficiency discussion to Appendix D, while retaining the main section structure.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the introductory medical illustrations and expands the main trade-off figures from three wrapped panels to full-width five-panel displays. Benchmark and hyperparameter tables gain columns, new ablation and counterfactual-example tables are added, and the expanded timing figure moves to Appendix D.

R1.justification: V3 adds positioning against concept discovery and causal inference through Stammer, Louizos, and Xia, and expands discussion of concept interactions and memory reasoning. It also cites the new datasets and encoders. These extend the existing positioning without replacing its central comparison with CBMs and counterfactual generators.

T1.justification: The graphical-model factorization, objectives, Appendix A ELBO derivation, and Appendix C.2 metric definitions are retained. V3 adds explanatory prose but no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical support for applicability beyond supplied concept annotations through object and chest-X-ray evaluations. Table 7 exposes tuning trade-offs, and Appendix E makes feasibility claims inspectable through actual outputs, addressing important gaps in v2. These gains outweigh reporting problems: unexplained Figure 5 rescaling, inconsistent loss-weight numbering, and the overstated SIIM highest-validity claim despite 99.9% versus 100.0% for several baselines.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Counterfactual Concept Bottleneck Models. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds CIFAR10 and SIIM Pneumothorax results, loss-weight sensitivity experiments, and generated counterfactual examples.

before.justification: V2 reports original classification, counterfactual-generation, intervention, and robustness experiments on dSprites, MNIST addition, and CUB.

results.title: Counterfactual Concept Bottleneck Models

C1.justification: v3 qualifies the broad standard-GP endorsement by explicitly tying successful optimization to Matérn kernels and UCB. Its abstract and contribution list add diffuse-prior MAP training and failure modes under alternative settings. This materially narrows applicability and expands the central contribution beyond demonstrating strong performance.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds proposed explanations involving L-BFGS instability, restrictive priors, vanishing EI gradients, inadequate Thompson-sampling candidate coverage, and SE covariance becoming nearly diagonal. It also discusses log-EI and alternative SE priors as remedies. These substantially qualify v2's predominantly positive interpretation of standard GP performance.

D1.justification: v3 adds MAP tolerances and priors, BNN implementation and tuning details, TS sampling instructions, and disclosure that surrogate examples came from optimization trajectories. It removes NN-Prune details, explicit NUTS priors, and SVM/Mopta08 implementation provenance. A new ambiguity remains: Section 4.1 specifies Gamma(1.1, 0.05) for noise variance, whereas Figure 10 specifies Gamma(1.1, 0.5).

E1.justification: v3 removes NN-Prune, including its ResNet-152/Tiny ImageNet task, while retaining the six synthetic and five other real-world optimization benchmarks. Appendix B.1 newly reports a high-dimensional polynomial optimization rerun. Both versions actually evaluate ten main surrogate-learning tasks, despite v2's introduction claiming twelve.

E2.justification: v3 adds BNN Laplace and BNN HMC to the optimization comparisons in Figures 1-2. Surrogate-learning comparisons add Add-GP and report a generic Proj-GP instead of separately labelled ALEBO-10/20 columns. These substantially broaden the evaluated surrogate families.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce MAP/L-BFGS settings, BNN architecture selection through leave-one-out cross-validation, Thompson sampling with 3,000/10,000 candidates, and kernel evaluations across 50-300 dimensions using 500 training and 100 test examples. Original BO budgets and the main 300/100 surrogate sample sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained kernel-length-scale and MLE/NUTS comparisons, Appendix B systematically tests training optimizers and priors, EI and Thompson sampling, SE versus Matérn kernels, dimensional sensitivity, and UCB exploration strength. Figures 10-20 and Tables 8-9 provide substantial new evidence about failure conditions.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 8 adds standard-deviation reporting for optimization trajectories, including selected best, median and worst baselines. v2's corresponding trajectory figures show averages only. Ten-run optimization and five-run surrogate evaluations are retained; an increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: Surrogate-learning values are extensively revised: Mopta08 ARD-GP MSE changes from 0.048±0.015 in v2 Table 5 to 0.034±0.006 in v3 Table 4. Identical sampled data are not established, so this is a revised result rather than a demonstrated same-setting gain. v3 also adds MAP/BNN results and substantial prior, acquisition and kernel failure findings, while removing NN-Prune results.

M1.justification: v3 adds SBO-1, which trains the standard GP using diffuse-prior MAP estimation with L-BFGS. The earlier ADAM/MLE GP-ARD and single-length-scale GP configurations remain as SBO-2 and SBO-3. The underlying GP/UCB optimization procedure is retained.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title and method terminology, revises the abstract, shortens the conclusion, promotes the original results subsections, and introduces a failure-modes section and appendix. Much of the introduction, GP background, related-work discussion and original experimental narrative remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v3 adds the settings-summary table and numerous ablation displays, redraws comparisons with additional methods, and presents SBO-3 separately with selected baselines. Existing tables and figures are resized or relocated, including the surrogate metrics and prediction-alignment plot. The document also adopts a substantially different template with wrapped tables and figures.

R1.justification: New references include Ament et al., Hvarfner et al., Li et al. on BNN surrogates, and Sobol, supporting the new experiments and discussion of earlier failures. Pruning-related references and Papenmeier et al. are removed. The principal additive, embedding and sparsity-based related-work taxonomy remains.

T1.justification: Formal changes are limited to definitions: v3 explicitly specifies EI and SE in Equations 6-7, while v2 Appendix A.2's penalized NN-Prune objective is removed. The central GP/UCB equations and synthetic-function definitions remain equivalent. No theorem, proof or formal guarantee is added.

improvement.justification: v2's broad endorsement lacked systematic tests of common alternative settings. v3 Appendix B establishes important failure conditions, while the abstract and contribution statements qualify when standard BO succeeds. This substantially strengthens the paper's evidential support and practical guidance. Removing NN-Prune reduces coverage, and the inconsistent noise-prior specification weakens reproducibility locally, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the central gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same standard-GP Bayesian optimization study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison despite the changed title and layout.

after.justification: v3 reports original optimization, surrogate-learning and timing results, together with additional baseline comparisons and failure-mode experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original optimization experiments over ten runs, surrogate-learning evaluations over five runs, and computational timing results.

results.title: Standard Gaussian Process is All You Need for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

C1.justification: v4 makes identifying a training-failure mechanism and proposing theoretically motivated initialization central contributions. Its abstract, introduction and conclusion newly claim that suitable initialization can restore strong SE-kernel BO performance. The Matérn performance headline remains, while the separate ten-dataset surrogate-learning contribution is dropped.

C2.justification: v3 Appendix B.3 emphasizes rapid covariance decay and potentially inadequate SE modeling capacity. v4 instead attributes failure primarily to initialization-induced vanishing gradients and explains why Matérn kernels and larger initial length-scales help. It also connects concentrated priors to this mechanism. New Appendix D explicitly acknowledges that the maximum workable input dimensionality remains unknown.

D1.justification: v4 explicitly discloses the default initialization of approximately 0.693, additional NUTS prior choices and the BoTorch log-EI implementation. It removes v3's experiment-code link and explicit 400/300-step budget sentence, although those budgets remain visible in plots. Hardware information and most baseline implementation sources are retained.

E1.justification: The eleven main BO benchmarks remain, but v3's separate ten-dataset surrogate-prediction evaluation is removed rather than relocated. v4 retains narrower prediction checks on Hartmann6/Rosenbrock and Mopta08/DNA, substantially reducing prediction-task coverage. The briefly reported polynomial-optimization experiment in v3 Appendix B.1 also disappears.

E2.justification: VBO is newly evaluated in the main BO comparisons, and log-EI joins the acquisition-function comparison. Removing the regression study also removes its ProjGP, AddGP and SaasBO surrogate comparisons. BNN Laplace/HMC remain in v4 Appendix C.1, so their absence from the main figures is not an overall removal.

E3.justification: v3 Appendix B.3's kernel-learning experiment becomes a crossed dimension/initialization study in v4 Section 4, extending the dimension range from 50–300 to 50–600 and measuring gradients and parameter changes alongside MSE instead of reporting test log likelihood. The SE BO comparison is now specified with L-BFGS MAP training in v4 Section 6.1, whereas v3 Appendix B.3 specified MLE.

E4.justification: v4 adds initialization sensitivity experiments and direct gradient/update measurements during training and SVM/Rosenbrock BO runs, linking failure to the proposed remedy in Figures 1–2. It also tests log-EI rather than merely suggesting it. v3's quantitative prior-sensitivity prediction Tables 8–9 disappear; MAP/MLE/NUTS and UCB exploration analyses largely remain.

E5.justification: The redesigned Hartmann6/Rosenbrock experiment reports twenty repetitions per dimension and initialization, versus five repetitions for v3 Appendix B.3's experiment. This does not establish additional runs of unchanged experiments. BO comparisons retain ten-run reporting and variability displays.

E6.justification: v4 adds initialization-dependent failure thresholds, RI/VBO optimization results and log-EI scores, while removing v3's regression Tables 4, 5, 8 and 9. The main SVM Matérn outcome changes from approximately -0.14 in v3 Figure 2 to -0.05 in v4 Figure 4, but v4 Figure 7 retains the older MAP range; this is not a verified same-setting gain. Timing values in v3 Tables 6–7 are unchanged in v4 Tables 4–5.

M1.justification: v4 Section 5 introduces dimension-dependent length-scale initialization, ℓ0 = c√d, with c = 1 in experiments, producing SBO-SE(RI). This adds an explicit procedure for preventing SE-kernel training failure that v3 did not propose. Existing Matérn MAP/MLE and single-length-scale variants largely remain under revised names or appendix placement.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, result discussion and conclusion are substantially rewritten around initialization and gradient failure. GP background is compressed, related-work subsections are flattened, and training/BNN analyses are reorganized into the appendices. New proof and limitations sections change the narrative structure; the author list also expands.

P2.justification: v4 adds gradient-diagnostic plots and threshold tables, redraws main comparison panels for RI/VBO, and consolidates trajectory displays using best/median/worst baseline summaries. BNN/training displays and timing tables move, while regression tables and several standalone endpoint plots disappear. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: The structural-BO related-work discussion largely remains. v4 adds Bengio/Hanin gradient-vanishing citations, removes the Batlle operator-learning connection and Li BNN-study discussion, and expands the already-cited Hvarfner/VBO work into a focused comparison between dimension-dependent prior regularization and initialization.

T1.justification: v3 provides standard GP/BO formulas and a heuristic explanation of SE-kernel decay. v4 adds gradient derivations, threshold Propositions 4.1 and 4.3, probability-bound Lemma 4.2 and initialization Lemma 5.1. New Appendix A supplies proofs, with the probability bounds assuming independently sampled uniform inputs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially advances v3's tentative explanation of SE failure by connecting initialization to gradient diagnostics, formal bounds and an experimentally tested remedy in Sections 4–5 and Figures 1–5. This improves both explanatory and practical value. The bounds remain limited by their sampling assumptions, and removing regression comparisons and the code link reduces breadth and reproducibility. The unexplained main/appendix SVM discrepancy limits confidence in exact scores, but the broader mechanism-and-remedy evidence supports a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and retain matching optimization benchmarks. All 26 pages of v3 and 24 pages of v4, including appendices, figures, tables and equations, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v4 reports original optimization results, initialization experiments and gradient diagnostics in Sections 4–6 and Appendix C, including synthetic experiments repeated twenty times.

before.justification: v3 reports original repeated optimization experiments, surrogate-prediction results, ablations and computational timings in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Standard Gaussian Process is All You Need for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

C1.justification: The architecture contributions and principal performance and teacher-preference claims are retained. v4 softens the abstract's guarantee of human-centric interpretability into an objective of optimizing human understanding, and more explicitly limits the claimed explanation to local feature/concept use.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly explains that the black-box discriminator's selection rationale is outside the explanation's scope. It adds warnings about misleading correlations and discussion of auditing, interpretable-input requirements, specialization, noise reduction and overfitting. Sections 6 and Appendix I also substantially expand architectural tradeoffs and applicability boundaries; the earlier user-study presentation caveat is retained.

D1.justification: The core reproducibility appendix retains its hardware, training-time, epoch and tuning details. v4 adds sensitivity-grid settings, FRESH's BERT backbone and rationale fractions, RF tree counts/depths, and guidance on specifying feature groups. The explicit MIT-license statement for the authors' code/models disappears with v2's checklist; the public code link remains.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same eight primary benchmarks, the supplementary Structures and Venture MOOCs, and the same teacher study. The added experiments reuse existing datasets. Raw speech, video and graph-based time-series applications are prospective discussions, not evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: v4 adds FRESH to the AG News/SST comparison in Table 2, Integrated Gradients, LIME and SHAP to the synthetic explanation comparison in Table 4 and Appendix I.2, and Random Forest to the tabular comparison in Figure 19. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator families beyond v2's original baselines.

E3.justification: v4 adds top-5 Rank Agreement and Feature Agreement to the synthetic evaluation; PRA is retained in Appendix I.2. New experiments introduce temperature/threshold sweeps, cross-routing controls for specialization, and FRESH evaluations using BERT with specified rationale fractions. Existing benchmark splits, core training budgets and teacher-study procedures are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix D.2 tests Gumbel parameter sensitivity and sparsity on DSP and Breast Cancer. D.3 tests whether experts predict better on their assigned data across DSP, SST and Breast Cancer. Appendix I.1 adds an RF-versus-ICC feature-importance comparison. Earlier regularization, prediction-horizon and grouping analyses remain present.

E5.justification: Appendix I.4 newly specifies five random seeds for FRESH, while the general three-seed setup remains; this does not establish increased runs for existing results. The new sensitivity analysis selectively omits confidence intervals from performance plots and lists high-variance configurations. Existing mean/std reporting and teacher-study significance tests are retained.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive comparator, explanation-metric, sensitivity and specialization results. For example, FRESH scores 88.73 ± 0.69 on AG News and 82.05 ± 0.56 on SST. Existing Table 2 entries and teacher-study scores remain unchanged. However, new Figure 19 reverses the synthetic scores 89.51 ± 0.51 and 84.67 ± 4.04 between ICC FG and SENN Concepts relative to Table 2 in both versions.

M1.justification: The principal feature-gating and group-routing methods remain unchanged. Appendices I.3 and I.5 newly propose optional tree/SVM discriminators and graph-based components. These extend the proposed architectural options, but are explicitly unevaluated alternatives, not changes to the models producing the reported benchmarks.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and terminology refinement. v4 removes the NeurIPS checklist, adds acknowledgements, introduces a taxonomy appendix, and reorganizes and expands the appendix narrative. These changes extend beyond inserting new scientific results.

P2.justification: v4 expands Tables 2 and 4, adds sensitivity plots, specialization heatmaps, the RF comparison and an extractive-rationale comparison table. It relocates the existing Tukey plot into the main text and AG News examples into the appendix, changes Table 1's layout, and corrects Figure 1's feature-gating caption to match the existing method.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning against extractive-rationale methods, including FRESH, Bastings et al. and Yu et al., with a dedicated discussion and comparison table. It adds XAI taxonomies, expert-informed concept approaches and classical MoE foundations. It also revises the characterization of post-hoc sparsity and replaces Table 1's coverage axis with predictive stage.

T1.justification: The routing equation and Gumbel derivation remain unchanged. Appendix I.2 adds quantitative definitions separating Ground Truth Alignment from Ground Truth Faithfulness, with asserted faithfulness bounds in Table 4. This extends metric definitions and formal properties without adding a proof of the guarantees.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation where v2 lacked an external interpretable text baseline, direct post-hoc explanation comparisons, and Gumbel-parameter and expert-specialization checks. These additions test central performance and interpretability claims more thoroughly, while the discriminator-scope discussion improves their interpretation. Figure 19's swapped synthetic scores and stale user-study cross-references introduce reporting defects, but the broader comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InterpretCC research, with matching architectures, datasets and teacher study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures and equations, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, parameter-sensitivity experiments and expert-specialization analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original predictive benchmarks, synthetic explanation evaluations, routing analyses and teacher-study outcomes.

results.title: Intrinsic User-Centric Interpretability through Global Mixture of Experts

C1.justification: V2 broadens its central theoretical contribution from strongly convex and PL-conditioned results to general non-convex convergence guarantees under both learning-rate policies. The abstract and introduction also make heterogeneous, time-varying resource availability a central contribution, while retaining the claim that DSpodFL unifies existing decentralized methods.

C2.justification: V2 revises the learning-rate and participation interpretation of the optimality gap, replacing v1's simple proportionality claims with participation-dependent residuals. Appendix O explains the tradeoff between accuracy per iteration and delay, and decomposes the resource savings. Section 6 acknowledges limited dataset/task validation, although O.5's new assertion that all methods converge to the same global model exceeds the general non-convex stationarity guarantee.

D1.justification: Section 5 newly identifies a cluster of three NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 40 GB memory. This adds reproducibility information absent from v1; it does not establish a hardware change between experiments.

E1.justification: Fashion-MNIST/SVM and CIFAR10/VGG11 image classification, including IID and non-IID cases, are retained. Appendix O.4 adds a distinct environment with computation and communication availability changing during training; v1's empirical participation probabilities remain fixed.

E2.justification: Corresponding empirical comparisons retain DGD, DFedAvg, Randomized Gossip, and Sporadic SGDs. The additional experiments reuse these comparators; changes to the related-work comparison in Table 1 do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The main experimental settings remain stable. New protocols resample participation probabilities every 1000 iterations, sweep CIFAR10 client counts, and evaluate accuracy by iteration and delay components at specified accuracy targets. Figure 6b changes its stated measurement delay from 5000 to 500, without establishing that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained heterogeneity and connectivity sweeps, Appendices O.4-O.6 add temporal-resource robustness tests, accuracy-by-iteration comparisons, and processing-versus-transmission delay decomposition. These analyses substantially extend the examination of whether DSpodFL's advantage comes from iteration efficiency or reduced resource costs. Figure 6c also extends the client-count sensitivity analysis to CIFAR10.

E5.justification: V1 does not describe repeated-run uncertainty reporting. V2 explicitly reports means and one-standard-deviation uncertainty across multiple runs, adding bands and error bars to the main experimental figures. Exact run counts and seeds remain unspecified, so an increase in runs cannot be established.

E6.justification: V2 revises existing plotted results, particularly Figure 2, and adds Figure 6c, Figure 7, and Tables 2-5. Newly reported findings include FMNIST non-IID accuracy of 0.70 for DSpodFL versus 0.75 for DGD at iteration 15000, alongside target-accuracy delay decompositions. These substantially expand the quantitative record without establishing performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The core sporadic SGD and aggregation updates remain unchanged. Algorithm 1, line 13, revises the stated Metropolis-Hastings weight calculation from time-indexed neighbor counts to fixed neighbor counts, which v2 explicitly defines using the graph union.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and related-work discussion are substantially rewritten. Method exposition is reordered, proofs are consolidated into grouped appendices, and the PL discussion moves out of the main analysis. These are extensive narrative and organizational changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column main-text layout with a single-column format, revises Figure 1, expands and restructures Table 1, and adds uncertainty displays. It also adds a third panel to Figure 6, a new Figure 7, and four numerical tables, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references on local decentralized SGD, Cooperative SGD, and optimization over directed graphs, while removing several uncoordinated-step-size references. Section 2 sharpens distinctions from the already-cited Anarchic FL and asynchronous framework of Even et al., but retains the central positioning around joint sporadic computation and communication.

T1.justification: V2 adds general non-convex stationarity analysis under Assumption 4.2, with constant and diminishing learning-rate results and proofs in Appendices G-H and K-L. The earlier PL analysis is retained and revised in Appendices M-N. Theorem 4.11 now treats time-varying probabilities through uniform bounds, and the PL recursion gains the previously omitted alpha-dependent participation residual, changing the resulting gap bound.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens theoretical scope through the additional non-convex analyses and improves precision by correcting the participation-dependent PL residual and gap interpretation. Dynamic-resource experiments, uncertainty reporting, and iteration/delay decomposition provide stronger support for the practical claims. These gains outweigh the overstrong common-global-model assertion in Appendix O.5; exact run counts also remain an unresolved reporting limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DSpodFL research, with matching authors, core update equations, and benchmark tasks. The main text, figures, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix O report original benchmark results, including additional experiments with time-varying resource availability and new accuracy and delay analyses.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix V report original Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR10 experiments comparing DSpodFL with decentralized-learning baselines.

results.title: Decentralized Sporadic Federated Learning: A Unified Algorithmic Framework with Convergence Guarantees

C1.justification: v1 already claims that PGW defines a metric, but emphasizes efficient solvers. v2 newly claims the first GW-based metric for non-probability metric measure spaces, introduces barycenters as a contribution, and adds principal claims about shape discrimination and robustness in interpolation. The original solver contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 attributes retrieval behavior to metric discrimination and some UGW behavior to Sinkhorn regularization. It qualifies interpolation advantages under overlapping noise and explains that MDS requires manual orientation alignment because GW/PGW are invariant to rotations and reflections. Appendix Q expands the line-search limitation, although disabling line search for PU learning was already disclosed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 documents new preprocessing and implementation settings, including k-means with 1,024 centers, SVM kernel scale 10, barycenter iteration limits and tolerances, and task-specific mass and penalty choices. It specifies a PU penalty bound where v1 only requested a sufficiently large value, adds dataset-access directions, and revises the hardware description to an EPYC 7713, 256 GB RAM, and one RTX A6000 rather than v1's four-GPU description.

E1.justification: v2 adds two shape-retrieval datasets and noisy shape-interpolation tasks. It replaces the square/circle-to-cube/sphere mixture-matching experiment with moon and circle–sphere matching under outlier contamination. MNIST, EMNIST, Caltech Office PU learning, and the synthetic solver-timing task remain.

E2.justification: Existing distance and solver comparator families remain, with primal-PGW renamed MPGW. The substantive extension is evaluating GW barycenters against PGW barycenters in the new interpolation experiments, Figures 3 and 5. The MPGW barycenter algorithm is introduced but is not shown as an evaluated interpolation baseline.

E3.justification: v2 introduces random-representative nearest-neighbor classification, stratified 10-fold kernel-SVM evaluation, and SMACOF reconstruction of barycenters. Table 3 adds PU timing configurations with 2,000 source and 10,000 target samples, beyond the retained 1,000/5,000 configuration. Cross-feature POT-initialized comparisons are dropped. Interpolation settings contain an unresolved discrepancy: Appendix M.1 says 0.5% noise where Section 5.3 and Figure 5 say 5%.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled outlier tests for matching and interpolation robustness across three spatial noise distributions and two figure-labeled noise levels, 5% and 10%. Figure 5 includes noise overlapping the signal region, where the methods behave more similarly. Retrieval confusion matrices also expose class-specific errors. These analyses are absent from v1.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 newly specifies 10,000 randomized representative-selection repetitions and reports SVM accuracy averaged across 10 folds. These are new repetition and aggregation practices, not evidence of additional runs for retained experiments. Neither version provides seed identities, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds retrieval results, including PGW accuracies of 96.25% and 100% versus GW's 98.13% and 80.83%, plus new matching and interpolation findings. PU timings and Caltech Office accuracies change: POT-initialized PGW on SURF(A) to SURF(A) changes from 100% to 74.7% in v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 4. Digit accuracies remain unchanged. Additional timing rows are reported; differing hardware descriptions preclude treating revised runtimes as clean performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: The original PGW objective and two solvers are largely retained, but Section 5.3 and Appendix M introduce barycenter optimization, alternating coupling/matrix updates, and a mass-constrained variant in Algorithms 3–4. The pruning text also changes from rows containing no negative entries to rows containing a nonnegative entry; this documents an inconsistent rule without establishing an implementation change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around the metric. Solver 2 and its conversion result move into Appendix G; runtime and PU experiments move into Appendices O and P. Background and proof exposition are reorganized, and primal-PGW terminology becomes MPGW throughout.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the original matching illustration, adds retrieval distance/confusion matrices and interpolation grids, and introduces barycenter algorithm displays. The runtime figure moves to Appendix O and is redrawn. PU tables separate initialization method from accuracy/time and add displays for expanded timing results. The original t-SNE visualization is retained as Figure 10.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning from providing solvers to distinguishing a claimed metric from existing unbalanced discrepancies. New Appendix L develops the comparison with Chapel et al.'s mass-constrained formulation, including non-equivalence and a distinguishing example. Added references cover robust optimal transport, metric geometry, and linear GW; the change is substantive beyond citation additions.

T1.justification: v1 Proposition 3.4's transport-cost cutoff and its proof are removed. The metric proof is substantially rewritten using three auxiliary points and an untruncated cost, with explicit compact-space and equivalence assumptions. v2 also develops Lipschitz-based existence arguments, proves the large-penalty PGW-to-GW limit, formalizes the relationship with MPGW, and derives barycenter updates. These exceed renumbering or expanded explanation.

improvement.justification: The revised metric argument, derived barycenter procedure, and controlled retrieval and contamination experiments substantially improve support for PGW's mathematical role and practical usefulness beyond v1's solver-focused demonstrations. More implementation detail and explicit MDS limitations improve assessability. New defects remain, notably the pruning wording and inconsistencies in Appendix M's interpolation equation and noise level, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains in justification and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PGW formulation and Frank–Wolfe solvers despite the changed title and substantial expansion. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original outlier matching, shape retrieval, and barycenter interpolation results, alongside retained and revised runtime and positive-unlabeled learning experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original solver runtimes, synthetic shape-matching experiments, and positive-unlabeled learning accuracies and timings in Section 5 and Appendix L.

results.title: Partial Gromov-Wasserstein Metric

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the central explanation to claim that AM achieves LMC through the same mechanism as WM. v4 also qualifies v3's assertion that WM outperforms STE, describing a possible advantage for LMC among three or more models. The distance-reduction and dominant-singular-vector claims remain.

C2.justification: v4 interprets ImageNet's failure despite strong alignment through mismatches between input directions and dominant singular vectors, and connects learning-rate/weight-decay effects to low-rank structure. These materially develop applicability conditions. However, v3's explicit limitation concerning same-dataset image classification and untested image-generation applicability is omitted.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds software versions, batch sizes, training epochs, CIFAR10 augmentation, permutation-update counts, and AM implementation references. It also documents the ImageNet training configuration, blurpool setting, and BatchNorm-repair sample size. These substantially expand reproducibility information; newly documented settings for retained experiments do not prove procedural changes.

E1.justification: v4 adds actual training and evaluation on ImageNet in Appendix H.8, extending coverage to substantially larger-scale image classification. MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR10 remain; the added coverage is not merely a change of network architecture.

E2.justification: v4 adds activation matching as a systematically evaluated comparator across the retained dataset/network combinations, with Table 3 and Figures 14–15 directly compared against WM. v3 evaluated WM and STE without these AM comparisons. Newly discussed multi-model merging papers are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include the learning-rate/weight-decay sweep using VGG11 at twice its original width and Ainsworth's WM implementation, plus ImageNet evaluation using ResNet50, a 40-epoch training configuration, and 50,000 training images for BatchNorm repair. Newly disclosed batch sizes and training epochs for retained experiments do not establish that their settings changed.

E4.justification: v4 adds learning-rate/weight-decay sensitivity analysis, a broader alignment-threshold sweep, AM mechanism comparisons, and analysis of why ImageNet merging fails to achieve LMC. Most earlier width and input-projection analyses remain, but v3 Figure 9's width-dependent alignment between original and merged models is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix H.4 newly specifies six trained models grouped into three merge pairs per hyperparameter condition, reporting three-run averages without plotted uncertainty. Retained experiments preserve mean/standard-deviation reporting. Both versions retain conflicting three-versus-five merge counts for the three-model comparison; an increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: v4 adds AM, sensitivity, and ImageNet results, plus accuracy and distance-reduction columns in Table 1. ImageNet merged accuracy is 40.239% with WM versus 0.179% without, still below the originals' approximately 75.8%. Existing alignment scores also change: Table 2's VGG11 STE R becomes 0.036 ± 0.007 from 0.008 ± 0.002, while its barrier and distances remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The principal WM and STE objectives and their adopted Sinkhorn procedures remain unchanged. Activation matching is an existing method newly evaluated and analyzed, rather than a proposed algorithmic component. Using another WM implementation in the new hyperparameter study changes that experiment's procedure.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and analysis narrative, expands the title, reorganizes Section 4, and introduces a dedicated AM section. Related work moves to Appendix A, much of v3 Appendix E enters the main analysis, and the remaining appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensively resized and rearranged figures. New AM, sensitivity, and ImageNet displays are added, while existing input-projection results are partly redisplayed in the main text. Table 1 gains columns; v3 Table 3 becomes v4 Table 4 with corrected barrier headings and removed R columns.

R1.justification: Beyond moving related work to Appendix A, v4 adds substantial discussion of low-rank bias, recent LMC theory, and multi-model merging, including Galanti, Timor, Ferbach, and Crisostomi. Appendix E expands the critique of Zhou's commutativity explanation, while the discussion of Singh and Jaggi's relationship to WM is revised.

T1.justification: v4 adds an explicit thresholded-R definition and bound in Appendix B, formal commutativity analysis in Appendix E, and local derivation corrections. The principal Taylor and SVD results remain. Theorem 4.2 and its proof largely reproduce v3's Appendix E.1 and Equation (13), rather than constitute a new central theorem.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens testing of the proposed explanation: AM examines extension beyond WM, sensitivity studies probe its conditions, and ImageNet documents failure despite strong alignment. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh removal of the width-dependent post-merge analysis and explicit limitations paragraph, although unexplained alignment-score revisions and the retained run-count inconsistency still limit precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WM/LMC research, with matching authors, experiments, and mathematical results despite retitling and reorganization. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and adds activation-matching results, hyperparameter and threshold analyses, and ResNet50 experiments on ImageNet.

before.justification: v3 reports original model-merging experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR10, including loss barriers, singular-vector alignment, and model-width analyses.

results.title: Analysis of Linear Mode Connectivity via Permutation-Based Weight Matching: With Insights into Other Permutation Search Methods

C1.justification: The central contribution remains sample-based generative-model assessment without fitting auxiliary models. v2 narrows headline scalability to moderately high-dimensional data and frames the abstract's test around multinomial bin-count equality. Its introduction adds upper-bound language and qualifies general applicability by requiring a definable metric.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds substantive limitations concerning small samples, extreme region counts, unsuitable tessellations, correlated model outputs, and distance metrics. Appendices G and I explain scaling blind spots of cosine/correlation distances, dependence between retessellations, and permutation-testing tradeoffs. These materially qualify the earlier broad applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future implementation release; v2 supplies a repository link. v2 newly documents MCMC subsampling, tabular encoding, sequence distances, simulation settings, astrophysical sample allocations, and A100 runtime information. Hyperparameter documentation is revised, although v1's explicit VAE batch size of 512 is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds FFHQ256, ImageNet, Adult Census, Probes, SKIRT TNG, JWST detector images, and ESM Metagenomic Atlas sequences. Coverage also expands to class-omission, small-mode, corruption, scaling, and rotation scenarios. The original Gaussian-mixture mode-dropping and time-series experiments remain in Appendix F.

E2.justification: Appendix H adds weighted and unweighted Schilling nearest-neighbor tests as direct statistical comparators. Figure 8 adds C_T and authenticity-score comparisons to the memorization experiment, although those metrics already appeared in v1's human-judgment comparison. Wasserstein, MMD, and JSD comparisons remain; FLS and FLD refer to the same cited Jiralerspong et al. method.

E3.justification: The Gaussian-mixture null evaluation expands from a stated sample size of 5,000 to a 128–16,384 sample-size sweep. New experiments introduce controlled class removal, noise corruption, geometric perturbations, and a 50-samples-per-distribution comparison. The reported VAE learning-rate decay changes from 0.1 to a factor of 0.9 every 50 steps; whether existing training curves were regenerated is unspecified.

E4.justification: v2 adds MNIST class-dropping, small CIFAR-10 mode detection, ImageNet corruption, distance-metric sensitivity, permutation calibration, and qualitative failure analyses. These test sensitivity and validity beyond v1's analyses. The CIFAR-10 hyperparameter ablation is retained, while the Bayesian translated-distribution validation is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix I introduces permutation-based p-values for the mean over dependent retessellations, substantially extending statistical calibration. v2 also reports 2^14 null-test repetitions, replacing v1's inconsistent statements of 200 in the text and 500 in the caption. Existing reporting of standard deviations over 20 tessellations remains in several comparisons.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the CIFAR-10 ablation table retain their numerical results. Substantial new results include FFHQ evaluations, missing-mode tests, astrophysical comparisons, and permutation tests. For example, v2 Table 2 reports ImageNet PQMass values increasing from 95.55 to 4495.07 across noise variances 0 to 1. The Bayesian likelihood curve is removed.

M1.justification: v1 Algorithm 1 selects reference points from one sample set and includes them in the counts. v2 Section 2.2 selects references from both sets and removes them before counting. v2 also changes the main p-value calculation to the upper tail, removes the Bayesian variant, and introduces optional permutation calibration in Appendix I.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten. Separate theory and algorithm sections become Theory and Methods; image experiments are consolidated, and time-series and Gaussian-mixture analyses move to Appendix F. A dedicated limitations section and reorganized appendices substantially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensively resized and repositioned displays. Figure 2 becomes a sample-size comparison; the human-judgment figure gains an FFHQ row, and the memorization figure expands from two to four panels. Numerous new plots and tables accompany the added analyses, while the Bayesian figure disappears.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around scientific inverse problems, simulation-based inference, privacy, and synthetic-content detection. It adds Voronoi-theory references, Schilling's two-sample tests, and literature supporting the new application domains. Several Bayesian-integration and alternative-sampling references disappear; publication updates to retained works are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: v2 introduces quantized-measure definitions and two consistency propositions with proofs under explicit smoothness and support assumptions in Section 2.3. It removes the Bayesian likelihood and posterior-predictive derivations. The main p-value integral changes substantively from the lower tail in v1 Equation 12 to the upper tail in v2 Equation 5.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validity gaps by separating reference selection from counted samples, correcting the main p-value tail, and providing permutation calibration for dependent retessellations. New stress tests and explicit limitations make sensitivity and applicability substantially easier to assess, while the repository link improves reproducibility information. The Bayesian branch is lost, and both versions still overinterpret p-values as probabilities of hypotheses, but the calibration and validation gains support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PQMass and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Inspection of all 14 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2 supports comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on image corruption, missing classes, tabular data, astrophysical images, protein sequences, distance metrics, and permutation calibration.

before.justification: v1 reports original null tests, sampling-method evaluations, mode-dropping and time-series experiments, MNIST training measurements, CIFAR-10 assessments, and a Bayesian experiment.

results.title: PQMass: Probabilistic Assessment of the Quality of Generative Models using Probability Mass Estimation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: clustering and risk minimization improve distilled-data generalization and subgroup robustness, with theoretical and empirical support. The emphasized Double-DRO terminology describes nesting already present in v2's analysis. The first-work positioning is also retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations connecting excessive clustering and small batches to insufficient samples for CVaR optimization, discusses initialization insensitivity, and acknowledges additional computation. It also interprets transfer and domain-generalization results as broader applicability evidence. These refine practical boundaries and interpretations while retaining the original account of group coverage and robustness.

D1.justification: Appendices G–H newly disclose dataset statistics, RGB-space KMeans evaluation with ten groups, hardware, baseline-specific details, and distillation schedules, including network-training sample budgets and image-update counts. Earlier architectural and default hyperparameter information is retained after relocation. v2's direct code link disappears; v3 instead states that code accompanies supplementary material, whose availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: v3 adds MetaShift, ImageNetBG, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-50-to-CUB-200 transfer. It also introduces unseen-class retrieval from ImageNet-10 to the existing ImageNet-A/B subsets, changing task requirements beyond their original within-subset classification evaluations. The original SVHN, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-subset coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates IDM in Table 5 and DREAM and PDD in Table 8, each with and without the proposed robust optimization. Table 12 additionally compares MMD, RSC, and HYPO as training pipelines combined with GLaD and its robust variant. The original Random, DSA, DM, KIP, IDC, and GLaD comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50-IPC subpopulation-shift evaluations, downstream fine-tuning, and nearest-neighbor retrieval on unseen classes with the query excluded from candidates. Appendix D adds controlled cluster-count, batch-size, and initialization comparisons. Original settings such as alpha=0.8 and batch size 256 are retained; the additional implementation disclosure does not establish changes to those experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained CVaR-component ablation, alpha sensitivity, cross-architecture tests, and visualizations, v3 tests sensitivity to cluster count, mini-batch size, and initialization in Tables 9–11. It adds transfer and subpopulation robustness tests, compatibility with domain-generalization pipelines, and an efficiency analysis reporting the additional optimization cost.

E5.justification: Uncertainty reporting expands substantially. v2 provides ± values mainly for robust-method results in its standard-accuracy table; v3 also supplies them for baseline results and the retained robustness, cross-architecture, ablation, and ImageNet-subset comparisons. Five-run averaging was already stated in v2 and is specified for several new v3 tables. The PDFs do not establish increased run counts for retained results.

E6.justification: The matched original tables retain their central accuracy values, while v3 adds substantial new results. Table 3 reports GLaD/GLaD-robust worst-group accuracies of 51.3/57.0 on MetaShift and 32.2/38.6 on ImageNetBG; Table 6 reports 49.2/54.6 on CUB-200 transfer. Additional method, sensitivity, and timing outcomes also appear. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance gains over v2 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The proposed formulation is substantively generalized. v2 Algorithms 1–2 define L(S) through the optimized cluster-CVaR objective and update synthetic data using Gaussian zero-order estimates. v3 Algorithm 1 alternates robust network optimization with synthetic-data optimization under a plug-in matching objective. The clustering/CVaR criterion remains, and the original zero-order update survives as an optional procedure in Appendix B. This does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The introduction and algorithm exposition are extensively rewritten. Analysis becomes a separate main section; related work and implementation details move to appendices; robustness results precede standard accuracy; and the existing additional ImageNet results move to Appendix D. New appendix organization and a reproducibility statement substantially reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: The main document changes from two columns to one, with extensive table and figure rearrangement. Original Tables 3 and 4 become paired panels in v3 Table 4, and the ImageNet-subset table moves to Table 13. Numerous new tables are added. Existing sample visualizations are retained and relocated, while the alpha plot is reformatted without changing its reported trend.

R1.justification: v3 broadens the cited research context to subpopulation shift, transferability, and domain generalization through works supporting the new evaluations. It also adds dataset-parameterization and recent adversarial-distillation literature, plus Nash and Morse-Saard references for the convergence argument. The original DD/DRO positioning and first-subgroup-DRO claim remain, but the supporting literature coverage expands substantially.

T1.justification: v3 strengthens Assumption 3.1 with a positive lower bound on subgroup probability and adds Theorem 3.3 asserting fixed-point convergence under Morse-Saard and compact-solution-set conditions, supported by a brief cooperative-game argument. v2 explicitly excluded training convergence guarantees. The existing large-deviation proposition and its appendix proof remain substantially unchanged after renumbering.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central robustness claim by adding subpopulation-shift benchmarks beyond v2's clustered and corrupted test sets. Sensitivity, initialization, transfer, and timing analyses address important validation gaps, while expanded uncertainty reporting and implementation details improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the less explicit code access and weaknesses in the newly asserted convergence theorem, which lacks a developed proof and refers to Algorithm 2 despite the surrounding discussion of Algorithm 1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset-distillation work and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Relocated material, including the zero-order algorithm and ImageNet-subset results, can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds subpopulation-shift evaluations, transfer experiments, additional method comparisons, and sensitivity analyses in Section 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 Section 4 reports original distillation experiments, robustness evaluations, cross-architecture comparisons, ablations, and parameter analyses.

results.title: Group Distributionally Robust Dataset Distillation with Risk Minimization

C1.justification: The central efficiency, information-utilisation and oversmoothing claims remain. v4 additionally presents the unified aggregation framework as a distinct contribution, explicitly claims the first decoupling of structural processing from model learning, and replaces the Cora-CA headline example with a large-scale Trivago claim.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations attributing performance to fewer trainable parameters and reduced overfitting, and attributes SIGN's disadvantage to its classifier's feature-merging burden. It adds explicit hyperedge-node importance learning as future work. Existing oversmoothing and heterophily interpretations, and the lack of hypergraph-level evaluation, remain.

D1.justification: Appendices I, K and L supply dataset descriptions, negative-sampling construction and per-dataset model depths, widths, learning rates, alpha and regularisation settings missing from the supplied v2. The text changes promised code release to claimed code/data availability at the TF-HNN address. These improve documentation without establishing changed implementation; settings for Trivago and several added comparisons remain incomplete.

E1.justification: v4 adds Trivago, an accommodation/browsing-session hypergraph with 172,738 nodes, for classification and hyperlink prediction. Appendix J also extends hyperlink prediction from Cora-CA, Citeseer and House to DBLP-CA, Congress and Senate. The original classification datasets remain.

E2.justification: v4 evaluates SGC and SIGN with clique expansion in Table 6 and adds HyperGCL and HDSode classification comparisons in Appendix J. The MLP-only comparator from v2 Table 5 disappears. The original nine classification HNNs and four hyperlink-prediction HNNs remain; the EDGNN figure label becomes ED-HNN.

E3.justification: v4 adds controlled experiments replacing only the message-passing module with SGC or SIGN while keeping other components fixed. Its new Trivago evaluation reports 64-layer Deep-HGNN for classification and two layers for hyperlink prediction. Existing splits, accuracy/AUC metrics and the 5:1 negative-to-positive ratio remain unchanged; appendix settings are disclosures rather than established revisions.

E4.justification: The new module-replacement study tests the proposed propagation against training-free graph alternatives across four datasets. Conversely, v2's MLP-only ablation testing the benefit of structural propagation is removed. The depth/alpha sensitivity analysis and weighted-versus-unweighted comparison remain, although v4 reverses the latter's row labels.

E5.justification: v4 newly specifies five runs for hyperlink prediction and reports numerical uncertainty for absolute training times in Tables 4–5, 10 and 12. Ten classification runs and existing score uncertainty are retained. The five-run statement is new disclosure, not evidence of increased repetitions; neither PDF clearly defines the meaning of all ± values.

E6.justification: The original six-dataset classification scores are identical, but v4 adds substantial results for new benchmarks and comparators. Trivago classification reports 94.03% for TF-HNN versus 84.06% for Deep-HGNN, with training times of 38.09 versus 3352.35 seconds. Appendix J adds hyperlink results, including ED-HNN outperforming TF-HNN on Senate. MLP-only and CE-homophily entries disappear. Table 7 assigns retained ablation scores to opposite weighted/unweighted labels, contradicting its discussion.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains parameter removal and linearisation followed by precomputed propagation using the same hyperedge-size weighting, symmetric normalisation, self-loops and residual mixture. v2's SHNN becomes the TF-MP-Module within TF-HNN; the task-specific training pipeline is unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes from Simplifying Hypergraph Neural Networks to Training-Free Message Passing for Learning on Hypergraphs. Abstract, introduction and methodological framing are extensively rewritten around MP-Modules and TF-HNN. A method overview is added, discussions are reorganised, and named appendix sections replace unsupported generic appendix references.

P2.justification: v4 changes the document from two columns to one, redraws Figure 1, merges method formulas and complexity comparisons into Table 1, and transposes the dataset table while dropping homophily/task fields. It adds experimental and hyperparameter tables and restructures the component ablations. Figures 2–4 largely retain their plotted content with revised sizing and labels.

R1.justification: v4 expands positioning through a four-mechanism HNN taxonomy, graph-filter applicability restrictions and optimisation connections, adding references such as Kim et al. (2024), Ortega et al. (2018) and Yang et al. (2021). It strengthens the first-decoupling novelty claim and develops comparisons with training-free graph methods.
