The earlier SIGN/SGC inspiration and distinction from inference-focused hypergraph methods remain.

T1.justification: Relative to v2's available statements and proof sketches, v4 supplies extensive formal material in Appendices B–H and M: mechanism-specific derivations, propagation-support proofs, explicit weighting assumptions, entropy arguments and the limiting optimisation derivation. Most main mathematical results are retained or reformulated; Proposition 3.3 adds an explicit i != j restriction. This establishes expanded documented support, not that every argument was newly developed.

improvement.justification: The direct SGC/SIGN comparisons and large-scale Trivago experiments address important gaps in evidence for the method's distinctiveness and efficiency. Supplied proofs and reproduction settings substantially improve inspectability over the available v2. These gains outweigh the removed MLP control, incomplete settings for new experiments and Table 7's reversed labels, although those defects weaken reproducibility and the component analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching core equations and experiments despite renaming. The supplied pages are readable, but v2 refers to appendices absent from its PDF, whereas v4 includes Appendices A–M. Earlier supplementary proofs and settings therefore cannot be compared directly.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and reports additional Trivago results, training-free module comparisons and supplementary benchmark results in Tables 4–6 and Appendix J.

before.justification: v2 reports original SHNN classification results, hyperlink-prediction experiments and ablations in Table 4, Figures 3–4 and Table 5, even though some baseline classification scores are borrowed.

results.title: Training-Free Message Passing for Learning on Hypergraphs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: training-free hypergraph message passing, a unifying framework, training efficiency, information utilisation, and resistance to oversmoothing. The headline Trivago claim is unchanged. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v5 explicitly qualifies Proposition 4.1's entropy as conceptual in Section 4 and Appendix U. Appendices N and R add explanations involving information loss during learned feature projection and memory-constrained latent dimensions. Appendix Q explains zero-degree applicability, and Appendix S interprets hyperparameter interactions. The future-work discussion replaces explicit hyperedge-node importance learning with automated hyperparameter search.

D1.justification: v4 provides selected final hyperparameters but little tuning documentation. v5 adds Trivago configurations to Tables 13–14, extensive model-specific search ranges, validation-based checkpoint and hyperparameter selection, memory restrictions, and the eight-RTX-3090 setup for search timing. It also documents zero-degree handling and changes the code-access disclosure from an anonymous address to a GitHub link.

E1.justification: Appendix P and Table 18 add node classification on the Yelp hypergraph. The seven original hypergraphs and both existing tasks remain. This extends the evaluated data by one benchmark without introducing a new task; the added sensitivity and timing experiments use retained datasets.

E2.justification: Tables 15–16 newly compare against APPNP with the clique expansion from Equation (5) on Cora-CA and Citeseer. Table 17 also evaluates parameter-free variants of four existing baselines. The original HNN, SGC/SIGN, and appendix HyperGCL/HDSode comparisons are retained; those appendix baselines are not new additions.

E3.justification: v5 adds procedures measuring complete grid-search runtime and preprocessing separately, plus paired validation/test evaluations across hyperparameter combinations. The retained experiments keep their 50%/25%/25% splits, accuracy/AUC metrics, and negative-sampling settings. Newly documented search ranges and final configurations do not establish changes to the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix O tests removing only learnable parameters from four baselines on Cora-CA and Citeseer, isolating a design step not separately tested in v4. Appendix S adds extensive pairwise hyperparameter sensitivity analysis on DBLP-CA, beyond the retained depth/alpha analysis. Appendices S and V additionally investigate tuning cost and preprocessing overhead, substantially broadening the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten node-classification runs and five hyperlink-prediction runs and retain the same plus/minus uncertainty reporting. The additional results introduce no explicit changes to run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimation, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

E6.justification: Tables 15–21 and Figure 5 add substantial comparison, ablation, sensitivity, and timing results. For example, TF-HNN achieves 36.06 ± 0.32% accuracy on Yelp with 6.54 ± 0.96 seconds training time. Original benchmark scores are retained. Table 7 swaps the condition labels: v5 assigns average accuracy 77.02 to weighted S and 76.02 to unweighted S, reversing v4's attribution and aligning the table with the discussion.

M1.justification: The TF-HNN procedure remains unchanged: fixed linear message passing with the weighted clique-expansion operator is precomputed before training the task-specific module. Equations (1) and (4)–(6) retain the same operations. New explanations and baseline ablations do not establish a modification to TF-HNN.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative and existing appendices remain recognizable. v5 makes local paragraph edits, replaces 'model learning' with 'model training,' expands introductory explanations and cross-references, and adds acknowledgements and equal-contribution information. The substantial appendix additions mainly document new evidence and discussion rather than extensively reorganizing existing prose.

P2.justification: v5 adds seven tables and Figure 5, which presents 15 pairs of validation/test heatmaps. Tables 13–14 gain Trivago rows, and Table 7's condition labels are corrected. Existing figures and tables are retained with caption shortening, resizing, and reflow. The new comparative and diagnostic displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 3.1 and the new Appendix N substantially expand positioning against APPNP, explaining its relationship to GCN/PageRank and distinguishing training-time propagation from TF-HNN preprocessing. Additional references support the new discussions of entropy, tuning, datasets, and hypergraph applications; Eswaran et al. (2020) is removed. The principal change is the detailed treatment of closely related methodology.

T1.justification: Appendix T adds Lemmas T.1–T.2 and proofs connecting the clique-expansion operators, including their dependence on hyperedge size. Section 2 drops the prohibition on duplicate hyperedges, and Appendix V adds an O(m) preprocessing-complexity statement. The central propositions and earlier derivations remain largely unchanged, with several proof cross-references corrected.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens reproducibility and support for the efficiency claim by documenting search spaces and selection rules and measuring previously unreported tuning and preprocessing costs. The APPNP comparison, parameter-removal controls, sensitivity analyses, and Table 7 correction also address important evidential gaps. These gains outweigh remaining theoretical problems: the conceptual entropy qualification does not fully reconcile the formal equality claim, and the new UniGNN derivation in Lemma T.2 contains a normalization inconsistency with Appendix D.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TF-HNN research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across pagination changes.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and adds APPNP comparisons, Yelp evaluation, parameter-removal experiments, sensitivity analyses, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v4 reports original TF-HNN node-classification and hyperlink-prediction results, training times, and ablations in Section 6 and Appendix J.

results.title: Training-Free Message Passing for Learning on Hypergraphs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate modality-sequential training and adaptive stopping into central contributions alongside fusion. Claimed empirical scope expands to seven tasks, including touch and thermal reasoning. The efficiency claim changes from approximately 96% fewer trainable parameters to over 90%, with the stated per-modality requirement changing from under 5M to 4–10M.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds substantive explanations involving incompatible modality representations, dominant-modality convergence, and the benefits of sequential optimization. It also attributes weak alternative fusion results to architectural changes and limited downstream data. Appendix C newly identifies limited temporal modeling from image-only pre-training and overhead from computing additional modalities as specific limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds dataset-construction descriptions, split sizes, and additional modality settings; Table 11 extends prompts to four new tasks, and the license section adds their sources. Most encoder, hardware, and pre-training details remain unchanged. v2 drops the explicit cross-entropy-loss statement and OneLLM reimplementation description, and does not specify a numerical early-exit threshold.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from three benchmarks to seven. v2 adds TouchQA material recognition from Touch&Go, ThermalQA past-action recognition from Thermal-IM, PerceptionTest multiple-choice QA, and VGGSound classification reformulated as QA. These extend the represented sensory domains and task requirements. Existing benchmarks and appendix-documented pre-training sources remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds Mirasol3B to the NExT-QA comparison, CMC to TouchQA/ThermalQA, and CAV-MAE plus Mirasol3B variants to VGGSound. It removes the 13B and 33B LLaMA-VQA entries from NExT-QA while retaining the 7B variant. OneLLM and X-BLIP zero-shot comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates expanded modality configurations, including V/P/D/N on SQA3D and V/A/F/D/N on MUSIC-AVQA. New protocols include reduced-epoch controls for adaptive stopping, a fixed-batch single-GPU memory comparison, and VGGSound accuracy both before and after excluding out-of-vocabulary predictions. These substantially extend evaluation design; retained benchmarks keep their stated evaluation splits.

E4.justification: v2 adds adaptive-exit convergence and training-budget analyses (Table 6 and Figure 2), joint-versus-sequential training ablations (Table 16), and a training-memory comparison (Table 14). Fusion and easy/hard analyses are revised. Pre-training and LoRA-rank ablations remain, and the qualitative examples are retained and regrouped rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests for its experimental results. Both primarily report point estimates; parenthesized improvements are score differences rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Many results are added or replaced. For NExT-QA, the original fused variant reports 73.0 accuracy and 1.46K GFLOPs, whereas the revised method reports 73.9 and 2.47K. New SQA3D and MUSIC-AVQA configurations report 54.6 and 81.7, respectively, under expanded modality inputs. Four added benchmarks and new training analyses supply further results. Baseline parameter counts also change, including BLIP-2 from 188M to 108M for one modality; zero-shot and rank/pre-training results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Equation 3 changes fusion from element-wise addition of video and gated supporting features to concatenation. Section 3.3 introduces modality-sequential updates within each minibatch and gradient-based adaptive early exit. These substantially change fusion and optimization, while retaining the frozen backbone and modality-specific adapters.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, integrates the separately named Espresso variant into the CREMA narrative, rewrites Section 3.3 around modular training, and reorganizes quantitative analysis around research questions. Qualitative analysis and broader impacts move into the appendix, while experimental discussions and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: The document changes from a predominantly two-column to a single-column layout. The introductory comparison schematic is removed, the architecture diagram is redrawn with additional modalities and training information, and an early-exit plot is added. Tables are added and reorganized, while the same eight qualitative examples are regrouped into appendix figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new datasets and comparators, alongside works such as VAST, ViT-Lens, and SOK-Bench. Sections 3.3 and B.4 newly acknowledge alternating adaptation and distinguish CREMA from MLA's shared classifier and gradient projection. The broader positioning against existing multimodal LLMs remains largely intact.

T1.justification: Equation 3 revises the mathematical definition of fused queries. Sections 3.3 and 4.3 introduce a gradient-threshold stopping rule and an early-stop indicator. Existing LoRA equations remain, and neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs; the mathematical changes are limited algorithmic definitions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for CREMA's central generality and practical-efficiency claims through touch/thermal evaluations, controlled sequential-training and early-exit analyses, and a matched-batch memory comparison (Tables 4, 6, 14, and 16). Specific temporal-modeling and preprocessing-cost limitations also improve qualification of those claims. Removed larger LLaMA-VQA comparisons, an unspecified stopping threshold, and unclear SQA3D configuration matching in Table 7 weaken parts of the presentation, but the added controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement beyond higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CREMA by the same authors, with substantial shared methods and experiments. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support a reliable comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional task evaluations, sequential-training and early-exit ablations, and training-memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning and zero-shot experiments on SQA3D, MUSIC-AVQA, and NExT-QA, together with fusion, modality, pre-training, and LoRA-rank analyses.

results.title: CREMA: Generalizable and Efficient Video-Language Reasoning via Multimodal Modular Fusion

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on running uncompressed Mixtral on 24GB GPUs with large single-batch gains over offloading systems. V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the central claim to adaptive heterogeneous execution outperforming specialized competitors across ordinary generation, long prefills, and beam search.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of the complementary strengths of CPU-based and offloading baselines, and interprets Appendix D/E results as evidence of distribution robustness and applicability beyond Mixtral. The underlying communication/computation explanation, compression compatibility, and assumption that non-expert weights fit on the GPU remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds baseline version numbers, llama.cpp ngl settings, specific CPU models, initialization-time latency profiling, and disclosure of an AVX512_BF16 expert kernel. V1's explicit non-persistent DeepSpeed pipeline statement disappears. These are bounded changes in implementation and reproducibility documentation; the PyTorch basis and code-access URL remain.

E1.justification: V2 extends short-input ShareGPT generation evaluation to long-context prefilling and beam-search generation, introducing substantially different workload requirements. Appendix D also adds LMSYS-Chat-1M as a second conversation corpus.

E2.justification: V2 adds llama.cpp to the main comparison alongside the retained DeepSpeed-MII and Mixtral-Offloading, plotted as Eliseev & Mazur. This introduces an important CPU-based competitor missing from v1's offloading-only comparisons. Llama.cpp also supplies the beam-search comparison.

E3.justification: Environment 2 changes from L4 with a 32-core CPU to RTX 6000 Ada with a 112-core CPU, with revised expert residency and offloading settings. V2 changes sequence-length configurations and adds TTFT/ITL measurements, beam widths 4-16, and Phi-3.5-MoE evaluation. Its exact main length grid is inconsistent: Section 4.1 specifies four input and four output lengths, while Figure 4 plots five input and three output lengths.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds an input-distribution sensitivity study comparing conversation datasets, and Appendix F separates prefill and decoding latency through TTFT/ITL breakdowns. These substantially broaden the diagnostic evidence. The sparsity and expert-popularity analyses are retained, while microbenchmarks and hardware-dependent popularity calculations are revised.

E5.justification: V1 specifies averaging 10 runs for Fiddler and three for baselines; v2 omits these end-to-end repetition counts. Both retain 32 microbenchmark executions with means and standard deviations. This is a limited loss of statistical reporting, without evidence that the actual repetition counts decreased.

E6.justification: V1 reports 8.2x/10.1x speedups over Mixtral-Offloading in its two environments. V2 reports 1.26x over llama.cpp across revised environments, 11.57x for beam search, and 6.5x over DeepSpeed-MII for Phi-3.5-MoE, alongside new sensitivity and latency-breakdown results. These are new or replaced comparisons, not matched-setting performance changes. Microbenchmark and Environment 2 hit-rate results also change; Table 2's sparsity values remain identical.

M1.justification: The reported scheduling rule changes substantially. V1 Section 3.2 jointly partitions experts to minimize the maximum aggregate CPU/GPU latency; v2 Algorithm 1 independently assigns each uncached expert by comparing CPU latency against GPU computation plus weight-transfer latency. Popularity-based initial placement already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, design explanation, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Design is reorganized into overview, execution strategies, algorithm, and optimizations, with explicit contribution bullets. The original sparsity and microbenchmark appendices exchange order, and new appendices D-F are added.

P2.justification: V2 adds high-level and initialization/execution diagrams, redraws v1 Figure 1 as a three-case execution diagram, and introduces an algorithm display plus multiple benchmark and diagnostic panels. Existing plots are also redesigned. The sparsity table and popularity heatmap are retained. Several v2 plot legends inconsistently call the proposed system Twiddler while captions use Fiddler.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning by acknowledging CPU-based hybrid inference, particularly llama.cpp, and distinguishing Fiddler through adaptive execution rather than CPU computation alone. Related work and motivation expand to newer MoE models, heterogeneous deployment, long-context applications, and additional inference systems.

T1.justification: V1's central min-max optimization over disjoint CPU/GPU expert sets, justified by parallel completion time, is removed. V2 substitutes an expert-wise latency inequality with separate GPU computation and transfer costs. This substantively changes the formal scheduling model, while retaining the linear-CPU and constant-GPU latency assumptions. Neither version provides an optimality proof.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's evaluation: it adds the stronger CPU-based llama.cpp comparator and tests workloads that expose different execution tradeoffs. Dataset sensitivity, a second MoE model, and latency breakdowns substantially strengthen evidence for applicability and performance. Omitted end-to-end run counts and setup/plot inconsistencies weaken reproducibility and clarity, but the broader, more relevant comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fiddler and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and reorganization, supporting comparison despite the substantial revision.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original generation, long-prefill, and beam-search benchmarks. The appendices additionally report dataset sensitivity, Phi-3.5-MoE performance, and latency breakdowns.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original Mixtral inference benchmarks. Appendices A-C report activation sparsity, CPU/GPU microbenchmarks, and expert-selection measurements.

results.title: Fiddler: CPU-GPU Orchestration for Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Models

C1.justification: v1 presents a general program for zero-shot ODE-system inference, with imputation as an application. v2 makes zero-shot imputation of hidden ODE solutions the central contribution, explicitly separating point-wise and temporal missingness, and adds phase-portrait reconstruction from one observed coordinate as a headline capability. Arbitrary-dimensional application without downstream fine-tuning remains a core claim.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanation of applicability and failure. It distinguishes local interpolation from global information needed across temporal gaps, explains normalization problems for nearly constant noisy signals, and identifies sparse-coordinate failures of channel independence using PhysioNet. It also discusses window-resolution tradeoffs, rapid-derivative failures and errors introduced by PCA. v1's limitations mainly concerned high-frequency dynamics and its approximately 32-point context requirement.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents normalization and output rescaling, detailed temporal-module architecture and optimization, dataset masks and preprocessing, and LatentODE search grids, training schedules and runtimes. It also reports high-dimensional inference costs and describes a reproduction script. The availability statement changes from pretrained models being online in v1 to forthcoming online availability in v2, although supplementary code and weights are still asserted.

E1.justification: v2 adds air-quality, traffic, solar-power, electricity and healthcare evaluations, including PhysioNet2012 and PhysioNet2019 in Appendix F. It also adds single-coordinate phase-portrait reconstruction and four synthetic regression tasks. ODEBench, Lorenz, motion capture and Navier-Stokes remain; the separate ETTh2, ETTm1 and ETTm2 interpolation demonstrations from v1 disappear.

E2.justification: Reported comparisons expand substantially to include Neural ODE Processes, BRITS, SAITS, GP-VAE, CSDI, BayOTIDE and numerous additional imputation methods. Cubic splines join the retained Lorenz comparison, while motion-capture comparisons include LatentODE, npODE, GPDM and VGPLVM. ODEFormer, ODEFormer-opt and PySR remain in v2 Table 9; their move out of the main comparison is not removal.

E3.justification: The default local-model training dataset changes from 8M to 2M trajectories, with revised sampling distributions and a separate temporal-gap training dataset. Evaluation adds window sweeps and derivative scoring. Lorenz corruption is described as additive rather than v1's multiplicative noise. Motion capture and Navier-Stokes expand from single examples to 43 and 61 trajectories, with PCA and direct-space evaluation. v2 inconsistently states minimum contexts of four and eight observations.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled studies of parameter count, training-set size, BiLSTM versus transformer encoding, context limits, temporal-gap sizes and training trends (Tables 4-8). It also studies window-count sensitivity, including the Lorenz sweep in Figure 8, and PCA versus direct-space imputation. v1's explicit FIM denoising comparison with and without Savitzky-Golay filtering is not retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report ODEBench variation across ten corruption realizations and trajectory-level standard deviations. v2 additionally displays predictive derivative uncertainty in Figure 3 and identifies imported TSI-Bench baseline deviations as coming from five training rounds (Tables 21-22). These extend uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repeated FIM training runs.

E6.justification: Existing scores are replaced and substantial new results appear. At 50% subsampling and noise 0.05, v1 Table 1 reports R2 accuracy of 80.2 ± 1.7 for FIM and 79.6 ± 1.5 for FIM-N; v2 Table 9 reports 83.7 ± 0.7 for four-window FIM-ℓ and 91.6 ± 1.9 for sixteen windows. These involve revised configurations, not controlled version-to-version gains. New results include derivative errors, quantitative imputation comparisons and clinical-data failures.

M1.justification: v2 adds a learned temporal-gap imputation module above the frozen local estimator FIM-ℓ: a transformer processes local embeddings and scale statistics to predict the missing interval's representation, followed by boundary-conditioned integration (Section 3.2.2; Appendix C). This substantially extends v1's upsampling and window-composition approach. The stated local reconstruction objective also changes from squared to absolute error.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method narrative are extensively rewritten around imputation. Experiments are reorganized into phase-portrait reconstruction and two missingness categories; limitations are integrated into the conclusion, and a reproducibility statement is added. The appendices are substantially reorganized into model-specific documentation and task-specific evaluations, beyond simply appending new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. v2 introduces a graphical-model/architecture schematic, phase portraits, derivative-uncertainty panels and a window-sensitivity plot. Lorenz plots are redesigned to include derivatives, and tables become extensive window/dimension breakdowns and benchmark matrices, including landscape appendix tables. v1's ETT panels and Navier-Stokes image demonstration are removed.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from ODE identification and analogies with language models toward amortized inference and time-series imputation. v2 adds discussion and citations for Stuhlmüller, Paige and Wood, zero-shot learning, channel-independent modeling, and major imputation families and benchmarks. Much of v1's neural-ODE training and transfer-learning discussion is removed. ODEFormer's preprint-to-publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: The path-wise ODE reduction and overlapping-window interpolation are retained. v2 adds derivations for rescaling derivatives and variances (Appendix B.1) and constructing continuous solutions across a missing interval (Appendix C.6), while removing v1's alternative kernel-operator formulation. These are localized mathematical developments rather than a new theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v1's imputation evidence was largely illustrative. v2 supplies an explicit temporal-gap method, broad quantitative comparisons, controlled ablations, detailed implementation information and concrete failure analyses, substantially strengthening validation and reproducibility. Reporting problems remain: minimum-context specifications conflict, Table 23's Navier-Stokes RMSE contradicts the claimed benefit of avoiding PCA, and Table 22 shows linear interpolation outperforming FIM on some datasets highlighted favorably in Table 2. These qualifications limit particular claims but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FIM research, retaining the synthetic-training framework, local ODE estimator and several benchmarks. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial changes in title, scope and organization.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, derivative-estimation and imputation results, including extensive benchmark comparisons and architecture, training-data and windowing ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original FIM experiments on ODEBench and Lorenz trajectories, alongside motion-capture and Navier-Stokes imputation demonstrations and ETT interpolation.

results.title: Zero-shot Imputation with Foundation Inference Models for Dynamical Systems

C1.justification: V2 adds empirical effectiveness and scenario-specific guidance as central contributions in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. V1 foregrounds the claim that BALD captures only part of epistemic uncertainty; v2 foregrounds a unified family containing BALD and EPKL, while retaining the partial-uncertainty argument in Appendix C.

C2.justification: V2 connects weak excess-risk performance on hard-OOD inputs to possible failure of the conditional-distribution approximation. It adds recommendations about matching training and uncertainty scores, choosing risks for noisy misclassification, and avoiding universal approximation rankings. These interpretations substantially extend v1's retained theoretical limitations (Section 6, Appendices G–J).

D1.justification: Unlike v1, v2 documents experimental implementation: label-swap pairs, ensemble-specific class omissions, Gaussian-blur parameters, architectures, 200 training epochs, SGD with momentum and weight decay, and learning-rate schedules. Appendix F also adds links to two training-code repositories, although some hyperparameter values are deferred to that code.

E1.justification: V1 has no dataset-based evaluation. V2 introduces out-of-distribution and misclassification detection using CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN, blurred and label-corrupted CIFAR variants, and a CIFAR10 scenario with classes omitted from selected ensemble members (Section 6, Appendix E).

E2.justification: V2 introduces empirical comparisons among Bayes-, total- and excess-risk measures. Tables 6–9 explicitly compare BI, RBI and EPBD, whose log-score instances are BALD, RMI and EPKL. V1 discusses these quantities mathematically but evaluates no comparators; the new comparisons are among uncertainty measures within the framework.

E3.justification: V2 adds an AUROC-based evaluation protocol using 20-member ResNet18 and VGG19 ensembles, log/Brier/spherical training losses, and matching versus mismatched uncertainty scoring rules. Main results aggregate approximation choices, while Appendix J separates them and excludes the identically zero excess-risk approximation. V1 contains no empirical protocol.

E4.justification: New analyses examine training/uncertainty-score matching, distribution shifts, label noise, class omissions and inner versus outer approximation strategies. Appendix G additionally excludes Neglog to test whether its instability alone explains the mismatch effect (Figure 7). V1 has no corresponding empirical ablations or robustness analyses.

E5.justification: V2 adds ensemble-member performance distributions (Figures 4–5), AUROC distributions and aggregate mean ± summaries in Appendix J. Those summaries describe variation across datasets or dataset pairs, rather than repeated full-ensemble trials. Seed identifiers, confidence intervals and significance tests are not reported.

E6.justification: V2 adds all empirical results in Tables 2–9 and the experimental plots. For CIFAR10 versus blurred CIFAR10, Table 2 reports excess/Bayes AUROC of 87.80/84.38; for noisy CIFAR100 misclassification, Table 3 reports Bayes/excess AUROC of 82.64/72.30. These are newly reported results, with no corresponding v1 measurements.

M1.justification: V2 extends the Bayesian averaging choices to the predictive argument as well as the unknown distribution, adding posterior-mean predictor options and the zero-excess case (Section 4, Appendix C). The core risk framework, EPBD, reverse-Bregman estimate and risk-difference/BALD quantity already appear in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, Bayesian section and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Risk definitions and proper scoring rules become separate main sections, while much of the existing derivation and approximation discussion moves into Appendices A–D. This materially reorganizes the retained argument as well as accommodating the experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adds AUROC boxplots and histograms, ensemble-performance violin plots, and numerical comparison Tables 2–9. Table 1 receives revised labels and formatting. V1's risk-estimation diagram is retained as Appendix Figure 3, while the original illustrative Figure 1 remains.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted positioning relative to DEUP, Bregman information and bias–variance decomposition work, plus citations covering Bayesian approximations and the new experiments. The existing Bayesian, deterministic and second-order uncertainty taxonomy remains. Publication-metadata updates to retained references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: The core decomposition and score-specific risk derivations are retained, often relocated. V2 corrects the Bregman-divergence sign in v1 Equation (6), adds explicit loss derivations and relations involving the expanded approximation cases, and shifts spherical Bayes/total risks by a constant (Appendices A–D).

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the practical support for the framework. Section 6 and Appendices G–J test previously untested recommendations, reveal different behavior on soft versus hard OOD inputs, and check whether Neglog alone explains scoring-rule mismatch failures. The expanded approximation recipe, corrected mathematics and implementation details improve usability. Statistical reporting and some implementation details remain incomplete, but the direct evidence and clearer applicability boundaries provide substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same risk-based uncertainty framework. All 12 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, figures and tables, support comparison. Relocated derivations and illustrations can be matched.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices E–J report original deep-ensemble experiments for out-of-distribution and misclassification detection, including numerical results in Tables 2–9.

before.justification: V1 contains theoretical derivations and conceptual illustrations, including Appendix A, but no original experimental or data-analysis results.

results.title: From Risk to Uncertainty: Generating Predictive Uncertainty Measures via Bayesian Estimation

C1.justification: The central convergence-and-acceleration contribution remains, but the headline explicit-parameter guarantees expand from bounded-support targets to finite-second-moment targets with early stopping and sharper δ dependence. Acceleration is now advertised under Lipschitz Hessians without the former score-Lipschitz requirement. The introduction drops the separate claim that handling estimation error distinguishes the work from prior acceleration.

C2.justification: New Section 1.2 discusses dimension-versus-accuracy tradeoffs against D-SDE guarantees and explains the different parameterizations. The conclusion changes the remaining challenge from improving δ dependence to improving dimension dependence. V1's detailed practical interpretation contrasting its covariance estimator with the prior accelerated sampler is removed.

D1.justification: Neither version provides code or data access, hardware, measured runtime, or an implemented training configuration. The documented Hessian-matching procedure is retained; revised estimator-error conditions are mathematical assumptions.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or conducts training or evaluation experiments. The revised coverage of distribution classes concerns mathematical guarantees, not empirically tested tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates experimental baselines. V2's additional D-SDE and accelerated-DT comparisons in Table 1 concern cited analytical bounds.

E3.justification: No experimental protocols, splits, training budgets, or evaluation procedures are reported in either version. The noise-schedule formula and KL, total-variation, and Wasserstein distance framework remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Neither PDF reports ablations, empirical robustness tests, or supplementary experimental analyses. The appendix revisions concern mathematical error bounds and proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Score and Hessian estimation-error assumptions are theoretical conditions, not empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The analytical result entries change substantially: Theorems 4 and 8 replace leading KL-bound factors δ^-2 and δ^-3 with log^2(1/δ) and log^3(1/δ), under revised target assumptions. V1's additional linear-in-dimension special-case bound disappears. Gaussian-mixture rates in Theorems 3 and 7 remain unchanged, although v2 Table 1 omits their mixture-component factors. These are analytical changes, not measured performance gains.

M1.justification: The score-based reverse mean, Hessian-corrected Gaussian covariance, Hessian-matching objective, and early-stopping schedule are retained. V1 Section 5.1 matches v2 Sections 5.1–5.2; the changed guarantees do not establish a changed sampling algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around DT and D-SDE terminology. A comparison section is inserted, related work is reorganized, Hessian matching receives its own subsection, and proof exposition is substantially condensed and restructured. The general accelerated corollary moves from the main text to Appendix H.3.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a sampler column, separate D-SDE/regular-DT/accelerated-DT groups, additional rows, and blue highlighting for this paper's results. Author affiliations and some equation layouts also change. The overall single-column format remains, with no figures added.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning through a dedicated DT-versus-D-SDE comparison section and an expanded Table 1. It adds Li et al.'s accelerated diffusion work and newer references on probability-flow ODEs, flow matching, Gaussian-mixture learning, and score estimation. Existing references updated from preprints to publications are retained works, not new additions.

T1.justification: Assumption 4 replaces derivative envelopes and summability requirements with moment conditions at Xt and the reverse mean. Jensen's inequality simplifies Appendices A and G, removes Theorem 1's extra trace term, and eliminates auxiliary mismatch conditions from Theorem 5; Theorem 6 drops score Lipschitzness. New derivative-moment and change-of-measure arguments support the revised early-stopping theorems. Assumption 1 also strengthens the dimension-uniform requirement from a second-moment matrix bound to E||X0||² <= M2. V1's general accelerated Corollary 3 is retained as v2 Corollary 2 in Appendix H.3.

improvement.justification: The revised derivations in Appendices E, F, and H address v1's explicitly unresolved polynomial δ dependence and provide explicit guarantees for unbounded finite-moment targets. The direct Jensen argument also simplifies the central proofs and removes auxiliary conditions. These are substantial theoretical and explanatory gains. Drawbacks include the stronger dimension-uniform moment assumption, removal of the special linear-d bound, and inconsistent summaries: v2's text after Theorem 1 states O(ε^-1) steps despite its T^-1 KL bound, while Table 1 suppresses mixture-component factors. These limit, but do not outweigh, the improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same samplers and theoretical framework, with the same title and authors. The main text, equations, comparison table, and complete Appendices A–I support comparison despite substantial proof revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 likewise contains theoretical guarantees and proof appendices, without original experiments, simulations, or data-analysis results.

before.justification: V1 reports convergence theorems and mathematical proofs. Table 1 compares analytical guarantees; neither the main text nor appendices report original empirical outcomes.

results.title: Broadening Target Distributions for Accelerated Diffusion Models via a Novel Analysis Approach

C1.justification: Both versions identify gradient conflict and mixed BN statistics as central obstacles, propose AR-AT to improve the robustness-accuracy trade-off, and connect these mechanisms to knowledge-distillation defenses. v3 emphasizes understanding and broader empirical support, but these changes do not materially redefine the central scientific claims. The conclusion retains the same claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds a substantive explanation for component interaction: stop-gradient weakens invariance regularization and can exacerbate clean/adversarial feature separation, explaining its dependence on split-BN. Appendix E interprets persistence across batch sizes as evidence of distribution-wide conflict, while Appendix F develops the BN-statistics explanation. The existing limitations concerning layer selection and architectures without BN remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly identifies cross-entropy as the adversarial-example generation loss, adds a single-A100 timing protocol and per-batch resource measurements, and promises code release upon publication. Existing optimizer settings, predictor dimensions, dataset details and baseline implementation links are retained. The attack-loss statement is additional disclosure; SWA-specific implementation settings remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Imagenette for image classification. v3 Appendix B.4 adds L2-bounded adversarial training and evaluation on both CIFAR datasets, extending the threat scenarios beyond the earlier L-infinity setting without adding datasets or application domains.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands the reported comparator set while retaining earlier baselines. Tables 11-12 add NuAT2 and NuAT2+WA on CIFAR-10, TRADES+HF on CIFAR-100, and AT+HF, TRADES+Rand and TRADES+AWP+Rand on both datasets. These entries are explicitly identified as results copied from prior papers, rather than newly reproduced experiments.

E3.justification: The default 100-epoch training schedule, PGD-10 training attacks, PGD-20/AutoAttack evaluation and dataset splits remain unchanged. Additional protocols include training-perturbation sweeps, L2 attacks with epsilon 0.5, batch-size diagnostics spanning 128-1024, and AutoAttack-based component comparisons. The original PGD-20 component table is retained as Table 15. The new L2 comparison uses PreAct ResNet-18 for AT and ResNet-18 for AR-AT.

E4.justification: v3 directly tests mechanisms previously supported more indirectly: Figure 2 isolates the two stop-gradient directions, Figures 3-4 examine feature divergence and predictor stability, Appendix E tests batch-size sensitivity, and Appendix F analyzes feature separation and BN running-statistic stability. Component ablations also extend across both CIFAR datasets and architectures. Earlier layer, loss-weight and component studies remain present.

E5.justification: v2 reports point estimates for benchmark accuracies without repeated-run counts. v3 Table 3 reports means and standard deviations over five runs for LBGAT and AR-AT variants, substantially strengthening uncertainty reporting for the principal comparisons. This establishes newly reported repetition, not an increase from a known earlier run count. Table 19 also introduces timing variability.

E6.justification: Principal estimates change and substantial new results appear. For CIFAR-10/WRN-34-10, v2 reports AR-AT clean/AA accuracy of 90.81/51.19; v3 Table 3 reports five-run means of 90.89/50.77 and adds AR-AT+SWA at 90.06/54.03. New L2, mechanism, comparator and runtime results broaden the findings. Imagenette results and several earlier ablations remain unchanged. Appendix Tables 11-12 are not fully reconciled with Table 3's updated estimates.

M1.justification: The core stop-gradient, predictor, split-BN, automatic loss balancing and multilayer regularization procedures remain unchanged. v3 adds an optional combination with stochastic weight averaging, AR-AT+SWA, in Section 5.2 and Table 3. This is a limited procedural extension rather than a redesign of AR-AT.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around understanding invariance regularization, and Section 5.1 is reorganized into a more detailed component-analysis narrative. Earlier appendices are regrouped into experimental-details and performance-comparison sections, alongside new explanatory appendices. v3 also adds acknowledgments, ethics and reproducibility statements and adopts the ICLR document style.

P2.justification: v3 redraws Figure 2 as a two-panel diagnostic, adds feature-divergence, predictor-stability, trade-off, batch-size and BN-statistics plots, and expands table structures for uncertainty and SWA results. The original component table moves to Appendix B.5, while earlier UMAP, parameter-sharing and Asym-TRADES figures remain. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering and numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting SWA, the trade-off metric and additional defenses: Izmailov et al., Sitawarin et al., Sriramanan et al., Jin et al. (2023), and Li et al. Existing positioning relative to TRADES, MART, knowledge distillation and split-BN remains substantially intact. The author-year citation conversion is a presentation change.

T1.justification: v3 corrects Equation 1 to distinguish the adversarial example x + delta from the optimizing perturbation. Equation 5 adds a factor of one-half to the stop-gradient decomposition. These are local mathematical revisions; the new explanatory appendices do not introduce a substantial theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens previously indirect support for the central mechanisms through isolated-loss, predictor-stability and BN-statistics diagnostics. Five-run uncertainty reporting and broader comparator coverage also make the empirical claims more assessable. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: incomplete SWA implementation details, unreconciled main-text/appendix results, and an architecture mismatch in the new L2 comparison. The improvement rests chiefly on stronger evidence and analysis, rather than higher reported performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AR-AT research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison. Earlier material can be matched despite substantial appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds component diagnostics, repeated-run results, AR-AT+SWA evaluations, L2-bounded experiments and computational-time measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original AR-AT experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Imagenette, including component ablations, representation analyses and hyperparameter studies.

results.title: Rethinking Invariance Regularization in Adversarial Training to Improve Robustness-Accuracy Trade-off

C1.justification: The central dataset, MACM, two-part evaluation, and character-alignment claims remain. v6 adds an explicit novelty claim for Jung-based human-simulation data and standard simulation experiments, and highlights personality-dependent but rigid conformity as a main finding. These extend the contribution claims without replacing the original research proposition.

C2.justification: v6 interprets conformity results as exposing rigid personalities that fail to reproduce changing human responses. Section 6 and Appendix A add substantive discussion of Jung's limited empirical support, omitted nationality/race attributes, target selection, and the cost-constrained dataset size. Conversely, v5's explicit warning that the proposed approach inherits adversarial vulnerabilities is not retained as a comparable limitation.

D1.justification: v6 adds construction pseudocode and scoring weights, attribute-sampling rules, retrieval details, questionnaires, judge rubrics, full prompts, and hardware/cost information (Appendices A, D, F, and G). Its reproducibility statement supplies a code/data access link, replacing v5's future-release promise. These substantially expand documentation; they do not establish changes to the underlying implementation. v5's option-shuffling detail is no longer documented.

E1.justification: The same 11-character Human Simulacra dataset remains, but v6 adds an Asch-style conformity task requiring decisions under group pressure and subsequent interviews (Section 5.2, Appendix E). Table 12 also introduces conflicting multi-turn interactions. These extend evaluation beyond the earlier self-report, observer-report, and isolated dialogue scenarios.

E2.justification: The existing None, Prompt, and RAG comparison methods remain. v6 adds a Human reference row to Table 2 and compares MACM with Character.ai and published human results in the conformity experiment (Figure 7). Character-LLM and Role-LLM appear in a descriptive dataset comparison, not as newly evaluated experimental baselines.

E3.justification: v6 expands the ten-model evaluation to fourteen models by adding three Claude-3 variants and Qwen-turbo. Its new conformity protocol uses 18 trials, including 12 critical trials, across 11 characters, followed by interviews; Table 28 supplies numerical line lengths through text prompts. Component-removal experiments introduce additional controls. Existing evaluation scores are also rescaled from 50 to 100 points.

E4.justification: v6 adds agent-removal and memory-source ablations across three LLMs (Table 4), character-diversity analysis (Appendix A.3), a worked retrieval/reasoning example (Table 10), and a conflicting multi-turn case (Table 12). Appendix E analyzes conformity across models and simulation methods. The earlier Mary Jones dialogue examples largely reappear in Table 11 and are not new analyses.

E5.justification: v6 Table 3 first reports inter-judge intraclass correlations: 0.86 for description matching and 0.95 for response similarity. Both versions retain three repeated self-report tests and majority-selected dialogue examples from three tests. No increase in repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance testing is established.

E6.justification: v6 adds four model rows, previously missing MACM results for Llama-2-70b and Llama-2-70b-Chat (56.00 and 58.66), and ablation, conformity, and dialogue findings. Shared Table 2 scores are equivalent after rescaling and rounding. Some Table 3 entries change beyond rescaling: Prompt's total changes from 34.63/50 to 69.00/100. Figure 12 also exchanges James's and Kevin's reported story lengths relative to v5 Table 1.

M1.justification: The character-generation pipeline, Jung-based personality modeling, and four-agent MACM retain their procedures. v5 Section 4 matches v6 Section 4.3 and Appendix B: memory construction, retrieval, logical/emotional analysis, and response aggregation remain. The new pseudocode and prompts disclose implementation details rather than establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten. MACM moves from a standalone section into the evaluation framework with details in Appendix B; qualitative analysis moves to Appendix C. Dataset-generation subsections are merged, and a substantial Discussion, reproducibility statement, and organized appendices replace the earlier compact structure and standalone limitations/ethics treatment.

P2.justification: v6 changes to a single-column conference layout and substantially redesigns the visual presentation. It combines the earlier information-chain and generation diagrams, expands the evaluation and MACM diagrams, presents character information through cards and charts, and converts the earlier dialogue figure into Table 11. New conformity figures, ablation tables, ICC columns, and extensive appendix displays further change presentation.

R1.justification: v6 substantially expands positioning beyond v5's memory-systems discussion and brief role-playing comparisons. It adds a dedicated role-playing discussion and dataset comparison table, engages work such as Generative Agents and critiques of LLM personality self-assessment, and develops comparisons among personality theories. Asch-related literature also supports the newly introduced psychological application.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly defines inter-character distance as d_total = (d_L1 + 1 - tau)/2, combining normalized attribute distance and personality-ranking similarity. v5 has no equivalent definition. The cognitive-psychology foundations remain, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v6 addresses important weaknesses in v5: missing component-level validation and insufficient detail to reproduce the method and human evaluation. Table 4's ablations, the full prompts and judge rubrics, and agreement statistics substantially strengthen assessability. The conformity study also exposes a concrete behavioral limitation. These gains outweigh remaining problems, including limited comparability with human visual trials and the introductory observer score of 77.75% conflicting with Table 3's 77.50.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Human Simulacra dataset, MACM framework, and psychology-guided evaluation. Their text, tables, figures, and equations support reliable comparison. v5 has no appendix; v6's Appendices A-H are available and readable.

after.justification: v6 retains original self-report and observer evaluations and adds conformity simulations, component ablations, and character-diversity analysis in Section 5 and Appendices A, B, and E.

before.justification: v5 reports original self-report evaluations across LLMs, human-judged observer evaluations, and dialogue case studies in Section 6, Tables 2-3, and Figure 5.

results.title: Human Simulacra: Benchmarking the Personification of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion extend the empirical applicability claim from three search spaces and two tasks to four spaces and three tasks, explicitly including decoder-only language modeling. The central claims of single-search Pareto profiling and zero-shot device transfer remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds discussion of when single-objective constrained optimization is useful, interprets the GPT results as evidence of effectiveness beyond convex Pareto fronts, and introduces environmental implications in Appendix A. These extend the interpretation while retaining the earlier mechanism and scalability explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds GPT predictor architecture, architecture encodings, hardware splits and training configurations; identifies SyneTune as the baseline implementation source; and provides pipeline runtime breakdowns in Table 4. Appendix C adds explicit sampler pseudocode. The original three spaces’ hyperparameter settings and MODNAS code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds autoregressive language modeling on OpenWebText using the GPT-S space from HW-GPT-Bench, evaluating perplexity and energy across eight GPU types. This substantially extends task and hardware coverage beyond the retained image-classification and machine-translation experiments.

E2.justification: v1 primarily evaluates RS, RHPN, HELP and HAT. v2 adds extensive actual comparisons with methods including NSGA-II, qEHVI, MO-ASHA, MO-RE, CMA-ES, LaMOO combinations and scalarization-based Bayesian optimization. HELP also enters the NAS constraint analysis but disappears from the reported HAT comparisons.

E3.justification: v1’s 24-sample random-search comparisons expand into budgeted searches and 50-evaluation NAS-Bench-201 tests. v2 specifies larger HAT baseline budgets, 192-hour OFA baseline searches using an accuracy predictor, and a new GPT evaluation protocol. Frozen OFA weights become the main setting, having been supplementary in v1. HAT runtime statements are not fully reconciled with Table 4.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial search-efficiency and budget-sensitivity analyses through evaluation-count curves and doubled-budget comparisons (Figures 4, 16 and 19). The separate MobileNetV3 0.2-constraint analysis in v1 Figure 21 is absent. Existing sampler, gradient-update and device-count ablations remain, while the frozen-supernetwork variant moves into the main evaluation.

E5.justification: Both versions report means of three independent NAS-Bench-201 searches and already use shaded variability plots. v2 introduces no explicit increase in runs, seed disclosure, new uncertainty definition or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline scores, budget curves and GPT Pareto fronts. Whereas MODNAS led v1’s displayed HAT comparator set, v2 Figure 23 reports Xeon BLEU-based hypervolume of 0.81 for NSGA-II versus 0.80 for MODNAS. Figure 9 newly reports average OFA hypervolume of 0.76 for MODNAS versus 0.74 for LS-BO. These are expanded or revised comparisons, not established same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same four components, preference conditioning, ReinMax sampling and MGD updates. GPT experiments adapt the existing framework to another search space. The frozen-supernetwork option emphasized in v2 already appears in v1 Figure 22.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites and reorganizes the explanation: the main hypernetwork description is simplified, detailed mathematics and sampler descriptions move to appendices, computational complexity becomes Section 4.4, and the appendices are restructured. Introductory and related-work paragraphs are also substantially edited.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive figure and table rearrangement. v2 adds a simplified architecture overview, budget curves, GPT plots and a runtime table, expands comparison legends, and replaces the main OFA radar with aggregate and per-device bar charts. Figure 6 introduces a device-caption mismatch: Eyeriss in the caption versus gold_6226 in the plot.

R1.justification: The dedicated baseline discussion in v2 Appendix D substantially expands positioning against evolutionary and Bayesian multi-objective optimization. New references include LaMOO, qEHVI, MO-ASHA, random-scalarization Bayesian optimization and HW-GPT-Bench. This goes beyond citation-format changes and broadens the comparison with prior research.

T1.justification: The Pareto definitions, bi-level formulation, MGD dual problem, Frank-Wolfe reasoning, objective penalty and normalization are substantively retained. Mathematical material is condensed or relocated; added sampler pseudocode documents existing procedures rather than introducing new theory or proofs.

improvement.justification: The expanded evaluations address v1’s important weakness of relying mainly on random and constrained-search comparators. Direct MOO comparisons and budget-sensitivity tests substantially strengthen the evidence for the central efficiency claim, while the GPT task and additional implementation details broaden its assessment. Removal of the OFA constraint analysis, inconsistent runtime accounting and overly broad HAT superiority wording are drawbacks, but the stronger empirical scrutiny provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MODNAS. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original search experiments and reports expanded baseline comparisons and new GPT-based language-modeling results, including predictor-based evaluations in Appendix J.4.

before.justification: v1 reports original architecture-search experiments on NAS-Bench-201, ImageNet-1k and WMT’14 En-De, including hardware comparisons and ablations.

results.title: Multi-objective Differentiable Neural Architecture Search

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the headline calibration advantage from approximately 10× to 5× on average; the conclusion similarly reduces its stated factor. The central contributions concerning dual-head calibration, confidence-aware selection, initialization, and improved clustering remain.

C2.justification: New discussion explains mini-cluster penalty strength, SSL thresholding failures, initialization-related stability, computational tradeoffs, and applicability to other clustering models and OOD rejection. The explicit v2 limitation that cluster count must be known is removed, although v3 still assumes predefined clusters.

D1.justification: v3 adds a CDC code-access link, identifies the solo-learn library, describes K-means++ initialization and a PyTorch implementation, and reports parameter counts, runtime, and memory in Table 7. These supplement an otherwise largely retained implementation recipe; they do not establish that existing experiments changed.

E1.justification: The original six benchmarks remain. Appendix C adds ImageNet50/100/200 subset evaluations and a distinct OOD-detection task using CIFAR and Tiny-ImageNet near-OOD inputs and SVHN, Textures, and Places365 far-OOD inputs, substantially broadening evaluated conditions.

E2.justification: Appendix C.1 adds evaluations of FlexMatch and FreeMatch thresholding both directly and integrated into CDC, plus CDC augmented with Gradient Synchronization Filter and Prototype Proximity Filter. These introduce substantive alternatives to CDC's sample-selection strategy. Comparator membership in the original benchmark tables is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include transferring ImageNet-10 hyperparameters to larger ImageNet subsets with ResNet-50, evaluating OOD detection through maximum-softmax scores, and applying CDC for 100 epochs after SCAN or SeCu. The original six-benchmark splits, main training budgets, and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds batch-size/mini-cluster sensitivity, hidden-width and expanded entropy-weight ablations, a label-smoothing sweep, alternative sample-selection analyses, hyperparameter transfer, and OOD robustness tests. Conversely, v2's all-versus-selected-samples head-training ablation and MLP-depth sweep disappear. The principal component ablations in Table 2 remain.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies eight runs and reports mean and standard deviation for CDC and several baselines across all six benchmarks in Tables 10–11. v2 lacks explicit run counts and corresponding uncertainty tables. Table 5 additionally reports variability across hyperparameter settings, distinct from repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Numerical entries in the original Tables 1, 2, and 4 are unchanged, but substantial new results are added. For example, Table 12 reports ImageNet50 ACC/ECE of 77.8%/7.5% for CDC versus 76.8%/14.2% for SCAN-3 under the added setting. The CIFAR-20 calibration comparison in prose is corrected from 52.3%→40.6% to 52.3%→4.9%, matching both versions' Table 1.

M1.justification: The reported pseudo-label selection rule changes: v2 multiplies average confidence over all samples assigned to a class by floor(B/C), whereas v3 sums confidence over its top floor(B/C) samples and rounds down. This refines sample selection while retaining the dual-head architecture, losses, initialization, and inference procedure.

P1.justification: Contributions, related work, and several method explanations are extensively rewritten. Initialization moves from Section 3.1 to 3.3, Algorithm 1 moves from the appendix into the main method section, and experiments and appendices are reorganized. Citation style, affiliations, and conference headers also change.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICLR layout, revises framework labels, restructures tables, and adds sensitivity, sample-selection, and OOD displays. Existing appendix Figures 5–7 become Figures 6, 7, and 9 with retained content; Figures 5, 8, 10, and 11 provide new displays. Figure 3 also corrects ARPC to AURC.

R1.justification: Positioning expands beyond the original deep-clustering and supervised-calibration survey. v3 discusses CLIP-based SIC/TAC, distinguishes domain-adaptation calibration using labeled source data, and substantially relates CDC to moderately confident sample selection and FlexMatch/FreeMatch thresholding in Appendix C.1.

T1.justification: v3 corrects Theorem 1's reversed region indices: confidence is penalized in unreliable region F and preserved in reliable region T, consistent with the existing proof. Appendix A.1 also adds an explicit feature-normalization assumption. The principal propositions, theorems, and derivations otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: The eight-run uncertainty tables, relevant SSL comparisons, and transfer/OOD evaluations substantially strengthen evidence for CDC's stability and applicability beyond v2's original evaluations. Resource reporting and code-access information further improve reproducibility. Removed ablations and the explicit cluster-count limitation are drawbacks, as is overstated robustness prose: Table 5's CIFAR-20 ACC spans 58.1–62.6%, exceeding the claimed ±1.4-point variation. These issues temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial empirical strengthening.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same calibrated deep clustering (CDC) work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original sensitivity studies, repeated-run results, transfer evaluations, and out-of-distribution detection experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original CDC experiments on six image benchmarks, including clustering, calibration, failure rejection, and component ablations.

results.title: Towards Calibrated Deep Clustering Network

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes OM superiority for preventing reward drops and regularizing away from hacking policies. v2 makes a new formal definition and a proxy-quality-dependent improvement guarantee central contributions, adds claims about χ² versus KL including RLHF, and recommends replacing current KL regularization. The regularizing-away contribution is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 explains hacking through breakdown of reward correlation under distribution shift and motivates χ² through its stronger penalty on unlikely behavior. It newly acknowledges that the RLHF evaluation reward model can itself be hacked and discusses limits of OM/AD equivalence for future multi-turn or tool-using agents. Earlier AUROC-based explanations and the λdrop recommendation disappear.

D1.justification: v2 adds ORPO pseudocode, a 1%-per-tail trimmed divergence estimator, proxy-reward scale values, pandemic network details, and RLHF model, dataset and software specifications. Appendix D explains previously tabulated clipping behavior but removes discriminator-training epoch counts and earlier glucose history/feature-selection guidance. These are substantive changes to implementation documentation.

E1.justification: The tomato gridworld, Flow traffic, SimGlucose and pandemic environments remain, sometimes under renamed headings. v2 adds language-generation/RLHF experiments using AlpacaFarm preference and SFT data, substantially extending domain and task coverage (Appendix C.4).

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from KL-based AD and OM regularization to comparisons across both divergence families, including a new AD χ² comparator against χ² ORPO. The best-case early-stopping baseline in v1 Table 1 disappears. Base-policy, unregularized and true-reward-training comparisons remain for the original environments.

E3.justification: v2 introduces held-out-prompt RLHF evaluation with separate proxy and evaluation reward models, plus new χ² coefficient sweeps. Appendix D also revises the reported traffic/tomato discriminator depth from four 256-unit layers to two and specifies this architecture across non-LLM environments. Original PPO budgets remain unchanged; the revised documentation does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds proxy/true-reward correlation analyses across environments and controlled ablations of discriminator update order and reward clipping (Figure 2 and Appendix E.2). It removes v1's AUROC detection analysis and the λdrop coefficient-selection experiment. These changes substantially replace the questions investigated by the supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds and median rewards with standard deviations in tables. The main coefficient-sweep plot changes from standard-deviation error bars in v1 Figure 3 to shading showing the range across seeds in v2 Figure 5. No increased repeated-run count is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds χ², RLHF, correlation and ablation results, while removing detection, early-stopping, λdrop and regularization-away results. New RLHF best-coefficient scores are 16.94 ± 0.07 for χ² and 16.81 ± 0.27 for KL. Some changed summaries reuse earlier results: gridworld AD KL changes from 6.19 to 6.33, but 6.33 already appears in v1 Table 4. Several retained appendix standard deviations also change.

M1.justification: v1 primarily optimizes proxy reward minus an occupancy KL penalty. v2 introduces a square-root χ² occupancy penalty, changing the discriminator-based reward adjustment from a linear score to an exponential score normalized by estimated divergence (Section 6 and Appendix B). It also implements direct χ² regularization for RLHF and omits v1's regularizing-away variant.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The narrative is reorganized into preliminaries, definitions, mitigation and experiments; much ORPO derivation moves to Appendix B and environment descriptions to Appendix C. Terminology changes from safe policy to base policy, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. New correlation, glucose-distribution and RLHF graphics replace earlier toy, ROC and regularization-away displays. The coefficient-sweep figure becomes separate χ²/KL rows across five environments; result tables are redesigned, and algorithm and ablation displays are added. Existing training-board and traffic illustrations remain in Appendix C.

R1.justification: v2 repositions the contribution around formalizing reward hacking, explicitly contrasting correlated proxies with prior unhackability and bounded-error robust-MDP formulations. It expands the distinction from offline RL and adds relevant robust-RL, RLHF and multi-turn-agent references, including Derman, Gadot and Coste. Earlier early-stopping and TV-bound supporting references are removed.

T1.justification: v1's AD counterexample, TV return bound and tightness argument are replaced by correlated-proxy/reward-hacking definitions and Theorem 5.1's correlation-dependent χ² improvement bound with occupancy-support assumptions. Appendix A introduces contextual-bandit equivalence for general f-divergences, and Appendix B derives the new optimization gradient. Definition 4.1 does contain a normalization inconsistency: its stated standard deviations are printed as variances.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between proxy quality, a theoretical improvement bound and the implemented regularizer, addressing a limitation of v1's generic return-distance argument. New RLHF comparisons and controlled ORPO ablations add relevant empirical support and identify implementation failures. These gains outweigh losing earlier diagnostic and alternative-strategy studies, although removing the λdrop experiment weakens practical coefficient-selection evidence. Definition 4.1's normalization error and remaining discrepancies between main and appendix result summaries still require correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-hacking and ORPO research, despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments in the retained environments and an added RLHF setting, including reward correlations, regularization comparisons and implementation ablations (Figure 2, Table 1 and Appendix E).

before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments in four environments, including regularization comparisons, reward-hacking detection and regularization-away results (Tables 1–3 and Appendix B).

results.title: Correlated Proxies: A New Definition and Improved Mitigation for Reward Hacking

C1.justification: The abstract changes from introducing a novel importance-sampling loss to using an existing weighted loss, and removes the exploration/exploitation claim. The introduction emphasizes feasibility and practical design insights while retaining the central state-value-only learning and high-dimensional-control claims.

C2.justification: v3 extends the twin-critic regularization interpretation by suggesting greater benefits in higher-dimensional problems, and discusses overactuated systems and categorical critics as future directions. The HalfCheetah weakness remains in Section 4.3, although the conclusion no longer repeats it.

D1.justification: Table 2 now explicitly documents the hyperparameters for MyoHand by sharing the dog-task configuration. Existing algorithm details, hyperparameter values, hardware and training-time disclosures remain; the new reproducibility statement mainly directs readers to this material.

E1.justification: v3 adds ten 39-dimensional MyoHand tasks from MyoSuite, covering pose, reaching and object manipulation with standard and hard variants (Figure 3). This substantially extends coverage beyond locomotion; all five Gymnasium and three DMC dog tasks remain.

E2.justification: The retained benchmark comparisons still evaluate SAC, MPO, PPO, on-policy TRPL and one-step V-trace, and the component variants remain the same. The new MyoHand comparison uses existing comparators SAC, PPO, TRPL and V-trace; Figure 3 does not report MPO results.

E3.justification: v3 introduces success-based MyoHand evaluation and cross-task IQM aggregation (Figure 3), supplementing the existing per-task return evaluations. Settings for the retained tasks in Tables 1–2 and the controlled one-step V-trace comparison remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Component ablations expand from Humanoid-v4 alone to Ant-v4 and, in Appendix C Figure 6, Hopper-v4, Walker2D-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4. These substantially broaden the investigation of whether importance sampling, TRPL, twin critics and clipping are beneficial across tasks.

E5.justification: v3 adds an interquartile-mean estimate with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval across MyoHand tasks (Figure 3). Per-task reporting continues to use ten seeds, means and 95% bootstrapped intervals; no increase in runs for retained results is stated.

E6.justification: v3 adds MyoHand success curves showing Vlearn's highest aggregate performance with task-specific exceptions, plus results from the expanded component ablations. Figure 6 also shows that removing twin critics improves HalfCheetah performance. The retained benchmark curves and the reported 25% Humanoid improvement over SAC are unchanged.

M1.justification: The weighted Bellman-error objective, TRPL policy update, twin critics, importance-weight clipping and replay-buffer procedure remain unchanged. Renaming the loss to LWIS and moving the unchanged Algorithm 1 to Appendix B do not change the method.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative around high-dimensional control, expands the WIS explanation and restructures experiments into high-dimensional tasks, design choices and low-dimensional tasks. It also retitles the paper, moves pseudocode into the appendix, adds a reproducibility section and removes the broader-impacts appendix.

P2.justification: Existing Gymnasium and dog plots are regrouped into Figures 2 and 5; a new MyoHand Figure 3 and appendix ablation Figure 6 are added. Figure 4 becomes a wider three-panel comparison, and the algorithm moves from a wrapped main-text display to a full-width appendix display.

R1.justification: v3 expands the connection to prior linear WIS and TD(0) work and clarifies attribution. It adds references for MyoSuite, double sampling, Sutton and Barto's textbook, and recent critic/stabilization approaches, while retaining the overall positioning against Q-function methods and V-trace.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, the upper-bound and consistency proofs, and the bandit variance/effective-sample-size analysis in Appendix A remain mathematically unchanged. Loss renaming, notation corrections and expanded explanations introduce no new formal result.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central generality claim: v2 evaluated locomotion and examined components only on Humanoid, whereas v3 adds musculoskeletal hand control and checks component effects across all five Gymnasium tasks. The new results expose task-dependent exceptions, while clearer attribution distinguishes the existing WIS foundation from the practical algorithm contribution. These changes materially improve validation and scientific clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Vlearn research despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original MyoHand evaluations and component ablations on additional Gymnasium tasks.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on five Gymnasium tasks and three DMC dog tasks, plus Humanoid component and replay-buffer ablations.

results.title: Efficient Off-Policy Learning for High-Dimensional Action Spaces

C1.justification: v2 broadens the abstract's reconstruction claim from Mel-spectrograms to Mel-spectrograms or discrete tokens.
