The contributions now emphasize three enhanced losses and reduced GPU memory use, and the introduction newly claims the fastest diffusion-based waveform reconstruction to the authors' knowledge. The headline speed changes from approximately 90 to 97 times real-time.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for stronger guidance effects with tokens, the STFT loss's magnitude-versus-phase tradeoff, and ViSQOL's apparent preference for GAN outputs despite audible artifacts. It also discusses bandwidth saturation and MBD's sound-effect performance. v1's disclosure that preliminary direct text-to-complex-spectrogram TTS underperformed a cascade is removed, although the proposed future direction remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds auxiliary-loss weights and their gradient-norm rationale, overlap size, codec feature-extraction settings, training hardware and durations, baseline repository links, and detailed external-test construction instructions. Existing optimizer, crop, batch-size, and backbone details largely move to Appendix A.1. Conversely, v1's direct RFWave repository link and explicit TTS-checkpoint availability statement are omitted; this does not establish that the resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 retains the principal Mel-reconstruction datasets but removes the Universal-dataset experiment. It adds actual EnCodec-token reconstruction experiments, training with Common Voice, DNS Challenge speech, Jamendo, FSD50K, and AudioSet. The external evaluation suite in Table A.4 substantially broadens coverage across speech, vocals, and sound effects.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares RFWave with Vocos. v2 adds evaluated PriorGrad and FreGrad comparisons for Mel reconstruction and EnCodec and Multi-Band Diffusion comparisons for token reconstruction. Vocos also becomes a comparator in the Jamendo experiment, where v1 reports only RFWave. The speed comparison expands accordingly.

E3.justification: v2 replaces UTMOS and Mel-SNR evaluation with human MOS, ViSQOL, voiced/unvoiced F1, and periodicity error, while retaining PESQ. Jamendo testing changes from 1,397 files to 50. New codec experiments evaluate bandwidths from 1.5 to 12 kbps. CPU timing is removed, while the RTX 4090, batch-one LJSpeech GPU benchmark is retained.

E4.justification: The retained time/frequency-domain and balanced-loss ablation is expanded with overlap-loss, STFT-loss, and guidance combinations in v2 Table 3. Appendix A.3 expands spectrogram case studies to additional methods and music artifacts. Conversely, v1's 100-step sampling comparison and 80-versus-100-dimensional Mel-input comparison disappear.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v2 adds uncertainty to human MOS results, explicitly identifying 95% confidence intervals in Table 1 and displaying intervals in the detailed results. This is a new reporting practice, but training-seed replication, listener counts, and interval-construction procedures are not specified.

E6.justification: v2 substantially replaces and expands the reported results, adding MOS, codec-bandwidth results, and new ablation outcomes. For example, Table 1 reports average MOS of 3.95 for RFWave, 3.47 for Vocos, and 3.75 for PriorGrad. Reported RFWave GPU throughput changes from 91.46 to 97.01 times real-time. Universal, CPU, and preliminary direct-TTS results disappear. Many quality scores use revised configurations or test subsets and therefore do not establish controlled performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: v2 introduces overlapping subbands with a consistency loss, an STFT loss applied to the estimated clean signal, and classifier-free guidance, including its use for EnCodec reconstruction. These change training and inference. The shared ConvNeXtV2 backbone remains, and v1's time-balanced loss is renamed energy-balanced with the same Equation 5. EnCodec conditioning was already described in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten, the method is reorganized into model structure and loss functions, and the results place application comparisons before ablations. Implementation details move into a structured appendix with separate resources, examples, and tables sections. Terminology and the author block also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overlap schematic, restructures results into aggregate and detailed tables, and expands the compact spectrogram comparison into three appendix figures with ground truth and additional methods. The weighting plot is redrawn, the model schematic is restyled, and resource and dataset-construction tables are added. Page geometry and headers also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around neural codecs and diffusion competitors through discussions of PriorGrad, FreGrad, SoundStream, VALL-E, and UniAudio, and adds flow-matching TTS context. The earlier Parallel WaveNet, ClariNet, and WaveGrad discussion disappears. Together with the new fastest-diffusion claim, this changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic maintenance.

T1.justification: The original Rectified Flow formulation and balanced-loss Equation 5 remain. v2 adds formal overlap/subband dimension definitions and Equations 6–7 connecting predicted velocity to an estimated clean signal for STFT-loss computation. These are limited mathematical additions; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's central quality and efficiency claims relied largely on automatic metrics and comparison with Vocos. v2 adds human listening evidence with uncertainty, direct diffusion competitors, codec reconstruction tests, and ablations addressing the new losses and guidance. These substantially strengthen support for the paper's central claims, while the appendix improves reproducibility. Listener counts and confidence-interval procedures remain unspecified, and removal of the negative preliminary TTS result and direct code/checkpoint disclosures weakens transparency. Those losses do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RFWave and retain identifiable corresponding architecture, equations, and experiments. Their main text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion in v2.

after.justification: v2 reports original Mel-spectrogram and EnCodec-token reconstruction experiments, human listening evaluations, ablations, and efficiency measurements, including detailed appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original waveform-reconstruction scores, domain and loss ablations, spectrogram comparisons, and inference-speed measurements in Tables 1–3 and Appendix A.

results.title: RFWave: Multi-band Rectified Flow for Audio Waveform Reconstruction

C1.justification: The central claims about efficient, high-quality, frame-level multi-band reconstruction remain. v3 adds sampling-time selection as a fourth stated contribution, updates the headline speed from 97 to 160 times real-time, and explicitly claims speed comparable to GAN-based methods in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting time-domain performance to periodic signals introduced by ISTFT, relating this mechanism to Snake activation, and attributing cross-domain advantages to better preserved harmonics. It also discusses the necessity of Rectified Flow, backbone efficiency, and scaling tradeoffs. Earlier discussion of MBD's sound-effect strengths and CFG's approximately 50% latency overhead is removed.

D1.justification: New details include sampling-grid calibration using one batch of 96 examples and 100 integration steps, half/double-size backbone configurations, explicit STFT-loss formulas, and the BigVGAN repository. Most optimizer, preprocessing, hardware, and training-duration information is retained. v3 omits v2's explicit Mel-test subset sizes of 20, 300, and 50; this establishes reduced documentation, not changed sample selection.

E1.justification: The existing training corpora and broad speech, singing, music, and codec coverage remain. v3 adds a focused scenario: Mel-spectrogram reconstruction on MUSDB18 using LibriTTS-trained models, covering vocals, drums, bass, other instruments, and mixtures. MUSDB18 already contributed codec-test samples in v2; its speech-to-music transfer role is new.

E2.justification: BigVGAN becomes an evaluated comparator in quality and speed benchmarks, and Table 6 adds DDPM and ResNet alternatives. Vocos is removed from the original multi-dataset comparison in Tables 1 and A.5 and its corresponding spectrogram panels, while participating in separate GAN comparisons. The Vocos, PriorGrad, and FreGrad rows from v2's LJSpeech ablation table also disappear.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a separate GAN listening study, a 50-step DDPM control, a similarly sized ResNet backbone, and half/double-size model configurations. The speed benchmark adds GPU-memory measurement and explicit 44.1-kHz comparisons. These extend the experimental protocol substantially; the retained default training configuration and ten-step RFWave budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of equal-straightness sampling, Rectified Flow versus DDPM, backbone choice, model scaling, and speech-to-music generalization. Figures A.8–A.9 newly illustrate artifacts from omitting STFT and overlap losses. Conversely, the frequency-domain energy-balanced variant and two CFG ablation rows reported in v2 are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report MOS with confidence intervals, explicitly identified as 95% intervals in Table 1. Additional interval-bearing results in v3 use the existing reporting practice. Neither version supplies training-seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results: MUSDB18 average MOS is 3.67 for RFWave, 3.51 for BigVGAN, and 3.10 for Vocos; the equal-straightness ablation reports PESQ 4.275 versus 4.211 without it. Reported RFWave speed changes from 97.01 to 162.59 times real-time, without explaining the cause. Original diffusion and EnCodec scores are largely retained, while some Vocos/CFG entries disappear. The new LibriTTS MOS comparison is explicitly a separate listening study.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds equal-straightness selection of nonuniform Euler sampling times, with implementation in Appendix A.5. This refines inference while retaining the multi-band architecture, ConvNeXtV2 backbone, normalization procedures, and three training losses. Appendix A.4 documents existing STFT losses rather than introducing another objective.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively condensed and rewritten. Previously separate experiment and results sections become a structured experiments-and-analysis section separating diffusion, GAN, codec, ablation, and speed evaluations. Subband details move to the appendix, appendix explanations are reorganized, and the conclusion loses the future-TTS and ethical-concerns discussion.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn as an integrated architecture diagram. Existing spectrogram comparisons change from five to four panels, while new sampling, GAN-comparison, and loss-effect figures are added. Tables are reorganized around separate comparison groups, and the speed table gains memory and high-sample-rate entries. The document also adopts different headers, typography, and table formatting.

R1.justification: v3 expands context through references to flow matching, stochastic interpolants, additional diffusion vocoders, and BigVGAN/Snake, and explicitly distinguishes energy-balanced loss from PriorGrad's adaptive prior. Some codec and future-TTS references are removed. These refine the existing research positioning; citation-style and bibliography-format changes do not themselves constitute substantive changes.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 introduces the straightness functional S(v) and uses equal accumulated deviation to define sampling intervals. The original Rectified Flow and loss equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added. Appendix A.4 mainly supplies formulas for previously specified STFT-loss components.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through speech-to-music transfer tests, BigVGAN comparisons, controls isolating Rectified Flow and backbone choices, and diagnostic loss examples (Tables 2–6; Figures A.6–A.9). These address important gaps in evidence for generalization and design decisions in v2. Some earlier Vocos/CFG results and explicit test-subset counts are lost, and the speed revision is unexplained, but the added diagnostic and comparative evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RFWave work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds GAN comparisons, cross-domain evaluation, sampling and backbone analyses, and resource measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original listening tests, objective reconstruction measurements, ablations, and inference-speed benchmarks in Tables 1–4 and A.5–A.6.

results.title: RFWave: Multi-band Rectified Flow for Audio Waveform Reconstruction

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds simple diffusion-backbone initialization and transfer using limited target data. v3 makes systematic identification of effective adaptation choices a principal contribution, with headline findings about annotation quality, stochasticity and image-level supervision. It emphasizes dense perception while retaining GenPercept's transfer claim and moving pose evidence to the appendix.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for LoRA's limitations, annotation quality and supervision effects on detail, and depth-versus-disparity tradeoffs. It explicitly qualifies semantic generalization with failures on unseen cats and cars (Figure 4). Meanwhile, v1's MAE/CLIP/CoCa representation-learning discussion and interpretations of the removed data-volume and PixArt experiments disappear.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository pointer and documents sampling ratios, noise/ensemble defaults, prompt strings, LoRA ranks and MMPose rendering. It omits v1's explicit learning-rate decay, DIS/matting normalization and clipping instructions, and runtime/memory measurements. These change reproducibility documentation within an otherwise retained implementation framework; the link alone does not establish external code availability.

E1.justification: v3 adds ScanNet depth evaluation, Sintel normal evaluation, and Taskonomy/Cityscapes training for the data-quality comparison (Tables 5–7). Appendix E.6 additionally reports MHP pose experiments. The original COCO pose coverage is retained in Appendix C, rather than removed.

E2.justification: The depth benchmark gains DepthAnything, DepthAnything v2, Metric3D v2, Marigold, GeoWizard and DepthFM. Normal comparisons replace FrameNet, VPLNet, TiltedSN and Bae et al. (2021) with Omnidata variants, Metric3D v2, DSINE and GeoWizard. Matting adds HATT, SHM and MODNet. Conversely, v1's DINOv2 depth and semantic-segmentation comparisons disappear. P3M becomes P3M-Net with the same comparator scores.

E3.justification: Default ablations change from Hypersim-only training at resolution 768 and batch size 16 (v1 Section 3.5) to 90:10 Hypersim/Virtual KITTI sampling at 480×640 and batch size 32 (v3 Appendix D). Normal evaluation drops RMSE and adds 5° and 7.5° thresholds. v3 also introduces average ranks across depth metrics. These are substantive reported protocol changes.

E4.justification: v3 expands the noise/component studies to test both noise forms, multi-resolution noise, image-level losses, prompts, timesteps, LoRA ranks and synthetic versus real training data (Tables 1–5). It adds qualitative ablation and semantic failure examples. Conversely, v1's training-data-volume sweep, PixArt and VAE-encoder tests, and explicit ensemble/runtime analysis are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Inference ensembles and discussion of diffusion stochasticity do not establish statistical uncertainty reporting; both versions principally report point estimates.

E6.justification: v3 substantially replaces and extends geometry and ablation results under revised settings. DIS overall maxFβ changes from 0.840 to 0.863 (v1 Table 4; v3 Table 8); matting SAD/MSE change from 12.44/0.0037 to 12.77/0.0027 (v1 Table 5; v3 Table 10). These are revised reported outcomes under changed training, not controlled same-setting improvements. GenPercept's semantic mIoU and COCO pose scores are retained.

M1.justification: The one-step backbone and optional decoder mechanism remain, but task-specific learning changes substantially. v3 adds disparity prediction, uses MSE/scale-shift-invariant/gradient depth losses instead of v1's VNL/HDN/MSE/L1 combination, and adds image-angular supervision for normals. Colormap segmentation changes from latent-space supervision to pixel-wise MSE. These revise outputs and objectives beyond merely documenting the existing architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The method-first narrative becomes a preliminary overview followed by question-driven analyses and explicit findings before task experiments. Detailed formulations move to Appendix A, human pose moves to Appendix C, and implementation and supplementary results receive separate appendices. This is substantial narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: Figure 2 becomes a multi-panel visualization of noise forms, schedules and predictions; Figure 4 gains generalization and failure examples. Geometry tables expand to additional datasets, methods and training-sample columns, while the semantic table loses baseline and architecture columns. Boxed findings and extensive appendix comparison grids are added, alongside relocation of the pose table and figure.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts from broad foundation-model transfer and NLP/pretraining analogies toward identifying unresolved diffusion-adaptation choices. Marigold and DMP remain but become central reference points. GeoWizard, DepthFM, DepthAnything, Metric3D v2 and newer inverse-rendering work substantially expand the contemporary context, while much of the earlier NLP, DINOv2 and representation-learning discussion is removed.

T1.justification: The diffusion formulations and beta-equals-one derivation in v1 Section 2, Equations 1–8, are retained in v3 Appendix A. No new theorem, proof or substantive formal derivation is introduced. The expanded empirical explanations do not change this mathematical content.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the justification for adaptation choices: Table 1 investigates both stochastic and deterministic noise schedules, and Tables 2–5 isolate supervision, conditioning and fine-tuning choices that v1 examined less fully. Broader geometry comparisons and explicit semantic failure cases improve the assessment of applicability. Removing DINOv2 comparisons, data-scaling evidence and measured runtime/memory results loses useful support, but the stronger investigation of the central design questions provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe the same GenPercept work, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. However, v1 refers to supplementary DIS comparisons that are absent from its supplied PDF, limiting comparison of that material. The principal method, experiments and revisions remain assessable.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and extensive adaptation ablations, with additional empirical comparisons and qualitative results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original GenPercept experiments on depth, surface normals, segmentation, matting and human pose, together with component and training-data ablations.

results.title: What Matters When Repurposing Diffusion Models for General Dense Perception Tasks?

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the explicit finding that stochasticity harms perception with the scheduler-special-case claim that multi-step generation can become one-step without performance loss. The principal contributions—GenPercept, data-quality analysis and task-specific supervision—remain.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 replaces the earlier Gaussian-versus-RGB difficulty explanation with ground-truth shortcuts and training/inference mismatch; new Appendix B develops this interpretation. V4 acknowledges weaker benchmark performance against MVANet and ViTAE-S while emphasizing generalization, recommends depth versus disparity by scene type, and identifies LAION data scale versus diffusion pretraining as an unresolved source of benefits.

D1.justification: V4 specifies scheduler interpolation and UperNet class-channel outputs, identifies geometry results evaluated using released weights and Marigold/DSINE protocols, and documents runtime hardware and measurement settings. Existing training hyperparameters largely persist. The GenPercept code URL in v3's abstract is removed without replacement, reducing documented access information.

E1.justification: Matting coverage expands substantially beyond portraits: v4 adds zero-shot AIM500 evaluation and Composition-1K training, including semi-transparent and hollow objects (Table 10; Appendix H.4; Figures 16–17). It also adds ADE20K training, whereas v3 used ADE20K only for zero-shot evaluation on overlapping semantic classes.

E2.justification: V4 adds MVANet to DIS comparisons, Mask2Former with ResNet50/Swin-T/Swin-L to semantic segmentation, and ViTAE-S to matting comparisons. Table 6 also adds DMP Official to the final depth comparison, although DMP already participated in v3's ablations. These additions substantially strengthen comparator coverage across tasks.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include 1024-pixel DIS inference, training subsets ranging from 90K to 5.6K images, and runtime/memory measurements averaging 100 images at 768×768 on an RTX 4090 (Tables 8, 11–12). Supervised ADE20K and matting-transfer evaluations also introduce additional settings. The newly identified Marigold/DSINE protocols for retained geometry scores are documentation, not evidence that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: V4 adds training-volume sensitivity, runtime/ensemble/decoder comparisons, and synthetic-versus-real training comparisons under challenging visual conditions (Tables 11–12; Figure 9). Expanded cross-dataset DIS comparisons and portrait-to-general-object matting tests provide additional robustness evidence. The original architecture, timestep, prompt and training-strategy ablations remain.

E5.justification: Section 3.1 newly reports varying random seeds during training and inference when investigating scheduler performance. V3 does not report these checks. V4 provides no run counts, seed identifiers, error bars or confidence intervals, so this is a limited reporting addition rather than a documented increase in repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include supervised ADE20K mIoU of 50.2, AIM500 SAD of 75.5 versus ViTAE-S's 112.52, 1024-pixel DIS results, runtime measurements and data-volume results (Tables 8–12, 14). Tables 6–7 add baseline entries distinguished from authors' evaluations. Retained GenPercept geometry and pose scores are unchanged; the added training and inference settings should not be read as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The deterministic one-step GenPercept procedure, U-Net fine-tuning, optional decoders and task-specific losses are retained. The clarified UperNet output format and applications to additional datasets do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries and Section 3.1 undergo substantial rewriting, including an equation-led explanation and a different mechanism narrative. Findings and conclusions are revised, the appendix is reorganized into additional thematic sections before the references, and matting implementation details move into the appendix.

P2.justification: V4 expands comparison tables and adds provenance markers, training/test-dataset columns, and runtime/data-volume tables. Figures 5–6 gain comparator columns; the cross-dataset segmentation display expands considerably; new synthetic-versus-real and general-matting figures appear. Figure 2's plot styling and several captions change. Numerous older qualitative panels are retained despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: V4 replaces the DINO object-detection citation with Caron et al.'s self-supervised vision-transformer work, adds DINOv2 discussion, and cites the newly included comparators and Composition-1K source. Most of the related-work narrative and the positioning around repurposing diffusion priors remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly gives an explicit mathematical definition of the variance schedule using interpolation between square-root endpoints (v4 Equation 5). The diffusion objectives and one-step reduction otherwise retain v3's mathematics; equations brought into the main text largely restate material already in v3 Appendix A.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens previously under-supported practical claims through measured runtime and data-volume analyses, stronger baselines, and broader generalization tests. Tables 8–10 also expose task-specific weaknesses and produce more balanced conclusions, while baseline-provenance disclosures improve interpretability. These gains outweigh removal of the code link and reporting weaknesses: seed variation remains unquantified, and Appendix C's claimed 27% GPU-memory reduction conflicts with Table 11's 6.95-to-6.32 GB change, approximately 9%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenPercept study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains these original results and adds runtime measurements, training-data-volume experiments, stronger benchmark comparisons and general-object matting results.

before.justification: V3 reports original experiments on depth, surface normals, segmentation and matting, plus component ablations and appendix results on human pose estimation.

results.title: What Matters When Repurposing Diffusion Models for General Dense Perception Tasks?

C1.justification: v1's central empirical claim concerns inadequate separation in unmodified models. v2 expands the stated contributions to mitigation evaluation and claims that the tested prompting and fine-tuning approaches do not reliably provide both separation and high utility (abstract, introduction, and Section 7). This substantially broadens the scientific claim.

C2.justification: v2 interprets separation alongside instruction-following utility and adds substantive qualifications: system/user roles are imperfect instruction/data proxies, GPT-4 may benefit from generating SEP, and unsuccessful mitigation experiments cannot establish impossibility. It discusses alternative optimization choices and residual failures despite high aggregate scores, substantially expanding the applicability and limitations analysis.

D1.justification: Where v1 Appendix B mainly identifies evaluated models, v2 Appendices B.1–B.4 document mitigation-data construction, prompt templates, optimization settings, TRL/PEFT implementation, and NVIDIA A6000 hardware. Table 10 supplies LoRA and training hyperparameters. These are substantial reproducibility details for the new experiments; the code and SEP access statement is retained.

E1.justification: The 9,160-element SEP evaluation dataset and Appendix A task inventory are retained. v2 additionally uses SQuAD-based inputs and Alpaca-derived probes for mitigation training and validation, including open-ended probes without witnesses. This substantially expands the represented training data and task requirements beyond the original synthetic evaluation setup.

E2.justification: The model comparison removes Llama-2-13B, OpenHermes 2.5, and Dolphin 2.2.1, while adding Gemma-2B/7B, Phi-3-mini-4k, Llama-3-8B, and Starling. Tables 3–4 also introduce comparisons between original models and prompt engineering, prompt optimization, and fine-tuning.

E3.justification: v2 adds utility evaluation, separate 10,000-example training and 1,000-example validation datasets, validation-based selection, and optimization/fine-tuning budgets. It introduces textual system/user delimiters for Gemma and Starling. GPT-3.5 changes from the reported 0613 endpoint to 0125, and GPT-4 from 0125 to 2024-04-09, preventing direct same-checkpoint comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analysis of mitigation effectiveness versus utility, including Figure 2 and failure cases despite engineered prompts in Tables 8–9. The insistence, probe-position, and task-domain analyses are retained in Appendix D with updated results. v1 Appendix C.1's separate diagnostic of GPT-4's witness agreement across prompt locations is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard errors without specifying benchmark replication counts or seeds. v2 adds a fitted linear regression summarizing the utility–separation relationship in Figure 2. This is a limited statistical addition; the expanded result tables otherwise retain the existing uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported SEP scores change for retained models: Llama-2-7B changes from 44.7% to 44.3%, and Zephyr from 29.1% to 30.0%. GPT results are replaced under newer endpoints. New mitigation results show, for example, average open-model separation rising from 37.5% to 81.8% after fine-tuning while utility falls from 67.8% to 19.2%. Appendix subgroup results also change.

M1.justification: v1 introduces measurement and benchmarking without implementing mitigations. v2 adds template-based prompt selection, adapted gradient/coordinate prompt optimization targeting task-specific outputs rather than fixed refusals, and LoRA fine-tuning (Section 6 and Appendix B). These are substantial new procedures; the original separation computation remains equivalent.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and formal exposition undergo substantial rewriting. A dedicated mitigation section reorganizes the narrative, and the appendices are restructured around experimental details, failure cases, and dataset-factor results. Terminology shifts from instruction prompt to task prompt; authorship, affiliation, and document-header text also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a ChatGPT screenshot, a utility–separation scatter plot, model-output and failure-case tables, and parameter tables. It replaces v1's dataset-example figure with a different example table and expands the main results into separate separation and utility tables. Retained appendix result tables are transposed and reformatted, alongside a changed document template.

R1.justification: v2 positions the work as both a measurement study and a mitigation investigation, adding substantive discussion of StruQ, spotlighting, and robust prompt optimization. It newly emphasizes dataset diversity and adaptations of prior defenses, with corresponding method and dataset references. This extends the earlier positioning around defining and benchmarking instruction-data separation.

T1.justification: Definition 4 adds a formal empirical utility score, while the KL-based separation definition and empirical separation ratio remain equivalent to v1. No theorem or proof is added. The revised witness reasoning introduces an internal inconsistency by associating small empirical separation with many surprise witnesses despite linking witnesses to large divergence.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses an important limitation of v1's separation-only evaluation: apparent separation may accompany poor instruction following. Utility measurements and three concrete mitigation experiments, selected using separate data, make this distinction empirically assessable. Detailed implementation information, residual failure cases, and explicit caveats strengthen reproducibility and interpretation. Utility remains a narrow proxy and the witness discussion contains inconsistent reasoning, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEP study and retain matching core definitions and dataset documentation. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of nine models, mitigation experiments, utility measurements, and qualitative failure cases in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original SEP evaluations of seven language models in Table 1, with further experimental breakdowns in Appendix C.

results.title: Can LLMs Separate Instructions From Data? And What Do We Even Mean By That?

C1.justification: The central claims of standardized ASR robustness evaluation, fairness utility, and the importance of model size remain. The abstract and introduction expand claimed coverage from 69 to 114 perturbations and broaden the released dataset collection, while dropping the explicit promise to measure prediction stability. These adjust contribution scope while preserving the main research claims.

C2.justification: v2 treats gender disparities as dependent on the dataset and calls for further examination, qualifying v1's predominantly female-disadvantage discussion. It adds application-specific interpretations of MMS and Wav2Vec weaknesses, a learned-front-end hypothesis for adversarial robustness, and explicit language/scenario generalization limitations. Earlier stability interpretations and attack-specific model-selection recommendations disappear.

D1.justification: v2 adds a dataset repository address, dataset licenses, Bridges-2/V100 hardware information, additional effect parameters, and detailed selection rules for accented and conversational speech. Appendix B newly discloses punctuation removal and lowercasing before WER computation; this does not establish that preprocessing changed. v1 already supplied code access and substantial perturbation implementation details.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's LibriSpeech and Spanish Multilingual LibriSpeech evaluations, v2 adds TEDLIUM, selected Common Voice accents, and CHiME-6/AMI conversations with near- and far-field recordings. Evaluated conditions also expand to music, crosstalk, real room responses, and additional audio effects. These introduce substantive speech-domain and input-environment coverage.

E2.justification: The seven-model English corruption/attack comparisons in v1 expand to sixteen models in v2 Figure 3, including Canary and SpeechT5. Additional Whisper, Wav2Vec, HuBERT, and MMS participants enter these comparisons; some were already represented elsewhere in v1. Spanish comparisons add Canary and Whisper-base. DeepSpeech remains evaluated despite losing its normalization-reference role.

E3.justification: Primary evaluation changes from baseline-normalized WER and WERV to WER degradation and speech-quality-normalized metrics. Gaussian/environmental noise severities change from 10, 5, 1, -10 dB to 30, 20, 10, 0 dB (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1). Simulated-RIR severity changes from SNR-based grouping to RT60, while real RIRs use SRMR.

E4.justification: v1's prediction-stability analysis under repeated Gaussian and environmental noise is removed. v2 adds a focused Canary-versus-Whisper failure analysis for acoustics and effects (Figure 4), Spanish adversarial diagnostics, and gender-disparity analysis across additional corpora. Existing severity and within-family model-size analyses remain, with revised evidence.

E5.justification: Removing WERV also removes v1's explicitly documented 30 noise draws per type and associated variance estimation. v2 adds robust linear regression for model-attribute trends in Section 4.5. These are localized statistical changes; neither version reports confidence intervals or training-seed replication. WERV measured prediction variability, not confidence in estimated mean performance.

E6.justification: Result sets and rankings change substantially. v1 Figure 5a ranks Spanish Wav2Vec-large ahead of Whisper-large, with NWER 0.335 versus 0.379; v2 Figure 3e ranks Whisper-large first, followed by Canary and MMS under NWERD. Different metrics and perturbation settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting performance gain. Numerous model, natural-speech, Spanish-attack, and speech-quality results are added, while WERV results disappear.

M1.justification: The benchmark pipeline changes substantially. v1 requires target and baseline ASR transcriptions and includes repeated perturbations for prediction stability. v2 replaces the baseline-ASR branch with DNSMOS/PESQ speech-quality estimation, processes inherently noisy recordings directly, and removes the stability component (Section 3 and Figure 1).

P1.justification: The introduction and benchmark-positioning discussion are extensively rewritten. Evaluation is reorganized into separate model, clean-accuracy, non-adversarial, and adversarial sections. Definitions and model documentation move into expanded appendices; a limitations section is added, the conclusion is shortened, and v1's impact statement and acknowledgments are removed.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one, diagrams are redrawn, and result plots become reorganized panels and per-perturbation small multiples. Speech-quality and license tables are added, and the model table moves to the appendix. v1 Figure 12 is reused unchanged as v2 Figure 10. v2's taxonomy figure partly extends beyond the page boundary.

R1.justification: The introduction and Section 2.3 substantially reposition SRB as integrating existing speech benchmarks and complementing the Open ASR Leaderboard. This replaces much of v1's emphasis on limited benchmarking beyond digit recognition. New discussion and references cover conversational/noisy datasets, additional models, speech-quality estimation, and fairness through robustness.

T1.justification: Mathematical revisions concern metric definitions: baseline-ratio NWER is replaced by speech-quality normalization, WERV's definition is removed, and WERD is explicitly defined. WER degradation already appeared in v1's language comparison. WER, LWERR, and the SNR/PGD derivations are retained or relocated; no theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: The added accented and conversational speech evaluations substantially strengthen the basis for real-world robustness conclusions: they expose additional model weaknesses and show that gender-disparity direction depends on the corpus. Separating clean accuracy from degradation and adding curation, access, licensing, and hardware information improve interpretation and reuse. Losing prediction-stability testing and retaining prose/chart ranking inconsistencies, such as Section 4.4 versus Figure 3c, are drawbacks, but the broader diagnostic evidence and better-qualified conclusions provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Speech Robust Bench. All 15 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including their appendices, support matching the methods, equations, experiments, and displays. Minor clipping of v2's taxonomy figure does not prevent comparison because its embedded image and accompanying descriptions are available.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original experiments across expanded speech datasets and model comparisons, including robustness, gender disparities, and estimated speech-quality results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original ASR experiments on perturbed English and Spanish speech, including accuracy, prediction stability, adversarial robustness, and gender disparities.

results.title: Speech Robust Bench: A Robustness Benchmark For Speech Recognition

C1.justification: The central contributions remain literature synthesis, a curated benchmark, architectural baselines, and reusable code. v3 refines the earlier multi-class/multi-label framing toward standardized multi-label PAM evaluation and explicitly includes standardized training protocols and released trainable model parameters among its contributions. The new empirical evidence principally supports already stated goals.

C2.justification: v3 develops substantive explanations of covariate shift, label uncertainty, task shift, and adaptability beyond v1's brief challenge list. It adds interpretations of architecture and training-regime differences, validation-leakage concerns, and limitations concerning restricted test environments and the absence of detailed rare-species or location-specific failure analyses (Sections 2, 4.2, and 5; Appendices B.2 and C.6).

D1.justification: v3 adds model and optimizer settings, preprocessing and augmentation parameters, sampling limits, hardware descriptions, metadata schemas, licensing, and dataset-maintenance information (Table 8; Appendices B–D). It also provides trained-checkpoint and detailed-results access information beyond v1's high-level dataset/code links and tracking statement.

E1.justification: v1 presents generic XC training and soundscape testing without dataset-specific experiments. v3 reports training on XCL/XCM and dedicated subsets, testing on PER, NES, UHH, HSN, NBP, SSW, and SNE, and using POW for validation and VOX for augmentation. This establishes substantial empirical coverage across American and European environments (Table 4; Appendix B.5).

E2.justification: v1 promises unspecified architectural baselines but reports no comparisons. v3 evaluates EfficientNet, ConvNext, AST, EAT, and W2V2 across three training regimes, with inference-only Perch included in the LT comparison (Tables 5 and 9–11). BirdNET is explicitly excluded for leakage; it was not an evaluated comparator in v1.

E3.justification: v3 adds operational protocols for newly reported large, medium, and dedicated training experiments. These specify five-second evaluation segments, the 0.5-second label-overlap rule, cmAP/AUROC/T1-Acc metrics, POW validation for LT/MT, a 20% validation split for DT, checkpoint selection, and model-specific training budgets (Sections 3–4; Appendix C). v1 provides only a schematic protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds illustrative validation-loss curves examining early overfitting in AST and ConvNext versus continued improvement in EAT (Appendix C.6, Figure 10). Appendix B.6 also adds descriptive species-composition, vocalization-overlap, and geographic analyses. These are limited diagnostic additions; v1 contains no corresponding analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports neither repetitions nor uncertainty. v3 introduces repeated-seed means and standard deviations throughout Tables 9–11. Section 4.1 and Table 8 specify three seeds for LT/MT and five for DT, but Table 11's caption says five for LT. The reporting addition is clear, although the actual LT run count is unresolved.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive numerical outcomes where v1 supplies none, including dataset-level DT/MT/LT results and aggregate scores. For example, Table 5 reports ConvNext's LT AUROC score as 0.85. These are newly reported outcomes, not version-to-version performance gains. Some entries disagree internally: EAT's LT AUROC score is 0.80 in Table 5 versus 0.82 in Table 11.

M1.justification: Figure 1 in both versions retains focal training, complete or species-specific training sets, soundscape evaluation, and test-species logit restriction. v3 specifies standard baseline architectures, losses, and augmentations, but this expanded documentation does not establish a revised proposed algorithm or architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. The brief challenges discussion becomes reordered, developed subsections organized around problems, related work, and BirdSet's response. Separate dataset, experiment, conclusion, and appendix sections create a substantially different narrative structure; the title and author block also change.

P2.justification: v1's full-width pipeline diagram is redrawn and placed compactly beside the introduction in v3. New comparison matrices, dataset and results tables, spectrogram and evaluation schematics, distribution plots, geographic mapping, radar charts, and validation curves substantially expand the visual presentation. The title block and text/table wrapping are also redesigned.

R1.justification: v1's brief literature motivation expands into a structured comparison of dataset selection, architectures, training, robustness, and evaluation practices (Section 2; Tables 1–3). v3 adds numerous relevant works, including BEANS, and explicitly differentiates BirdSet from BEANS, BirdCLEF, and the already cited BIRB benchmark.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. Appendix C.5 in v3 supplies standard formulas for cmAP, T1-Acc, and AUROC; these explain the evaluation metrics rather than introduce new theory.

improvement.justification: v1 asserts an empirical benchmark without supplying results or an operational setup. v3 makes that contribution assessable through dataset specifications, explicit protocols, comparative results with uncertainty, and substantial reproducibility documentation. Conflicting LT seed counts and some main/appendix scores weaken reporting precision, but the addition of inspectable evidence and implementation details substantially resolves v1's central deficiency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BirdSet and share the focal-training/soundscape-evaluation design. All supplied pages and visual material, including v3's appendices, support comparison. v1's limited content is a document difference, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: Section 4 and Tables 5 and 9–11 report original model evaluations. Appendices B.6 and C.6 additionally present dataset statistics and validation-loss curves.

before.justification: v1 claims an extensive empirical analysis but reports no experimental or original data-analysis outcomes. Its five pages contain introductory material, a pipeline schematic, a brief challenges section, and references; there is no appendix.

results.title: BirdSet: A Large-Scale Dataset for Audio Classification in Avian Bioacoustics

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from optimizing acceptance within one block through optimal transport to a verifier with optimal expected token production across iterations in the standard decoding loop. V2 also recommends default adoption and quantifies its headline wall-clock improvement as 5%–8%, while retaining the lossless-generation claim.

C2.justification: V2 explains how greedy acceptance can impair later iterations through target-distribution modifications and why that procedure cannot simply replace verification in the unchanged loop. It explicitly qualifies the new optimality guarantee by this algorithmic scope and adds an interpretation connecting drafter quality to verification gains.

D1.justification: V2 adds NumPy implementation sketches and explicit input-array shapes in Appendix A, plus dataset-source references for GPT Prompt and ShareGPT. These extend v1's pseudocode documentation, although the new implementations are explicitly described as illustrative and unsuitable for practical use.

E1.justification: V2 adds GPT Prompt, comprising ChatGPT prompts sourced from LearnGPT, while retaining all seven datasets evaluated in v1. This modestly expands prompt coverage within the existing language-generation evaluation.

E2.justification: Token verification remains the principal baseline. V2 Appendix C, Table 3 adds a three-way comparison by evaluating the earlier proposed procedure, renamed greedy block verification, against the new block verifier and token verification. The additional methods discussed in related work are not experimental baselines.

E3.justification: V2 expands from one reported Gecko/Bison pairing to XXS and XXXS drafters with an S target; the PDFs do not establish how the original names map to these checkpoints. Both retain 1000 prompts, 512-token input limits, 128-token output limits, and draft lengths 4, 6, and 8. Timing tables change from normalized latency to speedup ratios.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's draft-length analysis, v2 investigates the effect of drafter choice and directly compares greedy and non-greedy block verification. Figures 3–4 and Appendix C, Table 3 address whether better drafters amplify gains and whether maximizing acceptance within one block improves iterative decoding.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging across three random seeds. V2 newly reports standard deviations for efficiencies, speedups, and relative improvements in Table 1 and Tables 4–8. This improves uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results for the new verifier, GPT Prompt, and the second drafter. Table 3 reports LM1B efficiencies of 3.21 for token, 3.49 for new block, and 3.30 for greedy verification; the last retains v1's 3.299 after rounding. Some baseline values change, while detailed greedy timing and shorter-block results disappear. Changed procedures and unmapped model names limit direct cross-version score comparisons.

M1.justification: V1's verifier uses block probability ratios and modifies target distributions for subsequent tokens; it survives as greedy block verification in v2 Appendix C. V2 introduces a different main verifier with recursively clipped acceptance probabilities and a revised residual distribution, allowing subsequent iterations to use the unchanged target model.

P1.justification: The main text is substantially rewritten around a motivating example and a directly usable verifier, replacing the earlier optimal-transport-led narrative. Related work becomes a separate section, experimental setup and results are separated, and the appendices are reorganized around implementation, new proofs, and greedy verification. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the decoding diagram, places verification algorithms side by side with highlighted differences, and adds boxed formulas, performance summaries, and implementation figures. The earlier Bernoulli plot is removed. Result tables gain uncertainty and average rows, and new drafter and three-way comparison tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 7 and Table 2 expand the existing taxonomy with TriForce, Online Speculative Decoding, multi-token prediction, and self-speculative or early-exit approaches. V2 also adds stochastic-dominance and dataset references and removes Shazeer 2019. The central positioning of verification improvements as complementary to drafting improvements remains.

T1.justification: V1's single-block optimal-transport result largely survives for greedy verification in v2 Appendix C. V2 adds a validity characterization for the unchanged decoding loop and proofs of distribution preservation and optimal expected token production after any fixed number of iterations for the new verifier (Theorems 1–2, Appendix B).

improvement.justification: V2 addresses the important gap between v1's single-block acceptance objective and performance across decoding iterations. It introduces a verifier that avoids future target-distribution modifications, supplies corresponding theory, and directly compares it with the earlier procedure (Theorem 2; Appendix C, Table 3). Drafter analyses, standard deviations, and clearer algorithm presentation substantially strengthen the paper. Some earlier greedy timing details are omitted and implementation sketches remain limited, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger formulation and supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same evolving work on block verification for speculative decoding. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments across eight datasets, two drafters, and three draft lengths, including comparisons of token, block, and greedy block verification in Sections 5–6 and Appendices C–D.

before.justification: V1 reports original block-efficiency and wall-clock experiments across seven datasets and three draft lengths in Section 5 and Appendix C, Tables 2–4.

results.title: Block Verification Accelerates Speculative Decoding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of lossless joint verification, optimal expected token production, simple substitution for token verification, and reported 5–8% wall-clock gains. Renaming 'Strict improvement' to 'Optimal improvement' does not change the contribution's meaning.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly states that zero-temperature decoding receives no additional speedup and interprets larger gains at higher temperatures through coordinated acceptance randomness. It also explains the batching computation tradeoff and why wall-clock gains peak at intermediate draft lengths despite increasing block efficiency.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses temperature 1.0 and batch size 1 for the retained PaLM-2 experiments, without establishing that those settings changed. It documents the new Vicuna checkpoints, single H100 GPU, generation limit, and competitor draft-count selection. Appendix A also changes the illustrative block-verification initialization from None to an empty list.

E1.justification: The eight original prompt datasets remain. Section 6.2 adds Spec-Bench evaluation covering multi-turn conversation, retrieval-augmented generation, summarization, translation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, extending the evaluated task requirements beyond the earlier coverage.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates token verification and greedy block verification as comparators. v3 additionally evaluates SpecTr and SpecInfer in Appendix D.1/Table 5, extending comparisons to multiple-draft systems. These methods were discussed in v2 but were not experimentally compared there.

E3.justification: New protocols include Vicuna-7B-v1.3/Vicuna-68M evaluation with a 1024-token generation limit and temperatures 0.2, 0.6, and 1.0; a batch-size-8 comparison selecting two competitor drafts from {2,4,8}; and a toy simulation with draft length 10. The original PaLM-2 prompt counts and length limits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds temperature sensitivity analysis, an empirical acceptance-length comparison explaining block verification's behavior (Figure 3), and a batching study examining the tradeoff between block efficiency and actual latency. Existing draft-length, drafter-quality, and greedy-verification analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The retained tables preserve their three-run reporting and standard deviations where previously supplied. The new Vicuna table also averages three runs. No increased run count, new uncertainty estimator, confidence interval, or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: All retained empirical tables match numerically after renumbering. New Table 2 reports Vicuna block-efficiency improvements of 3.72–8.70% and wall-clock improvements of 1.66–6.07%. New Table 5 shows block verification achieving the highest batched wall-clock speedups despite lower block efficiency than SpecTr/SpecInfer. Figure 3 adds acceptance-tail results. Section 6.2's stated 6.7% maximum conflicts with Table 2's 6.07%.

M1.justification: The acceptance rules, residual distributions, speculative-decoding loop, and greedy variant in Algorithms 1–6 remain unchanged. Expanded explanations and the illustrative Python initialization edit do not establish a changed decoding method.

P1.justification: The existing method and theory exposition is reorganized, with parameter intuition moved and expanded into separate distribution-matching and optimality explanations. Appendix B's proof exposition is substantially rewritten. Results and Appendix D gain clearer subdivisions, although the main section sequence and much introductory wording remain.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICLR layout throughout, places the residual-distribution box beside the algorithm comparison, adds the acceptance-distribution figure and two result tables, and replaces the appendix's code-image figures with typeset listings. Existing plots and result tables are retained with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 7 newly acknowledges Hu and Huang's independent verification work and distinguishes its improvement guarantee from the claimed optimality here. Chiang et al. and Kwon et al. are added for Vicuna and serving context. The broader related-work organization remains; Xia et al.'s publication update is the same cited work.

T1.justification: Although the main theorem statements remain, Appendix B substantially revises their supporting mathematics: it adds Lemma 6 and its proof, changes conditional-probability calculations in the optimality argument, corrects the acceptance-probability index in Appendix B.3, and rewrites Lemma 4's case analysis. Definition 1 also explicitly specifies permitted inputs and outputs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence previously confined to PaLM-2 and token/greedy comparisons: Vicuna experiments test transfer across model families and temperatures, while Appendix D.1 tests practical latency against external competitors under batching. Expanded and partly corrected proof arguments improve auditability. These gains outweigh localized defects, including the new token-verification argmin description conflicting with Algorithm 1 and the 6.7% versus 6.07% reporting discrepancy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same block-verification research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D support comparison, including the image-based Python listings in v2.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds Vicuna/Spec-Bench results, batched comparisons with SpecTr and SpecInfer, and an empirical toy-model acceptance-length distribution.

before.justification: v2 reports original PaLM-2 experiments measuring block efficiency and wall-clock speedup, including comparisons with token verification and greedy block verification.

results.title: Block Verification Accelerates Speculative Decoding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: efficient one-step generation from scratch and pretrained models, one-step PixArt and LoRA capabilities, resolution adaptation, and downstream compatibility. Added methods and evidence do not materially redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6.4 adds a bootstrapping explanation for reducing distribution shift and improving compatibility, replacing v1's narrower remedy and discussion of full-fine-tuning style loss. It also attributes transfer failures partly to LoRA capacity. Appendix B newly states fairness, detail-generation, and object-count limitations, while the central self-cooperative mechanism interpretation remains.

D1.justification: Appendices C, D, and G add pseudocode, optimizers and betas, learning rates, EMA coefficients, clipping, loss weights, image selection, and synthetic-data filtering details. Section 6 adds training iteration counts and LoRA batch information. Reproducibility documentation expands substantially, although LoRA batch guidance is ambiguous between 64 in Section 6.3.2 and 256 in Appendix G.2, and v1's explicit no-augmentation statement disappears.

E1.justification: Figure 5 replaces the prompted turtle example with a null-prompt test of the text-to-image models, adding an evaluation condition without text guidance. CIFAR-10, JourneyDB, HPS, resolution transfer, image editing, ControlNet, and the named community-model coverage are otherwise retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes Score SDE (VP), Probability Flow (VP), and FastDDPM. Table 4 adds pretrained SD1.5, and Table 5 introduces an unaccelerated Realistic-vision reference comparison. The principal text-to-image comparators remain; newly discussed DMD is not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces an equal-budget comparison using 5,000 total iterations, including 1,000 adaptation iterations where applicable, with matched prompts and initial noise. Table 5 adds evaluations at different sampling budgets, while Table 4 drops one-step LCM-LoRA and evaluates SD1.5 at 25 steps. Existing benchmark metrics remain unchanged; newly disclosed training details do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix F and Figure 7 add a controlled ablation testing whether quick adaptation improves convergence under equal training budgets. Figure 5 adds a null-prompt case, and Section 6.4, Table 5, and Figure 6 investigate whether retraining improves one-step community-model compatibility. These substantially extend the retained CIFAR-10 and initialization analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, explicit random-seed values, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate and qualitative reporting; matching initial noise in Figure 7 supplies experimental control rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 3 changes YOSO-PixArt-α's reported HPS/AeS from 28.21/6.18 to 29.83/6.14, placing its HPS above SDXL-Turbo's unchanged 28.91. Table 5 adds compatibility results, including one-step Realistic-vision with YOSO-LoRA-v2 at 27.13/6.12. Figures 5–7 also add or replace qualitative outcomes. These are revised or newly evaluated model results, not evidence of a controlled same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: Section 5.1 adds decoupled adversarial and consistency schedules with different time gaps, k=250 and m=25, replacing their shared target timestep in v1's objective. Section 6.4 also introduces retraining on community-model/YOSO-generated data to produce YOSO-LoRA-v2. These change the training procedure beyond the retained latent discriminator, perceptual loss, IPI, and quick-adaptation components.

P1.justification: The main Sections 1–7 retain their sequence and much of their wording. v3 makes localized language and terminology edits, expands the introductory explanation, adds an author, and moves the general text-to-image related-work paragraph into Appendix E. The new appendix organization does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is substantially revised: Figure 1 corrects branch labels and gradient annotations, Figure 5 replaces comparison samples and its final scenario, and Figure 6 is rearranged and extended with LoRA-v2 outputs. v3 adds Table 5, Figure 7, and Algorithm 1, and revises existing table structures and headers. These changes extend beyond numerical updates or pagination.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of DMD and its relationship to variational score distillation, with new references to DMD, ProlificDreamer, and Diffusers. It removes the FastDDPM reference and v1's criticism of InstaFlow's fixed data-noise pairings. The general positioning against diffusion-GAN hybrids remains.

T1.justification: v1's Equation 3 asserts an equivalence between marginal and joint KL objectives; v3's Equation 2 instead explicitly defines a joint KL formulation. Section 5.2 revises the teacher's v-prediction target to use its denoised estimate, and the final consistency objective revises the noise coupling and explicitly includes stop-gradient. These are local mathematical revisions; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens reproducibility and evidence for the text-to-image extension. Appendix G supplies previously missing training details, Appendix F tests quick adaptation under an equal total budget, and Section 6.4 provides evidence for addressing v1's acknowledged one-step transfer failure. Mathematical corrections also improve precision. LoRA batch-size ambiguity and absent uncertainty estimates remain, but the overall gain rests on better documentation and experimental support rather than higher reported scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe YOSO and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting comparison. v1 ends with references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A–G, which were included in the assessment.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds YOSO-LoRA-v2 results in Table 5 and a quick-adaptation experiment in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 experiments and ablations, text-to-image fine-tuning results, and downstream application examples in Section 6.

results.title: You Only Sample Once: Taming One-Step Text-to-Image Synthesis by Self-Cooperative Diffusion GANs

C1.justification: v5's abstract explicitly claims state-of-the-art one-step performance even with LoRA, whereas v4 claimed high-quality LoRA generation. The explicit first one-step diffusion-transformer claim is dropped. The central self-cooperative generation and zero-shot 512-to-1024 resolution-transfer contributions remain.

C2.justification: v5 adds capacity-based motivation for annealing, timestep-approximation reasoning for decoupled schedules, and a data-versus-teacher explanation for outperforming EDM. It discusses possible human-feedback metric bias and revises mode-collapse interpretations toward DMD and SD-Turbo. The data-flywheel interpretation is removed; Appendix B's general limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v5 newly supplies a code repository link, a CIFAR-10 fine-tuning learning rate, and additional evaluation-data instructions. Most optimizer and EMA details remain. It removes the explicit CIFAR-10 training-budget table and Appendix C safeguards disclosure, including synthetic-data filtering details; LoRA data-generator provenance becomes less explicit.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10, JourneyDB, the HPS benchmark, and the principal generation and downstream tasks remain. v5 adds COCO-5k evaluation and reports internally collected data for LoRA training in Appendix G.2, although that collection's composition is unspecified.

E2.justification: v5 adds Tract, Diff-Instruct, DMD, CTM, and SiD to CIFAR-10 comparisons. Text-to-image comparisons add Hyper-SD-LoRA, PeRFlow, TCD-LoRA, PixArt-DMD, and additional base-model controls. SDXL-Turbo and StyleGAN2 without ADA disappear, as does the budget-matched CT/iCT comparison; standard CT/iCT results remain.

E3.justification: Main CIFAR-10 experiments switch from DDGAN-style networks with LPIPS to EDM networks with MSE and add pretrained-EDM fine-tuning; the smaller architecture remains for ablations. Text-to-image evaluation adds ImageReward and CLIPScore and changes the stated non-HPS evaluation corpus to COCO-5k. Reported LoRA batch size changes from 64 to 128, although Appendix G.2 still states 256.

E4.justification: v5 Tables 3-4 add scheduler and annealing ablations on CIFAR-10 and quantitative text-to-image tests of perceptual loss, IPI, adversarial formulations, and training strategies. Qualitative comparison and application cases are revised. The compute-matched analysis and data-flywheel study disappear, while the discriminator-loss plot and Appendix F quick-adaptation study are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for benchmark outcomes. The discriminator training curves do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v4's CIFAR-10 FID 3.82 survives as YOSO-Base; v5 adds 3.30 and 3.05 in the smaller-backbone ablations and 2.26 from scratch and 1.81 with EDM fine-tuning. PixArt HPS changes from 29.83 to 30.52, and one-step LoRA HPS from 23.34 to 28.33. These span revised training conditions. ImageReward/CLIPScore results are added, while full SD1.5 fine-tuning, budget-matched, and data-flywheel results are removed.

M1.justification: v5 introduces annealing of KL and consistency-loss weights to zero and extends the decoupled scheduler, already present for text-to-image in v4, to CIFAR-10 training. These change the training procedure. v4's explicit YOSO-LoRA-v2 data-flywheel retraining procedure is no longer presented.

P1.justification: v5 substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, moves related work from Section 2 to Section 7, and creates a dedicated CIFAR-10 section before text-to-image scaling. LoRA discussion is integrated into the main evaluation, and the application section is shortened. Author, affiliation, header, and citation formatting also change.

P2.justification: v5 reorganizes CIFAR-10 results into main and ablation tables, replaces separate text-to-image tables with a backbone-grouped table containing additional metric columns, and removes the cost and data-flywheel tables. Qualitative comparison and application figures are substantially replaced or reorganized. Figure 1 and the quick-adaptation images are retained within a different document layout.

R1.justification: Related-work positioning is updated around SDXL-Lightning, Hyper-SD, and Diff-Instruct, with additional references supporting the new baselines, metrics, and COCO evaluation. The central distinction between self-cooperative clean-data matching and other diffusion-GAN formulations remains. Citation-style changes and relocation of related work are presentational.

T1.justification: v5 adds Proposition 1 and Appendix C, arguing that the cooperative adversarial loss has a data-matching global optimum under sufficient model capacity. This is a focused theoretical addition to the largely retained probabilistic definitions and derivations.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens evidence for the central method through comparisons using matching backbones and quantitative text-to-image component ablations, addressing v4's limited evidence isolating its scaling techniques. CIFAR-10 ablations also separate the effects of the added training strategies. Removing compute-matched comparisons and weakening some training-data documentation are material losses, but the improved experimental support is substantial; this judgment does not rely on treating revised-setting scores as direct performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe YOSO and its self-cooperative diffusion-GAN framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renamed material.

after.justification: v5 reports original CIFAR-10 training and fine-tuning results, text-to-image evaluations, quantitative component ablations, and downstream demonstrations.

before.justification: v4 reports original CIFAR-10 experiments, text-to-image and LoRA evaluations, component ablations, downstream applications, and an appendix quick-adaptation study.

results.title: You Only Sample Once: Taming One-Step Text-to-Image Synthesis by Self-Cooperative Diffusion GANs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and closing section retain the same central contributions: exposing limitations of VQA/captioning-based ICL evaluation, introducing a broad multimodal benchmark, and identifying VLLM strengths and weaknesses. The expanded experiments support this existing agenda.

C2.justification: v1 primarily attributes poor shot scaling to context and image-token limitations. v2 qualifies this explanation by arguing that context extension alone is insufficient, interprets model-size comparisons as evidence of an emergent ICL threshold, and discusses progress over release dates. Its Discussion also explicitly acknowledges limited text-to-image model coverage.

D1.justification: Appendix Table 6 expands configuration documentation with connection modules, image-token representations and context windows for newer models. Conversely, v2 removes v1's code/dataset access link and A100-80GB hardware disclosure. These are documentation changes; the PDFs do not establish that the resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: The main suite expands from eight to ten tasks, adding Fast Counting and Fast Attribute Matching, which require generating images using newly learned count or attribute names. v2 also evaluates an artificial-label Fast Matching MiniImageNet variant; conventional Matching MiniImageNet results remain in Appendix Table 23.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated models including IDEFICS2, VILA, Mantis, Phi3-Vision, LongVA, LLaVA-OneVision and InternLM-XComposer2.5. Appendix Table 27 additionally evaluates Anole-7B on text-to-image MiniImageNet. LongVA and Mantis also join the retained many-shot comparisons in Tables 42–45.

E3.justification: v2 introduces peak accuracy, normalized ICL efficiency and average-rank summaries, plus controlled 4K-to-16K SelfExtend evaluations and LLaVA-OneVision comparisons at 0.5B, 7B and 72B parameters. The COCO judging protocol is inconsistently described: Section 2.2 now names GPT-3.5, while Table 12 retains v1's LLaVA-Next attribution, so an actual judge replacement is unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds context-extension and model-size studies, efficiency-versus-zero-shot analysis, and performance trends by model release date. It expands the existing 64-shot study to additional models. Earlier prompting, repetition and instruction-tuning analyses remain, while v1's aggregate per-shot accuracy-increment analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds and retain the same average and plus/minus reporting practices in detailed result tables. Additional rows extend these practices without introducing new uncertainty procedures, significance tests or an increased run count.

E6.justification: New tasks, models, metrics and controls add substantial results, and the expanded comparison identifies LLaVA-OneVision-72B instead of GPT4V as the overall image-to-text leader. LLaVA-Next-7B's 4-/5-shot Fast Open-Ended MiniImageNet entries change from 0.00/0.33 to 37.24/36.95 (v1 Table 12; v2 Table 16). However, v2 Table 54 retains the old values, preventing a clean performance-gain interpretation.

M1.justification: The work remains a benchmark using pretrained models and support/query prompting, without proposing a revised learning algorithm, architecture or objective. SelfExtend appears as an additional controlled evaluation of an existing technique.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the title and several task descriptions, folds Text Variation into a paragraph, renames Conclusion to Discussion, and relocates qualitative discussion to Appendix C. Most introductory prose, motivation and the main section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The main results presentation shifts to summary Tables 2–5 and selected curves. The updated radar plot moves earlier, while full benchmark curves and qualitative images move to the appendices. Figure 1 gains two task illustrations, and new model-size, efficiency, context-extension and temporal plots substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds recent model and SelfExtend references, cites additional multimodal ICL studies, and explicitly distinguishes its scope from Jiang et al. (2024b)'s recognition-focused many-shot evaluation. The existing related-work organization and principal novelty positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: v2 defines ICL efficiency through normalized area above zero-shot performance and states the bound that zero-shot accuracy plus efficiency cannot exceed 100% (Section 4.1 and Appendix B.7). The original probabilistic ICL formulation remains unchanged; no substantial theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the benchmark's diagnostic value by experimentally probing context length and model size, addressing v1's largely conjectural explanation of shot-scaling failures. Added generation tasks and artificial-label matching broaden the learning abilities tested, while efficiency summaries distinguish adaptation from zero-shot competence. These gains outweigh the reduced reproducibility documentation and reporting inconsistencies, particularly conflicting LLaVA baseline entries and caption-judge attribution, which still require clarification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VL-ICL Bench work. Their complete text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, allowing retained, revised and added material to be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of further tasks and models, context extension and model-size scaling.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLLM benchmark evaluations, image-generation results and analyses of shot scaling, prompting and instruction tuning in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: VL-ICL Bench: The Devil in the Details of Multimodal In-Context Learning

C1.justification: The central claims about training-time physical constraints, residual reduction, unchanged inference, and regularization remain. However, the contribution statement replaces the explicit '1–2 orders of magnitude' claim with 'significantly reduces,' drops the claim of minimal additional training cost, and explicitly extends applicability to differentiable surrogate constraints or objectives.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes ideal sample-based consistency from the conflicting objective introduced by mean estimation and uses this to explain convergence differences. It adds qualifications about discretization bias, excessive residual weighting causing collapse, and reduced accuracy with an uninformative prior. The topology discussion acknowledges that compliance comparisons are affected by differing volume errors, adding an important interpretation boundary.

D1.justification: v2 adds DDIM implementation details, topology conditioning and finite-element assembly/interpolation instructions, and expanded hyperparameter tables. Appendix G discloses GPU hardware and training times, including 13/16/22 hours for standard/mean-estimation/sample-estimation Darcy models. v1 promised code upon publication; v2 states that code is available and supplies a repository link. Availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

E1.justification: v2 adds conditional structural topology optimization using 30,000 optimized structures, with both seen and unseen boundary-condition test scenarios (Section 4.2). This extends coverage from unit-circle sampling and unconditional Darcy fields to constrained mechanical design. The original toy and Darcy tasks remain, partly relocated to Appendix F.
