E2.justification: The Darcy comparison retains standard diffusion, PG-Diffusion, and CoCoGen. v2 adds evaluated topology-optimization comparisons against TopoDiff-G and DOM in Table 1, alongside standard diffusion. TopoDiff's earlier citation in v1 did not constitute an experimental comparison.

E3.justification: Toy training changes from 200 to 400 epochs and from learning rate 0.001 to 0.0005. v2 introduces batch size 16 for Darcy sample estimation versus 64 for mean estimation, and a larger topology model trained for 600k iterations with batch size 4. The new topology protocol reports residual, compliance, and volume-fraction metrics and explicitly evaluates DOM without SIMP post-processing (Appendices F–G).

E4.justification: v2 compares mean and sample estimation on Darcy residuals and convergence, and extends the four toy loss/data ablations to both estimators (Figures 2, 5–6). The topology study additionally tests generalization to unseen boundary conditions. These introduce substantive questions about estimator behavior and robustness beyond v1's retained toy ablations.

E5.justification: The toy results newly report averages over ten training runs with different seeds and 25th/75th-percentile bands (Figures 5–6). v1 Figure 2 reports averaging over generated samples without training-run uncertainty. This is a meaningful but localized reporting improvement; comparable repeated-run uncertainty is not added to the main PDE benchmarks.

E6.justification: v2 adds sample-estimation results, replaces toy curves under revised training settings, and adds the topology results in Table 1. For example, PIDM's in-/out-of-distribution residuals are 1.24e−3/1.29e−3 versus standard diffusion's 1.86e−3/1.97e−3, while standard diffusion has lower compliance error. The new results establish additional tradeoffs; revised toy and Darcy curves should not be interpreted as same-setting gains between versions.

M1.justification: v2 adds a two-step DDIM sample-estimation alternative to evaluating constraints on the predicted conditional mean (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1, Appendix D). The written loss also changes residual aggregation and variance weighting relative to v1 Eq. (19). The topology-optimization adaptation introduces conditioning inputs, joint density/displacement outputs, and finite-element residual evaluation.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the toy study moves to Appendix F.1, detailed Darcy setup to F.2, loss simplification to C, and inequality/optimization objectives to E. Section 3.3 is rewritten around two estimators, while related work and the conclusion are condensed. The appendices gain a thematic A–H structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised to show both estimators, the Darcy learning-curve display gains another method, and the toy display becomes two appendix figures with uncertainty bands. v2 adds the topology comparison table and design/residual figures, expands the architecture/training tables, and reorganizes Darcy sample displays with an additional appendix gallery. These are substantive display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its theoretical context through DDIM, score-based SDEs, Jensen-gap analysis, consistency models, and score-matching literature. Section 5 additionally positions PIDM against topology-specific TopoDiff and newly cited DOM, emphasizing the absence of auxiliary datasets or surrogate models. The original comparison with inference-time physics corrections remains.

T1.justification: v2 adds an idealized continuous-time score-model consistency proposition and proof in Appendix A, replacing v1's brief consistency argument with a formal treatment. Section 3.3 identifies the Jensen-gap inconsistency of mean-based residual evaluation. The residual becomes a concatenated constraint vector, with MAE separately defined for evaluation. Much of v1's likelihood-ratio and auxiliary-objective mathematics is retained in Appendices C and E.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's consistency rationale by identifying the mean-estimation approximation, providing an explicitly idealized proof, and testing a sample-based alternative. Conditional topology optimization substantially broadens validation, while seeded toy results, implementation details, timing disclosures, and reported code access improve transparency and reproducibility. The topology comparisons remain limited by differing volume errors and training budgets, and the proof does not guarantee practical discretized behavior, but the overall gains in scientific support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Physics-Informed Diffusion Models work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on unit-circle sampling, Darcy flow, and topology optimization, including estimator comparisons, generated samples, and quantitative benchmark results in Table 1.

before.justification: v1 reports original unit-circle and Darcy-flow experiments, including generated samples, residual errors, and training/test-loss curves in Figures 2–4.

results.title: Physics-Informed Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central no-box vulnerability claim and three stated contributions remain. The introduction explicitly broadens the transferability claim to differing watermarking algorithms and extends the superiority claim to adversarial-example purification, beyond the earlier architecture and watermark-length comparisons.

C2.justification: v3 explains that attacks on smoothed models exceed their certified perturbation bounds, interprets MI-CWA's low success as a limitation of classifier-based transfer, and discusses DiffPure's image-quality tradeoff. It also explicitly connects expected bitwise-accuracy bounds to double-tail detection. Earlier mechanism explanations and finite-sample caveats remain.

D1.justification: v3 identifies use of Meta's public Stable Signature model, the original StegaStamp architecture, regression smoothing and public DiffPure code. It also specifies the two-watermark classifier's image sources and new ensemble configurations. These add implementation information; the existing attack hyperparameters and learning-rate table are unchanged.

E1.justification: The Stable Diffusion, Midjourney and DALL-E 2 source datasets remain. However, evaluation expands beyond HiDDeN and DWT-DCT to images protected by StegaStamp, Stable Signature and smoothed watermark defenses, plus Tree-Ring under common post-processing. These substantially broaden the tested watermarking environments.

E2.justification: v3 Figures 5 and 14 add the ensemble-classifier attack MI-CWA and diffusion purification method DiffPure to the corresponding attack comparisons. The two-watermark classifier baseline is recast as AdvCls-Enc-WM1&WM2 with explicit target-encoder access. WEvade-B-S, AdvEmb-RN18 and AdvCls-Real&WM remain.

E3.justification: New experiments use equal numbers of HiDDeN and StegaStamp surrogates, regression-smoothed target models, and 100 ResNet-18 classifiers for MI-CWA. MI-CWA and DiffPure are constrained to approximately 0.9 average SSIM. The two-watermark baseline's stated access now includes the encoder. Original sample counts, attack budgets, detection thresholds and Table 1 learning rates remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds smoothed-versus-unsmoothed defense evaluations in Figure 6, common post-processing stress tests of DWT-DCT and Tree-Ring in Figure 10, and successful perturbed-image examples in Figure 1. Existing sensitivity, attack-variant and theory-versus-empirical analyses are retained, including their appendix results.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over test images without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals or significance tests. Surrogate-training bootstrapping and the empirical estimation of theoretical bounds are retained; no new uncertainty-reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: v3 newly reports over 77% evasion across five watermarking targets with 100 surrogates in Figure 6, MI-CWA/DiffPure results in Figures 5 and 14, and non-learning watermark post-processing results in Figure 10. Original HiDDeN attack curves remain unchanged, while several post-processing perturbation and SSIM curves change numerically. The PDFs do not explain those numerical revisions.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same surrogate training, target-watermark choices, ensemble objective, gradient updates and early stopping. The mixed HiDDeN/StegaStamp ensemble used in a new experiment changes the surrogate configuration, without introducing a new attack procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction and baseline descriptions are revised, epsilon is renamed sensitivity, the standalone transfer-adversarial-examples subsection is removed, and formal definitions and assumptions move to Appendix F. The eight-section organization and most method and results prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v3 adds an image montage and two experimental figures, expands comparison bar charts, changes several graph scales and legends, and extensively reformats typography, captions and page layout. The DWT-DCT attack plot moves to the appendix. Appendix figures now interrupt proof sequences, rather than largely following them.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Stable Signature, certified image watermarking, DiffPure, Tree-Ring and Liu et al.'s transferable adversarial examples, while removing the Tramèr et al. reference. Positioning against classifier ensembles becomes more explicit. Chen et al.'s ensemble-attack paper was already cited in v1; its publication update is not a new work.

T1.justification: v1 assumes equal surrogate and target watermark lengths. v3 introduces separate lengths, applies the existing reasoning to their shared bit range, and extends Theorem 3 and Appendix E with trivial bounds of zero and one for unmatched target bits. The central derivations and independence assumptions remain; their relocation to Appendix F is not new theory.

improvement.justification: v1's broad claim relies chiefly on one learned watermark family and lacks an ensemble-classifier comparison. v3 addresses these important gaps through additional watermark families, smoothed defenses and image-quality-constrained MI-CWA/DiffPure comparisons. This substantially strengthens the evidence for generality and comparative effectiveness. Limited documentation of some new settings, unexplained numerical revisions and a more fragmented appendix reduce clarity but do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same paper. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation of material.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by evaluations of additional watermarking methods, defenses and attack comparators.

before.justification: Sections 6–7 and the appendix report original attack evaluations, perturbation measurements, ablations and comparisons between theoretical bounds and empirical results.

results.title: A Transfer Attack to Image Watermarks

C1.justification: V1 presents a general toolkit illustrated by a grounding dataset and an online task suite, with video learning largely a future direction. V2 makes GroundUI, IDMBench, and CriticBench central contributions alongside the environment and tools, turning video-action labeling and broader success detection into explicit benchmark contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning screenshots steering models toward inefficient GUI actions, difficulty terminating action sequences, and the limited benefits of action information for success detection. Its limitations also explicitly address automatic recaptioning errors, dataset leakage or exploitation, and the restriction of online experiments to Ubuntu Docker, extending v1's discussion of evaluator difficulty.

D1.justification: Unlike v1's brief implementation and access descriptions, v2 supplies model versions, decoding settings, execution limits, prompts, response parsing, dataset-source counts, recaptioning costs, task configurations, and detailed tool workflows in Appendices A and C-G. It also adds Hugging Face hosting information. These disclosures do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: V2 extends desktop grounding to evaluated web, desktop, and mobile GroundUI data, introduces single-action and multi-action video-labeling tasks, and broadens the earlier critic evaluation into cross-environment CriticBench. The online suite also expands into additional application tasks, including GIMP. The original 227-example grounding dataset remains represented.

E2.justification: The online comparison changes from GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, and Gemini-1.0 Pro to GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, and adds humans. GroundUI comparisons additionally evaluate CogAgent, CogVLM2, MiniCPM, and PaliGemma variants, among others. The original grounding comparator set is retained in v2 Table 11.

E3.justification: V2 introduces recaptioned, coordinate-only GroundUI evaluation, paired-frame versus sequence-based IDM protocols, and balanced success/failure trajectory evaluation with additional classification metrics. Its expanded online suite uses functional evaluators with manual validation, whereas v1 relied on human evaluation for level-3 tasks. Controlled comparisons also vary screenshot observations and the availability of action information.

E4.justification: V2 adds instruction-recaptioning ablations, text-only versus screenshot observation comparisons, and action-information ablations for success detection. It also adds a five-category failure analysis, active-finish analysis, and detailed successful and failed trajectories. V1's location/type and element-size analyses are retained in v2 Figures 4 and 7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. V2 adds evaluation metrics and decoding settings, but no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V1 Table 2 is preserved numerically in v2 Table 11, while the original 77-task results are replaced by results for the expanded online suite. New findings include 36.6% overall success for Claude 3.5 Sonnet versus 72.2% for humans, and 61.1% GroundUI-1K accuracy for SeeClick. IDMBench, CriticBench, and ablations add substantial further results. These are new comparisons under revised settings, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The Python-based GUI/API control backbone remains, but v2 substantially extends the toolkit's data-construction procedures. It adds trajectory recording followed by video refinement that removes noisy operations and aggregates atomic actions, plus GPT-4o-based instruction recaptioning (Sections 3 and 5.1; Appendix G), beyond v1's stepwise annotation workflow.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around three desiderata. Environment and tools receive separate sections, online benchmarking precedes fine-grained evaluation, related work moves later, and parts of the earlier actionable-insights discussion are reorganized into Appendix B. Extensive explanations and dedicated appendices substantially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, restructures the environment-comparison table, and adds task/data composition charts, ablation plots, and numerous results tables. The original grounding table moves to Appendix A, and its paired analysis figure is split and reformatted. New appendix screenshots, annotated examples, and prompt/trajectory panels substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially updates its positioning through comparisons with OSWorld and AndroidWorld and discussion of WebLINX, MoTIF, and other added references. It emphasizes lightweight setup, combined GUI/API interaction, and decomposition of agent abilities, and explicitly positions IDMBench and CriticBench as filling benchmark gaps. This goes beyond relocating related work.

T1.justification: V2 adds an explicit POMDP formalization with observation, action, reward, and language-feedback spaces, and formalizes inverse-dynamics prediction and trajectory-outcome classification. These extend v1's simple task tuples, but neither version develops theorems, proofs, or theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited illustrative validation through targeted capability benchmarks, controlled ablations, human comparisons, evaluator validation, and detailed failure evidence. Its appendices make experimental procedures and toolkit use much more reproducible. These gains materially improve support for the toolkit's claimed usefulness, while the expanded limitations clarify remaining annotation errors, evaluator reliability concerns, and the restricted online testing environment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AgentStudio, with matching authors, core infrastructure, and retained experiments. Text, tables, equations, and figures support reliable comparison, including all v2 Appendices A-G. V1 ends with references and has no appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original evaluations on the 205-task online suite, GroundUI-1K, IDMBench, and CriticBench, together with human comparisons, ablations, and failure analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations on 227 GUI-grounding examples and 77 online tasks, including task success and critic accuracy (Tables 2-3).

results.title: AgentStudio: A Toolkit for Building General Virtual Agents

C1.justification: The pruning-and-replacement and stability contributions remain central. v4 extends the headline retention claim from 7B to 7B or 13B models and explicitly claims training-efficiency advantages over concurrent pruning methods, broadening the earlier emphasis on accuracy and stability.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations based on hidden-state magnitude and calibration-data sensitivity for choosing cosine similarity, and recasts replacement versus LoRA as local knowledge recovery versus redistribution across remaining layers. It qualifies the earlier GSM8K failure observation with recovery under more training, discusses the associated cost, and adds Appendix E's stated limitation relative to quantization.

D1.justification: v4 revises the documented LoRA hyperparameters, lists selected layer indices in Table 8, and specifies the full-data training size and reported computational cost. Captions clarify that dagger-marked networks halve the intermediate dimension. Existing replacement-training hyperparameters, A800 hardware information, and data-mixture proportions are retained.

E1.justification: The classification and generation benchmarks, including the smaller-OPT benchmark suite, are retained. v4 Appendix A adds Wikitext and standalone C4 calibration scenarios alongside SlimPajama to test pruning-data sensitivity. The additional model families do not introduce new downstream tasks or languages.

E2.justification: v4 Appendix A adds an evaluated perplexity-based pruning comparator explicitly identified as SLEB in Table 9. Existing LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT, LaCo, and LoRA comparisons remain. Shortened Llama appears in the related-work comparison table but receives no new performance evaluation.

E3.justification: v4 adds Llama2-13B and four Baichuan/Baichuan2 model configurations, plus a 5.49M-sample post-training condition. The reported LoRA protocol changes from rank 384 to 128, 30,000 to 300,000 training samples, ten epochs to one, and learning rate 5e-5 to 1e-4 (Section 4.7 and training appendices). These are substantive setting changes, not evidence of a same-setting performance comparison.

E4.justification: New Appendix A tests whether cosine- and perplexity-based pruning select consistent layers across calibration corpora and preserve downstream performance. New Appendix D.5 tests whether substantially more post-training data improves recovery and at what computational cost. Earlier architecture, initialization, and pruning-ratio analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark results. The existing perplexity standard deviations used to construct the stability metric remain unchanged and are not estimates of uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results for Llama2-13B, Baichuan models, calibration sensitivity, and training-data scaling. For example, Llama2-13B FFN reports 53.2 average classification accuracy and 84.9 stability. Under revised settings, Table 6 replaces LoRA accuracy/stability of 44.6/82.6 with 44.5/82.1 and GPU memory of 47.6 G with 56.4 G. Earlier main Llama2-7B and OPT results are retained.

M1.justification: Both versions select contiguous layers using hidden-state cosine similarity and train a lightweight replacement using MSE. The replacement architectures, initialization alternatives, and optional language-model post-training remain unchanged; additional comparisons and explanations do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: The introduction, methodological discussion, results narrative, and related-work section are extensively rewritten. Sections 4.5–4.7 gain explicit takeaway statements, appendices are reorganized, and citation style and terminology are revised. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental material.

P2.justification: Main Tables 2–4 now pair Llama2-7B with Llama2-13B, while the original OPT-6.7B blocks move into separate appendix tables. New tables display concurrent-method characteristics, calibration comparisons, Baichuan results, and data scaling. Figures receive styling and legend updates, alongside a different document header and heading layout.

R1.justification: The brief earlier positioning is expanded into a detailed comparison with concurrent layer-pruning approaches, including newly cited SLEB and Shortened Llama. Table 7 contrasts selection criteria, training requirements, data, and trained modules. Existing ShortGPT and UIDL references receive substantially fuller treatment, and additional literature supports the cosine-similarity rationale.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same residual-layer formulation, cosine criterion, MSE objective, confidence statistic, and stability definition. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added; the new methodological discussions are conceptual explanations.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation through larger and additional model families and direct tests of previously untested pruning-criterion and training-data choices. Appendix D.5 also qualifies v3's mathematical-task failure observation by documenting partial recovery and its reported 100-fold computational cost. Expanded research positioning and an explicit quantization limitation clarify scope. Broader efficiency claims still lack uniform matched comparisons, and the revised LoRA scores are not directly comparable across versions, but the additions resolve important empirical validation gaps.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLM-Streamline. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, experiments, and results can be matched despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and adds Llama2-13B and Baichuan evaluations, calibration-data sensitivity tests, and a larger-data post-training study.

before.justification: v3 reports original pruning experiments on Llama2-7B and OPT models, including benchmark evaluations, replacement-network ablations, pruning-ratio analyses, and a LoRA comparison.

results.title: Streamlining Redundant Layers to Compress Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central claims remain that sinusoidal activation increases low-rank matrices' rank without additional trainable parameters and improves performance across language, vision and 3D applications. Rewritten contributions emphasize its drop-in character, while the expanded experiments support the existing broad applicability claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds discussion of small or zero frequencies, explains frequency-induced gradient amplification and the gain factor's stabilizing role, and explicitly acknowledges that frequency selection lacks a principled rule and requires tuning. The principal limitation concerning the remaining accuracy gap to full-rank models is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 supplies previously unspecified gain scaling, experiment-specific frequencies, learning rates, epochs and batch sizes, alongside codebase, hardware and timing information. This substantially expands reproducibility documentation. One disclosure remains unclear: Table 13 associates Thai Statue rank-1 IoU 90.8 with frequency 200, whereas retained Figure 9 places that value near frequency 700.

E1.justification: v2 adds commonsense evaluation on BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c and OBQA. Occupancy evaluations expand from Thai Statue to include Lucy and Dragon. The original GLUE, image-classification and LLFF coverage remains; ConvNeXt uses the already evaluated CIFAR100 dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds DoRA comparisons in Table 7, implementing the rank-8 baseline and using cited results at ranks 16 and 32. It also removes the unactivated low-rank reference from the ViT frequency comparison, formerly v1 Table 5 and now v2 Table 10. Existing principal LoRA, low-rank and full-rank comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include LLaMA 3-8B adaptation of five attention/MLP modules at ranks 4–32 and ConvNeXt-Tiny experiments decomposing the final stage's linear layers with a 150-epoch training budget. DoRA introduces additional rank/configuration comparisons. These extend evaluation substantially; newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices A.2.1 and A.2.4 add training-memory measurements for LLaMA and NeRF, plus LLaMA training-time comparisons, testing practical overhead beyond parameter counts. The existing activation comparisons and ViT, NeRF and occupancy frequency sweeps are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.2 explicitly states that GLUE results average five random seeds. v2 retains those scores but removes this statement without supplying replacement run-count or uncertainty information. This is reduced statistical reporting, not evidence that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: v2 adds LLaMA/DoRA, ConvNeXt, Lucy/Dragon and resource-cost results. Retained GLUE scores are unchanged. NeRF improvement entries are corrected from 3.12 to 3.10 at rank 5 and 0.74 to 0.77 at rank 60. ViT training-loss entries disappear when the tables become plots. New Table 2 contains a rank-16 delta inconsistency: 84.35 minus 82.90 equals 1.45, although 2.45 is reported.

M1.justification: The core sine transformation in Equation 3 is unchanged. Appendix A.2.1 adds a sine-DoRA variant that applies this transformation to the direction update within DoRA's magnitude/direction parameterization. Newly specified gain and frequency choices are implementation disclosures rather than evidence of a redesigned core method.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, revises introduction/contribution and conclusion passages, places language-model experiments before ViT, and reorganizes appendices around application-specific experiments. These are localized narrative and structural revisions; much of the existing methodological and interpretive prose remains close to v1.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes a four-application overview, ViT tables become performance-versus-parameter plots, and the full NeRF image grid moves to the appendix while selected examples join a redrawn rate-distortion plot. Numerous new tables, an expanded occupancy table, revised plot styling and the conference-template layout substantially alter presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning and citations involving DoRA and circular-convolution parameter-efficient fine-tuning, plus references supporting ConvNeXt, commonsense datasets and implementation choices. The existing low-rank decomposition and parameter-efficient learning discussion is largely retained; bibliography-format and publication-metadata changes do not constitute new positioning.

T1.justification: Proposition 1, Theorem 1, both supporting lemmas and their proof arguments are substantively unchanged. Appendix A.1 adds an explicit reminder of the operator norm already used in the proofs and explanatory remarks, without a new theorem, revised assumption or corrected derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's sparse implementation documentation by specifying gain, frequencies and training settings, while resource measurements make practical efficiency assessable. LLaMA/DoRA and ConvNeXt experiments strengthen support beyond the earlier model and comparator coverage. These gains outweigh the loss of five-seed disclosure and ViT training-loss values, although the new numerical and frequency inconsistencies limit confidence in some details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sine-activated low-rank research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite the changed title and organization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds LLaMA 3-8B, sine-DoRA, ConvNeXt, additional shape-reconstruction and resource-cost results. Some DoRA baseline scores are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original ViT training, GLUE fine-tuning, LLFF reconstruction and Thai Statue occupancy results, together with frequency ablations.

results.title: Efficient Learning with Sine-Activated Low-Rank Matrices

C1.justification: The headline contribution broadens from tree-search reasoning to general tree-structured inference, explicitly encompassing few-shot prompting and speculative decoding. v2 promotes both Node and Flatten implementations and replaces the two-task 1.7–2.4× claim with separate end-to-end and attention claims of up to 2.52× and 3.82× across three workload families.

C2.justification: v2 explains how KV materialization dominates unpaged execution and how paging shifts the bottleneck toward attention (Section 4.2). It attributes modest reasoning gains to narrow trees and limited attention overhead, and explicitly limits substantial gains to sufficiently large shared contexts or numerous queries (Sections 4.3 and 5). Appendix A.6 additionally explains declining benefits as suffixes grow.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the retained pseudocode with a backend/paging matrix, an explicit depth-first layout description, and workload specifications covering stopping criteria, tree shapes, and recorded speculative acceptance lengths (Tables 5–6 and 10; Appendix A.5). However, v1's explicit 100-tree workload count is no longer reported.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates sorting 128 numbers and document merging. v2 retains these and adds keyword counting, set intersection, and APPS-based few-shot prompting and speculative-decoding workloads (Tables 6–7 and 10), substantially broadening the tasks and tree-structured inference scenarios evaluated.

E2.justification: Radix Attention from SGLang becomes an evaluated comparator, including on the retained reasoning tasks, alongside Flash-Decoding and Tree Attention-Medusa (v2 Tables 7, 11–12). It provides the strongest end-to-end baseline. The stated Flash-Decoding implementation also changes from CUDA in v1 Section 4.1 to Triton in v2 Table 5.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated model from Llama2-7B-HF to Llama3-8B, although v2's citation still identifies Llama 2. v2 introduces explicit paged/unpaged configurations, separate attention timing, and expanded partial-result IO accounting. New protocols include approximately 4,000-token prompts with 400 decoding iterations and speculative token trees of 32–256 queries.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Node-versus-Flatten split ablation linked to node-length dispersion (Figure 5), memory-management latency decompositions (Figures 4 and 13), and tree-width sensitivity analysis (Figure 14). v1's thought-length distributions and task-averaged reasoning iteration plots (Figures 7–8) are not retained. The questions investigated therefore change substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed timing experiments, confidence intervals, significance tests, or defined uncertainty estimates for performance. v2 Figure 5's standard deviation describes tree-node lengths, not uncertainty in measured speedups; v1's 100 trees are workload samples rather than reported repeated runs.

E6.justification: Reasoning measurements are replaced under revised model and memory settings: DEFT-Node sorting/document latency is 305/272 seconds in v1 Table 4 versus 114.06/81.87 seconds in v2 Table 11. v2 adds extensive Flatten, Radix, and new-task results, including 1.03–1.10× reasoning and up to 2.52× speculative end-to-end speedups over Radix. These do not establish same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The core attention algorithms persist: Algorithms 1–4 match across versions after the DEFT-Subtree-to-DEFT-Flatten rename. v2 reports adapting DEFT kernels to paged as well as unpaged KV storage (Table 5 and Appendix A.1), a limited system extension. Balanced splitting, bit masks, and global reduction already appear in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around general tree-structured inference. System, kernel, and workload explanations are reorganized between the main text and appendices; experiments gain dedicated bottleneck and ablation sections, and the appendix gains a contents list and expanded organization.

P2.justification: The interaction and QKV-grouping diagrams are substantially redrawn, and results are reorganized into separate attention, end-to-end, and IO tables. New bottleneck, split-ablation, and width-sensitivity plots accompany these changes. Existing diagrams are also relocated, including v1 Figures 2 and 5 becoming v2 Figures 6 and 11, while the document template changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A.3 substantially expand positioning against ChunkAttention, Hydragen, and Bifurcated Attention. Table 8 distinguishes shared IO-reduction ideas from DEFT's claimed support for deeper trees and balanced workloads. Additional citations cover Prompt Cache, APPS, few-shot learning, self-consistency, and inference systems.

T1.justification: The core definitions and prefix-sharing argument remain. v2 Table 4 introduces a QKV-group factor into query IO accounting and includes scaling, mask, and masked-logit costs; the worked crossover changes from 32 to 29 queries. Appendix A.3 also supplies an explicit LogSumExp attention-merging argument in Equation 2.

improvement.justification: v1 tests only Node on two reasoning workloads and leaves its balanced variant without results. v2 evaluates that variant, introduces the stronger paged Radix comparator, and separates attention gains from memory-management costs through breakdowns and ablations. Broader workloads and explicit limits substantially strengthen the evidence and interpretation of speedups. Reporting remains imperfect: v2 omits the earlier 100-tree count and has a model-label/citation mismatch. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial empirical and analytical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DEFT and retain matching core definitions and algorithms. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison without material extraction gaps.

after.justification: v2 reports original latency and IO measurements across few-shot prompting, four reasoning tasks, and speculative decoding, plus ablations and bottleneck analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original latency and IO measurements for sorting and document-merging workloads, including averages over 100 trees in Table 4 and per-iteration results in Figure 8.

results.title: DeFT: Decoding with Flash Tree-attention for Efficient Tree-structured LLM Inference

C1.justification: The central IO-reduction claims and headline 2.52×/3.82× speedups remain. V3 centers the contribution on DeFT-Flatten, explicitly adds comparison of three splitting strategies, and extends the conclusion to claim effectiveness across LLM models and GPU architectures. These are bounded extensions of the original contribution.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands interpretation: Node-Chunk's weakness with many small nodes, chunk-size tradeoffs between query IO and GPU scheduling, reduced gains when larger models increase FFN overhead, and floating-point explanations for numerical discrepancies. The dedicated limitations paragraph disappears, but the substantive qualification about limited benefits for small trees remains in Section 4.3.

D1.justification: V3 newly discloses a default KV chunk size of 128 and NVIDIA Nsight Compute as the profiling tool, and specifies hardware, model, and measurement details for added experiments. The default-size disclosure does not establish a change to earlier experiments. Existing system descriptions and pseudocode are largely retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use APPS, the same four GoT-derived reasoning tasks, and Medusa-derived speculative decoding traces. The added experiments vary models, hardware, prompt padding, and metrics within these workloads, without introducing an identifiable new dataset or task.

E2.justification: V3 adds DeFT-Node-Chunk to evaluated comparisons and Hugging Face vanilla attention as the numerical reference in Table 15. Flash-Decoding, Tree Attention-Medusa, and Radix Attention remain the main external comparators. DeFT-Node's end-to-end latency and IO comparison rows disappear, although its attention comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain, but v3 adds CodeLlama-7B/34B, MHA/GQA comparisons, RTX 4090 experiments, sorting prompts padded to 5K–10K tokens, and chunk-size sweeps from 128 to 1024. New protocols measure GPU utilization and attention/PPL agreement, substantially broadening evaluation beyond the original latency and IO measurements.

E4.justification: V3 adds Node-Chunk ablations, GPU utilization profiling, numerical accuracy checks, and sensitivity studies covering prompt length, model size, architecture, GPU, and chunk size (Tables 6–8, 14–15, 18–21; Figure 15). The earlier topology and tree-width analyses remain. V2's Figure 13, containing four reasoning-task latency breakdowns, is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained node-length standard deviation describes tree structure. V3's new attention and PPL errors measure numerical agreement, rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: The main DeFT-Flatten latency and IO values are retained across v2 Tables 7/11/12 and v3 Tables 16/5/17. V3 adds extensive accuracy, utilization, Node-Chunk, and configuration-dependent results. DeFT-Node's b=30 attention latency changes from 11.41 to 10.62 seconds, and previously unsupported cases receive results. Its end-to-end/IO rows and the four-task latency breakdowns are removed.

M1.justification: V3 introduces DeFT-Node-Chunk, which subdivides individual nodes into KV blocks while retaining node-wise grouping (Section 3.3). This is a limited procedural addition. DeFT-Flatten's existing flattening, masking, and reduction procedure remains unchanged; Algorithms 1–4 are identical apart from formatting.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method exposition are substantially rewritten around prefix-aware and balanced QKV partitioning. Segmented attention becomes introductory material, the IO analysis moves to the appendix, and the final section becomes a conclusion. This reorganizes the argument substantially beyond merely appending experiments.

P2.justification: V3 redesigns the overview and partitioning diagrams, expands and transposes Table 2, and adds a supplementary tree-attention diagram. End-to-end results move into the main text while attention results move to the appendix. Numerous analytical tables and a chunk-size plot are added, and the four-panel reasoning latency breakdown is removed.

R1.justification: V3 adds references to Quest and NVIDIA Nsight Compute documentation and refines descriptions of baseline partitioning and load balancing. The principal positioning against Flash-Decoding, Medusa, SpecInfer, SGLang, and concurrent prefix-sharing methods remains. The switch to author-year citations is a presentation change.

T1.justification: V2's explicit decoding-tree and tree-attention definitions are omitted. The IO analysis moves from Section 3.4 to Appendix A.5 and gains Radix Attention and Node-Chunk entries, including the latter's sum-of-ceilings group-count formula. The segmented-softmax equation restates the existing merging identity rather than establishing a new theorem.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation that was concentrated on latency and IO in v2. Numerical fidelity checks, direct GPU utilization measurements, the Node-Chunk comparison, and broader model/hardware experiments provide stronger evidence for correctness, the proposed mechanism, and applicability boundaries. The rewritten explanation also makes partitioning choices easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed reasoning-task latency breakdowns; the improvement comes from stronger support for retained results, rather than higher headline performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeFT research, with matching algorithms, workloads, and core results. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains the original experiments and adds numerical accuracy checks, GPU profiling, and experiments varying splitting strategies, models, hardware, prompt lengths, and chunk sizes.

before.justification: V2 reports original latency and IO measurements for few-shot prompting, multi-step reasoning, and speculative decoding, together with splitting-strategy and tree-width analyses.

results.title: DeFT: Decoding with Flash Tree-attention for Efficient Tree-structured LLM Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: zero-shot composition of video and multiview priors, parallel generation without 4D training data, efficient reconstruction and flexible conditioning. The additional experiments and qualifications do not redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: A.2–A.3 explicitly discuss textureless backs, corrupted motion and rotations that violate the independence assumption, extending v1's limited caveats. A.4 explains domain and viewpoint biases; A.5 explains choosing image-mediated text generation and attributes reconstruction-score advantages partly to camera alignment. These materially qualify applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies eight A6000 GPUs, a 33.8-degree field of view, a 2 m camera radius, dataset provenance, four-view CLIP averaging, and 50 user-study participants evaluating eight named samples. A.4 adds initialization and view-weighting formulas, including a 25-step preliminary pass. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the repository link is unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds partial-observation reconstruction using both a front-view video and reference-frame multiview images from six animated models, introducing a distinct conditioning scenario and data population. Figure 6 also demonstrates explicit text-to-4D prompts. The Animate124, Consistent4D and Objaverse sources newly identified for the original experiments are provenance disclosures, not established dataset replacements.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 is unchanged. For the new partial-reconstruction comparison, A.5 adapts Consistent4D by adding reference-view pixelwise reconstruction loss and rendering inputs with Zero-1-to-3 camera intrinsics. This changes the evaluated comparator variant without introducing a new baseline family.

E3.justification: A.5 introduces a ground-truth reconstruction protocol with joint conditioning observations and PSNR/SSIM evaluation on six animated models. Figure 5 also revises the reported extreme controls from pure SVD/SV3D to logistic schedules with s0=0 or 1 and k=20. This establishes changed reported settings, not that the retained ablations were rerun.

E4.justification: The original schedule-sensitivity analysis remains, with its extreme settings recharacterized as model-dominant mixtures. A.4 adds an unquantified experimental finding that two-pass initialization reduces failures more effectively than simply doubling inference steps. No dedicated numerical ablation accompanies this additional comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's participant count describes the existing user study; its two sampling passes are algorithmic steps, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All scores, preference percentages and generation times in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. New Table 3 reports PSNR/SSIM of 18.41/0.87 for Consistent4D, 20.45/0.89 for Diffusion2-stage1 and 21.55/0.90 for stage2. Figures 6–7 add text-conditioned and reconstruction results. These extend the evidence to new settings rather than establish same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core SVD/SV3D score-composition and Gaussian-reconstruction framework remains. v3 adds an explicit text-to-image-to-4D input procedure with background removal and recentering (A.5). A.4 also documents two-pass initialization and view-dependent mixing, but does not establish whether these refinements were already used for v1's retained experiments.

P1.justification: Substantial paragraph rewriting extends across the introduction, related work, method and experiments. Separate task-result subsections become one Main results section; conditioning and parallelism explanations are reorganized, and ablation discussion gains parameter-specific headings. These narrative revisions extend beyond simply appending new scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, Figure 3 rearranges stage rows and method labels, and Figure 5 gains revised labels and separate parameter panels. Existing tables are restyled and relocated, while Figures 6–7 and Table 3 add new displays. The changes substantially affect visual presentation, despite retaining many original examples.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly credits MultiDiffusion and SyncDiffusion as inspiration and adds references for FreeInit, variational autoencoders and additional Gaussian representations. It removes the HexPlane and Sora-geometrical-consistency references. The broad positioning against SDS-based generation and Efficient4D remains.

T1.justification: Assumption 3.1 changes from independence between entire row/column sets to a pairwise-image formulation. New A.3 supplies a rotation counterexample, continuity and local-independence assumptions, and an approximate derivation of the score decomposition. This substantially expands and revises the theoretical conditions, although the main theorem's displayed conclusion remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves auditability by supplying study, dataset and hardware details missing from v1, whose user-study appendix reference had no accompanying appendix. It adds ground-truth fidelity evaluation beyond CLIP similarity and explicitly identifies failures of the central assumption. These address important documentation and applicability gaps. A.3 remains an approximate argument and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, so the improvement does not establish fully resolved theoretical or statistical rigor.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Diffusion2 and contain readable text, equations, figures and tables. v1 ends after its references; v3 additionally contains Appendix A.1–A.5. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds text-to-4D examples and a partial-observation reconstruction evaluation in Appendix A.5, Figures 6–7 and Table 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation examples, a user study, quantitative video-to-4D comparisons and schedule ablations in Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: Diffusion$^2$: Dynamic 3D Content Generation via Score Composition of Video and Multi-view Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central claims remain output-based reconstruction of model relationships and inexpensive benchmark prediction. The Discussion adds a claim that PhyloLM reveals how quantization fidelity depends on model size, modestly broadening its stated utility.

C2.justification: v2 identifies chat-interface prompting as a confound in interpreting model distances, substantially qualifying v1's interpretation of isolated proprietary-model branches. It also argues against family-only prediction using new controls, acknowledges the code reconstruction's incorrect root, expands family-specific interpretations, and adds the limitation that temperature effects were not investigated.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C substantially expand reproducibility information: dataset fields and sizes, sampling temperature 0.7 and top-p 1, A100 memory and GPU allocation, the Falcon180B precision exception, API access details, benchmark-score sources and prompting settings, and algorithm pseudocode. These are principally newly documented details, not evidence that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Reported benchmark coverage expands from MMLU and ARC to include HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande, and GSM8K. The analyzed model population also adds Gemma and proprietary Claude, PaLM/Gemini, and Mistral models. Open-Web-Math and MBXP remain the context sources.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing genealogy-inference or benchmark-prediction methods against PhyloLM. The added LLMs are study subjects, while GPTQ and AWQ in Appendix H concern quantized model inputs rather than alternative PhyloLM baselines.

E3.justification: Prediction changes from leave-one-model-out to leave-one-family-out evaluation. v2 also separates completion and chat interfaces and expands model configurations. Section 2.6 states that prediction excludes proprietary models, but Tables 4–5 include GPT results, leaving the precise inclusion protocol inconsistent.

E4.justification: v2 adds within-family correlations addressing whether prediction merely identifies model families, analyses of chat/completion interface effects in Appendix G, and quantization sensitivity across Qwen1.5 model sizes in Appendix H. The existing gene-count/probe-count sensitivity studies and math/code comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use eight independently sampled gene sets and show hyperparameter error bars; v2 newly identifies those bars as SEM. It additionally reports correlation summaries with SEM and confidence-interval displays, Student's t-tests, family-specific p-values and sample counts, and a quantization significance test. No increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: The two-benchmark prediction plots are replaced by substantially expanded results under the revised predictor and family-held-out protocol. Tables 4–5 newly report overall MMLU correlations of 0.88 for math contexts and 0.79 for code contexts. Appendix H adds quantization rankings and model-size trends. These are new results under changed conditions, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 2.6 replaces 15-dimensional MDS of distances and a 200-hidden-unit MLP with 15-dimensional ICA of similarities and sigmoid logistic regression. This substantially changes the performance-prediction component. The underlying Nei similarity, distance transformation, and four-character sampling procedure remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methods explanations, results narrative, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Headings and terminology are revised, including replacing much of 'genome' with 'set of genes'. Limitations are integrated into the Discussion, and the appendix is reorganized into dedicated algorithm, interpretation, prediction, and quantization sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. The analogy and reconstruction diagrams are redrawn, global rooted dendrograms become separate unrooted completion/chat displays, and model tables gain benchmark columns. New statistical panels and quantization figures substantially change the visual presentation; named dendrograms are supplied separately in Appendix I.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the expanded study, including PaLM, Gemini, Gemma, Mixtral, GPTQ, AWQ, MergeKit, the Open LLM Leaderboard, and GPT-Fathom. The central positioning as an adaptation of population-genetic methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The Nei similarity formula, negative-log distance transformation, population/context/token analogy, and variability computations are retained. Explicit averaging notation and Appendix C pseudocode clarify existing computations without introducing substantive mathematical results, formal assumptions, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly leaves unresolved whether predictions merely reflect model families. v2 directly addresses this weakness through family-held-out evaluation and within-family analyses, while recognizing interface confounds and substantially improving experimental documentation. These changes strengthen the paper beyond simply adding benchmarks. Inconsistent GPT inclusion, retained MLP/point-held-out caption wording, and discrepancies between statistical summaries and appendix tables weaken auditability, but the overall methodological and reproducibility gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PhyloLM. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original phylogenetic analyses, predictions across six benchmarks, within-family analyses, and quantization experiments. These analyses qualify independently of the externally sourced benchmark scores.

before.justification: v1 reports original hyperparameter experiments, similarity matrices, phylogenetic reconstructions, and MMLU/ARC performance predictions, including code-context replications in Appendix D.

results.title: PhyloLM: Inferring the Phylogeny of Large Language Models and Predicting their Performances in Benchmarks

C1.justification: The main LMB/LRM contributions and first-binarization claim remain. However, the abstract, introduction, and conclusion now describe 1.1-bit rather than 1-bit weights and revise headline savings from 16.0× FLOPs/27.1× storage to 9.3× OPs/24.8× storage, narrowing the quantitative efficiency claim.

C2.justification: Appendix B.3 adds substantive interpretations of placement tradeoffs, diminishing returns from additional bases, and LRM's weaker FID performance than MSE at four-bit weights. It also attributes differences from EfficientDM partly to full-model training and access to original data. Section 4.3 newly identifies generic layerwise activation quantization as a limitation.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies CPU/A800 80GB hardware, 20-step DDIM sampling for ImageNet, and training-step/time pairs. Its checklist promises supplementary code, without establishing accessible code in the supplied material. Existing batch sizes, approximate training duration, and relative learning-rate descriptions remain.

E1.justification: All five image datasets and the unconditional/conditional generation tasks are retained, including relocated FFHQ results. However, v2 removes v1 Appendix C's human evaluation of image quality and condition-image consistency, involving 50 users and 20 image sets.

E2.justification: v2 Table 10 newly evaluates Q-DM and TDQ on LSUN-Bedrooms; Q-DM was previously only cited. Table 18 adds EfficientDM to ImageNet comparisons, while Tables 16–17 introduce mixed-precision LSQ and QALoRA controls. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparisons beyond v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces detailed LMB placement/basis-count sweeps, higher-precision LRM controls, and ImageNet training budgets from 10K to 150K steps. Appendix B.1 also revises reported efficiency accounting from scaled FLOPs to OPs combining BOPs/64 with full-precision FLOPs. The original 50,000-sample generation evaluation remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 already ablated component inclusion, LMB scope, PCA reduction, and initialization. v2 retains these and adds head/tail versus central placement, finer placement sweeps, additional binary bases, higher-precision distillation, mixed-precision controls, QALoRA training, and training-duration analyses (Tables 10–18). These substantially deepen tests of the design rationale.

E5.justification: v2 checklist item 7 newly states that random seeds were fixed for all experiments. It supplies neither seed values nor repeated-run counts or newly defined uncertainty estimates; this disclosure does not establish additional runs or statistical significance.

E6.justification: Most original generation scores are retained. The main ImageNet/DDIM result changes from IS 163.14/FID 10.00 to 190.36/10.40; the earlier values reappear at 150K steps in v2 Table 18, so a matched-setting gain is not established. Numerous new comparison/ablation results, revised costs such as LDM-4 BinaryDM's 40.8 to 42.1 MB size, and removal of user-study outcomes substantially change the evidence.

M1.justification: The default dual-basis LMB, PCA-based LRM objective, and progressive initialization remain unchanged. Appendix B.3 adds a limited extension to three- and four-basis LMB variants (Table 12). Relabeling the default weights from 1 to 1.1 bits does not itself establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The title drops the BinaryDM prefix, and the abstract and portions of the introduction and method receive targeted rewrites. Method headings change, Appendix B separates quantitative results from additional analyses, and a checklist is appended. The main narrative sequence and substantial portions of the prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text to a single-column layout, redraws the overview, adds an accuracy-efficiency plot, and splits or relocates major tables. Original sample images are retained and rearranged, while user-study plots disappear. Some revised captions incorrectly describe eight- and 32-bit activation panels as four-bit, including Figures 10–11.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to MeliusNet, attribution-rank-preserving mixed-precision quantization, and GWQ to support efficiency accounting. It also expands discussion of differences from EfficientDM. The broader related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The LRM projection definition changes multiplication order: v1 Equation 12 places the PCA matrix before the features, whereas v2 Equation 11 places it afterward while retaining the stated tensor shapes. This is a localized mathematical revision; the principal derivations remain and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central accuracy-efficiency argument through placement and matched mixed-precision controls that test whether gains merely reflect extra precision. Explicit 1.1-bit reporting, fuller operation accounting, and acknowledgment of EfficientDM's different training/data access address important weaknesses in v1's comparisons. Removing the user study and introducing misleading sample captions are losses, but the improvements to core validation and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BinaryDM and provide readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, and appendices. Renamed sections and relocated results can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original generation experiments and adds quantization, architectural-control, and training-budget results in Appendix B.3.

before.justification: v1 reports original DDIM/LDM generation experiments, component ablations, efficiency measurements, and a 50-person user study.

results.title: BinaryDM: Accurate Weight Binarization for Efficient Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The common-cause claim about information imbalance and the principal object-bias findings remain. However, v2 adds the connection between modality gap and logit entropy as a central abstract, introduction, and conclusion contribution. This substantially extends the claimed explanation to a functional role in representing uncertainty.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 introduces the interpretation that embedding changes associated with the gap permit entropy adjustment, distinguishing this from global temperature control and explicitly qualifying causality. Appendix D.2 adds explanations involving CLIP-A training and data filtering. v1's standalone discussion of synthetic-to-real generalization, scale, and applicability beyond contrastive models is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices F.1–F.5 document architectures, training schedules, learning rates, batches, caption truncation, initialization, and fine-tuning for the new experiments. For example, CC12M training specifies RN50, 30 epochs, and batch size 1760. Appendix E.1 explicitly supplies MOAD normalization factors. Existing MAD hyperparameters and the OpenCLIP access reference remain.

E1.justification: v1's controlled caption-information interventions use synthetic MAD. v2 adds natural-caption truncation experiments on CC12M and image-image matching with selectively cropped views on MS COCO (Appendices F.1 and F.4). These introduce materially different information-imbalance scenarios while retaining the original evaluation benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds a real-words baseline within the ideal-word and shifted-ideal-word comparison; v1 Section 4.3 reports only their alignment similarities. Appendix F.1 also evaluates L2I alongside RMG as an alternative gap measure. The established CLIP/SigLIP and RMG/L2M comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 filters the analytical cohort from 112 to 98 models, changes the medium-dataset cutoff from 128M to 140M, and replaces Spearman with Kendall correlations. Dimension-ablation plots use RMG instead of L2M, and Table 5 revises the stated centering treatment for shifted ideal words. New caption-length, temperature-freezing, and image-image experiments introduce additional controlled evaluation designs.

E4.justification: v2 adds caption-truncation and temperature ablations, CommonPool filtering analysis, CLIP/CLIP-A stratification, controlled word-prior experiments, and image-image/direct-embedding tests distinguishing information imbalance from loss or initialization effects. The ideal-word analysis now tests downstream accuracy. Existing MAD and dimension-ablation analyses remain, but v1 Figure 7b's caption-presence classification-accuracy panel is removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports three-seed MAD averages without correlation significance tests. v2 adds significance indicators in Table 1 and numerical p-values in Table 3 and Appendix D.2, materially expanding uncertainty assessment for central evidence. MAD's three-seed practice remains; five seeds are reported for the new image-image experiment, rather than an increase for retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial caption, entropy, filtering, word-prior, and image-image results; Table 8 reports RMG 0.006 without versus 0.149 with information imbalance. Table 5 replaces v1's CLIP/MIT-States ideal-word cosine values 0.19/0.56 with 0.388/0.858 and adds accuracies. Revised correlations and shifting procedures preclude interpreting these replacements as same-setting gains. Table 2's neighborhood distances remain identical.

M1.justification: The core CLIP objective, MAD construction, and intended RMG/MOAD procedures are retained. New temperature and encoder configurations serve as experimental controls. Formula corrections and additional evaluation measures do not establish a revised proposed learning algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and explanatory prose; reorders the modality-gap analyses; absorbs the former Section 4.3; and reorganizes Section 6 into two subsections. Detailed definitions and examples move into reorganized appendices, while the standalone Discussion section disappears.

P2.justification: v2 changes page format and typography, redraws the information-imbalance and MAD diagrams, reorganizes v1 Figures 3–4 into Figures 4/11, and redistributes Figure 8 across Figures 7/12. New experimental plots and Tables 3–9 substantially expand the displays. Figure 7a's new subtitle incorrectly reverses the bias trend shown by its curves and main caption.

R1.justification: v2 engages Fahim et al. (2024)'s contrastive-gap explanation through replication and discussion, and adds references to language rewrites and UMAP. It removes v1's discussion connecting the work to multimodal identifiability and captioning-based representation learning. The broader positioning around information imbalance versus existing gap explanations remains.

T1.justification: v2 corrects RMG's matching-pair and exclusion indices, corrects the second mismatch pair in the retained toy construction, and defines L2I. The expanded MOAD and loss expressions largely restate existing mathematics. Appendix F.3 also introduces an inconsistent nonnegative coordinate restriction despite retaining solutions with negative coordinates.

improvement.justification: v1 Section 7 acknowledges that controlled validation relies on synthetic MAD. v2's CC12M interventions provide direct real-data evidence for the modality-gap hypothesis, while temperature and alternative-cause controls substantially strengthen its empirical explanation. Correlation p-values also improve transparency. These substantive gains outweigh the local inconsistencies introduced in Figure 7a and Appendix F.3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of modality gap, object bias, and information imbalance. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and adds CC12M training, temperature interventions, word-frequency controls, and image-image experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of pretrained models, controlled MAD training experiments, embedding ablations, and a numerical toy experiment.

results.title: Two Effects, One Trigger: On the Modality Gap, Object Bias, and Information Imbalance in Contrastive Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from TR-DPO to a class covering DPO, IPO and KTO, with an explicit claim that reference updates offer benefits beyond lowering beta. v2 withdraws level-of-detail improvement from the headline HC claims and changes the conclusion from consistently improved performance to improvement in the majority of scenarios.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new sweeps as evidence for benefits beyond weakened KL regularization and explains its preference for HC scoring through possible reward-model distribution shift. It connects the lack of detail improvement to shorter responses and discusses a repetition-related length anomaly. The discussion adds specific qualifications concerning GPT-4 evaluation, untested generalization and the unexplained length mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents eight 80GB A100 GPUs, 3–12 hours of training per model, DeepSpeed, maximum gradient norm 2, KTO loss weights and dataset/model licenses. These are additional disclosures, not evidence that previously unspecified implementation choices changed. Conversely, v1's explicit five-generations-per-sample detail for diversity evaluation is no longer stated.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Anthropic-HH dialogue alignment and Reddit TL;DR summarization using the same described datasets. The 150-example provocative HH subset for human-centric evaluation is already present in v1. No new dataset, domain or task is introduced.

E2.justification: The DPO-only comparisons expand to include IPO and KTO as evaluated baselines for their respective TR variants in Table 1 and supplementary analyses. v2 Figure 1 also introduces explicit comparisons against SFT, which served as an initialization/reference policy without this reported comparison in v1.

E3.justification: The reported DPO beta changes from 0.1 to 0.05, and maximum generated tokens increase from 256 to 512. v2 removes the 410M configuration and concentrates cross-size comparisons on alpha = 0.6 and tau = 512. It adds beta-sweep controls, removes reward-model scoring, and revises the HC judge prompt with six scored examples in Appendix H.3. These are documented protocol changes, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds beta sweeps testing whether reducing regularization substitutes for reference updates, relating HC quality to KL divergence and Self-BLEU. It extends update-rate sensitivity and gradient analyses to IPO/KTO and adds a beta-dependent length analysis. The earlier reward-based diversity/KL analyses disappear, and the illustrative generation cases are replaced.

E5.justification: Both versions report bootstrapped Probability of Improvement confidence intervals and Fisher's exact tests. v2 extends these existing practices to additional results without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure. Neither version specifies training seed counts or repeated-training-run counts.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced, added or removed. For Pythia 2.8B with alpha = 0.6 on HH, Table 1 changes from 49.4% wins and 30.4% losses to 42.4% and 32.4%. Because beta and evaluation settings also change, this is not a same-setting performance decline. v2 adds IPO/KTO, SFT-comparison and beta-sweep results, removes reward-model and 410M results, and reports no improvement in level of detail.

M1.justification: v1 proposes TR-DPO and leaves IPO/KTO extensions for future work. v2 introduces TR-IPO and TR-KTO, applying reference updates within their different training objectives. The soft and hard update rules remain unchanged, but the proposed algorithm family substantially broadens.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and closing discussion are substantially rewritten around the broader TR family. The separate update-rate, diversity and gradient narrative is reorganized around the new Section 4.4 question about lowering beta. The appendices are restructured, and the conclusion becomes a discussion with explicit limitations and societal impacts.

P2.justification: v2 adds the SFT comparison chart, redesigns Table 1 around three methods, introduces multiple IPO/KTO and beta-analysis panels, and removes the reward-based displays. Generation examples change from prose sections to comparison tables. The original method schematic is retained as Figure 2, so that particular change is relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: The literature coverage remains largely intact. v2 develops IPO's stability positioning, adds Kahneman and Tversky and DeepSpeed citations, and removes Tang et al. and the accompanying rationale for concentrating solely on DPO. The Anonymous-to-Liu citation update concerns the same rejection-sampling paper, rather than a newly added work.

T1.justification: v2 adds IPO/KTO loss definitions and their gradient expressions, including separate chosen/rejected KTO terms, in Equations 3–4 and 9–10. These extend the existing gradient explanation; the reference-update equations, DPO gradient and trust-region argument remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or formal trust-region guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: Section 4.4 and Appendices D–E directly address an important weakness in v1: whether the reported benefits merely reflect weaker KL regularization. Together with actual IPO/KTO experiments and more qualified claims, these controls substantially strengthen the paper's evidential foundation. Removing reward-model cross-checks and unexplained numerical discrepancies remain drawbacks: for example, v2 Table 1 gives a 39.8% HH win rate for 2.8B TR-DPO at tau = 512, while Table 3 gives 209/500, or 41.8%. These limit confidence in exact figures but do not outweigh the substantial analytical improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reference-policy updating study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the substantial expansion in v2.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices C–G report original experiments with DPO, IPO, KTO and their TR variants, including benchmark results, parameter sweeps and gradient analyses.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original Pythia experiments comparing TR-DPO with DPO, including GPT-4 evaluations, reward-model scores and training-dynamics analyses.

results.title: Learn Your Reference Model for Real Good Alignment

C1.justification: v2 centers its contribution on overcoming an unnecessarily restrictive static reference policy. v3 makes mitigation of offline reward overoptimization a central claim and explicitly extends claimed effectiveness to general-purpose Llama3 assistants. This changes the principal scientific framing and claimed application scope while retaining the reference-update contribution.

C2.justification: v3 introduces a vanishing-curvature/reset hypothesis and interprets preserved sequence probabilities as reduced leakage into OOD outputs. It replaces broad near-optimality claims for α = 0.6 and τ = 512 with task-dependent guidance, acknowledges mixed KTO results and absent KTO toy overoptimization, and adds limitations concerning large update intervals on small datasets.

D1.justification: v3 documents toy-RNN dimensions and training trajectories, Llama3 training and generation settings, new dataset access information, and additional licensing details (Appendices B, D, and F). Pythia settings, hardware, training-time information, and judging prompts are retained. The explicit KTO setting λw = λl = 1 from v2 Appendix D.2 is omitted.

E1.justification: v3 retains Anthropic-HH and Reddit TL;DR and adds general instruction-following coverage through UltraChat-200k, UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval 2, and Arena-Hard. It also evaluates a synthetic trajectory-preference task in a toy MDP, substantially broadening the training and evaluation domains.

E2.justification: DPO, IPO, and KTO remain the principal comparison methods. However, v2 Figure 1's Pythia comparison against SFT on Anthropic-HH disappears; SFT instead appears in the new Llama3 benchmark comparison. Newly cited methods such as SimPO and Nash-based approaches are not evaluated as additional comparators.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama3-Base/Instruct protocols, including PairRM selection among eight generated responses, length-controlled win rates, and GPT-4-1106-preview benchmark judging. It also introduces toy-RNN and matched-KL probability-analysis protocols. The reported Reddit preference-validation size changes from 26,198 to 21,198 (v2 Section 4.1; v3 Table 4), without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test ID/OOD probability dynamics in toy MDPs, chosen/rejected sequence probabilities on Anthropic-HH, and hyperparameter sensitivity through expanded Pythia and Llama3 sweeps (v3 Appendices B, C, and E). Existing HC, KL, and diversity analyses largely remain, but v2's IPO/KTO gradient-time-course analyses are removed.

E5.justification: Beyond v2's Fisher tests and bootstrap PoI intervals, v3 reports 100 different seeds with means and standard deviations for toy simulations, plus benchmark standard deviations and 95% confidence intervals. Existing Fisher and PoI results remain, although the explicit bootstrap-description sentence disappears. The new reporting does not establish repeated LLM training runs.

E6.justification: Main Table 1 and the Fisher-test results are unchanged. v3 adds extensive benchmark, simulation, and ablation results; for example, Table 2 reports Llama3-Base Arena-Hard scores of 21.3 for TR-DPOα versus 10.5 for DPO. v2's SFT-relative scores and IPO/KTO gradient traces disappear. New Table 6 also reports a 22.8% tie rate for TR-DPO at α = 0.5, conflicting with the retained 21.8% result.

M1.justification: The soft parameter-averaging and periodic hard-copy rules remain unchanged, as do the underlying DPO, IPO, and KTO objectives (v2 Equations 5–6; v3 Equations 8–9). Explicit stop-gradient notation and clarified parameter replacement document the existing procedure rather than establish a new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related work, motivation, and discussion are substantially rewritten around overoptimization. Methods gain separate motivation and implementation subsections; experimental setup is subdivided; HC discussion moves into the appendix; and appendix organization is extensively revised. These changes exceed routine renumbering or added scientific paragraphs.

P2.justification: The opening SFT comparison is replaced by two benchmark panels, and v3 adds MDP/probability figures and benchmark/ablation tables. Existing KL panels are combined into Figure 5, HC plots are relocated, DPO gradient axes are rescaled, and IPO/KTO gradient panels disappear. The title, headers, typography, and overall page layout also change.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around overoptimization, adding Gao, Coste, and Rafailov studies and contrasting offline TR methods with online Nash approaches by Rosset and Munos. The earlier target-network/EMA motivation and TRPO citation disappear, while new alignment, dataset, and benchmark references expand the research context.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the DPO Hessian and its derivation (Equation 7 and Appendix A), substantially changing the mathematical analysis. Conversely, v2's explicit KL-constrained trust-region objective and IPO/KTO gradient derivations are removed. The rearranged DPO gradient itself is algebraically equivalent to the earlier expression.
