improvement.justification: The Llama3 evaluations and probability-dynamics experiments substantially address v2's narrow empirical coverage and largely speculative mechanism explanation. Hyperparameter sweeps also replace overbroad default-setting claims with better-supported guidance. These gains outweigh removed gradient analyses and reporting inconsistencies, including TR-KTOα's Arena-Hard score of 15.3 in v3 Figure 1 versus 14.9 in Table 2. The proposed mechanism remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TR-DPO/TR-IPO/TR-KTO research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original Llama3 benchmark evaluations, toy-MDP simulations, probability analyses, and hyperparameter experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original Pythia experiments on Anthropic-HH and Reddit TL;DR, including preference comparisons, human-centric scores, and training-dynamics analyses.

results.title: Learn Your Reference Model for Real Good Alignment

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the empirical scope from two custom benchmarks to evaluation on three benchmarks. The central claims about compositional world modeling, cooperative tree-search planning, and generalization across agent counts remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds explanations of intent adaptation through observation history, attributes VLM advantages to pretrained knowledge and multimodal integration, and proposes causes of generation failures involving guidance conflicts and action misunderstanding. It also discusses limits from restricted cooperator diversity and hidden physical variables. Appendix B adds possible alternatives when reachability information is unavailable; the existing slow-inference limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents 4,000 training environments, 40,000 intent-tracker rollouts, 138,000 evaluator examples, shared submodule models, and one-epoch LoRA fine-tuning with batch size, GPUs, and runtime. Appendix C.2 supplies the supervised comparator's architecture and training details, and Appendix D describes real-world fine-tuning. Existing diffusion-model sizes and budgets are retained. The project-video access link also changes.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained TDW tasks, v2 adds visual 2D-FetchQ cooperation with replayed human trajectories and a physical human–XArm puzzle task using collected real-world training data. It also extends TDW-Game transfer evaluation to two agents. These substantially broaden task requirements and interaction environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds reported comparisons against BC-single, BC-GAIL, and Co-GAIL on 2D-FetchQ, plus a CLIP/BERT-based supervised model against the three VLM planning modules in Table 7. Existing TDW comparators and AVDC remain; Oracle Cooperator is renamed Shared Belief Cooperator, rather than removed.

E3.justification: v1 specifies a 60-step maximum and 10 episodes for the main TDW evaluation; v2 Table 1 reports success over a 30-step horizon and 20 episodes. New protocols include 60-episode human-trajectory replay, five physical trials, and component prediction-accuracy evaluation. Some v2 successful-episode averages exceed 30 steps, leaving their relationship to the stated horizon unclear.

E4.justification: v2 adds intent-tracker adaptation cases and prediction-error analysis, supervised-versus-VLM component comparisons, and a classification of world-model failures with visual examples in Appendix C. Agent-count generalization also extends to two agents. The existing loss-scaling and search-budget analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based variability, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Changed evaluation-episode counts and the new physical-trial count describe sample sizes, without introducing a different statistical uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main-table values change under revised reported settings: COMBO with TDW-Cook Cooperator 1 changes from 1.0 success/21.3 steps to 0.90/22.8, which is not a same-setting performance comparison. New results include 81.3% on 2D-FetchQ versus Co-GAIL's 53.3%, 100%/10.5 steps for two-agent TDW-Game, component accuracies in Table 7, and 4/5 physical successes with 8.4 average successful-trial steps. v1 Tables 2–3 retain their values as v2 Tables 3–4.

M1.justification: The proposed COMBO procedure retains two-stage compositional diffusion training, agent-dependent loss scaling, state inpainting, three VLM planning modules, and the same tree-search algorithm. Explicit initial-frame conditioning clarifies the existing state-conditioned procedure. Appendix C.2 introduces a supervised comparison model without replacing the main COMBO method.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the explanation: Problem Statement becomes part of expanded Preliminaries, Section 4 is rewritten around current-state and future-frame conditioning, and task and implementation descriptions move into separate appendices. The original appendix is reorganized into task and implementation sections alongside new analysis and real-world sections. Introduction wording, terminology, authorship, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, clarifies state and prediction labels in Figures 2 and 4, and adds Figures 8–13 for the new environment, intent tracking, failures, and physical experiments. It adds Tables 2, 7, and 8, combines success/steps within Table 1 cells, and expands the agent-count table. The conference template also changes typography, margins, headers, and figure placement throughout.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 sharpens the comparison with VLP and newly discusses RoboDreamer's compositional robot planning. New citations support Co-GAIL evaluation, implementation details, and proposed extensions, while generic references such as Genie and NOPA disappear. These refine the existing multi-agent research positioning without replacing it.

T1.justification: The DEC-POMDP formulation, score composition, diffusion losses, and sampling relationships retain their substance. New preliminary subsections reorganize and explain the existing diffusion mathematics, while explicit initial-frame conditioning clarifies notation. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was confined to two custom simulated tasks and left planning-module training substantially underspecified. v2 addresses these weaknesses through an additional cooperation benchmark, a physical pilot, component comparisons, intent and failure analyses, and concrete fine-tuning documentation. These materially improve empirical support and reproducibility. The physical study remains preliminary at five trials, and the stated 30-step horizon is difficult to reconcile with some reported averages, but these reporting limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe COMBO and retain matching core methods and experiments. All 23 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports retained and revised TDW experiments, plus original COMBO results on 2D-FetchQ, component-level analyses, and a five-trial human–robot experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original TDW-Game and TDW-Cook experiments, generated-video evaluations, component ablations, and planning-budget and agent-count comparisons.

results.title: COMBO: Compositional World Models for Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine the central contribution around implemented weighted point cloud embeddings and connect the retained approximation theorem to that proposal. V1's operational proposal uses uniform point sets and explicitly reserves weighted architectures for future work. The underlying PMI and downstream-classification claims remain.

C2.justification: The central PMI and representation-capacity interpretation remains. V2 adds interpretations of negative weights and nonlinear kernels, tentatively attributes nonlinear-only training failure to vanishing gradients, and explains weight divergence and temperature saturation. Its linear-classification discussion now distinguishes two feature settings and acknowledges the Gaussian/CC3M exception, replacing v1's explicit discussion of the gap to before-projection CLIP.

D1.justification: V2 adds weight-head stabilization and inverse-temperature parameterization details, expanded RFF implementation guidance, cuML and regularization-search specifications, and dataset split counts in Table 4. These go beyond relocating existing settings into Appendix A. Conversely, v2 reports kernel-search ranges without identifying the selected settings as explicitly as v1 and omits v1's specific FP16/BF16 choices.

E1.justification: CC3M and CC12M pretraining remain. V2 adds Aircraft, Flowers, EuroSAT, DTD, and Pets, removes MNIST, and adds ImageNet linear classification. Evaluation expands from nine zero-shot and eight linear-classification benchmarks to thirteen for each, including new remote-sensing and texture domains.

E2.justification: CLIP and its before-projection linear baseline remain. V1's cossim ◦ mean comparator disappears from the main comparisons; v2 adds positive-weight WPCE and WPCE Linear controls in Table 3. These are changed controls, not renamed versions of uniform mean pooling.

E3.justification: Reported CC3M training changes from 64 to 50 epochs, batch size 384 to 2048, and weight decay 0.2 to 0.5; CC12M batch size changes from 4096 to 2048. Training RFF dimension increases from 512 to 1024, and linear-evaluation dimension from 256 to 512. Linear evaluation replaces momentum SGD with validation-tuned, regularized L-BFGS logistic regression and adds WPCE before-projection features. Caltech-101 evaluation changes from top-1 to mean per-class accuracy.

E4.justification: V2 introduces dedicated tests of signed versus positive weights and mixed versus linear-only kernels (Section 6.4), plus qualitative training-stability investigations motivating its stabilizers. V1's uniform-mean control and coefficient-by-coefficient performance grid are no longer reported. The existing analysis of sensitivity to RFF randomness is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five zero-shot evaluations varying RFF randomness, means in the main tables, and standard deviations in the appendix. Both use a single fixed RFF realization for linear evaluation. V2 does not introduce uncertainty over independent pretraining runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The result tables are extensively replaced for revised models, protocols, and coverage, including new CC12M IMQ and WPCE before-projection results. For example, v2's CC3M before-projection averages are 73.66 for WPCE IMQ and 72.14 for CLIP. These are newly reported results, not same-setting gains over v1. V2 also contains conflicting CC12M CIFAR-10 values: Gaussian/IMQ score 77.64/79.46 in Table 1 but 46.77/45.59 in Table 5.

M1.justification: V1 implements uniform averaging of point representations and leaves architectures with learned weights as future work. V2 implements learned signed weights through additional projection heads, uses weighted vector and random Fourier feature sums, and bounds weights with a tanh activation (Section 5.3, Algorithm 1, Appendix A.1). This changes the representation and similarity computation, beyond introducing the WPCE name.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the abstract, motivation, and conclusion around WPCE. It removes the introduction's contribution list, reorganizes Section 5 around the weighted formulation, theorem, and implementation, and moves the algorithm and substantial implementation material into Appendix A. This is extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are revised to depict weights and weighted embeddings. Separate CC3M/CC12M result tables become grouped displays, new ablation and dataset-split tables appear, and the uncertainty tables are consolidated. Algorithm 1 moves to the appendix with a revised, numbered presentation. These substantially change the visual organization beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds Chen et al. (2024) on CLIP transfer and Zhai et al. (2024) on RKHS-based analysis, alongside new dataset and optimization references. It removes the related-work paragraph on auxiliary-loss extensions and associated citations. The main positioning relative to contrastive-learning theory and alternative similarities remains.

T1.justification: The principal theorems, excess-risk bounds, weighted-class approximation guarantee, and proof strategies are retained. V2 corrects the missing logarithm in the PMI definition in Assumption C.2(d) and changes the printed RFF normalization from sqrt(1/(2D)) to sqrt(2/D), with an unbiased-estimator derivation in Appendix A.1. These are localized mathematical corrections.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially narrows v1's acknowledged gap between its weighted-class theorem and its uniformly weighted implementation by implementing and testing learned signed weights. Targeted ablations, broader domain coverage, and before-projection comparisons for both WPCE and CLIP strengthen support for the actual proposal; localized mathematical corrections improve accuracy. The conflicting CIFAR-10 entries and less explicit selected hyperparameters remain reporting weaknesses, but the gains in methodological coherence and empirical support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe the same multimodal contrastive-learning work despite the changed title and revised method. Corresponding theoretical results, experiments, figures, and Appendices A–C support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original weighted-point-cloud experiments, zero-shot and linear classification results, and weight/kernel ablations in Tables 1–3, with additional uncertainty reporting in Table 5.

before.justification: V1 reports original CC3M/CC12M pretraining experiments, zero-shot and linear classification results, and repeated-evaluation results in Tables 1–6.

results.title: Weighted Point Set Embedding for Multimodal Contrastive Learning Toward Optimal Similarity Metric

C1.justification: The synthesis-aware generation claim remains, but v2's main contributions expand to backward-policy learning, large-action-space scaling, novelty against stronger baselines and experimental-fragment-guided design. v1's explicit claim of comparability to bioactive ChEMBL compounds and its 'first application' conclusion are dropped. The title also shifts from guaranteed synthesis pathways to synthesis constraints.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of backward-flow leakage, fingerprint-driven cluster exploitation and baseline novelty differences, plus qualifications about molecule-size effects and docking's omission of water-mediated interactions. It removes v1's explicit discussion of reward-proxy generalization uncertainty, uncertain laboratory yields and the proxy-versus-experimental-activity validation (v1 Limitations; v2 Sections 3.2, 4.1–4.5 and Appendix B.3).

D1.justification: Beyond v1's basic model and training table, v2 documents reaction preprocessing, backward-training algorithms and replay, baseline training budgets and hyperparameters, clustering tools, docking preparation and fragment-curation procedures (Appendices A–B). These substantially expand reproducibility information. The SynFlowNet source-code link itself is retained.

E1.justification: Coverage expands beyond sEH to GSK3β, DRD2, Mpro and HSP90, and adds recovery of synthesis routes for previously unseen reachable molecules. The earlier ZINC250k and high-affinity ChEMBL property-control comparisons disappear; ChEMBL instead serves as a novelty reference in v2.

E2.justification: The retained fragment-GFlowNet comparison adds FragGFN SA. v2 also evaluates Soft Q-learning, REINVENT4 and SyntheMol, substantially expanding the comparator families. v1's standalone random-trajectory quality comparison in Figure A.4 is no longer reported.

E3.justification: The default building-block count changes from 6,000 to 10,000, and the reported template count from 71 to 105 after preprocessing. Typical sEH training changes from 1,000 steps with beta 64 to 5,000 with beta 32, with revised trajectory limits. Evaluation changes from 1,600 molecules to 1,000 random samples, and AiZynthFinder selection changes from the top 100 to 100 random samples. Mode-count and novelty metrics are added, while SCScore and ligand-efficiency evaluation disappear.

E4.justification: v2 adds backward-policy and entropy ablations, fingerprint-selection comparisons, building-block scaling and cluster/runtime analyses, and fragment-curation and docking-pose case studies (Table 1, Figures 7–8 and Appendix B). Trajectory-length analysis changes scope. v1's reward-exponent sensitivity and proxy-versus-IC50 correlation/ROC analyses are removed.

E5.justification: v1 presents molecule-level distributions and point summaries without declared repeated-run counts or cross-seed uncertainty. v2 reports standard errors from three training seeds in Table A.2, three seeds for Figure 7, and eight seeds for Figure A.3. This establishes substantially expanded statistical reporting, without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the main comparison results and adds substantial baseline, target, backward-policy and scaling outcomes. For example, v1 reports 47% AiZynthFinder success (Table A.3); v2 reports 40% for L=4 and 62% for L=3 in Figure 4, but 65% for L=3 in Table A.2. Changed settings prevent interpreting these as direct gains. Table 1 newly reports 32.3% and 44.3% unseen-route recovery for maximum-likelihood and REINFORCE policies, respectively.

M1.justification: v1 trains forward and backward policies through trajectory balance. v2 introduces separate maximum-likelihood and REINFORCE backward-policy objectives, including replay and reversibility constraints, and replaces learned building-block output weights with fixed fingerprint representations. It also introduces target-informed building-block selection (Sections 3.2–3.3, 4.6 and Appendix A.4).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Background becomes a separate section with four subsections; methods and results are reorganized around distinct research questions. The appendix is restructured into Extended Methods and Extended Results. Some original action-space and network descriptions remain or move, but the overall narrative is substantially revised.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn to explain fingerprint sampling and backward-policy constraints. The earlier boxplot-focused presentation expands into violin plots, mode-discovery and scaling curves, and docking-pose panels. Tables are restructured and algorithm boxes added. Earlier SCScore, ligand-efficiency, proxy-validation and top-50-molecule displays disappear or are replaced with different content.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially, especially through a dedicated backward-policy discussion positioning the approach against Jang et al. and Mohammadpour et al. v2 also acknowledges concurrent RGFN work by Koziarski et al., qualifying the earlier first-application positioning, and broadens discussion of synthesis-aware generation and modern comparison methods (Section 2).

T1.justification: v2 adds formal backward-training objectives (Equations 2–3) and a short constant-reward state-count argument, without developing new theorems or proofs. These are limited mathematical additions beyond v1's framework description. The REINFORCE specification is internally inconsistent: Section 3.2 describes maximization, while Algorithm 2 specifies minimization.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond v1's narrow single-target evaluation through stronger baselines, multiple targets, repeated-seed reporting and direct tests of backward-policy consistency and scaling. It also diagnoses an important previously unexamined MDP problem and documents proposed remedies. Losing v1's proxy validation and laboratory-feasibility caveats, the 62%/65% discrepancy, and conflicting REINFORCE optimization directions weaken the revision, but the broader controlled evidence and methodological detail provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SynFlowNet. All 14 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including their appendices, figures, tables and equations, support comparison despite substantial expansion and retitling.

after.justification: v2 reports original baseline comparisons, backward-policy experiments, scaling studies and fragment-guided generation analyses (Sections 4.1–4.6 and Appendix B). Previously published experimental structures provide inputs to these computational evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original molecule-generation experiments, property and diversity measurements, retrosynthesis evaluations and reward-proxy analyses (Figures 2–5 and Appendix A).

results.title: SynFlowNet: Design of Diverse and Novel Molecules with Synthesis Constraints

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the backward-policy contribution: v2 claims improved sample quality and diversity, while v3 claims correction of backward trajectories while retaining diverse, high-reward discovery. The abstract's central synthesis-aware generation claim and the conclusion otherwise retain their substantive scope.

C2.justification: New Appendix B.2 explicitly discusses linear synthesis paths, the two-reactant restriction, unmodeled selectivity, reaction conditions, stereochemistry, and inaccessible chemical regions. v3 also interprets rediscovery through chemical-space membership and proposes an explanation for FragGFN's lower rewards. Conversely, it removes v2's caveat about AiZynthFinder using a different reaction library.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 now specifies scaling-experiment budgets, batch size, evaluation samples, validity filtering, H100 hardware, and timing boundaries. Additional documentation covers docking reward penalties and normalization, reaction encoding, and ChEMBL building-block extraction. These materially expand reproducibility information without proving retained experiments were rerun. Table A.1 removes max_nodes=9; the source-code address is merely relocated.

E1.justification: v3 adds aripiprazole and celecoxib rediscovery, KRAS docking optimization, and JNK3 optimization. It also trains on building blocks extracted from ChEMBL molecules, whereas v2 used ChEMBL as a novelty reference. These extend task requirements, target coverage, and the represented training vocabulary.

E2.justification: SynNet becomes an evaluated comparator in v3 Tables A.4 and A.5, using published reference scores. The existing REINVENT, FragGFN, Soft Q-learning, and SyntheMol comparisons are retained. Extending existing comparators to KRAS does not itself introduce new baseline methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a 10,000-oracle-call evaluation using AUC of top-10 scores, top-10 rediscovery evaluation, and top-100 optimization comparisons. These are additional protocols, distinct from v2's retained sampled-molecule comparisons and larger training budgets. The ChEMBL-derived vocabulary experiment also introduces a control for differences in available molecular building blocks.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether novelty persists with ChEMBL-derived building blocks, whether known actives can be rediscovered, and how fingerprint selection affects molecular structural diversity across library sizes. These address substantive questions beyond the previous analyses. The backward-policy and entropy ablation is retained as Figure A.6, having appeared as Figure A.3 in v2.

E5.justification: The new sample-efficiency evaluation reports means and standard deviations over five independent runs; rediscovery reports mean and standard deviation over three seeded models. Existing three-seed standard-error reporting and the eight-seed backward-policy analysis remain. This adds statistical reporting for new protocols, without establishing increased replication of retained experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds rediscovery rewards of 0.90 and 0.48, KRAS results, SynNet comparisons, ChEMBL-vocabulary results, and sample-efficiency scores. Table A.5 reports SynFlowNet AUC above FragGFN but below REINVENT and SynNet on both tasks. Original entries in Table A.2 and the backward-policy table, renumbered from Table 1 to Table 2, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The reaction-based action space, graph-transformer policies, fingerprint-based selection, objectives in Equations 1–3, and Algorithms 1–2 are retained. Expanded reaction-encoding and docking-reward documentation does not establish a change to the underlying generation procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local wording corrections, shortened related work, moving the data description into Appendix A.2, and adding focused rediscovery, sample-efficiency, and outlook subsections. The publication header changes to ICLR 2025. This is a targeted expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the result displays with four new tables and figures for structural diversity and ChEMBL-controlled novelty. Figure 1 is redrawn with clearer flow directions and reaction-encoding information, and Table A.2 gains a row. The synthesis example moves from main-text Figure 3 to Appendix Figure A.3; several other figures are relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly connects fingerprint action selection to prior large-action-space reinforcement learning and expands the comparison with SynNet. It adds references supporting new evaluations while removing the TACO-GFN discussion and several diffusion-model references. The main research positioning remains intact; duplicated or differently dated citations to the same works are not new research coverage.

T1.justification: The GFlowNet definitions, mathematical reasoning, and forward/backward training objectives are unchanged; neither version supplies new proofs relative to the other. Added Equation 4 documents normalization of the already-used docking reward, rather than extending the theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens scrutiny of central claims: the ChEMBL-vocabulary control addresses a confound in the novelty comparison, budget-limited evaluations clarify practical competitiveness, and the new outlook qualifies real-world synthesizability. These address important validation and interpretation gaps in v2. Incorrect cross-references and Equation 4's inconsistency with its stated normalization range remain reporting defects, but are outweighed by stronger controls, broader evidence, and clearer applicability limits.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SynFlowNet research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material across moves and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds SynFlowNet results for rediscovery, KRAS docking, additional optimization tasks, vocabulary-controlled novelty, and sample efficiency.

before.justification: v2 reports original molecule-generation benchmarks, backward-policy and scaling ablations, and target-specific computational case studies.

results.title: SynFlowNet: Design of Diverse and Novel Molecules with Synthesis Constraints

C1.justification: v2 principally claims competitive generalization on three main benchmarks. v3 claims state-of-the-art OoD performance on five of six, convergence guarantees, interpretable representations and uncertainty estimation. It also elevates the benchmark collection to an explicit core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 develops contextual self-modulation, physical-parameter identifiability and explanations involving nonlinear adaptation and spurious associations. It adds substantive limitations concerning discontinuous dynamics, initialization sensitivity and hyperparameter tuning, while revising v2’s quadratic-cost discussion around context pooling and its accuracy–cost tradeoff.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands per-method architectures, optimizer and budget tables, hardware, frameworks, solver tolerances and regularization settings. It documents dataset parameters and a common split/tensor interface, and updates implementation examples for second-order expansion and pooling. Code and dataset links already existed in v2. Conflicting SP variant and LV pool-size descriptions still limit reproducibility.

E1.justification: v3 retains SP, LV, GO and GS, adding Sel’kov Model, Brusselator and Navier-Stokes evaluations. It also expands LV adaptation to a wider parameter range on a 25-by-25 grid and evaluates physical-parameter recovery. SP was already evaluated in v2’s appendix.

E2.justification: CAVIA and CoDA-l1 remain the main external baselines, and OFA remains the SP comparator. v3 additionally compares the earlier first-order NCF against NCF-t2 and includes a dedicated CoDA-versus-NCF parameter-recovery comparison in Figure 5 and Appendix A.2. The external baseline families are unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: v2 specifies 120,000 LV training epochs and GO context dimension 1024; v3 specifies 10,000 epochs for LV NCF-t1 and GO dimension 256. Optimizers, architectures and learning-rate schedules also change. New analyses introduce MAPE and matched-architecture parameter-recovery protocols. These changes do not establish that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds context-pool and Taylor-removal ablations, runtime analysis, grid-wide adaptation, attractor-specific errors, parameter recovery and GO context clustering. It replaces the SP context-size sweep with a broader LV sweep. The three-network ablation is retained, including v2 Table 4 as v3 Table 8.

E5.justification: Beyond v2’s existing uncertainty displays, v3 introduces predictive uncertainty from candidate trajectories: Figure 6 reports means and standard deviations across 9 LV and 21 SM forecasts, with deviations magnified tenfold for display. Figure 14 explicitly identifies seed-averaged results and standard-deviation bars, without specifying the seed count or establishing increased runs for retained results.

E6.justification: v3 Table 1 adds NCF-t2 and three benchmark result sets, with NCF-t2 achieving the lowest OoD MSE on five of six tasks. The first-order LV entries change from 9.56/9.83 to 6.73/7.92, in units of 10^-5 for InD/OoD, under revised settings. CoDA’s GO InD entry changes from 0.56 × 10^-3 to 5.06 × 10^-4. SP and architecture-ablation tables retain their values.

M1.justification: v3 introduces NCF-t2 with second-order Taylor expansion and proximal alternating minimization, configurable context pools and L2 weight regularization. Unlike v2’s cross-context adaptation, v3 disables Taylor expansion during adaptation. These substantially change training and adaptation procedures.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and discussion are substantially rewritten around meta-learning and contextual self-modulation. Extended related work moves into the main text; methods receive separate training, adaptation, pooling and testing subsections; results separate interpolation from extrapolation; and the appendices are extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v3 merges and expands the main benchmark tables, revises the NCF diagram and adds parameter-grid heatmaps, uncertainty plots, identification panels, runtime plots and trajectory displays. Existing SP and architecture-ablation figures are relocated, while the GS visualization is retained with a revised caption. Algorithms and page layout are also substantially reformatted.

R1.justification: Beyond relocating related work, v3 explicitly positions NCF relative to CAMEL/Blanke and Lelarge’s interpretable, linearly parameterized systems and claims an extension to nonlinear settings. It adds substantial positioning around proximal optimization, uncertainty estimation and scientific foundation models, supported by new references.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly leaves theoretical guarantees for future work. v3 adds Proposition 3.1 and its second-order JVP proof in Appendix A.1, plus a conditional convergence theorem under KL, smoothness and boundedness assumptions. The applicability of its smooth-loss assumptions to the stated L1-regularized objective is not reconciled.

improvement.justification: v3 implements the scalability remedy deferred in v2 and supports it with accuracy/runtime ablations. Broader nonlinear adaptation tests, parameter-recovery analyses and substantially fuller experimental documentation strengthen the paper’s practical evidence. These gains outweigh added tuning complexity, although conflicting settings and the unresolved applicability of the convergence theorem to the nonsmooth objective temper the stronger claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Neural Context Flows, with matching authors, methods and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, including additional Sel’kov, Brusselator and Navier-Stokes experiments, alongside adaptation, interpretability and ablation analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original NCF experiments on Lotka-Volterra, Glycolytic Oscillator, Gray-Scott and Simple Pendulum, including benchmark comparisons and appendix ablations.

results.title: Neural Context Flows for Meta-Learning of Dynamical Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion refine the central problem from performance-improvement collapse toward the insufficiency of a monotonicity condition that ignores representation changes. The principal contributions—identifying task representation shift, deriving conditional guarantees and demonstrating benefits from controlling updates—remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive guidance favoring less frequent encoder updates, expands the pretraining explanation to distinguish approximation error from the gap between mutual-information and return optima, and explicitly acknowledges that policy-learning improvements remain untreated. It also identifies the online Performance Control variant as impractical because of its evaluation cost, materially clarifying applicability limits.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-code link and a public UNICORN-code link, replacing v2's statement that UNICORN code was obtained from its authors. It clarifies update-frequency semantics and documents new dataset sizes, the controller parameter, NVIDIA 3090 hardware and approximately 3–6-day runtime. Most original architecture, learning-rate and batch-size information is retained.

E1.justification: Figure 2 and Table 2 add Walker-Param and Push to Ant-Dir, Reach, Dial-Turn and Button-Press, substantially broadening the evaluated locomotion and manipulation tasks. The original environments and Ant-Dir random, medium and expert data conditions are retained.

E2.justification: CSRO moves from cited and theoretically discussed prior work in v2 to an evaluated comparator in v4: Figures 8–9 compare original CSRO with controlled update schedules. The existing contrastive, reconstruction, cross-entropy and pretraining comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce materially different protocols: Appendix 8.3 varies sample size and measures representation discrepancy using MSE, while Appendix 8.5.1 uses online evaluations on three sampled training tasks to guide updates and retains evaluation on twenty test tasks. The original common settings in Table 1 remain unchanged; these additions do not establish reruns or protocol changes for the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v4 adds numerical tests of the sample-size dependence underlying Assumption 4.9 and an experiment testing whether performance feedback can guide encoder updates. Figure 5 also replaces the earlier visualization case study with a different pair of representations evaluated at 300K steps. The existing data-quality and pretraining analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v4 adds paired t-tests and reported p-values against each comparison's worst setting in Table 3, introducing statistical inference across the central results. Eight-seed means and standard-deviation bands already appeared in v2 and remain. The new Performance Control experiment separately reports six seeds; this is not an increase in the original experiments' run count.

E6.justification: v4 adds numerical summaries in Table 3, results for the added environments, assumption-check outcomes, Performance Control results and CSRO curves. For example, its new Walker-Param contrastive comparison reports 299.00 ± 35.42 for the original schedule and 450.47 ± 19.71 for Nk=2, Nacc=1. Figure 5 also replaces the illustrated models and returns; these are different cases, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: Appendix 8.5.1 adds Performance Control, which uses online evaluations with a pretrained representation to accumulate estimated policy improvements and adapt encoder-update timing. This is a concrete extension of the update gate; the encoder objectives, BRAC policy learning and original fixed schedules remain. Renaming the schedule parameters to Nk and Nacc is otherwise clarification.

P1.justification: Sections 4.2, 4.3 and 6.1 undergo substantial explanatory rewrites. v4 consolidates related work, moves objective descriptions into Appendix 8.4, makes encoder parameterization and schedule terminology more explicit, and reorganizes the appendix around proofs, assumption justification, implementation and additional results. These changes substantially reshape the exposition.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figure 1, expands Figure 2 from twelve to eighteen panels, replaces Figure 5, and adds Figures 6–9 and the numerical results Table 3. It also expands Table 2, changes legends and captions, relocates existing displays and adopts the ICLR page layout. The visual revision extends well beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v4 removes the broad Offline RL and Meta RL related-work paragraphs and their associated citations, while adding works by Li et al. (2021) and Zhang et al. (2024). It also revises the ContrBAR comparison from an OMRL framework-specific guarantee to an online, approximation-specific result contrasted with this paper's broader offline formulation.

T1.justification: Theorems 4.6 and 4.10 and Corollary 6.1 replace the mutual-information-optimal reference with the return-optimal representation. v4 removes the former support-coverage assumption, strengthens Assumption 4.7 to ensure a positive improvement margin, and replaces simplex volume with representation-space cardinality. It also adds Corollary 4.4 with its proof and Appendix 8.3 derivations for alternative approximation-error bounds.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially improves scrutiny of the central guarantee through revised assumptions, an explicit comparison condition, additional derivations and numerical checks of an assumption only briefly justified in v2. Added task and CSRO evaluations, exact result summaries and significance tests strengthen the empirical support, while clearer implementation information and limitations improve assessability. The gains remain qualified: the tests compare against worst settings, and the adaptive controller requires expensive online evaluations rather than providing a practical fully offline solution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same task-representation-shift research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, proofs, figures and tables, support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reformatting.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds benchmark evaluations, numerical assumption checks, performance-guided training and CSRO experiments, including Appendix Figures 6–9.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments, including update-schedule comparisons, data-quality tests, pretraining comparisons and task-representation visualizations in Figures 2–5.

results.title: Scrutinize What We Ignore: Reining In Task Representation Shift Of Context-Based Offline Meta Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements more carefully attribute SGA rate guarantees to its asymptotic approximation. The conclusion narrows the suggested convergence to DSE from existing GAN algorithms generally to the chosen GDA initialization algorithms. The principal contributions remain local convergence theory and its illustrative GAN application.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges that the attraction-region size and suitable initialization remain uncharacterized. Appendix N.2 adds explanations involving insufficient correction and amplified stochastic noise, plus a tentative global-convergence interpretation. The efficiency discussion now acknowledges that SGA can be slower on full Fashion-MNIST, refining the earlier account of its practical benefits.

D1.justification: v2 promises future PyTorch software, whereas v3 supplies a project repository address; its contents were not inspected. Appendix M adds dataset counts and initialization details, including previously unspecified T-shirt splits and pretraining. Appendix N.2 discloses that theta was tuned on MNIST digit 0 and transferred to other datasets. These materially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v3 adds unconditional image modeling over all ten classes of MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, substantially broadening the target distributions beyond digit 0 and T-shirts. It retains both single-class experiments, Gaussian modeling, and the deterministic example.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain GDA, SGA, and asymptotic SGA in the deterministic example. The new full-dataset experiments reuse GDA and SGA. Alternating GDA remains an initialization procedure; cited extragradient and Hamiltonian methods do not become evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: For retained single-class results, v2 Tables 2–3 become v3 Tables 3 and 5 with GDA budgets revised from 200,000 to 20,000 iterations and SGA budgets from 1–3 million to 100,000–300,000. Reported learning rates for retained timing plots also change. These are documented setting revisions, without establishing reruns. New full-dataset protocols use batch size 512, and Figure 1(c) replaces objective value with approximate distance to equilibrium.

E4.justification: v3 adds a correction-strength sensitivity study over theta from 0.01 to 0.5 at fixed tau = 5 (Appendix N.2, Figure 5). New timing analyses expose delayed GDA instability and a case where GDA is faster than SGA (Figures 4 and 6). Figure 1(c) supplies a direct convergence diagnostic through distance to the known equilibrium. These broaden the earlier tau sweeps and timing analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix M.7 newly specifies that test FID is computed without resampling. Ten resamplings for training/validation FID and for the objective and angle, with sampling standard deviations, were already described in v2. Neither version reports uncertainty across independent training seeds.

E6.justification: v3 Tables 2 and 4 add full-dataset results, including SGA validation FID of 7.6 ± 0.08 on MNIST and 16.6 ± 0.1 on Fashion-MNIST at 500,000 iterations. Section 4.2 changes the Gaussian covariance error at tau = 100 from approximately 0.3 to 0.2. The single-class table scores are retained under revised reported budgets, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The GDA and SGA update rules, asymptotic SGA approximation, and stochastic gradient estimator remain unchanged. The smooth DCGAN generator, scattering discriminator, and Stiefel geometry described in v3 were already present in v2, including its appendices.

P1.justification: v3 edits the abstract, introduction, mathematical explanations, and empirical narrative. It moves notation into Appendix A, relocates the digit-0 discussion to Appendix N.2, and separates experimental details from supplementary results into Appendices M and N. The five-section main structure and most theoretical exposition are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds two full-dataset result tables and Figures 4–6. Figure 1(c) becomes a logarithmic distance-to-equilibrium plot, and Figure 1(b) is redrawn. The retained single-class tables are relocated, with the T-shirt table changed from stacked to side-by-side comparisons. The original timing panels reappear as Figure 7, substantially reorganizing the empirical displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds Benaim and Miclo (2024) to the introduction and bibliography and explicitly attributes the expanded Theorem 3.3 to Jin et al. and Zhang et al. The related-work comparison and overall positioning against existing Riemannian optimization methods remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the step-size bound denominator from absolute eigenvalue to squared absolute eigenvalue and specifies negative real parts. Definition 3.1 and the Ostrowski proof distinguish the invariant neighborhood from its geodesically convex subset. Theorem 3.3 additionally gives an explicit step size and rate bound at tau = 1, supported in Appendix I. These revise central formal guarantees.

improvement.justification: v3 corrects a consequential step-size formula and repairs the local-stability formulation underlying its convergence results. Full-dataset experiments, correction-strength sensitivity evidence, and more complete reproducibility information substantially strengthen the paper beyond its earlier single-class demonstrations. The unexplained iteration-count revisions and speculative global-convergence suggestion remain limitations, but the improvements to mathematical rigor and empirical support provide a clear net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Riemannian min-max study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison; relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulations and GAN results and adds experiments on all ten classes of MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, plus parameter-sensitivity results.

before.justification: v2 reports original deterministic convergence simulations and Wasserstein GAN experiments on Gaussian data, MNIST digit 0, and Fashion-MNIST T-shirts, including appendix results.

C1.justification: The central claims remain automatic selection of expert counts and per-token activations, competitive performance across vision/language/vision-language tasks, and efficiency without extensive hyperparameter search. Added appendix evidence does not redefine these core scientific contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations of load-balancing versus sparsity, initialization strategies, aggregation weights, and routing overhead. It acknowledges inefficient routing and suggests optimized kernels. The memory limitation remains in Section 4.4, but the conclusion removes v2's explicit larger-model evaluation limitation. The broad preference for W-Average also needs qualification because Table 19 favors Average initialization.

D1.justification: v4 adds localized reproducibility details for new experiments, particularly ImageNet optimizer settings, learning schedule, MoE placement, hardware, batch sizes, and timing configurations. Existing Appendix settings and Table 5 remain. The repository link is unchanged, while the explicit statement promising Tutel and DeepSpeed-MoE implementations is omitted; this does not establish that implementations were withdrawn.

E1.justification: v4 adds TinyImageNet classification fine-tuning, CIFAR-10 pretraining, and ImageNet training from scratch (Tables 18–20). This substantially extends vision coverage beyond the original DomainBed domain-generalization experiments. The original language and vision-language benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds an evaluated adaptive top-p comparator with p=0.4 (Table 17), Dense-LLaVA in the runtime comparison, and top-1 timing controls. The efficiency baseline also changes from MoE-LLaVA using DynMoE's dispatcher to DeepSpeed's top-2 implementation. Existing main accuracy comparators remain.

E3.justification: The runtime evaluation adds first-token latency, wall-clock and component timings, exclusion of the initial allocation sample, and forced-top-1 controls. New vision experiments introduce separate training configurations, including 200-epoch ImageNet training with specified MoE layers and batch sizes. Original accuracy protocols are largely retained; the revised efficiency captions alone do not establish that retained FLOP measurements were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's fixed-k and auxiliary-loss comparisons, v4 examines load-balancing/efficiency-loss combinations and their activation patterns (Tables 13–16), expert initialization strategies, routing overhead under matched top-1 activation, and equal versus score-weighted output aggregation (Table 23). These address several previously untested design choices and efficiency mechanisms.

E5.justification: v4 first supplies per-task ± uncertainty terms throughout the retained GLUE comparison in Table 11 and specifies five-trial averaging for Table 4. Both versions already state three random seeds for language and vision experiments, so increased seed counts are not established. The statistic represented by ± remains undefined.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive results in Tables 13–23 and Figure 24 while retaining the original main accuracy means. StableLM throughput changes from 26 versus 19 to 30 versus 27 tokens/second for DynMoE versus MoE-LLaVA under revised implementation settings, not a demonstrated same-setting improvement. Qwen/Phi-2 throughput entries disappear; their FLOP, MAC, and memory values remain in Table 24.

M1.justification: The core top-any router, expert addition/removal procedure, and original auxiliary loss remain unchanged. Section 8.4 adds alternative expert initialization procedures using averaging, weighted averaging, or the most activated expert. Additional loss combinations, including DynMoE-B in Table 20, extend the method through optional variants.

P1.justification: Most of the original narrative is preserved. Changes include localized prose edits, a rewritten conclusion, a subdivided experimental appendix, relocation of Algorithm 1 to Appendix 7, acknowledgments, and updated author/header and citation formatting. The additional experiments account for much of the new prose.

P2.justification: v4 adopts the ICLR layout, substantially resizes and redistributes existing displays, adds Tables 13–23 and Figure 24, and redesigns the main efficiency table. The earlier FLOP/MAC/memory comparison moves to Table 24 without its throughput column. Figures 1–23 retain their artwork despite relocation and resizing.

R1.justification: Related work now discusses Huang et al.'s top-p routing and Yang et al.'s XMoE, distinguishing their hyperparameter or dense-training requirements. References supporting dynamic networks, layer skipping, additional losses, and new datasets are added. This is a focused expansion of positioning rather than a wholesale revision.

T1.justification: The mathematical development in Equations (1)–(8) is retained, with no new substantive derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof. The stated orientation of Wg is edited as a notation adjustment, and Algorithm 1 is relocated unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation of the central efficiency and routing claims. Native DeepSpeed comparisons and forced-top-1 controls expose routing overhead that v2's shared-dispatch comparison did not isolate. The adaptive top-p comparator and aggregation/initialization ablations address important validation gaps, while GLUE uncertainty reporting improves transparency. These gains outweigh narrower losses in throughput coverage and the removed larger-model caveat. Reporting weaknesses remain, including undefined ± terms and Table 14's unexplained activation frequency of 1.29.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DynMoE work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and reformatting.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds vision training experiments, adaptive-routing comparisons, method ablations, and runtime analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original DynMoE experiments on DomainBed, GLUE, and vision-language benchmarks, alongside routing analyses, ablations, and efficiency measurements.

results.title: Dynamic Mixture of Experts: An Auto-Tuning Approach for Efficient Transformer Models

C1.justification: V1 broadly suggests amplification when insertion is intermittent, even under adversarially chosen loss landscapes. V2 instead claims no amplification for sufficiently large batches relative to noise and restricts the amplification possibility to smaller batches. This substantially revises the abstract, contribution summary, and implications while retaining the every-step no-amplification claim.

C2.justification: V2 explains competing effects of noise and batch size on propagation of the initial private signal, materially narrowing applicability. It adds initialization and pretrained-model interpretations and refines the difficulty of realizing worst-case landscapes in ordinary networks. The federated-learning application discussion is removed. Its prose describing the amplification-ratio trend conflicts with Figure 4b's direction.

D1.justification: V2 documents A_CotS gradient generation and cosine scoring in Algorithms 6–7, identifies ImageNet as public pretraining data, specifies last-layer AlexNet fine-tuning, and describes bisection for privacy-parameter conversion. Existing implementation libraries, hyperparameter table, and approximately 3,500 GPU-hour disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: CIFAR10 and Housing remain the evaluation datasets. V2 adds auditing with unknown initialization, changing the adversary's information-access scenario (Appendix G, Figure 12). ImageNet supplies pretrained AlexNet weights for a CIFAR10 experiment; it is not an additional evaluated benchmark.

E2.justification: Appendix G newly evaluates A_CotS, adapted from Andrew et al. (2024), against the proposed and loss-based adversaries on Housing. Figure 8's caption names A_GC-R while its legend names A_GC-S, but A_CotS participation is clear. The ConvNet/ResNet comparator curves from v1 Figure 5 are absent from the replacement landscape experiments.

E3.justification: The landscape evaluation expands to B in {1,2,4,8,16}, noise parameter σ in {1,...,8}, and trajectories through T=25, introducing the ε25/ε1 ratio. V2 also adds unknown-initialization testing, last-layer fine-tuning of pretrained AlexNet, and full privacy-profile evaluation. The original real-data training settings and Table 2 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 4 and 14 add systematic batch-size/noise sensitivity analysis central to identifying amplification regimes. Appendix G tests robustness to unknown initialization and examines tightness across privacy profiles. Existing dimension-selection ablations, GDP approximation checks, and threshold-search validation are retained, despite relocation and renumbering.

E5.justification: The 5,000 auditing runs, 95% Clopper-Pearson procedure, Figure 1's 30-run reporting, and Housing repetitions remain unchanged. However, the replacement landscape plots in v2 Figures 4 and 14 omit the explicit five-run averaging statement and variability band accompanying v1 Figure 5. This establishes a reporting change, not fewer actual runs.

E6.justification: New landscape results reveal strong batch-size dependence: v2 Figure 4b reports ε25/ε1 of 0.25 at B=1, σ=8, versus 0.99 at B=16, σ=8. Appendix G adds comparator, initialization, pretrained-model, and privacy-profile findings. These are results under expanded conditions; Figures 1–3 and the retained appendix analyses preserve their earlier plotted data.

M1.justification: Section 6 substantially generalizes the loss-landscape adversary: its gradient function changes from values bounded by C to batch-gradient sums bounded by BC, and updates explicitly divide the gradient sum and noise by B. This changes the modeled dynamics and adversary capabilities. The real-data A_GC-R and A_GC-S procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Rewriting concentrates on the abstract, contribution summary, landscape analysis, and discussion, with new remarks and Appendix G. The main section sequence, background, core gradient-crafting descriptions, and much experimental prose remain intact. Citation and heading styles also change.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the main landscape displays with trajectory panels and a numerical heatmap, adds several appendix plots and an algorithm display, and regroups/resizes retained appendix figures. The document template, title block, headings, and figure placement also change substantially. Relocated existing analyses are distinguishable from genuinely new displays.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning through comparison with Annamalai's concurrent no-amplification result, discussion of Asoodeh and Diaz's constrained nonconvex guarantees, and Feng and Tramèr's privacy-backdoor constructions. These qualify novelty and practical realizability beyond merely adding citations. It also adds black-box auditing literature and removes the federated-learning reference associated with the deleted discussion.

T1.justification: Section 6 revises the formal stochastic model through explicit batch averaging and the admissible range g in [-BC,BC], replacing the earlier [-C,C] formulation. Its optimality discussion shifts from a T=2 worst-case conjecture to batch-dependent tightness claims. Appendix A's definitions, lemma, and corollary remain substantively unchanged; no new formal proof establishes the new regime claims.

improvement.justification: The batch-dependent formulation and Figures 4/14 address an important omission in v1's landscape analysis, replacing a broad amplification suggestion with substantially better-supported regime boundaries. New comparator and robustness checks strengthen the empirical assessment. Caption inconsistencies, contradictory ratio wording, and reduced uncertainty reporting for the replacement landscape plots are drawbacks, but do not outweigh this central scientific improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same privacy-auditing work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds batch-size/noise experiments, a comparator evaluation, unknown-initialization tests, pretrained-model auditing, and privacy-profile results.

before.justification: V1 reports original auditing experiments on CIFAR10 and Housing, synthetic loss-landscape experiments, and appendix analyses of adversary variants and auditing approximations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: UnKEBench, non-local block key-value storage, cause-driven optimization, and effectiveness on structured and unstructured editing with batch and sequential capabilities. Additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 materially revises the comparative interpretation. Where v2 emphasizes UnKE's leading FactScore and little general-capability impact, v3 acknowledges IKE's much higher FactScore, attributes it to reading comprehension with supplied answers, and characterizes this as 'cheating'. It also introduces a locality tradeoff attributed to UnKE modifying more parameters. Appendix F qualifies KnowEdit advantages by dataset.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents benchmark checks, including matching thresholds of 0.8 and 0.9, entity consistency, regeneration rules, and a 15-token sub-answer limit. Appendix J adds LoRA/AdaLoRA settings, RECT tuning information, and IKE templates, retrieval, and inference details. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; they do not establish that the previously used benchmark was regenerated. UnKE's own settings and code link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual KnowEdit evaluation on WikiData_recent, ZsRE, WikiBio, WikiData_counterfact, ConvSent, and Sanitation (Appendix F, Table 8), substantially extending evaluated coverage. UnKEBench also gains unrelated knowledge questions constructed from Wikipedia triples for locality evaluation. Its original 1,000 counterfactual texts and the earlier evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds LoRA, AdaLoRA, RECT, and IKE with and without ICL to the retained FT-A, FT-L, ROME, MEMIT, and MEND comparisons. The new KnowEdit comparison additionally includes SERAC, ICE, and FT-M as labeled in Table 8. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 adds Loc-FactScore evaluation on unrelated questions and KnowEdit evaluations reporting editing success, portability, locality, and fluency. New baseline protocols include IKE answer-containing prompts with or without five retrieved examples and LoRA/AdaLoRA tuning. The retained UnKEBench batch size, decoding temperature, editing layer, and human-evaluation design are unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a direct assessment of unrelated-fact preservation through Loc-FactScore and qualitative LoRA/AdaLoRA convergence and hyperparameter-sensitivity observations in Appendix J. The original module/loss ablations, layer sweep, batch and sequential editing analyses, human-correlation analysis, and generation case study remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same three-annotator evaluation of 36 samples per method, Fleiss' kappa of 0.57, and Pearson correlations with p-values. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or other uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: v3 adds baseline, locality, and KnowEdit results. IKE obtains FactScores of 94.60 without ICL and 93.08 with ICL, exceeding UnKE's retained 42.49. Existing metric assignments also change: Table 4's UnKE Bert-Score changes from 98.63/76.85 to 99.61/93.09. The layer-7 MMLU entry changes from 29.72 to 29.68, and reported FT-L/FT-A runtimes change from 24/31 to 14/21 hours. These are added or revised reported results, not demonstrated improvements to UnKE itself.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same non-local block key-value representation, last-token optimization, and three-loss objective. Equations 1–7 and UnKE's two-stage editing procedure are unchanged.

P1.justification: Most core prose remains unchanged. Benchmark construction moves from Section 5.1 to Appendix A, Section 5.1 becomes Evaluation Metrics, and the experimental discussion and appendix documentation expand. There are localized wording, cross-reference, author-header, and acknowledgement edits rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The principal comparison in Table 2 is substantially expanded with baseline rows and a locality column, while v3 adds the extensive KnowEdit table and two IKE prompt tables. Figure 1 moves earlier and its caption is shortened; appendix tables and prompt examples are relocated or reformatted. The original four figures are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds AKEW and LEME and distinguishes their entity-concept editing from UnKEBench's direct unstructured-text editing. Additional references address parameter memory and downstream applications. These are localized additions; the existing related-work taxonomy and principal research positioning remain.

T1.justification: The knowledge-localization hypotheses, mathematical representation, and optimization derivations are retained. Equations 1–7 are unchanged, and v3 introduces no new theorem, proof, or substantive formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v2's empirical support: Table 2 introduces competitive parameter-efficient and in-context baselines and directly tests unrelated-knowledge retention, exposing meaningful tradeoffs. KnowEdit broadens the test of applicability, while benchmark-validation and implementation details improve reproducibility. Corrected metric assignments also improve consistency across tables. The dismissive treatment of IKE's advantage and the unfinished RECT configuration sentence are weaknesses, but the gains in evidential coverage and transparency clearly outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UnKE method and UnKEBench benchmark. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, locality measurements, and UnKE results on KnowEdit.

before.justification: v2 reports original automatic and human evaluations, structured knowledge editing experiments, ablations, and batch and sequential editing results.

C1.justification: v2 makes inexpensive online likelihood evaluation an explicit central contribution, whereas v1 emphasized pretraining, PTT sampling, and PTT-based likelihood estimation. Its conclusion also qualifies pretraining's benefits for tightly clustered datasets and acknowledges limited benefits during long training, narrowing v1's broadly positive generative-quality claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains why pretraining offers limited benefits on less clustered data and why long training can again lose equilibrium, recommending combination with optimized MCMC methods (Section 6). It also connects train/test likelihood divergence with increasing privacy loss and analyzes exchange-acceptance versus computational-cost tradeoffs (Appendices H and B.1). These substantially extend v1's interpretations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 supplies RCM dimensionalities, hidden-unit counts, and pretraining times (Table 5), total training times (Table 4), and implementation details for persistent online-AIS chains (Appendix D.2). The printed code/data pointer changes from nbereux/fast-RBM to anonymousrbm/iclr-2025. These are additional reproducibility disclosures; repository accessibility itself cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds generative-model evaluation on 2D Ising configurations, 32-by-32 black-and-white CelebA images, and full MNIST, while retaining MNIST01, Mickey, and human genome data (Table 2, Figures 2 and 16). This materially broadens coverage to physical configurations, faces, and the remaining digit classes.

E2.justification: v2 directly evaluates Parallel Tempering, reference-distribution Parallel Tempering, and Stacked Tempering against PTT on retained datasets (Figure 4); v1 directly compared PTT with Gibbs sampling and discussed Stacked Tempering through published speedups. v2 also adds reference-distribution AIS comparisons. JarRBM disappears from the plotted training comparisons, although its implementation and failure discussion remain.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes HGD hidden units from 185 to 200 and Mickey from 100 to 200. v2 introduces small-RBM exact-enumeration validation and varying AIS schedules. Sampling comparisons count Gibbs steps across all replicas instead of v1's per-replica steps, and the main PTT acceptance target changes from approximately 0.30 to 0.25. Figure 10 additionally selects models at comparable privacy loss.

E4.justification: New Appendices B.1 and F examine equilibration, exchange-acceptance sensitivity, and learning-rate/hidden-width sensitivity using autocorrelation curves, cost curves, and likelihood grids. Appendix H adds longitudinal privacy and overfitting analyses beyond v1's endpoint comparison. Conversely, v1's supplementary sampling case studies for PCD- and JarRBM-trained machines are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports jump-count averages over 100 chains without corresponding uncertainty reporting or a stated training-replication count. v2 Figure 2 newly reports 10 trainings and standard-deviation bands conditional on a common low-rank initialization. Figure 4 increases the sampling ensemble to 1000 chains and reports errors of the mean; Appendix B.1 also specifies uncertainty estimation for autocorrelation times.

E6.justification: v2 adds exact-likelihood error curves, broader training results, runtimes, sensitivity scores, and equilibration estimates, while removing JarRBM curves and v1's acceleration-factor table. For example, its new MNIST01 grid reports test likelihoods of -73.99 ± 2.71 for PCD and -66.37 ± 1.10 for pretraining plus PCD at 1000 hidden units and learning rate 0.01 (Figure 7). Results involving changed widths, estimators, or cost accounting are not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: v2 adds online Tr-AIS using persistent evaluation chains and per-update importance weights, and separates standalone offline Tr-AIS from PTT-based estimation (Section 5.1, Appendix D). It extends the existing bias treatment with a separate dataset-mean direction entering only the visible bias (Appendix A.3). The underlying RCM pretraining framework and PTT swap rule are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 5 is reorganized around trajectory annealing with separate likelihood-estimation and sampling subsections, and the main-text privacy section moves into Appendix H within a substantially reorganized supplement. The title, citation style, and headers also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from three-method density maps to scatter plots, marginal histograms, and likelihood curves; Figure 4 expands the sampler comparison and changes its cost axis. v2 adds accuracy, sensitivity, and equilibration plots plus timing tables. Low-rank generation panels move from Figure 1 to Figure 15, while the existing PTT schematic is retained as Figure 5.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly positions its approach as a practical extension of earlier RCM work, identifying bias and sampling developments needed for real datasets. It substantially expands AIS/PT, equilibration, phase-transition, and neural/biomedical references, including Neal, Hukushima and Nemoto, Sokal, and Bravi. Several quantum and AdS application references from v1 are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds AIS path-weight identities, and Appendix E derives forward/backward transition corrections before applying the symmetric-update assumption already stated in v1. Appendix G introduces substantial Curie-Weiss and phase-transition mathematics, while Appendix A.3 formalizes the additional bias direction. The new Appendix G nevertheless contains an internal inconsistency: its positive Hm term favors negative magnetization for positive H, contrary to the accompanying interpretation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through exact-likelihood checks on small RBMs, direct comparisons with stronger samplers that account for replica count, replicated trainings, and equilibration diagnostics. These address important weaknesses in v1's evidence, while the new applicability limits make the conclusions better qualified. Removing explicit JarRBM results and introducing the Appendix G sign inconsistency are drawbacks, but they are outweighed by the stronger validation of the central methods.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same low-rank RBM pretraining and Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT) work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained and additional datasets, including exact-likelihood validation, sampler comparisons, sensitivity studies, and equilibration measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original training, generation, likelihood, sampling, and privacy results on MNIST01, Mickey, and human genome data.

C1.justification: The claims about general architectural applicability, tensorial communication and normal-regression performance remain. V3 adds iterative local-frame refinement as an explicit main contribution and claims that it strictly generalizes static local canonicalization, materially extending the paper's claimed contribution.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations for why refinement benefits from an expanding receptive field, why normal estimation is noise-sensitive, and why Gram–Schmidt makes later frame axes less robust. It newly acknowledges discontinuities and symmetric degeneracies in canonical frames and interprets PCA-versus-learned frame performance as task-dependent. These substantially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: V3 documents refinement MLP dimensions, ShapeNet inputs and a full segmentation architecture and hyperparameter configuration. It revises existing architecture specifications and hardware/training-time reports, and newly discloses random-direction handling of parallel frame vectors. These additions materially expand implementation information beyond v2's two-task setup.

E1.justification: V2 evaluates only ModelNet40 normal regression and classification. V3 retains both and adds ShapeNet part segmentation, real-world ScanObjectNN classification and evaluations under Gaussian input noise, substantially broadening tasks and input conditions.

E2.justification: Normal-regression comparisons expand from Luo et al. alone to include RS-CNN, DGCNN and GC-Conv (Table 1). ModelNet40 classification expands from CRIN alone to numerous comparators, including PointNet, TFN and both Vector Neurons variants (v3 Table 4). These are actual comparison rows using published scores; the PDFs do not establish that those baselines were rerun.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: the regression learning rate falls from 5e-3 to 2.5e-3, encoder sampling fractions change, and classification feature configurations and frame-prediction MLP sizes change. Figure 4 replaces classification-error scaling with normal-regression cosine-error scaling. V3 also introduces noise/jitter protocols and a 500-epoch ScanObjectNN setting.

E4.justification: V3 retains the learned/random-frame and scalar/tensor-message ablation, adds comparisons with and without iterative refinement, and tests PCA frames against learned frames. Appendix D and Figure 5 add noise-sensitivity analyses of predictions, complete frames and individual frame axes, including training with versus without jitter. The data-efficiency analysis also changes task.

E5.justification: V3 extends uncertainty depiction to robustness results through shaded bands in Figure 5, but does not explain their statistical meaning or sampling basis. Runtime reporting remains mean plus standard deviation over ten test-set loops in both versions. No increase in repeated training runs or newly specified seed counts is established.

E6.justification: Under revised settings, unrefined learned-frame tensor results change from 0.86 to 0.87 cosine similarity and from 88.3% to 88.0% ModelNet40 classification accuracy. V3 adds refined-model results, including 0.88 cosine similarity, 80.2 ShapeNet IoU and 81.0% ScanObjectNN accuracy, plus PCA and noise findings. Runtime values and Figure 4 results also change. These are not controlled performance gains across versions.

M1.justification: V2 keeps predicted local frames fixed during message passing. V3 adds iterative frame refinement: an MLP predicts an SO(3) rotation after each layer, updates the local frame and transforms features into that updated frame (Section 4.3.1, Equations 14–15). This substantially extends the retained tensorial-message procedure.

P1.justification: V3 changes the title and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and method explanations around local canonicalization. ModelNet40 classification moves into Appendix D, while experimental details become a separate Appendix E. The revised narrative emphasizes communication between frames and their iterative refinement.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the scalar-message illustration as an early scalar-versus-tensor comparison, adds refinement to the pipeline diagram and redraws the frame-transformation illustration. It replaces Figure 4's plotted task, adds the six-panel robustness Figure 5, expands comparison tables and relocates classification results. These are substantial display changes beyond the conference-template update.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises positioning around canonicalization, adding frame averaging, learned canonicalization, approximate frame transitions and gauge-equivariant approaches, including Puny, Kaba, Du and Cohen. The earlier survey of handcrafted local-frame construction is removed. V3 also connects its data-efficiency discussion to newer work on broken symmetries and equivariant scaling.

T1.justification: The central representation framework and invariance derivations remain. V3 adds a short proof of equivariance for local-frame construction in Appendix B and mathematical justification for refinement and feature transport in Equations 14–15. Equation 13 also corrects the missing inverse in v2's derivation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens scrutiny of the central mechanism: refinement ablations, PCA alternatives and noise tests address frame-estimation questions left largely untested in v2, while segmentation, real-world classification and broader comparator tables address its narrow empirical validation. Added mathematical justification, explicit degeneracy caveats and clearer diagrams improve assessability. Accuracy results still lack repeated-run uncertainty, and Figure 5's bands are undefined, but these remaining weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same tensorial message-passing framework and PointNet++ adaptation, despite the changed title. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 reports original experiments on ModelNet40, ShapeNet and ScanObjectNN, including frame-refinement, noise-robustness and PCA-frame comparisons.
