before.justification: V2 reports original ModelNet40 normal-regression and classification experiments, frame/message ablations, data-efficiency curves and runtime measurements.

results.title: Beyond Canonicalization: How Tensorial Messages Improve Equivariant Message Passing

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims about generating diverse, learnable tasks through code. However, the introduction removes the explicit 'under the reward hypothesis' qualification from the claim of creating any simulatable task, making that claim less explicitly conditional.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the ablations as evidence that both the archive and interestingness guidance contribute to diversity, and the ANNECS-OMNI curves as evidence of continued innovation during the measured runs. Existing limitations concerning simulator constraints, specialist agents, and VLM success detection remain.

D1.justification: The new evaluation describes the control's prompt/filter modifications and the embedding-to-PCA-to-bin processing procedure. Existing generated-code listings, prompts, model identifiers, training hyperparameters, and hardware disclosures are retained in the renumbered appendices.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate task generation and R2D2 learning in PyBullet using the same three seed tasks and broad navigation/object-interaction coverage. The additional runs generate further instances within this retained setting.

E2.justification: V1 has no evaluated comparison controls. V2 introduces OMNI-EPIC w/o archive and OMNI-EPIC learning progress only, comparing both against the full method in the diversity and learning-progress experiments.

E3.justification: Section 6 adds controlled evaluations using cell coverage after two-dimensional PCA and progress measured by ANNECS and ANNECS-OMNI. These are new protocols; the original t-SNE visualization and reported DreamerV3 training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New ablations test the contributions of archive conditioning and interestingness guidance. The latter control removes both interestingness requests from task-generation prompts and post-generation filtering. Figures 4, 33, and 34 supply evidence absent from v1.

E5.justification: V2 expands the reported learning experiments from one run to five and reports three simulated-learning runs per method for the diversity comparison. It adds median curves, 95% confidence intervals, and Mann-Whitney U tests reporting p < 0.05; v1 lacks this statistical reporting.

E6.justification: The original 16-success, 6-failure, 1-uninteresting-task result is retained. V2 adds four runs and quantitative control comparisons: Figure 4 shows median ANNECS-OMNI reaching 10 for the full method versus 4 for each control at plotted learned-archive size 13. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The archive, task and environment generators, interestingness filtering, specialist-agent training, and success detection remain unchanged. Calling the filter the post-generation model of interestingness clarifies an existing component; the corresponding prompts are retained.

P1.justification: Localized method rewrites distinguish task-generation interestingness from post-generation checking. V2 adds a quantitative-results section and two appendices, changes citations to author-year style, and makes small wording edits, while retaining most existing prose and appendix listings.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 4 and Figures 29–34, introducing quantitative plots and four additional task-outcome image grids. It also relabels Figure 1, relocates Figure 3, and changes document styling. Existing figures and both hyperparameter tables are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Mackiewicz and Ratajczak (1993), Mouret and Clune (2015), and Pugh et al. (2016) for PCA and diversity measurement. Section 6 also positions ANNECS-OMNI as an extension of ANNECS informed by OMNI; the main related-work discussion remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 6 introduces a limited new metric definition: ANNECS-OMNI adds an interestingness condition to ANNECS's accumulated count of qualifying solved environments. No theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee accompanies this definition.

improvement.justification: V1 relies primarily on qualitative generation examples and one learning run. V2 addresses an important evidential gap through component ablations, additional learning runs, and quantitative comparisons with uncertainty reporting. Small samples and model-judged interestingness still limit the conclusions, and removing the reward-hypothesis caveat slightly reduces precision, but the new controlled evidence substantially strengthens support for the paper's central design.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OMNI-EPIC and provide readable main texts, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained task descriptions, code, prompts, and settings can be matched across renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by four additional learning runs and quantitative comparisons against two controls in Section 6 and Appendices D–E.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original task-generation and reinforcement-learning experiments, including a 200-iteration generation run and a learning run reporting 16 successes, 6 failures, and 1 uninteresting task.

results.title: OMNI-EPIC: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness with Environments Programmed in Code

C1.justification: The abstract changes 'can endlessly create' to 'has the potential to endlessly create,' and the conclusion similarly qualifies endless generation. The core contribution—code-generated, interesting and learnable curricula—remains, with more cautious claims about indefinite continuation.

C2.justification: v3 adds caveats about resemblance to foundation-model training data, cyclic task rejection and the absence of demonstrated cross-task generalization. The generalist-training discussion, moved from Section 5 to Appendix O, changes 'straightforward' feasibility into a substantial future undertaking. These refine the retained applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly states that all code is open-sourced and provides a direct repository link. v3 also documents pooled PCA/binning, human-study instructions and compensation, the learning-progress ablation prompt, and Ant action bounds. Existing hyperparameter tables, hardware disclosures, core prompts and task code remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The R2D2/PyBullet task coverage is retained. Appendix P adds Ant-robot training with eight-dimensional continuous control and four illustrated task demonstrations, extending embodiment and control requirements beyond the original six-action R2D2 setting within the same simulator.

E2.justification: v3 retains OMNI-EPIC Learning Progress Only and OMNI-EPIC w/o archive, while adding evaluated variants using training from scratch, uniformly sampled archive examples, successful examples only, and no learning-progress prompting. Appendix G and Figure 41 substantially expand the comparison set around the system's central components.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include transfer-versus-scratch comparisons on the same generated tasks with equal two-million-step budgets, a 50-participant video-rating study, and diversity measurements at additional discretization levels. These extend the evaluation protocol; v3's clarification of pooled PCA and the original binning procedure does not establish that retained experiments changed.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's archive and interestingness controls, Appendix G tests transfer learning, example retrieval, failed-task examples and learning-progress prompting. Appendices H–I add human checks of success judgments, diversity sensitivity to discretization, and analysis of learned-task fractions over time. These substantially strengthen component and robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report three simulated-learning runs, five RL runs, medians with 95% confidence intervals, and Mann-Whitney U tests. New results extend these existing reporting practices. Neither increased replication of retained experiments nor a new statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Original results, including Figure 4 and the illustrated run's 16 successes, six failures and one uninteresting task, are retained. New findings include median success of 63.2% with transfer versus 36.8% from scratch, 5/7/0 learned generated tasks in the three prompt/retrieval ablations, and 72.7% human–detector agreement. Added sensitivity results show that short-run diversity differences are not always significant. These are new comparisons and findings, not improvements over v2 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The archive retrieval, task/environment generators, interestingness filtering, DreamerV3 transfer learning and success-checking procedure remain unchanged. Core prompts and task code match. v3 clarifies the use of code-based success detection and relocates existing VLM material to Appendix C; these do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: There are targeted language corrections and clearer method and metric explanations. Existing VLM discussion and prompts are consolidated in Appendix C, and generalist-training discussion moves to Appendix O. The main narrative and extensive existing appendices remain largely intact, alongside bibliography and conference-header edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial visual material: three ablation montages, the human-annotation interface, two sensitivity figures, a learned-task-fraction curve and Ant demonstrations. Existing plots are retained and rearranged, including v2 Figures 33–34 becoming v3 Figures 37 and 40. Main-text figures also move within the revised layout.

R1.justification: v3 adds intrinsic-motivation and procedural-generation context, including Oudeyer, Baranes, Colas, Shaker, Juliani and Justesen references. The relocated VLM discussion cites Du et al. (2023) in place of Christiano et al. (2017). Positioning relative to OMNI and environment-design approaches remains broadly unchanged; many other citation edits concern the same works.

T1.justification: The Darwin Completeness concept and ANNECS-OMNI criterion are retained. No new theorem, proof or formal derivation is introduced. Expanded descriptions of embeddings, PCA and binning clarify existing empirical measurement rather than introduce new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the curriculum mechanisms through controlled transfer comparisons and component ablations, tests diversity-metric robustness, and independently checks success judgments with humans. These address important evidential gaps in v2, while qualified claims improve calibration. The 72.7% human agreement still leaves success measurement imperfect, and generalist performance remains untested, but the added evidence and transparency provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OMNI-EPIC. Their main text, figures, tables, prompts and extensive task-code appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds component ablations, human evaluation, sensitivity analyses and Ant-robot demonstrations.

before.justification: v2 reports original task-generation experiments, five short RL-training runs, and quantitative comparisons of diversity and open-ended progress in Sections 4–6 and the appendices.

results.title: OMNI-EPIC: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness with Environments Programmed in Code

C1.justification: v2 foregrounds Sparse Expansion as an efficient, leading one-shot sparsification approach. v3 redefines its central contribution around measuring neuronal entanglement and using Sparse Expansion as an experimental framework, adding claims involving mapping difficulty and empirical computational bounds. The earlier pruning-performance claims survive, particularly in the appendix, but no longer organize the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking entanglement to superposition, early training dynamics, effective feature counts, and disproportionate pruning despite modest weight magnitudes. It explains why preserving high-WD neurons can fail under a fixed sparsity budget. Section 3.6 also explicitly judges practical deployment unlikely without memory-footprint optimizations, substantially qualifying v2's efficiency emphasis and narrower acknowledgment that end-to-end timing remained future work.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies calibration on a Wikitext-2 training subset and evaluation on its test set, and explicitly identifies GPTQ in the retained compression setup. It removes v2's A100 counts and MI100 hardware disclosure. The code-access information, RAPIDS dependency, 16-cluster default, pseudocode, and RTX3090 latency setup remain.

E1.justification: v2's evaluation centers on Wikitext-2. v3 retains it and adds SQuAD 2.0, TriviaQA-Wiki, GSM8K, MMLU, and BBH capability tests, plus zero-shot transfer evaluations including ARC-e, ARC-c, Lambada, and SciQ (Section 2.3 and Appendix A.3). This substantially broadens the evaluated task requirements.

E2.justification: The principal pruning comparators remain magnitude pruning, Wanda, and SparseGPT; all already appear in v2's plots. v3 adds neuron-selection comparators based on output mean, output variance, and weight magnitude in Figure 3, and a GMM/BIC component-count predictor in Figure 7's comparison with Wasserstein distance.

E3.justification: v3 replaces the cosine-input/L1-output characterization with normalized L2 distances and mapping difficulty, and changes the central neuron-ablation model from Llama-2-7B to Llama-3-8B. New protocols include specified few-shot and zero-shot evaluations, 17 training checkpoints, and fixed-total-sparsity interventions. Figure 9 accounts for routing in its efficiency axes. These additions and revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of performance recovery after targeted neuron expansion, weighted WD/MD reductions, training-time emergence, weight-magnitude confounds, GMM predictors, PCA-based computational frontiers, and expert-count benefits by neuron group. Appendix A.7 tests preserving high-WD neurons at fixed total sparsity and finds deterioration. The earlier quantized-neuron sensitivity experiment in v2 Figure 4 is removed; existing cluster-count and distribution analyses largely remain.

E5.justification: v3 Figure A10 explicitly identifies its shaded spread as group minima and maxima, whereas the corresponding shading in v2 Figure A.5 is unexplained. Standard-error reporting already existed in v2 and continues in v3; its application to additional analyses does not establish a new uncertainty practice. Neither version reports repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial benchmark and mechanistic results. For example, Table A1 reports Llama-3.2-1B MMLU scores of 28.729 for Sparse Expansion and 25.046 for SparseGPT at 50% sparsity. Figure 1 revises displayed RI values from 1.11/1.53 to 1.18/1.77. Earlier quantization-sweep results are removed, while v2 Tables 1 and 2 retain identical values as v3 Tables A5 and A3. These are additions, removals, and numerical revisions, not an established across-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The matched pseudocode and architecture retain PCA/K-means routing, copied dense weights, cluster-specific SparseGPT pruning, and expert selection without retraining. The new diagnostic metrics and experimental interventions do not change the proposed Sparse Expansion procedure. Explicit GPTQ attribution accompanies retained compression results rather than establishing an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Sparse Expansion and Neuronal Disentanglement' to 'Wasserstein Distances, Neuronal Entanglement, and Sparsity.' The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Neuron analysis now precedes the method, performance becomes a subsection of the experimental framework, and substantial existing material moves into reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: v3 adds capability radar charts, mechanistic scatterplots, training trajectories, and benchmark tables. It redraws input-output plots, merges the retained scaling and sparsity comparisons into Figure 9 with revised efficiency axes, and adds fitted lines to appendix plots. Existing performance and latency tables move to the appendix, while several quantization panels disappear.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts substantially toward polysemanticity, special-neuron research, and computational superposition, adding discussion of Bricken, Lecomte, Gurnee, Stolfo, Hänni, and Adler–Shavit. v3 also distinguishes its use of Wasserstein distance from SWAP and WD-based channel pruning. Much of v2's discussion of DejaVu, MoEfication, activation sparsity, and sparse upcycling is removed.

T1.justification: v3 introduces a central formal definition of mapping difficulty: the average ratio of normalized output and input distances, using median-output and maximum-input normalization (Equation 2). Appendix A.8 develops the normalization rationale, replacing v2's qualitative characterization with an explicit mathematical quantity. The Wasserstein definition remains unchanged; Section 3.5's computational bounds are empirical observations, not new proved theorems.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's relatively qualitative characterization of entanglement and Wikitext-centered validation. Mapping difficulty, measured WD/MD reductions, alternative neuron controls, the negative fixed-sparsity intervention, and downstream-task evaluations make the central hypothesis more explicit and better tested. The memory limitation also improves the qualification of practical claims. Removed hardware details and some quantization results are meaningful but limited costs relative to these gains; the computational-bound evidence remains empirical.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Sparse Expansion and Wasserstein-neuron research despite the changed title and emphasis. Their main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds downstream-task evaluations, training-checkpoint analyses, neuronal controls, and experiments connecting clustering to entanglement measures.

before.justification: v2 reports original pruning benchmarks, neuron-distribution analyses, sparsification interventions, expert-count experiments, and layer-level latency measurements.

results.title: Wasserstein Distances, Neuronal Entanglement, and Sparsity

C1.justification: The introduction removes v3's assertion that the scalar-direction decomposition is impossible for first-order methods and acknowledges a related first-order construction. This narrows the exclusivity claim. The central claims about dimension-free communication, convergence under low effective rank, and empirical communication savings remain.

C2.justification: Appendix A.5 newly attributes advantages over gradient projection to smoothing and higher-order effects, and discusses additional backpropagation and gradient-storage costs. Appendix A.2 adds an explicit memory comparison with FedZO. Appendix B.3 distinguishes direct small-model Hessian evidence from indirect LLM scaling evidence. Existing computational-cost and heterogeneity limitations remain.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code URL and a reproducibility statement identifying the execution, configuration, and README files. It newly specifies LoRA rank=8, alpha=8, and Q/V targets, explains seed generation, and supplies complete multiple-perturbation pseudocode. These expand disclosure without establishing that the retained LoRA implementation changed.

E1.justification: v4 adds CIFAR10 training for the custom-ResNet Hessian analysis in Appendix B.3.1. MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and the six NLP tasks remain. Additional OPT sizes extend model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds FedAvg to the full-parameter LLM comparisons, where v3 evaluated only MeZO, FedZO, and DeComFL configurations. Figure 4 additionally evaluates the first-order gradient-projection adaptation against DeComFL. These substantially broaden the empirical comparison with first-order alternatives; FedZO's perturbation-count change is a setting change.

E3.justification: Section 5 changes the stated MNIST FedAvg learning rate from 0.001 to 0.1, while retaining 0.001 for DeComFL. Table 2 changes FedZO from P=5 to P=10. New analyses introduce OPT-350M/2.7B configurations, Hessian-spectrum estimation, and Top-k settings of 5% and 1%. Existing client sampling, data partitioning, and documented DeComFL fine-tuning budgets remain.

E4.justification: New Figures 4–6 examine finite differences versus gradient projection, the low-rank rationale through Hessian spectra and convergence across model sizes, and sensitivity to stronger Top-k compression. These substantially extend the original P/K and LoRA analyses. The full-parameter P=5 DeComFL comparison is removed from Table 2, although the LoRA perturbation comparison remains.

E5.justification: Figure 2 already displays DeComFL means and standard-deviation bands in v3, and v4 retains that practice. Neither version supplies experimental replication counts, replication seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added seed-generation explanation concerns the algorithm, not repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds FedAvg results, replaces FedZO P=5 results with P=10 results, and removes full-parameter DeComFL P=5 entries; retained DeComFL P=10 scores are unchanged. Figure 2's left-panel FedAvg curves change, and Figures 4–6 add findings. In the retained LoRA comparison, FedZO's SST-2 accuracy stays 85.34%, but its reported cost changes from 279.40 TB to 0.66 TB (v3 Table 5; v4 Table 6).

M1.justification: Appendix A.5 introduces an optional DeComFL variant that replaces finite-difference scalars with projections of backpropagated gradients, formalized in Algorithm 5. Algorithm 2 also removes a redundant history summation. The core DeComFL framework remains intact; Algorithms 3–4 document the multiple-perturbation method already described and used in v3.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose are retained, with local wording corrections, updated affiliations, author-year citations, and expanded explanations. Acknowledgments, a reproducibility statement, and additional appendix subsections are added without a wholesale narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: v4 adopts the ICLR layout, changing typography, spacing, and figure/table placement throughout. Figure 1 gains reset annotations; Figures 4–6, a memory-comparison table, and Algorithms 3–5 are added. Table 2's comparison columns are restructured. This is a substantial display and layout revision beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v4 discusses Yue et al.'s CORE projection approach and distinguishes its distributed setting from FL. It also adds an attributed criticism of FedMeZO's proof and references supporting the ResNet and Hessian analyses. The broader communication-efficient FL and zeroth-order research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 corrects the Gaussian smoothing normalization exponent from P/2 to d/2. Appendix A.5 adds projection equations and a Taylor-expansion argument relating first-order projection to finite differences. The principal convergence rates and most of the Appendix C proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central communication-efficiency claim by adding the missing first-order LLM comparison, reporting FedAvg learning-rate tuning, revising extreme communication-cost entries, and testing the low-rank rationale and stronger compression. Implementation disclosures also improve reproducibility. The removed full-tuning P=5 comparison and unresolved 'Figure ??' reference for learning-rate tuning reduce completeness, but the gains address important weaknesses in the earlier empirical comparisons and reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DeComFL and contain readable main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C. Their corresponding content can be matched despite the formatting changes and expanded appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains original benchmark results and adds gradient-projection comparisons, Hessian-spectrum analysis, model-scaling experiments, and compression-sensitivity results.

before.justification: v3 reports original MNIST and Fashion-MNIST experiments, OPT fine-tuning results across six NLP datasets, and additional LoRA results in Appendix B.

results.title: Achieving Dimension-Free Communication in Federated Learning via Zeroth-Order Optimization

C1.justification: The central claims about unsupervised task creation, in-context learning, and prediction without fine-tuning remain. The introduction changes superiority across 'all datasets' to 'several datasets,' and the introduction and conclusion relax the main hardware-efficiency claim from 4GB to 8GB VRAM.

C2.justification: Multi-dataset training is reinterpreted as offering little benefit to CAMeLU because task generation already supplies diversity, replacing v1's modest-improvement interpretation. The default extractor is now justified by comparison fairness, and Appendix A.7 qualifies scalability through quadratic support-set cost. Existing noisy-data and fixed-way limitations remain after relocation.

D1.justification: Implementation documentation updates the GPU from an RTX 3050 Ti with 4GB to an RTX 3070 Ti with 8GB, describes ResNet-50 pretraining and BECLR configuration, and identifies 25 queries for the main comparison. Code release remains promised upon acceptance. Appendix A.1 introduces an inconsistent CLIP description that reverses the earlier image-feature and concatenated-input dimensions.

E1.justification: Meta-iNat adds another fine-grained classification domain for evaluation and baseline training, extending coverage beyond the four retained benchmarks. The few-shot task family remains unchanged. ImageNet-964, miniImageNet, MSCOCO, and Fungi training experiments remain present; multi-dataset training moves to Appendix A.3.

E2.justification: The small-scale training comparison adds BECLR alongside PsCo and CAMeLU (v1 Table 8 versus v2 Tables 2 and 11). Appendix A.5 also introduces a k-means task-generation comparator. The existing external baseline families remain represented.

E3.justification: The main CAMeLU configuration changes from CLIP-ViT-B/16 to supervised ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet-964, increasing the transformer input width from 1024 to 2304. Cross-domain PsCo training changes from ImageNet-1k to ImageNet-964 to remove overlap with miniImageNet evaluation classes. Appendix A.1 changes image normalization from [0,1] to zero mean and unit variance. Appendix A.7 adds a one-query evaluation condition; these are substantive reported setting changes.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands task-generation testing with quantitative augmentation-only and k-means comparisons in Table 7, replacing v1's leakage-versus-no-leakage learning-curve comparison. It adds an extractor-pretraining overlap control and a one-query analysis. The embedding case study gains centroid distances while dropping the CIFAR-fs illustration. Pixel-versus-patch mixing, Beta-parameter sensitivity, and logistic learning-phase analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across three complete runs, with evaluation averaged over 500 tasks. v2 relocates the main tables' standard deviations to Appendix A.10 rather than removing uncertainty reporting. No new statistical testing or repeated-run practice is specified.

E6.justification: Main and ablation results are extensively replaced or supplemented. For example, Table 1's CAMeLU miniImageNet 1-shot/5-shot accuracies change from 69.63/90.95 to 76.51/92.14 under revised settings, so these are not same-setting gains. New Meta-iNat, BECLR, clustering, and one-query results appear. The small-scale CAML learning curve changes from increasing in v1 Figure 6 to approximately flat in v2 Figure 3.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the specified query construction from mixing an existing support image with another image to mixing a separately augmented view of the support source image. ResNet-50 replaces CLIP as the default extractor, although both architectures were already evaluated in v1. The class encoder, transformer-based inference, and training objective remain.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: small-scale generalization moves from Appendix 7.6 to Section 4.5, multi-dataset training moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix A.3, and limitations move to Appendix A.9. Appendix analyses are reordered, with embedding analysis brought forward, and several experimental explanations are rewritten.

P2.justification: Main comparison tables are redesigned with Meta-iNat columns and means only, while full uncertainty tables are redisplayed in Appendix A.10. A new task-generation ablation table is added. The embedding figure is substantially redrawn with shaded clusters, centroids, and distances; learning-curve displays are revised and several figures and tables are relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds BECLR and distinguishes its contrastive few-shot framework from meta-learning. It also adds citations for deep residual learning and the Meta-iNat source. The broader positioning relative to UML, image mixing, and in-context learning remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 restores the missing '1 minus' in the simplified class-collision probability, correcting its inconsistency with the preceding expression. Appendix A.7 adds a computational-cost argument of O(Q(NK+1)^2 d). The existing training formulation and logistic-phase mathematics remain, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the main comparison by replacing v1's mismatched default backbones and leakage-affected PsCo evaluation with common ResNet-50/ImageNet-964 settings. Additional task-generation controls and the BECLR comparison better test the method's contribution beyond its feature extractor. New reporting defects, including reversed CLIP dimensions in A.1 and inconsistent multi-dataset values between Tables 5 and 6(b), limit reproducibility, but the improved experimental controls provide a substantial net gain in evidential quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAMeLU research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial experimental revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification results and ablations, including additional Meta-iNat evaluations, BECLR comparisons, clustering-based task generation, and a one-query experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original few-shot classification experiments, learning curves, feature-extractor ablations, and task-generation analyses in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Unsupervised Meta-Learning via In-Context Learning

C1.justification: v1's introduction and conclusion emphasize performance against individual fixed hyperparameter configurations. v2 explicitly claims superiority over competitive AutoRL baselines and extends the abstract's empirical scope to Atari. This broadens the central comparative contribution while retaining the shared-target selection idea.

C2.justification: The fixed-population and discount-factor limitations in v1 are replaced by implemented extensions in v2, while the reward-related restriction remains. v2 explicitly connects the theorem's ideal condition to infinite data and drops v1's interpretation that greedy selection necessarily yields the smallest achievable cumulative approximation error. Appendix C adds a concrete tradeoff: the 16-network configuration is sample-efficient but slower than random search.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds Atari preprocessing, search-space tables, tournament and mutation rules, weight preservation, optimizer resets, and Meta-gradient DQN settings. It also newly discloses horizons for the existing LunarLander and MuJoCo experiments, without establishing changed settings. The explicit GPU model and detailed overhead percentages in v1 are omitted. The promise of supplementary code and release upon acceptance remains unchanged.

E1.justification: LunarLander and the six MuJoCo environments are retained. v2 adds vision-based Atari control: three games for finite hyperparameter selection and six for population search, comprising eight distinct games across Figures 20 and 21. Discount-factor experiments additionally evaluate BattleZone and Freeway, both within that Atari coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds random-search references computed from individual runs to the existing MuJoCo comparisons, and evaluates SEARL, DEHB, and random search in the population-search experiment. Figure 8 adds Meta-gradient DQN. These extend v1's individual configurations, grid search, and random-target variants. Figure 7 plots DEHB, although its caption incorrectly mentions grid search.

E3.justification: New Atari protocols introduce stacked grayscale observations, sticky actions, human-normalized scores, and extensive hyperparameter search spaces. Section 5.4 specifies a 40M-frame population-search budget, six random-search trials of 30M frames, and DEHB budgets of 20M–40M frames. It reports running maximum returns for random search/DEHB and population extrema for SEARL. These are added evaluation designs; the stated parameters of the retained LunarLander and MuJoCo experiments largely match.

E4.justification: v2 adds Atari hyperparameter sensitivity studies, robustness tests varying target-update and population-update intervals, and a Pong hyperparameter-evolution case study. Appendix B.1 reports comparisons involving truncation selection and weight resets, while Appendix C adds performance-versus-time analyses. LunarLander Figure 3 gains behavioral-selection distributions. Conversely, the MuJoCo actor-selection distributions shown in v1 are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions use IQM with pointwise 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals and retain 20 LunarLander seeds and nine MuJoCo seeds. v2 additionally specifies five seeds for Atari. This adds run-count information without establishing any increase in repetitions for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial Atari results, including aggregate advantages over SEARL with a BattleZone exception in Figure 21, and similar performance to Meta-gradient DQN in Figure 8. The MuJoCo finding of outperforming 13 of 16 configurations in final performance remains. Figure 2 revises the AdaDQN-max curve from negative to positive late-training returns. v1's detailed win-count and resource-overhead tables disappear; Appendix C adds clock-time results and Atari memory measurements.

M1.justification: The original AdaDQN/AdaSAC procedures remain, but Section 5.4 and Appendix B.1 implement a population-based extension with selection and mutation, inverse-loss behavioral selection, and L2 ranking across networks trained with different losses. v2 also introduces training with different discount factors and a common cross-validated discount for network selection. v1 described population evolution as future work and excluded discount-factor tuning.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 3, the performance bound moves from the preliminaries to Appendix A, and the method's theoretical motivation is substantially rewritten and integrated into Section 4. The experimental narrative is reorganized around finite and infinite hyperparameter spaces, with an expanded setup appendix. These changes substantially alter the paper's structure and exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adds Atari plots, robustness radar charts, a population-workflow diagram, clock-time plots, and two Atari configuration tables. It merges v1's MuJoCo Figures 5 and 6, removes actor-selection panels, adds a behavioral-selection row to LunarLander Figure 3, and restructures legends and appendix plots. The original resource and win-count tables are removed, alongside a document-wide transition to the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: The AutoRL taxonomy and most related-work discussion are retained. v2 adds relevant references for Atari protocols, hyperparameter landscapes, evolutionary selection, and evaluation, including Mohan et al., Eimer et al., and Obando-Ceron et al. It expands the comparison with meta-gradient methods to discuss target tuning, first-order optimization, and non-stationarity, citing Xu et al.

T1.justification: The formal performance-loss bound, empirical-error selection theorem, and bias-variance proof are retained. v2 moves the cited bound to Appendix A and states the empirical conditional-expectation assumption explicitly in Theorem 4.1, but that assumption already appears in v1's Appendix A proof. The mathematical changes otherwise concern notation and presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly avoided direct AutoRL comparisons despite making AutoRL its central motivation. v2 substantially addresses that gap through comparisons with SEARL, DEHB, random search, and Meta-gradient DQN, alongside Atari validation and tested population and discount-factor extensions. Expanded implementation details and runtime analyses strengthen assessability. Some reporting quality is lost through omitted hardware and overhead details and inconsistencies involving Figures 2 and 7, but the gains in comparative evidence and demonstrated applicability outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AdaQN and contain readable text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained content can be matched across the reorganization, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original LunarLander and MuJoCo results and adds Atari experiments, AutoRL comparisons, robustness analyses, and discount-factor selection results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LunarLander and six-environment MuJoCo experiments, including learning curves, ablations, hyperparameter-selection analyses, and resource measurements.

results.title: Adaptive $Q$-Network: On-the-fly Target Selection for Deep Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The core optimizer and performance claims are retained. v2 adds an explainable Fisher measure to the stated contributions and extends the ImageNet conclusion to multi-GPU training. The introduction also drops v1's explicit restriction of the diagonal-energy finding to the examined architectures, layers, and losses.

C2.justification: The existing Fisher/Hessian convergence explanation moves to Appendix B.1. New discussion interprets Fisher histograms and component effects, and qualifies square-root-free Adam comparisons through a batch-size scaling requirement. v2 removes the distributed-training limitation, expands the caveat about literature ImageNet settings and augmentations, and drops the architecture-specific diagonal-dominance qualification.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands tuning documentation with damping, Hessian-power, and decay-factor search grids, and documents distributed hardware use and NNgeometry-based diagnostic procedures. It revises the available GPU inventory from eight to six and removes the experimental appendix's previously selected decay-factor pair. Selected learning-rate tables and the code-access link remain unchanged; some final parameter selections remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds Penn Treebank language-model evaluation in Section 4.3 and a MNIST subset for Fisher-approximation diagnostics in Appendix B.2. Existing image-classification, language-modeling, and IRIS visualization coverage is retained. Larger batches and multiple GPUs change settings rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The established benchmark comparator sets are retained, including KFAC renamed K-FAC. The new component experiment in Figure 13(A) adds square-root-free Adam as a comparator against AdaFisher variants; this is an evaluated modification rather than merely a citation.

E3.justification: v1 describes recommended/default settings for several CNN baselines; v2 reports learning-rate searches across optimizers and broader damping, Hessian-power, and decay-factor searches in Appendix D.2.1. This changes the reported protocol without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols also include distributed GPU/batch configurations, scheduler and component controls, and a 50-epoch MNIST reference-Fisher comparison using MAE.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained spectral, batch-size, learning-rate, and cutout analyses, new Appendix B directly tests schedulers, square-root omission, EMA, and normalization-layer Fisher computation. It adds Adam/AdaFisher Fisher-distribution diagnostics and comparison with a reference Fisher diagonal. Appendices A.4 and D.2.4 additionally examine distributed scaling and larger-batch behavior.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 newly reports Monte Carlo sampling for estimating the reference Fisher, adding a statistical estimation procedure without specifying its sample count. The existing five-initialization CIFAR mean/standard-deviation reporting and single-trial Tiny ImageNet/ImageNet practice remain unchanged; additional repeated training runs are not established.

E6.justification: Matched existing benchmark table values are unchanged. New results include PTB perplexities of 41.15 for AdaFisherW, 44.70 for AdamW, and 59.43 for AdaHessian (Table 4); ImageNet top-1 accuracies of 77.01 and 77.09 at batches 512 and 1024 (Figure 5); and distributed timing, ablation, and Fisher-diagnostic results. These are added results under new conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the core diagonal-Fisher, normalization, momentum, and EMA procedures remain unchanged. Appendix A.4 adds a distributed adaptation that averages normalized Kronecker factors across GPUs before constructing the preconditioner.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose are preserved. v2 adds a methodology roadmap, selectively rewrites contributions, stability discussion, and conclusions, and reorganizes tuning details into lists. The impact statement moves into the main text, while the visualization and experiment appendices shift after the new ablation appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds Fisher histograms, scheduler/component plots, distributed-training displays, and an ablation-summary table; expands the language-model table and plot for PTB; redraws Figure 2; and changes the document template and display placement. Most existing benchmark plots are retained. New presentation errors include Figure 13's caption describing panel A as the MAE analysis, which is actually panel D.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MNIST (Deng, 2012), Penn Treebank (Marcus et al., 1993), NNgeometry (George, 2021), and normalization (Jiang et al., 2024b). Section 5 largely retains the earlier positioning relative to Fisher approximations and adaptive optimizers. Expanded author names and bibliography formatting do not represent additional works.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds a conditional unbiasedness argument for averaging distributed Kronecker-factor estimates, using linearity of expectation. Section 2 makes the model-output distribution in the Fisher expectation explicit. The existing convex/nonconvex propositions, convergence bounds, and appendix proofs remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: Appendix B substantially strengthens evidence for design choices that v1 supported mainly indirectly, through controlled EMA, square-root, and normalization-layer ablations plus Fisher-approximation diagnostics. Appendix A.4 specifies and tests distributed training, addressing an explicit v1 limitation. These gains outweigh incomplete tuning selections, new caption/reference errors, and weakened caution about diagonal dominance. The improvement comes from stronger validation and documented applicability, while matched benchmark scores remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AdaFisher, with matching core algorithms, theoretical results, and benchmark results. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Penn Treebank results, distributed ImageNet experiments, and component and Fisher-approximation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification, transfer-learning, and WikiText-2 experiments, plus optimizer stability and Fisher-structure analyses in the appendices.

results.title: AdaFisher: Adaptive Second Order Optimization via Fisher Information

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: causal transparency by design, competitive predictive performance, improved intermediate and downstream predictions through interventions, and support for causal reasoning and verification. Renaming and reordering these contributions do not materially change their scientific scope.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's existing distinction between model inference and real-world causality, v3 explicitly discusses non-identifiability of learned graphs, interval-valued PNS, computational tradeoffs, and CIFAR-10 intervention failures attributed to out-of-distribution embeddings. These additions materially expand the interpretation of results and the stated applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code-repository link, CIFAR-10 training and workstation details, and updated total/reproduction compute estimates of 60/8 hours versus 40/2 hours. Most existing implementation information is retained. Appendix G.4 still promises a future code release, so actual repository availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: v3 adds CIFAR-10 with automatically extracted concepts and a synthetic tabular benchmark with controllable concept incompleteness (Appendices G.1 and H.4–H.6). These extend coverage beyond the original three datasets to automatically annotated images and systematically incomplete concept information.

E2.justification: Black box, CBM, and CEM remain the evaluated baselines. The renamed supplied-graph +CD variant remains in corresponding original experiments. New benchmark comparisons reuse these methods; +CD is unavailable on CIFAR-10 because of stated computational cost, rather than being removed from an existing comparison.

E3.justification: Additional protocols measure concept-only intervention accuracy, vary synthetic concept counts across 10/30/60/100 and incompleteness across 0/0.1/0.5/0.9, compare one to three unfolding steps, and measure parameters and training/inference time. CIFAR-10 receives a 25-epoch budget. The documented protocols for the original benchmarks are retained.

E4.justification: The original CaCE-regularization ablations remain. v3 adds controlled concept-incompleteness tests, computational scaling analysis, and an unfolding-depth ablation in H.4–H.6. It also adds concept-only intervention analysis, explicit CelebA counterfactual examples, and broader PNS analysis, substantially expanding examination of robustness and model behavior.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds, 1–5, and retain the existing uncertainty-reporting practices. v3 Appendix I newly explains that unidentifiable PNS queries yield intervals, and Figure 17 explicitly reports upper bounds. This adds identification-uncertainty reporting; no increase in repeated runs or new significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores and regularization-ablation values are retained. New CIFAR-10 label accuracies are 93.32±0.03 for Causal CGM, 94.85±0.03 for black box, 92.17±0.11 for CBM, and 92.04±0.06 for CEM. Numerous intervention, incompleteness, scaling, unfolding, and counterfactual results are added. The added blocking-results column has an ambiguous duplicated CelebA heading.

M1.justification: Causal CEM is renamed Causal CGM, but the encoder, concept copies, embedding aggregation, adjacency learning, training objectives, unfolding, and intervention procedures are retained. v1's neural parametrization and unfolding descriptions move to v3 Appendices D–E; the CaCE regularizer already appeared in v1 Appendix B.4.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around Pearl's hierarchy and CBM assumptions. The method narrative is reorganized, with derivation, neural parametrization, and unfolding moved into separate appendices; causal reasoning becomes Section 3.4 and the conclusion becomes a standalone section. Terminology changes throughout from Causal CEM to Causal CGM.

P2.justification: v3 expands Table 1 with CIFAR-10 and transparency columns, restructures the opening schematic, and adds equivalence diagrams, concept-only intervention plots, counterfactual tables, scaling/incompleteness plots, and PNS heatmaps. Existing figures and tables are resized, regrouped, or relocated within a substantially revised page layout.

R1.justification: v3 removes several general XAI and feature-attribution references and adds sources on opacity, causal bounds, CIFAR-10, and the synthetic benchmark. Appendix K explicitly distinguishes the approach from causal representation learning. The central positioning relative to CBMs, causal discovery, and post-hoc surrogate explanations remains consistent with v1.

T1.justification: v3 introduces Theorem 3.2 and its Appendix C proof concerning replacement of copy-variable parents by endogenous parents, invoking identical variables and full observability. It also adds computational-complexity and k-step-unfolding arguments. v1's cyclic and dissected PGM definitions remain in Appendix B, so their relocation is not a theoretical removal.

improvement.justification: v1's evaluation lacked direct tests of incomplete concepts and computational scaling and used relatively small annotated concept sets. v3 addresses these important applicability gaps through CIFAR-10 with automatic concepts and controlled incompleteness, scaling, and unfolding experiments. Explicit counterfactual examples and new limitations also make the evidence easier to assess. Reporting weaknesses remain, including Table 3's duplicated heading and sparse details for the new synthetic experiments, but the added validation substantially strengthens the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The model renaming and relocated material can be matched. A duplicated dataset heading in v3 Table 3 creates a localized reporting ambiguity.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds CIFAR-10 experiments, synthetic-benchmark analyses, computational measurements, and counterfactual examples in Section 4 and Appendices H–I.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy, intervention, causal-structure, blocking, and regularization-ablation results on Checkmark, dSprites, and CelebA in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Causal Concept Graph Models: Beyond Causal Opacity in Deep Learning

C1.justification: The central adaptive-weighting and conditional-coverage claims remain intact. The abstract extends the empirical claim to synthetic data, and the conclusion now identifies a preliminary adaptive-window implementation where v1 discussed only future work.

C2.justification: V2 explains how residual mixing can coexist with nonstationary observations and attributes performance to rapid adaptation to volatility. Section 5 newly acknowledges brief local coverage failures from aggressive adaptation, qualifying the retained favorable interpretation.

D1.justification: Adds the AAPL data source and date range, synthetic generation equations and coefficients, and the adaptive-window testing rule with an example 0.01 threshold. It also clarifies the window-selection criterion. Existing implementation links remain unchanged; the new simulations are not fully specified, including sample lengths and the seasonal model's beta coefficients.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained electric, wind and solar datasets, v2 evaluates AAPL daily closing prices, a heteroskedastic AR/GARCH mixture and a seasonal nonstationary synthetic process. These substantially broaden the domains and temporal conditions tested.

E2.justification: The corresponding original comparisons retain all nine baselines, including Plain NW, SPCI, EnbPI and the adaptive conformal methods. SAOCF in v1's Table 1 is corrected to SAOCP. Added benchmarks use subsets of existing baselines; newly cited methods are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The original ten-tree random forest, 7:1:2 split, coverage target and evaluation metrics remain unchanged. Added setups include an 80:20 chronological stock-data split, 100-lag predictors for the seasonal simulation and a fixed-versus-adaptive window comparison.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds targeted robustness experiments under heteroskedastic volatility bursts and nonstationarity. Appendix E tests adaptive versus fixed window selection, while Figure A.3 adds a solar interval case study. The original rolling-coverage analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 reports no repeated-run counts or between-run uncertainty. V2 adds standard deviations from five independent trials to Table 1, reports three trials for AAPL and five for the nonstationary and adaptive-window studies, and presents five independent heteroskedastic paths. This establishes new reporting, not a documented increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores and rolling plots are retained. Tables A.1–A.4 add substantial results, including KOWCPI coverage/width of 0.912/15.74 on AAPL and 0.90/11.41 in the seasonal simulation. New interval and window trajectories are also reported. Table A.4 lists fixed-window electric width as 0.23, although Table 1 retains 0.22.

M1.justification: The RNW weighting and interval-construction algorithm remain unchanged. Appendix E implements an optional adaptive window-selection procedure using two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests between adjacent residual blocks; v1 treated adaptive selection as future work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are preserved. V2 refines algorithm wording and explanations, standardizes notation, subdivides Appendix C, adds Appendices D–E and removes the acknowledgments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with clearer residual blocks and a PACF panel. Table 1 is expanded to display uncertainty, four appendix tables and two figures are added, and typography and page composition change throughout. Existing benchmark plots are retained.

R1.justification: Adds Angelopoulos et al. (2024), Yang et al. (2024), and two Masry–Tjøstheim references, expanding discussion of online threshold adaptation and mixing assumptions. The central research positioning remains stable; Gibbs–Candès 2022 to 2024 is a publication update.

T1.justification: The RNW definitions, Assumptions 4.2–4.5, coverage results and Appendix A–B derivations are mathematically retained. Notation standardization, equation renumbering and explanations of the Hessian and decomposition do not change the theory.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support previously limited to point estimates on three energy datasets: repeated-trial uncertainty, targeted robustness tests and the adaptive-window comparison address reliability and practical tuning. The coverage-failure discussion also improves balance. New interpretations sometimes overstate the evidence—SPCI has narrower intervals with valid coverage on Table A.2's fourth path—and Tables 1/A.4 disagree on one electric width. These reporting issues temper the claims but do not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KOWCPI research. Text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained content to be matched despite formatting and appendix expansion.

after.justification: Retains the original experiments and adds stock-price, synthetic-data and adaptive-window results in Appendices C–E.

before.justification: Table 1 and Figures 2, A.1 and A.2 report original coverage and interval-width experiments on electric, wind and solar data.

results.title: Kernel-based Optimally Weighted Conformal Time-Series Prediction

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes achieving leading results without synthetic data. V2 makes data curation, including synthetic generation and example-based labeling, an explicit contribution and claims sustained leadership across two model releases. It also adds claims of leading clustering/classification performance and generalization to AIR-Bench, extending the original MTEB-centered contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of reversed-stage training trade-offs and latent specialization for review sentiment. Appendix A argues that MTEB improvements need not transfer to out-of-domain retrieval, illustrating this with the SFR models, while interpreting NV-Embed's AIR-Bench results as generalization evidence. These extend the earlier pooling and attention explanations.

D1.justification: V2 documents the mining teacher and cutoff, synthetic generator and prompt templates, uniform training-data sampling, and optimizer restarts between stages. Training counts and instruction tables are revised and expanded. The abstract changes from promising an NV-Embed-v1 release to reporting an NV-Embed-v2 release with a different model link; actual external availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 56-task MTEB evaluation but adds AIR-Bench evaluation on eight English QA and fifteen long-document datasets, including law and book domains. Training expands through additional retrieval, classification and clustering datasets and 120,000 synthetic examples spanning 60,000 tasks (Sections 4.1–4.3 and Appendix A).

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Bge-en-icl, Stella-1.5B-v5, SFR-Embedding-2R, Gte-Qwen2-7B-instruct and Bge-multilingual-gemma2, while removing Gte-Qwen1.5, Voyage-lite, Google-gecko and LLM2Vec from that comparison. The detailed per-dataset comparator set also changes, and AIR-Bench comparisons introduce Linq-Embed-Mistral.

E3.justification: Reported warm-up steps change from 500 to 50. Training sample counts change substantially, including NLI from 20k to 270k and PAQ from 100k to 500k, and several training/evaluation instructions change. V2 introduces single-stage/reversed-stage controls and AIR-Bench protocols using nDCG@10 and Recall@10. The reported sequence limit, batch size and stage budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original attention/pooling ablations survive in v2 Table 2. New analyses test single-stage versus two-stage and reversed-stage training, label-based versus example-based supervision, and incremental effects of negative mining, additional public data and synthetic data (Tables 3–5). Appendix C adds a review-sentiment latent-attention case study, and Appendix A examines out-of-domain generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 retains NV-Embed-v1's 69.32 MTEB and 59.36 retrieval scores and adds NV-Embed-v2 scores of 72.31 and 62.65 under revised training and instructions. These are distinct model configurations, not an isolated same-setting architectural gain. New ablation and AIR-Bench results include 52.28 QA and 74.78 long-document averages. Some original per-dataset baseline and ablation entries are replaced in Table 11.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 introduce E5-Mistral positive-aware negative mining, replacing the earlier encoder-based/BM25 procedures, and use sampled examples instead of label texts for selected multiclass and clustering tasks. V2 also adds Mixtral synthetic-data generation and STS document-side instructions. The latent-attention architecture and two-stage training framework remain.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the architecture and training exposition remain intact. V2 revises the abstract, contribution list and conclusion, adds data-curation and ablation subsections, expands the appendix organization and adds acknowledgments. These are targeted narrative revisions accompanying the scientific additions.

P2.justification: V1 Tables 2–3 are merged into v2 Table 2. V2 adds several ablation and AIR-Bench tables, synthetic-generation prompt tables and the attention heatmap in Figure 2. The detailed benchmark table moves to the appendix with substantially different columns, and the document adopts ICLR formatting. Figure 1 remains materially unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 expands positioning around data curation and reproducibility, discussing Linq-Embed, explicitly adopting NV-Retriever's mining technique, and contrasting Bge-en-icl's few-shot training with zero-shot evaluation. It also discusses newer competitors' limited disclosure and adds references supporting the expanded datasets and methods.

T1.justification: Section 4.1.1 newly defines the negative-score cutoff as the positive score multiplied by a percentage margin, set to 0.95. This is a limited mathematical selection-rule addition. The latent-attention equation and associated definitions remain unchanged, and neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the training recipe: Tables 4–5 directly test training order and data-curation choices that v1 did not isolate, while AIR-Bench adds generalization evidence beyond MTEB. Expanded procedural documentation also improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh reduced per-dataset ablation detail and documentation errors, notably Table 9's Medrxiv instructions for Reddit/StackExchange. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, limiting confidence in small score differences.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NV-Embed and contain matching architecture descriptions and original experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds NV-Embed-v2 results, training and data-curation ablations, AIR-Bench evaluations and an attention visualization.

before.justification: V1 reports original MTEB/BEIR evaluations and experiments comparing attention masks and pooling methods in Tables 1–4.

results.title: NV-Embed: Improved Techniques for Training LLMs as Generalist Embedding Models

C1.justification: The central claims of contrastively aligning images, DNA and taxonomy for seen/unseen species classification remain. The abstract reduces the claimed zero-shot accuracy advantage from over 11% to over 8%. The introduction and conclusion more explicitly foreground DNA as a better alignment target than taxonomic text when labels are scarce.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking DNA's advantage to sparse species labels, attention patterns to successful insect recognition, and encoder prealignment to image-to-text performance. It argues that simple classifiers can make BZSL's complexity unnecessary and discusses accuracy–resource tradeoffs. The conclusion newly makes the two-dataset and CLIP-style-training limitations explicit, alongside the persistent cross-modal performance gap.

D1.justification: Implementation reporting expands substantially: v2 specifies bfloat16 AMP, the learning-rate schedule, alternative encoder checkpoints, attention-rollout blocks 2–6, and measured memory use and training times. Reported hardware changes from two to four 80GB A100 GPUs. Appendix A adds detailed class-overlap and sample statistics, while the earlier LoRA projection and parameter-count details are omitted.

E1.justification: BIOSCAN-1M and INSECT remain the experimental datasets; BIOSCAN-5M is discussed without being evaluated. Retrieval-scenario coverage narrows slightly: v1 Table 9 evaluates DNA queries against image references, whereas v2 reports DNA queries only against DNA references. Image-query classification and the seen/unseen-species tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds explicit majority/chance baselines in Table 7 and OpenCLIP-based image/text encoder comparisons in Table 11. The principal existing comparators—BioCLIP, BZSL, CNN DNA encoder, DNABERT-2 and BarcodeBERT—remain, so this is a targeted extension rather than wholesale replacement.

E3.justification: Main training changes from 15 epochs, batch size 800 and learning rate 0.001 to 50 epochs, batch size 2000, a one-cycle schedule spanning 1e-6 to 5e-5, and AMP. BioCLIP and threshold-based IS+DU evaluations move from validation to test, while thresholds remain tuned on validation; v1 already contained test retrieval results. Figure 2 also revises reported seen test-query/key counts from 6878/6530 to 4878/6350 despite retaining the Appendix A partitioning rule.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's modality, key-type and batch-size studies, v2 adds encoder/prealignment comparisons, temperature, AMP and LoRA-versus-full-fine-tuning ablations (Tables 11 and 14–16). It adds attention success/failure cases and compares UMAP embeddings across alignment configurations. The batch-size study is revised, while the averaged-image/DNA-key analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides no training-run variability reporting. v2 Appendix B.1 and Figure 9 newly report four random-seed training runs for the full trimodal model, with means and shaded uncertainty across retrieval settings and taxonomic levels. The uncertainty definition remains ambiguous: the text says standard deviation, while the caption says standard error.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and supplemented. For example, reported test-set species image-to-image macro harmonic mean for I+D+T changes from 32.4% in v1 Table 8 to 51.2% in v2 Table 1; the best aligned-encoder INSECT harmonic mean changes from 38.1% to 35.0% (v1 Table 6; v2 Table 4). These concern revised training/settings, not controlled cross-version gains or losses. New ablation results appear, while DNA-to-image and averaged-key entries disappear.

M1.justification: v1 trains the encoders through LoRA and fixes the contrastive temperature at 0.07. v2 uses full fine-tuning and learns the temperature initialized at 0.07 (Section 3.1; Appendix C). This substantially changes the optimized parameters, while retaining the encoder families, symmetric trimodal contrastive loss and nearest-neighbor retrieval framework.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming BIOSCAN-CLIP to CLIBD, v2 substantially rewrites the introduction, related work and experimental narrative. It creates a dedicated analysis subsection, consolidates cross-modal/BZSL discussion, moves classifier details into Appendix B.2, and organizes implementation ablations in a new Appendix C.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column layout and extensively restructures tables around query/key combinations, separating macro and micro results. Retrieval examples become a combined three-mode display, UMAP expands from one plot to four panels, and attention and uncertainty figures are added. The split and class-distribution diagrams are also revised.

R1.justification: Section 2 removes the broad fine-grained multimodal survey, including discussions of methods such as ImageBind, BLIP and CLOOB, and refocuses positioning on biological classification, DNA representations and label scarcity. New cited work includes MycoAI, BIOSCAN-5M and environmental-DNA/remote-sensing research. The BioCLIP publication update refers to the same retained work.

T1.justification: The symmetric contrastive-loss equations and trimodal sum remain mathematically equivalent. However, v2 removes v1 Section 3.1's explicit LoRA weight factorization and parameter-count argument, retaining only an empirical LoRA comparison. This is a limited reduction in mathematical method detail; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility: threshold-based IS+DU results are evaluated on test data rather than the validation set used for tuning, four-seed reporting addresses previously undocumented variability, and controlled ablations support important training choices. Added failure cases and explicit limitations improve interpretation. Removed retrieval analyses and reporting inconsistencies, particularly Figure 9's standard-deviation/standard-error ambiguity, temper these gains, but the stronger validation and supporting evidence establish a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same image–DNA–taxonomy alignment work, renamed from BIOSCAN-CLIP to CLIBD. All 16 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on both datasets, including revised classification results, additional ablations and four-seed training variability.

before.justification: v1 reports original BIOSCAN-1M retrieval experiments, INSECT zero-shot classification results, and modality and batch-size analyses.

results.title: CLIBD: Bridging Vision and Genomics for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale

C1.justification: The central claims about 3D scene conditioning, independent modality rendering and beneficial cross-modal learning remain. The abstract and introduction broaden stated validation to RAF. v1's prominent claim of outperforming prior work with half the audio data is no longer retained; v2's replacement few-shot statement requires 75% of the data for superiority across all metrics.

C2.justification: v2 reinterprets grid benefits using the capacity-preserving zero-grid control and explicitly presents loss selection as a T60-versus-C50/EDT tradeoff. It removes the lack-of-real-data limitation and adds distinctions between recorded-audio fitting and reusable RIR prediction, plus a grid-detail explanation for RWAVS House underperformance. v1's explicit single-source and difficult-RIR-acquisition limitations are omitted; scene-specific training and static-scene limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents NeRAF++ loss weights and batches of 34 complete STFTs, monaural output configuration, RAF camera selection and preprocessing, and RWAVS-specific settings. It newly specifies pose normalization with a 1 mm margin and the waveform-to-STFT evaluation procedure. Feature-size assignments conflict between Appendices B and F. v1's license-information table is removed, while the project-page reference remains.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates six simulated indoor SoundSpaces scenes. v2 retains these and adds RAF's two real rooms with monaural RIRs and directional sources, plus recorded-audio synthesis on RWAVS Office, House, Apartment and Outdoors scenes. Appendix J also evaluates visual synthesis in real scenes.

E2.justification: SoundSpaces Table 1 adds NACF and NACF w/T to the retained AAC/Opus, NAF, INRAS and AV-NeRF comparators. The new RAF comparison includes energy-decay-trained NAF++ and INRAS++ alongside NACF variants. RWAVS Table A2 additionally evaluates ViGAS. Nerfacto remains the visual comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces RAF's 80/20 audio split, 0.32-second recordings, 48-kHz processing and camera subsampling, plus RWAVS MAG/ENV evaluation and sparse-image protocols. Within SoundSpaces, feature dimensions become scene-dependent, time normalization changes from [-1,1] to [0,1], and loss ablations expand from three to six scenes. Grid ablations and runtime measurement move to RAF. The main SoundSpaces 90/10 split and audio preprocessing remain.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds a zero-filled-grid control that preserves the feature extractor, directly testing scene information beyond parameter count. It replaces the SoundSpaces grid study with a RAF study and expands the loss analysis. RAF few-shot curves, loudness-map visualizations and RWAVS cross-modal visual analyses add substantial evidence about data efficiency and model behavior.

E5.justification: v1 does not specify repeated-run counts. v2 Section 4.2 newly reports six repetitions per experiment and averaging; this does not establish an increase over v1's unspecified count. Neither version supplies seed identities, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: SoundSpaces Table 1 revises NeRAF's T60/C50/EDT errors from 2.04%/0.39 dB/0.011 s to 2.14%/0.38 dB/0.010 s alongside configuration changes. Vision scores, few-shot curves and ablation results also change. Extensive RAF and RWAVS results are added. RWAVS Table A2 reports mixed rankings: NeRAF's overall ENV is lower than AV-NeRF's, 0.144 versus 0.145, while MAG is higher, 1.596 versus 1.504.

M1.justification: The core pipeline remains, but v2 replaces positional direction encoding with spherical harmonics and introduces NeRAF++ with an energy-decay loss and full-STFT training. Appendix A adds a monaural, source-direction-conditioned RAF configuration. Appendix J adapts NeRAF to query frequencies, predict STFT masks and use magnitude-STFT MSE for RWAVS. These substantially extend the documented procedures.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and method explanations, replaces the contribution bullet list with prose, and removes the separate Task section. It reorganizes the appendices and moves societal impact out of the main discussion. These changes substantially revise the narrative independently of the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figures 1-4 are redrawn, and visual comparisons gain larger panels and highlighted artifacts. Table 1 combines SoundSpaces and RAF comparisons; Table 2 expands from averaged deltas to per-scene absolute scores and deltas. New loudness maps, RAF few-shot plots and RWAVS tables accompany extensive rearrangement of appendix displays and a changed document template.

R1.justification: v2 adds NACF discussion, distinguishing NeRAF's scene priors from NACF's assumed surface acoustic coefficients. It also adds RAF and VR-NeRF references and a ViGAS citation for the new evaluations. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix C adds the formal energy-decay objective through per-window energy, reverse cumulative energy and a log-space L1 discrepancy, following cited prior work (Equations 11-14). This is a limited addition to the mathematical loss formulation. No new theorems, proofs or theoretical guarantees are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked real-world validation, an important gap for its intended applications. v2 addresses this with RAF RIR experiments and RWAVS audio/vision results, while stronger comparators and the zero-grid control better test its central claims. Explicit loss tradeoffs and mixed RWAVS outcomes improve the assessment of applicability. Missing uncertainty estimates, inconsistent feature assignments and removed license information remain weaknesses, but the gains in empirical relevance and experimental control are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NeRAF and retain the same core radiance-field, voxel-grid and acoustic-field framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original SoundSpaces results and adds RAF and RWAVS experiments, including acoustic predictions, real-scene visual results and additional controlled analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original SoundSpaces RIR predictions, cross-modal image-synthesis results, few-shot experiments, grid and loss ablations, and inference measurements.

results.title: NeRAF: 3D Scene Infused Neural Radiance and Acoustic Fields

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and scientific conclusion retain the same contributions: utilitarian configuration over infinite spaces, anytime near-optimality guarantees, and improved finite-space performance over UP. The additional comparative evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 newly discusses comparisons across different objectives and guarantees, interpreting anytime refinement as avoiding sensitivity to fixed budget choices. Appendix D connects AC-Band's default metric to its racing mechanism. Existing limitations concerning benchmark breadth and choosing utility functions remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix D documents baseline budgets, cap grids, Hyperband multipliers, ICAR parameters, and SPC settings. It also describes correcting AC-Band's CPLEX cap from 900 to 10000 seconds. Section 5 newly discloses an environment where restarting runs is impossible; both versions retain the anonymous-repo-link placeholder.

E1.justification: Both versions use minisat, cplex_rcw, and cplex_region for SAT, wildlife-conservation, and combinatorial-auction configuration experiments. The log-Laplace and uniform utility families are retained; the additional comparisons introduce no new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: Section 5.3 adds evaluated comparisons with Successive Halving, Hyperband, AC-Band, ImpatientCapsAndRuns, and Structured Procrastination with Confidence. These substantially expand v1's comparisons with UP, the naive procedure, and OUP/COUP; AC-Band is evaluated with both log-Laplace and default objectives.

E3.justification: The new comparison measures percentage gap to the best configuration against CPU time. Its runtime setup uses uniform-utility caps of 100 for minisat and 3000 for CPLEX, quantile-capped evaluation with quantile parameters 0.1 and 0.2, and baseline-specific budget/cap grids. These supplement the retained experiments rather than replace their settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds a quantile-parameter robustness comparison: Figure 8 uses 0.2 versus Figure 5's 0.1. Section 5.3 and Appendix D also examine baseline parameter sensitivity and AC-Band's objective choice. The existing doubling-condition and exploration-schedule analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 provides no empirical seed counts or uncertainty regions. v2's new comparison reports averages over five seeds and minimum–maximum error regions in Figure 5, introducing substantial variability reporting. This does not establish an increased run count for retained experiments.
