E6.justification: Figures 5 and 8 add extensive percentage-gap results. Section 5.3 reports OUP/COUP eventually identifying the best configuration for every seed, Hyperband finding good RCW configurations earlier but retaining a gap, and weak AC-Band performance under log-Laplace utility. Retained runtime curves also change, notably Figure 3, without a stated method change.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same sampling, confidence bounds, selection, termination, and captime-doubling procedures. The improved doubling condition already appears in v1. v2's algorithm walkthroughs explain existing steps.

P1.justification: v2 adds walkthroughs in Sections 3–4, Section 5.3, and Appendix D, and refines algorithm terminology. It removes the generic societal-impact closing passage. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds a six-panel comparison figure and a three-panel robustness figure with uncertainty displays. Retained plots receive revised axes, legends, and panel labeling; old Figures 5–6 become Figures 6–7. Title, author, heading, and page formatting also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds Jamieson and Talwalkar (2016) and Li et al. (2018), and expands discussion of Successive Halving, Hyperband, and previously cited configurators with different guarantees. The established bandit and utilitarian research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Definitions 1–2, Lemmas 1–5, Theorems 1–2, and Appendix B's proofs retain the same mathematics. Appendix A's doubling-condition derivation is also retained. The added phase-sampling explanation restates Algorithm 2.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support primarily compares against UP and a naive baseline. Section 5.3 and Appendix D address this important gap through five additional configurators, explicit evaluation choices, five-seed variability, and detailed settings, substantially strengthening evidence of practical competitiveness while retaining the theory. Different objectives still limit direct comparisons, and code access remains a placeholder, but the gain in evidence and transparency is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OUP/COUP research. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, and appendices support comparison, including the new Appendix D in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original OUP/COUP evaluations and adds comparisons with five other configurators, including results across five seeds in Section 5.3 and Appendix D.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A/C report original OUP/COUP runtime evaluations, comparisons with UP and a naive procedure, and analyses of doubling conditions and exploration schedules.

results.title: Utilitarian Algorithm Configuration for Infinite Parameter Spaces

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: hard-label semantic 2DGS, alpha-based identification of unobservable regions, and time-reversal inpainting for reconstructing empty streets. Additional evaluation and the new 'A Simple Baseline' subtitle do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussion: it explicitly limits consistency guarantees to forward-facing cameras, discusses dynamic-object handling and segmentation failures, and interprets reconstruction cost and SDF-versus-TSDF geometry differences. v1's standalone limitations list is replaced; its explicit linear-cost and pretrained-inpainter bottleneck caveats are no longer stated in that form.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the A40 GPU, frontal-camera selection, 24 Waymo and nine PandaSet scenes, label inheritance during densification, and restriction of re-optimization to nearby Gaussians. It also documents new baseline settings, geometry preprocessing, runtime measurements and supplementary-video access paths. Newly specifying local re-optimization does not establish that its implementation changed.

E1.justification: v3 extends the Waymo-only evaluation to nine PandaSet street scenes, adding an independent driving dataset to the main comparisons and ablations. The task remains street unveiling; PandaSet's stated 360-degree sensor coverage does not establish surrounding-camera evaluation, since v3 specifies frontal sequences.

E2.justification: v3 adds an adapted LeftRefill comparator in Table 4 and evaluates StreetSurf for geometry in Table 7. These introduce direct comparisons with the inpainting backbone and a surface-reconstruction method, respectively. Both were cited in v1 but were not evaluated as these comparators; the original main comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: v3 revises the FID procedure from v1's stated framewise computation and averaging to comparison of image collections. It also introduces geometry evaluation using LiDAR, a 5-meter mesh-cropping rule, Chamfer Distance and F-score at 0.25 meters, plus timing protocols averaging eight scenes per dataset. These are substantive reported protocol additions and revisions, without establishing whether existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds stagewise computational profiling, segmentation-boundary failure cases, and analysis of naive LeftRefill failures when future references omit relevant regions. These investigate efficiency and failure mechanisms beyond v1's analyses. The time-forward comparison is retained and extended, not newly introduced: it already appeared in v1 Appendix B.1 and Table 3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. v3's averages over scenes and runtime measurements do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 replace the reported Waymo values: StreetUnveiler's LPIPS/FID changes from 0.241/157.970 to 0.216/127.581. v3 adds PandaSet results of 0.261/155.527 and new LeftRefill, runtime and geometry results. These are revised or additional estimates, not established same-setting gains. Both versions' Table 1 values give SDXL the lowest FID, despite their misleading accompanying wording.

M1.justification: Equation 8 changes the reported shrinking loss from summed opacity to mean opacity, dividing by the number of Gaussians while retaining its weight of 0.001. The core hard-label 2DGS, alpha-mask generation, time-reversal inpainting and re-optimization pipeline remains.

P1.justification: v3 adds the subtitle, updates affiliations and publication text, edits terminology and sentences, and expands the appendix into additional-results and thematic-discussion sections. Most main-text prose and the principal section sequence remain, so this is limited editing and reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 redesigns Tables 1–3 with dataset-specific columns, merges the main ablation presentation and redisplays the existing time-order comparison there. It adds Tables 4–7 and figures for LeftRefill, geometry accuracy, segmentation failures and additional examples. The conference template also changes layout; earlier semantic, geometry and mesh figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including Reffusion, Inpaint3D, InstantSplat and S3Gaussian, and develops distinctions from StreetSurf and dynamic/static scene decomposition. The principal related-work organization and street-unveiling positioning remain. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new works.

T1.justification: Equation 8 revises the mathematical definition of the opacity penalty from a sum to an average and defines the Gaussian count N. This is a limited, non-equivalent normalization change. The remaining mathematical framework is retained, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's Waymo results and qualitative geometry: PandaSet tests broader applicability, the LeftRefill comparison helps assess the pipeline's added value, and geometry and runtime measurements address previously unquantified properties. Explicit camera and segmentation limitations improve interpretation. Geometry validation still concerns scenes before removal, and PandaSet timings are not reconciled between Tables 5 and 6 (311 seconds for 80 frames versus 5.09 seconds per frame). These reporting limitations do not outweigh the stronger empirical support and clearer applicability boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe StreetUnveiler. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the expanded evaluation and revised layout.

after.justification: v3 reports original Waymo and PandaSet experiments, additional baseline comparisons, computational measurements and quantitative geometry evaluation in Tables 1–7.

before.justification: v1 reports original Waymo experiments, quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–3, and qualitative reconstruction, semantic-label and mesh results.

results.title: 3D StreetUnveiler with Semantic-aware 2DGS - a simple baseline

C1.justification: The first general black-box bias-certification framework and three prefix families remain the central contributions. V2 reframes the headline question around estimating unbiasedness and adds specific contribution claims about inexpensive bias-provoking distributions having no current defenses and alignment quality potentially mattering more than model size. These extend the advertised findings without replacing the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning prefix denoising, perturbations weakening jailbreaks, refusal versus helpful neutral responses, and alignment versus model size. Appendices A.4 and C explain how additional demographic groups affect detection and discuss annotator disagreement, detector errors, and missed emoji-based bias. These considerably expand v1's more general detector-dependence and sample-complexity limitations.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies the previously undocumented DT agreement-based detector, including its handling of multiple demographic groups, and provides four algorithms documenting certification and the retained prefix samplers. Baseline averaging is described explicitly, and reported hardware changes from four to two 40GB A100 GPUs. The code-access link, BOLD detector threshold, and human-study instructions remain; the new detector description does not establish a change to the earlier binary implementation.

E1.justification: The BOLD profession/gender and Decoding Trust stereotype/race tasks remain. V2 Appendix A.4 adds an evaluated three-race scenario covering black people, white people, and Asians with Mistral-7B, extending v1's binary racial comparisons. No new dataset or broad task domain is introduced.

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate the same two benchmarking baselines: prompting without prefixes and with the unmodified main jailbreak. Claude-3.5-Sonnet is an additional target of certification, not a competing certification method. Newly cited benchmarking works are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The reported certification budget changes from adaptive 50–200 samples to a fixed 50, removing the bias threshold of 0.1 and safety margin of 0.01. V2 also adds a sample-count experiment spanning 10–100 samples and evaluates Claude-3.5-Sonnet. The main dataset sizes remain 250 BOLD examples and 48 Decoding Trust statements.

E4.justification: V2 adds sample-count sensitivity analyses for all three prefix families and qualitative true-positive, false-negative, and false-positive analyses of the BOLD detector against human annotations. The existing prefix-hyperparameter ablations are revised to examine probability bounds instead of percentages certified biased. The original model-response case studies largely remain, with the DT case moved to Appendix E.

E5.justification: Both versions use 95% Clopper-Pearson intervals, but v2 changes the statistical stopping procedure from repeated threshold checks to estimation at a fixed sample count with explicit IID Bernoulli observations. V2 additionally reports averaging five evaluations per baseline prompt set; v1 does not specify that repetition count, so an increase in repetitions cannot be established.

E6.justification: Categorical certification percentages are removed, several numerical estimates change beyond complementing probabilities, and Claude, three-race, sample-count, and case-specific bound results are added. For example, v1 Table 3 gives DT/Llama-7B/random-prefix average bias bounds of (0.00, 0.06), equivalent to unbiasedness bounds of (0.94, 1.00); v2 Table 1 reports (0.79, 0.96). Given the revised sampling procedure, this is a changed reported estimate, not an established same-setting performance decline.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces adaptive sampling and threshold-based biased/unbiased/inconclusive decisions with fixed-sample estimation of unbiasedness probability bounds. The permissible-bias threshold and stopping decision disappear. This substantially changes the certifier's procedure and output, although the three prefix-generation mechanisms remain substantially the same.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, formalization, and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. V2 separates general from model-specific observations, expands the appendix organization, relocates the DT case study, and redistributes the former standalone limitations section into the conclusion and detector appendix. Terminology consistently emphasizes counterfactual prompts and unbiasedness.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, removes the prompt-distance illustration, and restructures the main results table around average bounds previously reported in v1's appendix. It adds algorithm boxes, sample-count plots, a three-race table, detector-error examples, and sampled-prefix figures. Existing case-study figures are resized and annotated with numerical bounds, while ablation axes and legends change to display lower and upper bounds.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its conceptual grounding through Counterfactual Fairness, representational harms, local neural-network specifications, and probabilistic programming, adding references such as Kusner, Blodgett, Suresh and Guttag, and Sankaranarayanan. It removes the QuaCer-C comparison and the introductory randomized-smoothing discussion. This changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: V1's approximate prompt-similarity condition using a user-defined distance and epsilon is replaced by Definition 1's counterfactual prompt sets, requiring identical non-sensitive components and an invariance condition for an unbiased generator. V2 also bounds prompt length by model context and replaces the earlier binomial justification based on similar prompt-level probabilities with an explicit IID Bernoulli formulation. Neither version supplies a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central certification account: its fixed-sample IID formulation better matches the stated Clopper-Pearson guarantee than v1's repeated threshold-based stopping. Specifying the DT detector fills an important reproducibility gap, while sample-count analyses and detector-error examples make the evidence easier to assess. Detector inaccuracies remain, and the new claim of no current defenses exceeds what the reported evaluations establish, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in statistical coherence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QuaCer-B by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material that was relocated or renumbered.

after.justification: V2 reports original certification results, including Claude and a three-race evaluation, alongside sensitivity analyses, case studies, and the retained human evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM certification experiments on BOLD and Decoding Trust, hyperparameter ablations, model-response case studies, and a human evaluation of its bias detector.

results.title: Certifying Counterfactual Bias in LLMs

C1.justification: The core contributions—online FCL and uncertainty-based replay across modalities—remain. The v3 abstract additionally claims maintained data confidentiality and competitive communication efficiency, extending the stated benefits without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 5 and the new appendices substantially expand interpretations of augmentation quality, communication tradeoffs and generative-model failure. Section 3.2.2 discusses operation without sharing class information. Medical-domain superiority is narrowed from all cases to most cases; the original TTA cost and estimator-bias limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds execution pseudocode, text-dataset subsampling information and training-time measurements. Architectures, optimizers, hardware and the augmentation list were already documented in v2. Reproducibility remains imperfect: Appendix A.3 reverses the DBPedia and Yahoo Answers sample counts relative to Table 6.

E1.justification: v3 adds CIFAR100, DBPedia and Yahoo Answers while retaining all four original datasets. This substantially expands class coverage in vision and the represented text-classification data; text classification itself was already evaluated in v2.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds distinct FedProx, FedCIL and weighted FedAvg comparisons, including on CIFAR10. It also evaluates FL and generative baselines on retained datasets beyond the original CIFAR10 comparison. ER, CBR and the four alternative uncertainty scores remain.

E3.justification: The main batch size, client count, models and default communication settings remain. New experiments introduce burn-in and communication-frequency sweeps, aggregation alternatives, 8/10/12-augmentation controls, runtime evaluation and subsampling for the added text benchmarks. These expand the evaluation design rather than establish reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.5 tests burn-in, aggregation, communication frequency and augmentation count. Appendices A.6–A.8 add communication-cost analysis, runtime comparisons and an MFCL generated-image case study addressing failure in the online setting. These analyses were absent from v2.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use three random seeds and retain the same plus/minus reporting in matched benchmark tables. No changed run count, significance test or uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported. The added ablation tables provide point estimates without specifying an additional statistical procedure.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive benchmark, baseline, ablation and runtime results. It also revises CRC-Tissue scores: bottom-BI at M=120 changes from A=59.06 and F=23.10 to A=62.33 and F=7.99, without explaining the revision. Matched CIFAR10, KC-Cell and 20NewsGroups table values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The BI/TTA estimator, class-balanced memory selection, random replay, burn-in, periodic communication and aggregation framework remain. O-FCIL is renamed O-FCL, and Algorithm 1 documents the existing procedure. Testing alternative aggregation strategies does not establish a change to the previously flexible method.

P1.justification: The title changes, O-FCIL becomes O-FCL, and the conclusion becomes a discussion-and-conclusion section with additional subsections and appendix references. Local wording and explanations are revised, but most introductory, related-work and methodological prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn from four clients to two and receives an expanded caption. The medical tables are merged side by side, the text-results table expands, and v3 adds benchmark and analysis tables, generated-image Figure 5 and an algorithm display. These substantially change the presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds Li et al. for FedProx and Zhang et al. for the added text datasets, and explicitly claims the first use of the cited decomposition for FCL memory management. The related-work taxonomy and principal positioning against offline generative approaches remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal online-learning setup, BI estimator and uncertainty/evaluation equations (1–8) remain. No theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is added. The new pseudocode and communication-count calculation document implementation and experimental costs.

improvement.justification: v2 left important component choices and computational practicality largely untested. v3 adds targeted ablations, measured runtimes and broader FL/FCL comparisons, substantially strengthening empirical scrutiny of the same method. Pseudocode also improves transparency. Benefits are tempered by reporting inconsistencies: Appendix A.3 and Table 6 disagree on text-subset sizes, and Figure 3 retains baseline scores unreconciled with Table 5. These limit precision but do not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same online federated continual learning framework and BI-based memory method. All 15 pages of v2 and 19 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds benchmark results, component ablations, runtime measurements and generated-image examples in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments on CIFAR10, CRC-Tissue, KC-Cell and 20NewsGroups, including accuracy and forgetting results in Tables 1–4 and Figure 3.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a small complementary solution set, TCH-Set and its smooth variant, efficient optimization, and theoretical and experimental support. The precise theoretical guarantee changes in the body, but these headline contribution claims are not substantively rewritten.

C2.justification: V2 explains the weaker guarantee for nonsmooth TCH-Set and contrasts it with STCH-Set. Appendix D adds interpretations involving smoothing and optimization landscapes, hard versus smooth clustering, preference-dependent objectives, computational scaling, and budget-dependent solution counts. The original limitation to fully observable deterministic objectives and the nonlinear-regression failure discussion remain.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation documentation: Appendix B.4 specifies CelebA tasks, backbone family, loss, optimizer, learning rate, decay, training duration, and the borrowed implementation source. Appendix D documents shared smoothing parameters, an annealing formula, and preference choices. The authors' own code remains promised upon publication. The annealing formula and stated endpoint are internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: V2 adds real-data deep multi-task grouping on nine CelebA attribute-classification tasks, extending coverage beyond v1's synthetic convex optimization and mixed regression problems. All original synthetic coverage, including 1,024-objective optimization and the regression noise levels, remains.

E2.justification: V2 Table 4 introduces Random Grouping, HOA, TAG, and DMTG as actual comparators for CelebA, using scores attributed to Gao et al. (2024). HOA and TAG were previously cited but not included in reported comparisons. The original synthetic comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include training two, three, or four ResNet-variant models on CelebA with cross-entropy and Adam for 100 epochs, evaluating task-level classification performance, comparing fixed and adaptive smoothing, sampling Dirichlet preferences, and measuring runtime. These extend the evaluation design; the original synthetic dimensions, sample counts, noise levels, and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests smoothing sensitivity with five fixed values versus an adaptive schedule, preference sensitivity with several Dirichlet distributions versus uniform weights, and runtime scalability across objective counts. These investigate optimization choices and computational behavior beyond the retained solution-count and noise-level comparisons.

E5.justification: The original experiments retain 50 independent runs, mean reporting, and Wilcoxon rank-sum comparisons at the 0.05 level. The added CelebA, sensitivity, and runtime results do not introduce new seed disclosures, uncertainty intervals, repeated-run specifications, or statistical testing procedures.

E6.justification: The original synthetic numerical results are unchanged, including v1 Table 1 retained in v2 Table 6 and v1 Tables 4–5 retained as Tables 7–8. V2 adds substantial new results: Table 4 reports a worst-task score of 11.89 for STCH-Set versus 12.18 for DMTG at K=2, while SoM has the better average, 5.80 versus 5.81. Tables 9–11 add sensitivity findings and runtimes, including 58 seconds for STCH-Set versus 5,500 seconds for MosT at 128 objectives.

M1.justification: The TCH-Set and STCH-Set objectives, smoothing formulations, and gradient update in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V2 newly documents and tests smoothing schedules, but does not establish that these replace a different procedure used in v1. Applying the method to CelebA does not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact. Changes include localized explanatory rewrites around assumptions and guarantees, additional cross-references and appendix organization, author-contact edits, and conversion to author-year citations. Table 3's caption is corrected from linear to nonlinear regression.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document template and typography, refreshes early illustrations, and adds Figure 4 plus Tables 4, 5, and 9–11. The full convex-results table moves to Appendix C as Table 6, while a shortened version remains as Table 1. These substantially change the displays and presentation beyond renumbering or numerical edits.

R1.justification: V2 adds context on strong linear scalarization, smooth scalarization in multitask and reinforcement learning, DMTG, homotopy optimization, and weighted clustering. These broaden supporting connections while retaining the central positioning relative to SoM, MosT, and Pareto-front approximation. Publication-status updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes from guaranteeing weak Pareto optimality for every member of an optimal TCH-Set set to asserting existence of an optimal set composed of Pareto-optimal solutions; the unique-set guarantee remains. Appendix A.1 replaces the corresponding proof. V2 also explicitly states nonredundancy and positive-preference assumptions and adds Appendix A.5's counterexample discussion and guarantee comparison.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's synthetic-only empirical support through CelebA evaluation and targeted sensitivity and runtime evidence. It also withdraws the overbroad universal TCH-Set guarantee and explains the weaker claim. These address important weaknesses in validation and theoretical qualification. The repair is incomplete: Appendix A.5's example does not establish strict domination and makes its second solution redundant, while Appendix D.1's smoothing formula conflicts with its stated endpoint. Those defects limit theoretical rigor and reproducibility, but the added validation and more cautious guarantee still provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tchebycheff set scalarization work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated results.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds author-trained CelebA models, parameter sensitivity experiments, and runtime measurements. It distinguishes its CelebA results from comparator scores taken from prior work.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on convex many-objective optimization and noisy mixed linear and nonlinear regression, including results over 50 runs in the main text and Appendix C.

results.title: Few for Many: Tchebycheff Set Scalarization for Many-Objective Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract expands the advertised context capability from 128k to 1M tokens, and Figure 1 claims the first base model achieving 100% accuracy at 1M on the specified retrieval task. The introduction also adds detailed analysis of Quest's design choices as an explicit contribution. The central synthesis and scaling-law claims remain.

C2.justification: v6 adds interpretations connecting query quality and random keyword selection to performance, attributes weaker summary-derived keywords to summaries' broader semantic space, and argues that matching document similarity alone cannot explain Quest's advantage. It also distinguishes sentence and numeric retrieval difficulty. v3's explicit warning about doc2query/RAKE biases disappears, although the computational limitation of larger query generators remains in Appendix C.2.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly reports synthesis costs: 24 hours on 16 H800 GPUs for query generation, then 0.5 and 3 hours on 128 CPUs for keywords and indexing. v6 clarifies equal-data controls and GPT-4-based retrieval scoring. Table 6's training configuration is retained, while the earlier disclosure of 32,768 KNN inverted lists is removed.

E1.justification: v6 adds HELMET's 17 subtasks, including retrieval-augmented generation and re-ranking, and a keyword-quality assessment task. Numeric-string retrieval extends from v3's 500k context scenario to 1M tokens. Pile training, LongBench, Longbook QA, and the seven short-text benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen2.5-7B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B-base, while removing LLaMA-2-13B-64K. Figure 4 adds those three models and Yi-9B-200K to the needle comparison. Tables 14–17 introduce alternative keyword sources, highest-RAKE selection, and KNN selection variants. Standard, KNN, and ICLM remain the core synthesis baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include HELMET averaging across 8k, 16k, 32k, 64k, and 128k; controlled query-keyword corruption; and keyword-selection comparisons. Appendix C.3 introduces a five-point rating rubric, 100 samples assessed by two PhD students and GPT-4o, followed by 1,000 GPT-4o-rated samples. Existing Pythia training settings in Table 6 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices C.2–C.4 and D.1 add analyses of query-keyword corruption, keyword extraction from queries versus documents or summaries, random versus highest-RAKE selection, and alternative KNN similarity rankings. These directly probe important design choices. Earlier training-progress, long-document, and split-ratio analyses remain; the split-ratio analysis moves to Appendix A.4.

E5.justification: Appendix C.3 adds correlation-based validation of automatic ratings, reporting Pearson correlation 0.7986 between human and GPT-4o scores on the 100-sample assessment. Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests for model performance.

E6.justification: Core Tables 1–3 and 5, detailed LongBench results, and scaling-law results are retained. New results include HELMET averages of 50.97 for Quest versus 48.08 for Standard, keyword-quality and selection outcomes, and additional baseline scores. Numeric retrieval is reported at 100% through 1M tokens instead of the earlier 500k evaluation; 128k sentence retrieval remains 97%, so this is expanded evidence rather than a same-setting accuracy gain.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains query prediction, RAKE keyword extraction, inverted indexing, index splitting, and oversampled document concatenation. The added oversampling equations elaborate the existing procedure; the PDFs do not establish an algorithm change. Alternative keyword and document-selection strategies are evaluated as comparisons.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around semantic relevance and diversity. Evaluation discussion is reorganized, analysis precedes scaling laws, split-ratio discussion moves into the appendix, and the standalone limitations section disappears. The appendices are reorganized around implementation, retained results, and new component analyses.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensive figure and table relocation and revised captions. Figure 4 expands from two to six retrieval heatmaps, a 1M heatmap becomes Figure 1, and Tables 12–17 are added. The domain-distribution pies move to the appendix, while the earlier absolute-volume bar chart is removed.

R1.justification: v6 adds references supporting newer comparisons and evaluations, including HELMET, LongVA, LWM, LLaMA 3.1/3.2, DeepSeek-V2, and Qwen2.5. It removes v3's explicit statement that earlier synthesis work was limited to 8k and adds the first-base-model-at-1M positioning. The related-work organization and central relationship to retrieval-based synthesis remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: Section 3 adds explicit mathematical definitions of oversampling sample allocation in Equations 1–2, introducing group sizes, an oversampling probability, and integer rounding. v3 described this allocation verbally. The scaling-law equation and algorithmic mathematics otherwise remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: Tables 13–17 substantially address v3's limited direct evidence for query generation, keyword selection, and the advantage over similarity-based aggregation. HELMET broadens validation, and synthesis-cost reporting improves practical transparency. These gains outweigh the removed bias caveat and some overstatements, including Section 4.3's claim that Standard is worst at 128k, contradicted by Table 2 at 6.9B and 12B. The improvement rests primarily on stronger experimental support, not the larger context-length claim; run-to-run uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Quest, with matching core algorithms and experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v6 retains original experiments and adds HELMET evaluations, keyword-quality assessments, and component analyses in Tables 12–17.

before.justification: v3 reports original continued-pretraining evaluations, retrieval experiments, scaling-law fits, and ablations, including Tables 1–3 and Sections 5–6.

results.title: Quest: Query-centric Data Synthesis Approach for Long-context Scaling of Large Language Model

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes ICL's limitations relative to instruction-tuned models and improvements from greedy selection. V2 adds central claims about decoding parameters and ICL being competitive with IFT in the low-data regime, claiming the first systematic comparison under matched data conditions. These additions materially broaden and qualify the paper's main contribution.

C2.justification: V1 interprets questions-only prompting as beneficial relative to its weak base-model result; v2 interprets it as harmful relative to the stronger reported baseline and finds answers-only prompting effective. V2 also proposes that fine-tuning stabilizes generation across decoding settings, attributes ICL's multi-turn weakness to imitation of single-turn style, and discusses how stronger pretraining may mitigate lower-quality alignment data.

D1.justification: V2 adds training hyperparameters, GPU counts, context lengths, checkpoint selection and a numerical greedy-search threshold (Appendix A, Table 4). However, it removes v1's detailed Evol-Instruct quality-filtering procedure and scoring prompt despite retaining associated results. Its decoding documentation also conflicts: Appendix A.1 states temperature 1.0 for greedy decoding, whereas Section 2.2 specifies 0.

E1.justification: V2 introduces SkillMix-4k, containing synthetic instructions combining skills, as the principal demonstration and training corpus. Evol-Instruct remains, while OpenHermes-2.5 and its diversity/unsupervised experiments disappear. This substantially changes the instruction data studied, although MT-Bench and AlpacaEval 2.0 remain the evaluation benchmarks.

E2.justification: V2 adds directly trained IFT comparators using the same instruction sources and matched dataset sizes as ICL (Section 4, Figure 5), extending substantially beyond v1's comparisons with official instruct models. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct joins the systematic comparison. V1's OpenHermes-Diversity and OpenHermes-Unsupervised comparators are removed.

E3.justification: V2 adds Llama-3.1-8B experiments, ICL scaling to 250 demonstrations, IFT training sweeps over 3–4000 examples, and decoding-parameter grids. Both conversation turns are tracked throughout the new scaling comparisons. Appendix A.1 also drops v1's stated MoE repetition-penalty exception, reporting 1.15 for base models; this documentation revision does not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test decoding sensitivity, URIAL rules versus demonstration subsets, answers-only prompts, data quality, and ICL/IFT generalization to second turns. The question-answer ablation expands to Llama-3.1-8B. OpenHermes diversity and unsupervised scaling analyses disappear. The earlier cross-model transfer analysis is retained in Appendix B, rather than removed.

E5.justification: V1 mentions repeated random sampling without specifying seed counts or reporting uncertainty bands. V2 reports ICL means and standard deviations over five seeds, and IFT results over five seeds for Mistral and three for Llama-3.1 (Appendix A.4; Figures 3 and 5). This substantially strengthens uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in the earlier experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive decoding, ablation, SkillMix and IFT results. Table 3 reports MT-Bench scores of 7.52 for Mistral with one additional SkillMix demonstration and 7.81 for Llama-3.1 with three. V1's Evol-Instruct greedy-search scores remain in v2 Table 5, so these are different-setting results. The Mistral no-demonstration entry changes from 2.93 to 6.52, without establishing a same-setting improvement. OpenHermes results and the earlier random-example table rows are removed.

M1.justification: The central URIAL prompting and sequential greedy selection algorithm remain: score candidate demonstrations with GPT-4-Turbo, select the best, and repeat within a restricted candidate pool. Changing the principal demonstration corpus and evaluating standard IFT introduce data and comparison changes, without establishing a new proposed algorithm, architecture or loss.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around decoding analysis and low-data ICL-versus-IFT comparison. Question-answer matching moves earlier into Section 2, transferability moves to Appendix B, and Section 4 becomes the direct ICL/IFT comparison. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative beyond simply inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column main-text layout with a predominantly single-column format and substantially redesigns the displays. It adds decoding heatmaps, prompt-component plots, multi-panel scaling comparisons with uncertainty bands and a training-configuration table. Ablation tables expand, greedy-search histograms become multi-stage displays, and retained transfer tables move to the appendix.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around low-data alignment and the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis, adding works such as Alpagasus, Platypus, Long Is More and SkillMix. It frames matched-data ICL-versus-IFT evaluation as a literature gap and expands discussion of alternative alignment approaches. The OpenHermes reference is removed.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations. The question-answer notation is retained. V2's additional hypotheses about alignment and generation are conceptual interpretations, not new formal theory.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves support for the central ICL-versus-IFT argument through direct comparisons at matched data sizes, decoding controls and multi-seed uncertainty reporting (Section 4, Figure 5, Appendix A.4). These address important weaknesses in v1's reliance on official instruct models and limited characterization of base-model performance, supporting more qualified conclusions. Conflicting decoding documentation and lost Evol-Instruct preprocessing details remain reproducibility drawbacks, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures and mathematical notation, support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds decoding studies, prompt-component ablations, SkillMix experiments and direct ICL-versus-IFT evaluations in Sections 2–4 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original demonstration-selection, scaling, question-answer matching and cross-model transfer experiments in Sections 3–4, beyond results attributed to earlier work.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same central claims about decoding, limited benefits from scaling ICL, and ICL versus IFT in the low-data regime. The new introductory contribution list consolidates claims already present in v2 rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive applicability and mechanism interpretations: multi-turn weakness depends on demonstration content and formatting, while demonstrations can harm an already instruction-tuned model. Appendix B.2 explains question-only failures through the model answering demonstration queries. Appendix C interprets IFT as producing more persistent distributional changes than ICL, even with three examples. The original resource and task-scope limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 prints the complete URIAL prompt in Figure 9, provides illustrative SkillMix examples, specifies the GPT-4o instruction for generating two-turn demonstrations, and describes the KL computation and response truncation. E2.justification: The retained experiments preserve their comparison methods: unprompted models, URIAL, official instruct models, random-demonstration ICL, greedy selection, and IFT. The added studies reuse these approaches or examine prompt variants rather than introduce a new baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: v3 adds several evaluation designs: three versus six two-turn demonstrations with formatting controls, ablations on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, token-level KL comparisons over 25 SkillMix examples using supplied response prefixes, and AlpacaEval scaling from zero to 50 demonstrations. Appendix A.1 also corrects the stated greedy-decoding temperature from 1.0 to 0.0; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether multi-turn demonstrations and separation tags improve second-turn performance (Section 2.4), whether prompt-component and matching findings hold for an instruct model (Appendix B), and how ICL and IFT affect token distributions (Appendix C). Appendix E.1 additionally checks demonstration-scaling saturation on AlpacaEval. The earlier ablations and transferability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 specifies three-run standard deviations for the new instruct-model component ablation in Table 7 and three-run reporting for AlpacaEval scaling in Table 10. The original five-seed ICL and five/three-seed IFT specifications remain unchanged. These are additional study-specific disclosures, not evidence of increased repetition for existing results.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the retained scores. Table 3 reports Llama-3.1-8B second-turn scores of 5.31 with original URIAL and 6.71 with three tagged two-turn SkillMix examples. Table 7 reports instruct-model first-turn scores of 7.92 unprompted versus 7.58 with URIAL. Figure 11 and Table 10 add KL and AlpacaEval scaling results. These concern added conditions, not across-version performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 2.4 adds a multi-turn prompting adaptation: GPT-4o supplies follow-up questions and answers, and prompts combine demonstrations with optional separation tags. The original greedy selection algorithm and instruction fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 adds contribution bullets, clearer background/setup/results signposting, and expanded URIAL and SkillMix explanations. New sections extend the existing organization, and author affiliations and conference headers change. Most retained prose and the main narrative remain stable.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with multi-turn and instruct-model tables, an AlpacaEval scaling table, SkillMix examples, the full URIAL prompt, and instruct-scaling and KL plots. R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged, but Section 2.4 adds a specific positioning argument: Lin et al. demonstrated multi-turn interaction without rigorously quantifying the role of multi-turn demonstrations. v3 presents its new experiment as addressing that gap.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs, and the existing mathematical notation is retained. The new KL-divergence analysis is empirical and introduces no new mathematical definition or formal result.

improvement.justification: v2 hypothesized that missing multi-turn demonstrations explained weak second-turn performance without directly testing that explanation. v3 supplies that control in Section 2.4 and independently checks scaling behavior on AlpacaEval in Appendix E.1, substantially strengthening the evidence and applicability boundaries of central conclusions. The instruct-model failure analysis and fuller prompt documentation add diagnostic and reproducibility value while preserving the original results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, with retained material identifiable across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds original multi-turn prompting, instruct-model, token-distribution, and AlpacaEval scaling results.

before.justification: v2 reports original instruction-following experiments, including prompt ablations, demonstration scaling, greedy search, and comparisons between ICL and instruction fine-tuning.

C1.justification: v3 presents a GFlowNet application with a relaxed reward for realistic, diverse CV-free sampling. v4 redefines the contribution around diffusion path samplers, log-variance training, and scale-based equivariant forces for high-dimensional problems. Its headline claims also extend to classical-baseline comparisons and resemblance to reference ensembles.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantial explanations linking performance to replay, annealing, and sparse training signals. Its revised Chignolin analysis emphasizes failure of force/potential variants and the role of scale-based guidance, whereas v3 emphasizes successful folding and advantages of conservative potential-derived forces. The stated limitations concerning larger systems and generalization remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 Appendix B newly specifies MLP depths, activations, Softplus scaling, gradient clipping, heavy-atom alignment, handedness atom selection, and the TICA data-collection and lag settings. It also adds an explicit code link and revises hyperparameter tables. Conversely, v3's GPU hardware and PyTorch implementation disclosures disappear. The net documentation change is substantial.

E1.justification: v4 adds a two-dimensional double-well transition task with two reaction channels and rejection-sampled reference paths. All three molecular systems remain covered, so the coverage expansion is limited to an additional controlled synthetic setting.

E2.justification: v3 compares against unbiased MD and PIPS. v4 systematically adds steered MD with multiple force constants on every retained molecular benchmark, introducing a substantial classical comparison missing previously. PIPS force and potential variants remain represented; their renamed descriptions do not constitute new comparators.

E3.justification: v4 replaces EPD with aligned heavy-atom RMSD, removes LL/EPCD/EFP, and extends THP and maximum-energy evaluation to Polyproline and Chignolin using handedness and TICA criteria. ETP is renamed ETS with its maximum-energy definition retained. Appendix B changes the reported integrator, Alanine solvent, and training budgets. The new double-well protocol evaluates 1,024 paths. Figures 3–4 have temperature captions conflicting with the main text, leaving those plotting settings uncertain.

E4.justification: v3 provides qualitative path analyses but no component ablations. v4 Section 4.5 adds five ablations covering the loss, control variate, replay, annealing, and variable path lengths, with convergence curves. It also adds an SMD force-constant sensitivity analysis and double-well comparisons against reference transition-state distributions.

E5.justification: v4 Figure 9b newly specifies that training curves average eight different seeds; v3 reports no corresponding repeated-training-run count. Both versions already report plus/minus values in benchmark tables and average molecular metrics over 64 paths. The new seed disclosure does not establish increased repetitions for the retained benchmark tables.

E6.justification: v4 substantially replaces the benchmark results and adds double-well, scaling-model, and ablation entries. Alanine potential-model THP changes from 100.00% in v3 Table 1 to 87.50% in v4 Table 1 under revised settings and criteria. v4 newly reports Chignolin THP of 59.38% for scaling versus 0% for force and potential variants. These are revised-setting findings, not demonstrated same-setting gains or losses.

M1.justification: v4 Section 3.3 adds positive scale-based bias forces with Kabsch alignment and replaces the pairwise-distance indicator relaxation with an aligned-coordinate RBF. These substantially change the parameterization and training signal. The squared log-ratio objective, learned scalar, replay buffer, annealing, and variable-length truncation already occur in v3; their reframing alone is not a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten around TPS-DPS terminology. Experiments are reorganized from separate quantitative/qualitative discussions into system-specific sections and ablations. Appendix A becomes a multipart method derivation, and the training algorithm moves there from the main text.

P2.justification: v4 changes the main text from two columns to one, consolidates benchmark results into a four-system table, and substantially redraws and reorganizes molecular visualizations. It expands the Alanine comparison panels and adds double-well landscapes/distributions, Chignolin TICA plots, ablation curves, and the SMD trade-off plot. These exceed renumbering or numerical table updates.

R1.justification: v4 removes the dedicated GFlowNet and learned-CV discussions and centers its positioning on log-variance diffusion sampling. It adds connections to Nüsken and Richter, Richter and Berner, relative trajectory balance, and concurrent Doob-based sampling, alongside newer trajectory-generation work. This changes the intellectual framing and novelty attribution beyond citation maintenance.

T1.justification: v3's one-step GFlowNet derivation is replaced by continuous path-measure definitions, a Girsanov-based log-variance derivation, and a derivation connecting the discretized loss to relative trajectory balance in v4 Section 3 and Appendix A. v4 also adds mathematical arguments for positive force alignment and claimed equivariance. This substantially expands the mathematical treatment despite equivalence of the central discrete objectives.

improvement.justification: v3 lacked controlled component tests and reference-ensemble validation. v4 addresses these central evidential gaps through Figure 9's ablations and eight-seed curves, Figures 2–3's double-well validation, and systematic SMD comparisons. More explicit implementation details further strengthen reproducibility. Removing whole-path likelihood checks and introducing conflicting temperature captions weaken reporting, but the gains in testing sampling fidelity and explaining training choices constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same transition-path sampling project, retaining the authors, molecular benchmarks, and central discrete training objective despite substantial reframing. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 reports original sampling results on a synthetic double-well system and the three molecular systems, together with component ablations and training curves.

before.justification: v3 reports original molecular simulations and TPS-GFN evaluations on Alanine Dipeptide, Polyproline Helix, and Chignolin in Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–5.

C1.justification: The central CV-free sampling and accuracy/diversity claims remain. That wording exceeds the new proposition's conditional guarantee for sufficiently small bias-only updates.

The original five component ablations remain, but v4's SMD force-constant sensitivity and THP–ETS trade-off study in Figure 8 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report RMSD and ETS with accompanying plus/minus values and average ablation learning curves over eight seeds. No new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are disclosed.

E6.justification: The double-well and Alanine benchmark values and most Chignolin entries are retained. New TPS-DPS(S) hit rates are 81.25%, 84.38%, and 43.75% for Trp-cage, BBA, and BBL, alongside new ablation and computational-cost results. Polyproline results and the SMD sensitivity results disappear. The replacement Chignolin SMD scores use a different force constant and cannot establish a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The log-variance objective, learned control variate, replay buffer, simulated annealing, scale-based bias force, and relaxed indicator are retained. Algorithm 1 moves from the appendix into the main text. Expanded explanations and the new proof do not establish a changed sampling procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations undergo substantial rewriting. Algorithm 1 moves into the main text, the experimental narrative is reorganized around fast-folding proteins, and the appendices gain separate proof, cost, visualization, and reverse-KL comparison sections.

P2.justification: v5 splits and expands the benchmark table, merges the double-well and Alanine trajectory figures, adds a bias-force-field illustration and comparison tables, and reorganizes case-study panels. The Chignolin trajectory display becomes a four-protein appendix grid. The SMD sensitivity plot and standalone Alanine/Polyproline snapshot figure are removed.

Background and implementation references also change. These refine the context while preserving the central research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix A.3 add Proposition 1 and its proof of strict distance reduction after a sufficiently small bias-only position update and realignment, assuming nonzero initial distance. This extends v4's positive-inner-product observation. Appendix C also adds asymptotic cost arguments; the existing log-variance and discrete-loss derivations remain.

improvement.justification: The added 20–47-residue protein experiments and computational measurements materially strengthen scalability and efficiency claims that v4 supported with only one 10-residue protein-folding benchmark and limited cost evidence. The conditional descent proof and additional controls strengthen justification of the method. These gains outweigh the loss of Polyproline coverage and SMD sensitivity analysis, although the unconditional MD-step wording and blanket failure interpretation should be narrowed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TPS-DPS and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained methods and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial revision and relocation.

after.justification: v5 reports original simulation results in Tables 1–2, component ablations in Figure 6, computational measurements in Appendix C, and additional comparisons in Appendix E.

GPT-2 fine-tuning specifies AdamW, a learning rate of 3e-5, and 500 warmup steps. The code pointer changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub project. Some earlier generation details, including ambiguity selection within ten probability-mass bins, are removed.

E1.justification: v3 adds Wikitext fine-tuning, syllogistic reasoning with ordinary and unseen-token subjects, and a bursty synthetic token-label prediction task adapted from Chan et al. Existing POS and syntax datasets remain. These additions substantially broaden training data and task requirements beyond the earlier syntax-focused study.

E2.justification: v3 Appendix F/Figure 14 adds an explicit plotted comparison with Chan et al. (2022b)'s observational baseline across different task settings. Existing vanilla training, active forgetting, and increased-weight-decay comparisons remain. Singh et al.'s regularization comparison already appeared in v2 Appendix A.7; its promotion to the main text is not a new baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include a four-layer autoregressive synthetic model, separate contextual and memorization tests, probability-based syllogism scoring, Pythia checkpoint evaluation, and 2,000-step GPT-2-large fine-tuning comparisons. Separately, v3 changes the stated MultiBERT Tail sampling from frequent to infrequent adjectives. This is a reported setting revision; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 Appendix E adds autoregressive sensitivity analyses across ambiguity, burstiness, distribution skew, and forgetting regimes, including trajectories testing whether structural ICL and memorization coexist. Most earlier layer, syntax, vocabulary, ambiguity, embedding, and distribution-shift analyses are retained. The original Figure 1 t-SNE analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 8 newly states that Pythia results are averaged over three trials. Both versions retain MultiBERT seeds 0, 1, and 2 and Figure 2 error bars of plus or minus one standard error. There is no documented increase in runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial autoregressive and syllogism results. Appendix D reports GPT-2 unseen-token syllogism accuracy rising from 0.02 to 0.927 during probabilistic forgetting, while ordinary-token accuracy changes from 0.933 to 0.923. Retained results also change: the temporary-forgetting head-IWL bar at alpha = 1.5 rises from approximately 0.74 in v2 Figure 5 to 0.84 in v3 Figure 4. The latter figure also plots tail accuracy above 1.0, an unexplained inconsistency. These revisions do not establish a reliable same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: v3 Section 7 and Appendix D introduce probabilistic temporary forgetting for pretrained models: approximately 10% of batch tokens receive random embeddings, and the pretrained embedding matrix is restored after each update. This substantially extends the procedure beyond v2's periodic embedding resets during pretraining. The original active and temporary forgetting procedures remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental explanations, and discussion are extensively rewritten. v3 creates a Definitions section, moves the main-text embedding analysis into Appendix N, absorbs Related Work into Discussion, replaces the grammar appendix with worked examples, and reorganizes the appendices. These changes substantially alter the narrative structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces its t-SNE panel with the relocated forgetting-duration plot. The decile comparison receives a new main-text presentation, and new autoregressive, syllogism, and sensitivity figures are added. Many older appendix plots are retained unchanged under new numbering. Figure composition, captions, placement, and conference formatting are substantially revised.

R1.justification: v3 adds positioning around autoregressive models and syllogistic reasoning, including Lampinen et al. and Kim et al., while removing much of the neuroscience and cognitive-control background. It also drops the explicit first-to-use-forgetting-for-ICL statement. The central relationship to Chan, Singh, and Chen remains.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A.5's explicit probabilistic grammar and truncated-Zipf probability-mass formula are removed, although the synthetic task remains described. v3 Section 2 introduces an explicit embedding-replacement invariance criterion for structural ICL. These are limited changes to formal definitions and exposition; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important limitation explicitly acknowledged in v2: forgetting interventions lacked validation on pretrained natural-language models. The controlled GPT-2 fine-tuning experiment, Pythia analysis, and autoregressive synthetic replication substantially strengthen the evidence beyond the original MLM setting while retaining most earlier analyses. The invalid accuracy bar in Figure 4 and removal of some generation details weaken reporting, and large-scale benefits remain untested, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Dual Process Learning study. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting, reorganization, and added experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds autoregressive synthetic experiments, Pythia checkpoint evaluations, and GPT-2 fine-tuning results.

before.justification: v2 reports original MultiBERT probing, synthetic masked-language-model experiments, forgetting interventions, and appendix analyses of embeddings and generalization.

results.title: Dual Process Learning: Controlling Use of In-Context vs. In-Weights Strategies with Weight Forgetting

C1.justification: The central claims remain novel-view synthesis from casual monocular videos through 3D-aware initialization and ordinal depth supervision, with advantages over existing DVS methods. Additional evaluations support these retained contributions without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds specular-reflection failures and a current video-length limit of approximately ten seconds, with longer videos proposed as requiring greater model capacity and training. It also explains alpha sensitivity and ranking-loss behavior. Existing limitations concerning unseen regions, training cost, and dependence on depth estimates remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents one-in-five flow keyframes, scene and depth normalization, exclusion of depth pairs differing by at most 0.02, Gaussian-center depth rendering, and Kaiming initialization. It also supplies DAVIS preprocessing instructions and promises future code release. These additions improve documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed implementation choice changed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates DyNeRF, Nvidia, and the self-collected MCV dataset. v2 additionally evaluates DAVIS natural videos, including animal and outdoor scenes with recovered camera poses (Appendix A.6 and Figure 11), substantially extending its benchmark coverage beyond the original datasets.

E2.justification: The principal SC-GS, Deformable-GS, HexPlane, and RoDynRF comparisons remain. v2 adds evaluated comparisons with Shape-of-Motion, prior depth-ranking losses, and depth-supervised HexPlane (Tables 3, 8, and 10), providing substantially broader controls for reconstruction quality and the proposed loss.

E3.justification: The reported initialization and joint-training budgets each fall from 30k to 20k steps. Quantitative evaluation expands from five to six DyNeRF scenes and three to eight Nvidia scenes, while new experiments introduce DAVIS pose recovery and controlled loss, noise, and initialization settings. Retained camera splits and metrics are unchanged; the budget revision alone does not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices A.7–A.13 add tests of alpha sensitivity, depth-noise robustness, ranking-loss alternatives, video-depth supervision, depth-supervised HexPlane, and zero-deformation versus Kaiming initialization. These investigate several previously untested explanations and dependencies. The earlier initialization, Pearson-loss, and depth-warping analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. The Gaussian distribution parameters in v2 Table 5 specify injected depth noise, not uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: All 96 overlapping per-scene metric entries and the original three-row ablation table are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results for additional scenes, comparators, and analyses. MoDGS's Nvidia average PSNR changes from 23.27 to 19.27 and DyNeRF from 22.90 to 22.64 because the evaluated scene sets expand; these are not same-setting performance declines. Reported training time and rendering speed also change under the revised training budget.

M1.justification: The canonical Gaussians, invertible deformation field, 3D-aware initialization, and ordinal-loss formulation remain substantially unchanged. Section 3.2 adds SAM2 segmentation as an alternative to flow thresholding for selecting static regions during depth-scale initialization; it does not establish which experiments used this option.

P1.justification: v2 corrects the title spelling, edits terminology and several paragraphs, renames headings, and moves implementation details into Appendix A.1. The main introduction–related work–method–experiments–conclusion narrative remains recognizable; much of the additional prose accompanies new scientific content.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned, comparison figures gain input-view columns, and the initialization figure is rearranged. Dataset summaries are consolidated into a main-text table while expanded per-scene tables move to the appendix, alongside new figures and analysis tables.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion adds an ordinal-depth lineage including Zoran, Fu, Chen, and Pavlakos, and distinguishes MoDGS's dense rendered-depth supervision from earlier approaches. It also positions MoDGS against concurrent DG-Marbles, Shape-of-Motion, and MoSca, emphasizing its use of pairwise RAFT flow rather than strong long-range correspondences.

T1.justification: The ordinal indicator drops its explicit equal-depth case between v1 Equation 3 and v2 Equation 2. Appendix A.5 also adds a derivation showing that the summed squared standardized rendered depths equal the pixel count, supporting a step merely asserted in v1's Pearson-equivalence argument. No new theorem or broader theoretical framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central contributions through fuller benchmark coverage, Shape-of-Motion comparisons, and targeted loss, depth-supervision, robustness, and initialization controls. These address important gaps in v1's comparative evidence, supported by clearer implementation details and applicability limits. The gains outweigh localized reporting problems: the Nvidia D-GS summary disagrees with the displayed per-scene mean, and Table 9's metric improvements are less consistent than its accompanying interpretation suggests.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MoDGS. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds benchmark results, Shape-of-Motion comparisons, and several quantitative ablation and robustness studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments, quantitative benchmark results in Tables 1–2, ablations in Table 3, and qualitative analyses.

results.title: MoDGS: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting from Casually-captured Monocular Videos with Depth Priors

C1.justification: The four principal contributions remain. v2 narrows the first-work novelty claim to neural inverse approximation using only matrix information and newly claims applicability to structured matrices supporting fast matrix products. These refine the contribution's boundaries without redefining the proposed approach.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the practical interpretation: total cost depends on reuse across right-hand sides, generalization across different matrices is limited, and implementation choices affect robustness and speed. Appendix D.3 acknowledges that AmgX constructs preconditioners faster but fails more often, and explains why comparable solution-time testing is omitted. New discussion also connects GNN matrix products to polynomial approximation.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly discloses GPU use whenever supported and identifies the AmgX driver, configuration file and aggregation-based setup. It also explains the C-versus-Python implementation obstacle to solution-time comparison. Existing GNP hyperparameters and hardware specifications remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate 867 square, real, non-SPD SuiteSparse matrices using the same size and sparsity filters. v2 specifies 50 application areas instead of v1's 'over 20', without documenting added coverage. Structured-matrix applicability is discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: Jacobi joins the direct GNP comparisons, alongside retained ILU, PyAMG, GMRES and unpreconditioned solves. Appendix D.3 additionally compares AmgX against PyAMG, although it does not provide a direct AmgX-versus-GNP solution-time comparison.

E3.justification: v1 uses a relative tolerance of 1e-8 and a 100-iteration limit throughout. v2 adds time-comparison runs with the iteration limit disabled and a shared timeout determined by the maximum solution time among the iteration-limited runs. This substantially changes the time-based evaluation budget; the AUC formulas and GNP training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds residual-advantage ratios, application-area breakdowns, construction-versus-solution cost analysis and a PyAMG–AmgX robustness study. The original sampling and scale-equivariance ablation questions remain. The convergence examples replace VDOL/kineticBatchReactor_5 with Hollinger/mark3jac040, including the corresponding appendix histories.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new residual-ratio percentiles and timing summaries describe variation across benchmark matrices rather than introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figure 2 reports GNP's time-based winner share changing from 3.9% to 19.4%, and the unpreconditioned share from 49.6% to 3.7%, under revised stopping conditions and comparator membership; these are not same-setting performance gains. v2 adds residual-ratio results and AmgX failure counts of 105 during construction and 36 during solution. The retained failure table also changes GMRES solution failures from one to two.

M1.justification: The scale-equivariant residual GNN, Arnoldi-based mixture sampling, residual training loss and nonlinear-preconditioned FGMRES procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A without changing its steps.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most method exposition remain intact. v2 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, evaluation rationale and results discussion, reorders several results questions, moves Algorithm 1 into the appendix and organizes supplementary experiments into named subsections.

P2.justification: The result displays are substantially revised: construction-time plots expand to include solution times and additional methods, with logarithmic and linear versions; breakdown figures gain application-area panels; and convergence plots incorporate Jacobi and a replacement case. Two new tables present residual-ratio percentiles and AMG-implementation failures, and the existing failure table gains Jacobi.

R1.justification: The research positioning expands through connections to structured-matrix solvers, polynomial interpretations of GNNs, deeper GCNs, FCG-NO, AmgX and continual learning. Sections 1.2 and 5 develop substantive arguments about fixed sparsity and problem-specific generalization, while qualifying the novelty claim. This goes beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, Corollary 2 and their original proofs are retained. New Appendix C derives an explicit Chebyshev-polynomial bound and approximately exponential residual decay under an origin-excluding spectral-ellipse assumption, extending the previously qualitative convergence discussion.

improvement.justification: The revised time-budget protocol addresses an important weakness in v1, where early iteration-limited termination could favor fast but inaccurate solves in Time-AUC. Combined with construction-versus-solution analysis, application-specific evidence and the AMG implementation check, v2 offers substantially stronger support for assessing practical usefulness and its limits. Comparable AmgX solution-time testing remains unresolved, so the timing conclusions still depend on implementation choices.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GNP research, with matching architecture, training approach, theory and SuiteSparse benchmark. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional residual-ratio, application-area, timing and AMG-implementation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on 867 matrices, including convergence, timing, preconditioner failures and architecture/training ablations.

results.title: Graph Neural Preconditioners for Iterative Solutions of Sparse Linear Systems

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the demonstrated contribution from reward design aligned with human driving standards to reward design reflecting implicit human knowledge across driving, locomotion and manipulation. v1 presented broader applicability as potential; v2 explicitly claims superior performance across three simulation settings.

C2.justification: v2 attributes REvolve Auto's smaller advantage in MuJoCo to less informative automated feedback and emphasizes its interaction with evolutionary search. It explicitly notes the absence of MuJoCo generalization tests and expands resource-efficiency arguments in Appendix D using indirect comparisons. The earlier visual-processing and closed-source-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds SAC/SB3 architecture and hyperparameters, MuJoCo training times, task-specific prompts and environment/reward code, storage estimates and a future public-code-release statement. However, v1's three-driver, ten-runs-per-driver description disappears. Added Adroit documentation conflicts internally: Table 1 versus Appendix A.1.3 gives 39 versus 97 observations, and Appendix A.1.3 versus Box 11 gives 30 versus 28 actions.

E1.justification: v2 adds MuJoCo humanoid locomotion and dexterous door opening with an Adroit Hand to v1's autonomous-driving coverage. These introduce substantially different behaviors and continuous-control tasks. The original driving environment and two AirSim generalization scenarios remain.

E2.justification: T2R Auto is removed from the driving fitness comparison, while Expert Designed is added to the driving Elo comparison and Eureka is added to both retained generalization scenarios. These are targeted membership changes; the principal REvolve/Eureka and automatic-feedback comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The added MuJoCo experiments use SAC with 5 million training steps per policy and task-specific velocity or completion-time fitness measures, versus the retained driving protocol using Clipped Double Deep Q-Learning and 500,000 steps. Mutation-only and crossover-only experiments introduce new controls. These substantially expand the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original driving training budget.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.5 and Figure 4 add a direct comparison of mutation alone, crossover alone and their combination, testing a central explanation for REvolve's performance that v1 did not isolate. The existing generalization analysis gains Eureka comparisons. Conversely, v1 Figure 9's population-average fitness analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v1 Section 5.2 explicitly reports a single random seed; v2 reports two, and Figure 3 adds shaded bands to the evolution curves. The existing generalization mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remains. No new significance tests or confidence-interval procedure are provided, so the statistical expansion is limited.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for both MuJoCo tasks and the operator ablation. Table 3 adds Eureka fitness scores of 0.73 ± 0.04 and 0.57 ± 0.05 in the two generalization environments, while retaining the earlier rows. Driving REvolve Elo changes from 1534 to 1575 in an expanded comparison pool, preventing interpretation as a direct performance gain. Population-average results are removed.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, island-based evolution and Elo-guided feedback remain unchanged. However, the documented driving crossover prompt in Box 3 drops the instruction giving collision and inactivity penalties precedence over other rewards. This is a limited revision to the specified LLM instructions; the PDFs do not establish its experimental effect.

P1.justification: The title, contribution paragraphs and conclusion are substantially rewritten around broader applicability. Experimental setup, training and baselines are reorganized; retained human-feedback related work and episodic-step discussion move into appendices. The appendices gain task-based organization, and ethics and reproducibility sections are introduced. This substantially changes the narrative structure beyond adding experiments.
