P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-task fitness display with three panels, adds an operator-ablation figure and task-summary table, and separates and expands v1's combined Table 1. It moves the framework-comparison schematic to Appendix D, adds task illustrations and a fitness diagram, removes the population-average plot, and reorganizes convergence plots. Typography and page styling also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 expands the existing evolutionary-versus-greedy positioning, explicitly arguing that Eureka does not qualify as an evolutionary algorithm. It adds references for SAC, MuJoCo, SB3 and resource comparisons, replaces Bäck and Schwefel with De Jong, and removes Salvador and Saludares. Most earlier literature remains, including the human-feedback discussion relocated to Appendix D.

T1.justification: The RDP objective, assumptions, Elo equations and selection reasoning remain. Appendix B.2 adds mathematical definitions for humanoid fitness, conditional on surviving the episode, and Adroit fitness, conditional on successful completion and elapsed steps (Equations 3–4). These are limited formal additions, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 evaluated driving without isolating genetic-operator contributions. v2's operator ablation and two additional continuous-control tasks substantially strengthen evidence for the search mechanism and broader applicability. Adding Eureka to generalization comparisons and reporting two seeds further support the evaluation. These gains outweigh the removed T2R Auto and population-average comparisons, although inconsistent Adroit dimensions, limited replication and indirect resource comparisons weaken reproducibility and some claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REvolve, with matching formalization, algorithm and driving experiments despite the changed title and broader scope. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original driving, humanoid locomotion and Adroit Hand experiments, human-preference rankings and genetic-operator ablations in Figures 3–4 and Tables 2–3.

before.justification: v1 reports original AirSim experiments, human-preference evaluations and reward generalization results, including Figures 4–5 and Table 1.

results.title: REvolve: Reward Evolution with Large Language Models using Human Feedback

C1.justification: The central claims remain vector representations for binary features, polytope representations for categorical concepts, and orthogonal structure for semantic hierarchy. v2 foregrounds polytopes, but v1 already defines them; its conditional simplex claim remains in v2 Appendix C. Additional model evidence supports the retained claims.

C2.justification: v1 interprets the observed geometry directly as evidence of semantic hierarchy. v2 explains how high-dimensional geometry and token-set inclusion can produce similar observations, distinguishes sibling from inclusion relationships, and interprets independent-subsampling controls. It also explains the empirical importance of LDA and the causal inner product, substantially refining the interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix E explicitly identifies displays using representations estimated from unsplit token collections, including retained visualizations. Projection captions also specify the normalized dot-product formula. These clarify implementation and reporting without establishing corresponding changes to previously unspecified settings. Existing preprocessing and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds a limited intervention scenario testing target-versus-subordinate logit changes for three parent-child contrast pairs in Table 1; v1 empirically examined representation geometry. English WordNet noun/verb coverage and the curated animal/plant examples remain. Adding LLaMA changes model coverage rather than introducing another dataset.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's random-word projection reference, v2 evaluates shuffled-unembedding controls in the retained WordNet analyses, random parent/grandparent assignments, a mean-vector estimator, and an unwhitened Euclidean alternative. Figures 3–5 and 10–12 substantially expand the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported train/test split changes from 80/20 to 70/30. v2 adds whole-token versus independently subsampled estimation, normalized-vector intervention tests, and LLaMA-3-8B noun evaluations. Hierarchy comparisons use inverse shortest-path distance instead of the earlier adjacency reference. These substantially revise and extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 tests whether apparent orthogonality arises from high dimensionality or token-set inclusion using random relatives, shuffled embeddings, and independent subsampling. Appendix F additionally tests mean estimation and removal of whitening. Table 1 adds intervention case studies. These analyses address alternative explanations largely untested in v1.

E5.justification: v1 Figures 4 and 9 report error bars of 1.96 times the standard error; the corresponding v2 projection analyses use standard deviation. Table 1 also reports standard deviation across token pairs. This changes statistical reporting, without establishing additional repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for interventions, controls, ablations, and LLaMA. For example, Table 1 reports a plant-to-animal intervention changing parent logit differences by 5.1265 ± 1.1731 and subordinate mammal-to-reptile differences by -0.0600 ± 1.2190. Revised projection plots use different splits, so they do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same whitening transformation and LDA representation estimator with Ledoit-Wolf covariance shrinkage in Equations 5.1–5.2. The added theoretical properties, comparator estimators, and evaluations do not change the proposed estimation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. The theoretical exposition is reorganized around binary and categorical vector representations; the simplex discussion and animal example move to appendices. The experimental narrative is restructured around representation existence, intervention, similarity, and controlled orthogonality tests.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the principal heatmap arrangement with shortest-distance, original-embedding, and shuffled-embedding panels, and introduces dedicated orthogonality line plots. Projection figures gain training curves and control panels. A numerical intervention table and additional analysis figures are added; the existing categorical visualization is relocated and its viewing angle revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds the LLaMA-3 reference and removes several citations, including Patchscopes, Representation Engineering, and Ri et al.'s contrastive-loss work. It condenses the embedding-literature discussion while retaining the central positioning as an extension of Park et al.'s formalization.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds Corollary 10 and a proof characterizing token projections onto categorical representation subspaces. Appendix G adds a Gaussian mean-vector derivation explaining inclusion-induced orthogonality. These extend the theoretical analysis. The earlier simplex theorem survives as Proposition 9, and the binary-contrast result is reorganized as Corollary 6 rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support left high-dimensional geometry and token-set overlap as substantial alternative explanations. v2 directly investigates these through shuffled embeddings, random relatives, and independent subsampling, materially strengthening support for the central interpretation. Intervention measurements and LLaMA replication provide complementary validation. Changed splits and error-bar conventions prevent direct numerical improvement claims, but the stronger experimental controls constitute a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated, revised, and added content.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original Gemma-2B and LLaMA-3-8B results, including projection measurements, intervention effects, and controlled comparisons of hierarchical geometry.

before.justification: Sections 5.2–5.3 and Appendix C report original Gemma-2B experiments measuring token projections and hierarchical representation geometry.

results.title: The Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a general CTMC guidance framework and an efficient approximation. The headline application emphasis shifts toward scientific generation, and v2's claim of improved unconditional image generation is explicitly reframed in v3 Appendix F.1.2 as a check of conditional sample quality and distribution coverage.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning approximation error, predictor miscalibration and why exact guidance can sometimes perform worse than TAG. It qualifies FBD as a heuristic and adds explicit limitations about TAG's missing theoretical guarantees and uncertainty over predictor-training strategies. These substantially extend v2's predominantly proof-of-concept interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds DiGress implementation settings, predictor-retraining details and molecular fingerprint specifications while retaining most existing architectures and resource links. Reproducibility also suffers limited regressions: Listings 1 and 4 introduce inconsistent variable names, respectively pred_model versus model and guidance_strength versus inverse_guide_temp.

E1.justification: The source datasets and four application domains remain; CIFAR-10 moves to Appendix F.1 rather than disappearing. Enhancer evaluation drops cell-type class 21, reducing nine evaluated classes across v2's main text and appendix to eight in v3 Appendix F.3.4. No new task family is introduced.

E2.justification: v3 evaluates DiGress against Discrete Guidance on molecules, enhancer DNA and proteins; v2 discussed DiGress without these empirical comparisons. GWG-Opt is removed from the protein comparisons. Dirichlet FM, ProteinMPNN and the unguided CTDD comparison remain.

E3.justification: The protein evaluation changes its sampling step size and structure-conditioning temperature, adds predictor training and expands from three to eight targets. The enhancer predictor-guidance strength grid also changes. Added experiments introduce DiGress protocols, molecular MAE and diversity evaluation, and enhancer success/diversity metrics. These changes prevent interpreting revised scores simply as same-setting improvements.

E4.justification: v2 compares exact and approximate guidance principally through molecular ring-count histograms. v3 extends this investigation across all three scientific applications, adds molecular diversity analyses and guidance-strength comparisons, and evaluates enhancer generation with alternative success/diversity metrics. Conversely, v2's image and enhancer noisy-classifier performance plots are removed.

E5.justification: v3 adds molecular MAE standard errors and Mann-Whitney tests, uncertainty for molecular validity, and five-bootstrap-replicate means and standard deviations for enhancer metrics. v2 already reported protein t-tests and qualitatively discussed seed variability, so this is a substantial expansion rather than the first statistical reporting. Bootstrap replicates do not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: New molecular MAEs, enhancer comparisons and expanded protein tables substantially change the reported evidence. DG outperforms DiGress on molecules and generally on proteins, while performing comparably on enhancer DNA. The new 6ACV case favors TAG over exact guidance, with maximum success rates of 74% and 46% respectively (v3 Table 10). Protein results are revised under changed settings; CIFAR IS/FID and PDB recovery values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core predictor-guided and predictor-free rate formulas, Taylor approximation and fixed-state handling remain unchanged. However, v3 Appendix F.4.3 adds a second training stage for the stability-guidance predictor using generated samples labelled by the clean predictor, beyond the initial training described in v2.

P1.justification: The empirical narrative and discussion are extensively rewritten, image modeling moves from the main experiments to the appendix, and Appendix F gains a detailed numbered subsection hierarchy. Guidance-strength terminology and exact/TAG naming become more systematic, while citations switch from numerical to author-year form. This exceeds local copyediting.

P2.justification: Molecular figures gain comparison and diversity panels; enhancer plots are consolidated and redesigned; and the main protein table is replaced by a comparative bar chart with expanded appendix tables. Image displays are relocated and noisy-classifier plots removed. Typography, captions and table formatting also change substantially.

R1.justification: Targeted additions cover Gat et al.'s discrete flow matching, literature supporting gradient approximations, and preference-based fine-tuning in Appendix E.1. The DiGress contrast becomes more prominent, and the Emami reference associated with GWG-Opt disappears. The central positioning around CTMC guidance remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 2 corrects the score definition from the gradient of the density to the gradient of its logarithm. The guidance derivations, assumptions and fixed-state mathematics otherwise remain substantively unchanged. v3's separate generality subsection, C.8, largely reproduces material already in v2 C.7.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important empirical weakness in v2 by directly evaluating the closely related DiGress approach and testing exact versus approximate guidance beyond ring-count generation. The added diversity analyses, uncertainty reporting and explicit failure interpretations provide substantially stronger scrutiny of the framework. Broader protein testing strengthens support, although changed settings preclude simple cross-version performance claims. Removing GWG-Opt and classifier diagnostics, and introducing code-listing inconsistencies, are drawbacks, but they are outweighed by the stronger comparative evidence and clearer limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Discrete Guidance work and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, code listings and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical investigations and adds DiGress comparisons, broader exact-versus-approximate evaluations and additional protein case studies in Section 6 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original guided-generation experiments on images, molecules, enhancer DNA and protein sequences in Section 6 and Appendix F.

results.title: Unlocking Guidance for Discrete State-Space Diffusion and Flow Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add the claim that PopT provides a computationally lightweight, more interpretable alternative with competitive performance against end-to-end methods. The title, abstract, and conclusion broaden the demonstrated scope from intracranial activity to multiple neural modalities and temporal encoders, while retaining the original decoding and interpretability contributions.

C2.justification: The limitations change substantially: v1 emphasizes unavailable comparable intracranial datasets and computational obstacles to end-to-end comparisons; v2 emphasizes dependence on meaningful spatial coordinates, individual brain variability, and difficulty identifying functional channels with low-SNR recordings. v2 also adds an explanation linking the Brant comparison to spatial aggregation and discusses potential geophysical and climate applications.

D1.justification: v2 adds temporal-embedding dimensions and parameter, hardware, and compute tables in Appendices A–B. It revises pretraining time from four to two days but removes the 80-CPU-core/700-GB memory disclosure, the explicit 500 ms temporal threshold, and subject identities for the pretraining-subset study. Core optimizer, schedule, split, and code-access information remains.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates movie-watching intracranial recordings on four auditory-linguistic tasks. v2 retains this coverage and adds TUEG pretraining and TUAB scalp-EEG pathological-versus-normal classification, which the paper labels seizure detection. This adds a distinct recording modality, population, and task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds fine-tuned Brant and removes the single-channel BrainBERT comparison row. Table 2 adds comparisons with BIOT and LaBraM using scores explicitly attributed to their original works. Deep NN also joins the sample- and compute-efficiency comparisons in v2 Figures 4–5, where v1 Figures 3–4 showed only Linear and the two PopT variants.

E3.justification: The added EEG evaluation uses 21 channels, excludes task subjects from pretraining, and reports balanced accuracy alongside ROC-AUC. New configurations use TOTEM for intracranial data and Chronos/TS2Vec for EEG. The channel-count sweep expands from 1–30 to 1–50 channels, while the original splits and training-step budgets in Appendix A remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds a reconstruction-only pretraining control beyond v1's added-reconstruction-loss ablation. The channel-count sensitivity analysis is extended to 50 channels. The existing loss/position ablations, held-out-subject study, pretraining-subject scaling, frozen-model analyses, and interpretability studies are retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds means and standard deviations across five random seeds for the EEG experiments in Table 2 and Figure 2b. Subject-level standard-error reporting remains for the intracranial experiments. No increase in repeated runs for the retained experiments is stated.

E6.justification: The original BrainBERT PopT AUROC means remain 0.69, 0.84, 0.86, and 0.89. v2 adds TOTEM/Brant results, EEG results, reconstruction-only scores, and additional scaling and efficiency entries. Table 2 reports PopT+TS2Vec AUROC of 0.8907 alongside quoted BIOT and LaBraM values of 0.8815 and 0.9162. Reported PopT pretraining time also changes from four to two days.

M1.justification: The transformer backbone, frozen temporal embeddings, two discrimination objectives, channel replacement procedure, and downstream fine-tuning remain. The ensemble encoding explicitly described in v2 was already depicted as sequence position in v1 Figure 1. Additional encoders and EEG inputs exercise the existing modular method without establishing a new algorithm.

P1.justification: Beyond the new experiments, v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, existing method explanation, discussion, and conclusion, and condenses interpretability descriptions and captions. It reorganizes the loss explanation, changes the title and terminology, and adds a compute appendix while renumbering retained appendices.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with separate objective panels and a detailed temporal-encoder pipeline. Table 1 is reorganized by encoder, and new EEG, parameter, and compute tables and a summary bar chart are added. Existing plots receive changed axes, legends, grouping, and placement within a new conference layout; the appendix connectivity and frozen-model graphics are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work structure and novelty argument for modular aggregation across variable channel layouts largely remain. v2 adds references for Chronos, TS2Vec, TUEG, BERT, and aggregation approaches, and removes the Nejedly and Islam references associated with the old limitations. Comparisons with already-cited end-to-end models become explicit empirical positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical substance remains the two discrimination tasks and their summed binary-cross-entropy objective. v2 replaces explicit BCE expansions with prose and expands position-encoding notation. These are expository changes; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for encoder/modality generality and its missing end-to-end comparisons through additional encoders, scalp-EEG evaluation, and the Brant comparison. Five-seed EEG reporting and the reconstruction-only control further strengthen the evidence while preserving the original results. EEG competitors remain partly indirect comparisons, and some reproducibility details are lost, but the gains in empirical support and applicability are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Population Transformer work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across the revised organization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments with alternative temporal encoders, a fine-tuned Brant comparison, scalp-EEG evaluation, and a reconstruction-only ablation. The EEG comparison scores attributed to earlier works are distinguished from these original results.

before.justification: v1 reports original intracranial decoding experiments, efficiency and generalization studies, ablations, and analyses of learned connectivity and attention.

results.title: Population Transformer: Learning Population-level Representations of Neural Activity

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: Bayesian aggregation of multiple weak supervisors, extension from classification to generation, token-level soft supervision, and further improvement through cDPO. Expanded experimental support and revised terminology do not redefine those claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanations of ensemble behavior: Bayesian priors provide fault tolerance, weak-model disagreement supports complementarity, TinyLlama's scoring can undermine Joint Decoding, and larger candidate pools exacerbate that failure. Appendix E additionally interprets dynamic weighting as redundant with token-level reliability information. The two-task applicability limitation remains, with the model-count limitation updated to three and five teachers.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the default beam size M=5, validation-based tuning of ceiling models and reuse of those settings, and checkpoint/license information for the added models. Appendix C updates cDPO hyperparameters while retaining most training and hardware details. Conversely, v1's explicit description of the DPO reference model and its SFT initialization is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use SciQ reformulated as binary answer-correctness classification and SLURP transcriptions for generative slot filling. Added weak models and ensemble configurations do not introduce new datasets, tasks, populations, or input environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds BLOOM-1B1 and TinyLlama_v1.1 as evaluated single-model and single-weak-to-strong comparators in Tables 1–4. Naive Multi-Weak and Joint Decoding remain the ensemble baselines. The separate full hard-label comparator panel in v1 Table 4 is no longer reported.

E3.justification: v2 adds five-model ensembles alongside the original three-model configuration, plus four-model controls, generation-versus-scoring controls, weighting comparisons, and beam-size experiments with M=3, 5, and 10. Appendix C changes the stated cDPO learning rate from 2×10^-7 to 5×10^-7 and beta from 10 to 2. These substantially expand the evaluation design; dataset splits and principal metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds model-agreement analysis (Figure 3), staged target-token versus other-token probability ablations (Table 6), weighting-strategy comparisons (Table 7), and Joint Decoding teacher-quality and beam-size analyses (Tables 8–9). The original auxiliary-loss comparisons persist, but v1's complete hard-versus-soft-label comparison is replaced by a narrower component ablation.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports point estimates and two classification p-value comparisons, without explicit repeated-run counts. v2 states three random seeds and reports means and standard deviations across the principal comparisons and ablations; the earlier p-value comparisons disappear. This is a substantial reporting change, but does not establish how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: Numerous retained results change: three-model Bayesian classification accuracy with auxiliary loss changes from 0.855 to 0.850±0.006, and the slot-filling ceiling changes from 0.781 to 0.748. v2 adds five-model results, including 0.866±0.006 classification accuracy and 0.724±0.015 SLU-F1 after cDPO, plus new ablation and agreement findings. Changed aggregation, ceilings, configurations, and cDPO settings preclude interpreting higher cross-version PGR values as comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: The Bayesian EDL objective, auxiliary self-training loss, word-mediated token probabilities, and weak-model-guided cDPO procedure are retained. Joint Decoding moves from Section 4.1 to the baseline description in Section 5.2. Expanded explanations and weighting ablations do not establish a change to the proposed core method.

P1.justification: The generation and experimental sections undergo substantial reorganization: Joint Decoding moves into the baseline section, dataset and model descriptions are separated, and results are rewritten around three-versus-five-model comparisons. Probability-estimation explanations are expanded, terminology is revised, and the existing appendices are reordered around the new analyses.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 receive revised labels, captions, and diagram presentation, while Figure 3 adds agreement heatmaps. Main comparison tables are restructured around ensemble size and uncertainty reporting, cDPO receives a separate table, and four appendix analysis tables are added. Title styling, headings, and page headers also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds boosting and bagging references to the ensemble discussion, along with citations for BLOOM and TinyLlama. The existing positioning around alignment, human-opinion variability, and weak-to-strong generalization remains substantially intact. The switch to author-year citations is a presentation change.

T1.justification: The EDL likelihood and regularizer, word-probability decomposition, cDPO objective, and PGR definition remain mathematically unchanged. The regularizer moves from Appendix B to G. v2's tokenwise teacher-forcing formula makes the existing naive generation baseline explicit; no substantive theoretical result, proof, or mathematical correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis of the ensemble approach through three-seed uncertainty reporting and targeted tests of component contributions, weighting, and teacher-scoring failures. These address important gaps beyond v1's point estimates and broad hard-versus-soft comparison. The lost full hard-label panel and an inconsistent TinyLlama PGR entry in Table 4 weaken parts of the reporting, but the expanded diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement. Higher PGR under changed ceilings and settings is not itself evidence of improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong research. All pages, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and slot-filling results, repeated-seed comparisons, model-agreement analysis, and additional ablations in Tables 1–9 and Figure 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original SciQ classification and SLURP slot-filling experiments, including ensemble, auxiliary-loss, soft-label, and cDPO results in Tables 1–5.

results.title: Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong from Text Classification to Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion replace exact-likelihood evaluation as a central contribution with diffusion/AO-ARM objective unification. The zero-shot contribution shifts from reevaluating SEDD to improved trained RADD variants. The sampling claim narrows from consistently better quality to similar quality while retaining the speedup claim.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 now acknowledges that different autoregressive orders generally define inconsistent distributions and interprets the objective as expected autoregressive negative log-likelihood and a diffusion likelihood bound. v2 also credits adopted hyperparameters for improved results and interprets the DSE comparison as supporting removal of time conditioning. The GPT-2-scale and fixed-length-output limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a RADD code-access link, explicit training budgets and regularization settings, the LayerNorm-bias correction, lambda-DCE pseudocode, and disclosure that sampling uses no top-p/top-k annealing. The hardware description changes from 16 V100/A100 GPUs to nodes with 32 V100 GPUs. Earlier attention/checkpointing details and the SEDD URL/license appendix are removed, materially changing reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions train on OpenWebText and evaluate LAMBADA, WikiText2, PTB, WikiText103 and 1BW. Unconditional generation, generation conditioned on prefix and suffix prompts, and forward/backward/random-order sampling already occur in v1. Additional losses and training budgets do not expand dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The external zero-shot baseline families remain GPT-2, D3PM, PLAID and the SEDD variants. Internal model comparisons expand to RADD-lambda-DCE and RADD-AO; the sampling-order comparison replaces RADD-DSE with RADD-lambda-DCE (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4). Newly discussed concurrent works are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v1 uses a common SEDD training configuration; v2 changes non-DSE variants to weight decay 0.03 and dropout 0.02 while retaining the DSE control. It evaluates variants using their corresponding losses and reports separate 400k- and 1000k-iteration experiments. Appendix G.3 also revises RADD's generation sample count from 1000 to 1024. v1's total training iterations are unspecified, so a direct budget increase cannot be established.

E4.justification: The existing loss comparison broadens from DSE/DCE to four training variants, and Section 4.3 explicitly analyzes the matched DSE comparison as evidence about time conditioning. Appendix G.4 revises the models examined in the retained sampling-order analysis, and Figures 3–6 replace the qualitative examples. These extend existing analysis questions; the scaling-trick ablation remains.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages over generated samples or orders. Neither supplies training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Many RADD results are replaced under revised model, training and evaluation conditions: RADD-DSE's LAMBADA entry changes from 96.62 to 51.83, and DCE/t-DCE's PTB entry from 116.74 to 109.03. Lambda-DCE, AO and 1000k-iteration results are added, while the SEDD-S 'exact likelihood' reevaluation disappears. RADD's 32-step generative perplexity changes from 135 to 158, with runtime values retained. The sampling-order winner changes from random to forward.

M1.justification: The time-independent RADD architecture and caching procedure remain. v2 explicitly fixes a missing time-independent LayerNorm bias (Section 4.3, footnote 2) and implements lambda-DCE and AO training variants alongside DSE and renamed t-DCE. The lambda and mask-count reformulations already appeared in v1; these are refinements of the existing framework.

P1.justification: The background is reorganized around continuous-time diffusion and AO-ARMs, Section 3.3 is extensively rewritten, and the introduction and experimental narrative are recast. The main-text NFE derivation is shortened, theorem proofs are regrouped, and the sampling appendix is reorganized into dedicated subsections. These are substantial structural and explanatory revisions.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is simplified from four curves to two with a revised legend and caption. The zero-shot table is regrouped, a separate training-budget table is added, and the runtime table moves to Appendix G.4. The license table disappears and sample figures are replaced. The overall visual format remains similar.

R1.justification: v2 adds the AO-ARM research lineage and substantial discussion of concurrent work by Shi et al. and Sahoo et al. Section 5 distinguishes overlapping losses, time-conditioning findings and caching from RADD's theoretical contributions, and credits Shi et al.'s hyperparameters. This substantially revises contribution positioning, beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Theorem 2 changes from an exact diffusion negative-log-likelihood identity to equivalence among diffusion and any-order autoregressive objectives. v2 reuses parts of the lambda/mask-count derivations but adds the DSE-to-t-DCE equivalence proof (Appendix C.1), Euler/Tweedie equivalence under a log-linear schedule (D.4), and mean-parameterization analysis (E). Theorem 1's score factorization remains.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is replacing v1's central exact-likelihood overclaim with the bound/expected-AO-likelihood distinction and explicitly acknowledging order inconsistency (Theorem 2; Section 3.3). The disclosed model repair, clearer experimental configurations and substantive concurrent-work discussion further improve reliability. Changed regularization limits attribution of performance gains, and some implementation/license detail is lost, but these tradeoffs do not outweigh the central conceptual correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RADD research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original results for revised RADD models, multiple training objectives and training budgets, together with generation experiments and appendix examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original RADD language-modeling perplexities, generation quality, inference timings, sampling-order comparisons and generated examples.

results.title: Your Absorbing Discrete Diffusion Secretly Models the Conditional Distributions of Clean Data

C1.justification: v3 removes the abstract's quantified 'up to 3.5 times faster' claim and emphasizes faster sampling convergence in the introduction. The core claims about score factorization, time-independent RADD, objective equivalence, and performance on five language-modeling benchmarks remain.

C2.justification: v3 explains that fp32 categorical-sampling errors can act as unintended annealing, making low perplexity misleading. The earlier conclusion that AO sampling performs worse is replaced by agreement with converged fp64 diffusion sampling under the revised evaluation. It also adds explanations involving finite-data gradient estimation and GPU utilization, and explicitly limits direct applicability to absorbing rather than multinomial diffusion.

D1.justification: v3 adds AO-ARM training/sampling pseudocode, dynamic-minibatching details, Gumbel-sampling precision, training-token totals, and timing-hardware information. A reproducibility statement points to setup instructions in the already-linked repository. Most existing implementation documentation remains, although the explicit seven-million-parameter reduction is no longer reported.

E1.justification: Both versions train on OpenWebText and evaluate LAMBADA, WikiText2, PTB, WikiText103, and One Billion Words. Unconditional generation and generation conditioned on prefix/suffix prompts remain covered. Added model sizes, precision settings, and batch sizes do not introduce different datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 compares RADD against both SEDD-Euler and SEDD-Tweedie; v3's corresponding runtime comparison retains SEDD-Tweedie but omits SEDD-Euler. Table 1's comparator membership is unchanged, with SEDD-U/S renamed SEDD-Unscale/Scale.

E3.justification: v3 adds medium-model evaluation and switches the principal generation comparison from small RADD-t-DCE to medium RADD-λ-DCE. Main timing measurements move from a 4090 with batch size 8 to an A800 with batch size 16. It introduces fp64/fp32 categorical-sampling comparisons, unigram entropy, and a separate batch-size experiment. Reported RADD-DSE weight decay changes from 0 to 0.03 and dropout from 0.1 to 0.02.

E4.justification: Appendix J.4 adds precision-sensitivity experiments measuring perplexity and entropy, plus a caching-efficiency ablation across batch sizes 1, 2, 4, and 8. Existing scaling/time-conditioning ablations extend to medium models, and the generation-order analysis is revised using medium-model results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Averaging over generated samples remains the reporting practice; the new experiment's sample count changes evaluation design rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces all five RADD-DSE scores, including LAMBADA 51.83 to 49.57, alongside changed regularization; other small-model rows remain unchanged. v3 adds medium-model scores, entropy and batch-timing results, and replaces generation/order results under revised conditions. For example, v3 reports RADD-medium perplexity 81 under fp64 versus 22 under fp32 at 4096 steps. v2 Table 2 is retained unchanged as v3 Table 7.

M1.justification: The time-independent RADD architecture, four objectives, and cached Euler/Tweedie sampling procedures are retained. The four corresponding algorithm bodies match across versions. Added AO-ARM pseudocode and dynamic-minibatching explanations document implementation rather than establish a changed underlying method.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative and much of the prose are retained. v3 makes localized rewrites, moves introductory notation into Appendix A, expands appendix explanations, reorders algorithm presentations, and adds contents and reproducibility statements. Citation style, affiliations, and conference-header wording also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds an architecture schematic and reorganizes the main plots, replacing the small-model perplexity-versus-NFE display with a medium-model perplexity-versus-time plot. It adds medium-model, precision/entropy, and batch-size tables, relocates the unchanged long-training table, and replaces generated-text figures. Table grouping, metric highlighting, captions, and conference layout are also revised.

R1.justification: Section 3.3 and new Appendix H explicitly acknowledge Hoogeboom et al.'s prior ARM–diffusion ELBO equivalence and position RADD's analysis as an alternative proof connecting four losses. New Appendix F compares Chen et al.'s sampler, while Section 5 clarifies differences from Sahoo et al. v3 also incorporates Zheng et al.'s categorical-sampling critique, substantially refining the work's positioning.

T1.justification: v3 corrects the missing minus sign in the AO-ARM objective, Eq. (2.11), making it consistent with negative log-likelihood minimization. The principal theorems, assumptions, and proofs in Appendices B–E remain substantively unchanged; the new AO-ARM exposition largely restates existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important evaluation blind spot: v2 assessed generation without precision or diversity controls, whereas v3 demonstrates the fp32 annealing artifact through fp64/fp32 and entropy comparisons and revises the AO-sampling interpretation. Medium-model experiments and clearer attribution of prior equivalence results further strengthen the paper. Changed RADD-DSE regularization weakens attribution of its better scores to architecture alone, but the improved generation controls provide a substantial net gain in scientific reliability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RADD research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original RADD experiments and adds medium-model results, numerical-precision comparisons, entropy measurements, and batch-size experiments in Section 4 and Appendices J–K.

before.justification: v2 reports original RADD language-modeling perplexities, sampling times, generation-order experiments, and generated examples in Section 4 and Appendices G–H.

results.title: Your Absorbing Discrete Diffusion Secretly Models the Conditional Distributions of Clean Data

C1.justification: The central steerability, locality and weight-sharing claims remain. However, the abstract and contributions expand claimed validation from reconstruction, classification and editing to fine-grained segmentation, forecasting and super-resolution/resolution transfer. The asserted applicability and downstream benefits therefore become substantially broader.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive qualifications about attention cost versus locality, insufficient shape reconstruction through meta-learning, and limited equivariance gains on aligned ShapeNet objects. Its class-only segmentation control supports a new interpretation involving positional shortcuts. It also discusses Functa overfitting on OMBRIA, initialization sensitivity and tentative parameter-efficiency benefits, extending v1's mainly general explanations of geometric representations.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's sparse experimental specifications, v4 Appendices A–C provide initialization guidance, autodecoding pseudocode, optimizer and learning-rate settings, RFF bandwidths, architecture sizes, training budgets, preprocessing and H100 hardware information. Section 6 and embedded links add implementation and data-access information, reporting partial experimental code availability while promising the remaining code.

E1.justification: CIFAR10 and CelebA remain, while STL10 disappears and ImageNet1K is added. The earlier 10-class ShapeNet study becomes 16-class occupancy/classification/part-segmentation and 55-class SDF evaluations. New domains include multimodal OMBRIA flood mapping and ERA5 temperature forecasting, with missing-observation and changed-resolution test scenarios.

E2.justification: v4 adds reported comparisons with PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN and NF2vec for shape segmentation, OmbriaNet for flood mapping, and an identity forecasting reference. Functa remains. The earlier ENF-abs-rel-pos/norm-rel-pos variant disappears from image comparisons, while translation and PONITA roto-translation variants remain under new names. The non-equivariant control changes from absolute coordinates x to concatenated pose and coordinate inputs.

E3.justification: Reported CIFAR10 latent configurations change from 16 points of dimension 32 to 25 of dimension 64; CelebA changes from 25 of dimension 128 to 36 of dimension 64. The downstream classifier changes from four layers using rotational invariants to three layers using attributes matched to the ENF. Added experiments introduce segmentation-specific evaluation, one-hour forecasting, observation subsampling and zero-shot resolution-transfer protocols.

E4.justification: v4 adds a roughly fixed-parameter latent-count/context-dimension ablation (Appendix D.1), a shape-segmentation control using only object class (D.2), and OMBRIA sparsity and resolution-transfer tests. Conversely, v1's shape stitching and appendix CelebA clustering, latent mixing and interpolation demonstrations are removed. Transformation and car–duck stitching demonstrations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional class/instance averages and random sampling descriptions in v4 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Image reconstruction values change: translation-equivariant CIFAR10 PSNR is 34.8 in v1 Table 1 and 42.2 in v4 Table 1 under revised model settings, while its classification accuracy remains 82.1%. Shape results are replaced by different class/modality settings. Substantial new results include segmentation, robustness, ablation and forecasting outcomes, such as OMBRIA full-observation IoU of 74.00 and ERA5 forecast MSE of 9.44e-06.

M1.justification: The bi-invariant cross-attention and FiLM backbone remains, but v4 introduces attention restricted to each coordinate's k nearest latents. It also specifies new downstream procedures: a second ENF for segmentation and a latent-update PONITA model for forecasting, including a reconstruction-error-aware forecasting objective (Section 4.2 and Appendix C.1). These substantially extend the implemented procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and background are extensively rewritten. Encoding background and meta-learning pseudocode move into an expanded appendix; the method is reorganized into architecture and latent acquisition, and experiments are reorganized around reconstruction and downstream tasks. A reproducibility section and structured technical appendices replace the earlier brief experimental appendix.

P2.justification: v4 substantially redesigns the introductory and method schematics, adds a locality illustration, combines image reconstruction/classification into one table, and introduces segmentation and forecasting displays. Several earlier editing figures disappear, while retained transformation and stitching examples receive revised panels or annotations. Table arrangements, captions, typography and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The principal lineage through Functa, cross-attention neural fields and PONITA remains. v4 adds Spatial Functa as context for global-latent limitations and neural ideograms/Kendall shape VAEs as inspiration, while dropping the earlier Field2Vec/metanetwork motivation. Additional neural-field and dataset references broaden the context without fundamentally changing the method's positioning.

T1.justification: The steerability/bi-invariance lemma and its proof are retained. The written Gaussian-window definition changes from a positive squared-distance term in v1 Section 3.4 to a negative squared-distance bias using positional pose components in v4 Section 3.1. This is a limited mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v4 resolves important evidential weaknesses: v1 Table 3 juxtaposes ENF SDF reconstruction with Functa voxel reconstruction, whereas v4 Table 2 compares both methods within each representation. New fine-grained tasks, robustness tests and the ShapeNet shortcut control substantially strengthen evaluation, while detailed appendices improve reproducibility. Some editing evidence is lost and reporting errors remain, including the CIFAR10 sentence using 68.7 where Table 1 gives Functa 68.3. Nevertheless, the stronger comparison design and technical documentation establish a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Equivariant Neural Fields work, with matching core definitions and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v4 reports original reconstruction, classification, segmentation and forecasting experiments, with additional robustness tests and appendix ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image reconstruction, CIFAR10 classification and ShapeNet experiments, plus qualitative latent editing and clustering results in the main text and Appendix A.

results.title: Grounding Continuous Representations in Geometry: Equivariant Neural Fields

C1.justification: The principal claims about the hypernetwork decomposition, HYLA, compositional generalization, and SRAVEN are retained. The revised abstract more explicitly claims that training-acquired latent codes are reused on unseen compositions, while the contribution list adds parametrically controlled SRAVEN difficulty and frames HYLA more explicitly as a test of the proposed mechanism.

C2.justification: v3 changes the explanation of HYLA's gains from primarily nonlinearity to the combination of nonlinearity and RMSHead. It adds interpretations involving shared codes for related rules, head-count dependence, and initialization scale explaining poor softmax-normalized HYLA performance. The language-modeling discussion now argues practical relevance from C4 results, while the earlier limitation discussing softmax-induced interactions between latent codes is removed.

D1.justification: The language-modeling reproduction recipe is substantially replaced: Appendix C documents NanoDo tokenization with a 32,000-token vocabulary instead of 6,144, rotary positional encodings, and revised architecture and optimization settings. Appendix D adds NanoDo and reports 16 Cloud TPU v5e devices, 72–100 hours per run, and approximately 163 TPU-days instead of the earlier GPU-based WikiText estimates. The code-access URL remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The language-modeling evaluation replaces WikiText-103 with C4. SRAVEN evaluation also expands from the standard four-feature setting to five and six features in Figure 5D, increasing the number of rules that must be resolved together. Fuzzy-logic testing on unknown terms was already reported in v1 and is not new coverage.

E2.justification: The principal softmax-attention and linear-attention comparators remain. Table A1 adds controls using linear attention with RMSHead and a nonlinear value network, HYLA with softmax normalization, and deeper HYLA; it also includes standard softmax results. The earlier HYLA linear rows are retained under names describing removal of the nonlinearity.

E3.justification: The replacement language experiment changes from a reported 2M-parameter model and context-length sweep to 50M-parameter models trained for 130B tokens. Appendix C changes its layer count, dimensions, batch size, positional encoding, vocabulary, and hyperparameter search settings. New analyses introduce logistic-regression decoding evaluated on unseen compositions and attention-head sweeps; these are added protocols rather than changes to the retained benchmark results.

E4.justification: v3 adds quantitative latent-code decoding on both reasoning tasks, SRAVEN head-count and feature-count sensitivity tests, and cosine-similarity analysis of rule codes. Appendix A expands architectural controls and supplies a quantitative plot for the previously described unknown-term failure. Conversely, the WikiText-103 context-length sensitivity study is removed.

E5.justification: Table A1 retains standard errors over three seeds, and Table A2 retains the same Monte Carlo uncertainty reporting. However, language-modeling presentation changes from error-barred WikiText-103 results in v1 Figure A2 to C4 training curves without reported uncertainty in v3 Figure 6. This establishes a reporting change, not a reduction in run counts.

E6.justification: Original Table A1 values are retained, including HYLA's reported fuzzy-logic R2 of 81.13 ± 7.77 and SRAVEN accuracy of 69.13 ± 1.90. New rows include deeper HYLA at 87.65 ± 4.54 and 66.59 ± 0.08, respectively. v3 also adds decoding and sensitivity results and replaces WikiText-103 perplexities with C4 learning curves; the latter do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: Standard HYLA's equations and Algorithm 2 remain unchanged. Appendix A.1 introduces HYLA+ with an additional hypernetwork-generated hidden layer and nonlinearity, formally defined in Equation 10. This is a limited architectural extension studied through ablation.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution list are substantially rewritten, the granularity subsection is incorporated into the discussion, and language modeling becomes a main-text section. SRAVEN and appendix subsections are reorganized, and the NeurIPS checklist is removed while reproducibility and acknowledgement statements are added. These changes substantially revise the narrative structure beyond introducing new results.

P2.justification: Figures 2 and 5 are substantially redesigned to integrate new analyses and selected latent visualizations, with existing all-layer plots retained in the appendix. The 16-layer visualization changes from a narrow vertical strip to readable grids. Table A1 merges duplicated method columns into a consolidated comparison, and the task-count figures are combined into a multipanel display.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Zoology, In-Context Learning and Induction Heads, RoFormer, and NanoDo, supporting the revised language-modeling discussion and implementation. It removes several linear-time-attention references and references associated with the discarded WikiText setup. The central positioning relative to fast-weight programmers, compositionality, and Raven benchmarks remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The central attention decomposition and standard HYLA derivation remain intact. v3 adds the mathematical definition of deeper HYLA in Equation 10, corrects the fuzzy-term count from 2^N to 2^L, and removes the assertion that HYLA preserves recurrent, linear-time inference. The earlier granularity discussion survives in prose in Section 7.

improvement.justification: v1 supports latent-code structure mainly through t-SNE visualizations; v3 adds decoding on unseen compositions and targeted architectural and sensitivity controls. These substantially strengthen the empirical basis of the central interpretation, while redesigned figures improve scrutiny. Tradeoffs remain: the WikiText context-length study disappears, C4 curves lack uncertainty reporting, and the claim that both HYLA components are required is too broad for Table A1's fuzzy-logic results. Nevertheless, the added diagnostic evidence provides a substantial overall improvement without establishing causal code reuse.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Attention as a Hypernetwork, with matching authors, core derivations, methods, and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original reasoning-task experiments and adds decoding, sensitivity, and architectural analyses, together with C4 language-modeling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original fuzzy-logic and SRAVEN experiments, latent-code analyses, model ablations, and WikiText-103 language-modeling results.

results.title: Attention as a Hypernetwork

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes being the first generalizable feed-forward human Gaussian framework and achieving superior novel-view synthesis. v2 removes that explicit priority claim, elevates structural SMPL-X tokens and iterative body-parameter correction to central contributions, and broadens its abstract and conclusion to claim state-of-the-art surface reconstruction as well as rendering.

C2.justification: v1 attributes tolerance of SMPL errors to implicit feature-volume guidance; v2 emphasizes iterative correction and semantically anchored vertex tokens. Its new discussion explains the advantage of side-view supervision over previous front-view alignment. Limitations change substantively: v1 identifies noisy, unregularized meshes and non-end-to-end extraction, whereas v2's appendix identifies poor hands and faces and proposes regional diffusion refinement.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents 500 training scans, 12 rendering cameras, ground-truth SMPL-X inputs during training, a negative diffusion prompt, side-mask updates every 10 fitting iterations, 200 mesh-optimization iterations and reconstruction/extraction timings. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings. The estimator changes from SMPLER to PIXIE, and the repository link becomes a project-page link. v1's explicit sampling strength, sampling-step count and U-Net initialization disclosure disappear.

E1.justification: Alongside retained THuman2.0, HuMMan and in-the-wild coverage, v2 adds quantitative cross-dataset evaluation on CustomHumans, including loose clothing and challenging poses. Appendix Figure 11 additionally presents THuman2.1 mesh examples, and Figures 12–14 expand targeted clothing and extreme-pose coverage. Cross-dataset evaluation itself already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: The THuman2.0 NVS comparison changes from PIFu, Impersonator++, TEXture, Magic123, S3F, HumanSGD and SIFU in v1 Table 3 to SiTH, LGM, SV3D and SIFU in v2 Table 1. The mesh comparison retains ECON/SIFU, adds SiTH and removes PIFu, PaMIR, ICON, D-IF and GTA. PIFu remains in v2's qualitative appendix comparisons. HuMMan's NVS comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v1 reports both ground-truth-SMPL and estimated-SMPL NVS variants; v2 removes the ground-truth variant and specifies testing all methods without ground-truth SMPL-X. Mesh evaluation replaces L2 normal-map error with Normal Consistency. v2 also introduces a 45-scan CustomHumans evaluation protocol and specifies fine-tuning its new LGM comparator on the same training data.

E4.justification: v2 Table 4 adds an ablation removing SMPL-X refinement and extends component ablations from rendering metrics to Chamfer, P2S and Normal Consistency. Figure 10 examines initial versus refined body geometry and side-view masks; Figures 12–14 add targeted clothing and pose comparisons. The visual guidance ablation from v1 Figure 7 is retained as v2 Figure 8, rather than constituting new evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. Quantitative results remain point estimates.

E6.justification: The THuman2.0 reconstruction and ablation results are substantially revised, and CustomHumans results are added, including HGM's 23.84 PSNR, 0.944 SSIM and 0.0514 LPIPS in v2 Table 1. HuMMan HGM PSNR remains 23.86, while LPIPS changes from 0.062 to 0.0591. v1's rendering-speed table is removed; v2 reports different speeds in Section 4.4. Method and protocol changes limit direct performance comparisons across versions.

M1.justification: v1's branch predicting Gaussians from projected SMPL features is replaced by SMPL-X vertex tokens, cross-attention and residual updates to image Gaussians. v2 introduces iterative SMPL-X parameter refinement through mask/normal matching and mesh optimization using normal and Laplacian losses. Back-view refinement also changes from the stated ControlNet-tile setup to explicitly trained ControlNet refinement with a frozen diffusion backbone.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, method explanation and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Section 3.3 gains separate model and refinement subsections, the reconstruction loss moves into Section 3.5, and a discussion section is added. Limitations move to the appendix, the broader-impact paragraph disappears, and authorship information changes.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the architecture diagram, adds refinement diagrams and comparative mesh visualizations, and restructures tables to display multiple datasets and both rendering and geometry ablations. The speed table disappears, and substantial appendix comparison panels are added. Retained v1 Figures 3, 4 and 7 become v2 Figures 4, 9 and 8 respectively, with relocation or display changes.

R1.justification: The three related-work strands remain, with focused new positioning around SMPL-X estimation failures and correction relative to ECON/SIFU. References add PIXIE, CustomHumans, SV3D, DreamAvatar and DreamGaussian, while removing works associated with discarded components or comparisons, including SMPLER, Magic123, TEXture and D-IF. Publication updates to retained works do not constitute new citations.

T1.justification: v2 adds explicit mathematical definitions of the SMPL-X mask/normal optimization objective and ControlNet denoising objective in Equations 3–4. The HGM reconstruction loss remains equivalent. These are limited additions to the formal optimization formulation; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for its central robustness claims through a direct refinement ablation covering rendering and geometry, quantitative CustomHumans generalization tests, and targeted clothing/pose comparisons. It also addresses v1's acknowledged lack of surface regularization and supplies important implementation details. These gains outweigh narrower baseline coverage and remaining reporting weaknesses: the broad mesh-superiority claim overlooks SIFU's better THuman2.0 Chamfer score in Table 3, and the main-versus-ablation LPIPS decimal inconsistency persists.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HGM research project. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original rendering, reconstruction and ablation results, including CustomHumans evaluations and additional appendix comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original novel-view synthesis, mesh reconstruction and component-ablation results on THuman2.0 and HuMMan, with additional qualitative examples.

results.title: Generalizable Human Gaussians from Single-View Image

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction explicitly extend the superiority claim to fine-tuned VLMs and add a strong cross-dataset generalization claim. The central contributions remain the CTN benchmark and CEN architecture; human evaluation supplies additional support for the retained caption-quality claim.

C2.justification: v2 newly describes the unchanged transfer results as strong generalization, while retaining v1's warning about substantial zero-shot performance drops. It also interprets human ratings as benchmark validation and BLIP results as architectural flexibility. The limitations section is unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds VLM implementation details: A100-80GB hardware, LoRA applied to the LLM at learning rate 2e-4, and full-model AdamW fine-tuning with initial rate 1e-3, cosine scheduling, and 0.03 warmup ratio. Original CEN implementation details and the benchmark-release information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Training and evaluation retain MSVD and MSR-VTT captioning coverage. Cross-dataset tests and the unlabeled-video demonstration already appear in v1. The human study samples existing CTN captions; the new NExT-QA examples illustrate benchmark differences without evaluating the method on that dataset.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds VideoLLaVA and ShareGPT4Video, each evaluated zero-shot, with LoRA fine-tuning, and with full-model fine-tuning. These substantially broaden the comparison beyond the retained SEM-POS, AKGNN, and GIT baselines. Figure 5 also adds outputs from both VLMs.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a human evaluation protocol with five experts rating 100 randomly sampled validation captions, 50 per dataset, on three criteria. It also adds VLM fine-tuning protocols and an alternative-encoder configuration. Existing CEN splits, training budgets, sampling rules, and automatic metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 adds systematic human assessment of causal accuracy, temporal coherence, and relevance. Appendix A.6 newly tests dependence on the visual encoder through CLIP-versus-BLIP results. Existing architecture, transfer, prompting, and automatic-filtering analyses are retained; Figure 5 expands comparative failure examples.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, v2 reports rating standard deviations and absolute-agreement intraclass correlation with a 95% confidence interval for the human study. This introduces substantive variability and reliability reporting. Neither version supplies repeated-run or seed-based uncertainty for the captioning-model scores.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 and Table 2 scores are retained, while VLM, BLIP, and human-rating results are added. On MSR-VTT, full-fine-tuned VideoLLaVA and ShareGPT4Video score 19.98 and 20.76 CIDEr versus CEN's unchanged 49.87. BLIP-CEN scores 43.01. New MSVD SPICE results make VideoLLaVA Simple FT, at 16.09, the runner-up ahead of GIT's 15.58.

M1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds an evaluated CEN variant replacing CLIP encoders with BLIP encoders, a limited component substitution. The principal CTN-generation pipeline, two-stage CEN architecture, and losses remain unchanged. Statements that both encoders process the whole video clarify the existing procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted passages in the abstract, introduction, related work, and results are expanded or rewritten. Results gain numbered subsections, and appendices A–F become subsections within Appendix A with new material inserted. Most method descriptions, prompt analyses, and limitations retain their wording.

P2.justification: Table 1 and Figure 5 expand to include VLM comparisons. New Tables 3–5 display human ratings, encoder results, and benchmark distinctions; a new Figure 18 illustrates NExT-QA. Existing later figures are retained and renumbered. Typography, running headers, and placement change, while the principal diagrams and plots remain intact.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to VideoLLaVA, ShareGPT4Video, BLIP, and AdamW. It expands positioning against recent VLMs and elaborates the distinction from the already-cited NExT-QA through Appendix A.7. The overall research positioning remains centered on holistic causal-temporal captioning.

T1.justification: The similarity definition, feature construction, contrastive objectives, decoding formulation, and losses in Equations 1–9 are unchanged. Neither version presents additional theorems or proofs; the new human-rating statistics do not introduce a mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 supports CTN caption quality mainly through automatic relevance filtering and selected examples. v2 adds direct expert assessment with reliability statistics, substantially broader VLM comparisons, and an encoder control, strengthening evidence for both central contributions. The human study's inconsistent 5-point versus 0–5 scale description and stronger interpretation of unchanged transfer results remain concerns, but the added validation and comparisons provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NarrativeBridge, the CTN caption benchmark, and CEN. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across formatting and numbering changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds vision-language model comparisons, a human evaluation study, and a CLIP-versus-BLIP encoder experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original captioning comparisons, architecture ablations, cross-dataset evaluations, and qualitative experiments on MSVD and MSR-VTT, including appendix analyses.

results.title: NarrativeBridge: Enhancing Video Captioning with Causal-Temporal Narrative

C1.justification: The headline theoretical scope narrows: v1 Table 1 and Corollary 4.2 advertise guaranteed ReluMPNN/AdaptMPNN exponents, whereas v2 removes those guarantees and leaves relevant lower-stability questions open. SortMPNN's guarantee remains central. The revised introduction also adds robustness to reduced model size to its stated empirical contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains why componentwise expected separation need not transfer to a network: one shared ReLU bias can fail to separate all required multiset pairs simultaneously. It treats wider-ReLU stability as conjectural and AdaptMPNN's epsilon-tree behavior as empirical. It also connects SortMPNN's small-model advantage to width-one stability, materially revising applicability and mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-access link, multiset experiment specifications in Appendix G.3, SortMPNN parameter-normalization details, 1K-model widths and parameter counts, and runtime information. These extend an already detailed experimental appendix; newly documented normalization does not by itself establish an implementation change.

E1.justification: Both evaluate moment-matched multisets, epsilon-trees, synthetic tuple embeddings, the same five TU datasets, peptides-func, peptides-struct, and ZINC12K. The added width experiment uses the existing multiset construction; smaller network budgets extend configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain their comparator sets: GIN/GCN/GAT for epsilon-trees, GIN/GCN/GraphSage for TU, GINE/GCN/GatedGCN for LRGB, and GIN within ESAN. The new timing comparison uses existing LRGB comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds a width sweep on one eight-element multiset pair, a 1K parameter budget, and timing averaged over 250 epochs. The reported SortMPNN collapse setting for peptides-struct changes from matrix to vector collapse. These are limited protocol/configuration changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Figure 1 examines how width affects ReLU versus smooth multiset separation. The existing small-model analysis extends to 1K parameters, and Appendix H adds computational-cost analysis. The epsilon-tree distortion plots also revise their ReLU reference exponents. These supplement the retained analyses without substantially expanding their scope.

E5.justification: Both specify stratified 10-fold TU reporting, LRGB reruns with four seeds after tuning, and ten ESAN test seeds, with means and standard deviations. Revised standard-deviation values change results, but the reporting practices and stated run counts remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 3–5 substantially revise the proposed models' results and rankings. AdaptMPNN becomes best on PTC and NCI109; SortMPNN's peptides-struct MAE changes from 0.2494 to 0.2464; its ESAN comparison changes from six wins and one tie against GIN to five wins. Changed LRGB/ESAN settings preclude interpreting all revisions as same-setting gains. Width, 1K-budget, and runtime results are added; Table 2's classification accuracies remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core multiset operators and four MPNN architectures remain. However, the ESAN adaptation changes: v1 Appendix I.6 combines node and edge features by addition, with optional subsequent processing; v2 Appendix G.7 instead specifies concatenation, linear projection, and ReLU. This changes a localized part of the procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around pairwise expected stability and width. Section 4.2 is reorganized around upper stability, failure of general lower-stability transfer, and SortMPNN. Earlier graph-proof appendices are consolidated into Appendix F, norm-equivalence lemmas move to Appendix C, and terminology changes throughout from continuity to stability.

P2.justification: v2 adds the width plot, counterexample diagram, and runtime table; restructures Table 1; extends the budget plot/table; and revises plot labels and reference curves. The document adopts a different template with widespread figure/table reflow, relocated captions, and second-place underlining. The original five figures remain identifiable across renumbering.

R1.justification: The introduction adds connections and citations concerning frames, phase retrieval, group-invariant max filtering, and high-dimensional set representations, including Wang et al. (2024). The central positioning relative to previous sorting methods and MPNN stability research remains. The additional publication entry for 'Towards a bilipschitz invariant theory' represents an already cited work.

T1.justification: v1's general theorem transferring lower-Hölder guarantees from components to MPNNs is withdrawn, along with the dependent ReluMPNN/AdaptMPNN exponent upper bounds. v2 supplies a width-one ReLU counterexample in Appendix F.2, an explicit upper-Lipschitz proof, and an independent proof of the retained SortMPNN lower-Lipschitz claim in Appendix F.1. This replaces a central mathematical argument.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is correcting v1's central erroneous MPNN lower-Hölder guarantee, explicitly acknowledged in v2 Section 4.2. The counterexample and independent SortMPNN proof replace an invalid general argument with a more defensible contribution and clearer limits. Added width analysis, timing, and code-access information provide further support. Although the proven scope narrows and benchmark revisions are mixed, the correction substantially improves the paper's scientific reliability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material reorganized between versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original synthetic and benchmark experiments, revises their results, and adds a multiset width experiment and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original multiset and epsilon-tree experiments, synthetic distortion analyses, and SortMPNN/AdaptMPNN results on TU datasets, LRGB, and ZINC12K.

results.title: On the Hölder Stability of Multiset and Graph Neural Networks

C1.justification: The central claim of an efficient hybrid with strong language modeling and length extrapolation remains. v2 adds a headline claim of superior Phonebook retrieval extrapolation, explicitly claims first-at-scale hybrid superiority, and clarifies the distinction between zero-shot perplexity extrapolation and fine-tuned recall. The introduction qualifies infinite extrapolation as potential.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability boundaries through failed passkey-to-Phonebook transfer and an explicit perplexity-versus-retrieval extrapolation trade-off. It adds explanations involving Mamba's contribution and hybrid I/O/cache costs, and explicitly restricts fair architecture comparisons to matched-data models in Tables 7–8. The original base-model retrieval and task-dependent performance limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies RoPE's 10,000 base frequency and documents the existing summarization evaluation's ZeroSCROLLS source, tokenizer, document-length statistics, greedy decoding, and generation limits in Appendix F. It describes implementation choices for added comparators and changes the code-availability statement from a sample implementation to open-data training code. Existing hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds multi-key retrieval and cross-task transfer scenarios through Phonebook, discourse word prediction through LAMBADA, and harder knowledge/reasoning evaluations through MMLU-Pro and GPQA. Earlier training corpora and evaluation tasks remain represented.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Mega-S6, Mamba-SWA-MLP, MLP2-SWA-MLP, and SAMBA-NoPE to the existing SlimPajama comparison. The new chat evaluation in Table 8 includes Phi3 (June), R-Gemma 9B, FalconMamba, Jamba-1.5-Mini, and Llama-3.1/3.2 instruction models, substantially expanding evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 100-step Phonebook fine-tuning at 4K length, testing over 20–480 name-number pairs, and evaluation of transfer from passkey tuning. It also adds the June post-training configuration and benchmark-specific chat evaluation protocols. Sliding RetNet's reported small-model size changes from 438M to 446M; this alone does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: New ablations test replacing Mamba with MLPs, removing RoPE, and alternative hybridization arrangements at two scales. Phonebook additionally tests memory load and transfer of passkey-trained retrieval skills. Earlier context-length, full-attention, attention-head, and short-convolution analyses are retained, including material moved to Appendix D.

E5.justification: Both versions report throughput averaged over 10 measurements and approximately ±0.3% perplexity fluctuation. Neither introduces new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance testing, or repeated-run uncertainty procedures; additional result rows use the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3, 4, and 8 and the Phonebook curves in Figure 4. For example, the new 1.3B SAMBA-NoPE result has 326.17 perplexity at 16,384 tokens versus SAMBA's retained 6.96, and the June chat evaluation reports averages of 66.1 for SAMBA and 64.4 for Phi3. Original base-model, preview-model, and other retained scores are unchanged; June results concern a separate post-training configuration.

M1.justification: SAMBA retains the same Mamba–MLP–SWA–MLP arrangement, Mamba computations, 2,048-token attention window, and SwiGLU components. Additional comparator variants and post-training configurations do not revise the proposed architecture or inference procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: instruction-tuned results lead Section 3.1, base-model results move to Appendix B, retrieval experiments are consolidated in Section 3.4, and selected analyses move to Appendix D. The abstract and introduction are revised, and the appendices are reorganized into dedicated evaluation, analysis, implementation, and related-work sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds two evaluation tables and the Phonebook figure, expands Table 3, and substantially rearranges existing displays. The introductory performance figure moves into Section 3.3, prompt throughput moves to the appendix, and several tables change main-text/appendix placement. The document also adopts a different title, heading, and page-header layout.

R1.justification: A new related-work appendix substantially expands positioning across hybrid recurrent models, sparse attention, and length extrapolation. It identifies Griffin as the closest architecture and distinguishes SAMBA from Griffin, Infini-Attention, Megalodon, and other approaches. These substantive comparisons go beyond the accompanying citation-style and bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The mathematical description of Mamba and the attention/selection entropy definitions are unchanged. The entropy material moves from Appendix C to Appendix E; no substantive theorem, proof, assumption, or derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in architectural attribution and retrieval generalization: Table 3 directly tests Mamba removal and positional encoding, while Figure 4 tests multi-item retrieval and exposes poor cross-task transfer.
