These controls, clearer comparison qualifications, substantive positioning against Griffin, and newly documented summarization procedures substantially strengthen the central empirical argument. Phonebook comparisons still mix model sizes and tuning conditions, and uncertainty reporting remains limited, but the added evidence materially clarifies both the architecture's benefits and its boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SAMBA and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds architecture ablations, Phonebook experiments, and downstream evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original model training, downstream evaluations, perplexity and throughput measurements, retrieval experiments, and architecture analyses.

results.title: Samba: Simple Hybrid State Space Models for Efficient Unlimited Context Language Modeling

C1.justification: Both versions claim the first comprehensive mixed-source benchmark, covering three misinformation sources and 12 forgery types, evaluate six detectors and 15 LVLMs, and propose MMD-Agent to improve detection. Naming MMD-Agent in the abstract and emphasizing fine-grained evaluation do not materially change these contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations of external-knowledge dependence, artificial versus natural rumor difficulty, inference-cost tradeoffs, and catastrophic forgetting after fine-tuning. New case analyses discuss overlooked physical anomalies and distraction by globally consistent semantics. The existing limitation concerning inadequate Wikipedia retrieval is relocated, rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies eight 3090 GPUs, the GPT-4 model identifier, deterministic decoding, a 512-token generation limit, and ten volunteers selecting manipulated images. It also documents dataset licenses and states that detection code is released, generation code withheld, and data access restricted to verified researchers under an agreement. These expand v2's configuration and access documentation; they do not establish changed inference settings or withdrawal of previously available code.

E1.justification: V3 adds standalone evaluations on NewsCLIPpings and Fakeddit and evaluates retention on DGM4 after adaptation to MMFakeBench (Tables 7 and 9). These datasets previously served as construction sources or detector background, rather than separately evaluated populations. MMFakeBench's own 11,000-pair coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: Human evaluation becomes an additional comparator in Tables 2 and 6. The original six-detector and 15-LVLM comparisons are retained. FKA-Owl matches the earlier FakeNewsGPT4 work through its authors, title, and citation context; it is not an additional detector.

E3.justification: V3 introduces an 80-participant study with 50 randomly selected questions per questionnaire from the 1,000-item validation bank, fine-tuning budgets of 10/100/1,000 examples, and efficiency and diversity evaluations. Section 3.1.1 also changes the reported supporting-image selection rule from exceeding a CLIP threshold to choosing the highest-scoring images, without establishing dataset regeneration. Original splits and classification metrics remain.

E4.justification: V3 adds removal/substitution of external knowledge, adaptation and forgetting analyses, efficiency measurements, relevancy maps, and dataset-diversity diagnostics. Four-model failure cases replace v2's two-model example comparisons. The original hierarchical ablations and misinformation-type analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V3's deterministic decoding disclosure and descriptive entropy measurements do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Previously reported model scores in Tables 2–6 are retained. Added results include human F1 scores of 35.9 for multiclass and 54.9 for binary classification. LLaVA-1.6-34B achieves 43.8 without Wikipedia and 48.5 with Google knowledge, versus the retained 49.9 with Wikipedia; inference takes 49.04 seconds with MMD-Agent versus 5.97 with standard prompting. Tables 7, 9, and 10 add cross-dataset, fine-tuning, and dataset-statistics results.

M1.justification: MMD-Agent retains its three-stage checks, intermediate reasoning/actions, and Wikipedia retrieval. V3's separate Thought/Observation terminology describes components already illustrated in v2; it does not establish a new model, objective, or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. Targeted revisions rewrite source definitions and the framework explanation, standardize reasoning terminology, subdivide the appendix, and move ethics/limitations into the main text. Conference headers, author ordering, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: The overview and framework diagrams are redesigned, and v2 Figure 2 is split and redrawn as v3 Figures 2–3. V2 Figures 6–7 are combined into v3 Figure 7. Expanded comparison tables, new Tables 7–10, replacement error-analysis displays, relevancy maps, diversity plots, and dataset-example galleries substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations concerning image generation/editing, co-attention detection, and LVLM interpretability, including Cui et al., Wu et al., and Stan et al. Related-work discussion is modestly revised while the mixed-source novelty positioning remains. FakeNewsGPT4's update to the published FKA-Owl reference is matched as the same work.

T1.justification: Equation (1) separates retrieved observations from reasoning traces, re-expressing knowledge retrieval already present in v2. No substantive mathematical assumptions, proofs, or theoretical guarantees are added. The new entropy calculations are descriptive benchmark measurements.

improvement.justification: V2 lacked direct measurements of human difficulty, retrieval's contribution, and computational overhead. V3 supplies these alongside cross-dataset and adaptation evidence, substantially strengthening benchmark validation and exposing MMD-Agent's accuracy–latency tradeoff. Configuration and access documentation also improve assessability. Fine-tuning protocols remain underspecified and uncertainty reporting is absent, but the added evidence materially improves the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MMFakeBench and MMD-Agent. The complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures, and equations, support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds human evaluation, knowledge-source ablations, cross-dataset comparisons, fine-tuning experiments, efficiency measurements, and benchmark analyses.

before.justification: V2 reports original evaluations of detection methods and LVLMs, MMD-Agent ablations, source-specific performance, and error analyses.

results.title: MMFakeBench: A Mixed-Source Multimodal Misinformation Detection Benchmark for LVLMs

C1.justification: The central claim of a first architecture guaranteeing jointly sparse and SPD outputs remains. v2 drops the abstract/conclusion's explicit comparative claim of a larger function class or higher expressivity than existing approaches, focusing the contribution on structural guarantees and demonstrated effectiveness instead.

C2.justification: v2 substantially extends the applicability discussion: it interprets the sample-size results as evidence of suitability for sample-deficient recovery and Animals as evidence of synthetic-to-real generalization. It qualifies EGFM's modularity advantage through its clustering-specific inductive bias. v1's explanation that UBG's stronger inductive bias permits fewer training examples is removed; the existing spectral-instability explanation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly specifies g's hidden layers, batch size, threshold scaling for PNP/E2E, and GLAD's implementation source/defaults, alongside revised architecture and training details. v2 also states that PyTorch implementations accompany the submission and will become public. Much existing information is relocated, while v1's RTX 2080 SUPER and EPYC 7302 hardware disclosure is omitted.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic Gaussian precision-matrix recovery only. v2 adds synthetic-to-real transfer for graph inference on Animals, comprising 33 species and 102 binary attributes (Section 5.2). This introduces a substantive new data domain and evaluation scenario.

E2.justification: v1 principally benchmarks recovery against Oracle GLasso and examines GLAD's structural failures separately. v2 adds inverse Ledoit-Wolf and OAS estimators, includes both GLAD outputs in reconstruction/support comparisons, and evaluates EGFM alongside GLasso on Animals (Figures 4–6). DeepGraph remains discussed rather than experimentally compared.

E3.justification: GLasso tuning changes from ground-truth oracle selection to sample-based cross-validation. v2 uses 1,000 training pairs for every learned model, versus 100 for v1's UBG, and expands the p=n=50 evaluation to several dimensions and sample-size sweeps. Initialization changes from (S+0.1I)^−1 to (S+I)^−1, and learning rates are revised. Animals introduces graph construction, Louvain partitioning and modularity evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds sample-size sensitivity (Figure 5), training-time conditioning and sparsity diagnostics (Figure 3), and GLAD positive-definiteness frequencies (Appendix B.3). v1's post-hoc GLAD threshold sweep and illustrative precision-matrix comparisons disappear. The original instability example without normalization is retained as v2 Figure 7, rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions display shaded bands without explaining their statistical meaning. Neither reports training seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence levels or significance tests. The additional curves do not establish a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v1 Figure 4 reports minimum PNP test NMSE of 0.316 against Oracle GLasso's 0.405. v2 replaces this fixed-setting comparison with broader reconstruction and sample-size results, plus GLAD SPD frequencies. New Animals modularities are 0.78 for UBG, 0.61 for GLasso and 0.86 for EGFM (Figure 6). Changed protocols prevent interpreting the revised scores as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The Schur-complement framework and three model families remain. However, v2 normalizes the final-layer preactivation instead of the network output, adds a quadratic-form input to g, and replaces its exponential output activation with absolute value. The stepsize network also changes from whole-matrix input to column input, with revised widths. These are actual procedural refinements, not merely expanded descriptions.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related work and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten. The Graphical Lasso and competing-method discussions are consolidated, experiments are organized into synthetic and real-data subsections, and appendices are reorganized into experimental details and model analyses. A reproducibility statement is added.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation is substantially rebuilt with multi-panel benchmarks, sample-size plots, Animals graph visualizations and new diagnostic figures. v1's threshold plots and matrix heatmaps are removed. Figure 1 is relocated, the instability figure moves to the appendix, and conference formatting changes headers, author layout and typography.

R1.justification: The same three research strands remain, but v2 sharpens positioning around simultaneous structural constraints and adds references including Shlezinger et al., Adler and Öktem, Arridge et al., and EGFM. Several optimal-transport, nonsmooth-Riemannian and application references are removed. GLAD's citation-year correction refers to the same work and is not a new comparator.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Appendix A.2's Proposition A.1 and proof characterizing the regularization threshold yielding a diagonal GLasso solution. The core SPD-preservation and efficient inverse-update propositions, their proofs, and the spectral-perturbation argument remain. Recasting the update using u and v is principally an equivalent mathematical presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the narrow empirical validation in v1: matched training sizes, broader recovery baselines, sample-size sensitivity and Animals transfer let readers assess practical advantages and applicability beyond one synthetic setting. Additional implementation details support reproduction. Important caveats remain: uncertainty bands are undefined, and replacing exponential g with absolute value introduces an unresolved zero case in the strict-positivity guarantee. Nevertheless, the retained core theorem and substantially more informative evaluation support a major overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SpodNet and its UBG, PNP and E2E variants. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: Sections 5.1–5.2 report original synthetic experiments and graph learning on Animals. Appendix B.3 adds empirical measurements of GLAD outputs' positive-definiteness.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic precision-matrix recovery experiments, including reconstruction, support recovery and sparsity/positive-definiteness analyses in Figures 4–6.

results.title: Schur's Positive-Definite Network: Deep Learning in the SPD cone with structure

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims: exact, efficient injective flows for star-like manifolds and applications to objective Bayesian inference and mixing models. The conclusion adds empirical support for efficiency and exact-Jacobian importance, both already claimed in v2.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies the consequences of coordinate singularities for exact density evaluation and numerical stability, and explicitly motivates its focus on variational inference through the codimension-one restriction. Existing dimensionality and expressivity limitations remain. Learning the radial function from observations is still discussed in Appendix A.5.

D1.justification: v3 documents small angular offsets near singularities and expands the circular-spline implementation description, including rational-quadratic segments and periodic boundaries. It identifies the approximation implementation and specifies Sinkhorn blur=0.05. Existing architecture sizes, Adam settings, GPU information and FlowConductor access information are retained.

E1.justification: Synthetic coverage expands to uniform-density learning on an lp manifold with p=0.5, and the spherical checkerboard example is replaced by a sinusoidal density on a deformed sphere. The regression, conjugate mixing-model and 10-stock, 200-step portfolio coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 adds direct computational comparators absent from v2: explicit determinant computation using Eq. (2), and otherwise identical flows trained with Hutchinson-estimated Jacobian gradients. The latter use the implementation attributed to Sorrenson et al. (2024), with several estimator sample counts. These substantially extend comparison beyond the retained prior-choice and MCMC experiments.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 introduces controlled comparisons across dimensions 3, 10, 50 and 100 and Gaussian estimator sample counts 1, 10, 50 and 100, subject to the stated dimensionality bound. Both training variants use exact Jacobians at evaluation; metrics include log-density MSE, energy-distance MMD, Sinkhorn divergence and runtime. The third 3D target also changes from 2 sin(6θ) sin(6ϕ) to sin(4θ) sin(4ϕ). Existing regression and MCMC settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figures 3 and 10 directly test the importance of exact Jacobian training by holding the flow architecture fixed and varying the approximation sample count and dimension. They assess density accuracy, sample quality and computational cost. v3 also adds an empirical scaling analysis of determinant computation; v2's prior-sensitivity and MCMC analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 reports 20 repetitions for the new determinant-timing experiment and displays variability in the added comparisons. This does not establish increased repetition of earlier experiments. Existing 95% posterior intervals remain unchanged; training-run counts and the definitions of the new error bars are not fully specified.

E6.justification: New results report fitted runtime scaling of approximately d^2.96 for explicit computation versus d^1.81 for the proposed approach, and better density and sample-quality scores with exact Jacobian training. The first two 3D examples retain MSEs 0.013 and 0.011. The old checkerboard MSE of 0.024 disappears when that experiment is replaced by a qualitatively evaluated deformed-sphere example. Bayesian and portfolio results are retained.

M1.justification: The angle flow, radial embedding, spherical-to-Cartesian transformation, exact determinant formula and reverse-KL training objective remain unchanged. Expanded spline explanations and newly documented numerical safeguards do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Section 3.3 becomes Further Details and Limitations with separate explanatory paragraphs, and a new Section 5.1 precedes the existing applications. Appendix mixing-model material moves from A.6.4 to A.7.1. There are localized prose edits and updated publication headers, while most narrative and section ordering remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the runtime/accuracy panels in Figure 3 and sample-quality/runtime panels in Figure 10, and redraws the third illustrative-density example. Figure 1 is smaller, and retained figures are renumbered or relocated, including the final appendix plots. The overall visual format and most existing displays remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Kothari et al. (2021) and Munkres and Spivak (1965), and removes Cayton (2005) and Krantz and Parks (2008). The related-work discussion and positioning against approximate injective flows remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Sections 2 and 3.2 add the relaxed change-of-variables condition of a diffeomorphism almost everywhere and explain why measure-zero coordinate singularities preserve the density calculation. Theorem 1, its quadratic-complexity argument, and the definitions, lemmas and proofs in Appendices A.1–A.4 otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 closes a central empirical gap: v2 argued for efficient, exact Jacobians without directly testing their computational advantage and training benefit against approximation. Section 5.1 and Figure 10 add controlled evidence on scaling, density accuracy and sample quality while retaining the original applications and proofs. The replacement 3D example loses quantitative scoring, and replication details remain incomplete, but these limitations are outweighed by substantially stronger evidence for the paper's central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Injective Flows for Star-like Manifolds. Their main text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical applications and adds original runtime and exact-versus-approximate Jacobian experiments in Section 5.1 and Appendix Figure 10.

before.justification: v2 reports original density-reconstruction experiments, synthetic Bayesian regression, comparisons with MCMC, and portfolio results in Section 5 and Appendix A.6.

results.title: Injective flows for star-like manifolds

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about scalable synthetic construction, skill-specific evaluation, VNBench's three task families, and insights for video-model development. The new experiments support these claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: Appendix J materially qualifies low-score comparisons: option-order sensitivity can affect circular accuracy, and Counting-E2 differences should not be interpreted as meaningful capability advantages. New discussion interprets real-benchmark correlations, construction robustness, and action-ordering failures. The existing Section 7 limitation about synthetic data complementing real-world benchmarks remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix G newly documents the visual-token and answer-loss computations and training for one epoch on 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Added analyses disclose sampling and replacement-needle details. Conversely, v3 removes the abstract's code/data availability statement and project link without replacing them elsewhere; the PDFs do not establish that the resources themselves became unavailable.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench in Appendix B.2. VNBench-Act adds retrieval, ordering, and counting of action-bearing clips from Something-Something V2, extending evaluation beyond static-image and subtitle needles. Something-Something V2 already appeared in the training mixture; its new evaluation role is the coverage change.

E2.justification: The evaluated model families and size variants remain present in the corresponding VNBench comparisons. Added experiments use models already evaluated in v2. Appendix J adds a 25% chance reference but does not document an additional evaluated comparison method.

E3.justification: Figure 8 changes from binary extraction outcomes to accuracy averaged over 32 distinct samples. New protocols compare 1350 versus 2700 samples, replace needle content at matched positions, and evaluate six frame-count configurations across real-world benchmarks. Appendix J introduces consistency and conditional-accuracy metrics. The main four-pass circular evaluation remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses testing agreement with real-world benchmarks, sensitivity to needle content and dataset size, and answer-option consistency across nine subtasks. It also revises the position-depth analysis using multiple samples. Existing model-configuration ablations and the one-to-four-pass circular-evaluation analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report correlation coefficients and one-to-four option-shuffled evaluations. v3 adds no seed information, independent-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Averaging 32 distinct test samples changes evaluation design; the new consistency scores are evaluation metrics rather than uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial cross-benchmark, action, robustness, and consistency results. For example, Table 6 reports GPT-4o action retrieval, ordering, and counting scores of 85.6, 11.3, and 10.0. Main Table 2 remains unchanged, but the detailed 30–60-second LLaVA-OneVision-7B overall score changes from 69.8 to 60.0, ending its reported tie with 72B. Several counting cells are also corrected between v2 Table 6 and v3 Table 11.

M1.justification: The synthetic construction procedure, CLIP filtering, and core circular scoring rule remain unchanged. Dynamic video-clip needles were already allowed in v2 Section 3.1; VNBench-Act evaluates that possibility. Appendix G expands documentation of the retained training model without establishing an architecture or objective change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local wording and typo corrections, expanded training explanations, an acknowledgment section, conference headers, and appendix subdivisions accommodating the new analyses. There is no extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 5 is redrawn with separately identified OneVision size variants, and Figure 8 replaces binary maps with annotated continuous-accuracy heatmaps and a color scale. v3 adds eight tables, a cross-benchmark correlation figure, and animal-needle illustrations. It also relocates existing plots and corrects illustrative options and table labels.

R1.justification: v3 adds ChatBridge and a brief discussion of integrating external modalities, a Something-Something citation, and Wang et al. and Wei et al. on multiple-choice evaluation and selection biases. The broader positioning against existing video benchmarks and synthetic language-model evaluations remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix J introduces definitions of answer consistency and conditional accuracy, with the reasoning that circularly correct predictions form a subset of consistent predictions. This mathematical treatment is absent from v2. Appendix G also formalizes visual-token construction and the training loss, without introducing a new theorem or demonstrated method change.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's validation: Appendix B.2 tests its relationship to real-world performance, F.2–F.3 examine construction sensitivity, and Appendix J explains why some low-score rankings are misleading. These address important evidential and interpretive gaps in v2. The validation remains limited to the tested configurations, while removal of the project link and Table 8's conflicting Ordering-I1/I2 labels weaken reproducibility. Nevertheless, the targeted evidence and more careful interpretation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoNIAH and VNBench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and task examples, support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds action-clip evaluations, comparisons with real-world benchmarks, construction-robustness tests, and answer-consistency analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original VNBench and VNBench-Long evaluations, task analyses, and experiments varying model size, frame sampling, visual tokens, and temporal prompts.

results.title: Needle In A Video Haystack: A Scalable  Synthetic Evaluator for Video MLLMs

C1.justification: v2 foregrounds hue/saturation equivariance, comparable parameter counts, and on-par or better classification. v4 adds central claims of luminance equivariance, improved sample efficiency, stability across hue discretizations, and over three orders of magnitude lower equivariance error than CEConv. Its abstract also claims consistent outperformance of competitive baselines.

C2.justification: v4 develops the earlier brief invalid-RGB observation into a projection/invertibility explanation, identifies the N=1 and N=3 exceptions, and attributes CEConv-4's poorer generalization to equivariance error. It removes v2's explicit lack-of-luminance-equivariance limitation after introducing luminance models. Computational and finite-discretization limitations remain, with a more concrete computational-cost explanation.

D1.justification: v4 adds a source-code availability statement and repository link, training recipes for added benchmarks, ImageNet's eight-GPU hardware configuration, and Stanford Cars reconstruction resources. Appendix E.3 and Table 8 document mask preparation and the segmentation backbone layer by layer. These substantially expand reproducibility information, while most original training recipes remain.

E1.justification: v4 retains the four original datasets and adds reported classification results on Caltech-101, CIFAR-100, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10, ImageNet, and small NORB. Small NORB introduces controlled lighting shifts, while Caltech-101 foreground-background segmentation adds a distinct prediction task (Tables 4-7).

E2.justification: The MNIST comparison replaces the reported CEConv-2 hybrid with CEConv-4; the earlier CEConv corresponds to CEConv-3. v4 also adds CEConv-4 on 3D Shapes, CEConv-3 on Camelyon17, and grayscale/color-jitter ResNet baselines in Table 4. Conversely, the ResNet18/44 comparisons in v2's 3D Shapes table disappear. Sorting analyses add ResNet and CEConv comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include training-fraction sweeps, rotation-restoration and relative-equivariance measurements, lighting-based NORB splits, and segmentation with a 6941/868/868 split and 224-by-224 resizing. The CIFAR-10 description changes from 40k training/10k validation/10k testing to 50k training/10k testing in v4 Appendix D.4, although that paragraph calls the dataset CIFAR-100. This documents an inconsistent setting revision, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds sample-efficiency analysis, rotation invertibility versus group order, quantitative equivariance error, expanded CEConv feature-map/sorting comparisons, and hospital saturation distributions (Figures 3, 4, 6, 18; Appendix B). However, most saturation-step sensitivity rows from v2's Camelyon17 and CIFAR-10 tables disappear, despite retained prose mentioning four discretizations.

E5.justification: The original three-seed MNIST/3D Shapes/CIFAR-10 and five-seed Camelyon17 reporting remains unchanged. v4 explicitly discloses one ImageNet seed, 1999, and introduces plots with shaded bands and error bars. It does not document increased repetitions for the original experiments or clearly specify run counts for every added dataset.

E6.justification: Many original scores persist, including Camelyon17's 16.08 (2.68), now labeled Sat-3. Major additions include NORB A/B errors of 18.45 for Lum-3 versus 37.70 for ResNet18, ImageNet Hue-3 error of 30.28, and segmentation errors of 9.67 versus 11.25 (Tables 5-7). New sample-efficiency and equivariance findings substantially expand the results. Some retained entries also change, including MNIST Hue-3's parenthesized A/B variability from 0.28 to 0.29.

M1.justification: The original hue/saturation lifting and group-convolution procedure is retained. v4 extends it to luminance and hue-luminance lifting, and introduces a segmentation adaptation with convolution/deconvolution layers, group pooling, and mask outputs (Section 4; Appendices E.1 and E.3). These substantially extend the method's capabilities.

P1.justification: Beyond the title and author-presentation changes, v4 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution framing, and experimental narrative around CEConv, sample efficiency, and equivariance error. Dataset descriptions move into appendices, which are reorganized from datasets/training/proofs into proofs, comparisons, datasets, implementation, and additional results.

P2.justification: The two-column presentation becomes a single-column ICLR layout. v2 Figures 1 and 2 are combined into v4 Figure 1, Table 4 becomes a six-dataset comparison, and color-sorting displays expand into multiple-model comparisons. New diagnostic, luminance, and segmentation figures and tables substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The established equivariant-network literature and closest predecessor, CEConv, remain central. v4 refines the distinction from CEConv by dropping the fully-equivariant-versus-hybrid novelty claim and adding luminance. Supporting citations include Elesedy on sample efficiency, Zhdanov et al. on equivariance measurement, and additional dataset/implementation references. CEConv's corrected bibliography represents the same prior work.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds definitions of the luminance group and its image/feature-map actions, following the existing saturation construction. The original hue/saturation proofs move from v2 Appendix C to v4 Appendix A with essentially unchanged reasoning, and the lifting-equivariance derivation is retained. The formal expansion is limited.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central lifting-layer advantage: the earlier mainly N=3/hybrid CEConv comparison gains matched N=4 comparisons and quantitative invertibility/equivariance analyses. Luminance and segmentation experiments test previously unsupported capabilities, while added controls and implementation information improve evaluability. These gains outweigh the removed sensitivity rows and remaining documentation problems. Qualifications remain: the CIFAR split is inconsistent, and the broad outperformance language exceeds Table 4's mixed results against conventional ResNet.

A1.justification: The renamed paper retains the same research identity, core lifting method, and original experiments. Both PDFs are readable in full, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices; no material extraction gaps limit comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds benchmark comparisons, sample-efficiency and equivariance measurements, luminance experiments, and foreground-background segmentation results.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments on MNIST, 3D Shapes, Camelyon17, and CIFAR-10, alongside feature-map and color-sorting analyses.

results.title: Learning Color Equivariant Representations

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the contribution from a training-free sparse attention mechanism to a serving framework addressing algorithmic cost, GPU computation, and memory management. New central claims concern a mathematical advantage over random pruning and offloading with O(log T) GPU-resident tokens. The training-free hierarchical attention contribution is retained.

C2.justification: v2 develops attention locality as the mechanism explanation and discusses nonzero means, correlated score differences, and failure of the independence approximation near the final pruning iterations. It explicitly identifies missed top-k tokens through early branch termination, qualifies vector-map versus hash-map memory/latency trade-offs, and analyzes hardware-dependent slowdowns. These substantially extend v1's limitations discussion.

D1.justification: A new reproducibility statement describes supplementary code, kernel and evaluation entry files, configuration classes, and serving integrations. v2 also documents FlashAttention versions, offloading memory limits, weight/cache precision, and the Arxiv healing recipe. Some earlier healing details disappear, but the new implementation and execution information is substantial.

E1.justification: v2 adds PG19, passkey retrieval, RULER, and Arxiv healing data. Its multimodal evaluation replaces ChartQA and InfoVQA with MME cognition/perception while retaining MMMU, DocVQA, GQA, and TextVQA (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 8). WikiText2, MMLU, LongBench, and BookSum remain represented.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's principal StreamingLLM and HyperAttention comparisons, v2 evaluates A, AVD, BigBird, and H2O in the main benchmark suite. BigBird also joins the MMLU and multimodal comparisons. Reformer and SEA remain in the corresponding appendix experiment; these additions are evaluated comparators, not merely citations.

E3.justification: The main evaluations switch from LLaMA2/Qwen models to Llama3.1-8B and separately test sparse prefill, sparse decoding, and both phases. BookSum introduces 32k–128k books, 2k-token summaries, an 8k-token GPU-cache budget, and window-size controls. Healing and latency settings also change, including the new 500-step Arxiv recipe and expanded offloading configurations.

E4.justification: v2 adds empirical checks of attention-locality assumptions, a neighboring-token patch study, representative-token-position ablations, SelfExtend configuration studies, and sorting-removal experiments on RTX 4090/H100. The mask-refresh analysis is revised under different benchmarks. Earlier block-size, dense-layer, ensemble, and summary-case analyses are substantially retained and relocated.

E5.justification: v2 introduces substantial statistical estimation absent from v1's corresponding analysis: fitted attention-score-difference distributions, distance-dependent means and standard deviations, correlation estimates, Gaussian-fit KL divergence, and logarithmic-fit NRMSE (Appendix A.3). These characterize the proposed stochastic model. Benchmark run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, and significance tests remain unreported.

E6.justification: Many earlier multi-model results are replaced by Llama3.1 measurements, with additional retrieval, context-extension, and offloading outcomes. For example, v2 Table 5 reports 6.83× decoding speedup at 128k with 96.0% relative LongBench performance, and Table 6 reports 95.45 tokens/s with vector-map offloading at 64k on RTX 4090. These are new-setting results, not direct improvements over v1's speedups. The Reformer/SEA perplexities remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The hierarchical pruning backbone remains, but v2 changes branch representatives from first tokens to center tokens and introduces strided sampling within blocks. Section 3.3 adds separate GPU hot-token caches and vector/hash page tables, substantially extending v1's preliminary UVM offloading. Appendix C.4 also integrates HiP with SelfExtend.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are extensively rewritten around three serving objectives. The document adds a theory section and reproducibility statement, reorganizes the experiments and appendices, shortens main-text related work, and moves MMLU and multimodal evaluation into the appendix. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: The introductory and method diagrams are redrawn, several radar-chart presentations become tables, and main comparisons use color-coded tables grouped by prefill/decoding configuration. New offloading schematics, latency breakdowns, memory-throughput plots, and statistical figures substantially change the visual presentation. Several earlier appendix plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds connections to MInference/SnapKV-style attention, SelfExtend/YaRN, SGLang, and newer models and benchmarks, while removing some earlier citations. The central positioning relative to StreamingLLM, HyperAttention, and SEA remains largely intact and is mostly moved to Appendix E.1.

T1.justification: v1 provides algorithm equations and complexity reasoning without comparable correctness theorems. v2 Section 4 and Appendix A introduce probabilistic attention-locality assumptions, lemmas, derivations, and proofs supporting center-token selection over random selection in a simplified top-1 setting, plus a conditional optimality theorem.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the previously limited evidence for effective long-context retrieval and practical memory offloading. Passkey/RULER tests, phase-specific comparisons against more baselines, measured offloading trade-offs, and detailed execution instructions make the central claims more assessable. These gains outweigh narrower main-model coverage. The theory remains conditional and simplified, and the logarithmic-space hash-map variant does not deliver the vector-map variant's throughput; the added discussion makes these limits visible.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HiP attention work despite the changed title and expanded serving framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised, and added material.

after.justification: v2 reports original PG19, passkey, RULER, LongBench, BookSum, multimodal, offloading, and attention-locality results, alongside retained experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-modeling, MMLU, LongBench, BookSum, multimodal, latency, and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: A Training-Free Sub-quadratic Cost Transformer Model Serving Framework with Hierarchically Pruned Attention

C1.justification: V1 claims improved covariance estimation and DDPM/DDIM sampling efficiency, with image applications deferred. V2's abstract, introduction and conclusion add claims about likelihood, recall/diversity and scalability across pixel-space and latent image generation, substantially broadening the asserted contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds a likelihood-versus-FID trade-off interpretation, acknowledging that SN-DDPM or NPR-DDPM can outperform OCM on individual metrics. It attributes SN-DDPM's likelihood difficulties to quadratic-term error amplification and links learned covariance to diversity. Appendix B.1 also qualifies the computational-efficiency discussion with measured overhead, including 11.2% on LSUN Bedroom.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's brief toy optimizer settings, v2 supplies a code-access link, pretrained-model sources, shared-backbone and prediction-head specifications, parameter counts, GPU hardware, AdamW training budgets, batch sizes, checkpoint selection, EMA, covariance clipping and evaluation details (Section 3.3 and Appendix B). These substantially expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only the nine-Gaussian toy distribution and leaves image modelling to future work. V2 retains that task and adds CIFAR10, CelebA 64x64, LSUN Bedroom, ImageNet 64x64 and class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 generation using latent diffusion.

E2.justification: V2 introduces NPR-DDPM/NPR-DDIM as important comparators in the image likelihood and FID experiments. Within the retained toy DDIM comparison, Figure 3d removes the beta-DDIM, iDDIM and True-DDIM curves present in v1 Figure 1d. Ana/A-DDPM and NS/SN-DDPM are matched as renamed methods.

E3.justification: The stated toy training budget and MMD kernels remain unchanged. New image experiments introduce linear/cosine schedules, pretrained image models, NLL upper-bound evaluation, FID on 50,000 generated samples, recall, classifier-free-guidance sweeps and time-adjusted comparisons at approximately FID 6. These are added protocols, rather than demonstrated changes to the original toy setting.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained toy analyses, v2 adds Rademacher sample-count sensitivity studies (Figures 1 and 5), guidance-dependent quality/diversity analysis (Figure 4 and Table 11), parameter and inference-overhead measurements (Table 8), and qualitative sample studies across sampling settings (Appendix C.4).

E5.justification: V1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty summaries. V2 Appendix C.2 reports three evaluation repetitions with different seeds, and Table 9 provides means and percentage-scaled standard deviations for OCM likelihood and FID results. This documents repeated evaluation, not three independent training runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive likelihood, FID, recall, runtime and qualitative image results, while largely retaining the toy trends and removing three toy DDIM result curves. For example, its new Table 11 reports ImageNet 256x256 FID/recall of 5.33/46.58% for OCM-DDIM versus 6.12/41.15% for DDIM at 10 steps and CFG=2.0. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over corresponding v1 image results.

M1.justification: The Hessian-diagonal regression objective, single-Rademacher-sample training approach, covariance construction and skip-step DDPM/DDIM updates are retained. V2 documents shared-backbone prediction heads and practical image-sampling details, but does not establish a revision of the existing OCM algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 revises the title and extensively rewrites the introduction, separates background into its own section, adds a dedicated training/inference subsection, and separates broader related work from the conclusion. It reorganizes the original proofs within Appendix A and introduces a structured appendix contents page and experimental sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. The original overview table and toy figure are relocated and revised, while v2 adds algorithm boxes, extensive benchmark and uncertainty tables, guidance plots, architecture/runtime tables and image grids. These materially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V1 primarily positions OCM among covariance estimators. V2 adds substantial positioning against numerical solvers, Schrodinger bridges, GAN hybrids and diffusion distillation, with new references such as Peebles and Xie and Salimans and colleagues. Section 6 also relates OCM to likelihood-sensitive sampling, compression and future video applications.

T1.justification: The original covariance identity and optimality proof are retained, but v2 strengthens Theorem 2 with an upper-bound statement and Jensen-based derivation. New Appendix A.3 develops second-moment identities and proves Theorem 3: OCM-DDPM and SN-DDPM recover identical optimal diagonal covariances under an exact score and optimal training.

improvement.justification: V1's practical validation rests entirely on a toy distribution and explicitly defers image modelling. V2 addresses that central limitation with pixel-space and latent image experiments, supported by computational measurements, three-seed evaluation summaries, expanded theory and detailed reproducibility information. Some reporting inconsistencies remain, notably Table 10's 256x256 caption versus its 64x64 experiment text, and advantages are setting-dependent. Nevertheless, the added validation and transparency substantially improve overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OCM research, and their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison. V1's Appendices A and B correspond to v2's Appendices A.1 and A.2; v2 adds substantial further material.

after.justification: V2 retains the toy experiments and reports original image-generation, likelihood, recall and computational-cost results, including Tables 3–5, 8, 11 and 12.

before.justification: V1 reports original covariance-estimation errors and DDPM/DDIM sampling results on a two-dimensional nine-Gaussian mixture, evaluated using MMD in Figure 1.

results.title: Improving Probabilistic Diffusion Models With Optimal Diagonal Covariance Matching

C1.justification: The central claim that incentive knowledge can improve the robustness–accuracy tradeoff remains. v2 additionally advertises preference-order opponents, mentions utility inference, and explicitly claims that misspecification risks are often manageable. Its novelty statement is qualified to multiclass strategic behavior over complex inputs.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of indirect protection across attack targets (C.3), reduced gains when the incentive set approaches the adversarial setting (C.5), and difficulty recovering rarely attacked targets (C.6). It also interprets utility-order alignment effects (C.7) and discloses difficulties obtaining comparable ViT performance (C.1).

D1.justification: Existing optimization, hardware, runtime, and code/checkpoint access statements remain. New details include the preference-training epsilon, CIFAR-100 semantic grouping, and utility inference's observation requirements, known-k assumption, and frequency-based reconstruction rule. These support the extensions without substantially revising the original reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10 and GTSRB. Appendix C also evaluates new scenarios involving preference-order and continuous-valued utilities, opponents targeting known gaps in defenses, and recovery of targets and utility matrices from previous attacks.

E2.justification: Clean and PGD-adversarial training remain the principal baselines. New comparisons evaluate prediction-based versus attack-vector-based utility inference (Table 7), and utility-weighted, sequential, sequential-with-adversarial-fallback, multi-targeted, and adversarial training (Table 8), substantially extending the comparison methods.

E3.justification: The original splits, training budgets, and PGD settings are retained. New protocols include average and worst-case targeted evaluations against informed opponents (C.3), epsilon=0.5 for preference training (C.4), target-prediction and matrix-recovery metrics with known k (C.6), and aligned versus misaligned utility orderings (C.7).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's 1-hot strength, semantics, and misspecification analyses, v2 adds sensitivity to larger k (Figures 6 and 9), tests attacks on explicitly undefended targets (C.3), and examines utility-order alignment and fallback choices (C.7). These substantially expand tests of robustness and modeling assumptions.

E5.justification: v1 already reports quantiles and mean/standard-deviation curves. v2 adds standard errors for the random 1-hot comparisons in Table 3 and specifies ten randomly drawn preference orderings with mean/standard-deviation reporting in Table 5. This does not establish additional runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their values, while Figures 6 and 9 and Tables 3–8 add substantial results. For example, Table 6 reports CIFAR-100 anti-semantic VGG accuracy of 20.2 for strategic versus 20.5 for adversarial training. Some new prose disagrees with its table: C.4 claims a 4.1-point VGG gain, whereas Table 5 implies 3.9.

M1.justification: The core minimax framework remains, but v2 adds a non-target penalty for preference attacks (Eq. 12), utility-inference procedures (C.6), and sequential strategic training with alternative fallback attacks (C.7). These extend the actual procedures. The epsilon=0.1 stabilization described in Section 5.1 was already disclosed in v1 Appendix B.4.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the exposition remain. v2 revises the abstract, introduction examples, risk-tradeoff interpretation, and several results passages, while adding acknowledgments and appendix cross-references. These refine the existing narrative alongside the newly added scientific material.

P2.justification: v2 adds six result tables and new k-dependent plots, expands opponent illustrations with preferences, and redraws or relabels existing plots. The conceptual panel from v1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 2, rather than a new analysis. Document typography, citation presentation, and page layout also change.

R1.justification: v2 adds Mo et al. (2022) concerning adversarial training of vision transformers and removes Rosenfeld and Rosenfeld (2024), including the connection to strategic classification under unknown costs. It also sharpens positioning relative to predominantly binary, linear, tabular strategic-classification work.

T1.justification: The central formulations and clean–strategic–adversarial inequality remain. v2 adds a formal preference-order utility definition and mathematical reasoning relating continuous utilities to their binary support and target ordering (C.4 and C.7). These are limited formal extensions, without new theorem-and-proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's central incentive assumptions through informed-opponent tests, preference and continuous-utility experiments, and utility recovery. The CIFAR-100 exception also establishes a useful boundary on gains. These address important evidentiary gaps in v1, although validation remains controlled and minor prose/table discrepancies, such as C.4 versus Table 5, reduce precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same strategic-robustness work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison; extracted text and rendered pages resolve the relevant content.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original CIFAR-100, preference-order, utility-inference, and continuous-utility results in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 and GTSRB experiments comparing clean, strategic, and adversarial training, including opponent-strength and misspecification analyses.

results.title: Adversaries With Incentives:  A Strategic Alternative to Adversarial Robustness

C1.justification: v2 newly highlights permutation invariance and pose-free operation in the abstract. Its conclusion qualifies superiority relative to point-cloud methods trained similarly, replacing v1's claim about almost all quantitative metrics. The central efficiency, flexible-view representation and text-alignment contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially extends v1's geometry and synthetic-data-overfitting discussion. It connects frozen MLPs and fewer trained layers to preserved transfer, interprets attention maps as cross-view correspondence, and explains camera-coverage tradeoffs. ScanNet results motivate stronger data/overfitting limitations, while the conclusion adds alternative-pretraining and hybrid image/point-cloud directions.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds numerical camera ranges, timing and memory measurement settings, the batch-size exception, and concrete ScanObjectNN/ScanNet image-preparation instructions. v2 also newly states MVPNet up-axis alignment, without establishing whether that preprocessing changed from v1. The front-page resource link changes from a repository address to a project-page address.

E1.justification: v2 retains Objaverse-LVIS, MVImgNet/MVPNet and Text2Shape coverage and adds two distinct real-world evaluation settings: ScanObjectNN using rendered point-cloud views and ScanNet using cropped RGB video frames (Section 4.1 and Appendix A.3). These substantially broaden evaluation beyond the original data.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the corresponding Objaverse-LVIS, MVPNet and Text2Shape comparisons. The added benchmarks reuse existing comparison methods, including OpenShape, TAMM, Uni3D and zero-shot CLIP. The new fine-tuning configurations are model ablations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces ScanObjectNN point-cloud rendering and ScanNet mask-ranked frame selection/cropping protocols. Appendix A adds camera-elevation controls, training-view ranges and MLP-tuning configurations, including a 1400 batch-size exception. These expand experimental settings substantially; the default 80-epoch, batch-1600 training remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds attention-map case studies (Figure 3), expands MVA testing across trainable-layer counts and three datasets (Table 6), and adds inference-cost, camera-sampling, training-view-count and MLP-freezing analyses (Appendices A.1–A.2). The original layer-count ablation is retained, while the Objaverse-LVIS six-inference-view MVA comparison is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions state that evaluations are averaged over three seeds (v1 Section 4.2; v2 Section 4.2.1). v2 introduces no additional repeated-run policy, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests.

E6.justification: Original Objaverse-LVIS and Text2Shape scores are retained. OpenShape† MVPNet Top1 changes from 3.55 to 10.80, and its MVPNet-trained counterpart from 54.35 to 54.59, alongside newly stated alignment preprocessing. New results include ScanObjectNN Top1 of 66.3 and ScanNet averages of 61.3/63.3 for trained variants versus 69.2 for zero-shot CLIP, plus extensive new ablation measurements.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same CLIP-initialized multi-view encoder, contrastive objective, cross-view attention, embedding averaging and selective attention-layer training. v2 explicitly describes frozen MLPs and pose-free, permutation-invariant inputs, but these do not establish a changed procedure. MLP fine-tuning is introduced as an ablation.

P1.justification: v2 revises introductory and related-work prose, groups classification experiments and model ablations under Section 4.2, and rewrites 'Limitations and Future Work' as a fuller conclusion. Most existing method and results prose remains recognizable; the new scientific appendix does not by itself constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds attention visualizations, camera-sampling illustrations and ScanObjectNN renders, plus Tables 7–12. Table 2 gains ScanObjectNN columns, and the MVA table is redesigned around layers and datasets. Schematics, typography and table placement also change, while original retrieval figures and view-count plots are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for ScanNet, SceneNN, ScanObjectNN, CyCLIP and sigmoid-loss pretraining. It removes MiniGPT-3D alongside the associated LLM future-work discussion. The main related-work coverage and positioning against point-cloud and multi-view representation methods remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3 corrects the written attention expression: v1 places multiplication by V inside softmax, whereas v2 places it outside. This changes the mathematical expression rather than merely its notation. No new theorem or proof accompanies the newly emphasized permutation-invariance property.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the training design and transfer claims through additional real-world benchmarks and targeted camera, view-count and MLP ablations. The appendix improves reproducibility and exposes limitations, particularly trained models trailing zero-shot CLIP on ScanNet. These gains outweigh limited reporting weaknesses, including claiming ScanObjectNN Top3 superiority where Table 2 shows a tie with Uni3D.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Duoduo CLIP work and provide readable text, equations, figures and tables. v1 ends after the references; v2 includes Appendix A, which is included in this comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ScanObjectNN, ScanNet and further ablation experiments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, text-to-shape retrieval and model-ablation results in Section 4, Tables 2–6 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: Duoduo CLIP: Efficient 3D Understanding with Multi-View Images

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: internal standardization removes benchmark sortability artifacts, prevents deterministic collapse under the stated conditions, and changes identifiability properties. Expanded experiments support these existing claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting PC/GES performance to near-deterministic dependencies and discussing GOLEM's differing noise assumptions. The conclusion introduces an energy-conservation analogy for physical systems. Existing qualifications about forest identifiability and potentially sortable iSCM configurations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds implementation choices, search grids, and final hyperparameter Tables 2-4 for the added learners. A new reproducibility statement reports supplementary code, configurations, and commands, whose availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs. Conversely, precise NOTEARS/AVICI timings are replaced by broader runtime bounds.

E1.justification: Coverage remains synthetic observational causal systems with linear or Gaussian-process mechanisms, ER and scale-free graphs, and chain examples. The added comparisons vary methods and configurations within this coverage; no new task, domain, or graph family is evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 adds GOLEM-EV, GOLEM-NV, PC, and GES to the retained NOTEARS, AVICI, and SortnRegress comparisons in Figures 5, 14, and 15. Figure 13 also evaluates the Mooij and Squires generation heuristics, which v1 discussed without reporting their sortability results.

E3.justification: Existing graph settings, sample sizes, metrics, and NOTEARS tuning are retained. New experiments introduce GOLEM and PC tuning, GOLEM-NV evaluation without GOLEM-EV initialization, Gaussian versus HSIC tests for PC, and heuristic-specific weight ranges (Appendix E.3-E.4 and Figure 13).

E4.justification: New Appendix F.3 and Figure 17 examine implied-noise distributions under smaller weights, testing the explanation for NOTEARS's smaller performance gap in that regime. Existing noise-transfer, graph-density, and weight-sensitivity analyses remain, with the weight comparisons extended to additional learners.

E5.justification: Both versions use 20 systems per structure-learning configuration and 100 for sortability, reporting median/IQR box plots or means and standard deviations. Added comparisons follow these practices; no changed repetition counts for retained experiments or new performance-significance testing are reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial F1/SHD results for the new learners. For example, Table 4b newly reports PC median validation F1 of 0.57 on standardized SCMs versus 0.79 on iSCMs for linear ER(100, 2) systems with weights from ±[0.5, 2.0]. Figures 13 and 17 add residual-sortability and small-weight noise-distribution findings. The retained NOTEARS Table 1 is unchanged.

M1.justification: The iSCM construction, internal standardization procedure, implied-model computation, and intervention semantics remain unchanged, including Algorithms 1-2 and Appendices A-B.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the metric explanation, experimental discussion, and conclusion. A reproducibility statement and Appendix F.3 are inserted, but the main section order, abstract, introduction, and most methodological and proof text remain intact.

P2.justification: v1 Figure 5 is split into v2 Figures 5 and 6, and the main and appendix performance plots are widened and reorganized for additional learners. v2 adds Figures 13 and 17 and Tables 2-4, alongside relocations of existing figures. These substantially expand and restructure the empirical displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for PC, GES, and the Causal Discovery Toolbox, and explicitly credits Wright (1934) for Lemma 1's trek rule. It also sharpens the comparison with the already-cited Mooij and Squires heuristics, while retaining the overall research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 corrects the stated variance used in the Squires normalization from the variance of x_j to the variance contributed by its parents. The main lemmas, theorems, assumptions, proofs, and counterexample are retained; the new trek-rule attribution changes provenance, not their mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmarking argument by addressing v1's limited learner comparisons and lack of empirical tests of alternative generation heuristics. GOLEM, PC, GES, and Figure 13 test distinct reasons for preferring iSCMs, while the noise-sensitivity analysis and documented tuning improve interpretability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the coarser runtime reporting and the speculative physical-system analogy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Standardizing Structural Causal Models and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A-F. Content can be matched reliably despite pagination changes and added experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds learner comparisons, evaluations of existing generation heuristics, and an implied-noise sensitivity analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations of sortability, causal structure recovery, noise transfer, and covariance patterns in Section 5 and Appendix F.

results.title: Standardizing Structural Causal Models

C1.justification: v2's central claims concern probing interpretable motion features and using them for inference-time steering. v3 retains these and adds central claims that sparse autoencoding improves control linearity and that calibrated vectors enable zero-shot compensation for unseen dataset characteristics with negligible computational overhead. These additions reshape the abstract, contributions and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations linking sparse representations to more distinct control features, interpreting speed/acceleration/agent-vector alignment, and attributing ConvSAE calibration behavior to feature shrinkage (Section 5.3 and Appendix A.16). It also develops the domain-shift interpretation, justifies the ±50% evaluation window, and identifies sensitivity to the low-speed class definition.

D1.justification: v3 documents SAE losses, the reported sparsity weight, Adam optimization, a 10,000-epoch training budget, intermediate dimensions, JumpReLU threshold and patch/kernel settings. Appendix A.11 specifies A6000 hardware, PyTorch Lightning profiling and eager execution for latency measurement. The repository link and original transformer hyperparameters are retained; moving v2 Appendix A.4 into Section 4.4 is not an implementation change.

E1.justification: Argoverse 2 Forecasting and Waymo remain the datasets. v3 adds one synthetic Waymo scenario with future motion slowed by approximately 50% to test zero-shot compensation (Section 5.4). This extends coverage to a specific simulated distribution shift within the existing forecasting task.

E2.justification: The RedMotion, Wayformer and HPTR comparisons are retained. v3 substantially expands comparisons of control-vector construction, explicitly evaluating plain PCA against fully connected SAE, Sparse MLPMixer and ConvSAE configurations (Tables 1–2). The new shifted-Waymo experiment also compares SAE steering against unsteered RedMotion (Table 3).

E3.justification: v3's comparative linearity evaluation targets relative speed changes within ±50%, with method-dependent temperature ranges, whereas v2 reports a single temperature sweep over [-50,50]. New protocols include interpolating the first half of future waypoints to simulate slowdown, SAE configuration sweeps, and an eight-focal-agent latency benchmark. The original transformer training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds explained-variance analyses, control-vector alignment comparisons, SAE-width ablations, encoder-module and speed-threshold sensitivity tests, and a JumpReLU feature-shrinkage analysis (Figures 12–13 and 15; Tables 1–2 and 5–9). It also tests synthetic distribution-shift robustness. The earlier correlation heatmaps and direction-control example are retained, with the latter moved from Appendix A.1 to A.9.

E5.justification: v3 Table 4 newly specifies latency means over 1,000 iterations per configuration. This adds limited repeated-measurement and aggregation information. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals or significance tests for forecasting and controllability results; embedding standard deviations describe representations rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Extensive vector-geometry, ablation, forecasting and latency results are added. v2 Figure 5 reports PCA R² of 0.821; v3 Table 2 reports 0.969 under the revised calibration range, so this is not a matched-setting gain. Within v3's comparison, ReLU SAE reaches 0.984. On the new slowed-Waymo scenario, Table 3 reports minADE of 3.271 without steering versus 1.174 for SAE-128 at temperature -50.

M1.justification: v2 constructs control vectors by applying PCA directly to differences between opposing-feature hidden states. v3 adds an auxiliary sparse autoencoder: differences are pooled in its sparse representation and decoded back into the motion encoder's hidden space before inference. Fully connected, convolutional and MLPMixer variants substantially extend the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around sparse autoencoding and generalization. Existing training details move into the main text, qualitative and quantitative results receive separate subsections, and the appendix is reorganized, including moving title origin to A.1 and the retained qualitative example to A.9.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show SAE encoding, decoding and control-vector construction. The single calibration display becomes a comparative figure, and v3 adds architecture, explained-variance and shrinkage figures plus nine numbered tables. Existing trajectory examples and distributions are relocated, while speed and acceleration panels are reordered in the probing figures.

R1.justification: v3 adds substantial positioning around sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning, JumpReLU and zero-shot generalization. Sections 2.1–2.2 introduce a robotics mechanistic-interpretability novelty claim and distinguish offline SAE use and last-module steering from earlier language-model approaches. The MotionLM citation is removed, and motion-threshold motivation is attributed to the already-cited Waymo dataset paper.

T1.justification: v3 adds the standard formula for the already-used CDNV metric in Appendix A.17 and briefly invokes Johnson–Lindenstrauss as motivation for SAE decoding. These additions provide mathematical explanation, but no new proof, formal assumption, derived guarantee or substantive revision of existing mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 provides probing results, one calibration analysis and selected steering examples, with little testing of control-design choices or failure conditions. v3's direct PCA/SAE comparisons and module, width and threshold ablations substantially strengthen validation and expose failures; documented slowdown and latency experiments make practical claims more assessable. These gains substantially improve empirical support and reproducibility. The broader generalization claims remain supported by only one constructed slowdown scenario, and performance uncertainty is still unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Words in Motion by the same authors. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds sparse-autoencoder comparisons, sensitivity analyses, simulated domain-shift forecasting results and inference-latency measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original probing accuracies, representation statistics, control calibration and qualitative steering results on Argoverse 2 Forecasting and Waymo, with additional distribution and correlation analyses in the appendix.

results.title: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on captioner and CLIP attacks demonstrating agent vulnerability. v2 makes ARE and component-level robustness central contributions, extending its main claims to reflexion and tree-search agents and to how additional components can either block or amplify attacks.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving adversarial verification, reflections, and value scores, and qualifies defensive benefits by whether components themselves are compromised. Appendix D newly characterizes attack results as lower bounds on risk and limits conclusions to the evaluated agent algorithms. v1's vision-only limitation is replaced as text attacks enter the study.

D1.justification: v2 adds evaluation-matching rules, safety-prompt excerpts, and configuration details for the new agent studies. It omits v1's explicit PGD initialization and checkpoint-selection descriptions, including GPT-4 scoring of CLIP candidates. Model identifiers, hardware, and the code/data repository remain unchanged; omitted details do not establish changed attack implementations.

E1.justification: Both versions use the 200-task VWA-Adv benchmark covering classifieds, Reddit, and shopping, with retained adversarial-goal templates and synthetic image-selection scenarios. v2 adds an evaluated text-access scenario alongside bounded image perturbations, extending coverage within the existing web domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated reflexion and tree-search agents and comparisons involving safety prompting, abstention prompting, paraphrasing, and explicit consistency checking. These substantially expand the comparisons beyond v1's base, captioner-augmented, and self-captioning agents. The four backbone model families remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce component-edge evaluations and controls that selectively supply clean or adversarial captions. Reflexion permits two attempts, and tree search uses branching factor 3 and depth 1. v1's stepwise-versus-episode evaluation comparison is removed; v2 explicitly describes terminal-state evaluation. These additions establish new protocols without demonstrating reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled analyses of attacking the policy, evaluator, or value function separately and jointly, plus empirical defense tests. It removes v1's cross-goal repeatability study and stepwise-versus-episode validation. The resolution, negative-text, ensemble, and synthetic-context analyses are retained, partly relocated to Appendix C.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and both specify temperature-zero decoding. v1's removed 'Repeated ASR' experiment concerns transfer across user goals, rather than statistical uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o text-injection ASR of 40%, reflexion outcomes of 25% with a clean evaluator and 36% under joint attack, and corresponding tree-search outcomes of 26% and 38%. Paraphrasing reduces ASR from 31% to 27.5%. Earlier goal-specific tables and repeatability results disappear, while synthetic-context and CLIP-ablation values remain unchanged. The differently grouped headline rates are not directly comparable performance changes.

M1.justification: v2 introduces ARE's procedure for representing agents as graphs and evaluating attack propagation through components. It also adds direct text injection and implemented defense pipelines involving paraphrasing and consistency checking. The original captioner PGD and CLIP ensemble optimization objectives remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The setup, method, and experimental narrative are reorganized around ARE and component robustness, replacing v1's attack-centered organization. Several retained explanations move to appendices, while much appendix implementation material remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 replaces much of the main results presentation with agent graphs, weighted attack-propagation diagrams, a robustness-utility scatterplot, and a defense bar chart. Earlier detailed result tables and attack examples are removed. The resolution heatmap moves to the appendix, while several agent illustrations and appendix tables are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around compound-agent robustness and distinguishes it from concurrent AgentDojo and EIA research. Related work expands to indirect prompt injection, Agent Smith, defense methods, and the tree-search agent, supporting the shift beyond v1's emphasis on image attacks and captioner vulnerabilities.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3 introduces formal agent graphs, adversarial influence AdvIn(c), expected edge weights, a deterministic-environment assumption, and conventions for unexecuted branches. This is substantial new mathematical formulation beyond v1's attack objectives, although it does not add theorem proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for system-level conclusions: Sections 5.2–5.4 isolate how evaluators and value functions block or amplify attacks and empirically test defense ideas that v1 largely proposed. ARE provides a common framework for these comparisons. These gains outweigh the loss of repeatability evidence, detailed result tables, and some optimization documentation. Reporting weaknesses remain, including introductory relative-change percentages that do not consistently match the displayed results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VWA-Adv research and retain identifiable attacks, experiments, and appendix material despite the changed title and substantial extension. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original text/image attack results, component-isolation experiments, and defense evaluations, alongside retained synthetic experiments and ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack experiments, cross-goal repeatability tests, synthetic-context experiments, and CLIP ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Dissecting Adversarial Robustness of Multimodal LM Agents

C1.justification: The central claim that limited relearning data lacking direct answers can restore unlearned knowledge remains. v2 adds an explicit abstract/introduction claim that generic public information can recover verbatim copyrighted text, extending the stated contribution while preserving its central message.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation through persistent token associations, model/data-format mismatch, claimed PEFT susceptibility, and the importance of knowing RMU's corrupted layer. Sections 8–9 also explain metric-dependent attack success and identify prompt filtering and guardrails as applicability limits, beyond v1's brief future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v2 Appendices A.1, B.1, C.1, and D.1 add optimizers, schedules, learning rates, batch sizes, weight decay, LoRA parameters, and method-specific settings. Appendix D supplies the new relearning prompt and generated text, and page 2 adds a code-access link. However, v1's explicit eight TOFU relearning QA pairs per author is no longer stated.

E1.justification: The original WMDP and TOFU/WHP keyword tasks remain. v2 adds verbatim Harry Potter passage recovery using generic character information, synthetic name-sequence recovery, and actual multiple-choice evaluation alongside generated answers for RMU. These substantially expand task requirements and test scenarios.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates gradient ascent for WMDP. v2 Figure 4 additionally evaluates gradient difference, KL minimization, NPO, and SCRUB; Section 7 evaluates RMU. Table 3 also adds gradient difference and NPO to the LoRA-unlearning comparison. These methods are evaluated, rather than merely cited.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3-8b evaluation and describes full-weight WMDP relearning in Appendix C.1, whereas v1 specifies LoRA. New protocols include 15 split 80-word passages scored with Rouge-L, 100 synthetic prefixes, and likelihood-based MCQ scoring. The TOFU control changes its reported model from OPT-1.5 to Phi-1.5 while retaining identical scores; this establishes revised reporting without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine token-pair repetition and relearning depth, full-weight versus LoRA unlearning, RMU's disagreement between MCQ and generation metrics, and zero-initialization. Appendix D adds successful and unsuccessful verbatim-recovery cases. The earlier checkpoint heatmaps, TOFU control, and qualitative failure examples are largely retained.
