E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. v2's token-pair repetitions and additional evaluation samples concern experimental design, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive WMDP, verbatim-recovery, synthetic, and RMU results. For example, Table 4 reports NPO Rouge-L scores of 0.0332 after unlearning and 0.7221 after relearning. Expanded settings prevent interpreting these as across-version performance gains. The retained example in v1 Table 9/v2 Appendix C.4.4 changes its relearned score from 8 to 9. v2 Figure 4's retain panels duplicate forget values, making its retention results ambiguous.

M1.justification: The core attack algorithm is retained and moved from v1 Appendix F into the main text. v2 Section 7 adds an RMU-specific zeroinit+relearn variant that zeros the known corrupted layer before finetuning. This is a limited but genuine procedural extension.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, and threat-model explanation. Experiments are reorganized around partial-data versus public-information access, the algorithm moves into the main text, and qualitative material moves into task-organized appendices with an outline. Discussion and conclusion become separate sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds a front-page recovery illustration, WMDP bar charts, a synthetic-loss plot, and new quantitative tables. Existing keyword examples are condensed into a combined table; many other example tables and boxed question lists become appendix prose or bullets. The retained heatmaps are resized and relocated. Figure 4 introduces duplicated forget/retain panels.

R1.justification: Related work shifts substantially toward contemporary LLM unlearning and robustness, adding work including RWKU, MUSE, Ununlearning, intrinsic knowledge traces, and benign-finetuning safety failures. Several classical unlearning and extraction references disappear. The central distinction from prior relearning work—excluding direct evaluation answers from relearning data—remains.

T1.justification: The substantive threat-model assumptions remain. v2 adds explanatory disjoint-set notation and standard objective formulas in Section 6 and Appendix E. Its correlation study provides empirical intuition, without a new theoretical result, proof, or substantive formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for v1's broad vulnerability claim through additional unlearning methods, direct verbatim-recovery evidence, and RMU analyses that expose evaluation limitations. Its technical appendices also address substantial reproducibility omissions. Figure 4's duplicated retain panels are a material regression from v1 Table 2 and weaken retention conclusions, but the distinct new experiments, analyses, and implementation disclosures provide substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same targeted relearning study. All 17 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable. Retained experiments, equations, and displays can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Sections 4–7 retain original experiments and add unlearning-method comparisons, verbatim text recovery, synthetic correlation experiments, and RMU evaluations.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original WMDP completion scores and TOFU/WHP attack success rates. The appendices include additional examples and a relearn-data-only control experiment.

results.title: Unlearning or Obfuscating? Jogging the Memory of Unlearned LLMs via Benign Relearning

C1.justification: Both versions identify limited ERFs as a barrier to Mamba extrapolation and introduce the first Mamba-specific decimation-based context extension, applicable without additional training. v2 replaces the abstract's 25x headline with qualitative wording and emphasizes faster inference, but the 25x result remains in Section 5 and reduced computational requirements were already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications and explanations: persistent zero-shot degradation on LongBench, the sparsity assumption motivating Lbase, and why short generated outputs need no decoding pooling while longer outputs might. Appendix D.5 explains the choice of attention-distance over gradient-based ERF measures, and Appendix F discusses applicability to other gated architectures. The original warning that pooling can discard critical information remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds pseudocode, prefill/decoding clarification, LongBench checkpoint and decimation settings, and hyperparameter-selection guidance. Its reproducibility statement reports code provision, replacing v1's release promise. Conversely, v1 Appendix A.3's dedicated free-text QA configuration—including approximately 90,000 training examples, layer 14, and evaluation Lbase=7000—is no longer documented despite retaining the QA results.

E1.justification: v2 retains the SQuAD, WikiText, and PG-19 evaluations and adds 16 LongBench tasks. These substantially expand coverage to summarization, code completion, few-shot classification and QA, passage counting, and additional single- and multi-document QA domains.

E2.justification: v1 compares primarily against Mamba and alternative pooling strategies. v2 Tables 4–6 add Pythia-160M to passkey and document retrieval, and Pythia-1.4B/2.8B to PG-19 comparisons. These introduce scored Transformer baselines into existing experiments. The attempted LongBench Pythia evaluation reports OOM rather than a performance score.

E3.justification: v2 adds instruction-tuned 2.8B LongBench evaluation with task-specific metrics and context-length groups, plus model/block timing over 8K–512K tokens. Appendix A.2 also changes the reported retrieval prompt and training document count from 11 to 12. However, v2 Section 5 states 11 and Table 5 states 10; these conflicting descriptions do not establish whether the original experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The original ERF visualizations and layer-selection, pooling-strategy, and pooling-mechanism ablations are retained. v2 adds decay-rate and decimation-layer-count sweeps in Tables 7–8, and a GovReport comparison of prefill-only versus additional decoding pooling in Table 9. These substantially extend analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity and the need for pooling during generation.

E5.justification: The document-retrieval plot retains its shaded bands without explaining their statistical meaning. v2 adds no repeated-run or seed counts, confidence-interval definitions, or significance-testing procedures. Query and needle-position counts concern evaluation samples rather than independent repetitions.

E6.justification: The original QA values are identical in v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2, and the principal retrieval and PG-19 plots are retained. v2 adds substantial results: LongBench, Pythia comparisons, timing, and new ablations. For example, LongBench TriviaQA scores are 3.93 for Mamba versus 12.61 for DeciMamba, whereas QMSum scores are 8.18 versus 7.08. These are newly reported comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The core delta-based scoring, Top-Ps schedule, layer selection, and PG-19 training loss are retained. Appendix E.4 introduces an experimental decoding-decimation variant that alternates prefill and pooling with 50-token generation chunks. This is a limited inference adaptation; the new pseudocode and prefill-only explanation otherwise document the existing method.

P1.justification: The ERF and method explanations are extensively revised, and detailed ablations move from Section 5.1 to Appendix E with a main-text summary. The appendices are reorganized around implementation, additional evaluations, hyperparameters, related work, ablations, and extensions. New inference, complexity, and reproducibility subsections also reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: The two-column layout becomes a single-column ICLR format. Existing figures are recomposed and relocated: v1 Figures 1 and 8 become v2 Figure 1, while v1 Figures 2 and 5 become v2 Figure 3. The schematic moves earlier, and new benchmark, comparator, timing, and ablation tables plus an algorithm display substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through gradient-based ERF studies, RAG versus long-context research, context-compression and prefill literature, and extensions to other gated recurrent architectures. Appendices D.3–D.5, E.4, and F develop these relationships beyond v1's mainly Mamba and efficient-Transformer discussion.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4 adds a complexity comparison of O(L log L) against O(L + P log P), explicitly setting aside the O(L log P) selection cost. The existing SSM equations, Mamba Mean Distance definition, and transition-product derivation remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the method by addressing v1's narrow task coverage, absence of Transformer comparisons, and lack of direct inference-timing evidence. LongBench also exposes nonuniform benefits, while new ablations clarify important design choices. These gains outweigh the reproducibility regressions from removing QA training details and introducing conflicting document-count descriptions. Statistical uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeciMamba work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds LongBench evaluations, Transformer comparisons, inference timing, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original document retrieval, question answering, passkey retrieval, language modeling, ERF measurements, and ablation results.

results.title: DeciMamba: Exploring the Length Extrapolation Potential of Mamba

C1.justification: The central contribution—joint generation of aligned objects enabling hybridization and structure-preserving editing—remains. v2 adds explicit claims about the necessity of transition plausibility and smoothness and effectiveness across backbones. Its introduction and conclusion qualify editing performance as on par with specialized methods, whereas v1 claims superiority in quality and semantic alignment.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the mechanism interpretation, separating plausibility regularization from prompt blending and discussing an alignment-versus-realism tradeoff. It explains why limited geometric editing can obtain favorable DIFT scores and discusses backbone-specific weaknesses. The static-object limitation remains, while v1's explicit warning about substantially different proportions is removed.

D1.justification: New Appendices B and C provide architecture, hash-grid, latent-sampling, regularization-weight, initialization, baseline-adaptation, and evaluation details. Examples include 0.5 probability of individual-object sampling, RichDreamer network specifications, MVEdit denoising strength, and the CLIP ViT-L/14 model. These greatly expand v1's sparse implementation information; newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E1.justification: The three tasks and 15 joint-generation prompt pairs remain, including plants already evaluated in v1. Demonstrated coverage contracts slightly: the plant-decoration editing case in v1 Table 2 and mosquito/wasp hybridization example in Figure 8 are absent from v2. RichDreamer adds a model configuration rather than new data coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares against MVEdit. v2 adds LucidDreamer and GaussianEditor to aligned generation. Editing adds GaussianEditor quantitatively and LucidDreamer through qualitative comparisons and successful per-case results in Table 6; LucidDreamer's failures prevent an aggregate comparison in Table 2.

E3.justification: v2 replaces Chamfer distance with normalized DIFT correspondence distance and adds six GPT-4o evaluation criteria using 90 comparisons per method pair. The editing table changes from 24 cases to 26, and new backbone and ablation configurations are evaluated. CLIP averaging over 120 views is retained.

E4.justification: v1's ablation qualitatively compares separate networks, a shared network without interpolation, and the full method. v2 adds empty-prompt transition guidance and network-depth controls, with aggregate and per-pair quantitative results in Tables 3 and 7. Appendix A additionally tests generalization to the RichDreamer backbone.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. v2's 90 GPT-based comparisons specify evaluation sample size, without adding uncertainty estimates or establishing repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Reported aligned-generation CLIP averages change from A3D/MVEdit 29.46/27.92 to 27.7/27.1; editing averages change from 29.56/28.76 to 27.8/27.9. Revised methods and evaluation prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. v2 also adds extensive DIFT, GPT-based, ablation, and RichDreamer results, while removing some qualitative examples.

M1.justification: v2 adds a substantive RichDreamer-based implementation using DMTet/SDF geometry, staged geometry and texture optimization, and normal-depth/albedo guidance (Appendices A and B.2). The core simplex interpolation, hybridization, and source-anchored editing procedures remain. Its main method description also emphasizes depth and normal-map regularization instead of v1's explicit spectral normalization, although removal of spectral normalization is not explicitly confirmed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Terminology shifts toward structural alignment and latent codes, metrics receive a shared explanation, and the single additional-results appendix becomes four focused appendices. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns comparison figures to include more methods and separate appearance/geometry views, expands the ablation display, and adds a RichDreamer figure. The combined comparison table becomes separate task tables with additional metrics. Existing hybridization examples are condensed and rearranged, while v1's trajectory Figures 3 and 10 are omitted.

R1.justification: v2 removes the broad 2D diffusion survey, expands discussion of 3D editing and amortized generation, and adds a dedicated latent-space regularization subsection. Connections to StyleGAN and adversarial interpolation substantially develop the methodological positioning. RichDreamer was already cited in v1; its new experimental use is a separate change.

T1.justification: v2 defines a normalized, bidirectional DIFT correspondence distance mathematically in Appendix C, adding a formal metric construction absent from v1. The existing NeRF, SDS, and simplex formulations remain substantially unchanged, and neither version develops theorem-and-proof results.

improvement.justification: v1's limited comparator coverage, qualitative-only ablations, and sparse implementation information leave important validation and reproducibility gaps. v2 substantially addresses these through additional baselines, quantitative component controls, a second implementation, and detailed appendices. Some illustrative examples disappear and uncertainty remains unreported, but the stronger experimental support and technical transparency provide a clear overall improvement despite mixed performance results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe A3D and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The shared method and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparative experiments, quantitative ablations, and RichDreamer-based results in Tables 1–7 and associated figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation and transformation measurements in Tables 1–3, alongside hybridization examples and qualitative ablations.

results.title: A3D: Does Diffusion Dream about 3D Alignment?

C1.justification: Adaptation without expert labels moves from a future direction in v1's conclusion to an achieved main contribution in v2. The introduction adds the shared codebook and replaces the emphasis on structurally close transfer with broader adaptation claims with or without supervision. The claimed number of tasks with state-of-the-art single-task results also changes from six to seven.

C2.justification: V1 interprets input-adapter instability as restricting successful transfer to compatible instance structures. V2 instead argues that low-rank sharing reduces task-specific representation separation and interprets its new controls as evidence of multi-task synergy. It also discusses the supervised/unsupervised cost tradeoff, explicitly limits applicability to easily enforced constructive feasibility, and sharpens the practical scaling limitation beyond roughly 1,000 nodes.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link, node/edge codebook dimensions of 8/4, the learning-rate decay factor, and expanded per-task feature, action and trajectory specifications. Hardware changes from eight A100s to eight V100s. Some documentation remains inconsistent: Section 4 names HiGHS as the UMSP oracle, whereas Appendix E.15 names ORTools.

E1.justification: Transfer evaluation expands from four to eight tasks, adding Prize-Collecting TSP, Sequential Ordering, Maximum Covering Location and Open Shop Scheduling, including a new location domain. The original eight training task families remain. OVRP/OCVRP and SDVRP/SDCVRP are retained tasks with revised naming, not additional tasks.

E2.justification: V1 compares transfer against training from scratch. V2 Figure 3 additionally compares the multi-task backbone against fine-tuning seven individually pretrained task models on four transfer problems. This substantially expands the controls for assessing multi-task pretraining, while Table 1 retains its external baseline membership.

E3.justification: Reported training settings change from batch size 128 to 256, validation sets of 512 to 128 instances, and approximately 500 to 400 epochs. UMSP changes from 100x10 to 100x20, and supervised transfer from 64 to 128 labeled instances. The appendices revise JSSP processing times from U(1,10) to U(1,100) and OP prizes from random integers to distance-dependent values. Unsupervised transfer adds a time-budget comparison. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish which changes reflect reruns versus documentation corrections.

E4.justification: V2 adds codebook ablations across eight transfer tasks and comparisons testing the benefit of multi-task versus single-task pretraining. The original mixed-attention and multi-type ablations are retained in Figure 5. V1's distance-shift experiments, large-instance JSSP analysis, adapter relearning/freezing observations and t-SNE analysis are no longer reported.

E5.justification: V2 first specifies best-of-ten reporting for supervised and unsupervised transfer curves and ten-run means with uncertainty bands for codebook ablations. V1 provides no comparable repeated-run reporting. Appendix C's phrase 'confidence interval of 100' leaves the interval construction unclear. These are new reporting practices, not evidence of an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise numerous gaps and runtimes: multi-task ATSP100 changes from 0.45% to 0.50%, and BQ-NCO's ATSP200 entry from 1.55% to 1.90%. V2 adds extensive transfer results, including best-of-ten unsupervised gaps of 0.11% for SOP and 2.92% for MCLP in Figure 4. Earlier shift and JSSP generalization results disappear. Changed training, data and transfer settings prevent interpreting the revisions as uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 introduces low-dimensional input projections followed by a shared codebook (Section 3.4). Transfer now trains fresh adapters instead of relying on compatible pretrained input adapters. Section 4.2 also adds unsupervised imitation-improvement: an expert samples 128 solutions from the current model and returns selected improvements for imitation. These change the architecture and adaptation procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, transfer section and conclusion are substantially rewritten, and the attention explanation is reorganized. The appendices are extensively restructured: hyperparameters move forward, supervised transfer and codebook sections are introduced, and task descriptions change from domain-grouped sections to an expanded alphabetical catalogue. The title changes from 'Agent Learner' to 'Agent Learning'.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to include the codebook. New transfer and uncertainty-band panels replace or supplement earlier displays, while the original attention and multi-type plots are merged into Figure 5. Table 2 moves to the appendix and loses its JSSP block. Grouped task overview tables become per-task specifications with relocated illustrations, and the t-SNE and distance-shift figures disappear.

R1.justification: V2 adds RouteFinder, Expert Iteration, self-labeling and self-improvement references, plus an HGS reference. It situates the new unsupervised procedure relative to these approaches. The broader positioning against specialized neural solvers and routing-focused multi-task approaches remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The tail-recursive BQ-MDP formulation, multi-task disjoint-union construction and mixed-attention mathematics are retained. V2 reorganizes v1's attention equation into equivalent expressions. It adds no substantive theorem, proof or formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: V1 identifies unstable learning of new input adapters as a central transfer bottleneck. V2 addresses it with a concrete codebook mechanism and ablations, demonstrates fresh-adapter transfer with and without labels, and adds single-task pretraining controls that better test the value of multi-task learning. Expanded implementation documentation further strengthens the paper. Removed shift/JSSP evidence, unclear uncertainty definitions and remaining oracle inconsistencies are drawbacks, but the central generalist-transfer contribution is substantially better supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GOAL by the same authors. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, supervised and unsupervised transfer experiments, comparisons with individually pretrained models, and architecture ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark results, transfer experiments, architecture ablations, distribution-shift tests and latent-representation analyses.

results.title: GOAL: A Generalist Combinatorial Optimization Agent Learner

C1.justification: The headline claims change from removing at least 90% of second-moment entries and saving 45–50% memory to removing at least 99.9% and saving 50%. Claimed LLM effectiveness expands from 125M–7B to 39M–13B. The central structural contribution is also revised: Value/MLP blocks previously described as dense wholes are replaced by neuron-level partitions, with token-level embedding/output partitions.

C2.justification: V6 replaces the whole-block and sparse-embedding rationale with token/neuron-level Hessian interpretations and a shared-backpropagation-error explanation for averaging. It adds qualifications about unclear Value structure, training-length-dependent partition choices, untested non-Transformer architectures, baseline tuning and uncertain generalization of the GPT-2 loss-spike finding (Sections 2.3–2.4 and Appendices B–C).

D1.justification: V6 replaces the TinyLlama implementation description with Torchtitan and adds scaling architecture/training tables, runtime information, synthetic-data and matrix-generation code, Hessian ordering instructions and the optimizer.wv_names switch. V1's CommonCrawl preprocessing/split instructions and GaLore configuration are removed. These materially change reproducibility documentation; the Adam-mini repository link itself is retained.

E1.justification: Llama pre-training changes from explicitly processed CommonCrawl 2019-30 data to C4. V6 also adds synthetic binary classification data for the MLP Hessian experiment. OpenWebText, UltraFeedback/MT-Bench, ImageNet, CelebA and OGBN-arxiv tasks remain; the changes are limited within the retained application domains.

E2.justification: V6 adds LAMB to the GPT-2-125M comparison, Adafactor-Zhai-version to Llama comparisons, and Lion evaluations in Appendix C.5. GaLore disappears from the GPT-2-125M comparison, while GaLore and SM3 disappear from the trajectory comparison. These are substantive comparator changes, verified in the corresponding plot legends.

E3.justification: V6 adds controlled scaling runs and 8B/13B evaluations, and reports revised Llama context lengths, batches and a 1% warm-up/linear schedule instead of 2,000-step warm-up/cosine decay. The Transformer Hessian study changes from four layers at initialization to one layer at 1% of training. The reported LoRA learning rate changes from 5e-6 to 2e-5. These are protocol revisions, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V6 adds MLP Hessian tracking throughout training, controlled matrix-density/preconditioning experiments, scaling analyses, detailed Adafactor/Lion sensitivity sweeps and an AdamW epsilon/loss-spike analysis. V1's layer-by-layer initialization Hessians and exceptional diagonal-block case study are removed or superseded. The trajectory comparison and LoRA analysis already existed in v1, although their reported comparisons are revised.

E5.justification: V6 Appendix E.2 specifies 100 Xavier initializations per matrix and 40 sampled angle configurations per dimension/condition-number pair, averaging results for Figure 5. This adds repeated-sampling estimation for a new diagnostic. It does not establish additional training seeds; the shared-seed trajectory design remains, and neither version provides systematic confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V6 adds scaling results, including 1B-model perplexities of 12.452 for AdamW and 12.372 for Adam-mini after 26.21B tokens (Table 5). Adam-mini's calculated Llama 2-7B optimizer memory changes from 28.04 to 26.96 GB (Table 1). Several training and trajectory curves change, and GPT-2-770M results disappear. MT-Bench and non-LLM table scores remain unchanged; revised experimental conditions preclude interpreting changed curves as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: V1 partitions Query/Key by head, otherwise generally uses whole parameter tensors, and retains coordinate-wise second moments for embedding/output layers. V6 Algorithms 1–3 instead partition embedding/output layers by token and Value/attention-projection/MLP matrices by output neuron, with a whole-Value option for short runs. This substantially changes learning-rate assignments and optimizer storage.

P1.justification: V6 extensively rewrites the abstract and method narrative, organizes motivation into explicit case studies, and revises the conclusion. Related work, the complete algorithm and non-LLM experiments move into appendices, which are reorganized from A–B into A–E. This substantially changes the document's narrative and organization.

P2.justification: V6 redraws Figure 2, replaces and expands Hessian displays, combines GPT-2 panels, and adds scaling, tuning and instability plots. Memory/throughput tables gain rows and subtables, and new configuration tables appear. Algorithms and LoRA/non-LLM displays are relocated or regrouped, alongside a changed page template and caption styling.

R1.justification: V6 Appendix A adds substantive comparisons with BAGM and NovoGrad, acknowledging earlier block/layer-wise adaptivity and distinguishing Adam-mini's Hessian-based partitions. It also distinguishes LAMB, discusses the relevance and limits of Das et al.'s preconditioning bounds, and substantially expands Hessian-related research positioning. These changes go beyond moving related work or updating citation style.

T1.justification: V6 adds an explicit cross-entropy Hessian expression for a one-hidden-layer network and its assumptions (Equation 1), plus mathematical definitions of matrix density and preconditioning effectiveness (Equation 3). These extend the mathematical reasoning beyond v1's qualitative discussion. The original quadratic construction remains, and no new convergence theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V6 substantially strengthens validation: the 26.21B-token Llama 2-1B run and scaling study test sustained training, while explicit Adafactor/Lion sweeps address v1's limited baseline-tuning evidence. Revised partition instructions and BAGM/NovoGrad comparisons clarify reproducibility and novelty. These gains outweigh the removed comparisons. A reporting weakness remains: v6's new blanket claim of identical AdamW hyperparameters conflicts with the different ReMax learning rates in Appendix E.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Adam-mini, with identifiable corresponding methods and experiments. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V6 reports original empirical results, including retained training experiments and additional scaling-law studies, Hessian diagnostics and optimizer comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization simulations, Transformer Hessian analyses, language-model training and alignment experiments, and vision and graph results.

results.title: Adam-mini: Use Fewer Learning Rates To Gain More

C1.justification: The training-free cascading-cache contribution remains, but v2 makes efficient linear prefill a central contribution, claiming a 6.8-fold advantage over Flash Attention at 1M tokens. Headline evidence shifts from v1's 59% cache-operation speedup and small-window benchmarks to much larger cache-speed claims, Booksum, and million-token retrieval. The claimed LongBench gain changes from 5.6% to 12.13%, while MMLU leaves the headline contributions.

C2.justification: v1 argues that homogeneous head decisions avoid positional misalignment and reports failure of naive independent selection; v2 Appendix B instead favors independent heads in its new experiments. v2 adds explanations linking stride size to dense attention and examines when token span stops predicting retrieval accuracy. Limitations shift toward bounded extrapolation and possible logarithmic retrieval, while v1's general positional-embedding limitation paragraph is dropped.

D1.justification: v2 documents stride settings, revised hardware allocations and model paths, and states that code accompanies the paper as a supplementary ZIP; the archive itself cannot be verified from these PDFs. It drops v1's explicit 16-bit precision statement and detailed MMLU prompting/cache protocol. Reproduction remains limited by missing Booksum-specific settings and Table 5's conflicting Llama3.1 labels and Meta-Llama-3 paths.

E1.justification: v2 adds Booksum narrative summarization and randomized passkey retrieval through 1M tokens. MMLU is retained in Appendix Table 4 and expands from STEM to humanities, social science, and other subjects. The Wikitext replay scenario in v1's introduction is removed. PG19 and the same six LongBench tasks remain.

E2.justification: PG19 removes both HyperAttention variants and adds BigBird. LongBench adds BigBird and truncated full attention to the retained Streaming LLM comparator, called Sink Cache in v1. MMLU adds full-context and truncated attention comparisons. New Booksum and latency comparisons introduce H2O and SnapKV.

E3.justification: v2 reports Llama3.1/Qwen2 backbones up to 70B/72B, changes sink tokens from 4 to 64, and replaces the cache-dependent EMA coefficient with 0.9999. PG19 changes from 25 books with 2K/4K caches to length-filtered subsets with 16K/32K/65K caches. LongBench replaces fixed 1024/2048 windows with prompt-dependent quarter-length budgets. Strided prefill, digit-level retrieval evaluation, and revised latency measurements introduce further protocol changes.

E4.justification: v2 adds stride-size studies of latency and perplexity and replaces the PG19 cascade-count study with passkey sparsity and expected-versus-observed accuracy analyses. Head-policy and reduction experiments are redesigned for the newer models and GQA. Token-selection ablation remains under changed settings, while v1's EMA-coefficient and cascade-acceptance-frequency sensitivity studies are removed.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports 20 randomized passkey trials per insertion-range/sequence-length cell, totaling 600 retrievals, and explicitly justifies omitting error bars through determinism (Section 7). Figure 6 also introduces polynomial estimation of latency beyond memory limits. These additions do not establish increased repetitions or improved uncertainty reporting for the retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: PG19, LongBench, MMLU, latency, and ablation results are extensively replaced under revised settings. For example, v1's Llama2-7B PG19 comparison at a 2048 window is 7.05 versus 6.97 perplexity; v2's reported Llama3.1-8B comparison at 32768 is 7.65 versus 7.60. New Booksum and retrieval results include average digit accuracy of 42.0% versus 17.8% at 1M tokens with a 65K cache (Figure 8). These are not same-setting improvements between versions.

M1.justification: v2 introduces chunked linear prefill, processing multiple queries jointly before updating the cache (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1); v1 describes tokenwise processing. Appendix B also introduces GQA-aware head reduction and permits independent head selection, replacing v1's prescribed homogeneous policy. Cascading eviction, attention-score EMA, and circular buffers already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, limitations, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The method gains a separate linear-prefill subsection and reorganizes the context-span and implementation explanations. Latency becomes the first experimental subsection, MMLU moves to the appendix, appendices are reorganized, and a reproducibility statement is added. The title and author presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a prefill illustration and retrieval heatmaps, replaces the latency table with three plots, and redesigns head and cascade ablations as heatmaps and curves. LongBench radar charts expand from two to four comparators. MMLU subject bar charts give way to an appendix category table. Existing attention diagrams receive revised annotations, alongside extensive table and page-layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 substantially reframes novelty around linear prefill relative to SnapKV and H2O, rather than primarily extending Streaming LLM's retained context. It adds discussion and citations for these methods, SEA, and GQA, while removing references including HyperAttention, LongLoRA, and positional-extrapolation work. This changes substantive research positioning beyond the switch in citation style.

T1.justification: The attention equations and exponential cache-span expression in Equation 4 remain mathematically equivalent, despite renaming approximate context length to token span. v2 removes v1 Appendix B's derivation of the cache-dependent EMA coefficient and adds the explicit sparsity definition 1 - |C|/token-span. These are limited formal changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the practical contribution: strided prefill addresses a prompt-processing gap in v1 and is tested for both latency and perplexity, while quality comparisons also give Streaming LLM the prefill adaptation. Million-token retrieval directly tests long-range retention beyond v1's small-window evidence. These gains outweigh the removed sensitivity analyses, although the 6.8-fold headline relies on extrapolated baseline latency, and incomplete experimental settings and conflicting model paths limit reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cascading KV Cache research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark, Booksum, passkey retrieval, latency, and ablation results. Appendix results include expanded MMLU evaluation and head-policy experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original PG19, LongBench, MMLU-STEM, Wikitext replay, latency, and ablation results, including additional experiments in the appendices.

results.title: Training Free Exponential Context Extension via Cascading KV Cache

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion broaden the reported empirical contribution from eight open-source model families with 10 checkpoints to 24 open-source entries and two closed-source models. The central claims about dynamic, scalable synthetic generation, perceptual coverage, and the validity of synthetic evaluation remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking performance to language-model capacity, question-type sensitivity to language-model biases, commercial-model responses to safety training, and marine-animal weaknesses to training-data scarcity. It also interprets blind, KMMD, and audit findings as evidence of fairness and reliability. v1's detailed common-versus-uncommon-style interpretation disappears. The existing limitation concerning rule-based generation of cognition questions remains.

D1.justification: v3 discloses the CLIP filtering threshold of 0.75, adds visual-encoder identifiers and evaluation JSON examples in Appendix I, and specifies details of the new audits. The repository address changes from Benchmark-Dysca/Dysca to Robin-WZQ/Dysca, and the datasheet supplies creator and maintainer/contact information. Hardware and licensing disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The 20 Dysca subtasks, 51 styles, and four image scenarios remain. v3 adds a text-only test scenario, including LLaVA comparisons on MMMU, ScienceQA, AI2D, and MathVista in Appendix D. Its new distribution analysis also uses additional image collections, including CCBench, COCO-Val, MMVet, MME, and MMStar.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from 10 checkpoints to 26 entries, adding methods including XComposer2-VL, GLM-4V, MiniCPM-V2.5, Yi-VL, mPLUG-Owl-2, Phi-3-Vision, GPT-4o, and Gemini-1.5-Pro. Additional BLIP2, InstructBLIP, and MiniGPT configurations are evaluated. v1's separate Shikra-VQA entry is absent from the corresponding principal comparison, although it remains in the retained stability plot.

E3.justification: v3 introduces SQ/SC evaluation metrics and image-withholding controls. New protocols include CLIP-feature KMMD comparisons using an RBF kernel and up to 3,000 images per benchmark, plus a 7.7K-image manual audit. Tables also revise Shikra's stated language backbone from Vicuna-7B to LLaMA-7B. Averaging the three question-type scores already appeared in v1 Appendix A and is not a new protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds hierarchical inter-task and animal-category analyses, blind controls, distribution comparisons, and new failure cases. Appendix C audits 7.7K images, identifies 167 problematic images, and measures the effect of excluding them; Appendix B adds a NudeNet safety audit. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's correlations and size-stability analysis. The original stability analysis remains, while the detailed 51-style heatmap analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The new SQ/SC variances measure performance variation across question types and styles, rather than uncertainty in estimated performance. The retained stability plot also provides no uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Many retained-model values change: BLIP2/Flan-T5-XL's clean style TF accuracy is 88.62 in v1 Table 3 and 35.45 in v3 Table 8. v3 adds expanded rankings and blind, sensitivity, KMMD, and audit results, while omitting some question-format and noisy-subtask breakdowns. The correlation coefficients in v1 Table 5 and v3 Table 4 are identical. Revised cleaning prevents treating updated scores as established same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: v3 Section 3.3 extends the stated construction procedure with rejection using the top six LVLMs and subsequent removal of problematic metadata vocabulary and associated samples. v1 already included manual metadata screening and CLIP/OCR filtering, but not these additional components. The reported filtering rate changes from approximately 15% to 40%, while the underlying image and rule-based question generation remains.

P1.justification: The existing results narrative is substantially rewritten and reorganized into separate Key Observations, Inter-task/Intra-task Analysis, and Validity sections. Cleaning and introductory comparison passages are expanded, and the appendix presentation gains dedicated validation and documentation sections. Much background prose and the example/datasheet material remain, but the empirical narrative undergoes substantial restructuring.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the main results presentation with a colored 26-model matrix and moves the expanded clean-subtask tables into Appendix A. It removes the original style heatmap and question-type example panel, adds clustering and KMMD heatmaps, radar charts, audit tables, and failure-case panels, and substantially reworks the appendix leaderboards. Pipeline diagrams, metadata displays, and most example figures are retained with layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting newer models, statistical tools, label-error comparisons, and safety auditing, and briefly discusses commercial LVLM APIs. The principal benchmark taxonomy and positioning of Dysca against existing-image benchmarks and JourneyDB remain. The introduction more explicitly presents the annotation-cost comparison with MME, without substantially redefining the research positioning.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.4 adds mathematical definitions of chance-normalized question-type sensitivity SQ and across-style sensitivity SC in Equations 1–2. These are new metric definitions, absent from v1, but constitute a limited mathematical extension without accompanying theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct measurement of annotation correctness. v3's 7.7K-image audit, reported 2.2% error rate, and score comparison after excluding errors substantially strengthen that evidence. Blind and distribution comparisons further examine benchmark validity, while broader model comparisons and diagnostic analyses improve its usefulness. These gains outweigh the loss of some detailed result breakdowns, although filtering based on top-performing models leaves a selection-bias concern, and blind performance alone does not establish freedom from data leakage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Dysca and retain its central benchmark framework. The main texts, tables, figures, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 reports an expanded 26-model main comparison and original blind evaluations, clustering analyses, distribution comparisons, and dataset correctness and safety audits.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 10 LVLM checkpoints, including perceptual-task scores, attack robustness, benchmark correlations, and evaluation-size stability experiments.

results.title: Dysca: A Dynamic and Scalable Benchmark for Evaluating Perception Ability of LVLMs

C1.justification: Both versions claim that token-gradient identification and a routing regularizer reduce expert interference, provide a plug-in for MoE-based LVLMs and improve performance, particularly with more diverse training data. Rewritten motivation and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds the limitation that detecting conflict with a current expert does not identify the optimal alternative expert. It also explains the mean-gradient choice through training stability, discusses training overhead, interprets residual conflicts in shallow layers, and develops explanations involving routing pathways, loss optimization and feature-gradient relationships.

D1.justification: Sections 6.1–6.4 disclose bias-gradient extraction, cosine averaging, parameter freezing, training hyperparameters, hardware, precision, data-mixture prompts and comparator implementations. They explicitly identify the 1021K training setting behind Table 1 and report throughput and memory estimates. These substantially improve implementation documentation; the promised code-release location remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Section 6.5 and Table 12 extend evaluation from vision-language tasks to text-only GLUE tasks: CoLA, MRPC, QNLI, MNLI and RTE. Existing visual benchmarks and the 665K/1021K training-data comparisons remain; the newly detailed training-mixture constituents do not establish additional coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 4 expands the earlier embedding-versus-gradient comparison with feature-based and task-based routing implementations within MoE-LLaVA, documented in Section 6.2. Table 10 also introduces comparisons with Batch Prioritized Routing enabled. The headline LVLM comparator set in Table 1 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce BERT-large with eight experts and Top-2 activation, inference-capacity tests at 2.0 and 0.5 with and without Batch Prioritized Routing, and additional gradient-diagnostic metrics and procedures. Newly disclosed training settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments were changed or rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds load-balancing-weight and loss-design ablations, capacity robustness tests, activated-pathway analysis, gradient distributions, feature-gradient correlations and confusing-token case studies. Threshold and regularizer-weight sweeps are retained. Conversely, v2 Table 4(a)'s layer-subset ablation and Figure 3(a)'s direct routing-score diagnostic are removed.

E5.justification: Section 6.3.3 and Figure 8 newly report standard deviation of gradient consistency across experts, extending v2's mean-based summaries. This measures across-expert dispersion, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Headline benchmark scores in Tables 1–2 and the relocated scalability results remain unchanged. The expanded embedding comparison replaces results, including GQA 56.1 in v2 Table 3(a) with 57.0 in v3 Table 4. New results include GLUE averages of 81.5 for reimplemented MoE and 82.8 with STGC, computational overhead, robustness and diagnostic findings; several older ablation entries disappear.

M1.justification: The central STGC identification procedure and regularizer remain unchanged; L_token is renamed L_CEL. Section 6.3.4 adds an optional integration with Batch Prioritized Routing during inference. Bias-only gradient extraction is newly documented implementation information, without establishing a redesign of the method used for retained results.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and methodological explanations receive extensive rewriting around router optimization and conflicting-token identification. Ablation discussion is reordered, a limitations subsection is added, and a structured seven-part supplement is introduced. Terminology, author information and conference headers are also updated.

P2.justification: Figure 3 removes panels and rearranges retained curves; the threshold and loss-weight tables are consolidated, and the scalability table is relocated. Expert-loading displays are revised and expanded with routing pathways. Numerous new supplementary tables and plots present implementation settings, diagnostics, robustness, computational costs and language results.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against recent MoE and LoRA approaches, including Octavius/LoRA-MoE, MoLA, MoME, CuMo and Uni-MoE. It adds distinctions from PCGrad and discussions of compatibility with V-MoE and MoNE. DEMIX and several broad LLM references disappear.

T1.justification: Beyond v2's conflicting-token definition and first-order interference argument, Section 6.6 introduces convexity and Lipschitz-gradient assumptions, a learning-rate restriction and a descent/convergence derivation around Equation 15. This substantially expands the theory, although its purported loss-increase case requires an unattainable cosine condition.

improvement.justification: v2 leaves practical gradient extraction and training costs largely unexplained. v3 documents the bias-gradient approximation, training settings and approximately 21% step-time overhead, substantially improving reproducibility and feasibility assessment. New routing, loss and capacity controls plus language-task results strengthen validation. These gains outweigh removed diagnostics and introduced weaknesses: Section 6.6 uses an impossible cosine condition, and Table 4 reports a task-based average of 48.9 although its listed scores average about 55.0.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe STGC and retain matching core formulations and benchmark results. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v2 ends after its references; v3 additionally contains supplementary Sections 6.1–6.7.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds routing comparisons, language-task evaluations, computational measurements and gradient diagnostics, including Tables 8–14.

before.justification: v2 reports original STGC benchmark comparisons, ablations, gradient analyses and expert-loading results in Tables 1–5 and Figures 1, 3 and 4.

results.title: Solving Token Gradient Conflict in Mixture-of-Experts for Large Vision-Language Model

C1.justification: The contribution list replaces the scalable-data-pipeline contribution with image-coordinate action alignment for data-efficient transfer, which the conclusion also emphasizes. The claim of requiring no external data is narrowed to requiring no extra action labels or task/action supervision. The central policy-learning and auxiliary-data claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix B.3 more explicitly attributes auxiliary-data gains to information rather than additional optimization steps, extending v1's underfitting discussion. Section 6.2 interprets the new tests as preserved generalization after tuning. Limitations more specifically associate textual-description and detector constraints with additional reference images; the main noise and 3D-movement limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 specifies cosine scheduling, a 0.03 warm-up ratio, maximum learning rate of 2e-5, xArm7/Logitech C140 hardware, and cropping from 640×480 to 640×320. It also clarifies baseline action encoding. These are newly documented details, without evidence that retained experiments changed; the code/data/model access statement already existed.

E1.justification: V2 adds testing with ten unseen complex rephrasings of real-world task instructions. VIMA and xArm coverage otherwise remain stable: distractors and the weighing-and-return task already appear in v1's Figures 11–12. Using all 660k VIMA trajectories expands training volume, rather than establishing new task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 introduces and evaluates D-RT-2 Style (I), which encodes image-coordinate actions with special tokens, providing an important control for the natural-language formulation. It also expands the VIMA comparison to include RT-2-style baselines trained on the full dataset (Table 9), substantially strengthening the comparator design.

E3.justification: New experiments train RT-2-style baselines on all 660k VIMA trajectories for one through four epochs (Table 20). Appendix B.7 adds random, absent, and fifteen fixed inference-prompt conditions, while Section 6.2 adds explicit zero-shot/finetuned generalization evaluations. These extend the evaluation design; retained experiments keep their existing metrics and settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds a systematic action-prompt sensitivity study (Appendix B.7, Figure 13) and quantitative robustness tests involving distractors, complex rephrasing, and weighing-and-return behavior (Table 4). Existing auxiliary-data, action-history, planning, multiple-image, and detector ablations are retained. The longer-training analysis already existed and is extended with the new comparator.

E5.justification: V2 first explicitly reports twenty randomly initialized real-world episodes per setting. Simulation evaluation retains twenty random seeds, now described as per task. This is additional reporting, not evidence of increased repetition; neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Matched existing numerical results retain their values. V2 adds image-coordinate baseline results, full-VIMA baseline results, and prompt-sensitivity measurements. Its new Table 4 reports distractor/rephrasing/weighing success rates of 10/0/0% zero-shot and 75/40/20% after finetuning. These substantially extend the empirical record rather than show same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The LLaVA-based policy, image-coordinate action representation, inBC/D-inBC conversion, six auxiliary tasks, action history, and multi-step planning remain unchanged. Action prediction and planning details emphasized in v2 already appear in v1's figures and Appendix A.1.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and reorganizes the narrative: related-work discussions are consolidated, method subsections become compact thematic paragraphs, auxiliary-task descriptions are paired, and real-world details move into a dedicated appendix. The expanded experiments gain numbered subsections, and a reproducibility statement is added.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, merges v1's Figures 6–7, relocates training curves and qualitative examples, and adds robot-setup and prompt-sensitivity figures. It expands comparison tables and adds generalization/full-data tables, alongside widespread layout and table-format changes. Relocated results remain available in the appendices.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds SpatialVLM and sequence-model/self-supervised-learning references and develops explicit distinctions from PaLM-E and SpatialVLM. It removes the designation of 3D-VLA as the closest work while retaining its citation. These refine positioning around direct action generation and auxiliary supervision without replacing the overall research framing.

T1.justification: The MDP, demonstration-dataset, and history-conditioned policy formulations are unchanged. Neither version adds substantive theorems, proofs, derivations, or formal guarantees; revised notation and action-space explanations do not alter the mathematics.

improvement.justification: The coordinate-matched token baseline and full-data RT-2-style experiments address important gaps in v1's evidence for its action formulation and data efficiency (Appendices A.4 and B.2). Quantitative generalization tests make previously anecdotal capabilities assessable, while implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. Some new generalization language exceeds what the 40% rephrasing and 20% weighing results justify, but the stronger controls and more transparent evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLaRA work. Their main text, figures, tables, mathematical formulation, and complete appendices support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds baseline evaluations, prompt-sensitivity results, and quantitative real-world generalization tests.

before.justification: V1 reports original VIMA-Bench evaluations, ablations, and real-world robot experiments under zero-shot, finetuning, and joint-training protocols.

results.title: LLaRA: Supercharging Robot Learning Data for Vision-Language Policy

C1.justification: v3 adds last-iterate convergence as an explicit theoretical contribution and broadens its empirical superiority claim from iterative DPO to online RLHF methods including SPPO. The abstract and introduction remove the earlier contribution claim concerning KL regularization for response-length control.

C2.justification: The explanation for academic benchmark gains changes from the small training-prompt budget to better use of pretrained knowledge and abilities. Appendix B attributes smaller gains from instruction-tuned initialization to prior RLHF limiting further improvement. The response-length-control interpretation is withdrawn; finite-sample analysis remains future work.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds SPPO implementation-source information and the instruction-tuned checkpoint reference, and revises the documented eta selection. Section 4.1 explicitly identifies other LLM comparison scores as copied from Dong et al. Existing scheduler, warm-up, batch-size, and tournament details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same training prompt collections, three alignment benchmarks, and six academic benchmarks. Appendix B adds an instruction-tuned model initialization, which changes the model configuration rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated SPPO comparisons to both the main alignment and academic benchmark tables while retaining the existing comparators. This substantively strengthens comparison against general-preference methods: v1 cited SPPO as the closest related work but did not report its performance.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes the reported eta from 0.0075 to 0.005, retaining tau = eta/3, and adds experiments initialized from LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct. Average response length is no longer reported. The principal benchmark metrics, judges, three training iterations, and eight-response sampling remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The KL-with/without ablation remains, but v3 removes its response-length measurements and associated length-control analysis. Appendix B adds an examination of whether alignment gains persist when training starts from an already instruction-tuned checkpoint.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The expanded tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Many scores are replaced: Table 1 INPO (PM) changes from 41.5/38.3/8.35 to 42.6/37.8/8.43 on AlpacaEval/Arena-Hard/MT-Bench. The academic GPQA comparison reverses from INPO 30.5 versus SFT 27.8 to 28.9 versus 30.2. SPPO rows and Appendix B Tables 4–5 are added, while response-length results disappear. Changed hyperparameters and incompletely explained score revisions prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same OMD update, pairwise squared loss, current-policy sampling, and final-iterate output. The tournament selection details in v3 Section 4.1 already appear in v1 Appendix B. The new convergence analysis does not replace the experimental procedure.

P1.justification: v3 locally rewrites the preliminaries and algorithm exposition, replaces the detailed Online IPO subsection, swaps the academic-results and ablation subsections, and moves tournament details into the main text. Appendix B gains separate implementation and results paragraphs. The title and overall six-section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds two appendix tables and SPPO rows in retained benchmark tables, removes parenthetical response-length entries, and updates captions and highlighting. The academic and ablation tables exchange order. The table style and single-column layout remain substantially unchanged; neither version contains figures.

R1.justification: v3 adds Tang et al. (2024) to motivate online rather than offline alignment and expands discussion contrasting current-policy sampling with prior geometric-mixture approaches. The existing game-theoretic positioning and core related-work coverage remain largely unchanged; SPPO was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Assumption A changes from bounded negative log reference probability to bounded log-density ratios along feasible iterates. Lemma 2 and Theorem 3 replace reference entropy with D = max KL(pi || pi1), with corresponding proof revisions. New Theorem 4 and Appendix A.3 establish last-iterate contraction and an O(1/T) KL bound using eta_t = tau(t+2)/2.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the theoretical foundation through revised assumptions and initialization-dependent regret bounds, plus last-iterate analysis where v1 justified only the averaged policy. Evaluating SPPO, the closest general-preference competitor, also addresses an important comparative gap. The new convergence rate requires a varying eta, unlike the reported fixed experimental setting; unexplained score revisions and removed length diagnostics limit verification. Nevertheless, the stronger foundational analysis and direct comparative evidence constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same INPO research work. Their main text, equations, tables, and Appendices A–B are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations and ablations, including additional experiments initialized from LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original INPO evaluations on three alignment benchmarks and six academic benchmarks, plus a KL-regularization ablation.

results.title: Iterative Nash Policy Optimization: Aligning LLMs with General Preferences via No-Regret Learning

C1.justification: The central claim that min-p improves the creativity–coherence balance, especially at high temperatures, is retained. v2 adds an explicit claim of human preference and identifies practical parameter guidelines as a contribution in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning scaling to larger models, the accuracy–diversity frontier, parameter sensitivity and practical efficiency relative to eta/epsilon sampling. Appendix A adds specific limitations about hyperparameter selection and evaluating pre-generated rather than interactive outputs, alongside new connections between uncertainty and chain-of-thought reasoning.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands documentation of tested hyperparameters and selection rationale, human-study procedures, A100 runtime observations, and inference-engine integrations. It retains the implementation code and adds an anonymous repository address. However, v1's identification of Claude as the AlpacaEval judge and its explicit Exact Match reporting statement disappear.

E1.justification: GPQA, GSM8K and AlpacaEval Creative Writing remain the benchmark coverage. v2 adds a small creative-story study using the prompt 'Write me a creative story?' and English-fluent regular LLM users. Larger models and self-consistency extend evaluation settings rather than benchmark domains.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds top-k, eta and epsilon sampling to the GPQA/GSM8K comparisons, which previously evaluated min-p against top-p and unrestricted sampling. Table 3b also adds epsilon sampling to the creative-writing comparison. Mirostat was already evaluated in v1 Table 3.

E3.justification: v2 adds Mistral Large 123B evaluations, GSM8K self-consistency with an embedding-based entropy measure, and a Llama 3 70B human-study protocol using three outputs per configuration and 1–10 ratings. It also reports additional temperature settings. The existing 5-shot GPQA and 8-shot GSM8K prompting are retained.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 2 introduces an accuracy–diversity frontier and parameter-sensitivity analysis; Appendix B.2 adds runtime and high-temperature failure analysis for eta/epsilon sampling. The original case studies and temperature plots remain. The newly titled AlpacaEval ablation mostly repackages v1 Table 3, while omitting its weaker min-p configurations at temperature 1.5.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without corresponding uncertainty estimates or formal significance tests. v2 Table 4 introduces mean±SD human ratings, and Section 6 reports a paired t-test with p < 0.05. Benchmark seed counts and repeated-run uncertainty remain unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline, larger-model, accuracy–diversity and human-rating results. For example, Table 3a newly reports Mistral Large GPQA accuracy of 22.77% for min-p versus 2.01% for both top-p settings at temperature 3. Original plots survive in Appendix C.3, but Table 6 omits v1's temperature-1.5 min-p results with win rates 48.13% and 42.09%.

M1.justification: The threshold pbase × pmax, token filtering and renormalized sampling remain equivalent. The MinPLogitsWarper implementation in v1 Appendix A is retained in v2 Appendix B. Self-consistency is introduced as an evaluation procedure without changing the min-p algorithm.

P1.justification: The title and much of the prose are rewritten. Related work moves near the beginning, the separate background section is absorbed into other sections, methodology expands into several subsections, and experiments and results are reorganized. Human evaluation, reproducibility and ethics statements are added, and limitations move to Appendix A.

P2.justification: The main document changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 is rearranged into a grid, the case-study tables are merged, and original benchmark plots move to the appendix. New benchmark summaries, human-rating tables and an accuracy–diversity plot substantially change the presentation. Figure 1's revised caption incorrectly identifies several retained panels.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around computationally costly entropy-based methods and connects min-p to risk-based parameter calibration, self-consistency and uncertainty-guided reasoning. It adds relevant work such as Zhou et al. and Wang et al., while dropping v1's dedicated discussions of locally typical sampling and contrastive decoding.

T1.justification: The defining mathematics of min-p remains equivalent, and neither version provides theorems or proofs. v1's background decoding formulas are condensed into prose. v2's threshold example explains the existing rule, while its entropy measure is an evaluation addition without a formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly identifies its single-model scope and lack of human evaluation as limitations. v2 substantially addresses these through larger-model results and direct human assessments of quality and diversity, reinforced by the new accuracy–diversity analysis and broader baseline comparisons. These additions strengthen evidence for the central claim. The single-prompt human study, omitted weaker AlpacaEval configurations, incomplete experimental details and Figure 1 caption errors qualify—but do not outweigh—the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same min-p sampling method and share identifiable experiments, implementation code and figures. Their main text and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments, a GSM8K accuracy–diversity analysis, larger-model evaluations and a human study with 54 retained responses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Mistral 7B experiments on GPQA and GSM8K across sampling parameters and temperatures, including results in Figures 2–5.

results.title: Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs

C1.justification: The central claims about dynamic truncation, high-temperature quality/diversity, and human preference remain. The introduction explicitly broadens the experimental contribution to multiple model families and sizes and extends the practical-impact claim to advanced reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1.

C2.justification: V3 newly diagnoses limitations of the original human study, including sampling-order differences and participants overlooking incoherence. It adds explanations for low-temperature convergence, possible problems with combined samplers, and the diversity cost of higher min-p thresholds, plus an argument against universally optimal greedy decoding. Appendix A.5 also acknowledges false positives behind the earlier adoption estimates.

D1.justification: V3 substantially expands reproducibility documentation: it identifies benchmark inference frameworks and details the original survey's recruitment, compensation, presentation, filtering, and data processing. New evaluations include schemas, constraint libraries, prompts, parameter grids, judge instructions, and logging information. These disclosures extend far beyond v2's implementation listing and general experimental descriptions, although some new study details remain incomplete.

E1.justification: The principal reasoning and creative-writing tasks are retained. Appendix C.3 adds three creative-writing prompts requiring schema-constrained outputs, extending coverage to structured generation. The added Llama models concern experimental configurations; cited EQ-Bench, DeepSeek-R1, and agent-training work do not establish additional original task evaluations.

E2.justification: V3 substantially broadens reported comparisons: Table 7 adds greedy and configurations labeled tfs, quad, and dynatemp to AlpacaEval comparisons; Table 12 evaluates combined top-p/top-k sampling. Table 4 newly reports standard-sampling controls for the original human study, alongside the retained min-p and top-p results.

E3.justification: New benchmark settings cover Llama 3.2 1B/3B and Llama 3.1 8B/70B. The second human study changes the inference engine and reported temperature/truncation ordering, thresholds, recruitment, story presentation, and rating instructions. Appendix C.3 introduces structured generation, randomized blind comparisons, and five judge-rated metrics. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial analyses of low-temperature behavior, combined top-p/top-k sampling, higher min-p thresholds, and greedy decoding comparisons (Tables 10–14). Tables 17–18 analyze temperature and configuration effects in constrained writing. The original entropy/Pareto analysis remains, while v2's full benchmark sweep plots are omitted.

E5.justification: Human-evaluation reporting changes from mean ± SD to mean ± standard error, with condition-specific paired-test annotations. Tables 2–3 newly state approximate standard errors of 1–1.5 percentage points and mark results accordingly. Table 7 identifies a seed1337 configuration, but neither version establishes a general repeated-run protocol or an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 and the original min-p/top-p human means remain unchanged, but v3 adds extensive model, control, ablation, and evaluation results. Under the new human-study protocol, Table 15 reports temperature-3 quality scores of 5.80 for min-p=0.1 versus 1.23 for top-p=0.9. AlpacaEval metric assignments also change: v2 Table 6 reports 58.12/56.54 for win rate/LC win rate at min-p=0.1, temperature 1.5; v3 Table 7 reports 56.54/58.12. This reversal does not establish a performance gain.

M1.justification: The core min-p equations and implementation remain unchanged. Appendix D.2 introduces an exploratory min-z variant with a median-centered logit selection rule; it is not incorporated into the reported min-p experiments.

P1.justification: V3 reorganizes the appendices into implementation, benchmark results, additional evaluations, and applications/future work, moving the original limitations discussion to D.2. It extensively documents the existing human study and revises the evaluation narrative and resource discussion. Much of the core method prose remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V3 retains Figures 1–2 but removes v2 Figures 3–6. It redesigns the human-evaluation table to include controls and statistical annotations, expands the AlpacaEval table with configuration identifiers and output lengths, and adds numerous benchmark, analysis, and evaluation tables. Conference formatting also changes headings, headers, and the author block.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially through connections to Top-Nσ as a successor method, independent replications, greedy-decoding studies, adaptive decoding, reinforcement-learning exploration, and DeepSeek-R1 deployment. These relationships are developed in the reproducibility statement and Appendix D, beyond the largely retained traditional-sampler review. Two earlier Shwartz-Ziv information-theory references are removed.

T1.justification: The original min-p mathematical definitions are retained. Appendix D.2 adds explicit threshold and selection-set definitions for Top-Nσ and the proposed min-z variant. No new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee for min-p is supplied.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation through additional model families and sizes, broader comparisons, and a second human study addressing the reported temperature/truncation-order problem. Detailed protocols and correction of misleading adoption estimates improve transparency. Important reporting problems remain: Table 14 conflicts with underlying benchmark tables, and the second study's sample size is unspecified. Nevertheless, the gains in empirical validation and methodological accountability constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same min-p sampling work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds Llama benchmark results, a second human evaluation, and a structured creative-writing evaluation using an LLM judge.

before.justification: V2 reports original GPQA and GSM8K experiments, a self-consistency analysis, and a human evaluation with 54 retained respondents.

results.title: Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes language inequality and GPT-3/GPT-4 differences in dominant moral justifications. v2 removes the justification claims and foregrounds generally weak human alignment across 19 models. It also redefines the inequality question around high- versus low-resource languages and concludes that systematic disadvantage is not demonstrated, rather than treating cross-language differences themselves as inequality.

C2.justification: Interpretations of utilitarianism/fairness shifts and language-specific comprehension failures give way to explanations involving preference diversity, influential moral dimensions, and speaker-count correlations. v2 newly argues that procedural generation avoids training exposure when interpreting those correlations. It also expands discussion of dimension-dependent refusals and the limits of treating trolley-task alignment as real-world moral competence.

D1.justification: v2 adds open-model checkpoint identifiers and VRAM requirements, five exact paraphrases, dataset statistics, translation-checking information, and details of demographic-source collection and first-language weighting. Conversely, v1's explicit system-role prompt and full response transcripts disappear. The code/data link is retained. Some documentation remains inconsistent, including the vignette total and model identifiers.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same trolley-problem domain, six moral dimensions, random-character scenarios, and Moral Machine human reference data. Appendix B.1 contains the same 107 language codes in both versions; v1's references to 106 do not establish narrower coverage. Paraphrases test the retained task within existing languages.

E2.justification: v1 Table 4 compares nine GPT variants; v2 Figure 2 compares 19 models, adding Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen, and GPT-4o Mini. Older GPT variants and GPT-3.5 disappear from the reported preference comparisons, although GPT-3.5 remains in v2's API documentation table.

E3.justification: v2 introduces global speaker-weighted model scoring, language-sensitivity measurement, four-cluster analysis, and a five-paraphrase evaluation on 14 languages using Llama 3 8B and 70B. The latter adds agreement, kappa, F1, and accuracy metrics. The underlying L2 distance and zero-temperature decoding were already present in v1.

E4.justification: v1's character-level preference analysis, reason decomposition, answer-eligibility analysis, order-consistency results, and extended response case studies are removed. v2 adds model-specific language clustering, analyses of dimensions associated with misalignment, speaker-count correlations, and paraphrase robustness tests. These substantially replace the questions investigated by the supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports descriptive frequencies without inferential uncertainty assessment. v2 adds Pearson correlations with significance reporting for moral dimensions and speaker counts, including coefficients and p-values for all 19 models in Table 10. It also newly states that generation uses a fixed random seed. Neither version establishes repeated-run uncertainty estimates or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v1's reason-distribution results, including GPT-4's 52.72% utilitarianism and 41.85% fairness, disappear. v2 newly reports three Llama models with global misalignment below 0.6, near-zero speaker-count correlations, and paraphrase results of 75.9% four-of-five agreement, 78% F1, and 81% accuracy. Its world map evaluates Llama 3.1 70B instead of GPT-4, so this is a replacement result rather than a same-model improvement.

M1.justification: The core MULTITP construction and prompting approach remains: controlled trolley scenarios, automatic translation, and forced-choice completion. The prompt called token-forcing in v2 already appears in v1 Section 4.3. New scoring and analysis procedures change evaluation rather than establish a new model or inference method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, dataset exposition, and conclusions are extensively rewritten. The results narrative becomes five research questions with separate methods and findings, replacing the moral-tendencies/meta-behaviors organization. The appendices are substantially reorganized, and the extended multilingual-example appendix is removed.
