P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format. Reason-decomposition charts and capability histograms are replaced by ranked bars, violin plots, radar plots, and cluster boxplots, with several new tables. Figure 1 is reformatted, and the world map moves to the appendix with a different model, scale, and legend.

R1.justification: v2 substantially reframes the study around pluralistic alignment and psychological evaluation, explicitly distinguishes it from Takemoto's Moral Machine LLM study, and expands Table 1 with MoCa, GlobalOpinionQA, OffTheRails, and PRISM. It also recognizes controlled variation in MoralExceptQA, qualifying v1's stronger contrast with prior datasets. Literature supporting the removed moral-reason categories is dropped.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5.3 introduces a formal definition of cross-language sensitivity using dispersion of language-specific preferences. The displayed L2 misalignment equation otherwise formalizes the distance already described in v1 Appendix D. Neither version contains substantial theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for general claims about LLM alignment: v1's GPT-centered comparisons and descriptive language examples are supplemented or replaced by comparisons across multiple model families, explicit speaker-count tests, and quantified prompt robustness. These address important weaknesses in generality and evidential support, while checkpoint documentation improves reproducibility. The loss of detailed rationale analyses is a meaningful tradeoff. Dataset/model documentation inconsistencies remain, and null correlations do not prove equal alignment, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the MULTITP study, despite the changed title and substantially revised analyses. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 19 LLMs, language clustering, correlation analyses, and paraphrase robustness results in Section 5 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM preference measurements, reason classifications, and language-specific capability and consistency results in Sections 5–6 and Appendices D–E.

results.title: Language Model Alignment in Multilingual Trolley Problems

C1.justification: The dataset and MVDiT contributions persist, but v3's introduction makes superiority on video restoration an explicit third contribution. This substantially extends the claimed usefulness beyond v2's text-to-video-focused contributions. The motivation also shifts from manageable dataset size toward maintaining million-scale coverage with better videos and captions.

C2.justification: The central quality and alignment interpretations remain. v3 adds explanations of caching redundancy and restoration benefits, and acknowledges caption hallucinations and remaining motion-description weaknesses. Its limitations remove the explicit inability to model long-duration dynamics and add a hypothesis that more high-quality training data could improve physical realism.

D1.justification: v3 Table 1 adds GPU counts and processing times; Appendix A.1 details scoring, three cascaded cut detectors, and human-guided filtering thresholds; Section 6.1 expands staged-resolution training documentation. Conversely, v2's hosting, CC-BY-4.0 licensing, maintenance discussion, and frozen-encoder statement disappear. These are documentation changes, not evidence that access or encoder training actually changed.

E1.justification: v3 extends evaluation beyond text-to-video generation to arbitrary-resolution video restoration, including a low-resolution UDM10 example in Figure 7, and adds direct human assessment of caption quality. Existing generation coverage remains; Panda-50M-HD is a resolution-selected subset of previously used data.

E2.justification: Relative to v2 Table 2, v3 Table 3 adds CogVideoX-5B and replaces OpenSoraPlan-V1.1 with V1.2 in the quantitative comparison; V1.1 remains in qualitative figures. The restoration experiment introduces Upscale-A-Video as a comparator. The earlier qualitative comparison against Gen2 is removed.

E3.justification: v3 adds a native-HD Panda training control, restoration training using approximately 130K synthesized samples with fidelity, perceptual, and temporal metrics, and a caption study covering 1,117 samples and 10 volunteers using four five-point criteria and preferences. These introduce substantial evaluation designs; the retained 700-prompt generation benchmark and existing 50K-step controls remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 Table 7 adds MHCA and scaling-parameter ablations, with a further reported failure when MMTA is removed. Caption-error assessment and attention-redundancy/caching analyses add new diagnostic evidence. Existing resolution, architecture, and training-data ablations remain in Table 6; v2's filtering ablation moves unchanged from Table 5 to v3 Table 9.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v3's caption-rating means and preference percentages remain point estimates; the volunteer count describes study size rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained generation scores are unchanged, including Ours at 73.46 VQAA and 68.58 VQAT. Adding CogVideoX-5B at 76.86 VQAT changes the latter ranking to second. New results include the native-HD Panda control, restoration and module-ablation scores, 80.75% preference for generated captions, up to 1.7× inference acceleration, and replacement qualitative examples.

M1.justification: The core curation pipeline and MVDiT architecture remain unchanged. However, v3 Appendix C introduces an inference procedure that caches and reuses attention and feedforward outputs on alternating denoising steps without retraining. Expanded descriptions of filtering and MVDiT otherwise document existing components.

P1.justification: v3 revises and condenses introductory, related-work, curation, and method prose, updates conference front matter and citation style, and reorganizes the appendices. The dataset overview moves into Section 4 and filtering ablations move to Appendix B. The main section sequence and substantial portions of the scientific exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the opening mosaic with a dataset comparison, replaces earlier animated comparison panels with different examples displayed as frame sequences, and adds restoration, filtering, caching, and duration graphics. Tables gain resource and duration columns and new experimental displays. Figures 13–15 enlarge Figure 6's existing examples rather than adding independent comparisons.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for CogVideoX, Upscale-A-Video, DeepCache, and the restoration example's source. Appendix A.2 expands the relationship to MMDiT, and Section 5 explicitly asserts priority for the parallel visual-text structure in video generation. The dedicated OpenSora pipeline comparison is removed, while the broader related-work positioning remains.

T1.justification: The MVDiT mathematical formulation is retained, with v2 Equations 3–4 combined into v3 Equation 3 and subsequent renumbering. No substantive theorem, proof, formal assumption, or derivation is added. The caching discussion's standard quadratic-attention complexity statement is explanatory.

improvement.justification: v2 supported caption quality largely through length statistics and compared HD training chiefly against upsampled outputs. v3's human caption study, native-HD Panda control, and component ablations substantially strengthen evidence for the central dataset and model claims; processing details also improve auditability. Removing licensing information and the long-duration limitation weakens transparency, and the restoration comparison does not isolate dataset effects. Nevertheless, the stronger evidence addressing important gaps supports a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpenVid-1M, OpenVidHD-0.4M, and MVDiT work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and inspecting v2's embedded visual examples.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and adds restoration results, module ablations, human caption evaluations, and an inference-acceleration analysis.

before.justification: v2 reports original dataset statistics, text-to-video evaluations, qualitative comparisons, and controlled ablations in Figures 3–8 and Tables 2–5.

results.title: OpenVid-1M: A Large-Scale High-Quality Dataset for Text-to-video Generation

C1.justification: Both versions claim a reward-sum formulation of customization, direct learning of a residual-Q adapter without separately learning reward models, and mitigation of forgetting while learning new preferences. The rewritten abstract, title, and contribution list retain these central claims.

C2.justification: V1 emphasizes DSP performance often matching or exceeding the base model; v2 interprets its results as reduced forgetting despite remaining benchmark losses. V2 also recognizes Replay as competitive on HH-RLHF, identifies instability at large alpha0, and explains beta regularization as stabilizing training. The limitations concerning RLHF-trained base models and only one demonstrated customization round remain.

D1.justification: V2 Appendices B–C substantially expand baseline implementation, base-model preparation, benchmark task names, prompting and scoring configurations, and the judging prompt, explicitly documenting length-controlled win rates. Hyperparameters and the training-time estimate are revised. However, v1's training-loss code and some microbatch, memory, and DeepSpeed details disappear. The Q-Adapter repository address remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The four DSP domains and helpful-to-harmless HH-RLHF transfer remain. MathQA and HumanEval are removed, while MMLU Pro, BBH, and IFEval introduce harder knowledge questions, additional reasoning tasks, and explicit instruction-following evaluation. MMLU and GSM8K coverage remains; replacing their Tiny evaluations belongs to protocol changes.

E2.justification: Replay is newly evaluated in both DSP and HH-RLHF, adding a comparison family directly relevant to forgetting mitigation. PPO appears in v1's HH-RLHF Table 2 but is omitted from v2's corresponding comparison because of training instability. DSP retains SFT, DPO, and PPO; the PR labels rename the latter two.

E3.justification: The reported base model changes from Llama-3 8B to Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and LoRA rank changes from 16 to 8. Table 3 changes alpha-tilde from 0.1 to 1, alpha0 from 1 to 0.01, and gamma from 0.99 to 1. TinyMMLU/TinyGSM8K evaluations are replaced by standard benchmark tasks. Preference judging changes from GPT-4-turbo against the base model to GPT-4o against SFT, and the alpha0 sweep uses different values and scoring.

E4.justification: V2 adds training-checkpoint MMLU curves testing how forgetting develops (Figure 2) and a beta sweep testing the contribution and sensitivity of reward regularization (Appendix D, Figure 6). It revises the existing alpha0 tradeoff analysis and expands qualitative analysis to DSP style examples while replacing the HH-RLHF response case.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests for its experiments. The revised tables and plots continue to present point estimates.

E6.justification: The main benchmark and preference results are replaced under changed conditions. V1 Figure 2 reports DSP win rates against the base model; v2 Table 2 reports Q-Adapter's SFT-relative rates of 55.59%, 53.84%, 63.77%, and 58.20% across the four domains. V2 also replaces HH-RLHF results and adds checkpoint and beta findings. These are new or replaced measurements, not directly comparable performance gains, because models and evaluation protocols differ.

M1.justification: V2 Equation (10) corrects the regularization sign in v1 Equation (9), making the squared-reward term a positive loss penalty. V1 Appendix C already implemented a positive penalty, so this establishes a correction to the documented loss, not a newly introduced component. The residual-Q adapter, preference-learning procedure, and policy-composition rule otherwise remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Residual Q-learning becomes a preliminary subsection, customization formalization and Q-Adapter receive separate sections, and related work moves after experiments. The appendices are reorganized and subdivided, the Broader Impacts appendix is removed, and the title and author information change.

P2.justification: The original framework diagram moves from v1 Figure 1 to v2 Figure 5, alongside a new introductory illustration. DSP win rates change from a bar chart to a table, HH-RLHF results from a table to a scatter plot, and alpha0 analysis from a scatter plot to grouped bars. Checkpoint and beta plots are added, with substantial table and document-template changes.

R1.justification: V2 makes attribution to residual Q-learning more explicit through Section 2.3 and Proposition 2.2; v1 already cited and followed Li et al. It adds personalization, customization, forgetting, retrieval, and benchmark references, including Salemi, Wozniak, Liu, and Luo, while removing several earlier references. The central positioning relative to RLHF, DPO, IPL, and LoRA remains.

T1.justification: V2 replaces v1's incorrectly indexed soft-Q recursion with a discounted-return definition and adds a proof of the KL-regularized/maximum-entropy equivalence in Appendix A.1. Corollary 4.1 gains an explicit proof of the reward–residual-Q correspondence. The main residual-Q derivations remain, while v1's soft-optimality proof is replaced by a cited lemma.

improvement.justification: The added Replay comparison and training-checkpoint analysis substantially strengthen testing of the central forgetting-mitigation claim. The beta ablation and detailed benchmark/judge specifications address important gaps in v1's empirical justification and reproducibility, while formula corrections improve mathematical consistency. Removing coding evaluation, HH-RLHF general-benchmark results, and its PPO comparison narrows some evidence, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported. Nevertheless, the gains in testing and documenting the main contribution are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Q-Adapter and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The shared formulation, algorithm, and experiments can be matched despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original DSP and HH-RLHF experiments, training-checkpoint evaluations, hyperparameter analyses, and generated responses in Tables 1–2, Figures 2–4 and 6, and Appendices D–E.

before.justification: V1 reports original DSP and HH-RLHF experiments in Tables 1–2, preference evaluations and hyperparameter analysis in Figures 2–3, and generated responses in Appendix D.

results.title: Q-Adapter: Customizing Pre-trained LLMs to New Preferences with Forgetting Mitigation

C1.justification: Although the abstract's central message is retained, v2 reframes the contributions around deficiencies in single-turn evaluation and adds headline claims about temperature and fine-tuning effects. Its discussion extends the implications to training and alignment. The earlier contribution concerning between-chain semantic convergence is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking temperature to relaxed constraints and Base/Instruct differences to data curation and human preferences. It discusses the length exception in the constraint experiment and makes stronger alignment implications. v1's explicit warning that fitted fixed points do not prove attractor existence is omitted; B.3.1 additionally introduces a rationale for interpreting uncorrected KS-test trends.

D1.justification: v2 supplies exact paraphrased and graded-constraint prompts, adds environmental resource estimates, and explicitly identifies the repository as another source of generated data. Core decoding parameters, hardware descriptions, hashtag filtering, and existing code/data URLs remain. These are documentation additions rather than evidence that the original settings changed.

E1.justification: The scientific-abstract, news, and social-media sources and three principal tasks are retained. v2 adds heterogeneous Llama3-8B/Mistral-7B transmission scenarios and graded requirements for modifying texts (B.2.3–B.2.4). The 100-text replication increases sampling within existing data coverage.

E2.justification: v2 retains the five original principal models and adds GPT-4o-mini to their comparisons. Figure 5b additionally compares Base and Instruct versions of Llama3-70B and Mixtral-8x7B, extending the existing model families.

E3.justification: The principal 50-generation design persists, but v2 adds a 100-initial-text replication, five paraphrases per task, graded modification constraints, temperature sweeps, Base/Instruct conditions, and two starting orders for heterogeneous chains. It also removes the embedding-based cosine-similarity evaluation described in v1 Section 3.2.

E4.justification: v2 adds sample-size and prompt robustness tests, a direct control for task constraints, and temperature, fine-tuning, and heterogeneous-chain analyses (Figure 5; Figures S3–S6). The semantic-convergence analysis in v1 Section 4.4/Figure 7 is removed. The collapse case study and 10-to-50-generation attractor validation are retained.

E5.justification: v1 displays posterior-difference means and significance stars; v2 reports explicit 95% credible-interval endpoints in Tables 2–12. v2 also adds error bars to the principal attractor estimates and reports variability across prompt paraphrases. Both versions retain five seeds for the principal experiments; no increase is stated.

E6.justification: Beyond new model and control results, retained-model estimates change: Mixtral-8x7B's Rephrase toxicity-attractor strength is approximately 0.45 in v1 Figure 6 and 0.90 in v2 Figure 4. The revised Bayesian analysis no longer supports the between-model toxicity-position differences reported in v1 Figure 10; v2 Table 5 intervals all include zero. Semantic-convergence results are removed.

M1.justification: The iterative text-passing framework and linear-regression attractor estimator remain unchanged in Section 3. Added models, mixed populations, temperatures, and prompts are experimental conditions within that framework. Revised numerical estimates do not establish an algorithmic modification.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the contribution list and discussion, expands the explanation of culture, compresses the methods and qualitative-results narrative, and removes Section 4.4. Appendix B gains a detailed subsection structure, while reproducibility and ethics statements are added. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: v2 rearranges and substantially compresses the distribution and KS plots, moves the attractor-method illustration to Figure S1, and adds Figure 5 and Figures S3–S6. Posterior heatmaps become interval tables, attractor plots gain error bars, and the semantic-convergence figure disappears. Legends and appendix plots are updated for GPT-4o-mini.

R1.justification: Related work expands with dedicated discussions of Bayesian Iterated Learning and social-context evaluation, including Ren et al., Zhu and Griffiths, Zhou et al., and Huang et al. v2 substantively distinguishes its fixed-point approach from convergence-to-priors accounts and clarifies its cultural-evolution positioning. These changes exceed citation-style or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 retains the linear recurrence, convergence condition |s| < 1, position I/(1-s), and strength 1-s. Generalizing the generation-count notation adds no substantive theory. The Bayesian model definitions are also retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence: its direct manipulation of allowable text changes addresses confounding in v1's comparison of different tasks, while larger-sample and prompt-paraphrase checks test previously unexamined robustness (B.2). Temperature and Base/Instruct comparisons replace some speculation with empirical evidence, and explicit credible intervals improve scrutiny. These gains outweigh the loss of semantic-convergence analysis and less cautious claims about attractors and alignment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same telephone-game study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with six principal LLMs and additional robustness, temperature, Base/Instruct, and heterogeneous-chain comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original transmission-chain experiments with five LLMs, three tasks, and 20 initial texts, including statistical analyses, attractor estimates, and generated-text examples.

results.title: When LLMs Play the Telephone Game: Cultural Attractors as Conceptual Tools to Evaluate LLMs in Multi-turn Settings

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on random rewiring, graph-tailored attention, and the connection between message passing and sparse Transformers. v3 adds a novel efficient encoding contribution, D-RRWP, and makes the combination of encoding, rewiring, and attention central in the abstract and conclusion. The broad state-of-the-art performance claim remains.

C2.justification: v1 partly attributes performance to narrow, deep models and inductive bias on small datasets. v3 instead develops component-specific interpretations concerning D-RRWP efficiency, regular rewiring, attention alternatives, and the limited influence of minor design choices. Section 5.1 newly acknowledges that scalability on extremely large graphs has not been thoroughly evaluated; the nondeterministic-output limitation remains.

D1.justification: Both versions already provide detailed hyperparameter and timing tables. v3 updates encoding, hardware, compilation, and checkpointing information; discloses PyTorch Geometric implementations and ablation adjustments; and corrects pseudocode loop endpoints. It omits explicit 1cycle schedule naming and RAM/VRAM capacity rows. Both versions still promise a future GitHub release without providing access.

E1.justification: All eight original benchmark datasets remain, and v3 adds COCO-SP evaluation in Table 2. This extends the existing superpixel node-classification coverage to another image corpus. The new PascalVOC-SP ablations use a dataset already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add NeuralWalker, while Table 2 removes GatedGCN+RWSE. More substantially, v3 adds direct component comparisons against GAT, GatedGCN, and Transformer attention, plus LapPE encoding alternatives, in Tables 4 and 6. These substantially expand the comparisons testing the proposed components.

E3.justification: Retained benchmark settings change: CLUSTER training decreases from 100 to 50 epochs, PascalVOC-SP from 600 to 500, and PATTERN/CLUSTER rewiring degree from 15 to 6. Their edge-removal rates increase from 0.3 to 0.5. New ablations introduce parameter-budget matching, padded LapPE controls, and optimization adjustments. Table 2 also adopts externally retuned LRGB baseline configurations.

E4.justification: v1 provides ZINC component-removal ablations and a regular-graph degree sweep. v3 substantially expands these into encoding and attention replacement studies, regular versus non-regular rewiring, fully connected controls, optimizer replacement, and corresponding PascalVOC-SP analyses. Tables 3–6 additionally examine runtime, peak memory, and D-RRWP storage requirements.

E5.justification: Table 1 raises reported training-run counts from 8 to 16 for ZINC and from 6 to 8 for other GNN benchmarks. ZINC rewiring-variance estimation changes from 30 to 100 test evaluations, and Figure 4 adds standard-error bars. Mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remains, but v1's four-run preprocessing-time uncertainty is omitted in v3.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced under revised models and settings: ZINC MAE changes from 0.046 to 0.047, CIFAR10 accuracy from 82.471 to 83.750, and PATTERN accuracy from 90.997 to 89.177. COCO-SP MacroF1 of 0.4752 and extensive ablation/resource results are added. These are not controlled version-to-version gains. v3's claimed fifth-place Peptides-func ranking conflicts with Table 2, which lists eleven higher means.

M1.justification: Section 3 introduces D-RRWP, a truncated-eigendecomposition alternative to exact RRWP. It also concatenates forward and reverse RRWP edge encodings, replaces PN-V with batch normalization, removes degree-scaled attention, and includes the receiving node in attention neighborhoods. These change preprocessing and layer computations. Edge flipping and random edge removal were already present.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work section are extensively rewritten, and GRASS's expanded name changes. Methods explanations are reorganized, random-rewiring theory moves into Appendix A, and experiments gain separate benchmarking and ablation subsections. The conclusion gains dedicated limitations and reproducibility subsections, and the appendices are reorganized.

P2.justification: The architecture overview is redrawn and moved from the appendix into the main text. v3 adds a simplified attention diagram and an ablation chart, updates the detailed attention diagram, and substantially restructures ablation tables to display controls and resource costs. Benchmark tables gain comparator rows and a COCO-SP column, while appendix tables are regrouped.

R1.justification: The core relationship to RRWP/GRIT, GPS, Exphormer, and BigBird remains. v3 more explicitly credits existing random rewiring and locates novelty in the component combination and D-RRWP. It adds NeuralWalker, the LRGB reassessment, and decomposition/implementation references while pruning earlier background citations. The extensive prose rewrite exceeds the change in underlying research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds the D-RRWP derivation: a symmetric normalized transition matrix, truncated eigenpairs, approximate matrix powers, time/storage bounds, and an argument for setting walk length equal to the number of eigenpairs. The earlier random-regular-graph arguments largely move to Appendix A.1; the diameter bound is additionally qualified as asymptotic and applying to almost every such graph.

improvement.justification: v1 claims advantages for graph-tailored attention but provides only limited component ablations on ZINC. v3's alternative-attention, encoding, and rewiring comparisons on ZINC and PascalVOC-SP substantially strengthen evidence for its design choices. D-RRWP gains mathematical explanation and an empirical storage/accuracy comparison, and stronger LRGB baselines improve evaluation credibility. Explicitly acknowledging untested large-graph scalability also improves qualification of the claims. These gains outweigh the incorrect Peptides-func ranking and loss of preprocessing-time uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRASS research framework, despite the changed title and substantive revisions. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original GRASS results on nine benchmark datasets, expanded ZINC and PascalVOC-SP ablations, stochastic-output variance measurements, and computational and storage results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GRASS results on eight benchmark datasets, ZINC ablations, stochastic-output variance measurements, and computational timings in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Greener GRASS: Enhancing GNNs with Encoding, Rewiring, and Attention

C1.justification: The central claims about misleadingly high similarity, variance sensitivity, and dependencies between measures remain. v2 explicitly adds dataset dependence to its claim about good-score thresholds and qualifies the introduction's angular-Procrustes/CKA implication to the illustrated dataset, refining the scope of the conclusions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly rejects universal metric superiority and acknowledges that optimization dynamics combine optimizer behavior with similarity-measure behavior, materially qualifying the interpretation. It also introduces a tentative denoising explanation for above-reference decoding and reports that simply removing low-variance PCs does not explain it.

D1.justification: v2 adds the PyTorch lstsq implementation detail, explicit binarization information, and further explanation of joint-score optimization. Project, code, and package access addresses change. Conversely, v1's NVIDIA GeForce GTX TITAN X and less-than-one-day compute disclosure is removed. Much other apparent documentation growth is relocated material.

E1.justification: The five source datasets are retained, but functional decoding coverage expands substantially. Beyond v1's Mante/Siegel decision variables, v2 Figure 3 evaluates eight reaching directions, eight object categories, and texture-versus-noise classification using Hatsopoulos, MajajHong, and FreemanZiemba recordings.

E2.justification: v2 extends the Mante/Siegel decoding comparisons to angular CKA, NBS, and unregularized linear regression alongside the original three measures. These methods already appeared in other v1 analyses. The condition-average reference disappears from the corresponding decoding plots, although it remains in Figure 2.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a decoding-summary threshold at 90% of the improvement from chance to neural-data accuracy. Its new ridge experiment evaluates lambda values 1, 10, 100, 1000, and 10000 rather than only the previously reported default of 100. Existing five-fold decoding and regression protocols remain documented.

E4.justification: Figure S2 adds a substantive regularization-sensitivity analysis. Figure 6 replaces the single synthetic PC-perturbation example with validation on five neural datasets. Section 4.1 also briefly reports removing low-variance PCs to investigate above-reference decoding accuracy; this control did not resolve the observation.

E5.justification: Neither version introduces explicit repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing error bars and shaded bands remain without a newly documented uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds decoding curves and threshold results across more tasks and measures, regularization-dependent decoding outcomes in Figure S2, and five neural-data perturbation results replacing v1's synthetic example. Figures 2, 4, and 5 largely retain their results, and v1 Figure 3's decoding curves reappear in Figure S1.

M1.justification: The method still optimizes Gaussian-initialized synthetic data through differentiable similarity scores using Adam, including joint optimization of score pairs. The RNN architectures are unchanged. Expanded metric descriptions and disclosure of differentiation through PyTorch's lstsq do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract and introductory framing, adds an explicit contribution list, restructures the methods, and rewrites Sections 4.1 and 4.3. Optimization details move from the appendix into Section 3.2, while lengthy Figure 2 explanations move into the appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds a five-panel decoding Figure 3 and Figure S2, relocates the earlier Figure 3 to S1, expands the perturbation display, and separates joint-score diagrams into Figure 7. The latter removes displayed optimization trajectories. Captions, diagram arrangement, and the document's title and heading layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The reference to Cloos et al. 2022 on RNN evaluation is removed, while Cloos et al. 2024 on standardizing similarity measures is added. Related work additionally emphasizes joint-score optimization, but the principal comparisons with earlier similarity-measure research remain.

T1.justification: The perturbation assumptions and CKA/NBS derivation in v1 Appendix B.3 are retained in v2 Appendix C.2. The angular Procrustes rescaling already appeared in v1. v2 reorganizes and expands explanations of these relationships without adding a substantive theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the practical conclusions: functional decoding extends beyond two contextual-decision examples, the ridge sweep tests dependence on regularization, and neural-data perturbations support theory previously illustrated synthetically. Explicit dataset-dependent thresholds and the optimizer-confounding limitation make the conclusions better supported and more carefully bounded. These gains outweigh the limited reproducibility loss from removing hardware and compute-time information; uncertainty reporting remains a weakness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, optimization framework, neural datasets, and core analyses. The complete main texts, figures, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and reports additional decoding, regularization-sensitivity, and neural-data perturbation results in Figures 3, 6, and S2.

before.justification: v1 reports original RNN comparisons, decoding experiments, optimization dynamics, and principal-component perturbation simulations in Figures 2–6.

results.title: Differentiable Optimization of Similarity Scores Between Models and Brains

C1.justification: The contribution expands from depth-wise Transformer Alignment and trajectory regularity to coupling across both tokens and depth. The abstract and contributions also newly claim that coupling correlates more strongly with benchmark performance than parameter budget, model depth, or embedding dimension. These are substantive extensions of the central claims.

C2.justification: The in-context-learning discussion changes from claiming that coupling could only emerge through joint problem-solving to presenting a gradient-update analogy. v2 makes the exponential-growth explanation more explicitly conditional and adds layer normalization as a possible explanation for untrained singular-value scaling. The limitation concerning uncontrolled differences between independently trained models is retained.

D1.justification: Table 1 adds positional-encoding information and additional Pythia specifications, and corrects the Neo 2.7B and Pythia 6.9B parameter-unit entries. New captions disclose checkpoint selections, layer windows, and prompt counts. GPU, batching, quantization, and claimed supplementary-code information are retained; the smaller Jacobian prompt subset remains unspecified.

E1.justification: The six leaderboard datasets are retained. v2 Figure 19 additionally uses WikiText-2 prompts for representation and logit-entropy measurements, adding general-text input coverage within the existing language-model analysis.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 25 adds explicit comparisons of coupling with parameter count, layer count, and embedding dimension as predictors of benchmark performance. These competing reference predictors were not evaluated in the corresponding correlation analysis in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds Pythia checkpoint evaluations, normalized coupling with a layer-separation restriction, 11-layer measurement windows, and K=25/50/75/100 sensitivity settings. Expodistance also changes from growth rates of layer increments relative to the initial increment to adjacent representation-norm ratios (v1 Section 3.4 versus v2 Section 3.3). The original growth plot is nevertheless reused, so the PDFs do not establish that its measurements were recomputed under the revised definition.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of training-time emergence, sensitivity to the number of singular vectors, associations with model properties and positional encoding, and depth-resolved norms, linearity, spacing, and logit entropy (Figures 2, 4, 19–22, 25–29). These substantially expand the questions examined beyond v1's endpoint comparisons and spectral analyses.

E5.justification: The existing median and interquartile-range reporting is retained. New checkpoint plots, including Figures 4 and 21, display mean curves with extrema or range information. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts or significance tests; the added bands describe variability rather than establishing uncertainty across independent training runs.

E6.justification: The headline R²=0.7214 and reported mean LSS values of 4.25 trained versus 6.54 untrained remain. v2 adds cross-token and checkpoint results; Figure 25 reports benchmark R² values of 0.3254, 0.3547, and 0.3614 for depth, embedding dimension, and parameter count. Figure 26 adds R² values from 0.7331 at K=25 to 0.6933 at K=100. v1 Figure 3's fine-tuned-inclusive correlation panel is omitted.

M1.justification: v1 analyzes a token's self-Jacobian across layers. v2 Section 3.1 generalizes this to input-output token-pair Jacobians and introduces coupling analyses with matching input/output tokens, fixed input tokens, and fixed output tokens. This substantially extends the analytical procedure beyond renaming alignment.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around transformer block coupling and explicit research questions. Evaluation is separated from Methods, while PCA methodology and the ResNet comparison move into the appendices. The changes substantially reorganize the presentation beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds a coupling schematic, token-interaction heatmaps, checkpoint curves, and numerous diagnostic panels. The correlation display changes from two panels to one and moves forward; LSS is reordered and duplicated in the appendix. Existing spectral figures are enlarged and rearranged, and Table 1 gains a positional-encoding column.

R1.justification: The existing dynamical-systems and Residual Alignment foundations remain. v2 sharpens the distinction through transformer-specific token interactions and adds references to Su et al., Sarfati et al., and Wu and Papyan, while removing the introductory Brown et al. and Devlin et al. references.

T1.justification: v2 extends the mathematical definitions to token-pair coupling, introduces normalized mis-coupling, and revises the exponential-rate definition. Section 7 adds a short gradient-update argument linking coupling to in-context learning. The SVD framework and appendix linear-ODE derivation remain substantially unchanged, with no new theorem or substantial proof development.

improvement.justification: v1 supports training emergence mainly through randomly initialized versus final-model comparisons. v2 directly examines Pythia checkpoints, tests singular-vector-count sensitivity, and establishes a distinct cross-token extension through several interaction cases. These substantially strengthen the empirical foundation and contribution. The unreconciled expodistance definition and reused plot, together with removal of the fine-tuned-inclusive correlation panel, weaken reporting but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Jacobian and hidden-trajectory study, despite the changed title and expanded scope. Their main text, equations, figures, model table, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical measurements and adds cross-token coupling, training-checkpoint analyses, and supplementary representation and sensitivity results (Section 5 and Appendix A.6).

before.justification: v1 reports original measurements of Jacobian alignment, trajectory linearity, exponential growth, and singular-value scaling in trained and randomly initialized LLMs (Section 4 and Appendix A.4).

results.title: Transformer Block Coupling and its Correlation with Generalization in LLMs

C1.justification: The central claims about coupling, its correlation with generalization, and trajectory regularity remain. v3 adds adjacent-layer locality emerging through training to the contribution statement, refining the coupling claim without replacing the paper's central thesis.

C2.justification: v3 adds a subspace interpretation, an argument that stronger coupling complicates optimization, and an interpretation connecting stochastic depth to coupling. Table 2 claims implications for merging, pruning, projection, permutation and early exiting. Exponential growth is also qualified from occurring across all considered LLMs to occurring in the vast majority of trajectories; the heterogeneous-pretraining limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix A.7 supplies the new ViT experiment's architecture, hyperparameter grids, Adam learning rate, 500-epoch schedule, warmup, mixup, batch size, GPUs and training time. Appendix A.6 adds computational-cost details. Existing LLM hardware, batching, quantization and supplemental-code statements are retained rather than newly disclosed.

E1.justification: v3 adds CIFAR10 image classification, substantially extending the language-focused coverage of v2. It also evaluates difficulty-labelled Easy2Hard prompts and GSM8K prompts with appended zero-shot chain-of-thought instructions. The original leaderboard datasets and WikiText2 analyses remain.

E2.justification: Neither version benchmarks the coupling analysis against competing analysis methods. The new ViT sweeps and standard-versus-CoT probes compare experimental conditions. Compression, pruning and early-exit methods newly discussed in Table 2 are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a controlled 64-model ViT experiment with fixed architecture and an eight-by-eight weight-decay/stochastic-depth grid. It adds restricted-model regression subsets and embedding-noise testing. The Pythia coupling experiment also changes its reported checkpoint schedule and retains 6.9B/12B models while dropping the 1B series from that comparison.

E4.justification: New analyses examine regularization, model-size and score restrictions, training-token counts, prompt difficulty, CoT prompting and embedding perturbations (Figures 6–11, 15 and 30; Table 4). These substantially expand the questions tested. Conversely, the K=100 sensitivity panel and v2's Figure 29 misalignment maps are omitted; many other appendix analyses are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v3 adds regression p-values for the full model sample and restricted subsets in Table 4, including 1.56×10^-6 for the full sample. Figure 5(b) also supplies uncertainty intervals for untrained expodistance, whereas v2's Figure 18 showed points without intervals. Existing LSS median/IQR reporting continues; no repeated-seed protocol is introduced.

E6.justification: The main correlation plot is revised from R²=0.7214 to 0.75, with changed plotted coupling values and model membership; this is not a same-setting performance gain. New ViT results report R² values of 0.35, 0.48, 0.74 and 0.83 at stochastic-depth rates 0, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.3. Additional findings include model-dependent CoT effects and perturbation responses. Table 1 and many earlier appendix results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The Jacobian/SVD coupling procedure and LSS/expodistance measurements are retained. Although v3 simplifies the top-K notation in Section 3.1, Section 5.4 and Appendix A.6 still refer to truncated calculations. The ViT experiments apply the existing analysis rather than introduce a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, methods explanation, discussion and related work undergo substantial rewriting. Token-wise coupling is reorganized into self/context categories, linearity and exponential-growth results are combined, and the limitations and conclusion are condensed. These changes materially reshape the narrative beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: v3 rebuilds Figure 1 as a five-panel overview, adds axes and colorbars to enlarged coupling displays, and combines/restyles regularity plots. It adds Tables 2–4 and multiple experimental figures, while moving several earlier main-text figures into the appendix and regrouping existing appendix panels. These are substantial visual and layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens positioning through generalization bounds, dynamical isometry, subspace models, compression and early exiting, particularly in Sections 5.4–6.2 and Table 2. It adds associated references such as Arora, Pennington, Ashkboos and Gromov. The earlier information-processing subsection and its associated references are removed.

T1.justification: v2's continuous-ODE motivation is replaced and expanded with finite-depth matrix products and spectral derivations. v3's Appendix A.5 derives conditions yielding ED=0 and LSS=1, while Section 6.2 adds a gradient-based optimization argument. Appendix A.6 also introduces computational-complexity analysis. These are substantive mathematical additions beyond notation changes.

improvement.justification: v2's central generalization evidence relied primarily on heterogeneous pretrained LLMs. v3 adds fixed-architecture ViT training experiments and restricted-model correlation checks, providing substantial controlled and size-restricted support for the central relationship. Detailed training instructions and clearer comparative figures improve reproducibility and assessment. The new compression and early-exit explanations in Table 2 exceed the experiments presented, and LLM causality remains unresolved, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same transformer block coupling study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original LLM analyses and adds results from training 64 vision transformers, alongside new prompt and perturbation experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original measurements of Jacobian coupling, hidden trajectories and training dynamics across LLMs, including extensive appendix experiments.

results.title: Transformer Block Coupling and its Correlation with Generalization in LLMs

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds a 4.3% LongBench improvement over InfLLM and human-like event segmentation. V2 broadens the main claims to performance across five base LLMs and two benchmarks, superiority over RAG and full-context inference, and successful retrieval across 10 million tokens. The underlying human-memory contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations attributing advantages over RAG to layer-specific retrieval and advantages over full-context inference to reduced attention dilution. Appendix A.2 discusses retriever-capacity bottlenecks and pipeline complexity, while Appendix C.2 explains growing memory and retrieval-time costs and offloading tradeoffs. Existing cognitive interpretations and contiguity qualifications largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit backbone identifiers, RAG construction settings, Hugging Face integration details and offloading/parallelisation procedures. Appendix C.2 newly documents four-GPU nodes with 32GB per GPU, CPU-memory requirements, timing methodology and API use for full-context results. V1 provides substantially less implementation and hardware information.

E1.justification: V2 retains LongBench, PG-19 and the human podcasts, while adding six ∞-Bench tasks covering code debugging, mathematical finding, long-book multiple-choice questions and KV/passkey/number retrieval. Figure 1 also adds an extended passkey-retrieval scenario reaching 10 million tokens.

E2.justification: V1's downstream comparison uses InfLLM. V2 retains it and adds RAG pipelines using all-mpnet-base-v2 and NV-Embed-v2 in Table 8, plus full-context inference alongside NV-Embed-v2 RAG in Table 9. These introduce substantially different comparator families.

E3.justification: Alongside the retained 4K+2K evaluation, v2 adds LLaMA-3/3.1 configurations with 4K+4K contexts and Phi-3/3.5 configurations with 1K+3K contexts. New experiments introduce a 300-word, top-five-chunk RAG protocol and timing measurements over 100 chunks of 512 tokens. These do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 extends component ablations across additional models and ∞-Bench, adds a layer-specific retrieval case study in Figure 5, and extends human-segmentation comparisons to Mistral and LLaMA-3 in Figures 7–8. Runtime profiling and Figure 9's configuration comparisons add further analyses. V1's sensitivity plots remain as Figures 10–11.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 5 adds box-and-whisker summaries of retrieval-ratio variability across more than 500 chunks. Existing PG-19 plus/minus statistics and human-data plot bands are retained. Neither version reports a repeated-seed protocol or confidence intervals for downstream benchmark performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive benchmark, comparator, model and efficiency results. Corresponding original LongBench entries also change: the S variant's PassageRetrieval score changes from 85.42 in v1 Table 1 to 82.67 in v2 Table 3, while InfLLM remains 64.00. The configuration selection behind these revisions is unexplained. PG-19 Table 2 values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The surprise-based segmentation, boundary refinement and two-buffer retrieval algorithm remain. Appendix C.2 introduces execution adaptations for very long sequences: disk-backed LRU memory management, optional CPU offloading of representative tokens and layer parallelisation across GPUs.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the method and related-work prose remain. V2 revises the abstract and experimental framing, condenses the discussion and conclusion, and reorganises the supplemental material into thematic appendices with a contents list. These are focused editorial and organisational revisions.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns the main performance table around task groups and multiple models, and adds comparison, diagnostic, ablation and resource displays. It introduces the opening radar/scalability figure and redraws a subset of the human results for the main text. Original figures are preserved elsewhere, including v1 Figures 3–5 as v2 Figures 6, 10–11.

R1.justification: The existing long-context and episodic-memory reviews, including novelty relative to InfLLM, largely remain. V2 adds focused positioning against RAG and references covering NV-Embed, all-mpnet-base-v2, MTEB, RAG enhancements and ∞-Bench. Publication-status updates to existing citations do not introduce new works.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 revises the stated total retrieved-event count from k = ks + kc + 2 to k = ks + kc. The graph-based definitions, complexity argument and two k-NN/softmax approximation lemmas otherwise remain unchanged; the original complexity analysis and proof move to Appendices C.1 and E.1.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow downstream validation and largely theoretical efficiency discussion through broader model and benchmark testing, RAG/full-context comparisons, extreme-length retrieval evidence and concrete resource measurements. Implementation details also improve reproducibility. Reporting inconsistencies qualify this gain: Section 4.1's 30.5%/11.5% RAG improvements do not reconcile with Table 9, and Table 4's LLaMA-3 ∞-Bench results contradict uniformly superior performance. These issues limit claim reliability but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EM-LLM work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations across models and benchmarks, RAG/full-context comparisons, retrieval diagnostics and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original LongBench evaluations, PG-19 segmentation comparisons, analyses against human event boundaries and component ablations.

results.title: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs

C1.justification: v4 expands the headline claims to SOTA performance on six of seven datasets, training-free portability across LLMs, applicability to associated graph/document collections, and smaller-model reasoning comparable to GPT-3.5. It explicitly positions bidirectional KG×Text coupling as the contribution. v1 emphasizes accurate, interpretable graph-guided reasoning demonstrated on four datasets.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations concerning knowledge exposure, backbone capability, single-hop versus multi-hop tasks, and the respective roles of triples and documents. Appendix B.1 introduces substantive limitations involving missing knowledge, retrieval failures, misunderstood questions and exact-match false negatives. However, the new context-length explanation contradicts Figure 3b: LLM scores increase while reranker scores decrease overall.

D1.justification: v4 supplies pseudocode, full pruning/reasoning prompts, the Azure entity-linking implementation, explicit W=D=3 and K=10 settings, and financial-dataset construction procedures and statistics. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that newly disclosed defaults changed. v1's GPU configuration and 256-token generation-limit disclosures are dropped.

E1.justification: v4 adds Creak, Zero-Shot RE and ToG-FinQA, expanding coverage to additional fact verification, slot filling and Chinese financial multi-hop QA. ToG-FinQA contains 97 questions. The earlier HotpotQA evaluation is now identified as AdvHotpotQA, a challenging subset; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects a different underlying sample.

E2.justification: v4 adds explicit text-based Vanilla RAG and CoT-SC comparisons, evaluates GraphRAG on ToG-FinQA, and fills previously absent CoK comparisons on WebQSP and QALD-10-en. v1's Vanilla prompting corresponds to v4's Direct reasoning and is retained, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: FEVER changes from v1's blanket two-shot prompting to three-/six-shot demonstrations with an initial self-consistency step. Backbone experiments replace the reported Llama-2 configuration with Llama-3-8B, Qwen2-7B and GPT-4o. New experiments introduce retrieval-tool, context-count, width/depth and self-consistency-threshold comparisons, plus a manual analysis of 50 sampled outputs.

E4.justification: The original TP/RC/query-feedback ablation survives as Appendix B.2, Table 6. v4 substantially extends analysis with backbone comparisons, pruning-tool and context-count tests, width/depth sensitivity, self-consistency thresholds, measured runtime, evidence-source attribution, error categorization and additional QA cases (Sections 4.5–4.7; Appendices B and D).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v4's self-consistency experiments concern inference behavior, while its runtime averages and manual-category percentages are additional results rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive financial, backbone and diagnostic results and removes the Llama-2 result rows. Direct WebQSP changes from 74.55 to 65.9. Main FEVER results become 63.1/59.7 under revised prompting; the earlier 58.54 remains rounded to 58.5 in the appendix ablation. HotpotQA 40.91 versus AdvHotpotQA 42.9 is not an established same-setting gain. Proposed-method WebQSP/QALD scores only change rounding.

M1.justification: The core pruning, retrieval and reasoning loop remains. However, v1 scores chunks against a query containing the question, clue query and triple; v4 Equation 5 instead attaches a verbalized triple to the scored context. v4 also introduces a self-consistency prepass setting (Section 4.3; Appendix B.4). These are limited procedural revisions within the retained framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten and reorganized. v4 standardizes the ToG-2 name, changes the title, separates graph search, context retrieval and reasoning explanations, adds a conclusion and thematic appendices, and relocates the original component ablation.

P2.justification: The ACM two-column presentation becomes a single-column preprint. Both principal diagrams are redrawn, including a new loose-coupling hybrid panel in Figure 1. Performance tables are expanded and regrouped, the retained ablation moves to the appendix, and new sensitivity plots, runtime/error tables, case diagrams and prompt tables substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: Related work is reorganized around text-based, KG-based and hybrid RAG. Added discussion of GraphRAG and HybridRAG supports a substantive positioning change toward mutually improving graph and text retrieval through tight coupling. Additional references cover Self-RAG, self-consistency, context filtering and the expanded datasets.

T1.justification: v4 Section 4.6 adds explicit LLM-call bounds: 2D+1 for combined pruning, WD+D+1 for separate pruning, and 2WD+D+1 for ToG. This extends v1's asymptotic pruning-cost argument. Most other added equations formalize existing search and weighted scoring; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through explicit text-RAG and hybrid comparisons, financial-domain evaluation, controlled design studies, measured runtime and manual error analysis. Pseudocode, prompts and dataset documentation also make the framework substantially easier to assess. Reporting problems remain, notably Figure 3b's contradictory interpretation and the abstract's Llama-2 claim after its supporting result rows were removed, but these do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Think-on-Graph 2.0 framework. All six pages of v1 and 22 pages of v4 are readable, including figures, tables, equations and v4's Appendices A–E. v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark results, a newly constructed financial QA evaluation, sensitivity experiments, runtime measurements and manual analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark and component-ablation results for ToG2.0, including GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 experiments in Tables 1–2.

results.title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the headline contribution from NeRF editing to model-agnostic editing with claimed state-of-the-art results on both NeRF and 3DGS. The earlier priority claim about adopting decreasing timesteps for general 3D editing is dropped. The central diffusion-sampling and FreeU contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability and failure explanations: inherited IP2P prompt-following failures, improvement through detailed prompts, and segmentation/projection mismatch attributed to GE/DGE errors (Appendices C.2 and F.1). It also interprets the alternative-weight results as robustness to the precise coefficient choice, extending v1's discussion of the identity/editability trade-off.

D1.justification: v2 newly reports an official code repository, 3DGS implementation recipes, the complete evaluation prompt list and survey details including vigilance filtering, shared camera trajectories and randomized options. Existing NeRF and guidance details move to Appendix B. However, v1's timestep range [0.2, 0.9] and statement about retaining FreeU's original skip-feature scaling settings disappear.

E1.justification: Both versions report eight scenes and 40 prompt pairs from IN2N/PDS data. Figure 15 adds a limited input-condition scenario comparing simple and detailed prompts alongside the corresponding 2D-IP2P failure. The larger 3DGS evaluation primarily changes model configurations within the retained scene-editing coverage.

E2.justification: The NeRF comparison retains IN2N and PDS. The new 3DGS comparison evaluates GaussianEditor with DDS and IN2N guidance, plus DGE (Table 2 and Figure 8). These are substantial additions to the evaluated comparator set; DGE was only cited in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2 introduces separate Nerfstudio/splatfacto and Threestudio 3DGS protocols, with method-specific training budgets and densification settings. The reported user-study sample changes from 50 to 100 participants, and the prompt-alignment question drops its quality requirement. These are reported protocol revisions; unchanged preference percentages do not establish that the study was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative FreeU ablations, alternative-weight sensitivity tests, additional FreeU examples and an IP2P/prompt-specificity failure analysis. It removes v1's controlled 500-iteration random-versus-decreasing-timestep comparison for DreamCatalyst. Appendix C.1 instead tests PDS with decreasing timesteps, answering a different question.

E5.justification: Both versions retain Figure 5's linear-regression trend lines with 95% confidence bands. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, uncertainty estimates for the tabulated scores or significance tests. The participant-count revision concerns study sample size rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises retained NeRF scores: PDS CLIP directional similarity changes from 0.174 to 0.161, while the fast mode changes from 0.158 to 0.165, reversing their order. v2 adds 3DGS, weighting-variant, quantitative FreeU and failure-case results. NeRF timings and user-preference percentages remain unchanged. The score revisions are unexplained and cannot be treated as demonstrated method improvements.

M1.justification: The default identity-regularized DDS objective, decreasing timesteps, FreeU and IP2P guidance are retained. v2 adds two alternative DDS weighting functions and a GaussianEditor-integrated variant with a densification cutoff (Section 3.3 and Appendix B.2), extending the procedure without replacing its core.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. SDEdit preliminaries, text guidance and implementation details move into appendices; the preliminary and experimental subsections are restructured. New appendix organization and an ethics statement further change the document's narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds 3DGS and FreeU result tables, a full prompt table, comparison grids, survey screenshots and a limitations figure. Figure 2 gains weighting curves; Figure 6 replaces the FreeU examples and removes the timestep-ablation row. Existing displays are also relocated and resized, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning against model-specific GaussianEditor/DGE approaches and explicitly distinguishes its interpretation from DreamSampler's source–target equality assumption. It adds citations including DDS, GaussianEditor, 3DGS, Threestudio and DreamGaussian, while removing InstructHumans and the associated discussion of earlier decreasing-timestep editing.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines the DDIM noise coefficient from the schedule and changes the stated PDS noise-scale factor from beta_t to 1-alpha_t in Section 2. It also defines two additional weighting functions. The central DDS/SDEdit derivation is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility beyond v1's NeRF-only comparisons and qualitative component ablations. The 3DGS evaluations, quantitative FreeU and weighting tests, detailed prompts and implementation information, and illustrated IP2P limitation make the method more assessable. Unexplained score and participant-count revisions, removal of the original scheduling ablation, and lost setting disclosures are weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DreamCatalyst with the same authors and core framework. All 13 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2 are readable, including equations, tables and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 includes appendices A–F.

after.justification: v2 retains original NeRF results and reports additional 3DGS comparisons, quantitative ablations and qualitative analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original NeRF editing comparisons, quantitative metrics, human preferences and qualitative ablations in Section 4.

results.title: DreamCatalyst: Fast and High-Quality 3D Editing via Controlling Editability and Identity Preservation

C1.justification: v2 adds a headline claim that its quantitative survey reveals a growing capability gap in interpretability research. It also presents the intervention-graph architecture as an explicit contribution centered on separating experiments from deployment and improving reproducibility, alongside NNsight and NDIF. v1 primarily presents the library and service; their original access and flexibility claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of the research gap and remote-service costs, and explicitly limits current co-tenancy to sequential execution in its appendices. v1's graph-optimization and high-level-abstraction limitation discussions disappear, while the closed-model restriction remains. Section 4 also introduces a runtime-benefit claim for larger models that is not supported by Table 2's request latencies.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D substantially expand documentation of Ray routing, model sharding, distributed tensor handling, memory management, protocols and benchmark implementation. Additional examples cover LoRA training, gradient manipulation and remote probing; Appendix A documents survey curation. Conversely, v1's NNsight 0.2 syntax note and specific NDIF early-access eligibility/application instructions are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds a research-usage analysis covering 184 papers and evaluates standard remote inference, remote interventions and concurrent-user workloads. Attribution-patching timing evaluation disappears, although example code remains. IOI is newly identified as benchmark data; v1's unnamed 32-example batch does not establish whether the underlying dataset changed.

E2.justification: Petals becomes an evaluated comparator in Figure 6c, having appeared only in related work in v1. v2 also introduces direct HPC-versus-NDIF comparisons. The local baukit, pyvene and TransformerLens comparison remains, with TransformerLens now participating in the Gemma comparison where v1 reported missing results.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes from eight A100 GPUs with CUDA 12.4 to four H100 GPUs with CUDA 12.3, and replaces Llama3-70B with Llama-3.1-8B; both versions specify 32-example batches. New protocols measure setup time, sweep OPT model sizes, compare private Petals/NDIF deployments, and test concurrent requests over 30-second windows. The survey adds paper-selection and MMLU-imputation procedures.

E4.justification: v2 adds workload stress testing with 1–100 concurrent users in Appendix D.2, examining response-time growth and variability. Figure 6 analyzes setup and communication costs across OPT sizes. Appendix A additionally compares research-model and released-model size distributions. These analyses extend substantially beyond v1's library runtime comparison.

E5.justification: v1 already reports values with ± notation but provides no sample count or interval definition. v2 Figure 6 specifies n=128 and discusses 95% confidence intervals; Figure 10 reports medians, quartiles and extrema. These improve statistical documentation without establishing increased repetitions of the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 contains replacement timings under changed hardware/model settings: for example, NNsight's Gemma activation-patching time changes from 0.337 to 0.227 seconds. Attribution timings disappear, while setup, remote-service, survey and load-testing results are added. v2 Table 2 reports OPT-66B HPC/NDIF setup times of 23.697/0.423 seconds but request times of 1.889/2.739 seconds, distinguishing setup savings from request latency.

M1.justification: The core tracing, intervention graphs, Envoy/Proxy access and sessions remain. The reported serving procedure changes: v1 Section 3 says multiple users can be batched, whereas v2 Appendices B.2/D.2 specify queued execution with one forward pass per user and defer shared batching to future work. The PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or the earlier description was corrected.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the tutorial-oriented main text is reorganized around a survey, formal framework, evaluation and discussion. Much implementation material moves into Appendix B, with expanded examples in Appendix C. Separate ecosystem and limitations sections disappear, and ethics and reproducibility statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds survey plots, formal graph and infrastructure diagrams, a side-by-side code comparison, benchmark plots, a load-testing plot and three appendix tables. Table 1 replaces its attribution-patching block with setup times. The remote-pipeline diagram is substantially expanded, while v1's Envoy diagram is retained as v2 Figure 9.

R1.justification: The main positioning against Garçon, Petals and local intervention libraries remains. v2 extends it with S-LoRA, dLoRA and Punica, distinguishing their adapter-serving scope from general interventions, and adds sources supporting the survey and distributed implementation. Some background citations disappear. Publication updates to existing works such as Petals do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 adds formal computation/intervention-graph definitions, getter/setter edges and an acyclicity condition. Appendix E supplies a constructive equivalence argument between multiple-output and single-output apply nodes. v1 describes graph implementation without these mathematical definitions or derivations.

improvement.justification: v1's central remote-service benefits were largely asserted while its benchmark evaluated local libraries. v2 directly tests setup costs, remote interventions, Petals comparisons and concurrent demand, substantially strengthening evidence for the system's practical value. Formal definitions and expanded implementation documentation also improve assessability. Removing attribution-patching benchmarks and some limitations weakens coverage, and the runtime-benefit wording overstates Table 2, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gain in validation of the paper's central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NNsight and NDIF, with matching central architecture and examples. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v2 includes readable Appendices A–E; v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original library and remote-service benchmarks, concurrent-user testing, and an analysis of 184 research papers in Section 2 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 Section 6 and Table 1 report original activation-patching and attribution-patching runtime experiments across models and libraries.

results.title: NNsight and NDIF: Democratizing Access to Open-Weight Foundation Model Internals

C1.justification: v1's broad claim that smaller models memorize while larger models generalize becomes a task-dependent account: factual QA relies more on memorization, while translation and harder MMLU tasks rely more on generalization. Emergence and instruction-tuning contributions are dropped. Explaining LLM probabilities better than ∞-gram becomes a central claim.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations involving transferable translation skills, rare-knowledge retrieval and reasoning complexity, and interprets checkpoint influence as complementary causal evidence. These substantially revise v1's emergence and instruction-tuning interpretations. Appendix A additionally identifies checkpoint availability as a constraint, while retaining the limitations concerning older models and pair-filtering quality.

D1.justification: v2 supplies previously missing cosine-filter thresholds, explains the division between WIMBD and ∞-gram searches and zero-probability handling, and lists MMLU task groups. It promises code upon acceptance rather than documenting an available release. Hardware and dataset-access disclosures are largely retained, and the checkpoint schedule remains unspecified.

E1.justification: v1 analyzes Pythia/Pile and OLMo/Dolma and reports searching Tulu; v2's substantive corpus analyses focus on Pythia/Pile, although Tulu's license entry remains. WMT, TriviaQA and MMLU are retained. Appendix Figure 11 adds auxiliary pair-detection evaluations using FLAN-family texts spanning NLI, summarization, sentiment and other tasks, without identifying exact constituent datasets.

E2.justification: v2 introduces an evaluated ∞-gram language-model comparator for the central distributional analysis, absent from v1. The output-only n-gram control remains in the influence analysis. Appendix E additionally reports unsuccessful LLM-based and NER-based alternatives to semantic pair identification, although those alternatives are incompletely specified.

E3.justification: The reported MMLU analyses shift from OLMo base/instruction-tuned comparisons to Pythia size sweeps. v2 introduces an n=3 performance analysis excluding zero-count MMLU examples and n=3/5 correlation evaluations. Distributional evaluation changes from R² to Spearman correlation; the redesigned influence experiment specifies checkpoint aggregation and 50 retrieved documents per example.

E4.justification: v2 adds knowledge-versus-reasoning MMLU analyses, comparisons across n-gram lengths, a contamination check using overlaps longer than 14 tokens, unsuccessful pair-detection alternatives, and aggregate translation-alignment histograms. The OLMo instruction-tuning analysis disappears. Earlier illustrative examples and the WMT novel-pair chart are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 introduces correlation significance testing, p<0.05 markers, and omission of WMT correlation values because they are nonsignificant. Appendix Figures 10–11 add error bars. v1 provides R² fits and some fit annotations but no comparable significance-reporting scheme. v2 does not explain the appendix error bars or provide repeated-run and seed counts.

E6.justification: Central results are replaced under changed estimators: v1's R² curves and OLMo comparisons of 0.42 versus 0.51 give way to task-dependent Spearman correlations and checkpoint-influence results. v2 also adds MMLU accuracy curves and appendix findings. WMT and TriviaQA performance curves and WMT novelty counts are retained; the new correlations should not be interpreted as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 replaces v1's sequence-level count-product approximation and regression analysis with conditional pair probabilities and Spearman correlations against reference-output probabilities. It also replaces count-weighted gradient cosine similarity with gradient dot products accumulated across checkpoints. These change the analytical procedures beyond renaming the existing pair table.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and conclusions are extensively rewritten around distributional memorization and task-gram models. Influence analysis moves after the distributional results, related work moves from the appendix into the main text, and task-specific interpretive subsections reorganize the narrative. These exceed changes caused solely by added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with a revised pipeline diagram and substantially reorganized central plots. The retained novelty chart joins the new four-panel Figure 3, while the separate WMT performance-versus-size panel disappears. Example tables are reformatted, and appendix Figures 9–12 add new displays.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning against ∞-gram models and Merrill et al.'s novelty findings, and introduces phrase-table and long-range-dependency precedents. Gradient influence is now grounded in Pruthi et al. rather than Han et al. The novelty claim softens from the first effort to one of the first comprehensive analyses, and OLMo/Tulu-related references are removed.

T1.justification: v2 replaces v1's independent-pair product construction and approximately equal input-marginal assumption with an explicit conditional count ratio. Definitions 1–3 formalize the revised task-gram construction and memorization functional, while Section 6 introduces checkpoint-summed influence equations. These are substantive mathematical revisions, although neither version supplies a theorem-and-proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central analysis through explicit conditional definitions, an evaluated ∞-gram comparator, significance reporting and knowledge-versus-reasoning analyses. These support a more differentiated account than v1's broad scaling conclusions. Loss of OLMo/Dolma coverage reduces generality, and reporting defects remain: Section 5 states five-gram TriviaQA correlation exceeds 0.35 although Figure 3 stays below 0.25, and appendix error bars are undefined. Nevertheless, the methodological clarification and stronger comparative evidence constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same investigation of LLM capabilities through task-relevant pretraining n-grams. Their text, equations, figures and appendices are readable, allowing retained material to be matched despite substantial methodological and structural revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original task evaluations, distributional correlations and training-influence analyses in Sections 4–6, plus pair-identification and generation analyses in the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original corpus searches, downstream evaluations, gradient analyses, distribution regressions and generation analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendix.
