results.title: Generalization v.s. Memorization: Tracing Language Models’ Capabilities Back to Pretraining Data

C1.justification: v1 claims demonstrated 400K context extension and leaves faster execution and 1M scaling to future work. v2 claims achieved million-token scaling, a 128-fold extension to 4M, and efficient execution without additional overhead. It also explicitly conditions infinite context on sufficient memory. The 4M headline attribution to LLaMA3.2 conflicts with Section 3.3 and Figure 4, which assign that result to Qwen2-1B.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantive applicability limitation: poor performance on synthetic key-value retrieval, despite success on natural-context tasks. Section 4.3 and Appendix B propose disrupted cache coherence and positional ambiguity as explanations. Section 4.1 also explains semantic-fragmentation, local-context and selection-budget tradeoffs. These substantially qualify v1's predominantly favorable interpretation of position-agnostic selection.

D1.justification: Beyond revised cache settings, v2 documents the Triton operator-fusion implementation and profiling with real inference Q/K inputs on an A800-80GB GPU, a 48-core CPU and 256GB RAM. Appendix B.1 describes extracting Q/K states before and after positional embedding, reshaping them and applying t-SNE. These add implementation and analysis procedures absent from v1's evaluation settings and future optimization plan.

E1.justification: v2 adds InfiniteBench's English multiple-choice, question-answering and summarization tasks, RULER synthetic retrieval evaluations, and PG19 examples for cache analysis in Appendix B. These materially expand the evaluated data and input types beyond the retained LongBench, L-Eval and needle-retrieval coverage.

E2.justification: InfLLM changes from a cited method in v1 to an evaluated comparator on InfiniteBench and RULER in v2 Tables 1 and 3. v2 also compares the fused kernel against its PyTorch implementation. Full-attention and StreamingLLM comparisons remain, while v1's paired Dynamic NTK multi-needle comparison is no longer reported in the corresponding v2 retrieval experiment.

E3.justification: v1 uses model-dependent cache budgets; v2 standardizes local length to 4096 and k' to 127, replacing LLaMA3's k'=96 and most other models' local length 8192/k'=256. The benchmark roster adds LLaMA3.1/3.2 and 70B/72B models while dropping LLaMA2 and InternLM2 variants. Main needle tests change from four to eight A100s and extend their length ranges. New protocols include 32K/64K/128K InfiniteBench tests, 8K/16K RULER tests and controlled attention-budget ablations.

E4.justification: v1's correct/wrong attention-distribution case study is retained as v2 Figure 8. v2 additionally tests chunk size, span size, top-k and local-window sensitivity in Table 2, examines runtime and memory scaling, and investigates synthetic-retrieval failures through cache visualizations. Appendix B expands these diagnostics across natural and synthetic texts, layers, positional encodings and models.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experimental results. The added tables and efficiency plots continue reporting point estimates without statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Retained results are revised: LLaMA3's LongBench average changes from 35.07 for LongCache in v1 Table 2 to 35.03 for ReAttention in v2 Table 4, under changed cache settings. v2 adds extensive InfiniteBench, efficiency, ablation and longer-retrieval measurements. New negative findings include ReAttention's RULER MultiKey3 scores of 78.00 at 8K and 15.00 at 16K in Table 3. These are revised or newly reported outcomes, not evidence of a uniform same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The selection, voting, neighboring-span extraction and positional-reassignment procedure in Sections 2.1–2.2 remains unchanged. However, v2 implements a fused Triton kernel for attention-score computation and top-k selection, replacing separate PyTorch operations and intermediate-memory transfers; v1 leaves GPU optimization as future work. This is a limited execution adaptation rather than a new selection algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contribution statements are substantially rewritten around three conditions for infinite context and an attention-before-attention explanation. The discussion becomes three subsections, detailed benchmark reporting moves into Appendix A, and Appendix B introduces a separate diagnostic narrative. The method name, title, author information and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v1's two-part cache-operation diagram is replaced by a higher-level architecture diagram. Its separate benchmark tables become regrouped results in v2 Appendix Table 4 with main-text summary plots. v2 adds efficiency charts, ablation and RULER tables, and multiple t-SNE figures, while redesigning the retrieval panels. The existing attention maps are retained and relocated from Figure 4 to Figure 8.

R1.justification: The main positioning against full-attention extrapolation and sparse retrieval methods remains. v2 sharpens its distinctions from InfLLM and LongHeads, adds RetrievalAttention and references supporting the new evaluations and analyses, and removes the xPos/parallel-context-window/NBCE discussion. This refines the existing research positioning rather than replacing it.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3) retain the same mathematical operations, with only notation clarification. v2's three conditions for infinite context and its manifold-based discussion are conceptual arguments and empirical interpretations; they introduce no formal definitions, theorems, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1: efficiency was previously future work, the closely related InfLLM lacked direct comparison, and hyperparameter sensitivity and synthetic-retrieval failures were unexplored. Measured efficiency, controlled ablations, additional comparisons and explicit failure analysis substantially strengthen practical validation and clarify applicability. The inconsistent attribution of the 4M result and the unproven causal interpretation of t-SNE plots weaken specific claims, but the broader evidential gains support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cache-selection approach, renamed from LongCache to ReAttention. Their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. All 11 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2 were inspected, including v2's Appendices A–B; v1 has no appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and retrieval results, efficiency measurements, hyperparameter ablations, RULER experiments and appendix cache-visualization analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench, L-Eval, single- and multi-needle retrieval experiments, together with attention-distribution case studies.

results.title: ReAttention: Training-Free Infinite Context with Finite Attention Scope

C1.justification: The core contribution remains contrastive variational inference using self-generated soft labels. V2 makes stable, mass-covering objectives and lower forward KL more explicit in its headline claims, and its conclusion specifically emphasizes advantages on complex posterior geometries requiring flexible density estimators.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the explanation of low-alpha failures through log-ratio variability, label degeneracy, and dimensionality. It also explains restricted-support recovery failures, qualifies that the control variate need not reduce variance everywhere, and connects small-K degradation to gradient noise. These extend v1's shorter leakage and variance discussions with substantive applicability limits.

D1.justification: V2 newly states the linear-regression priors and documents the toy model and parameter controls; its FlowJax citation changes from version 12.3.0 to 14.0.0. Conversely, v1's learning rate of 1e-3 and eight-layer SLCP flow specification disappear. These omissions do not establish changed settings. The implementation and reproduction-code links remain the same.

E1.justification: The four main inference tasks remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 adds a Gaussian mean-inference toy task for gradient diagnostics, extending coverage beyond v1's experiments.

E2.justification: ELBO and SNIS-fKL remain the evaluated baselines in corresponding benchmark comparisons. The added benchmark analyses reuse these comparators, and the new gradient diagnostic compares against the existing SNIS-fKL baseline. SNIS-fKL-LV is identified with SoftCVI alpha = 1, rather than evaluated as a separate additional comparator.

E3.justification: The common training budget changes from 100,000 to 50,000 optimization steps. V2 adds K = 2 evaluations and controlled gradient sweeps in dimensions 1 and 50. The stated GARCH conditioning inputs also change from alpha1 and alpha2 to alpha0 and alpha1, although the PDFs do not establish whether this correction reflects an implementation change.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's leakage illustration and posterior marginals, v2 adds gradient signal-to-noise diagnostics, tests of posterior-based negative distributions, sensitivity to K = 2 versus K = 8, and posterior visualizations for six SLCP runs (Appendices A.3–A.5). These substantially expand the investigation of mechanisms, sensitivity, and failure behavior.

E5.justification: The stated number of independent seeded runs increases from 20 to 50. Both versions already display variation through boxplots. V2 additionally describes estimating gradient means and element-wise standard deviations across random seeds in Appendix A.3, without specifying that diagnostic's seed count.

E6.justification: V1 describes SoftCVI alpha = 1 and SNIS-fKL as performing similarly; v2 reports advantages for SoftCVI on most tasks and frequent poor SLCP mode approximation by SNIS-fKL. Performance, runtime, and marginal plots change, and new diagnostic and sensitivity results are added. Because the training budget changes, these are revised results rather than demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 proposes an explicit SNIS-fKL-LV loss with a mean-log-q control-variate term (Section 3.2, Equation 15). This is a limited auxiliary objective addition: it is gradient-equivalent to the existing SoftCVI alpha = 1 case, while Algorithm 1 and the main SoftCVI loss remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction, negative-distribution discussion, results, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work moves before the experiments, the expanded SNIS-fKL comparison moves from Appendix C into the main text, and Appendices A–C are reorganized into A.1–A.5. This materially changes the explanatory sequence.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes its calibration display from actual coverage to actual-minus-nominal coverage with a zero reference line. V2 adds gradient, alternative-negative-distribution, small-K, and six-run SLCP figures. The existing runtime and marginal displays are retained as Figures 5 and 8 with revised layouts and axes, rather than constituting wholly new analyses.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Chehab et al. on negative-distribution choice, Rainforth et al. on gradient SNR, and Blei et al. on variational inference, while removing references such as Rossi et al. and Wan et al. It sharpens the relationship to SNIS-fKL and other soft-label contrastive methods, retaining the central positioning between variational inference and contrastive learning.

T1.justification: V2 extends v1's Appendix C comparison by deriving the normalization-term gradient, establishing equality of expected gradients with SNIS-fKL, and identifying the control variate and inverse-K variance behavior (Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2). Appendix A.4 adds reasoning for posterior-based negative distributions. The original zero-gradient-at-optimum proof is retained as Appendix A.1.

improvement.justification: V2 turns v1's brief SNIS-fKL comparison into a substantially better-supported account of the method's gradient behavior. The derivations in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2, combined with gradient diagnostics and sensitivity experiments, explain both advantages and failure conditions. These gains strengthen the paper beyond its changed performance scores. Omitting the learning rate and flow depth weakens reproducibility, but this limited loss is outweighed by the stronger theoretical and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SoftCVI by the same authors. Their main texts, equations, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original 50-run main comparisons and additional gradient diagnostics, negative-distribution experiments, small-K tests, and SLCP case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original 20-run comparisons on Eight Schools, linear regression, SLCP, and GARCH, including performance, posterior marginals, and runtime results.

results.title: SoftCVI: Contrastive variational inference with self-generated soft labels

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraph, and conclusion retain the central claims: contrastively derived variational objectives, self-generated soft labels, zero gradient variance at exact approximation, and frequent calibration and forward-KL benefits. The additional applications do not redefine these principal claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability qualifications. It explains that model-parameter learning requires an additional objective and attributes the neural experiment's limited SoftCVI advantage to Gaussian posterior misspecification. It also discusses why predictive likelihood/calibration need not establish posterior accuracy, selection bias from validation procedures, and architecture-dependent runtime costs.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.7 supplies substantial model specifications, including eight-schools and GARCH priors, SLCP covariance construction, and reference-sampling details. v3 also discloses the four-layer SLCP flow and implementation settings for the added applications. The implementation package/link changes from softcvi to pyrox. Newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to the original implementations.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained Bayesian benchmarks and Gaussian diagnostic task, v3 adds MNIST generative-model training and synthetic nonlinear regression with Bayesian neural additive models. These extend coverage to image generation and neural-network posteriors with 1,500 or 3,000 parameters.

E2.justification: ELBO and SNIS-fKL remain the comparison methods in the matched benchmark experiments. The new neural additive-model study uses these same comparators, and the VAE example uses ELBO. Newly discussed adversarial methods are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: The original benchmarks retain their documented 50,000-step, K = 8 protocol and metrics. Added protocols include VAE training for 100,000 steps with batch size 1; neural-model widths 50/100, 300/150/1,000 training/validation/test samples, validation-based stopping, and predictive metrics; and a K = 2–64 sweep. These are additional protocols, not established changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v3 extends the existing K = 2 versus K = 8 investigation into a sample-count sweep measuring posterior fit and computational cost (Figure 7). Table 1 also compares neural-network widths. The original SNR, alternative-negative-distribution, and multimodal-posterior analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix A.5 newly specifies ten networks initialized with different seeds, and Table 1 reports values with ± terms, although their statistical meaning is unspecified. The original 50-run benchmark count remains. The replacement runtime curves no longer display the run-to-run spread shown by v2's timing boxplots.

E6.justification: v3 adds VAE manifolds, neural additive-model predictions and metrics, and accuracy/runtime curves across K, alongside small updates to Figure 1's plotted summaries. In new Table 1, width-50 ELBO achieves test log-likelihood -2.392 ± 0.005 versus -2.424 ± 0.007 for SoftCVI with alpha = 0.75. These are new-setting results, not performance changes relative to v2.

M1.justification: The core SoftCVI algorithm is retained. New Appendix A.4 introduces a limited extension for jointly learning model parameters: an additional ELBO-derived model loss trains the decoder and prior while SoftCVI trains the encoder, reusing proposal samples (Equations 28–29).

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the soft-label explanation and selected related-work passages, streamlines main-text task descriptions with a new detailed appendix, and adds acknowledgments and affiliation edits. The main section order and most existing exposition remain stable.

P2.justification: The ICLR format changes typography, headers, spacing, and figure placement throughout. v3 adds VAE and neural-component figures and Table 1, and replaces the fixed-K timing boxplots with accuracy/runtime curves. Other appendix displays are retained and renumbered, including v2 Figures 4 and 6 becoming v3 Figures 6 and 8.

R1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a focused comparison with adversarial variational methods using separate classifiers. v3 also adds chi-divergence and neural-model references while removing some generic contrastive-learning examples. The broader positioning between variational inference and contrastive estimation remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 explicitly adds the assumption that the variational family contains the true posterior and specifies optimality over all proposal sample sets, equivalently the expected objective. This tightens the posterior-recovery statement. The existing appendix proofs remain; the rewritten control-variate gradient formula is mathematically equivalent.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the evidence about SoftCVI's applicability and limits. The high-dimensional neural study tests a setting absent from v2 and transparently reports little advantage over SNIS-fKL, connecting this outcome to posterior misspecification. The expanded K analysis establishes practical accuracy/cost tradeoffs, while Appendix A.7 improves reproducibility. The VAE evidence remains qualitative and Table 1's ± terms are undefined, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation and more informative account of failure conditions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SoftCVI by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the revised formatting and additional material.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark results and adds MNIST variational-autoencoder experiments, Bayesian neural additive-model results, and expanded sample-count experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on eight schools, linear regression, SLCP, and GARCH, plus gradient signal-to-noise and negative-distribution analyses.

results.title: SoftCVI: Contrastive variational inference with self-generated soft labels

C1.justification: Both versions claim that equivalent-gradient matching with closed-form adapter gradients can narrow the LoRA/full-fine-tuning gap. v2 foregrounds the equivalence already developed in v1 and explicitly extends claimed demonstrated applicability to dialogue, mathematics, coding, and vision. This broadens the empirical contribution without replacing the central scientific claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds overfitting and distribution-mismatch hypotheses explaining GLUE and MT-Bench behavior, acknowledges failure of the full-rank assumption at zero initialization, justifies the Sylvester choice using reported variability, and discusses memory/stability tradeoffs between AdamW modes. These interpretations and qualifications were absent from v1. The overfitting explanations remain hypotheses rather than controlled experimental findings.

D1.justification: v1 supplies optimizer pseudocode but almost no experiment-specific settings. v2 documents learning rates, batch sizes, sequence lengths, rank/scaling, adapted layers, scheduling, warmup, weight decay, hardware, and DeepSpeed configuration. It also provides efficient-mode pseudocode and announces a public code repository. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the GLUE settings are newly disclosed rather than demonstrably changed.

E1.justification: The five GLUE datasets are retained. v2 adds WizardLM training with MT-Bench evaluation, MetaMathQA with GSM8K, and CodeFeedback with HumanEval, covering dialogue, mathematical reasoning, and coding. It also adds image classification on StanfordCars, DTD, EuroSAT, GTSRB, RESISC45, SUN397, and SVHN, substantially expanding task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: The entire GLUE comparator set is retained, including LoRA-GA, which already appears in v1 Table 1. v2 adds zero-shot CLIP as an evaluated comparator in Table 3. The LLM experiments otherwise extend the existing comparator methods to new tasks; additional LoRA-GA ranks are configuration changes.

E3.justification: New protocols include Llama-2-7B training on 52k WizardLM and 100k MetaMathQA/CodeFeedback samples, GPT-4 judging of first-turn MT-Bench responses, GSM8K accuracy, and HumanEval PASS@1. v2 also introduces CLIP visual-backbone fine-tuning with a frozen classifier, rank sweeps, and dedicated memory/time measurements. Newly disclosed GLUE hyperparameters do not establish that its previous settings changed.

E4.justification: v1 contains no empirical ablations. v2 tests zero, Sylvester, and symmetry choices for X in Table 4; rank scalability in Table 2; the full-rank assumption during training in Figure 2; resource costs in Table 5; and efficient versus full AdamW in Appendix C, Table 7. These substantially extend analysis of design choices, assumptions, and practical tradeoffs.

E5.justification: v1 Table 1 already reports plus/minus values but does not identify their statistical meaning or run count. v2 explicitly states that results are means and standard deviations from three runs with different random seeds. This clarifies reporting; it does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains all baseline values but revises all five LoRA-Pro results: its average changes from 88.80 to 88.44, MNLI from 86.92 to 86.03, and QNLI from 92.89 to 93.42. Identical underlying settings are not established. v2 adds extensive LLM, vision, ablation, rank, and resource results. Some new prose disagrees with its tables: Table 2 gives a GSM8K gain over LoRA of 12.15, not the stated 11.98.

M1.justification: The core objective and closed-form adapter gradients remain. However, v2 Appendix C introduces default efficient AdamW, maintaining moments separately for adjusted A and B gradients instead of the full equivalent gradient. This substantially changes the update procedure and optimizer-state requirements. v1 Algorithm 2 is retained as v2 Algorithm 3, with its first Sylvester solve simplified to X=0.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the low-rank-gradient connection. Related Work moves from before Method to after Experiments, the experimental narrative gains distinct task and ablation subsections, and appendix proof/optimizer explanations are reorganized. Authorship, headings, terminology, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds the method illustration and rank-tracking figures, five results/analysis tables, and an additional algorithm display. v1's notation Table 2 is retained as v2 Table 6. Existing Table 1 is regrouped and gains row shading and second-best underlining. Running headers, typography, theorem boxes, and proof formatting are also substantially redesigned.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new models, datasets, evaluation tools, and infrastructure, including Llama 2, WizardLM, MetaMath, MT-Bench, image benchmarks, and DeepSpeed. The substantive PEFT/LoRA positioning remains largely unchanged, with a limited expansion of the GaLore description. LoRA-GA's publication update refers to the same work already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The three central theorems remain. v2 adds a lemma proving equivalent-gradient rank at most 2r, restores the missing right-hand projector in v1 Equation 20 through v2 Equation 30, and corrects the dB sign in the descent proof. It also introduces the symmetry formula in Equation 16, although its inverse of A^T A is invalid under the stated r<n dimensions.

improvement.justification: v1's broad effectiveness claims rest on one GLUE table with little experimental documentation. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through language-and-vision validation, design and assumption analyses, measured resource costs, explicit settings and run reporting, and an efficient optimizer option. Proof corrections also help. These gains outweigh new defects, including inconsistent GSM8K margins and the invalid inverse in Equation 16, which weaken specific explanations and the auxiliary symmetry variant but do not erase the substantial gains in empirical support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LoRA-Pro, retaining the equivalent-gradient objective and corresponding theorems and algorithms. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 Sections 3.1–3.4 and Appendix C report original T5, Llama-2, and CLIP experiments, including ablations, rank tracking, and resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 Section 4 and Table 1 report original T5-base fine-tuning experiments on MNLI, SST2, CoLA, QNLI, and MRPC.

results.title: LoRA-Pro: Are Low-Rank Adapters Properly Optimized?

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes memory-efficient gradient matching and its convergence benefits. v2 centers its contributions on overcoming source imbalance and Adam-specific selection problems, while extending applicability claims to additional models and classification tasks. It additionally claims superiority to four-times-larger batches and 2.7x speedups under the expanded comparison settings.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations concerning unreliable small-source medoids and the need to match Adam-normalized gradients. It attributes superiority over larger batches despite higher gradient variance to more uniform learning across sources (Section 5.2). Section 5.4 newly discusses the dependence of source-free application on clustering quality and proposes using a fine-tuned proxy model.

D1.justification: Most existing learning-rate, sequence-length, LoRA, hardware and decoding details are retained, with material relocated to Appendix B. v2 adds Zephyr-specific LoRA target modules, explicit clustering warm-up/update details, the small-source threshold and a reference identifying the memory-efficient random-projection implementation.

E1.justification: The MathInstruct training dataset and six mathematical evaluation datasets are retained. v2 adds SST-2, CB and MultiRC classification experiments, including data without supplied source labels (Sections 5.1 and 5.4, Table 7). This substantially broadens task coverage.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's random small- and large-batch training comparisons, v2 Table 1 evaluates Big Loss, Grad Norm, Middle Perplexity, Completion Length, Least Confidence and hidden-state facility-location selection. These are actual additional comparators; FT denotes the retained random-batch training baseline.

E3.justification: The existing Phi-2 mathematical training and decoding settings largely remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce Phi-3 training for 4K iterations, Zephyr training for 2K iterations, batch-size-256 comparisons and additional CoLM batch sizes. Classification uses 250 CB examples or 3K SST-2/MultiRC examples, 80 iterations, a 20-iteration clustering warm-up and four clustering updates.

E4.justification: The weighted-sampling ablation is replaced by component tests of small-source retention, separate source selection and Adam normalization. v2 also examines weighting and distance choices, extends sparsification tests, and adds gradient-approximation and layer comparisons, gradient-variance measurements, batch-size sensitivity, completion-length analysis and alternative clustering procedures (Tables 2–7; Figures 3 and 5).

E5.justification: Both versions specify three experimental repetitions and report ± values in tables. However, v1 Figure 1 includes error bars on convergence curves, whereas the replacement convergence plot in v2 Figure 3a omits them. No increase in repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: For Phi-2 at 1K iterations, Table 1 replaces SSM's 54.0 average accuracy with 56.6 for the revised CoLM method; matched random-batch results remain 50.1 and 52.6. v1's 2K SSM results are absent. Numerous baseline, model, classification and ablation results are added. Table 7 reports 75.8 for online clustering and 81.9 for fine-tuned-model clustering, versus 78.9 for larger-batch FT.

M1.justification: SSM's inverse-source-size sampling and batch-wide selection become CoLM's retention of all small-source examples within each candidate batch and separate selection from large sources. v2 adds Adam-history-normalized gradients, source-specific sparsification masks and clustering to infer unspecified sources. Zeroth-order V-projection gradients and uniform selected-example weights are retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution narrative and substantial portions of the method exposition are rewritten. The problem formulation becomes a gradient-matching preliminary section, and the method is reorganized around imbalance, Adam and dimensionality. Training details and pseudocode move to separate appendices, replacing the previous single-proof appendix structure.

P2.justification: v2 restructures Table 1 around additional comparators, replaces the weighted-sampling table and adds Tables 5–7. Performance and timing plots are redesigned, the two convergence panels become one, and new illustrative, multi-model, variance, batch-size, source-distribution and completion-length graphics appear. Pseudocode is reformatted and relocated to Appendix C.

R1.justification: The related-work organization is retained, but v2 adds completion-length selection, Big Loss, projection, model and benchmark references. It foregrounds prior mini-batch coreset work as its starting point and removes v1's blanket assertion that existing selection methods cannot provide theoretical guarantees. Several older optimization-background citations are also removed.

T1.justification: v1's conditional nonconvex-SGD convergence theorem and Appendix A proof are replaced. v2 introduces dense-region, Lipschitz and boundedness assumptions, source-size and local-medoid statements, and a variance-reduction theorem (Theorems 4.1–4.3), supported by new lemmas and derivations in Appendix A.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation: Table 1 tests alternative selection methods, Tables 2 and 5–6 examine the proposed components, and additional models and classification tasks test broader applicability. This provides materially stronger evidence for the method's advantages and dependencies. Missing convergence error bars and the dependence of larger-batch superiority on fine-tuned-model clustering in Table 7 temper the gains but do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same mini-batch selection research, despite the changed title and SSM/CoLM terminology. Both versions' complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with Phi-2, Phi-3 and Zephyr, mathematical and classification tasks, selection baselines and component analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Phi-2 fine-tuning experiments on MathInstruct, including six mathematical evaluation datasets, training-time comparisons and ablations.

results.title: Mini-batch Coresets for Memory-efficient Language Model Training on Data Mixtures

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions and headline claims: source-aware mini-batch coresets, adaptation to Adam and high-dimensional gradients, memory savings, and performance exceeding larger random batches. The expanded model list supplies additional support without redefining these claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 newly explains that CoLM reduces activation memory, distinguishing it from weight and optimizer-state savings and explaining why benefits grow with batch size. Appendix D adds a rationale for emphasizing downstream performance over perplexity and explicitly notes MathInstruct's lack of a held-out validation set.

D1.justification: Appendices C/E newly disclose eight-step gradient accumulation, effective-batch accounting, per-device capacity constraints, and an estimated selection overhead below 200 MB. Appendix F and Table 8 document pre-training mixture weights, token chunking, training duration, and hardware. These materially extend reproducibility information, particularly for interpreting the memory comparisons.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds language-model pre-training on five Pile components: EuroParl, GitHub, HackerNews, NIH Exporter, and English Wikipedia. It adds downstream evaluation on SQuAD, WiC, and COPA. This substantially extends training domains and task coverage beyond the retained MathInstruct and classification experiments.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds a low-rank MeZO gradient comparator using GaLore-style SVD projection. The existing actual-gradient, projected-gradient, and MeZO rows are retained with clearer names. The main fine-tuning comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama-3.2-1B/3B and Llama-3.1-8B evaluations, extends batch-size testing, and introduces memory measurements across batch sizes. Appendix F adds a Llama-60M setup with 10K training iterations, 1024-token sequences, held-out perplexity, and downstream accuracy. These are additional experimental settings; the newly disclosed gradient accumulation does not establish a change to retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct analysis of memory scaling with batch size and selection overhead (Figure 2c and Appendix E), materially strengthening investigation of the central efficiency premise. It also adds training-loss trajectories (Figure 5a) and the low-rank gradient ablation (Table 5). Existing component, sparsity, layer, and completion-length analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments are repeated three times and retain the same uncertainty-reporting format for corresponding fine-tuning tables. No new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or estimation procedures are documented. Revised Table 7 means and uncertainty values are result changes.

E6.justification: v3 adds Llama evaluations, memory and loss results, the low-rank ablation, and pre-training outcomes; Table 9 reports average accuracy 43.9 for CoLM versus 42.5 for larger-batch pre-training. Under the same stated fine-tuning setup, Table 7 changes online-clustering accuracy from 75.8 to 78.7 and fine-tuned-clustering accuracy from 81.9 to 81.0. Reported memory savings versus batch sizes 128/256 change from 2x/4x to 20%/45%. Table 1 accuracy values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: CoLM retains the same source-aware selection, Adam normalization, zeroth-order V-projection gradients, sparsification, and facility-location objective. Algorithm 1 adds explicit gradient-estimation, normalization, and masking steps already described in v2 Sections 4.2–4.3; these are documentation expansions.

P1.justification: v3 revises the title, adds the conference header, makes localized wording edits, reorders results paragraphs, moves dataset details into the appendix, and exchanges the pseudocode and settings appendix order. Pseudocode explanations expand, but most existing narrative and theoretical text remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 are substantially reorganized: the model comparison expands, memory displays are added, and existing panels move. v2 Figures 4–5 become the two panels of v3 Figure 4. New Figures 5–6 and Tables 8–9 present supplementary and pre-training material, while Table 5 gains a row. Figure 5b redisplays convergence against training time rather than adding an independent experiment.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for Llama 3, the Pile, SQuAD, WiC, COPA, and the relationship between pre-training loss and downstream performance. GaLore also becomes the basis of an evaluated gradient approximation. The related-work discussion and overall research positioning otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, Theorems 4.1–4.3, and Appendix A assumptions, lemmas, proofs, and variance-reduction result are unchanged. Moving the small-source definition and expanding pseudocode introduce no new mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the paper's central memory-efficiency evidence. It replaces v2's 4x memory-saving assertion for the main comparison with a quantified 45% reduction, adds memory-scaling and overhead analyses, and discloses gradient accumulation. Additional model and pre-training experiments broaden empirical support. A new Section 5.4 inconsistency remains: the claimed 6.8-point benefit over online clustering is only 2.3 points in Table 7. This localized reporting error does not outweigh the substantial improvement in resource accounting and empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoLM, despite the revised title. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original fine-tuning experiments and adds model evaluations, memory analyses, and pre-training results in Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original language-model fine-tuning results, comparisons, convergence measurements, and ablations in Tables 1–7 and Figures 2–3.

results.title: Mini-batch Coresets for Memory-efficient Language Model Training on Data Mixtures

C1.justification: The central claims of physical-world vulnerability and three distinct risk mechanisms remain. v3 adds explicit comparative-superiority claims and foregrounds applicability to established frameworks and the benchmark as contributions. This refines the claimed contribution scope while retaining the original central scientific finding.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations involving conflicts with robotic system prompts, speech-recognition losses, jointly malicious outputs defeating consistency checks, and fine-tuning's uneven safety effects. Appendix F also qualifies ProgPrompt success as attempted execution despite incomplete tasks and acknowledges VisProg's differences from embodied systems. These materially extend v2's mechanism discussion and limitations.

D1.justification: v3 supplies exact attack and system prompts, action interfaces, the automated judging rubric, benchmark composition, prompt-collection procedures, server specifications, and expanded robot/camera details (Appendices B, E-J). Much of this was only referenced or briefly described in v2. However, v3 omits v2's direct project and benchmark-repository links; this changes access information without establishing that the resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: Beyond v2's prototype demonstrations, v3 evaluates RLBench object-interaction and spatial-composition tasks, VirtualHome household tasks, PyBullet tabletop scenarios, and VisProg image editing and object tagging (Section 4.3; Appendix F). These substantially extend task and environment coverage. The benchmark's seven harmful-action categories remain the same.

E2.justification: v3 reports a systematic comparison against Disguised Intent, Role Play, Structured Response, Virtual AI Simulation, and Hybrid Strategies, using 100 collected prompts and a Vanilla control (Tables 1/A1). v2 illustrates direct-query and role-play behavior and discusses structured responses, but does not report this expanded comparator suite.

E3.justification: v3 introduces quantitative protocols using manipulation success rate and GPT-4 harmfulness ratings, a five-model evaluation including LLaVA-1.5-7B, and 35 physical evaluations per attack. The retained benchmark's reported size changes from 230 to 277 queries. New simulation protocols are specified, although Code as Policies query counts conflict between Section 4.3 and Appendix F.3.

E4.justification: v2 discusses potential mitigations without reporting their effectiveness. v3 tests consistency validation and world-model fine-tuning on LLaVA (Table 3), analyzes failures of conventional jailbreak transfer (Appendix D.1), and quantifies the suffix/no-suffix contrast (Tables 2/A2). These add substantial controlled robustness and component analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix E.1 newly documents averaging results over three contextual-jailbreak prompts to reduce prompt-specific instability. This adds a limited aggregation practice, not evidence of increased independent repeated runs. Neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive quantitative findings absent from v2's qualitative demonstrations. Table 2 reports GPT-4-turbo MSRs of 0.83, 0.66, and 0.65 for the three attacks versus 0.25 Vanilla; Section 4.4 reports physical MSR of 68.57% versus 22.85%. Simulation results, harmfulness scores, and mitigation outcomes are also added. These are newly reported measurements, not same-setting improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The three attack procedures are retained: contextualized jailbreak prompts, structured-output enforcement, and GPT-4-assisted semantic rephrasing. v3 renames Jailbreak Exploit as Contextual Jailbreak and supplies pseudocode and exact prompts, without establishing a different attack algorithm. The semantic-consistency defense formula is also retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, terminology, and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around BADROBOT. Risk analysis becomes a separate conceptual section; general background and policy material move to appendices; related work moves near the end; and conclusions and limitations are combined. This substantially reorganizes the retained material.

P2.justification: v3 adds comparison and mitigation tables, harmfulness radar charts, simulation plots, algorithm panels, benchmark graphics, and extensive simulation and UR3e demonstration grids. It also revises the pipeline graphic and attack illustrations and removes v2's separate linguistic-versus-action-space comparison diagram. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 retains much of v2's general background in Appendix A but adds dedicated positioning against embodied-system adversarial robustness, discrimination, safety frameworks, and backdoor research (Section 6). Newly discussed works include Wu et al., Hundt et al., Azeem et al., SafeEmbodAI, and RiskAwareBench. Novelty is positioned more specifically around no-box malicious robotic manipulation.

T1.justification: v3 Section 2.2 adds an expected-safety maximization objective in Equation 1, beyond v2's universally quantified safety condition. Most remaining formalization changes preserve the existing binary safety logic or make prompt transformations explicit. Neither version supplies substantive theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v2's principal evidentiary weakness: broad vulnerability claims supported mainly by demonstrations. Comparative evaluations, tests across external frameworks, quantified physical trials, and mitigation experiments provide substantially stronger support, while the appendices make procedures inspectable. Limitations remain: some Table A1 averages conflict with displayed category scores, Code as Policies query counts disagree, and direct artifact links disappear. These shortcomings temper confidence in exact estimates but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe the same research, retaining the three vulnerability mechanisms and robotic prototype despite the BADROBOT retitling. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. The supplied v2 ends after its references without the mentioned appendix; v3 includes Appendices A-J.

after.justification: v3 reports original digital, simulation, physical-robot, and mitigation experiments in Sections 4-5, Tables 1-3, and the supplementary results.

before.justification: v2 reports original robotic demonstrations in Figures 1 and 5 and observed model interactions in Sections 4.2-4.3. These qualitative experimental outcomes qualify despite the absence of quantitative result tables.

results.title: BadRobot: Jailbreaking Embodied LLM Agents in the Physical World

C1.justification: The central channel-pruning novelty and memory-saving claims remain. v2 extends the headline empirical comparison to quantization and adds claims of 2.8-fold peak-memory reduction and up to fivefold batch capacity for ThinK combined with KIVI. Its contribution paragraph narrows the stated linear savings from both computation and memory to memory.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 3.3's argument that masked-query decoding should require less computation than zero-filling, and emphasizes the batch-capacity implications of the new KIVI measurements. Existing qualifications about aggressive pruning, small cache budgets, and value-cache pruning on Mistral remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 and Figure 7 newly document KIVI integration, including prefill ordering and residual-buffer handling. v2 also specifies the synthetic workload lengths and quantization precisions. It omits v1's zero-filling/FlashAttention implementation discussion and changes the hardware disclosure from one A100 to A100 GPUs without specifying their count.

E1.justification: LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack coverage remains unchanged. v2 Section 4.4 adds synthetic batched-generation workloads for peak-memory evaluation, providing a limited additional test scenario. The additional LLaMA backbones are changes in experimental configuration.

E2.justification: v2 extends the evaluated comparator families beyond token eviction by adding KIVI: Table 4 compares KIVI with KIVI plus ThinK, and Figure 3b includes 2-bit and 4-bit KIVI configurations. KIVI was cited but not experimentally compared in v1. H2O, SnapKV, and the magnitude-pruning comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds LLaMA-3-70B evaluations across cache budgets and LLaMA-2-7B-chat memory tests using 160-token inputs, 338-token outputs, varying batch sizes, and 2-bit/4-bit caches. These introduce substantial new configurations and peak-memory measurements. The magnitude-plot attribution also changes from LLaMA3-8B in v1 Figure 2 to LLaMA-2-7B in v2 Figure 4; this does not establish that the plot was regenerated.

E4.justification: v2 adds a batch-size sensitivity analysis of peak memory for KIVI with and without ThinK at two precisions, shown in Figure 3b. The recent-size, equal-memory, joint key/value-pruning, and retrieval-depth analyses are retained; their relocation or renumbering does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for its experiments. v2 continues the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: All original table values are retained. v2 adds 70B results, including LongBench averages of 46.27 for SnapKV and 46.45 with ThinK at pruning ratio 0.4 and cache size 512. New Table 4 reports 31.92 for KIVI versus 31.77 with ThinK, while Figure 3b adds peak-memory curves. These are newly reported comparisons under additional configurations.

M1.justification: The channel-selection objective, query-dependent score, observation window, and value-pruning rule remain unchanged. v2 Appendix C.1 adds a KIVI-specific inference procedure: pruning before quantization during prefill and pruning/quantizing accumulated decoding keys when the residual buffer reaches G tokens. The masked-query implementation illustrated in v2 was already described in v1.

P1.justification: v2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, experimental discussion, related work, and conclusion. It removes the contents page, replaces 'End Note and Future Direction' with 'Conclusion', and reorganizes supporting material into Appendices A–D. These are substantial editorial and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different, more compact layout. It expands Table 2 with 70B blocks, adds the KIVI table and workflow diagram, combines the existing equal-memory plot with a new memory-scaling panel, and redraws the decoding diagram. Magnitude plots, SVD plots, retrieval heatmaps, and the joint-pruning table move to appendices.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the introductory Frankle–Carbin and Blalock pruning references with SparseGPT and Sun et al. (2023), adds mathematical-reasoning references, and removes Bordes et al. The principal positioning as channel pruning complementary to eviction and quantization remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The pruning optimization, channel scores, selection constraints, SVD energy formula, and value-pruning equations are mathematically unchanged. The SVD formula and value-pruning formulation move to v2 Appendices A and D. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 asserted compatibility with quantization without experimentally validating it. v2 supplies the KIVI accuracy comparison, peak-memory measurements across batch sizes, and an implementation description, substantially strengthening the practical compression claim. The 70B results also strengthen evidence beyond the original smaller models. Denser tables and incomplete KIVI configuration details limit readability and reproducibility, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ThinK, the same query-driven KV-cache channel-pruning work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the equations, tables, and figures can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds LLaMA-3-70B results, KIVI comparisons, and synthetic-workload peak-memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack experiments, channel-pruning ablations, and comparisons under equal cache-memory budgets.

results.title: ThinK: Thinner Key Cache by Query-Driven Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract narrows resistance from thousands to hundreds of fine-tuning steps. The introduction replaces robustness against 28 adversaries, including 5,000-step attacks, with 26 adversaries and hundreds of steps. This substantially narrows the central robustness claim while retaining the proposed method and its claimed advantage over prior safeguards.

C2.justification: V4 explains contamination and shuffling-related vulnerabilities, emphasizes sensitivity to adversary distributions, and explicitly excludes input-space robustness from its optimization goal. Appendix A newly discusses low post-attack benign performance and the resulting risks for legitimate fine-tuning with contaminated data. Appendix D.4 shifts the initial safeguard's interpreted benefit toward pre-attack restriction rather than the large post-attack robustness benefit reported in v3.

D1.justification: New Appendix C.1 documents the sampler's seed override and the data-cleaning/retraining correction. Training configuration descriptions are updated, and Appendix D.1 newly identifies the benign fine-tuning optimizer. Existing hardware, distributed-training and memory-management details, and code/model access information remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: The main datasets and tasks remain unchanged. However, Appendix D.1 replaces cybersecurity with chemical security in the benign fine-tuning evaluation, including the corresponding WMDP forget-subject check. Biosecurity and the economics adaptation task remain, making this a limited change in that experiment's domain coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain Max Entropy, Min Posterior, LLMU, RMU, MLAC-AR, and SOPHON-AR for knowledge restriction, and Refusal Trained, R2D2, RepNoise, and RR for refusal. Newly cited Booster and Lisa are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix C.1 reports retain-data cleaning, retraining, and correction of overlapping train/test shuffling orders. Table 9 replaces the main 1,000-step attacks with 500-step attacks and removes the two 5,000-step biosecurity attacks. Section 5.1 and Table 7 revise the chemical loss weight and chemical/cyber training adversaries. Appendix D.1 changes benign fine-tuning from 800 steps with batch size 64 to two epochs with batch size 32. These are substantive reported setting changes, despite C.1's general statement that hyperparameters were unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds a five-seed shuffling-sensitivity study in Figure 5 and entropy diagnostics in Figure 6, materially revising the evidence about robustness and convergence. It removes the ablation isolating the retain loss's squared-distance term from Table 5. The existing inner-loop-length and DPO analyses remain; the earlier generalization analysis is moved and extended rather than entirely new.

E5.justification: V3 does not report seed replication counts. V4 explicitly reports averaging three different-seed attack replicates for the main knowledge-restriction results and displays five separate seeded trajectories in Figure 5. This substantially changes replication and variability reporting, although confidence intervals and significance tests are still absent. V3's undisclosed run count does not establish that it used only one run.

E6.justification: Knowledge-restriction results change throughout Table 1, Tables 3–6 and 12, and the heatmaps. TAR's average post-attack accuracies change from 31.3/27.6/29.5 to 35.2/27.1/28.6 for biosecurity/chemical security/cybersecurity under revised conditions, not directly comparable performance gains or losses. Table 5 changes the no-initial-safeguard result from 46.9 to 35.5, versus full TAR's 31.3 and 35.2 respectively. Refusal results in Tables 2 and 11 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the two-stage TAR procedure remain unchanged: initial safeguarding followed by first-order adversarial training, using entropy or DPO objectives and a retain loss. Data cleaning, sampler corrections, and revised training configurations do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: Most prose and the overall section hierarchy remain intact. V4 adds the implementation-update subsection, revises robustness and limitations passages, moves the generalization discussion from Section 5.3 into Appendix D.3, and expands the acknowledgements. These are focused edits and reorganizations.

P2.justification: V4 consolidates v3's Figures 4 and 8 into a three-domain Figure 4, revises heatmap scales and labels, adds the seed-sensitivity figure, and relocates the generalization plot with an added entropy trace. Table 5 loses one ablation row. The overall document format and most other display structures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds Booster and Lisa to the concurrent-defense literature and cites Qi et al.'s On Evaluating the Durability of Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs when acknowledging and corroborating vulnerabilities in the earlier release. The broader related-work structure and existing references are retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, first-order approximation, Random Mapping formulation, and baseline loss definitions remain unchanged. The added entropy and convergence discussion interprets empirical trajectories; it introduces no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses important validity deficiencies: Appendix C.1 reports correcting retain-data contamination and train/test shuffling overlap, while repeated-seed results and Figure 5 expose limitations obscured by v3's stronger claims. Narrowing the headline robustness claim and documenting practical fine-tuning limitations substantially improve credibility and calibration. The shorter main attack horizon and removed retain-loss ablation reduce evidential scope, and some reporting inconsistencies remain, but these costs are outweighed by the correction of central evaluation flaws.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TAR research. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison, including matching content across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical experiments, reports revised knowledge-restriction results, and adds an original analysis of sensitivity to dataloader shuffling seeds.

before.justification: V3 reports original safeguarding experiments on WMDP/MMLU and HarmBench/MT-Bench, plus benign fine-tuning, targeted patching, and component ablations.

results.title: Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs

C1.justification: The introductory contribution statement now explicitly claims exploration through both reward perturbations and higher rewards for unvisited states; v3 emphasized stochastic reward-driven policy diversification. The central claims about autonomous shaping, computational efficiency, sample efficiency, and convergence stability remain.

C2.justification: V3 stresses randomly rewarding arbitrary states, whereas v4 explains an implicit novelty preference: failed visited states lose success probability while unvisited states retain Beta(1,1). V4 also discusses dimensionality and distribution mismatches as disadvantages of adding actions to KDE inputs. The dense-reward and retention-rate limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V4 adds a source-code access link, explicitly defines the linear reward-scaling function, and supplies task state dimensions in Table 14, including 84×84 Atari inputs. It also documents the added tasks' reward conditions and episode limits. Existing architecture, default hyperparameter, hardware, and RFF timing disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: V4 adds RobotSlide, RobotPickPlace, and five Atari games: Pitfall, Frogger, Montezuma's Revenge, Solaris, and Freeway. AntSpeed, AntVeryFar, and WalkerKeep disappear from both the main evaluation and task appendix. The new manipulation objectives and image-based Atari domain substantially change coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 and Figure 3 retain the eight previous baselines and add DRND-online and GFA-RFE, materially expanding the main comparative evaluation. RND also joins the MountainCar exploration-density comparison in Figure 5; its presence in v3's main benchmark did not previously extend to that analysis.

E3.justification: V3 describes Table 1 as summarizing returns throughout training; v4 specifies evaluation of final models over 100 episodes. New experiments introduce SASR-normalized maximum-memory and training-time metrics, plus task-specific horizons such as ten million training steps for Pitfall and Montezuma. Shared network and hyperparameter defaults remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds a six-task state-only versus state-action reward ablation, comparative runtime and memory analyses, and RND to the exploration-density case study. The previous bandwidth sensitivity analysis remains in Appendix A.5 and Table 11 despite losing its main-text plot. The original RFF timing ablation is retained as Table 5.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten instances with different random seeds and report means with standard errors. V4's 100-episode final-model evaluation changes the testing protocol, but no different uncertainty estimator, increased training-run count, confidence-interval procedure, or significance test is specified. Changed error values alone are result changes.

E6.justification: Main comparison and retained ablation values are extensively replaced, alongside new task, comparator, and resource results. For example, Table 1's SASR AntStand entry changes from 39.12±2.86 to 94.9±0.0 under the revised evaluation summary, not a demonstrated same-setting gain. New Montezuma results report DRND-online at 6828.5 versus SASR at 6737.9.

M1.justification: The core SASR procedure, Algorithm 1, losses, and network architectures remain unchanged. New Appendix A.4 proposes optional procedures for automatically selecting kernel bandwidth and RFF dimension. These are limited procedural additions, not documented replacements for the fixed settings used in the experiments.

P1.justification: V4 copyedits and condenses passages, swaps the implementation and complexity subsections, moves the bandwidth discussion into the appendix, and regroups appendices under A.1–A.7. Author and acknowledgement text also changes. These are localized editorial and organizational revisions within the retained narrative.

P2.justification: The ICLR template changes typography and page layout throughout. Figures 2–3 reorganize and expand the task panels; Table 1 is transposed to task rows; Figure 5 gains an RND row; and Figure 6 introduces the state-action comparison while removing the bandwidth panel. New resource, ablation, and state-dimension tables substantially revise the displays.

R1.justification: V4 adds several references, including Mahankali et al. (2024), Zhang et al. (2024), and Wilcox (2011), while removing the multitask reward-agent preprint and Ma et al. (2023). The intrinsic-motivation versus inherent-value taxonomy and principal comparison with ReLara remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: The existing RFF and computational-complexity derivations are retained. Appendix A.4 adds Silverman's bandwidth formula, the dimension prescription M = O(epsilon^-2 log(N/delta)), and a kernel-approximation norm criterion. These are limited mathematical additions without a new convergence or optimality proof.

improvement.justification: V3's efficiency evidence chiefly compared SASR with its RFF ablation and SAC; v4 adds direct runtime and memory comparisons against reward-shaping competitors, addressing an important gap behind the efficiency claim. Added competitive baselines, visual Atari tests, and the state-action ablation substantially strengthen validation, while the code link improves reproducibility documentation. Three control tasks are lost, and the changed evaluation summary prevents interpreting higher scores as method improvements, but the net gain in relevant empirical support is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SASR research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and revised material.

after.justification: V4 reports original experiments on fourteen tasks, including Atari games, together with ablations, exploration analyses, and comparative runtime and memory measurements.

before.justification: V3 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on ten tasks, exploration case studies, component ablations, and training-time measurements.

results.title: Highly Efficient Self-Adaptive Reward Shaping for Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The main contributions remain theoretically motivated asynchronous closed-loop diffusion control, reduced sampling cost, compatibility with DDIM, and strong physical-control performance. The expanded experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges the absence of optimization-performance bounds under guided sampling, replacing v2’s future-work discussion of incorporating PDE priors. It also interprets short-horizon failure through inaccurate objective estimation, discusses memory tradeoffs, and explains sparse-control effects. Offline-training and broader-applicability limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds explicit synchronous and asynchronous DDPM implementation formulas. New appendices document noise injection, actuator placement, boundary-control data and sampling settings, and pendulum simulation, training, and evaluation details. The anonymous code link in v2 is replaced by a named GitHub link. Conversely, v3 drops the previously disclosed half-domain RDM threshold pair.

E1.justification: v3 adds Burgers’ control with actuator bounds, system noise, measurement noise, and sparse sensors/actuators; fluid boundary control; and a distinct double-pendulum task. The earlier FO and PO experiments remain as noise-free and half-domain settings, and the original fixed/random fluid maps are retained.

E2.justification: The original PDE comparator sets remain. The pendulum comparison adds DiffPhyCon-4, -8, -12, and -16 variants in Figure 7, extending the existing DiffPhyCon family. Its prose and Figure 8 instead name DiffPhyCon-15, leaving an inconsistency in one comparator label.

E3.justification: New protocols include full-domain scoring for sparse-observation/control experiments, 30,000 boundary-control training trajectories with 120-step DDIM sampling, and horizon comparisons at H=6, 10, and 15. Pendulum evaluation introduces PPO-generated training data, 290,000 training steps, 100 systems per evaluation, 200-step episodes, success rate, and function-evaluation efficiency. Main-table runtimes now average across settings rather than reporting each setting separately.

E4.justification: Beyond v2’s partial-observation and random-map tests, v3 adds explicit noise and actuator-restriction robustness tests. Appendix G.3 investigates horizon sensitivity, while Appendix H examines pendulum perturbation rates and supplies trajectory and phase-space case studies. These substantially expand diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v2 reports averages and mentions repeated qualitative evaluations without specifying seeds or uncertainty estimates. v3’s pendulum experiment reports five differently seeded runs and mean results with ±1 standard deviation in Figure 7. This reporting improvement is confined to the added experiment; additional runs for the retained PDE results are not established.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical and graphical results, including boundary-control objectives of 0.6169/0.7003 for fixed/random maps, horizon sensitivity, and pendulum performance-efficiency curves. Retained PDE objective scores are unchanged. The half-domain CL-DiffPhyCon runtime changes from 3.7516 seconds in v2 Table 1 to 9.7516 in v3 Table 4 without an explained setting change. Revised main-table runtime averages are not directly comparable to the earlier per-setting timings.

M1.justification: The two-model asynchronous controller, training losses, and Algorithm 1 are retained. The added pendulum implementation uses a Transformer and midpoint-ODE sampling, extending the architecture and sampler instantiations beyond v2’s U-Net DDPM/DDIM implementations. Appendix C primarily documents existing DDPM procedures rather than changing the original controller.

P1.justification: The problem setup and method explanations are extensively revised, with transition-model training presented before guided sampling and efficiency separated into Section 4.5. Proposition 2 moves to Appendix E, limitations move into the conclusion, and experimental appendices are reorganized. Terminology, the title, affiliations, and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 are substantially restructured around expanded scenarios and pooled timing columns. v3 adds sensor/actuator and fluid-domain diagrams, a horizon table, and pendulum schematic, Pareto, and trajectory plots. The earlier main-text Burgers’ comparison figure is removed, but its examples remain in the retained appendix visualizations; the fluid comparison figure is renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds references covering MPC, Diffusion Policy, noisy dynamics, numerical integration, and double-pendulum control. The central positioning against DiffPhyCon, adaptive replanning, and sequential diffusion generation remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes from deterministic action-sequence optimization to expected-objective optimization over a state-conditioned policy with explicitly stochastic dynamics. Proposition 2 receives a different brief proof argument. Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 and their proofs are retained; relocating Proposition 2 and spelling out DDPM specializations do not constitute new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for robustness and the performance-efficiency tradeoff through noisy feedback, restricted actuation, horizon sensitivity, and a distinct pendulum task with five-seed uncertainty. Expanded implementation information and explicit theoretical limitations also improve assessability. Incorrect noise-improvement percentages, inconsistent pendulum baseline labels, and the unexplained half-domain timing change weaken reporting, but do not outweigh these gains. The improvement comes from broader and more diagnostic evidence, not higher scores on retained settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CL-DiffPhyCon. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching renamed experiments and relocated proofs.

after.justification: v3 retains the original empirical results and adds constrained and noisy control experiments, horizon sensitivity, boundary control, and double-pendulum simulations.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulations comparing control performance and inference time on Burgers’ equation and incompressible-fluid tasks, with additional visual results in the appendices.

results.title: CL-DiffPhyCon: Closed-loop Diffusion Control of Complex Physical Systems

C1.justification: The benchmark, toolkit, and file-tuning contributions remain. However, v2 drops the abstract's claim of a new miniF2F state of the art for 1.3B models and foregrounds context benefits for both prompting and fine-tuning, together with miniF2F's inability to capture those benefits. This refines the advertised findings.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes unchanged accuracy after removing preceding proofs in its Rectangle.lean ablation; v2 interprets its different-file ablation as evidence of learning proof strategies and discusses model-dependent benefits from comments. v2 also replaces a largely prospective discussion of cross-file context with observed retrieval limitations and a proposed interference mechanism when retrieved premises dominate the prompt.

D1.justification: v2 documents selection criteria, additional premise/import metadata, a 2023 training snapshot, and more specific extraction and Lean-version instructions. Conversely, it omits v1's three training epochs, validation interval of 4,000 steps, search budgets S=32 and T=100, and several direct artifact links. These substantially change reproducibility information without establishing that the omitted settings changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds HepLean physics problems, SciLean scientific-computing problems, and a PFRcross scenario targeting extensive cross-file dependencies. These substantially broaden the represented domains and contextual requirements. miniF2F and the appendix Math2001 evaluations were already present in v1.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 retains the original five baseline configurations and adds retrieval-augmented GPT-4o and file-tuning comparisons, addressing an important alternative way to supply context. GPT-4o also joins the context-component ablation in Table 4, which previously evaluated only file-tuning.

E3.justification: GPT-4o evaluation changes from pass@1 in v1 Section 5.2 to eight generated proofs and pass@8 in v2 Section 4.1. The reported Prime sample changes from 87 to 85 problems and HTPI from 185 to 45. The component ablation also changes its stated test file from Rectangle.lean to PFR.ForMathlib.Entropy.Basic and expands its controls.

E4.justification: The earlier context ablation is replaced by a seven-condition study separating environment, definitions, lemma statements, proofs, and comments for two models. v2 adds cross-file dependency analysis and an analysis relating retrieved-premise length to success in Appendix D.3. The earlier Math2001 automation tests, proof/context-length analyses, and illustrative proof examples remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run variability, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new pass@8 setting changes the evaluation budget, while the premise-length distribution plot describes examples rather than estimating uncertainty in model performance.

E6.justification: v1 Table 2 reports file-tuning/state-tactic averages of 31.65%/9.31%; v2 Table 3 reports 35.94%/19.53% on the revised benchmark. New results include file-tuning at 44.19% on PFRcross, falling to 16.28% with retrieved premises. Changed coverage and GPT-4o's pass@8 protocol prevent interpreting aggregate differences as same-setting gains. miniF2F and appendix Math2001 scores are retained.

M1.justification: The core file-tuning formulation is retained. v2 Section 4.1 adds an optional inference component that appends the top 20 LeanDojo-retrieved premises from imported, non-Mathlib modules to the context for GPT-4o and file-tuned models. This extends input construction without establishing a change to the underlying architecture or training objective.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and benchmark narrative are extensively rewritten. NTP-TOOLKIT moves into the benchmark section, the standalone file-tuning exposition becomes part of the baseline descriptions, and discussion becomes a separate section. The introduction gains an explicit contribution structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds a benchmark-comparison table, a temporal-update diagram, and new dependency and premise-length plots. Dataset and performance tables gain columns and rows, and the ablation becomes a component matrix. The earlier main-text dependency chart is redrawn and moved to Appendix D.2; other retained charts are also restyled.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around premise selection and existing contextual datasets, adding a benchmark-feature comparison and discussion of Graph2Tac, Magnushammer, and DeepMath. It more explicitly acknowledges prior contextual proving methods and locates miniCTX's distinction in richer context, multiple sources, and temporal evaluation.

T1.justification: Equation 1 retains the same expected proof-correctness objective, and the theorem-, context-, and project-level generalization definitions are unchanged. The Lean proof examples are retained; no substantive theoretical result, derivation, or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The cross-file cases and actual retrieval comparisons address an important gap in v1 between its repository-level framework and experiments focused on preceding-file context. Expanded ablations and failure analysis provide substantially stronger evidence about useful context and retrieval limitations. These gains outweigh the loss of training/search details and the new inconsistency between 376 theorems in the text and 384 in Table 2. The assessment rests on stronger validation, rather than higher scores under changed settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe miniCTX, file-tuning, and NTP-TOOLKIT. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–F are readable and support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent matching the work across versions.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, retrieval comparisons, context-component ablations, and supplementary analyses in Appendices B and D.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on miniCTX and miniF2F, context ablations, and Math2001 experiments in Appendix B.

results.title: miniCTX: Neural Theorem Proving with (Long-)Contexts

C1.justification: v1 describes the released model as generating 720×480, six-second videos at eight fps. v2 claims generation up to 768×1360, ten seconds, and 16 fps across multiple aspect ratios without super-resolution or frame interpolation. Its introduction also expands the release contribution to both 2B and 5B text-to-video and image-to-video models and introduces a commercial-grade priority claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds discussion of convergence difficulties under aggressive VAE compression, explains resolution generalization through the absence of attention modules, and acknowledges that competing VAEs use fewer latent channels. It also positions Expert AdaLN's simplicity as advantageous for scaling. The earlier warning that high-quality fine-tuning slightly harms semantic ability remains in Appendix A.

D1.justification: Tables 5–6 newly disclose training budgets, batch sizes, model dimensions, optimizer settings, and precision. v2 also specifies VAE frame counts, resolution, GAN warm-up, image sources, and caption-model access. Some settings remain unreconciled, including 512-pixel training in Section 3.2 versus 480 pixels in Table 5. The earlier human-evaluation blinding/randomization statement is omitted, without establishing that the procedure changed.

E1.justification: v2 newly uses WebVid for ablation and reconstruction evaluation, extending evaluated data coverage within the existing video domain. Text-to-video, image-to-video, and video-to-video generation already appear in v1. Naming LAION-5B and COYO-700M provides training-source information but does not itself establish new domain coverage, since v1 already trains jointly on images and videos.

E2.justification: The main generation comparators and Kling remain unchanged. New comparisons evaluate SDXL's 2D VAE, Open-Sora and Open-Sora-Plan VAEs, MMDiT variants, and a model without Expert AdaLN. The previous learnable-position and Expert AdaLN-plus-MLP comparisons are removed from the revised ablations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces FVD evaluation on 500 WebVid videos, VAE reconstruction testing on 256×256, 17-frame videos, and filter evaluation using a 10% test subset. MMDiT controls match either parameter count or layer count. Training is described with four stages in Table 5 rather than v1's three-stage outline; the PDFs do not establish that retained benchmark results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds compression/channel ablations, architecture and separated-attention tests, FVD evidence for uniform sampling, and filter validation. The learnable-position and additional-expert-MLP ablations disappear. The RoPE-versus-sinusoidal and sampling loss curves remain, while the interpolation/extrapolation example moves to Appendix A.
