Appendix G also adds a captioning case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added evaluations continue to report point results and training trajectories without identified uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial VAE, FVD, and filter results. Table 2 reports flickering/PSNR of 85.5/29.1 for its VAE, versus 92.4/28.5 for Open-Sora and 90.2/27.6 for Open-Sora-Plan; Table 11 reports filter accuracies of 0.89–0.99. All main generation and human-evaluation scores remain unchanged. The prose now attributes five metric wins specifically to 5B, although Table 3 gives it four outright maxima; the fifth belongs to 2B.

M1.justification: The stated VAE reconstruction loss changes from L2 to L1. Section 2.2 replaces explicitly spatial-only patching with a formulation permitting temporal patches and first-frame repetition. Section 3.1 extends Frame Pack to mixed resolutions. These revise substantive procedures while retaining the central VAE, Expert AdaLN, and full-attention architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion, and several methodological and evaluation passages are substantially rewritten. v2 adds a contribution list and dedicated ablation subsection, introduces an appendix contents list, and reorganizes training details and loss curves into Appendices A–B. Earlier Appendices A–F become D–I, with additional material moved from the main text.

P2.justification: v2 adds an opening showcase, VAE and training tables, FVD plots, and caption/filter illustrations; redraws Frame Pack; and replaces two panels in the relocated loss-curve figure. Typography, figure wrapping, and table placement change throughout. Many existing showcases are retained. The new Figure 8 incorrectly swaps the FVD and training-step axis labels.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for SDXL, CogVLM2, LAION-5B, and COYO-700M and explicitly positions Expert AdaLN against MMDiT. Several baseline and long-context references are removed, even though the corresponding generation baselines remain evaluated. The new commercial-grade priority claim also adjusts novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 revises the token-count expression from T(H/p)(W/p) to (T/q)(H/p)(W/p), introducing temporal patch size q. This is a limited mathematical specification change. The diffusion objective in Equation 1 remains unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central design choices that v1 supported mainly through explanation and limited loss ablations. Reconstruction benchmarks, architecture controls, attention tests, and detailed training specifications improve validation and reproducibility without changing the headline benchmark scores. These gains outweigh the removed smaller ablations and reporting defects, including swapped FVD axes, unreconciled settings, and the overstated attribution of five metric wins to 5B.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CogVideoX. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, and retained material can be matched despite substantial renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical evaluations and adds VAE comparisons, architecture and attention experiments, and held-out data-filter results.

before.justification: v1 reports original automated and human evaluations in Tables 1–2, training-loss ablations in Figure 4, and generated examples in the appendices.

results.title: CogVideoX: Text-to-Video Diffusion Models with An Expert Transformer

C1.justification: Both versions present the same two central contributions and claim efficient, stable unlearning with better preservation of retained capabilities. The added TOFU evidence broadens support for these claims without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limits to the robustness narrative: FILA can cause excessive unlearning, and choosing a stopping point is difficult without an oracle reference model. It interprets this behavior through the Streisand effect and discusses reference-free evaluation as future work. It also removes v1's suggestion that merging adapters provides security by concealing unlearning history.

D1.justification: v2 supplies TOFU learning rates, epoch counts, batch size, and AdamW optimizer information, and newly specifies rank 32 for the existing module ablation. Hardware disclosure changes from 16 A100 GPUs on GCP to A100 40GB GPUs without the count or provider. Moving the retained evaluation-dataset list to Appendix C adds no new implementation information.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluation on TOFU author-profile question answering, including retention tests on real authors and world facts. Appendix D.1 also introduces sequential TDEC deletion requests. These extend coverage beyond v1's single-stage TDEC experiments; the original reasoning and dialogue datasets remain.

E2.justification: GA and GD remain the evaluated unlearning baselines. The new TOFU comparisons additionally include retain-set-only finetuned reference models, explicitly plotted in Figure 5. Newly discussed methods requiring auxiliary models or full training data are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: TOFU introduces Phi-1.5B and Llama2-7B experiments, 1%/5%/10% deletion splits, reference-model comparisons, Forget Quality and Model Utility metrics, and five-epoch tuning protocols. Appendix D.1 adds four sequential tasks. TDEC's learning-rate description also changes from separate full-tuning and LoRA rates to a stated fixed 2e-4, without establishing that the retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a four-task continual-unlearning test of cumulative capability retention. Section 4.3 examines TOFU behavior across deletion fractions, adapter ranks, and epochs, including excessive unlearning. The existing rank and target-module ablations remain.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported number of TDEC forget sets from three to five, although the retained results do not establish additional runs. TOFU introduces Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-values for distributional comparison; these are evaluation statistics rather than uncertainty intervals for mean performance.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the plotted results in Figures 2–4 are unchanged. v2 adds substantial TOFU and continual-unlearning results in Figures 5–6, including better utility retention with IHL, faster forgetting with FILA in many settings, and excessive unlearning in some TOFU configurations. These are new findings, not improvements to the original same-setting scores.

M1.justification: The inverted hinge loss, relative-Fisher weighting, low-rank initialization, base-weight compensation, and retain-set regularization remain the same. FLoRA is renamed FILA; the new evaluations do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial portions of the method and results prose are rewritten. FLoRA becomes FILA, the experimental narrative is expanded and reorganized, and dataset descriptions move to a new experimental-details appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds the extensive multipanel TOFU display in Figure 5 and the continual-unlearning plots in Figure 6. Existing figures are resized and repositioned, captions are revised, and Table 1 is reformatted. The retained plots display the same results despite their changed dimensions and tick layouts.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Liu et al.'s two-stage unlearning method, references Llama 3 and AdamW, and clarifies its positioning against approaches requiring auxiliary models or full training data. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for works already cited.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 removes v1's sign-inconsistent equality identifying the negative log-likelihood loss gradient with the positive log-probability gradient. The IHL derivative formulas, Fisher-weighted approximation, and mathematical material in Appendices A–B otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's small TDEC deletion sets by testing structured author-profile removal on additional model families and cumulative effects of sequential deletion. It also identifies excessive unlearning and reference-dependent stopping, making the practical limitations more informative. These gains address important gaps in the original evidence and outweigh the remaining ambiguity about TDEC setting changes and whether retained results were rerun.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renaming, reformatting, and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds TOFU evaluations in Section 4.3 and continual-unlearning results in Appendix D.1.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-Neo unlearning experiments on TDEC, including downstream performance, computational cost, and rank and module ablations in Table 1 and Figures 2–4.

results.title: Towards Robust and Parameter-Efficient Knowledge Unlearning for LLMs

C1.justification: Both versions claim that IHL stabilizes unlearning and FILA accelerates LoRA-based forgetting while preserving other capabilities. The new contribution bullets and parameter-efficient title retain this substantive scope; the additional experiments broaden supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly explains that FILA can accelerate GA's divergent behavior, making its downstream benefit depend on the loss being optimized. Sections 3.4 and 4.3 also attribute slow IHL optimization to limitations of randomly initialized LoRA weights. The existing over-unlearning and oracle-dependent stopping limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v3 adds an implementation-repository link, specifies TOFU utility's component metrics, and documents the additional baselines' regularization and reuse of experimental hyperparameters. It removes v2's direct TDEC dataset link. Hardware and principal training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use TDEC, WikiText retention, the same nine reasoning and four dialogue datasets, Pile perplexity, TOFU's 1%/5%/10% forgetting tasks, and continual unlearning. Real-author and world-fact evaluations were already documented in v2 Appendix C.

E2.justification: TOFU comparisons expand from GA/GD and the proposed variants to include KL, DPO, NPO, GA+FILA, and GD+FILA, documented in Figure 7 and Tables 2–9. GA remains in the appendix even though GD+FILA replaces it in the main Figure 5 display.

E3.justification: Figure 4 revises the stated model from GPT-Neo-2.7B to GPT-Neo-125M; this establishes a reported setting correction, not that experiments were rerun. Table 1 adds full-parameter IHL controls. The principal learning rates, ranks, sample sizes, epoch budgets, and stopping criteria remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 extends component testing through full-parameter IHL controls in Table 1 and GA/GD-with-FILA controls on TOFU. Existing rank, target-module, and continual-unlearning analyses remain. GD+FILA's TDEC rank analysis already appeared in v2 Figure 3, so its new table rows do not establish a new ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions report five TDEC forget sets and use Kolmogorov–Smirnov p-values for TOFU forget quality. The additional p-values do not change the statistical procedure, and v3 introduces no new seed, repetition, confidence-interval, or uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds full-parameter IHL results, additional TOFU comparator trajectories, and detailed component metrics across models, ranks, and forgetting fractions in Tables 2–9. Table 1 also revises GPT-Neo-2.7B full-parameter GD reasoning accuracy from 44.0 to 51.8. These are substantial additions to the reported evidence, not a demonstrated performance improvement between versions.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 revises the prescribed FILA initialization from row-sum weighting and inverse rescaling to square-root weighting and inverse-square-root rescaling. This is a limited correction to the written computation; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change. Removing IHL's outer max(0, ...) is mathematically equivalent for probabilities.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work receive substantial rewriting and compression, explicit contribution bullets are added, and the IHL/FILA motivation and results discussion are extensively revised. The title and affiliations also change, although the overall section sequence remains stable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes a fuller method overview; Table 1 gains rows, explicit method labels, colored performance differences, and highlighting. Figures 3–5 receive revised legends or displays, and Figure 7 plus eight detailed TOFU tables are added. The document also adopts the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: v3 adds Rafailov et al. (2024) for DPO and Zhang et al. (2024) for NPO, discussing them as alternative unlearning approaches. The broader positioning relative to GA, LoRA, and PiSSA remains substantially the same.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 corrects the claimed closed-form WLRA solution's weighting and inverse scaling to match its square-root-weighted objective, and fixes the relative-Fisher matrix dimensions from d×r to d×k. The core derivative calculations and Appendix A proof otherwise remain equivalent.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important weakness in v2's predominantly GA/GD-based validation through KL/DPO/NPO comparisons and additional controls separating IHL's and FILA's effects. Detailed TOFU metrics make the forgetting–utility trade-offs substantially easier to assess, while corrected FILA algebra and an implementation link improve method documentation. Losing the direct TDEC dataset link is a limited drawback relative to these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IHL/FILA research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite the revised title and formatting.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports additional comparisons and detailed TOFU results in Appendix D.2 and Tables 2–9.

before.justification: v2 reports original TDEC and TOFU experiments, component analyses, and continual-unlearning results in Appendix D.1.

results.title: Towards Robust and Parameter-Efficient Knowledge Unlearning for LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add theoretical justification as a central contribution: JDR improves label alignment under a stylized GOE model, with extension to cSBM suggested conjecturally. v1 principally presents a heuristic with empirical support and leaves theoretical guarantees open. v2 also explicitly frames its comparisons around preprocessing rewiring.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive boundaries concerning graph-level tasks, strong adversarial perturbations, million-node scalability and Minesweeper's failure case. Its alignment discussion explains why improved accuracy need not accompany increased alignment for other methods. The earlier nonlinear-feature limitation is retained in Appendix A.2, rather than removed.

D1.justification: v2 extends the existing detailed documentation with large-graph configurations, FoSR iteration counts and resource disclosures, including roughly 60 minutes and 500 GB of memory for Twitch-gamers. Code access remains unchanged. Conversely, v1's explicit final feature-blending equation is replaced by a brief interpolation description.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained cSBM and ten original benchmarks, v2 evaluates Roman-empire, Amazon-ratings, Minesweeper, Tolokers, Questions, Penn94 and Twitch-gamers (Tables 4 and 7). Coverage expands to a game-grid task and larger user/social networks, reaching 168,114 nodes.

E2.justification: FoSR, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator across the retained GCN/GPRGNN benchmark settings and spectral-clustering comparisons. This adds a directly relevant spectral-rewiring alternative throughout the evaluation. DIGL was already evaluated in v1's appendix; its appearance in v2's main tables is retained evidence.

E3.justification: The added benchmarks introduce source-provided splits, ROC AUC for imbalanced Minesweeper, Tolokers and Questions, and dedicated large-graph model configurations. Table 15 specifies five-layer GCN with residuals for Questions and four-layer GCN for Twitch-gamers. The original sparse/dense protocols and settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a focused extension of the alignment analysis: DIGL comparisons on cSBM and comparisons among rewiring methods across the original real graphs (Appendix A.5.4, Figures 7–8). The existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity/transfer studies and Gaussian-MSE analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The general practice remains 100 random-split runs with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from 1,000 resamples; Gaussian simulations retain ten trials and standard-deviation bands. v2 additionally specifies ten splits for the new Twitch-gamers experiment in Appendix A.8. This does not establish changed run counts for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results for new datasets, FoSR and alignment analyses. Newly reported Penn94 accuracy is 82.30% for GCN+JDR versus 80.40% for GCN (Table 4). FoSR also becomes the highest reported mean on dense-split PubMed with GPRGNN: 89.28% versus the unchanged JDR score of 89.24% (Table 8).

M1.justification: The decomposition, sign-corrected eigenvector interpolation, iterative synthesis and final update procedure remain unchanged. Appendix Algorithm 1 is identical apart from spacing. The new formal analysis and truncated-decomposition discussion do not establish a changed JDR algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution statement are substantially rewritten. Related work moves from before the method to after the experiments and gains topic-based organization; the low-dimensional resonance discussion moves to the appendix. The appendices are reorganized, and citations change from numbered to author–year style.

P2.justification: v2 adds a method-comparison table, large-graph and additional heterophilic result tables, and alignment plots. Existing benchmark and hyperparameter tables gain rows or columns, while DIGL results are also displayed in the main text. Existing figures are resized or relocated, and the principal cSBM performance plot gains labeled regime shading.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to distinguish preprocessing from end-to-end rewiring and discuss graph transformers, regularization and additional cSBM research. New works include Gutteridge et al., Qian et al. and Ando and Zhang. JDR's positioning relative to adversarial graph structure learning is also substantially clarified.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 1 and its Appendix A.3 proof of asymptotic one-step label-alignment improvement under independent GOE noise, lambda > sqrt(2), and sufficiently small interpolation. It also supplies a rotational-invariance proof, a computational-complexity derivation and explicit norm bounds in Equation 4. v1's earlier random-matrix discussion remains.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the justification and validation of JDR: the restricted GOE proof adds formal support, FoSR supplies a directly relevant missing comparison, and broader benchmarks test practical scope beyond v1's evaluation. Comparative alignment evidence and explicit failure conditions improve interpretation. The guarantee remains narrow and the final feature-blending update becomes less explicit, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and clarity about applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JDR research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds benchmark, scalability, FoSR-comparison and alignment results.

before.justification: v1 reports original cSBM and real-graph experiments, component and hyperparameter ablations, spectral-clustering results, and Gaussian-model simulations.

results.title: Joint Graph Rewiring and Feature Denoising via Spectral Resonance

C1.justification: The principal alignment, node-classification and rewiring-performance claims remain. Section 5 sharpens the novelty claim from the first generally applicable algorithm when features are available to the first joint graph-and-feature denoising method, explicitly asserting that no directly comparable method exists.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of graph-to-feature information transfer, explains ESNR–accuracy disagreements through feature information, and discusses hyperparameter-dependent runtime tradeoffs. It also reframes comparison fairness in Section 5. One new interpretation is inaccurate: A.5.3 claims GCN+JDR beats MLP+JDR on three heterophilic datasets, whereas Table 11 supports two.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1.4 newly specifies the timing setup: an NVIDIA A100 with 80 GB, Python-process timing, and outputs/logging left enabled. Table 5 supplies detailed measured runtimes. The existing code-access information, hyperparameter tables and general hardware disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: The cSBM scenarios and real-world dataset coverage are retained, including the additional heterophilic benchmarks and larger graphs. The new MLP, runtime and ESNR evaluations reuse existing datasets and task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds MLP and MLP+JDR comparisons against the GNN configurations on real-world datasets in Tables 10–11, and adds MLP+JDR to synthetic comparisons in Figure 6. V2 already included an unprocessed MLP on cSBM. DIGL, FoSR, BORF and AMP-BP remain; GPS is discussed but not directly benchmarked.

E3.justification: New evaluations tune JDR using an MLP downstream model, measure ESNR, and time preprocessing plus GCN training/evaluation on 100 splits using a common A100 setup. Existing splits, benchmark metrics and tabulated hyperparameters remain unchanged; these are additional protocols rather than revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.5.3 tests whether transferring graph information into features makes MLPs competitive with GNNs. New A.5.7 tests graph denoising through ESNR and examines its relationship to classification accuracy. These substantially extend the diagnostic evidence beyond the retained component ablations, sensitivity studies and spectral-clustering analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 100 random-split runs and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals using 1,000 resamples. Appendix A.9 retains ten independent trials with standard-deviation shading. The new classification results follow the existing confidence-interval practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results in Table 5, Tables 10–11 and 16–17, and Figures 6 and 12. Examples include Cora accuracy of 50.79% for MLP versus 62.66% for MLP+JDR, and higher ESNR for DIGL than JDR on every tested homophilic dataset. These are newly reported comparisons; the original benchmark scores in Tables 2–4 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same spectral decomposition, vector matching and interpolation, graph/feature synthesis, iteration and final update procedures. The revised theoretical model and additional downstream MLP experiments do not change JDR.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion receive focused rewriting, and the spectral motivation gains explanatory text. New appendix subsections organize the additional analyses, while the main section order and most existing prose remain. Equal-contribution and acknowledgment text are also added.

P2.justification: V3 adds five tables for runtime, MLP comparisons and ESNR, plus two corresponding comparison figures. Figure 2 is redrawn and its amplitude labeling and caption are revised. The conference template changes typography and headers, and numerous retained displays are repositioned without changing their reported benchmark values.

R1.justification: V3 adds references supporting the revised random-matrix analysis and multiclass motivation. Section 4 and A.5.7 expand the relationship to Dong and Kluger's already-cited work by discussing GPS and ESNR, and add connections to link-prediction-based denoising. The principal positioning within preprocessing graph rewiring remains.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 and Appendix A.3 are substantially replaced. V2 analyzes two symmetric spiked GOE matrices with a common signal parameter and requires lambda > sqrt(2). V3 analyzes a Gaussian graph matrix together with rectangular noisy features, requires lambda > 1 and mu > sqrt(gamma), and develops a different perturbation argument for graph and feature label alignment.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the connection between the method and its supporting evidence: Proposition 1 now treats rectangular features, MLP controls test the need for downstream graph processing, and runtime and ESNR analyses expose practical and interpretive limits. These address important gaps in v2's justification. The new three-versus-two win-count error in A.5.3 is a limited reporting defect that does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JDR research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained content to be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds runtime measurements, MLP comparisons and edge signal-to-noise ratio analyses.

before.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and real-world node-classification experiments, spectral-clustering results, ablations and simulations in its main text and appendices.

results.title: Joint Graph Rewiring and Feature Denoising via Spectral Resonance

C1.justification: v2 retains the original claims about general, model-agnostic COG combinations and adds a central contribution: normality tests can diagnose unsuitable interpolation seeds even when they reconstruct images well. This becomes an explicit introduction contribution and a recommendation in the conclusion, substantially broadening the paper's contribution beyond COG itself.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation of inversion failures through normality diagnostics and newly acknowledges that standard tests may not capture the characteristics required by a network. Appendix D also interprets differences among tests. Its claim that Cramér–von Mises separates every failure case at the specified percentiles overstates Table 2: the duplicated-coordinate upper value, 7e-4, exceeds the real-sample lower value, 2e-4.

D1.justification: v2 documents diagnostic implementation choices, including 30 histogram bins for chi-square and explicit coordinate-perturbation constructions in Appendix D/Table 2. Appendix B newly specifies v=0.5 for the existing beta-interval calculation. The main inversion, guidance, grouping and classifier settings remain documented as before.

E1.justification: ImageNet1k images and ShapeNet point clouds remain the real-data coverage. v2 Appendix D extends the synthetic latent-input scenarios beyond v1's mode and constant-vector examples to ramps, scaling, shifts, duplicated coordinates and sparse coordinate rescaling. The chair and point-cloud examples moved into the main text already existed in v1.

E2.justification: The interpolation and centroid comparator sets remain unchanged. However, v2 Table 2 introduces a substantial diagnostic comparison: Kolmogorov-Smirnov is evaluated alongside Shapiro-Wilk, chi-square, Cramér–von Mises, Gaussian likelihood and norm likelihood. The newly discussed Zheng et al. interpolation method is not experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 200-image normality/reconstruction study, a broader inversion-budget sweep, a 0.001 acceptance threshold, LPIPS reconstruction measurements and Q-Align evaluation of central spherical interpolants. The existing 400-step COG benchmark remains. Separately, Section 5.1 rewrites the mode-norm target as sqrt(D), while Appendix E retains v1's square-root-of-chi-square-mode definition; this inconsistent description does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v1 already illustrated inversion-budget failures and the insufficiency of likely norms. v2 substantially extends these analyses with systematic diagnostic comparisons, acceptance versus reconstruction quality, and seed normality versus interpolant quality (Figures 4–5 and Appendix D). These investigate additional failure mechanisms rather than merely redisplaying the earlier examples.

E5.justification: v1 reports 99% intervals from 10,000 Gaussian draws in Appendix B. v2 retains these and adds normality-test p-values, 0.1%–99.9% percentile ranges over 10,000 samples in stochastic test cases, and reported 50%/95% intervals around reconstruction and quality summaries. No increase in repeated runs of the retained COG benchmark is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the matched appendix benchmark tables retain their scores, including COG interpolation accuracy 67.4% and FID 38.9. v2 adds extensive diagnostic outcomes: Table 2 reports, for example, p=0 for Kolmogorov-Smirnov versus p=1 for Shapiro-Wilk on the zero-vector case. Figures 4–5 add acceptance, LPIPS and Q-Align results linking seed normality to generation quality.

M1.justification: COG's affine correction (v1 Equation 3; v2 Equation 4), interpolation weights and subspace construction remain unchanged. v2 Section 3 adds an auxiliary procedure for diagnosing seed-latent validity using normality tests, particularly Kolmogorov-Smirnov. This does not establish that the retained COG benchmark pipeline incorporated filtering.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around explicit contributions, and the document gains dedicated Background, Normality Assessment, Related Work and Conclusion sections. Existing methodology and experiments are reorganized, and v1's appendix discussion of atypical high-likelihood vectors is integrated into the main narrative. The title, author ordering and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds diagnostic Figures 4–5 and the colored normality-comparison Table 2. v1 Figure 11 is condensed and rearranged into v2 Figure 3, while the existing rocking-chair and point-cloud figures move into the main text as Figures 6–7. Typography, running headers, captions and figure placement are extensively revised.

R1.justification: New background and related-work sections substantially expand positioning against non-Gaussian-prior approaches, conditional generation and latent editing methods. Added discussions include Fadel, Davidson, Park's pullback metric and Zheng's interpolation approach, alongside classical normality-testing literature. The Haas preprint-to-publication update itself is not a new research comparison.

T1.justification: The five lemmas and their proofs in Appendices A–C remain substantively unchanged. Section 3.1 adds a mathematical reduction asserting equivalent standard-normal testing after z=Σ^(-1)(x−µ). This is new mathematical reasoning, but the stated transformation does not whiten a general covariance matrix; the reported unit-covariance examples avoid that particular problem.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's qualitative warning about invalid inversion seeds into a concrete, quantitatively evaluated diagnostic, substantially improving practical assessment of a key assumption (Section 3, Figures 4–5, Appendix D). Expanded background and research positioning also clarify applicability. The covariance-normalization error and overstated Cramér–von Mises separation claim need correction, but are localized and do not invalidate the reported unit-Gaussian Kolmogorov-Smirnov evidence. The improvement comes from stronger diagnostic support and explanation, not improved COG benchmark scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COG research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds normality-test comparisons and quantitative analyses linking latent validity to reconstruction and interpolation quality.

before.justification: v1 reports original interpolation and centroid experiments, generative subspace examples, inversion-budget analyses and Gaussian simulations.

C1.justification: The central claims about the benchmark, subtasks, professional-level tasks, and unguided difficulty ceiling remain. v3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the evaluation contribution from one agent scaffold to four and add the finding that scaffold effects depend on the model.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving action-space expressivity versus complexity and GPT-4o's lower answer-submission rate. New limitations acknowledge that the scaffolds are far from the capability frontier and that CTFs emphasize short tasks, small codebases, and constructed vulnerabilities. It also qualifies the single-attempt memory experiment and comparisons with externally reported AISI results.

D1.justification: v3 supplies prompts and interaction examples for the new scaffolds, clarifies that observation parsing credits flags rather than intermediate subtask answers, and adds extensive token, runtime, and iteration reporting in Appendix L. Existing model identifiers move to Appendix J, and the original prompt and public code/data access statement are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 40 tasks from four competitions across six cybersecurity categories. The new experiments reuse these tasks and their subtasks. Scaffold and memory changes alter evaluation procedures, not dataset or task coverage; v2 already permitted network access.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 adds direct comparisons between structured bash, action-only, pseudoterminal, and web-search agents for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o. These substantially expand the evaluated comparison methods. The original eight-model comparison remains unchanged; the cited AISI evaluation is external discussion, not a newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: v3 adds best-of-three scaffold evaluations and a separate full-history experiment with 128K input tokens for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 126K for GPT-4o. Appendices B–C add submission-based and log2(FST)-weighted metrics. The original iteration limits and token budgets are retained for the original experiment.

E4.justification: v3 adds scaffold ablations and case studies examining interpretation failures, terminal interaction, and search use (Appendix A), submission-rate analysis (B), difficulty-weighting analysis (C), and a memory-budget experiment (I). Appendix N also expands refusal analysis. These investigate important questions absent from v2's analyses.

E5.justification: v3 explicitly identifies the original results as single-attempt and specifies three attempts with maximum-performance aggregation for the added scaffold experiments. Usage tables report medians across those attempts. This adds replication and aggregation information, but neither version reports confidence intervals, seed-based variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 scores and corresponding per-task performance entries are retained. New best-of-three results include Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieving 27.5% subtask-guided success with pseudoterminal versus 17.5% with structured bash (v3 Table 3); these are new experimental conditions, not same-setting gains over v2. v3 also adds memory, weighted-score, submission, and usage results, expands refusals to Sonnet, and changes Opus's Delulu subtask label from Attempted to Refusal.

M1.justification: v2 uses one structured bash agent. v3 adds action-only responses, continuous pseudoterminal interaction, and a web-search tool as alternative scaffolds (Section 5 and Appendix A). These change response generation or available actions; the original agent is retained under the structured bash name.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 standardizes FST and structured bash terminology, streamlines related-work descriptions, revises Section 5's organization, moves model details into an appendix, and reorganizes the appendices around the added analyses. Author order and contribution statements also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds three prompt figures with highlighted additions and deletions, colored scaffold-comparison tables, submission and weighted-score tables, and extensive performance and usage matrices. The refusal table gains model/scaffold information and expands across pages. Existing overview diagrams, difficulty plots, and original result tables are largely retained or relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to 3CB, work on reporting train-test overlap, and the joint US/UK AISI evaluation, while removing the chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought references. It extends its positioning to claim first use of Kali Linux, web search, and pseudoterminal access for CTF agents. Most related-work coverage remains.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces the mathematical weighting rule log2(FST) for new difficulty-weighted performance measures. The act–execute–update equations and formal environment definitions are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantial theoretical derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2's capability assessment depended on one scaffold. v3 substantially strengthens it through scaffold comparisons, failure analyses, a memory-budget experiment, and explicit limits on generalization (Table 3 and Appendices A–C and I). Prompt and resource reporting also improve reproducibility. Best-of-three results still lack uncertainty estimates, and the broad scaffold-effect claims need qualification across metrics, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Cybench and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original tasks, experiments, and example logs can be matched across relocation and renumbering, supporting reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds scaffold comparisons, repeated-attempt evaluations, memory-budget experiments, and analyses of submissions, refusals, and resource usage.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of eight language models on 40 cybersecurity tasks, including aggregate results in Table 2, per-task results in Tables 4–6, and agent logs.

WikiText-2, PTB, Alpaca and the previously evaluated downstream tasks remain; the 70B model addition is a model-size expansion rather than new task coverage.

E2.justification: V4 adds SLEB to the retained 7B/13B perplexity comparison and evaluates OWL as a competing sparsity-allocation strategy in Tables 5 and 27. These extend an already broad comparator set. The feature-mimic, SVD-based and semi-structured comparisons from v1 remain in v4 Tables 17–19.

The earlier 8,000-sample recovery experiment remains separately. V4's new '2048 characters' wording conflicts with Table 3's '2048 tokens', leaving that specific setting unresolved.

Layer-rank distributions and broader task-degradation analyses provide additional diagnostic evidence. V1's calibration, temperature, module-compression and high-compression analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. V4 Table 27's sparsity standard deviation describes variation across layers, not uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: V4 adds substantial results for new evaluations: Table 5 reports 70B zero-shot averages of 65.51 and 66.79 for WikiText-2 and Alpaca calibration, respectively, versus 70.02 for the dense model. Table 28 reports 2722.98 tokens/s for the new block-allocation variant versus 2490.15 for uniform module sparsity. LLM-Pruner's 13B row also changes: 20% compression perplexity becomes 6.67 instead of 14.21, and numerical results replace OOM entries. Most existing MoDeGPT scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 replaces C_sigma^(1/2) with C_sigma in both ridge leverage scores and down-matrix reconstruction. Appendix B.11 also introduces separate MLP and MHA importance scores and weighted block-level sparsity allocation, extending v1's layer-level procedure. These change the specified computations; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution list are rewritten, Section 3.2 gains a substantial explanatory roadmap, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around scalability and performance–throughput tradeoffs. Earlier main-text comparisons move into dedicated appendix subsections. These changes substantially revise exposition and organization beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V4 adds a module-characteristics table, a perplexity–throughput plot, and new experimental tables and allocation figures. V1 Figure 3 survives as v4 Figure 12; its replacement in the main text is a different visualization. Figure 4 loses its parameter-share pie chart, those shares enter a table, and existing appendix memory results are also displayed in the main text.

R1.justification: V4 adds references for SLEB, FinerCut, LLaMA-3 quantization, COPA, LAMBADA and MMLU, and develops its comparison with the already cited OWL method. FinerCut positions the new block-allocation extension but is not experimentally benchmarked. The broader related-work framework remains substantially the same.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, Proposition 1 and Appendix A.1 revise the Type-I reconstruction and Nyström derivation, introducing an inverse-correlation factor and squared spectral-tail terms. Appendix A.4 corrects the Lagrangian derivation. B.11 adds a weighted optimization and claimed solution in Equations 42–43. These are substantive mathematical revisions, although some Type-I expressions remain unsynchronized and Equation 43 does not generally satisfy Equation 42's weighted budget.

improvement.justification: Measured 70B results, approximately matched computational budgets, and allocation comparisons substantially strengthen claims that v1 supported mainly through smaller-model experiments and extrapolation. The corrected Type-I least-squares update also addresses an important mathematical defect. These gains outweigh localized problems: Type-I formulas are not fully synchronized, and the new block-allocation solution in Equation 43 does not generally satisfy Equation 42's weighted constraint. Those issues weaken the extension and theoretical presentation, but the evidence supporting the core method is substantially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MoDeGPT. Their complete main texts and appendices, including algorithms, proofs, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V4 retains these original experiments and adds results for LLaMA-2 70B, additional tasks, computational-budget comparisons and sparsity-allocation variants.

before.justification: V1 reports original compression experiments on OPT and LLaMA models, including perplexity, downstream accuracy, throughput, ablations and calibration sensitivity.

The contribution positioning also narrows: hybrid attention is adopted from prior work rather than presented as newly invented, while multimodal sharding and the full-stack system remain central.

The main interpretations of sharding efficiency, captioning improvements, and convergence preservation otherwise remain.

D1.justification: v4 explicitly identifies the benchmark and ablation backbones, documents the convergence configuration as two Ulysses by two Zigzag degrees, and specifies dynamic resolution for the new image evaluation. It removes the stage-ablation caption's explicit 128-frame evaluation setting and the approximate ten-minute training-video description. The 17B-token context-extension budget, 336 A100 GPU hours, and project access link remain.

E1.justification: v4 adds evaluation of the Stage 3 checkpoint on ten image benchmarks, including VQAv2, GQA, VizWiz, MMB-CN, and MM-Vet, and introduces subtitle-assisted VideoMME evaluation. Appendix Figure 12 changes its training coverage from Shot2Story, AI2D, and ChartQA to Shot2Story alone. The principal video and text training datasets remain.

Needle training/evaluation increases from 1024/1400 frames to 2048/6000 frames. Appendix convergence changes from eight A100 GPUs and 100 plotted steps to eight H100 GPUs and over 600 steps. The new image evaluation explicitly uses the Stage 3 checkpoint.

The stage-removal, frame-count, sharding, and FSDP-versus-Zero-3 ablations otherwise persist, as do both qualitative captioning examples.

E5.justification: Both versions report timing averages over five iterations after ten warmup iterations. Neither introduces model-run seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands. The longer convergence trace is not additional repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: v1 Table 5 reports LongVILA-8B overall VideoMME scores of 49.2/50.5 at 128/256 frames. v4 Table 3 reports 57.5/57.4 without subtitles and 60.6/61.8 with subtitles for the different 7B configuration. Needle results change from 99.5% over 1400 frames to 99.8% over 6000 frames with increased training length; these are not same-setting gains. Appendix Table 8 adds image results, including 85.4 VQAv2 and 51.7 MM-Vet. Captioning scores remain unchanged. v4 Figure 10 changes Hugging Face's 128K result from OOM to 26.0 seconds, despite retaining a 96K maximum-support result.

M1.justification: The five-stage training recipe, two-stage image/token sharding, hybrid attention communication, and distributed inference procedure remain substantively unchanged. v4 corrects the inconsistent stage overview and changes attention attribution. Its Qwen2-7B benchmark configuration does not establish a new algorithm or architectural mechanism.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, the contribution bullets become a shorter narrative, and training now precedes the system description. VideoMME evaluation precedes needle retrieval, and the five-stage overview is corrected to match the already-present pipeline. These are extensive editorial and structural changes beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: System tables and plots are reorganized into paired throughput/scalability and inference panels, with throughput displayed as iterations per second. The needle figure gains a LongVA panel, VideoMME gains subtitle and model-size columns, and an image-benchmark table is added. The attention illustration moves to the appendix, convergence is redrawn, and ablation tables become side-by-side. Captioning example figures remain identical.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's limited comparison with competing long-context models by adding LongVA and other relevant baselines, subtitle-separated evaluation, and a much longer retrieval test. More precise attribution separates inherited hybrid attention from the multimodal contribution, and the reorganized pipeline is clearer. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, particularly the conflicting 128K Hugging Face latency and 96K support limit. The improvement is stronger comparative evidence and clearer contribution boundaries, not a demonstrated same-setting performance gain; the new image results concern only Stage 3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LongVILA and MM-SP. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and reports revised video evaluations, an extended convergence experiment, and new image-benchmark results.
