results.title: Near, far: Patch-ordering enhances vision foundation models' scene understanding

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and discussion retain the claims about abstraction, discriminative world modelling, sample efficiency, transfer, planning and learning abstraction components. Additional comparisons support these claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Appendix B.1.3 adds explanations of attention-mediated object interactions and the restrictions of NCS-style dynamics; B.1.4 develops possible robotics applications. The existing limitations concerning labelled object mappings and failures of single-item planning are retained.

D1.justification: v2 expands the attention architecture description and documents the learned encoder's observation/action inputs, convolutional encoder, output heads, loss, batch size and learning rate. Appendix G.3 adds MuZero's implementation source, search ranges and selected settings. These address substantial implementation gaps in v1.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same three 2D Crafting tasks, five MiniHack skill environments, sandbox transfer and compositional scenario. New experiments reuse this coverage. The robotics examples in v2 Table 1 are proposed applications, not evaluated domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds MuZero to the five MiniHack comparisons in Figure 4b and NCS-style k-means/greedy planning plus a k-means/Dijkstra variant in Appendix F.1.3 and Figure 23. Existing comparators remain. DAC-MDP and DLP-EIT appear in the conceptual comparison table without corresponding benchmark results.

E3.justification: Additional protocols vary encoder training fractions from 1% to 90%, fixed optimization budgets from 100 to 2500 steps, Dreamer training ratios and MuZero self-play delays. These substantially expand controlled evaluation; the original benchmark metrics and default MEAD, Dreamer and PPO settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds encoder-data sensitivity and downstream planning analysis (Figure 25), an additional fixed-budget optimization analysis (Figure 30), and Dreamer/MuZero training-setting analyses (Figures 35–36). Figure 23 also compares greedy versus Dijkstra planning with the NCS-style model. Earlier ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 states a minimum of three independent seeds. v2 Table 6 specifies counts by main experiment and method, including four/five MEAD seeds for Crafting/MiniHack. This is additional disclosure, not evidence of increased runs. Existing confidence-interval and stated exception conventions are retained.

E6.justification: New MuZero, NCS and sensitivity results materially expand the evidence. v2 Figure 23 shows the k-means/Dijkstra variant failing four-step Crafting but learning in Freeze-Wand; Figure 25 shows poor planning with very small encoder datasets. Retained main mean curves are unchanged, although some confidence bands differ slightly.

M1.justification: The discriminative transition model, count-based exploration, MCTS, Dijkstra planning and training algorithm are retained. Expanded attention-network and learned-map descriptions document existing components; the PDFs do not establish a changed MEAD procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main-section/Appendix A–G organization are retained. v2 makes local wording corrections, expands explanations, introduces targeted appendix subsections and consolidates the semantic-embedding headings, without extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds five experimental figures and four tables, expands Figure 14 into three environment panels, and revises Figure 4's comparator display and Figure 11's labels. It also changes title/heading styling and introduces running headers throughout. Most earlier graphics remain, often relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B.1.3 substantially expand positioning against object-centric research, including NCS, DLP-based methods and CEE-US. Table 5 compares representation, function approximation and planning choices. Additional MuZero and robotics references extend this substantive comparison beyond bibliographic restyling.

T1.justification: New Appendix B.1.3 supplies mathematical correspondences between Ab-MDP and OO-MDP, NCS and DLP representations, including a comparison of transition-dependency assumptions. The existing Ab-MDP definitions, Remark B.3 and single-/multi-item counterexample analysis remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by adding online-planning and object-structured comparators missing from v1, including a control separating model choice from planning choice. Encoder-data and training-budget analyses better expose performance dependencies, while fuller implementation and seed reporting improve reproducibility. These gains address important comparison and documentation gaps; the dependence on supplied or supervised abstractions remains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Ab-MDP/MEAD work. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds baseline comparisons and sensitivity analyses, including Figures 23, 25, 30, 35 and 36.

before.justification: v1 reports original 2D Crafting and MiniHack experiments, transfer results, learned-component evaluations and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix F.

results.title: Efficient Exploration and Discriminative World Model Learning with an Object-Centric Abstraction

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims about normal deflection, adaptive prior supervision, guided optimization, and recovery of detailed indoor geometry. The additional experiments support these existing contributions rather than introduce a new core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands explanations of geometric localization, robustness when smooth-region priors are wrong, and the relationship between inverse variance and surface sharpness. Appendix C.4 adds discussion of unbiasing failures and limitations of delaying unbiasing. Section 4.1 also replaces ScanNet++ superiority 'across all metrics' with a recall-focused interpretation. The original coverage and prior-dependence limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 identifies Grid/MLP comparator representations, explicitly locates the main ablations on ScanNet++, and documents SAM masking and normal rotation for the new robustness test. Conversely, Table 2 drops its explicit resolution of 768; the appendix specifies 2048 for qualitative comparisons only. Core implementation details, hardware, training time, and project access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate indoor reconstruction on ScanNet, Replica, Tanks and Temples, and ScanNet++. Appendix B.4 in v3 adds a distinct input condition: deliberately corrupted normal priors in smooth regions of one existing ScanNet++ scene. No new dataset or application domain is added.

E2.justification: DebSDF, already included in v2's ScanNet table, is added to the Tanks and Temples, ScanNet++, and Replica comparisons. It replaces MonoSDF in Figure 4 and NeuRIS in the Tanks and Temples qualitative comparison. New Figure 12 also compares NCC, edge, and uncertainty maps against the proposed angle map, substantially expanding the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: The new robustness experiment uses SAM-selected smooth regions and normal rotations of 0, 5, 15, 30, 45, and 60 degrees; comparator results are reported only at the endpoints. Figure 11 adds a rendering-weight analysis across inverse-variance settings. Existing training budgets and metrics remain stated as before; the protocol behind revised Tanks and Temples scores is not fully established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, v3 adds confidence-map localization comparisons in B.3 and controlled corruption of smooth-region normal priors in B.4. B.1 adds training curves and rendering-weight profiles to investigate convergence under partial versus uniform unbiasing. These directly examine robustness and mechanisms previously supported mainly by ordinary reconstruction results and component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability bars, or statistical significance tests. The new inverse-variance curves and uncertainty-map comparisons concern model quantities, not statistical uncertainty in experimental outcomes.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces ND-SDF's Tanks and Temples mean F-score of 9.35 with 14.46, while Table 4 changes MonoSDF's Replica F-score from 86.18 to 85.91. These are reported-value revisions, not established same-setting improvements. Added DebSDF results change some metric rankings. New Table 10 reports ND-SDF F-scores of 0.750 at zero bias and 0.655 at 60 degrees, alongside additional qualitative and convergence findings.

M1.justification: The deflection network, adaptive losses, angle-guided sampling and rendering, and warm-up procedure remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix A. Equation 3 corrects the expansion of the already specified Laplace-CDF mapping; it does not establish a change to the implemented procedure.

P1.justification: The main exposition and section order remain largely intact. Changes include targeted wording and notation edits, more precise appendix references, acknowledgments, and the conference header. New appendix subsections and an expanded C.4 extend the narrative without extensively rewriting or reorganizing the existing paper.

P2.justification: v3 adds diagnostic Figures 11–13, qualitative comparison Figures 16–17, and robustness Table 10. Figure 4 and the Tanks and Temples comparison are replaced, and several benchmark tables gain comparator rows. Figure 2 relabels depth and normals as priors rather than ground truth. Earlier Replica and extraction-resolution figures are retained and relocated, not newly added results.

R1.justification: New Appendix C.4 acknowledges NC-SDF's similar SO(3) residual-field idea and argues differences in training, boundary information, and generalization, materially expanding positioning against a close concurrent approach. It also expands comparisons with NeuS, TUVR, and DebSDF. References for edge-aware reconstruction, edge detection, and Lang Segment Anything are added; DataP-SfM and FedSurfGS are removed. NC-SDF is discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

T1.justification: Equation 3 corrects the sign domains of the piecewise density formula: the first exponential branch changes from s(x) <= 0 to s(x) >= 0, and the second from s(x) > 0 to s(x) < 0. This fixes a mathematical inconsistency with the stated Laplace CDF. The remaining derivations and formal assumptions are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of how ND-SDF handles unreliable priors: it adds DebSDF comparisons across additional benchmarks, directly tests corrupted smooth-region priors, and supplies localization and convergence diagnostics absent from v2. Equation 3 and the ScanNet++ interpretation become more accurate. The robustness test remains limited to one scene, and revised Tanks and Temples scores lack a clear protocol explanation, but the added evidence substantially reduces important gaps in support for the central mechanism.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ND-SDF research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, convergence diagnostics, confidence-map comparisons, and experiments with deliberately biased normal priors.

before.justification: v2 reports original quantitative and qualitative reconstruction experiments on four datasets, plus component, prior-model, warm-up, and rendering ablations.

results.title: ND-SDF: Learning Normal Deflection Fields for High-Fidelity Indoor Reconstruction

C1.justification: The central dataset, architecture, long-context and benchmarking contributions, including headline performance and efficiency gains, are retained. However, v4 removes the introduction's blanket assurance that synthetic songs are free from copyright issues; its ethics statement instead acknowledges copyright concerns and specifies noncommercial licensing, qualifying an important dataset-use claim.

C2.justification: v4 introduces interpretations of token complementarity, external-generator performance declines, possible overfitting and audible classification failures. It also discusses English-only applicability, gender imbalance and copyright concerns. Appendix A newly argues that genre shortcuts are absent, although the distribution plot alone does not establish this. The original limitations paragraph is retained in Appendix G rather than removed.

D1.justification: v3 promises a future resource release; v4 states that code and data are available and that supplementary materials contain source code and configurations. It additionally specifies CC BY-NC 4.0 licensing, distribution of real songs through YouTube links, and manual collection of external-generator samples. Existing hyperparameters, hardware, generation costs, pseudocode and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: v4 adds evaluation on 394 SkyMusic and 36 SeedMusic songs from external generator families (Appendix D.1, Table 8). This substantially extends generalization coverage beyond the existing Suno/Udio generator variants. The original SONICS and SingFake coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 newly evaluates AASIST, ResNet + Spec., ResNet + LFCC and Wav2Vec2 + AASIST against SpecTTTra in Table 9, with additional external-generator results in Table 8. These specialized comparators were not evaluated in v3; the original ConvNeXt, ViT and EfficientViT comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include temporal-only and spectral-only controls, varying spectral clip size while holding temporal clip size fixed, external-generator testing with randomly initialized controls, and manual vocal/style audits using 50 samples each. Section 6 also describes inspecting the 50 closest synthetic/real song matches. Existing splits, training budgets and benchmark settings are retained rather than demonstrably revised.

E4.justification: v4 adds component ablations in Section 4.4, external-generator robustness tests in Appendix D.1, genre-distribution analysis, vocal/style quality audits, a similarity-based copying check and analyses of correct and incorrect classifications in Appendix E. These address architectural contributions, dataset validity and failure modes beyond v3's existing duration, embedding and style analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging 100 inference-timing runs after five warm-up runs. Neither provides training-seed counts, confidence intervals, performance error bars or significance tests. The new randomly initialized controls do not introduce seed or repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original numerical entries in Tables 2–6 are unchanged. New Table 7 reports 120-second F1 scores of 0.91 for temporal-only tokens, 0.92 for spectral-only tokens and 0.97 for their combination. Table 8 adds external-generator results, including SpecTTTra-γ scores of 0.80 on SeedMusic and 0.60 on SkyMusic at 120 seconds. Table 9 adds detector results and failures, including AASIST's 0.91 F1 at five seconds and out-of-memory failure at 120 seconds.

M1.justification: The dataset-generation pipeline, spectral and temporal tokenizers, positional embeddings, Transformer encoder, pooling, classifier and three SpecTTTra variants remain unchanged. The tokenizer pseudocode and training objective also match. New component-removal experiments are ablations, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing method, experiment and prompt prose is retained, with limited abstract and contribution-list editing. Dataset costs and limitations move to appendices, acknowledgments are removed, and new section headings and an appendix contents page organize the additions. The revision does not extensively rewrite the retained scientific narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column ICLR format, extensively repositioning and resizing retained displays. v4 adds the genre-distribution figure and Tables 7–9, adds total hours to Table 1, and expands benchmark captions and unseen-generator annotations. Existing figures and prompt tables are retained despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: The largely retained related-work section is substantially supplemented by Appendix F's direct positioning against specialized song detectors and Appendix D.1's connection to cross-generator media-forensics research. New references also contextualize imperceptible artifacts and generated-dataset practices. This expands the substantive research positioning beyond citation-format changes.

T1.justification: The token-count expressions and tokenizer equations, Equations 1–3, retain the same mathematical content. Neither version contains additional theorems or proofs, and the new empirical ablations do not revise the formal model.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important validation gaps in v3 through component ablations, specialized detector comparisons and external-generator tests that expose generalization failures (Tables 7–9). Dataset-quality audits further strengthen the dataset contribution without changing the original headline results. Some reporting remains problematic: Table 7's short-audio token counts conflict with the stated dimensions, and genre-robustness and broad superiority interpretations overreach their evidence. Nevertheless, the added controlled comparisons and failure evidence substantially improve the paper's empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SONICS dataset and SpecTTTra research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and additionally reports token ablations, external-generator evaluations, specialized detector comparisons and dataset-quality checks.

before.justification: v3 reports original detection experiments, a human evaluation and efficiency measurements in Section 4 and Tables 2, 4–6, alongside dataset analyses in the appendices.

results.title: SONICS: Synthetic Or Not - Identifying Counterfeit Songs

C1.justification: v2 elevates GSM8K-to-MATH easy-to-hard generalization to a main contribution and adds empirical superiority over DPO and comparative model-scaling claims. The abstract's reported improvement range changes from 16-64% to 16-40%. Direct GenRM is described more cautiously as comparable or slightly better than discriminative RMs, with stronger emphasis on GenRM-CoT.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds concrete discussion of answer-checker false negatives and correct answers reached through faulty reasoning. Appendix D interprets the negligible GSM8K weighted-voting benefit as performance saturation, and Section 5 adds a tentative calibration explanation for generalization. The principal interpretations concerning joint training and noisy synthetic rationales remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds the exact LLM-as-a-Judge prompt, the greater-than-50% checker-agreement filtering rule, DPO initialization and hyperparameter searches, and weighted self-consistency K values. It also documents discriminative RM Z-loss and selected settings and revises training-budget information. Figure 1 announces a planned data-release location; the PDFs do not establish that release occurred.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation of GSM8K-trained verifiers on MATH500, extending coverage to high-school competition mathematics and cross-dataset easy-to-hard generalization. Existing algorithmic coverage is retained: Appendix A still specifies length-6 Last Letter Concatenation and length-5 Word Sorting evaluation.

E2.justification: DPO becomes an evaluated comparator on GSM8K and MATH, rather than only related work. v2 also compares self-consistency weighted by discriminative versus generative verifier scores and evaluates DPO scoring with and without reference-policy subtraction. Self-consistency remains evaluated despite its omission from the revised Figure 1.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes the reported GenRM budget from 200K steps with batch size 128 to 300K steps with batch size 64 and revises the discriminative RM dropout sweep. v2 adds MATH500 Best-of-32 evaluation, weighted self-consistency protocols, and the normalized gain metric in Figure 1. These establish reported setting changes without establishing which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds MATH subject/difficulty breakdowns, transfer model-scaling analysis, three MATH case studies, weighted self-consistency tests, and a DPO reward-function ablation. Existing rationale-count and solution-count ablations are retained or relocated. However, v1's direct-verifier data-scaling comparison and dedicated GSM8K model-size analysis are omitted, while the generation-loss-weight display is reduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Sampling multiple verification rationales is an inference procedure in both versions, not newly introduced uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial MATH, DPO, and weighted self-consistency results and revises existing performance curves. The introductory GSM8K GenRM-CoT result changes from 92.8% to 93.4%; Figure D.4 reports 93.5% with weighted self-consistency. These are revised reported outcomes under changed documented training settings, not a controlled same-setting improvement. Some original scaling results are removed, while the existing GSM8K appendix examples retain their scores.

M1.justification: The core next-token verification objective, joint generation training, CoT scoring, and rationale averaging remain unchanged. v2 adds a limited inference extension: weighted self-consistency selects the answer with the largest sum of its top-K solution scores (Section 4.1 and Appendix C). Newly documented rationale-filtering details do not establish a change to the underlying training procedure.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: task descriptions are consolidated, data-scaling discussion is redistributed between Section 4.4 and Appendix D, and separate details/results appendices precede the reordered examples. The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion receive substantial editing, and an author-contributions section is added.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 6 are redesigned around combined algorithmic results, GSM8K, and MATH. v2 adds transfer breakdowns, weighted-voting and DPO plots, a judge-prompt table, and MATH example tables. Existing ablation displays are split, relocated, or redrawn; the Digimon example disappears from the main text but remains in the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted connections to easy-to-hard generalization, calibration, weighted self-consistency, and implementation methods, including Sun, Kapoor, and Liu. Section 5 refines comparisons with DPO and critique-based reward models while retaining the original related-work framework. Chen et al. (2021) and Gulcehre et al. (2023) are removed with associated future-work discussion.

T1.justification: v2 Figure 1 newly defines normalized gain as Delta = (GenRM-CoT - Discriminative RM)/(Pass@N - Discriminative RM). This is a limited mathematical definition accompanying the new evaluation metric. The existing probability, training-loss, and verifier-scoring equations remain equivalent; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by testing generalization from GSM8K to harder MATH500 problems, evaluating previously untested DPO comparisons, and examining performance across subjects and difficulty levels. Added prompts, filtering rules, and baseline settings improve reproducibility. Some original scaling evidence is lost and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the broader tests and clearer comparison procedures substantially improve the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenRM research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and figures, equations, tables, and relocated material support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained tasks and adds MATH500 transfer results, DPO comparisons, weighted self-consistency experiments, and further analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Last Letter Concatenation, Word Sorting, and GSM8K, including scaling studies, ablations, and verification examples.

results.title: Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction

C1.justification: The central contribution—Bayesian graph SDE uncertainty modeling with variance and stability guarantees—is retained. V4 extends its stated empirical contribution to noise robustness, active learning, and Graph GP comparisons. Its abstract and conclusion describe overall performance as competitive, tempering v1's general outperformance conclusion.

C2.justification: V4 newly interprets entropy acquisition as selecting informative labels and links noisy-input results to the perturbation bound. It adds explanations of solver-controlled depth, a short-time-horizon qualification of the exponential stability bound, and Graph GP memory limitations. This substantially expands v1's discussion of entropy separation and general computational concerns.

D1.justification: V1 provides a brief uniform-hyperparameter table. V4 adds search ranges for training budgets, weight decay, solver step size, and model dimensions; an early-stopping value of 20; dataset split and label-count tables; the noise-generation rule; and active-learning training details. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although selected configurations and runtime hardware remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Both versions use Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, Amazon Computers, and Photo. V4 substantially expands task and input-condition coverage through active learning, classification with noisy test features, and feature-perturbation OOD detection; these are new scenarios on retained datasets.

E2.justification: V4 adds Graph GP to the standard-setting comparison, with completed results on Cora and Citeseer. Tables 13–14 introduce much broader OOD comparator sets, including GAT, GRAND, GREAD, MSP, ODIN, Mahalanobis, GNNsafe, GKDE, GPN, and GNSD. V1's comparisons contain GCN/GNN, GNODE, BGCN, and GCN ensembles.

E3.justification: V1 Table 2 specifies uniform hyperparameters, whereas v4 Tables 6–7 report validation-selected grid search. New experiments introduce test-only Gaussian noise scaled to feature variability, acquisition/retraining procedures, validation-selected thresholds for OOD accuracy, and additional AUPR/FPR95 metrics. The revised protocol description does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's entropy-distribution and label-leave-out analyses, v4 adds empirical noise robustness, random-versus-entropy acquisition comparisons, prior drift/diffusion sensitivity tests, GCN-versus-GAT backbone analysis, and runtime comparisons. These investigate robustness, uncertainty-guided selection, architectural dependence, and computational cost.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean ± standard deviation in their primary result tables. V4 newly specifies 20 weight initializations for fixed Planetoid splits and 100 random splits for other datasets; this discloses repetitions without establishing an increase. Its additional Tables 13–14 provide point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Standard-setting values are revised: LGNSDE's reported Cora AURC changes from 0.9968 in v1 Table 3 to 0.0702 in v4 Table 1, GNODE's Cora NaNs become finite results, and some AUROC/accuracy entries change. Original OOD AUROC/AURC values are retained. V4 adds extensive new outcomes, including broader comparisons where GNSD frequently leads. These are revised or newly reported results, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The prior/posterior SDE formulation, shared diffusion, variational objective, stochastic Runge-Kutta integration, and Monte Carlo prediction remain. Appendix C.1 adds an evaluated LGNSDE-GAT drift-backbone variant alongside the original GCN-based model, a limited architectural extension.

P1.justification: V4 extensively expands and reorganizes the exposition through a separate GNODE background section, rewritten abstract and conclusion, revised theoretical narrative, dedicated related work, and more granular experimental and appendix sections. Much of the original method and proof prose remains, but the explanatory structure changes substantially.

P2.justification: The standard-results table moves from Appendix C into the main text and expands; the OOD table gains accuracy rows. Figure 1 gains a latent-state axis and revised caption, while Figure 2 is restyled. New active-learning curves, a backbone entropy display, and sensitivity, benchmark, runtime, and complexity tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V4 adds a dedicated related-work section distinguishing its approach from earlier graph SDE formulations, stochastic diffusion, Graph Posterior Networks, and belief-theory methods. It adds Graph GP and evaluation/dataset references, and changes the existence argument's attribution from Pham (2009) to Lin et al. (2024). This substantially develops the work's positioning.

T1.justification: V4 adds a semigroup existence theorem attributed to Lin et al. (2024) and makes Proposition 1 conditional on it, replacing v1's strong-solution statement with a mild-solution statement. It also revises the time and memory complexity claims substantially. The original Lipschitz/growth assumptions, variance inequality, perturbation bound, and most Appendix A proof steps remain.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation and sparse experimental documentation. Noise tests, random-versus-entropy active learning, sensitivity/backbone analyses, and broader OOD comparisons provide better evidence about the utility and limits of its uncertainty estimates; split, tuning, and repetition disclosures improve assessability. These gains are substantial despite unexplained AURC revisions, underspecified Appendix C.3 protocols, and an unclear connection between the newly invoked existence theorem and the proposed model.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LGNSDE framework, with matching core equations and retained experiments. Their main text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical results and adds noise-perturbation, active-learning, sensitivity, backbone, runtime, and broader OOD comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original node-classification and leave-one-class-out OOD experiments on five graph datasets in Tables 1 and 3 and Figure 2.

results.title: Uncertainty Modeling in Graph Neural Networks via Stochastic Differential Equations

C1.justification: Both versions already claim single-quantizer compression to 40 or 75 tokens per second, strong reconstruction quality, rich semantic representations, and usefulness for generative models. v2 supplies substantially more supporting evidence, but these central contributions are not materially redefined.

C2.justification: v1's explanation of LJSpeech degradation through limited training data is replaced by a broad robustness/generalizability interpretation. v2 adds interpretations of downstream synthesis and training-data scaling. Appendix F newly identifies deficient ASR understanding as a barrier to unified understanding and generation, motivates stronger encoders, and leaves speech–text alignment in large multimodal models unresolved.

D1.justification: v2 documents dataset subsampling, ParlerTTS configuration and training, listener recruitment, sample counts, and annotation filtering. Appendix A relocates existing optimizer and cropping details while revising the GPU count from 16 to 8 and the iteration budget. Resource availability wording also changes: v1 advertises code, demos, and pretrained models as available; v2 links code but promises full code/model release in its introduction.

E1.justification: ARCH evaluation expands from four speech datasets to twelve datasets, adding music and acoustic-event tasks on FMA, MTT, IRMAS, MS-DB, ESC50, US8K, FSD50K, and VIVAE. Downstream text-to-speech evaluation replaces previously deferred experiments. LibriLight also disappears from the reported training corpora; MusicDB and AudioSet were already named in v1.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds DAC at 9 and 4 kbps to the LibriTTS test-other comparison and DAC at 9, 4, and 1 kbps to LJSpeech, where those comparators were absent in v1 Tables 2–3. Existing test-clean and speech-domain ARCH comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported training setup changes from 585-hour/5,000-hour/80,000-hour small/medium/large configurations to approximately 8,000 hours plus LibriTTS confirmatory training. The stated iteration budget changes from one million for v1-small to two million in v2. New protocols include 600M-parameter ParlerTTS training for 40 epochs and MUSHRA/CMOS listening evaluations. These reported changes do not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 retains the original codebook-size, context-window, and discriminator studies and adds reconstruction ablations removing attention or replacing the decoder with a mirrored structure (Table 7). Appendix D tests whether increasing training data from 585 to 4,000 hours raises codebook utilization. Appendix E tests semantic performance after jointly removing attention and extended context.

E5.justification: v2 Table 2 introduces ± quantities for MUSHRA scores, whereas v1 reports no comparable uncertainty estimates. The meaning of these quantities is unspecified, and neither version reports training-seed variability, repeated-run counts, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial MUSHRA, downstream TTS, music/audio semantic, and ablation results. Existing LibriTTS reconstruction scores are retained, but the 75-token LJSpeech UTMOS changes from 3.8753 to 4.2580 and Audio-MNIST accuracy from 0.6386 to 0.6957. Revised training descriptions prevent treating these as controlled same-setting gains. Tables 5–6 also remove previously reported V/UV F1 entries.

M1.justification: The encoder, single quantizer, attention/ConvNeXt/inverse-Fourier decoder, and loss equations are retained. However, Section 3.4 drops v1's separately named multi-scale discriminator and describes single-band amplitude and multiband complex MRD components. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the discriminator configuration or clarifies its description.

P1.justification: The introduction reorganizes five codec goals into two main research directions, and prose is extensively revised throughout. Experiments are consolidated into main results and a structured ablation section, training details move to Appendix A, the deferred-results section disappears, and new appendices organize evaluation details, analyses, and limitations.

P2.justification: Three reconstruction tables become one grouped table with shaded single-quantizer rows. The semantic table expands from four to twelve task columns; codebook and context ablation tables become compact side-by-side displays. New subjective, generative, and appendix tables are added. Figures 1–2 retain their plotted content with revised captions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Moshi, Qwen-Audio, SALMONN, and references supporting benchmark datasets and subjective evaluation. It explicitly identifies Single-Codec as the closest related approach and adds an attributed UTMOS assessment. The main related-work taxonomy and WavTokenizer's positioning remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: The STFT expression and loss formulations in Equations 1–7 remain mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and the new appendices add empirical studies and discussion rather than formal results.

improvement.justification: v1 claimed subjective quality, broad semantic capability, and generative usefulness while deferring much supporting evidence in Section 4.5. v2 substantially closes these validation gaps through documented listening tests, twelve-dataset ARCH evaluation, downstream TTS comparisons, and key decoder ablations. Weaknesses remain: its new all-test-set UTMOS superiority claim contradicts LJSpeech values of 4.2580 versus DAC's 4.3007, and MUSHRA uncertainty is undefined. These issues qualify the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WavTokenizer research. Their text, equations, figures, and tables support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2 includes readable Appendices A–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification and text-generation experiments evaluating Shadow Attack, Outlier Attack, and random perturbation in Tables 2-4.

results.title: Adversarial Attacks on Data Attribution

C1.justification: V3 adds asymptotic convergence-rate guarantees to its headline contributions and emphasizes learning expressive conditional generative models. The task is explicitly framed as active generation, with generative modeling promoted from a desideratum to requirement R5. V1 claimed effective variational search and empirical competitiveness but did not claim these convergence rates.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations linking expressive-generator gains to generalization and sampling from the adapting distribution. It cautions that diversity alone need not improve search, discusses prior overfitting, and notes that theoretical hit counts include duplicates. Earlier warnings about oracle extrapolation and dependence on informative priors largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly discloses optimization-iteration budgets and AdaLead's kappa setting, adds detailed LSTM/transformer configurations in Table 4, and describes early stopping, augmentation and Ehrlich CNN ensembles. Benchmark-specific settings and revised CPE specifications substantially expand reproducibility information. Previously unstated iteration budgets do not establish a change in actual training duration.

E1.justification: V3 retains all five biological datasets and adds conditional MNIST generation targeting digits 3 and 5, introducing image-generation coverage. It also adds closed-form Ehrlich sequence-optimization benchmarks using POLI and HOLO implementations, extending evaluation beyond the retained experimental landscapes and learned protein oracles.

E2.justification: V3 adds evaluated genetic-algorithm and LaMBO-2 baselines on the Ehrlich benchmarks (Figures 5 and 8), substantially extending comparison to guided diffusion. It also adds AdaLead curves to the GP-based landscape comparison (v1 Figure 5; v3 Figure 7). LaMBO itself is discussed but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: Normalized fitness performance in v1 Equation 18 becomes cumulative unique-sequence fitness in v3 Equation 16, and batch diversity becomes an additional metric. Reported CPE architectures and variational-model configurations change. New protocols include single-round MNIST adaptation and 32-round Ehrlich optimization from 128 initial observations; the retained biological experiments use ten rounds.

E4.justification: The existing GP-surrogate analysis continues in v3 Appendix C.1. New Appendices C.3–C.4 examine batch diversity and systematically compare uniform versus informed priors and independent, transition, LSTM and transformer posterior families. Figure 12 supplies direct ablation evidence beyond v1's qualitative observations about these choices.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly reports five random seeds in Section 4 and Appendix B.2; v1 does not state a run count. Both versions display error bars without clearly identifying their statistic. This establishes additional reporting, not an increase in the number of runs.

E6.justification: V3 adds MNIST samples and classifier results, including approximately 99% balanced accuracy, Ehrlich regret curves, diversity scores and prior/architecture ablation results. Existing biological-landscape and AAV/GFP curves are also revised. Changed architectures and the redefined performance metric prevent interpreting these revisions as controlled, same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The reverse-KL ELBO, classifier loss and score-function update remain. Algorithm 1 adds a final threshold/model refit and returns generator/classifier parameters instead of collected positive designs. LSTM and transformer instances replace the earlier simple autoregressive instance within the existing modular framework (v1 Appendix B.1; v3 Appendix B.3).

P1.justification: V3 substantially rewrites the introduction, problem formulation, related-work narrative and conclusion around active generation. Dataset descriptions and settings move into expanded Appendix B, supplementary experiments become Appendix C, and the former Section 2.4 moves to Appendix F. New theory occupies Section 2.4 and Appendices D–E.

P2.justification: V3 adds digit-sample galleries, Ehrlich plots, diversity panels, ablation displays and an architecture-configuration table. The three-panel BBO display becomes a two-by-three dataset/model grid. Tables 1 and 2 change their rows or columns, and existing result figures receive revised legends and performance-axis scales.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to latent-space optimization, LaMBO/LaMBO-2, guided generation and active level-set estimation, explicitly distinguishing these approaches from VSD. New GP/NTK references support the theoretical analysis, and v3 newly positions DHFR and TrpB as previously unused in machine-learning research.

T1.justification: V1's two optimization-bound propositions survive in v3 Appendix F. New Section 2.4 and Appendices D–E introduce assumptions and proofs for GP variance convergence, conditional-distribution convergence, an expected-hit bound and NTK-based neural-classifier rates. Section 2.2 also corrects the Gaussian probability-of-improvement expression.

improvement.justification: V1's high-dimensional validation relied on learned oracles, while its theoretical discussion offered only elementary optimization bounds. V3 adds closed-form Ehrlich comparisons, conditional convergence analyses and direct prior/diversity diagnostics, substantially strengthening evidence about applicability and design choices. Expanded settings improve reproducibility. Restrictive theoretical assumptions, undefined error-bar statistics and changed evaluation settings still limit interpretation, but the gains in evidence and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Variational Search Distributions by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V3 reports original biological-sequence experiments, MNIST generation, Ehrlich-function optimization, diversity measurements and prior/architecture ablations in the main text and Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original biological-sequence experiments, including fitness-landscape comparisons, AAV/GFP optimization and supplementary GP-surrogate results in Figures 2, 3 and 5.

results.title: Variational Search Distributions

C1.justification: V1's established main contributions concern continuous time, followed by a general assertion of discrete-time extendability. V3 makes a quantified discrete-time KSD guarantee a principal contribution. Its abstract changes the overall dimension-dependence claim from linear to polynomial while retaining the continuous-time linear bound, and explicitly confines the proved Wasserstein convergence to continuous time.

C2.justification: New Remarks 3–4 explain how tail growth, initial energy and a nonuniform Jacobian bound govern discretization error and step-size selection. Remark 6 adds a test-function explanation for Wasserstein's dimensional sensitivity. V3 also expressly defers discrete-time Wasserstein and propagation-of-chaos extensions, refining the scope of v1's broad extension discussion.

D1.justification: Where v1 only calls for sufficiently small steps, v3 Equation 10 specifies step-size dependence on particle count, dimension, tail-growth parameter and initial-energy threshold, together with an iteration count. Theorem 3 describes energy-restricted initialization. These are additional theoretical parameter prescriptions; neither version supplies implementation code, hardware or measured runtime.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical test scenarios. Examples of potentials, target distributions and kernels illustrate theoretical applicability rather than evaluated task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. Comparisons with Shi and Mackey, population-limit SVGD and modified particle algorithms concern published theoretical guarantees.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental protocols, splits, preprocessing or evaluation budgets. V3's explicit step-size and iteration formulas are conditions of its new theorem, not settings of a reported experiment.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity studies or case studies. The added energy-growth and Jacobian arguments are mathematical derivations assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. V3's additional probability bounds are theoretical guarantees rather than empirical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: There are no measured numerical results, empirical rankings or observed qualitative findings in either version. The additional convergence-rate results are formal theoretical contributions assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The discrete and continuous SVGD updates remain the same, as do the bilinear-plus-translation-invariant and Matérn kernel constructions. V3's initialization and step-size conditions specify guarantees for the existing iteration; it does not introduce a new update or model component.

P1.justification: The introduction is reorganized to present challenges and contributions before a separate past-work discussion. V3 separates continuous- and discrete-time sections and moves most retained proofs into a six-part appendix, while retaining Theorem 1's proof in the main text. Expanded notation, revised scope statements and explanatory remarks substantially change the document's organization.

P2.justification: V3 comprehensively changes the typesetting: the title and affiliation block is redesigned, centered small-cap section headings become larger left-aligned bold headings, running headers are removed, and equations and paragraphs are extensively reflowed. The existing convergence diagram moves from page 2 to page 4 with its conceptual content retained. No empirical figures or tables are added.

R1.justification: V3 adds Barp et al. (2022), Gorham and Mackey (2015), Lambert et al. (2021), Brooks et al. (2011) and Raginsky et al. (2017), and removes Blei et al. (2017). It adds discussion distinguishing its discrete finite-particle analysis from population-limit bounds. The central positioning against Shi and Mackey (2024) remains.

T1.justification: V3 adds discrete-time Assumption 2, Theorem 3 and Appendix A.3, with energy-growth and Jacobian bounds supporting explicit finite-step KSD rates. V1 only sketches discrete-time extendability. V3 also explicitly assumes existence and completeness of the continuous-time dynamics, strengthens initial-density regularity from C^1 to C^2 and several kernel conditions from C^2 to C^3, and corrects the Lyapunov derivative from average gradient of V to average V in the retained moment-bound proof.

improvement.justification: V1's discrete-time extension paragraph supplies no explicit finite-step bound or supporting proof. V3's Theorem 3 and Appendix A.3 provide quantified step-size and iteration requirements and detailed control of discretization error, substantially strengthening the connection to implemented SVGD. Explicit existence and regularity conditions also improve precision. The discrete-time guarantee remains restricted by tail-growth and initialization conditions, and Wasserstein/chaos extensions remain deferred, but these limits are now clearer.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SVGD convergence work. Their complete main texts, equations, conceptual diagram, references and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching proofs relocated in v3.

after.justification: V3 remains theoretical throughout its main text and Appendices A.1–A.6. Its additional discrete-time results are theorems and proofs, not empirical outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports mathematical convergence results and proofs, including Appendix A, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Improved Finite-Particle Convergence Rates for Stein Variational Gradient Descent

C1.justification: v3 broadens the headline efficacy claim from the earlier LLaMA-focused demonstration to effectiveness across LLaMA, Qwen, and Phi, reporting wins in 26 of 27 model-dataset configurations. Its headline numerical gains now compare against FRONT rather than v1's selected best baselines. The broad claim of being the first study of LLM hallucinations in RAG is removed.

C2.justification: Appendix F.8 adds an interpretation of non-monotonic data-size results through redundancy, insufficiently challenging samples, and possible overfitting, identifying document diversity as a pipeline limitation. Section 2 also explicitly acknowledges applications where parametric knowledge is appropriate while restricting this study to complete document grounding.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies full-parameter fine-tuning and documents complete document/question/answer input templates. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.1's embedding, UMAP, DBSCAN, and 30-nearest-question clustering details are replaced by a clustering-pipeline link in v3 Appendix E.1. These revise reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the underlying implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions use ASQA, QAMPARI, and ELI5 for training and evaluation, with ExpertQA for generalization testing. The added model families and training-data fractions do not introduce new datasets, task requirements, or input environments.

E2.justification: ExpertQA expands from ICL baseline comparisons in v1 Table 5 to include PostCite, PostAttr, and FRONT in v3 Table 7. GPT-4o becomes an evaluated comparator in Tables 7 and 16. FRONT also joins the retained LLaMA-3-8b comparisons, substantially broadening the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: v3 adds evaluated alignment configurations for LLaMA-3.2-1b/3b, four Qwen-2.5 sizes, Phi3.5-mini, and GPT-4o SFT. Appendix F.8 introduces training conditions selecting the top 10%, 25%, and 50% of augmented samples; Appendix I additionally reports 25% variants across open models. These substantially expand model configurations and training-data budgets.

E4.justification: v3 adds a dedicated empirical comparison of regular and calibrated correctness in Appendix F.1/Figure 6 and data-selection sensitivity in Appendix F.8/Figure 7. The SFT-versus-DPO analysis also expands across model families. Existing hallucination-type ablations, refusal ablations, SimPO comparisons, and answerability case studies are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The expanded results do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for additional models and training-data fractions, including GPT-4o SFT TRUST-SCORE values of 72.09, 56.99, and 48.99 on ASQA, QAMPARI, and ELI5 (Table 16). Some apparent changes are corrections across displays: v3 Table 2 uses LLaMA-3-8b scores 54.95/44.87 for QAMPARI/ELI5, already present in v1 Tables 21–22, instead of v1's main-table 55.31/46.88. v3 Table 12 still retains those conflicting older main-table values.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains question selection, document recombination, grounded positive-response generation, selection of hallucinating negative responses, and DPO on approximately 19K preference pairs. Applying the existing DPO or SFT procedures to additional models does not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten, the main method description is condensed, and related work and answerability nuances move into reorganized appendices with a contents page. Metric terminology and notation are revised throughout, including replacing calibrated EM labels with answer-correctness labels.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a single-column conference layout, redraws Figure 1, reorganizes the main results into model-family tables and a separate SFT comparison, and substantially expands the ExpertQA and detailed-results displays. Figures 6 and 7 add calibration and data-size plots; several existing figures and tables are relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds an introduction comparison identifying Thakur et al.'s refusal-focused work as closest and distinguishing the joint assessment of answers, citations, and refusals. It adds RAG background and model-family references while removing media examples and clustering references. Most of the earlier related-work discussion survives in Appendix C.

T1.justification: v1 Section 4, Equation 1 explicitly defines hallucination severity as e_q = sum_i w_i e_i. v3 continues referencing this score but omits its defining equation, including in Appendix E.5. The answerability and TRUST-SCORE mathematics otherwise remain equivalent after notation changes; no new proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 validates alignment on only two LLaMA bases; v3's evaluations across additional model families and expanded ExpertQA comparisons substantially strengthen evidence for broader applicability. The data-size analysis also exposes limitations of the sample-selection strategy, improving the qualification of the conclusions. These gains outweigh the omitted severity equation and clustering details, although unresolved duplicate-table discrepancies, notably Tables 2 and 12, still weaken reporting consistency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TRUST-SCORE and TRUST-ALIGN research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of additional model families, GPT-4o fine-tuning, and training-data-size sensitivity.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on ASQA, QAMPARI, ELI5, and ExpertQA, together with training ablations and hallucination analyses.

results.title: Measuring and Enhancing Trustworthiness of LLMs in RAG through Grounded Attributions and Learning to Refuse

C1.justification: The abstract, central introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about native-resolution encoding, dynamic compression, unified spatial-temporal understanding, and competitive performance. New appendix evidence supports existing claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning temporal localization and chemical-knowledge reasoning, with proposed causes and remedies in Appendix B. Appendices A and C also introduce interpretations of hallucination, memory overhead, shared-adapter feature distributions, and fixed-token Q-former limitations. These substantially broaden the account of applicability and mechanisms, although several explanations remain hypotheses.

D1.justification: Appendix D.2 fills a substantial encoder-pretraining documentation gap: Qwen2-0.5B, LoRA, 0.6B trainable parameters, 400M pretraining examples, CapsFusion/synthesized OCR sources, batch size 2048, and cross-entropy loss are specified. Existing main training details are relocated unchanged. The earlier explicit maximum positional-embedding size is omitted.

E1.justification: The benchmark suite and established training-task coverage remain unchanged. Appendix B adds targeted qualitative scenarios involving timestamp-specific video description and chemical-knowledge reasoning. CapsFusion and synthesized OCR data are newly identified pretraining sources, without establishing that the underlying training coverage changed.

E2.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their comparator sets. v3 adds LLaVA-OneVision responses to the four generation examples, separate image/video MLPs in Table 8, and standalone convolution and Q-former alternatives in Table 9(a). These extend supplementary comparisons without revising the main benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: Retained benchmark protocols and main training settings are unchanged. New protocols include A100 throughput and memory measurements at 1280 × 1280 pixels, batch size four for the memory comparison, a square-image memory sweep, and controlled data/adapter comparisons. Separate MLPs are initialized from pretrained image weights.

E4.justification: Appendices B–C substantially expand analysis with explicit failure cases, efficiency and memory scaling, ablations separating long-video data, 3D data and coarse correspondences, shared versus separate adapters, and additional downsampling alternatives. The earlier resolution, compression, and needle-in-a-haystack analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 and the relocated retrieval heatmap retain their results. Substantial new findings include OryxViT/SigLIP throughput of 146.5/157.7 images per second and memory of 49.1/48.7 GB, training-data ablation scores, and shared/separate MLP MLVU scores of 59.3/54.2. Qualitative outputs and failures are also added; the tennis caption is replaced. Table 9(b) repeats existing results.

M1.justification: OryxViT, variable-length attention, dynamic compression, the shared MLP, and the training procedure remain substantively unchanged. Appendix D.2 specifies previously underdocumented encoder pretraining; it does not establish a newly introduced procedure. The original compression settings remain in Appendix D.

P1.justification: Most original prose is retained. Bounded structural edits regroup data curation under Section 3.2, move implementation details and the retrieval experiment into appendices, place references after the appendices, and update the publication header. Added scientific material does not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the displays with Tables 6–9, two failure-case figures, and a memory curve. Existing generation panels incorporate baseline answers and colored emphasis. The original retrieval heatmap moves from Figure 3 to Figure 10, and the resolution plot becomes Figure 3; both retain their content.

R1.justification: v3 adds Insight-V (Dong et al., 2024) in the introduction and CapsFusion (Yu et al., 2024) for encoder-pretraining data. The related-work discussion and central positioning against previous approaches remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The native-resolution construction and cross-attention equation are retained, with no new proofs, derivations, or theoretical results. Generalized compression-ratio wording does not change the documented implementation or establish a substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v2: efficiency claims gain direct measurements, curated training data and adapter choices gain targeted ablations, and encoder pretraining receives essential technical documentation. Explicit failure cases also clarify limits missing from the earlier success-focused examples. Together these substantially strengthen evidential support and transparency while preserving the main results, outweighing the limited loss of positional-embedding size detail.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Oryx research work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds efficiency measurements, further ablations, qualitative comparisons, and failure cases.

before.justification: v2 reports original image, video, and ScanQA evaluations, architecture ablations, retrieval experiments, and generated examples.

results.title: Oryx MLLM: On-Demand Spatial-Temporal Understanding at Arbitrary Resolution

C1.justification: The main claims about retraining-free compression, performance through 60% compression, CPU acceleration and complementary attention patterns remain. The conclusion adds an explicit priority claim that this is the first work to reveal the potential of sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions for large-scale transformers, broadening v1's method-specific novelty claim.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges greater offline compression time and argues that deployment benefits justify this cost (A.2). It also explains why preserving outliers may matter more than minimizing activation reconstruction error (A.1), interprets the robust-scaling test, and discusses greater pruning resilience in vision transformers. Existing attention-rollout interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies an OATS code-repository link, NVIDIA A40 hardware and memory specifications, compression timings and parallelization details. It documents Qwen hyperparameters and identifies the implementation used for alternative perplexity evaluation. Existing calibration, baseline settings and attention-rollout details are retained after relocation.

E1.justification: Both use C4 calibration, the same ten-subject MMLU subset, eight zero-shot tasks, WikiText-2, ImageNet and COCO visualizations. Llama-3 70B and Qwen additions evaluate further model configurations on retained tasks; they do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: SparseGPT, Wanda and DSNoT remain the evaluated comparators, including the two DSNoT initializations in corresponding appendix comparisons. Added model evaluations use the same comparator set. Newly discussed methods such as SLOPE and SLIM are related work, not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3 70B and Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct configurations, Phi-3 Medium at 60% compression, a 20-iteration 70B experiment and broader rank/compression settings. Appendix A.12 additionally evaluates WikiText-2 with different normalization and segmentation. This supplements the retained LM Harness evaluation rather than replacing its protocol.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scaling, row-wise pruning and hyperparameter studies, v2 adds tests of median-based scaling, reversed thresholding order and scaling only the low-rank component (A.3–A.5). Additional rank-ratio configurations and the reduced-iteration 70B experiment examine sensitivity and the compression-cost tradeoff.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. Added experiments retain point-estimate reporting; task averages and the median-scaling ablation do not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores are retained, while v2 adds substantial model, timing and ablation results. For example, new 50%-compressed Llama-3 70B MMLU accuracy is 74.79 versus DSNoT's 72.76 (Table 2); median scaling yields 55.54 versus standard scaling's 59.99 on Phi-3 Mini (Table 11). Table 18 adds perplexities under another protocol, so its lower values are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains second-moment scaling, alternating truncated SVD and hard thresholding, inverse scaling, and the same rank/sparsity allocation. Row-wise and N:M options already appear in v1. v2 clarifies their description and tests alternative procedures as ablations without replacing OATS.

P1.justification: v2 extensively revises contributions, method explanations, experimental narration, related-work prose and the conclusion. It creates a dedicated alternative-sparsity subsection, separates structured-pruning discussion and reorganizes the appendix, relocating existing task and implementation sections. These editorial changes extend beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 expands model columns and appendix tables and adds displays for timings, ablations, hyperparameters, Qwen and alternative perplexity evaluation. Table 15 redisplays benchmark differences. Figures 1–2 revise axes and layout while retaining their plotted results; attention images remain unchanged. Original appendix Tables 9–11 map to Tables 17, 19 and 20.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.1 substantially expands positioning against earlier CNN sparse/low-rank compression, vision-transformer pruning, SLOPE pretraining and concurrent SLIM compression. It distinguishes objectives, training requirements and decomposition procedures. v2 also adds GoDec attribution and further outlier-related citations while retaining the earlier related-work discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an asymptotic time-complexity expression and defines its dependence on matrix dimensions and rank. Algorithm 2 repairs the dimensionally inconsistent activation multiplication, and N:M wording changes from N zero entries to N nonzero entries. The core optimization remains unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence and practical documentation. New mechanism ablations address the basis of outlier scaling, larger-model and Qwen evaluations broaden validation, and A.2 supplies compression-cost information absent from v1. The code link, expanded prior-work comparisons and explicitly distinguished perplexity protocols further improve reproducibility and interpretation. A material weakness remains: the retained blanket MMLU superiority statement conflicts with the new 30% Llama-3 70B result, where Wanda outperforms OATS. This inconsistency does not outweigh the substantial evidential and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OATS by the same authors. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds model evaluations, mechanism ablations, compression-time measurements and alternative-protocol perplexity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model and vision-transformer pruning experiments, ablations, CPU throughput measurements and attention visualizations.

results.title: OATS: Outlier-Aware Pruning Through Sparse and Low Rank Decomposition

C1.justification: v4's central validation concerns maintaining RAG accuracy while reducing prefilling cost. v5 broadens the claimed contribution to general and ICL capabilities, adds lossless switching between block and full attention as a central claim, and highlights game-AI applications in the abstract. The headline 32K latency/FLOPs reduction claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v5 interprets joint training as enabling both attention modes and removes v4's conjecture that passage independence might make block attention intrinsically more accurate. PromptCache's critique shifts from restrictive cache reuse to positional-encoding-related quality degradation. Discussion emphasizes real-time game agents instead of ReAct, and a new qualification explains the absence of subjective evaluations requiring OpenAI API access.

D1.justification: v5 announces public code, datasets, and model weights and supplies a project access link. It documents Tulu3 segmentation rules, the usable 23% fraction, and OpenCompass evaluation. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Conversely, v4's explicit DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage-2 and Flash-Attention V2 specifications are omitted.

E1.justification: v5 adds Tulu3 SFT training data, seven reported general/ICL benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, DROP, MATH, GSM8K, HumanEval, and IFEval), and an internal game scenario in Appendix A. The four original RAG benchmarks remain. NarrativeQA is also named, but its actual evaluation is unclear because no corresponding results are reported.

E2.justification: The reported comparison set expands to include Superposition and an original Tulu3-SFT control alongside the RAG-fine-tuned full-attention baseline. PromptCache was already evaluated in v4 through results identified as identical to its weak baselines; v5 reports it separately from block-without-fine-tuning, with distinct outcomes. The no-fine-tuning and no-position comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Sections 3.1-3.4 replace Llama3-8B/Mistral-7B with Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-8B-SFT and replace GPT-4-generated RAG answers with Llama3.3-70B-Instruct answers. Added evaluations use zero-shot general tests, four-shot GSM8K/MATH, and three-shot BBH/DROP. Hardware is reported as eight H20s rather than eight A800s; this does not establish that the unchanged timing results were rerun.

E4.justification: v5 adds a full-attention fallback ablation testing whether the block-trained model retains compatibility with full attention. Figure 4 changes from comparing separately trained models to comparing two attention modes of the adapted model. Existing fine-tuning and positional ablations remain, while Appendix A adds a game-state reuse case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Benchmark averages and checkpoint curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The Llama3/Mistral accuracy table is replaced by Tulu3 results, and seven-task results are added. Figure 4's reported adaptation point changes from about 400 to 800 steps under different training conditions. Appendix A reports TTFT decreasing from 2,800 to 100 ms. These are new or replaced results, not same-setting improvements over v4. The original latency/FLOPs table is numerically unchanged, moving from Table 2 to Table 3.

M1.justification: v4 adapts models through block-mask fine-tuning. v5 explicitly trains every training sample under both block and full attention to preserve both operating modes, substantially changing the training procedure. It also specifies segmentation of general SFT examples by turns, messages, and delimiters. The underlying block mask, cache reuse, and RoPE operations remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes from Efficient RAG to Efficient Prefilling. The abstract, experimental narrative, baseline descriptions, and results discussion are substantially rewritten. Related work is reorganized into three subsections, and acknowledgements and a game appendix are added. Author, affiliation, conference-header, and attention terminology edits accompany this restructuring.

P2.justification: v5 adds the general/ICL Table 2 and game illustration Figure 5. Table 1 drops the three average columns and reorders datasets. Figure 4 is redrawn with revised axes, legends, and curves; Figures 2 and 4 use text-wrapped placement. The unchanged efficiency table is relocated and renumbered Table 3.

R1.justification: A new concurrent-work section credits TurboRAG's independent similar contribution and distinguishes the approach from DecoupledRAG, NSA, and MoBA. Parallel-context positioning expands through Superposition, SGLang, and CacheBlend. The earlier general discussion of linear attention, mixture-of-experts, speculative decoding, and RAGCache is removed; PCW's duplicate references are consolidated.

T1.justification: The KV-state definitions and RoPE derivation in Equations 1-3 are unchanged. Appendix A's conditional-probability notation illustrates game tasks but adds no substantive mathematical reasoning, formal assumptions, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens practical validation by directly testing general-capability retention and switching back to full attention, concerns left untested in v4. The switching ablation, general/ICL evaluations, additional comparator, and new resource-access information improve evidential coverage and reproducibility. These gains are tempered by losing Mistral coverage, limited game-experiment documentation, and overstated accuracy claims: Section 3.5 claims RAG gaps of at most 1%, while Table 1 reports HQA scores of 72.3 versus 74.8. These weaknesses limit the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial added validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Block-Attention research, despite the revised title and expanded scope. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v4 has no appendix; v5's Appendix A is available and included.

after.justification: Section 3 reports RAG, general-capability, and in-context-learning experiments. Appendix A additionally reports original latency outcomes from an internal game application.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original RAG accuracy experiments, ablations, training curves, and latency/FLOPs measurements in Tables 1-2 and Figure 4.

results.title: Block-Attention for Efficient Prefilling

C1.justification: The abstract newly identifies context parroting as a mechanism for capturing chaotic dynamics and attributes success to in-context learning. This elevates a mechanistic explanation into a central contribution beyond v1's comparative forecasting and attractor-reconstruction claims, although the four enumerated contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the interpretation around motif matching and learning the attractor's natural measure. It adds limitations involving rare states and nonstationarity, interprets unsuccessful fine-tuning through task shift, and discusses possible adaptations. These extend v1's emphasis on generic features, dimensional lifting, and hypothesized in-context learning.

D1.justification: Appendix F.1 supplies implementation sources, architecture settings, and lookback search grids for all five trained baselines. Additional details cover pendulum coordinate conversion and downsampling, and fine-tuning data and scripts. These substantially improve documentation without establishing changes to previously used settings; code and data access statements remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained simulated dynamical systems, v2 adds measured double-pendulum data with experimental noise and dissipation (Appendix D) and systematically damped, nonstationary trajectories across the 135 systems (Appendix E). These substantially extend coverage to real measurements and distribution shift.

E2.justification: NBEATS, TiDE, NVAR, Transformer, LSTM, and the constant-forecast baseline remain. Appendix F.2 adds an explicit qualitative comparison of fine-tuned Chronos-base against zero-shot forecasts, expanding v1's brief preliminary fine-tuning remarks.

E3.justification: The principal 512-point context, 300-point test, and 135-system benchmark design remains. New protocols include shuffling context blocks while preserving the final block, a 200-trajectory initial-condition probe, pendulum preprocessing and evaluation windows, and exponential-damping sweeps. These are substantial additions to evaluation design.

E4.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendices C–F add context-overlap comparisons, shuffled-context ablations, attractor-density analysis, and nonstationarity robustness tests, while expanding fine-tuning diagnostics. Earlier multivariate, context-length, attractor-metric, and model-size analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 5 describes standard deviations; corresponding v2 Figure 6 specifies medians and standard errors. v2 also adds a matched t-test for context overlap. Figure 2 drops v1's disclosure of averaging 20 independent stochastic forecasts, without establishing that the actual run count changed.

E6.justification: New findings include benefits from shuffled long contexts, declining VPT with nonstationarity, and an initial-density/VPT correlation of 0.26 ± 0.03 across 2700 cases, plus pendulum and fine-tuning outcomes. Figure 3's VPT distributions and the context-length VPT curves also change. Changed aggregation reporting prevents interpreting these revisions as straightforward performance gains.

M1.justification: The same five pretrained Chronos variants perform channel-independent zero-shot forecasting. Added diagnostic experiments and expanded fine-tuning comparisons do not change this forecasting procedure; proposed architectural adaptations remain future work.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition is retained. Targeted edits revise the abstract and conclusion, replace numbered methods subsections with run-in headings, separate existing result discussions into focused subsections, and relocate the sMAPE explanation to Appendix B.2.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 2, expands the initial-condition illustration into paired Figure 8, and adds several mechanism and robustness figures. The former two-panel context-length figure becomes three-panel Figure 6 with a shuffling experiment. Plot axes, sizing, captions, and placement also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the measured dataset, Darts implementations, fine-tuning limitations, low-rank adaptation, and proposed robustness improvements. Section 2 also adds Ekambaram et al. on time-series foundation models. The broader related-work framing and first-large-scale-evaluation positioning remain.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a mathematical definition of exponential trajectory modulation and parameterizes nonstationarity through its damping strength, including stationary and damped limits. Existing Lorenz equations and forecasting-metric definitions remain equivalent; no new theorem or proof appears.
