improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the previously conjectural mechanism account with targeted context-matching and shuffling tests, examines real measurements and distribution-shift limits, and supplies missing baseline hyperparameters. These improve evidential depth and reproducibility. Unexplained VPT revisions and the pendulum experiment's seven-versus-eight-window inconsistency remain reporting weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with readable main text, figures, equations, references, and appendices. The retained material can be matched across restructuring and figure renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds context-shuffling, nonstationarity, initial-condition, and measured double-pendulum forecasting results.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments across 135 chaotic systems, including model comparisons, attractor reconstruction, and context-length analyses.

results.title: Zero-shot forecasting of chaotic systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: training-data-free joint reconstruction and motion estimation, projection-based optimization, and coarse-to-fine hash encoding. Claims of comparable in-domain performance and superior out-of-domain performance remain substantively unchanged; the 3D appendix expands evidence and capabilities without rewriting these main claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly identifies intra-acquisition motion, non-rigid motion, and spin-history effects as limitations and discusses deformation-field modeling as a possible extension. It characterizes the acquired-data validation as preliminary. Appendix A.2 also corrects the motion-error interpretation from higher-is-better to lower-is-better without changing its formula.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 newly specifies image contrasts, orientations, spacing, golden-angle sampling, spoke length, view counts, and 18 motion stages. It also discloses the MLP width and activation choices. Appendix A.1 supplies scanner, sequence, volume, and motion-state details for the new studies. These substantially expand reproducibility information; existing baseline implementation links remain.

E1.justification: V2 adds simulated motion on a 240×240×240 brain volume and actual motion-corrupted and motion-free T1w 3D acquisitions from one subject. This extends the original simulated 2D fastMRI/MoDL evaluation to volumetric reconstruction and real acquisition conditions.

E2.justification: The corresponding 2D comparisons retain NuIFFT, TV, DRN-DCMB, and Score-MoCo, with TV and Score-MoCo retained for motion estimation. The new 3D experiments reuse NuIFFT; no new comparator algorithm or substantive baseline modification is documented.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1 introduces 3D simulation protocols with 120 motion states, acceleration factors 2×/4×, and motion ranges ±5/±10. The acquired-data protocol uses 650 estimated motion stages, three instructed head movements, and a separate motion-free reference. Previously stated 2D splits and optimization budgets remain unchanged; newly disclosed 2D preprocessing details do not establish a protocol change.

E4.justification: The three existing component ablations retain their settings and aggregate results. V2 adds focused 3D motion-recovery case analyses: Figure 11 compares estimated trajectories with simulated ground truth, while Figure 13 examines consistency with the real subject's instructed movements. These provide limited additional diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: V1 reports ± values for component ablations but lacks statistical tests and uncertainty for the main image-quality comparisons. V2 adds mean±STD reporting for PSNR and SSIM in Tables 2 and 7 and t-test significance categories throughout Tables 1–7. Neither version specifies seeds or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: V2 adds 3D quantitative and acquired-data results. For example, Table 6 reports PSNR/SSIM of 31.58/0.844 for Moner versus 23.64/0.499 for NuIFFT at AF=2×, MR=±5. Existing 2D Moner means remain unchanged, but Score-MoCo's MoDL AF=2×, MR=±15 result changes from 32.49/0.762 to 33.90/0.795. Newly reported tests mark fastMRI PSNR differences between Moner and Score-MoCo as nonsignificant.

M1.justification: The original 2D method is retained, but Appendix A.1 adds an implemented 3D extension. It uses stack-of-radial data, a 2D inverse Fourier transform, 3D back-projection, and six rigid-motion parameters per motion state. V1 discusses 3D extension only as future work.

P1.justification: V2 selectively edits the abstract and introductory discussion, separates datasets from preprocessing in Section 4.1, removes the brief reproducibility statement, and inserts the 3D appendix section. Author information is reformatted. Most method and results prose remains intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the 3D schematic, reconstruction and trajectory figures, and Table 6. It splits the original combined PSNR/SSIM table into Tables 2 and 7, adds statistical annotations, replaces Figure 4 examples with annotated detail views, and labels the encoding-ablation trajectory by motion stages. Original appendix image grids are retained as Figures 15–18 rather than newly added.

R1.justification: V2 adds Catalán et al. (2023) and distinguishes its Fourier-slice neural-field approach from Moner. It also acknowledges that some earlier INR methods address dynamic range through relative L2 losses, replacing the blanket omission claim, and cites Reed et al. (2021) for possible non-rigid extensions.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds the formal 3D rotation matrix and translation vector in Equation 10 and the corresponding volumetric projection relationship. The existing Fourier-slice derivation, 2D method equations, and motion-error definitions remain unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's restriction to simulated 2D validation by documenting and testing a 3D extension, including actual motion-corrupted acquisitions. The added sampling and implementation details close important reproducibility gaps, while uncertainty and significance reporting make comparisons more assessable. The gains are tempered by the single-subject real study, NuIFFT-only 3D comparisons, and unexplained revisions to some Score-MoCo scores, but materially strengthen the paper's practical evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Moner and retain matching methods, datasets, and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including the new 3D material in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds simulated 3D reconstruction experiments and a real-acquisition study involving two scans of one subject.

before.justification: V1 reports original fastMRI and MoDL reconstruction experiments, motion-estimation results, runtime comparisons, and component ablations.

results.title: Moner: Motion Correction in Undersampled Radial MRI with Unsupervised Neural Representation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace the assertion of state-of-the-art depth/normal performance with promising performance, narrowing the claimed comparative standing. Section 5.2 specifies Lotus-G's best overall rank. The central formulation, detail-preservation, efficiency, and limited-training-data contributions remain.

C2.justification: Appendix B newly explains that AMRN reduces parameterization differences and can make single-step gains inconsistent, qualifying the original adaptation argument. Appendix F interprets frequency behavior as preserving geometric detail without copying texture, while Appendix E extends the applicability discussion through non-geometric tasks. These substantially expand the paper's explanations and applicability conditions.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly discloses normalization of depth and normal maps to [-1,1]; added analyses identify the Marigold codebase and FFT grouping procedure. Hardware, optimizer, training durations, and access links remain unchanged. Appendix B drops the explicit exclusion of test-time ensembling, a disclosure change that does not establish changed inference.

E1.justification: v5 adds DIODE depth evaluation and OASIS normal evaluation to Tables 1–2. Appendix E additionally trains and evaluates semantic segmentation and diffuse reflectance on Hypersim, substantially extending task requirements beyond geometric prediction. The original depth/normal training datasets remain.

E2.justification: Diffusion-E2E-FT is newly included in both depth and normal comparisons in Tables 1–2. The existing comparator membership is otherwise retained. Reusing Direct Adaptation for the new Hypersim tasks does not introduce another comparison method.

E3.justification: The added studies substantially expand evaluation design: Appendix E specifies 500 randomly selected test pairs and mIoU/mAcc or L1/L2 metrics; Appendix B introduces matched AMRN controls; Appendix F uses 100 sampled cases and eight frequency groups; Appendix G varies the single timestep while excluding detail preservation and mixed-dataset training. Existing geometric metrics and training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and training-step ablations, v5 adds disparity-target ablations in Table 3, parameterization/single-step/detail-preserver comparisons with and without AMRN in Tables 4–5, frequency analysis of geometry versus texture in Figure 13, and single-timestep sensitivity in Table 8. These test several previously unexamined explanations and conditions.

E5.justification: Tables 6–7 newly state that results are means from 10 independent runs. This adds explicit repeated-run reporting without identifying training versus inference repetitions or supplying dispersion. The original variance-band plots remain; the PDFs do not establish increased repetition of the original experiments.

E6.justification: v5 adds benchmark, comparator, and analysis results and revises Lotus scores. Table 3 retains the earlier Lotus-G KITTI AbsRel of 11.324 and adds 8.521 for disparity-space training, so these are different configurations. Table 2 changes Lotus-D's NYUv2 mean angular error from 16.8 to 16.2 without explaining the revision. New segmentation results include mIoU 21.2 versus Direct Adaptation's 14.1. Updated average ranks use expanded comparison sets.

M1.justification: v5 adopts disparity-space targets for depth training and prediction (Sections 5.1 and 5.3). Table 3 retains v4's final configurations and adds explicitly labeled disparity-space variants, establishing an actual procedural change. The architecture, single-step formulation, detail preserver, and generative/discriminative variants remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Changes include localized wording edits, clarification that the autoencoder contains an encoder and decoder, an expanded related-work paragraph, and new appendix subsections. Earlier appendices E–G become H–J without substantial rewriting.

P2.justification: v5 substantially expands visual presentation with Tables 4–8 and Figures 12–13, additional columns and rows in Tables 1–3, and revised Figure 1 comparison charts. The earlier qualitative and application Figures 12–14 are retained as Figures 14–16, with layout reflow rather than new experiments.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds substantive positioning against concurrent Diffusion-E2E-FT, acknowledging similar performance and distinguishing Lotus-G's stochastic predictions and detail preserver. References to Garcia et al., Disenvisioner, and DIODE are added. The broader related-work organization and existing comparisons remain.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds limiting-case reasoning for approximate equivalence between v-prediction and x0-prediction at t=T when the noise coefficient's complementary signal term approaches zero. The original numbered diffusion equations and Appendix C derivation are retained; no new theorem or substantial proof framework appears.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens the central adaptation argument by testing the previously unexamined AMRN interaction and adding a close concurrent comparator. Non-geometric experiments provide measured support for applicability beyond v4's geometric tasks, while headline performance claims become better calibrated. These gains outweigh remaining reporting gaps, including absent dispersion for ten-run means and Appendix A.2's outdated four-dataset descriptions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Lotus. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated or renumbered in v5.

after.justification: v5 retains original geometric prediction experiments and adds semantic segmentation, diffuse reflectance, and further controlled analyses.

before.justification: v4 reports original depth and surface-normal estimation results, component ablations, parameterization experiments, and qualitative applications.

results.title: Lotus: Diffusion-based Visual Foundation Model for High-quality Dense Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion add explicit claims of real-world task reasoning and generalization; v1 leaves physical-robot validation to future work. The central hybrid-method contributions and headline simulation improvement claims remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendices C–E add substantive explanations of training–inference distribution shifts, omitted rotation guidance, heuristic limitations, latency, skill-composition failures, and possible alternatives to GravMap representations. The cost-map ablation explanation changes from non-unit quaternion predictions to an encoder/zero-gradient problem. These materially expand and qualify the earlier interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v4 documents the physical-robot setup, RealSense D435i camera, image resizing, MoveIt/BiRRT execution, and demonstration/evaluation procedures. It also specifies the added oracle baselines and avoidance-map parameters, including the target exclusion radius and Gaussian smoothing. These substantially extend implementation coverage, while Table 3 and the existing prompt/video access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained 12 base and 8 novel simulation tasks, v4 evaluates Push Buttons Shape, Button Close Jar, and Pour From Cup to Cup, plus six base and four novel physical-robot tasks (Appendices D.4 and D.6). This substantially extends coverage to physical environments, skill composition, and unfamiliar objects and interactions.

E2.justification: The original VoxPoser, Act3D, and 3D Diffuser Actor comparisons remain. Table 7 adds VoxPoser (Manual), supplied with ground-truth object poses, and ChainedDiffuser (Oracle), supplied with ideal keyposes. Table 8 adds only ChainedDiffuser (Oracle). These are targeted extensions to the existing comparator suite.

E3.justification: v4 adds demonstration-count and camera-view sweeps, thresholded position/rotation accuracy metrics, runtime measurements, and a physical-robot protocol using 20 demonstrations per base task and 10 evaluation episodes per task. The original RLBench training and testing budgets remain. Table 5 and Appendix B.2.7 also revise the conditional block color from blue to black, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 substantially extends the original ablations and failure analysis with data/viewpoint sensitivity, runtime comparisons, keypose-filtering and touch-force case studies, and harder generalization probes. Appendix D.5 adds a no-cost-map ablation with gripper closure encoded as -1, addressing the encoder failure that confounded the original zero-success ablation.

E5.justification: The original three-seed evaluation and numerical uncertainty entries in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. New Figure 14 contains shaded bands, but its caption and Appendix D.3 do not define their meaning or associated run counts. Whether these introduce statistical uncertainty reporting, rather than another plotting convention, cannot be reliably determined.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 4 retain their results. Added findings include 62.66% success on Push Buttons Shape and zero on the other two added simulation tasks (Table 10), 10–100% across physical tasks (Table 11), and 44.75%/41.88% base/novel success for the differently encoded no-cost-map ablation (Figure 16). Baseline, runtime, and scaling results are also added. Table 8 reports a ChainedDiffuser average of 43.22%, although its displayed task scores average 50.04%, an unexplained discrepancy.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 adds an occupancy-derived avoidance map, smoothing and combining it with the distance cost. It also explicitly separates training-time random offsets from inference. These refine the reported map-generation procedure; the sub-goal discovery rules, diffusion architecture, and losses remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local wording and terminology corrections, publication-header and acknowledgment additions, moving Algorithm 1 into Appendix A, and organizing the expanded supplementary discussion, results, and limitations into Appendices C–E.

P2.justification: v4 substantially expands the visual presentation with task taxonomies, keypose and force illustrations, scaling curves, additional-task examples, a revised ablation display, physical-robot visuals, and Tables 6–11. Earlier figures are largely retained and relocated or renumbered; the original two main result tables are separated across pages.

R1.justification: v4 explicitly acknowledges earlier sub-goal approaches, adding references including Black, Kang, and Ma, and cites Garcia for task categorization. Appendix C.1 further distinguishes GravMap processing from VoxPoser. Additional references support proposed future extensions, while the broader imitation-learning/foundation-model positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 revises the mathematical cost-map construction from normalized Euclidean distance to a renormalized combination of twice that distance cost plus a smoothed occupancy map. This is a limited definition change. The problem assumptions and diffusion/loss equations (1)–(6) remain unchanged, with no added theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the simulation-only evidence in v1 through physical-robot validation, targeted comparator controls, and scalability and generalization tests. The revised cost-map ablation addresses an important experimental confound, while explicit failures and expanded limitations better establish applicability boundaries. Physical tests remain small and lack baseline comparisons, and Table 8 has an unexplained aggregate discrepancy, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GravMAD and retain matching formulations, experiments, and results. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and algorithms, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, scalability experiments, additional novel-task tests, and evaluations on 10 physical-robot tasks.

before.justification: v1 reports original RLBench experiments on 12 base and 8 novel tasks, component ablations, and failure-case analyses.

results.title: GravMAD: Grounded Spatial Value Maps Guided Action Diffusion for Generalized 3D Manipulation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion extend the claimed demonstrated applicability from a synthetic gene network to high-dimensional mixtures and real single-cell dynamics. The central contributions—learning RUOT without growth priors, avoiding false transitions and reconstructing landscapes—remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation beyond v1's false-transition and landscape explanations. It discusses growth-versus-transport ambiguity and temporal resolution, scalability difficulties at thousands of dimensions, numerical instability, and mechanisms behind training-stage failures (Section 6; Appendices B–C). The earlier unresolved microscopic Schrödinger-bridge interpretations remain in Appendix E.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, simulation parameters, an explicit initial-density estimator, dataset preprocessing, hardware specifications, loss weights, training schedules and epoch counts (Appendices A–C; Tables 3 and 5). These substantially expand v1's algorithm and library descriptions; newly disclosed settings do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic gene-network task, v2 adds Gaussian-mixture transport, mouse hematopoiesis and A549 epithelial–mesenchymal transition data. These extend evaluation to substantially different distributions and real biological populations (Section 6; Appendices B.2–B.4).

E2.justification: v1's reported baseline comparison centers on SF2M. v2 Table 1 retains SF2M and adds MIOFlow, unbalanced Action Matching, Unbalanced SB/UDSB and an Unbalanced OT implementation. Table 2 evaluates the expanded comparator set on hematopoiesis.

E3.justification: v2 introduces quantitative W1/W2 evaluation after fitting observed time points, using weighted distributions for DeepRUOT and uniform weights for comparators (Appendix C.1). Its quantitative gene comparison uses diffusion 0.05 for DeepRUOT versus 0.25 for SF2M, separately from the retained 0.25 visual comparison. Added experiments also introduce SPRING/PCA preprocessing and 10–100-dimensional mixture settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled ablations of growth, local mass matching, Fokker–Planck constraints and training stages (Table 4), plus epoch-scheduling and loss-weight sensitivity studies (Tables 6–7). Figures 4 and 7 additionally examine UDSB trajectory and population-mass errors, extending substantially beyond v1's qualitative SF2M comparison.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 1, 2 and 4 explicitly report means and one standard deviation across five runs. v1 provides neither repeated-run counts nor uncertainty summaries. This establishes new statistical reporting, without establishing an increase from any known earlier run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds quantitative comparisons, ablation and sensitivity scores, and mixture/real-data findings. Table 1 reports final gene-data W2 of 0.121 for DeepRUOT versus 0.124 for Unbalanced OT. Superiority is not universal: Table 2's final W1 favors Unbalanced SB, 0.128254 versus 0.132411. These are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The three-network solver and its principal losses remain. However, v1 specifies a CFM-only score warmup, whereas v2 Appendix C.3 augments that objective with a temporary penalty on positive log-density-network outputs before removing it. This is a limited revision to the stated training objective.

P1.justification: v2 extensively reorganizes the narrative: it rewrites and condenses the introduction, adds explicit contribution bullets and a separate related-work section, consolidates algorithm presentation, and moves substantial theory and training material into Appendices A–E. This exceeds routine language editing.

P2.justification: v2 combines v1 Figures 6.1–6.4 into a redesigned eight-panel Figure 2, revises the overview diagram, and adds six result figures and seven tables. The ICLR layout and redistributed scientific displays substantially change visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including Maddu et al. (2024), Meng et al. (2024), Weinreb et al. (2020) and Zhang et al. (2021). Section 4 also explicitly contrasts its Fisher cross-term with Baradat and Lavenant's formulation. The broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Most theorems, proofs and Schrödinger-bridge connections are retained and relocated. A local mathematical revision occurs in Appendix D.2: the entropy endpoint difference gains a sigma-squared factor absent from v1 Section 3.1. The central theoretical framework remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 relies on a qualitative comparison in one simulated system with sparse reproducibility information. v2 substantially addresses these weaknesses through quantitative baseline comparisons, five-run uncertainty reporting, component ablations, sensitivity tests, real-data applications and implementation details. Evaluation on fitted time points, unequal comparator settings and the overstated blanket superiority claim in light of Table 2 limit the conclusions, but the gains in evidence and reproducibility are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepRUOT work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching theory and experiments relocated in v2.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices B–C report original synthetic and real-data experiments, quantitative baseline comparisons, ablations and sensitivity results.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original synthetic gene-network experiments, including inferred trajectories, growth rates and developmental landscapes in Figures 6.1–6.4.

results.title: Learning stochastic dynamics from snapshots through regularized unbalanced optimal transport

C1.justification: The central claims of effective, practically endless attacks that exploit increasing model capabilities remain. V2 refines the headline contribution around universal, scale-adaptive sampling and explicitly presents the Pareto-frontier/computational-overload account as a contribution in Section 1.3, extending the earlier emphasis on scaling laws and failure modes.

C2.justification: V1 Section 5 anticipates that a sufficiently capable output filter could detect encoded harmful content. V2 Section 5 finds only modest mitigation even with a capability-matched guard, while attributing Haiku's apparent protection to severe overrefusal. V2 also develops computational overload as an alternative to mismatched generalization and identifies Gemini as an exception to the two-regime scaling pattern. The standalone limitations text remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds baseline implementation settings, identifies GPT-4o-2024-08-06, and labels Figure 7's MMLU evaluation as a 100-question subset. It removes v1's explicit 2048-token response limit. The detailed prompt and classifier appendices are unchanged. These are documentation changes, not evidence that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: AdvBench-50, HarmBench, HarmBench-35, and MMLU remain. V2 Section 5 adds a custom set of 100 benign intents to evaluate guardrail false rejections, a focused extension beyond the existing harmful-input and capability evaluations.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated PAIR, TAP, GCG-transfer, and an 11-encoding ensemble against the main benchmark results; v1 Table 1 contained only bijection learning. The universal-attack comparison also changes: v1 Figure 4 compares selected encodings with Pliny, whereas v2 Appendix F compares the retained selected encodings with average-case bijections.

E3.justification: V2 adds comparison protocols, including matched PAIR query budgets, a 58-query TAP budget, and GCG transfer from Llama Guard 3. Scaling evaluations add Claude 3 Sonnet, Llama 3.1, and Gemini 1.5 configurations. Guard testing expands to three guard models with common encodings and separate harmful/benign budgets. The reported human-judging rubric expands to PREFS with a copyright exception; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1 Appendix C's single-guard experiment becomes a substantially expanded capability-parity and overrefusal analysis in v2 Section 5. Figure 7 extends scaling analysis across four model families. Conversely, v2 narrows the failure-mode plots to digit attacks on HarmBench-35 and no longer separately reports the 20-teaching-example MMLU conditions shown in v1 Figure 6.

E5.justification: Both versions display error bars for MMLU attack conditions. However, v1 Figure 6 also shows separate baseline estimates with error bars; v2 Figures 6 and 11 replace these with horizontal baseline lines without displayed uncertainty. Neither version specifies seed counts or the error-bar construction.

E6.justification: The proposed method's Table 1 scores remain unchanged, including 86.3% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet on HarmBench. V2 adds extensive comparator results: the corresponding ensemble, PAIR, TAP, and GCG-transfer scores are 20.9%, 9.7%, 10.3%, and 0.3%. It also adds model-family findings and expanded guard results, while removing Pliny scores. Revised guard results should not be interpreted as same-setting performance changes from v1's explicitly LLM-only evaluation.

M1.justification: The encoding, in-context teaching, decoding, denoising, and best-of-n procedure remain unchanged. Dispersion reparameterizes fixed size as d = 26 - F; encoding length was already varied in v1. Appendices A and B retain the same templates and classifier instructions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methods exposition, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Desiderata move into the introduction, experiments gain a dedicated baseline section, guard evaluation moves into the main text, and universal-attack results move to Appendix F. Terminology changes throughout from fixed size and scale-agnostic to dispersion and scale-adaptive.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview to show the existing denoiser, restructures Table 1 around models and comparator rows, and replaces the combined scaling plot with four family panels. Failure-mode and guard figures are substantially redesigned. MMLU panels are split between the main text and Appendix E, and appendix tables are reorganized. Figures 9 and 10 retain their underlying graphics.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion shifts from broad safety, attacks, and robustness coverage to optimization-, persuasion-, and encoding-based attacks, with substantial distinctions concerning access, universality, and adaptability. V2 adds positioning against prompt-fuzzing approaches and mismatched-generalization explanations, supported by new citations including GPTFuzzer, Hayase et al., and Kotha et al.; much of the earlier defense-oriented discussion is removed.

T1.justification: The ASR definition is retained, and dispersion is an equivalent reparameterization of fixed size. Encoding length already existed in v1's experiments. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs; the expanded scaling and computational-overload discussion remains empirical and interpretive.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential gaps: Table 1 directly tests competing methods supporting the comparative claim, and Section 5 replaces speculative guard effectiveness with capability-parity and benign-input controls. Expanded scaling analysis also exposes a meaningful Gemini exception. These changes substantially improve validation and qualify the paper's interpretations despite unchanged headline attack scores. Removing the Pliny comparison and some uncertainty and supplementary detail is a drawback, but the stronger comparative evidence and better-controlled defense analysis outweigh those losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same bijection-learning work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including material moved between sections and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, model-family scaling evaluations, and guarded-system experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original jailbreak evaluations, parameter sweeps, MMLU measurements, failure-mode analyses, and a guarded-system experiment.

results.title: Endless Jailbreaks with Bijection Learning

C1.justification: v4 foregrounds Exploratory Learning within EXACT and frames the approach as building o1-like agents, while treating Imitation Learning as conventional. The headline changes from 97% performance recovery with roughly fourfold savings to Exploratory Learning's 87% recovery and 2.7-fold savings. These summarize different retained rows, rather than changed performance for one method.

C2.justification: v4 interprets the new OSWorld results as evidence of broader applicability and competitive performance using a single model, while distinguishing comparators that use additional resources, specialized models, or training. Existing mechanism explanations, error interpretations, and Section 8 limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 documents the new OSWorld search configuration and newly states that EXACT's system prompts slightly modify ReAct prompts to encourage exploration. It also clarifies that vision fine-tuning was unavailable at study time and updates the supplied code/data link. Appendix implementation and prompt details otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only VisualWebArena. v4 retains its three environments and adds WebArena's GitLab tasks in Table 2 and OSWorld's desktop, file-operation, and multi-application tasks in Tables 3-4. This substantially broadens the environments and task requirements evaluated.

E2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the flat ReAct reference with Best-of-N ReAct. New OSWorld comparisons include Agent-S, AgentStore variants, and Learn-by-Interact, using reported external results where indicated. Appendix Table 8 adds broader VWA comparisons, including ICAL and additional model-based agents. Existing VWA comparators remain.

E3.justification: v4 introduces separate OSWorld protocols using screenshot plus accessibility-tree inputs and accessibility-tree-only inputs, a 15-step limit, a 60-node search limit, and depth-decaying breadth starting at 10. These are settings for added experiments; the existing VWA settings and learning-data counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The revised compute-scaling analysis in Figure 1 compares R-MCTS with increasing Best-of-N ReAct computation, providing an additional check against repeated sampling. Component ablations, difficulty breakdowns, the qualitative example, error analysis, and Appendix B browser and task-instruction studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional tables and curve in v4 continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results: GitLab success reaches 23.5% for R-MCTS with MAD; OSWorld R-MCTS achieves 19.39% with screenshot plus accessibility-tree inputs and 16.6% with accessibility-tree-only inputs. Figure 1 adds Best-of-N results, and Table 8 adds leaderboard entries. Matched VWA, fine-tuning, and ablation scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v4 adds an OSWorld-specific search adaptation: breadth starts at 10 and decays exponentially with depth, whereas v1 documents fixed breadth. The core reflection, debate, and training procedures remain unchanged. Best-in-Tree SFT and Tree-Traversal SFT are renamed Imitation Learning and Exploratory Learning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and learning-related paragraphs are revised around EXACT and Exploratory Learning, with terminology updated throughout. The section sequence and most background, method, analysis, limitations, and appendix prose remain intact; this is focused rewriting rather than wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: v4 substantially expands the comparative displays through two OSWorld tables, the appendix leaderboard, and GitLab columns in Table 2. Figure 1 gains a Best-of-N curve, learning diagrams are relabeled, and the learning-results table gains a Search column. Existing appendix displays are retained with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: v4 adds references and comparison-oriented discussion for OSWorld, Agent-S, AgentStore, and Learn-by-Interact, emphasizing differences in resource use. It also positions best-action training as traditional imitation learning. Section 6's broader literature discussion and principal priority claim remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, policy/value definitions, reflection-error equations, and Appendix A search equations and pseudocode are retained. No new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations appear.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens empirical validation of R-MCTS beyond v1's VWA-only evidence. GitLab and OSWorld test materially different environments, while Figure 1's Best-of-N comparison makes the compute-scaling evidence more informative than the earlier flat ReAct reference. The learning evidence remains unchanged, and limited Best-of-N procedural detail and differing comparator resources constrain interpretation, but the broader validation provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same R-MCTS and search-based learning work, despite v4's EXACT branding. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-D are readable and support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds R-MCTS evaluations on WebArena's GitLab domain and OSWorld, alongside additional comparison results.

before.justification: v1 reports original VisualWebArena experiments, fine-tuning results, compute-scaling experiments, ablations, and error analyses, including additional browser and task-instruction experiments in Appendix B.

results.title: ExACT: Teaching AI Agents to Explore with Reflective-MCTS and Exploratory Learning

C1.justification: The central PnP/flow-matching contribution, efficiency claims, and main PSNR/SSIM claims remain. The conclusion modestly extends the explicit contribution scope by reporting preliminary Laplace-noise results and promising blind-inverse-problem applications.

C2.justification: Appendix A.10 newly interprets mixed LPIPS rankings through the perception–distortion tradeoff, extending v1's general oversmoothing discussion. New passages clarify likelihood requirements, restrictions of the blind examples, and the bounded-noise assumption. The conclusion also explicitly identifies posterior sampling as a future extension.

D1.justification: v2 newly reports PnP-Flow integration into DeepInv and documents DDRM/DPS checkpoint use and hyperparameter search grids in A.13. A.14 specifies Adam and operator constraints for the blind variant. Existing training details and the hyperparameter values in Tables 5–6 are retained.

E1.justification: Appendices A.11 and A.14 add Laplace-corrupted CelebA super-resolution and blind deconvolution and masking examples. These substantially extend the evaluated noise and operator-knowledge regimes. CelebA, AFHQ-Cat, CelebA-HQ, and Simplex-MNIST coverage already existed in v1; no new dataset is introduced.

E2.justification: Tables 10–11 add evaluated DDRM and DPS baselines across four restoration tasks on both main datasets. This substantially broadens diffusion comparisons beyond the existing PnP-Diff baseline. The original flow-based and PnP comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds LPIPS evaluation and a 100-image Laplace super-resolution protocol with 2× downsampling and noise levels 0.1 and 0.3. Blind tests introduce unknown operators, with known kernel size and a shared kernel across channels. Existing Gaussian protocols remain stated as before. Table 7's CelebA 4× header conflicts with 2× elsewhere and does not reliably establish a changed setting.

E4.justification: Appendix A.9 and Figure 13 add a case visualization separating gradient, interpolation, and denoising outputs. Appendix A.14 adds exploratory blind-restoration case studies. Existing initialization, Dirichlet-latent, and rectified-flow analyses remain; no systematic component-removal ablation is added.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments were seeded and report averages over test images, without introducing confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, or significance tests. Averaging five interpolation realizations remains an algorithmic operation, not new uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds LPIPS, Laplace-noise, DDRM/DPS, and blind-restoration outcomes. Table 9 reports PnP-Flow PSNRs of 30.30 and 26.50 dB at the two Laplace noise levels. Table 11 newly shows DPS exceeding PnP-Flow on AFHQ-Cat super-resolution PSNR, 27.83 versus 26.75 dB. Existing reconstruction scores are retained, but degraded super-resolution PSNR/SSIM changes from 7.527/0.012 to 10.17/0.182 in Table 1 and from 10.74/0.042 to 11.59/0.216 in Table 2.

M1.justification: The denoiser and core Algorithm 3 remain unchanged. Appendix A.14 adds a procedural extension for blind restoration: image updates alternate with Adam updates of an unknown blur kernel, and a related example jointly estimates a masking operator.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order remain. Changes include localized introduction and conclusion edits, shorter captions, expanded acknowledgements, an acceptance header, consolidation of existing appendix material, and additional appendix subsections. The retained narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 7–11 and Figures 13–17, covering perceptual evaluation, new comparisons, intermediate algorithm outputs, and new restoration scenarios. Figure 7 gains another example. Existing benchmark and hyperparameter tables are regrouped, and Figure 2 is resized. These substantially expand the visual presentation while retaining earlier displays.

R1.justification: Section 4 and new Appendix A.12 substantially expand positioning relative to diffusion approaches. v2 removes the assertion that the listed works are the only generative-model PnP methods, discusses Garber and Tirer, explicitly acknowledges similarity to He et al., and connects the method to decoupled posterior-sampling and null-space approaches. Cheng et al. is also credited for a related interpolation idea.

T1.justification: Proposition 4 adds the assumption that the latent distribution has bounded support. Appendix A.2 explicitly handles bounded iteration-dependent noise and removes an erroneous extra factor of (1−t_n) from the increment identity. These are substantive but localized corrections; Proposition 1 and its proof remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves correctness and critical evaluation: it repairs a missing convergence assumption and algebraic error, adds perceptual assessment beyond v1's distortion metrics, and evaluates additional diffusion baselines that expose performance limitations. Expanded related work also clarifies novelty. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including Table 7's conflicting downsampling label and disagreement between main and appendix degraded-image scores. The indirect FFHQ-trained diffusion comparisons and qualitative-only blind examples still limit the strength of the added evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PnP-Flow research, with matching authors, core algorithm, and substantial shared experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies in v2 do not prevent identifying the changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds perceptual-metric evaluations, diffusion-baseline comparisons, Laplace-noise experiments, and blind-restoration examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-restoration results and computational measurements in Tables 1–4, together with appendix experiments on Dirichlet latents, initialization sensitivity, and rectified flows.

results.title: PnP-Flow: Plug-and-Play Image Restoration with Flow Matching

C1.justification: v1 claims new state-of-the-art results in three languages. v2 qualifies the contribution as state-of-the-art-level performance from a non-ensemble model. The central SemInfo objective, correlation claim, and reported average 7.85-point improvement remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning robustness to noisy paraphrases, similar accuracy across optimization strategies, TreeCRF computational advantages, and possible PCFG expressivity limits suggested by supervised comparisons. Appendix A.6 introduces an agreement-based argument for potential ensemble benefits, without reporting an actual ensemble improvement. Section 3 also explicitly states the paraphraser-quality assumption.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project code-availability link, sampling and V-function computation details, and attribution of reused parser predictions to Shayegh et al. It also reports relative training speed and memory use. Existing dataset-processing instructions and paraphrasing prompts are retained.

E1.justification: Coverage remains constituency parsing on English PTB, Chinese CTB 5.1, and French/German SPMRL. The added studies vary optimization, supervision, and paraphraser configurations; they introduce no additional corpus, language, domain, or parsing task.

E2.justification: v2 adds supervised TreeCRF/PCFG reference models in Table 5, a right-branching baseline in Table 6, and heterogeneous agreement comparisons including ContextDistort and DIORA in Figure 13. Conversely, Table 3 removes StructFormer, reported at 54 English sentence-F1 in v1. These substantially expand and revise the comparison set.

E3.justification: The original splits, model sizes, preprocessing, and parsing metrics remain unchanged. New protocols compare training distributions and optimization strategies with supervised controls, vary seven paraphrasing models in Table 6, and evaluate pairwise parser agreement in Appendix A.6. The SF1i/SF1c terminology clarifies existing metrics rather than changing them.

E4.justification: New Appendices A.1, A.5, and A.6 investigate optimization choices, sensitivity to paraphraser quality, and diversity relevant to ensembling. Figure 8 expands sentence-level correlation examples, and Section 5.2 adds vocabulary-shift statistics. The earlier training-stage correlation and constituent-recall analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The original three-run mean/standard-deviation reporting, two-tailed t-tests, eight independently seeded correlation models, and Fisher Z aggregation remain unchanged. Additional tables extend the existing uncertainty-reporting format without specifying a new statistical procedure or increased run count.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark, correlation, and constituent-recall values are unchanged, apart from the removed StructFormer result. New Tables 5–6 and agreement figures add substantial results: Table 6 reports SemInfo-NPCFG scores from 59.01 with Qwen2.5-0.5B to 66.85 with GPT-3.5. Table 5 explicitly reports retrained comparisons, not replacements for Table 1.

M1.justification: v1 specifies TreeCRF REINFORCE with an average reward baseline. v2 retains this as Posterior-Avg but introduces V-function baselines, stepwise optimization with generalized advantage estimation, and direct PCFG-based counterparts in Appendix A.1. These are substantive alternative training procedures.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies instance-level versus corpus-level F1 terminology, expands the training explanation, simplifies the substring-frequency exposition, and adjusts abstract and conclusion wording. Existing sections largely retain their organization and prose; much of the appendix growth is new scientific content rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-pipeline diagram, optimization tables, two algorithm displays, a paraphraser comparison table, expanded correlation examples, and agreement heatmaps. Existing figures are repositioned and relabeled, and training-curve F1 axes change to percentage units. The enlarged training-curve display also overlaps the page-number area.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to mean-field reinforcement learning, generalized advantage estimation, recurrent neural network grammars, and ensemble distillation, while removing the StructFormer reference. It qualifies positioning around non-ensemble parsing; the main related-work discussion and relationship to Chen et al. remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds formal sampling distributions, value and advantage functions, dynamic-programming recurrences, and alternative optimization objectives. The stated TreeCRF distribution also changes from a sum of span posteriors in v1 Equation 4 to a product in v2 Equation 11. The original span-posterior proof survives as Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important gaps in v1: dependence on one paraphraser and limited evidence for the chosen optimization strategy. Tables 5–6 provide direct alternative-strategy and paraphraser-quality comparisons, while procedural detail, code-access information, and narrower performance claims improve assessability. Some weaknesses remain: ensemble benefits are only inferred, and the claimed 9-point robustness gain is 8.05 points in Table 6. These limited issues do not outweigh the stronger validation of central design choices.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SemInfo constituency-parsing research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds optimization comparisons, paraphraser robustness experiments, and parser-agreement analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on five PCFG variants across four languages, correlation analyses, and constituent-type recall results.

results.title: Improving Unsupervised Constituency Parsing via Maximizing Semantic Information

C1.justification: Both versions claim the same four contributions: the long short-term world model, zoom-based affordance generation, affordance-driven rewards, and mixed-imagination behavior learning. The central MineDojo performance claim remains. The abstract's added emphasis on long-horizon payoffs does not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v1's broad complexity and generalization caveats become concrete restrictions involving fixed viewpoints, 2D environments, and objectives beyond approaching objects. v2 also explains dependence on MineCLIP, possible failures on unfamiliar scenarios, stochastic jumping's learning rationale, and the observed evolution of jumping behavior (Appendices C.5–C.6 and D.2–D.4).

D1.justification: v2 substantially clarifies transition-data construction and intrinsic-reward matching for interval labels, discloses stochastic jumping probabilities and Gaussian parameters, and reports approximately 23 GB VRAM and 1.7 days on an RTX 3090. It also adds an explicit source-code address in a reproducibility statement.

E1.justification: The original five MineDojo tasks remain. v2 adds a stone-pickaxe crafting task involving seven subgoals and qualitative invisible or occluded-target scenarios, including village exploration (Appendices D.4–D.5). These substantially extend task requirements and tested observation conditions.

E2.justification: Director and PTGM are newly evaluated alongside DreamerV3, VPT, and STEVE-1 on the five retained tasks (Figures 4–5 and Table 3). This materially expands the comparator set, particularly its coverage of hierarchical approaches; Director's earlier citation did not constitute an empirical comparison.

E3.justification: The retained five-task budgets, input resolution, and episode limits remain unchanged. The new crafting evaluation specifies one million training steps per subtask and a 1,000-step testing limit under DECKARD planning. Appendix D.6 also adds a three-setting Gaussian-parameter sweep.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of jumping frequency, predicted transition intervals, and dynamic thresholds; occluded-target affordance case studies; and Gaussian reward sensitivity. Existing component ablations, series-versus-parallel comparisons, and the two earlier sensitivity analyses remain. The additions substantially broaden evidence about mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: The retained loss-scale and intrinsic-reward-weight sensitivity plots acquire shaded bands in v2 Figure 15; their v1 Figure 7 counterparts showed lines alone. Neither version explains these bands or supplies repeated-run or seed counts, so this establishes expanded uncertainty display without establishing additional runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds Director/PTGM results, crafting-subgoal outcomes, and jumping-dynamics findings. Figure 14 reports stone-pickaxe success rates of 69% for LS-Imagine and 32% for DreamerV3, with 684 and 923 steps respectively. The retained loss-scale and reward-weight sensitivity trajectories also change between v1 Figure 7 and v2 Figure 15.

M1.justification: The core architecture, losses, and mixed-imagination learning remain. Appendix D.5 adds a DECKARD planning layer for executing crafting subtasks, a limited procedural adaptation. Appendix C.5 presents the 0.7/0.3 stochastic jumping rule as a clarification; its disclosure does not establish an implementation change.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites notation and data-collection explanations, reorganizes experimental subsections, moves comparator descriptions and sensitivity discussion into the appendix, and regroups the appendices into expanded model-details and results sections. It also adds explanatory footnotes and ethics/reproducibility statements.

P2.justification: v2 adds a numerical comparison table, a series/parallel schematic, training-dynamics plots, occlusion examples, crafting results, and Gaussian visualizations. Baseline legends and sensitivity displays expand, while the original combined ablation/sensitivity figure is split. The complete imagination gallery is retained as Figure 12, formerly Figure 10.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated hierarchical-methods discussion and citations covering Dr. Strategy, PTGM, affordance navigation, STORM, and diffusion world modeling. Director and Gumbsch's hierarchical world models were already cited in v1. These additions refine the retained visual-MBRL and affordance positioning.

T1.justification: The jump-score formulas, world-model losses, and modified lambda-return retain their mathematical substance. Revised indexing and explicit interval-annotation and discounted-reward expressions clarify previously described operations. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: v1 relied on five fixed-objective tasks and omitted relevant hierarchical comparators. v2 adds Director/PTGM and a planning-assisted crafting evaluation, while making important training mechanics and applicability limits substantially clearer. These changes strengthen empirical assessment and reproducibility. The crafting results depend on an external planner, and uncertainty bands still lack definitions and run counts, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LS-Imagine and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original MineDojo experiments and adds baseline comparisons, crafting-task results, and analyses of jumping behavior and affordance maps.

before.justification: v1 reports original MineDojo performance comparisons, component ablations, sensitivity experiments, and qualitative imagination results.

results.title: Open-World Reinforcement Learning over Long Short-Term Imagination

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims: up to 10× faster SNF training, preserved generalization at moderate scaling, richer high-frequency representations and better conditioning. The added experiments support these existing contributions without redefining their central novelty.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the previously open question about other architectures with specific applicability boundaries: GaussNet and Sinc NF can fit faster while generalization worsens, and WIRE can deteriorate. It adds interpretations concerning Hessian outliers, learning-rate-dependent scale selection and extended-training generalization. The PDE discussion acknowledges unavailable ground truth beyond the initial time.

D1.justification: New Appendices F.1–F.3 disclose tuning grids and layerwise learning-rate compensation for existing analyses. Further additions document baseline settings, NeRF network sizes and codebase, and scheduled long-training learning rates. Conversely, v1's reproducibility statement promising public code is removed without replacement project-code access instructions.

E1.justification: v2 adds novel-view synthesis on NeRF-synthetic Lego and Drums, plus Gaussian-pulse wave-equation reconstruction and temporal extrapolation from initial observations (Appendices F.6–F.7). The original image, occupancy, spherical, audio and neural-dataset tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from seven to nine baselines by adding MFN and Sinc NF across the original domains. These methods also enter the qualitative comparisons, while Xavier panels disappear from the image, audio and spherical examples despite its retained quantitative row. MFN additionally enters the replacement long-training comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include two NeRF resolutions with 300/600-epoch budgets, a 40,000-step PDE experiment, and batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. The earlier longer-training comparison is replaced by a scheduled 5,000-step Kodak study. The stated spherical-data learning rate changes from 1e-4 to 1e-5; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained spectral, gradient-decoupling and conditioning analyses, v2 adds Hessian eigenspectrum snapshots, mini-batch sensitivity, scaling tests with other activations, and learning-rate dependence of the optimal scale (Figures 11 and 13–15). The earlier multi-domain continuation analysis is replaced by substantially longer Kodak train/test curves in Figure 23.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting for the principal data-fitting experiments. Added Table 1 baseline rows follow this practice. No changed run count, new confidence-interval procedure or significance test is documented.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 entries and Table 3 remain unchanged, but v2 adds baseline scores, diagnostic curves and new task outcomes. Examples include 28.17 dB for WS on 800×800 Lego after 300 epochs and initial-time PDE MSE of 2.8e-5. v1's longer-budget Table 4 is removed; the replacement Kodak study reports peak test PSNR of 37.45 dB under its different training protocol.

M1.justification: The initialization rule in Eq. (3), including leaving output-layer weights unscaled, remains unchanged. The new NeRF application introduces a limited adaptation: WS applies only to the volume-density network, leaving the color network outside the scaling procedure (Appendix F.6).

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely intact. Changes include targeted related-work and conclusion rewrites, publication-header and affiliation updates, acknowledgments, theorem renumbering, and reorganized appendices. Most expansion consists of new scientific material rather than extensive rewriting of retained content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces target-PSNR training-step bars with multi-method learning curves. Table 1 gains baseline rows, qualitative grids are rearranged, and new Hessian, sensitivity, NeRF and PDE displays are added. The earlier long-training table disappears, while a NeRF table and extended train/test plots provide different comparisons.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of sinusoidal activations beyond neural fields, including generative models, low-rank learning and compression. The new kernel and Hessian analyses substantially expand connections to Gaussian kernels, spectral conditioning and periodically activated networks. MFN and Sinc NF also broaden the comparison-related literature; the central training-efficiency positioning remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.3 develops a two-layer eNTK decomposition and conditional Gaussian-kernel/eigenvalue arguments relating scaling to conditioning (Eqs. 52–56), incorporating an explicitly attributed theorem. Appendix B.1 also restores omitted W^(3) factors in Eqs. (31)–(32). The original distribution-preservation and harmonic results otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central speed/generalization claim through additional baselines, mini-batch and learning-rate tests, training-to-saturation curves and held-out-view evaluation. Newly disclosed tuning procedures also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of the earlier multi-domain long-training table and code-release promise. The new theoretical argument remains conditional, and PDE extrapolation lacks later-time ground-truth validation, so those additions provide more limited support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core initialization rule and retained experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial appendix expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline evaluations, sensitivity analyses, novel-view synthesis experiments and wave-equation reconstruction results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments across several modalities, optimization analyses, and neural-dataset construction and classification results in Tables 1 and 3.

results.title: Fast Training of Sinusoidal Neural Fields via Scaling Initialization

C1.justification: The central unified-forecasting and TimeAttention contributions remain. The introduction adds an explicit claim of outperforming advanced zero-shot models at comparable model and pre-training scales, while the abstract recasts Timer-XL as a promising foundation-model architecture.

C2.justification: Section E.4 adds explanations involving selective attention versus attention to noisy context and mismatched normalization statistics during autoregression. The earlier inference that decoder-only models better accommodate the embeddings, based on the Moirai comparison, is removed. The limitations paragraph is retained.

D1.justification: Table 10 adds LOTSA training hyperparameters and Moirai configurations, Section E.2 identifies checkpoint-based evaluation, and Table 12 provides a model-checkpoint access link. Section 3.2 clarifies per-head variable biases. Existing implementation documentation largely remains, and the LOTSA training duration is unspecified.

E1.justification: Sections 4.4 and E.2 add LOTSA as a substantial pre-training collection alongside UTSD and ERA5-Large, including aggregated UTSD+LOTSA training. Downstream task families remain stable; the additional ETT result blocks concern datasets already listed in v2 Table 8.

E2.justification: Zero-shot comparisons expand beyond Timer to Moirai variants, TimesFM, MOMENT, Chronos and Time-MoE. DLinear joins Figure 3 and UniTST joins Figure 4. Tables 2–4 and 11 also reassign the former Moirai entries to UniTST while retaining their matched scores; the PDFs do not explain whether these were recomputed.

E3.justification: v3 adds LOTSA training configurations and a multi-horizon zero-shot protocol using official checkpoints, each model's maximum input length, and exclusions for pre-training overlap. Additional protocols include ERA5 one-day forecasting across daily-to-yearly lookbacks and 672-to-96 normalization comparisons. Existing supervised splits and settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine prediction quality through showcases (Figures 9–10), encoder-versus-decoder attention behavior (Figure 11), ERA5 context-length sensitivity (Table 14), and normalization dependence on three conventional benchmarks (Table 15). The original embedding ablation is retained as Table 13, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same three-random-seed standard deviations in Table 9. v3 introduces no additional uncertainty-estimation practice, significance testing or repeated-run disclosure.

E6.justification: Tables 6 and 12 add extensive zero-shot results, Table 11 adds three ETT result blocks, and Tables 14–15 add context and normalization findings. Figure 3 revises plotted results; Figure 4 adds UniTST temperature/wind MSEs of 7.356/3.807 against unchanged Timer-XL values of 7.172/3.786. Matched numerical entries in Tables 1–5 and the relocated embedding ablation remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The multivariate next-token objective, TimeAttention mask, positional embeddings and forecasting procedure remain unchanged. Clarifying that variable-bias scalars operate per attention head does not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and several method explanations receive localized rewrites. The embedding-ablation discussion moves to Appendix E.3, and supplementary material gains showcases and thematic subsections. The main section sequence and much existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 9–12 and new zero-shot, context-length and normalization tables; expands Tables 10–11; and redraws Figures 3–4 with additional comparators. The original Table 6 moves to Table 13, substantially reorganizing the presentation of experimental evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to MOMENT, Time-MoE and Deep Sets, removes the Touvron et al. 2021 citation, and shifts the discussion of prior multivariate encoder modeling from Moirai to UniTST. The overall related-work framework remains stable.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Appendix A complexity derivations are retained. Permutation-equivariance terminology clarifies the input/output reordering behavior already described in v2; no new mathematical result or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2's zero-shot evidence mainly compared Timer-XL with its predecessor. v3 addresses this important gap with broader foundation-model comparisons and adds context-length, linear-baseline and normalization controls, substantially strengthening evidence for its central claims. Unexplained Moirai-to-UniTST reassignment and inconsistent ECL entries between Tables 6 and 12 weaken reporting reliability, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Timer-XL. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds zero-shot comparisons, forecasting case studies and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting experiments, pre-training evaluations, ablations and efficiency measurements.

results.title: Timer-XL: Long-Context Transformers for Unified Time Series Forecasting

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: posterior sampling for text-guided editing, an inversion-free and training-free procedure, leading editing alignment, and approximately 1.5-second execution using 18 GB. The added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges limited background consistency and narrows the best-MSE statement to methods running below two seconds. It also explains parameter tradeoffs and states that the Fourier-based measurement improves reconstruction but edits poorly. These qualify the retained interpretation without changing the central mechanism explanation.

D1.justification: Existing hardware, checkpoint and noise-schedule information largely remains. v2 specifies 100 inner optimization steps, clarifies sampler roles and measurement usage, and provides the GPT4-o instruction-conversion template in Figure 18. Conversely, v1's code-availability statement and repository link disappear; this establishes lost access information, not repository unavailability.

E1.justification: PIE-Bench editing/reconstruction and the FFHQ-based layout analysis remain. v2 adds evaluation with paragraph-length source and target descriptions (Appendix A.6, Figures 8–11), extending the input scenario beyond v1's displayed short prompts. No additional named benchmark is introduced.

E2.justification: The editing comparison expands from seven baselines to twelve by adding SPD, GR, IP2P, OmniGen and SeedX (v1 Table 1 versus v2 Table 2). Figure 19 also includes GR and SPD in reconstruction comparisons, where they were previously absent. The original editing baselines remain, with some qualitative columns redistributed between figures.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 34-person preference-ranking evaluation and GPT4-o conversion of source/target descriptions for instruction-based comparators. The stated usual weight changes from 0.05 to 0.1, the hard-case weight from 0.1 to 0.2, and the fixed step size becomes scheduled. Figure 19 introduces a separate 10,000-step, approximately 15-second reconstruction setting. These reported changes do not establish that retained benchmark scores were rerun.

E4.justification: The original qualitative component ablations gain quantitative results in Table 5. New analyses examine mask probability, optimization steps and mixing weight (Table 4), compare reconstruction measurement operators (Table 6/Figure 14), visualize editing trajectories (Figure 13), and test high-frequency reconstruction (Figure 19). Long-text examples add a further input-sensitivity test.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new user-study participant count and raw preference votes add evaluation and results, without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All shared editing-table entries remain numerically unchanged, including PostEdit's CLIP scores of 26.76/24.14. v2 adds reconstruction scores, including PostEdit PSNR 24.39, plus sensitivity, ablation, measurement-comparison and preference results. The added SPD row reports background MSE 2.33 versus PostEdit's retained 3.24, in the displayed scaled units. Some supplementary editing examples are replaced, and the new Figure 19 results use a separate computation budget.

M1.justification: The posterior-sampling, LCM and measurement-based framework remains. However, v2 replaces v1's explicitly fixed optimization step size with an iteration-dependent schedule (Appendix A.2, Eq. 20). Algorithms 1–2 also correct the stated sampling flow, including removing Algorithm 1's premature return and moving reconstruction denoising outside the inner optimization loop. These are localized procedural revisions.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain. Introduction, method and comparison passages receive localized rewrites, and reconstruction/editing discussions gain clearer subdivisions. The appendix is reorganized, notably moving its former opening CFG, reconstruction-algorithm and proof sections to A.14–A.16. Conference headers and author-contact presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, expands the editing table, adds seven tables, reorganizes qualitative comparison columns and adds long-text, trajectory, measurement and high-frequency panels. The original supplementary editing grid in Figure 9 is removed. Retained displays are also relocated: v1's reconstruction Figure 10 becomes Figure 15, and its speed Figure 8 becomes Figure 17.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.1 substantially expands related work beyond the introduction, discussing textual/model-space optimization, exact inversion, instruction editing, inpainting and customization. Added works include EDICT, DreamBooth, Imagic and SmartBrush, alongside references supporting the new baselines and measurement discussion. This broadens research positioning substantially.

T1.justification: Equation 16 and the algorithms correct the mathematical update by applying a gradient to the loss terms, which v1 directly subtracts as scalar expressions. Propositions 1–2, the CFG derivation and the proof of Proposition 2 otherwise remain substantively unchanged, with the appendix derivations relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of reconstruction and the method's design choices: v1 largely supported these with qualitative examples, while v2 adds quantitative reconstruction, component ablations, sensitivity tests and measurement comparisons, alongside broader baselines. More explicit limitations improve interpretation of the tradeoffs. The user-study protocol remains brief, uncertainty reporting is absent, and removal of the code link weakens access documentation. Nevertheless, the new evidence resolves important validation gaps and produces a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PostEdit research, with matching authors, core framework and experiments. The complete main texts and appendices, including image-based figures and equations, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds quantitative reconstruction, sensitivity and ablation results, additional qualitative experiments and a 34-participant user study.

before.justification: v1 reports original PIE-Bench editing scores, reconstruction examples, component ablations and model-layout analyses.

results.title: PostEdit: Posterior Sampling for Efficient Zero-Shot Image Editing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the principal clustering claim from planar pushing to both discrete and continuous image-based control. V3 explicitly claims clustering by natural action labels in Lunar Lander and by control-oriented classes in pushing and stacking. The existing claim of improved low-data performance through NC pretraining is retained.

C2.justification: Appendix D substantially expands the interpretation of pretrained representations: ImageNet initialization benefits finetuning in visually complex scenes but shows little benefit on clean pushing, while frozen features remain inadequate. V3 also explicitly identifies ground-truth pose requirements as a scaling limitation for multiple or deformable objects and clarifies that extra pose information is unnecessary at test time.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly specifies the NC loss as 0.1 × CDNV + 10 × (STDNorm + STDAngle), four shuffled batches per pretraining epoch, and 50 pretraining plus 50 joint-training epochs versus 100 baseline epochs. These clarify previously underspecified experiments. Appendix A adds Lunar Lander architecture and expert-generation details, and the stacking section identifies the core stack_d0 dataset.

E1.justification: V1 studies a state-based double integrator and simulated and real planar pushing. V3 adds image-based Lunar Lander and MimicGen block stacking, substantially broadening task coverage. It also introduces simulated pushing with a LineMod background and real pushing with distracting objects and paintings, extending visual-environment coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds frozen versus finetuned and ImageNet-pretrained versus randomly initialized ResNet comparisons in Table 2. Table 3 introduces a DINOv2 baseline within the NC-pretraining comparison, although DINOv2 already appeared in v1's architecture experiments. These extend comparisons within existing model families; the original comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include Lunar Lander behavior cloning from 500 PPO demonstrations using four input frames and 600 training epochs, and block stacking with 1,000 demonstrations and 107,590 samples. The added complex-background robot experiment uses 200 demonstrations and 10 test tasks. Table 2 introduces initialization and freezing controls. These are added experimental designs; Appendix F's schedules for existing Table 1 experiments are newly disclosed details.

E4.justification: V3 adds analyses isolating ImageNet initialization and encoder finetuning, tests clustering and pretraining under complex visual backgrounds, and checks NC pretraining with DINOv2 (Appendices D, G.1, G.6 and Section 5). V1's k-means, REPO-granularity, LSTM, low-data, and continual-finetuning analyses remain present, often relocated.

E5.justification: The shared diffusion-model experiments retain means and standard-deviation bands over three random seeds, while LSTM results remain single-seed. V3 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or explicit repetition scheme. Additional tables and curves do not establish a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original clean-background robot success counts are unchanged. V3 adds clustering curves for Lunar Lander, stacking, and complex-background pushing; initialization results in Table 2; and DINOv2 pretraining results in Table 3, including 0.3747 versus 0.4602 on O. The new complex-background robot experiment reports 9/10 successes with NC pretraining versus 6/10 for baseline using 200 demonstrations. These are additional conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: V3 adds a discrete image-control instantiation using ResNet18, an MLP projection and action decoder, and cross-entropy supervision over four actions (Section 2, Appendix A). The continuous-control REPO classification and NC-pretraining procedure remain unchanged. Appendix F's explicit loss weights document the existing procedure rather than establish a revised loss.

P1.justification: V3 rewrites the abstract around discrete and continuous control, expands the introductory motivation, and reorganizes the central exposition into separate discrete- and continuous-control sections. Action-based classification and continual-finetuning discussion move into dedicated appendices, while the conclusion gains an explicit limitations paragraph. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is extensively redesigned to show three tasks, and the classification diagrams are revised and expanded. V1 Figure 5 is split between v3 Figures 6 and 21, while continual-learning figures move to the appendix. V3 adds new task plots, Tables 2 and 3, and complex-background robot montages; Figure 10 now juxtaposes clean and complex scenes.
