R1.justification: V3 adds references supporting Gym, MimicGen, LineMod, PPO, RL Baselines3 Zoo, and MuJoCo, and removes the Huh et al. representation-hypothesis citation. The related-work discussion is otherwise retained from v1 Appendix D as v3 Appendix I, with no substantial change in positioning against neural-collapse or imitation-learning research.

T1.justification: The double-integrator policy, neural-collapse definitions, CDNV and norm/angular metrics, and REPO construction retain their mathematical substance. Equations are relocated and renumbered. Neither version provides a formal proof of control-oriented clustering, and v3 adds no theorem or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v1's narrow empirical foundation through additional control tasks, visually complex environments, and initialization/freezing controls. Appendix F resolves important omissions in documenting the central pretraining procedure, while the explicit pose-annotation limitation improves scope calibration. Together these improve evidential support, interpretation, and reproducibility. Pretraining benefits remain demonstrated principally on pushing, and robot evaluations remain small, but these limits do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds experiments on Lunar Lander, block stacking, encoder initialization, DINOv2 pretraining, and visually complex pushing environments.

before.justification: V1 reports original behavior-cloning simulations, neural-collapse measurements, pretraining comparisons in Table 1, and robotic pushing experiments in Section 5 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract, RQ3 discussion, and conclusion replace the claim of identifying exogenous variables with the narrower claim that accuracy may fail to capture potential overoptimization. C2.justification: v3 gives a more specific explanation for why PPO favors evaluation on higher-ranked responses, clarifies diminishing benefits under annotation constraints, and adds interpretations of KL sensitivity and sample-size saturation. These extend the existing interpretation while retaining the central Goodhart-based account and qualifying its causal implications.

D1.justification: Appendix 8.10 and Table 8 newly disclose RM/PPO learning rates, batch sizes, sequence limits, regularization, scheduling, OpenRLHF use, BoN N = 1280, computational scale, and the base-2 KL calculation. Section 2 also clarifies relationships among corrupted training labels. These substantially improve documentation; they do not by themselves establish changes to previously used settings.

E1.justification: Appendix 8.4 adds GPT-4o-scored MT-Bench evaluation of downstream policies selected using open-source RMs, extending validation beyond synthetic RewardBench-based regret. MTBench-human already supplied preference-training data in v1; its earlier presence does not constitute this downstream evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains Mistral-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B, and Vicuna-7b. Table 4 retains the same reward-error metrics and Accuracy-pair baseline. The added architecture and downstream-model studies vary experimental configurations rather than introduce competing evaluation methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include Qwen2.5 reward models spanning 0.5–72B parameters, cumulative training-data subsets, Best-of-32 MT-Bench evaluation, a PPO KL-penalty sweep, sample budgets up to 10,000, and a Qwen2.5-7B downstream policy. Figures 6–7 also change the reported response-count sweep from 2–12 to 2–10. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained main experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices 8.3–8.7 add golden/proxy-pair symmetry diagnostics, architecture and training-data sensitivity, KL-penalty sensitivity, larger-sample saturation tests, and validation of response expansion with another downstream model. These substantially extend the robustness questions investigated in v1.

E5.justification: v1 already displays uncertainty bands and ± values. Appendix 8.10 newly specifies 64 test-set samplings, mean/variance reporting for Tables 2–4, and 95% confidence intervals for Figures 5–7; Figure 13 also reports p = 0.001. This documents uncertainty procedures without establishing an increase in training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical values, while Figures 4, 6, and 7 revise plotted results. New Figure 12 reports Spearman correlations of 0.8645 for model scaling and 0.458 for training-data subsets; Figure 13 reports 0.635 for RewardBench versus MT-Bench. Further results cover KL sensitivity, sample-size saturation, and another downstream model. These are additional or revised results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The synthetic golden/proxy RM framework, preference-training objective, BoN/PPO optimization, NDR calculation, and response-expansion strategy remain unchanged. Additional model configurations and implementation disclosures do not establish a revision to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Broad paragraph-level rewriting affects the abstract, introduction's research questions, experimental explanations in Sections 3–5, and conclusion. The expanded appendix places retained metric definitions and theoretical material in Sections 8.8–8.9 instead of 8.3–8.4. The main three-question narrative remains recognizable despite substantial prose revision.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 10–15 and Tables 7–8. Existing displays also change: Figure 3 gains fitted lines, uncertainty bands, and correlation annotations; Figure 4 gains explicit rank-bin axis labels; Figures 6–7 change their displayed ranges; and Figure 9 adds accuracy values to its legends. Several retained tables and figures are relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to ChatGLM-RLHF, OpenRLHF, Qwen2.5, RMB, and reward-model robustness for mathematical reasoning, and removes the Voorhees–Tice reference. It also connects the formal regret definition to existing MDP work. The overall positioning within reward evaluation and Goodhart-related research remains stable.

T1.justification: v3 adds a KL-constrained normalized definition of policy regret in Equation 2 and explicitly defines the overoptimization ratio, extending its derivation in Appendix 8.9. The Gaussian assumptions and final parametric relationship from v1 remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's narrow synthetic validation and sparse reproducibility reporting through model/data variation studies, MT-Bench evaluation, additional sensitivity tests, and explicit statistical and training details. These strengthen the evidence and make the experiments more auditable. Reporting limitations remain: the open-source RM roster is unspecified, and Table 7's zero-KL Spearman correlation of 0.4840 differs without explanation from Table 1's 0.6102. These limitations constrain particular comparisons but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-model evaluation study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds model/data variation studies, MT-Bench evaluation, and further sensitivity analyses in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original BoN and PPO experiments, response-distribution and annotation-budget analyses, and overoptimization curves in Tables 1–4 and Figures 3–9.

results.title: Rethinking Reward Model Evaluation: Are We Barking up the Wrong Tree?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and closing discussion retain the same central contributions: random-matrix analysis of diffusion spectra, experimental investigation of those spectra, three geometric phases, and an explanation of resistance to manifold overfitting. Additional validation does not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: v1 describes CIFAR10 and CelebA spectra as difficult to interpret; v4 Section 8 explicitly interprets their three phases and proposes explanations involving pixelation and correlations among latent variances. Appendix D adds curvature-scale conditions for applying linear intuition and discusses delayed nonlinear gap development. Appendix C newly attributes obscuring spectral slopes to perturbation sampling, while Section 5.4 expands the manifold-overfitting mechanism.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies use of the full available image datasets and 200,000 synthetic training examples. Appendix C documents normalization by the largest singular value and usual removal of the first singular value, alongside the revised algorithms. These disclosures improve reproducibility; the training-configuration table, training budgets, and V100 hardware information are retained.

E1.justification: v4 adds a controlled curved-manifold scenario using ellipsoidal synthetic data generated as y = F(z/||z||), evaluated in Appendix D and Figure 10. Existing linear-manifold datasets and MNIST, CIFAR10, and CelebA remain.

E2.justification: v4 Figure 9 adds a direct comparison between the standard Stanczuk et al. (2022) estimator and the orthogonalized estimator on CelebA and MNIST. v1 adopts the standard procedure but does not report this comparison. The analytical-versus-learned spectral comparison is retained.

E3.justification: Learned-model spectral evaluation changes from K random probes to d orthogonalized probes. Natural-image evaluation adds diffusion times through t = 200. The uniform-variance experiment changes from time-dependent spectra to a sweep over the number of variance groups, with equal column fractions and a caption-reported interval of [10^-2, 1] instead of [10^-3, 1]. Together these substantially revise the measurement and evaluation design; Table 1 training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds controls testing whether probe geometry obscures gaps (Figure 9), sensitivity to the number of variance groups (Figure 3, right), transfer to a curved synthetic manifold (Figure 10), and consistency across individual images (Figures 11–13). These substantially expand validation beyond v1's variance-swapping and theory-versus-network analyses.

E5.justification: v1 Section 8 explicitly describes averaging image spectra over 100 images; v4 removes that aggregation disclosure and separately reports individual-image spectra. This changes statistical reporting without establishing that the main-figure aggregation procedure actually changed. Both retain 100 matrix realizations for the random-matrix simulations and provide no confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The learned spectral curves in v1 Figures 5–7 are replaced by substantially different profiles in v4 Figures 3–5, with flatter leading portions and clearer gaps under the revised estimator. New results show estimator-dependent distortions, smoothing as variance groups increase, and broadly similar nonlinear-manifold behavior with delayed gap development. Individual-image results are also added. These are revised and additional measurements, not same-setting generative-performance gains.

M1.justification: Appendix C modifies the spectral estimator: independent Gaussian probes become d orthogonalized perturbations, and the central-difference algorithm revises its negative-perturbation construction. This changes an analysis component; the diffusion architectures, training objectives, and underlying generative procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most exposition and the main section sequence are retained. Targeted revisions move the manifold-overfitting discussion from Section 2.1 to an expanded Section 5.4, rewrite Section 8 as a phase-by-phase account, introduce 'stable latent set' terminology, and correct language and publication headers.

P2.justification: v4 combines the existing introductory illustrations from v1 Figures 1–2 into one multipart figure and relocates the single-variance display from v1 Figure 3 to appendix Figure 7. Empirical plots are redrawn with changed legends, additional curves, and an MNIST inset; new Figures 9–13 present comparisons and supplementary analyses. Table 1 remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds Goldt et al. (2020) and frames the data model through their hidden-manifold formulation. It also positions the orthogonalized estimator as an improvement over Stanczuk et al. (2022). Most other reference edits correct author names or bibliographic presentation rather than introduce new works.

T1.justification: v4 introduces the nonlinear hidden-manifold definition y = Phi(Fz) in Section 2 and Appendix D, extending the stated modeling framework beyond its linear special case. The spectral-gap formulas and replica derivations in Section 6 and Appendix A are retained. Appendix D supplies a heuristic applicability argument rather than a new nonlinear theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the central empirical validation. Its estimator comparison directly investigates distortions affecting v1's spectra, and the revised estimator produces closer analytical-versus-learned agreement in Figure 4. The curved-manifold and individual-image checks further support the proposed geometric interpretation beyond the original linear experiments and aggregate displays. Nonlinear applicability remains heuristic, and the missing averaging disclosure reduces reporting clarity, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, training table, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains original simulations and trained-model experiments and adds estimator comparisons, a nonlinear synthetic-manifold experiment, and individual-image analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original random-matrix simulations and experiments measuring trained diffusion-model spectra on synthetic linear data, MNIST, CIFAR10, and CelebA.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow the achievement from 162 theorems previously unproved by humans to 155 previously unproved formally, with seven exploits identified separately. V7 also moderates several case-study interpretations and removes the claimed human-proof-length advantage.

D1.justification: New Table 9 documents theorem and premise totals, including dependencies, for each repository. Appendix A.2 clarifies that the reported 4-to-9-day runtime applies to the Table 10 experiments. Hardware, optimization settings, repository commits, and core implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 23 repositories, curricula, and alternate PFR commit. The added MiniF2F test-set experiment changes the split and protocol within existing coverage. ProofNet and PutnamBench were not evaluated in v1, so deleting their exclusion discussion does not remove coverage.

E2.justification: ReProver and the same seven lifelong-learning variants remain the evaluated comparators. V7 also uses ReProver for its new MiniF2F protocol. TheoremLlama and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 scores are discussed as external context with comparability qualifications; Aesop is explicitly not evaluated.

V7 also adds a separate 244-theorem MiniF2F test evaluation using Pass@1 and explicitly excludes Test.lean from progressive training, while retaining the earlier combined-split experiment.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 extends the existing PFR case analysis by diagnosing two reflexivity proofs as artifacts of an unfinished multiDist definition. V7 also removes the one-line versus 175-line human-proof comparison for Wedderburn. The seven-variant ablations and most proof case studies remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or uncertainty estimates for the experiments. Both retain the same informal 3% threshold for calling an improvement significant; v7 adds no statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: The headline 162 proofs becomes 155 proofs plus seven exploits, a reclassification rather than demonstrated performance deterioration. TPPS scores and improvement ratios are replaced by proof counts and stage breakdowns. V7 adds separate MiniF2F test results of 38.1% (93/244) for LeanAgent versus 34.0% (83/244) for ReProver; the earlier 99-versus-85 result and lifelong-learning ablation scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proof-length curriculum, dynamic database, single-epoch progressive retriever training, and best-first proof search remain unchanged. Section 3.3 clarifies embedding refreshes before validation without establishing a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The overall section structure is retained. V7 revises headline wording and case-study language, clarifies embedding updates, corrects 'Matrix Workshop' to 'Math Workshop,' and moves TPPS exposition into the expanded Appendix A.7. Most methodology and lifelong-learning analysis prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 2 is substantially redesigned from two TPPS columns into proof totals and learning-stage breakdowns, and a repository-statistics table is added. Figure 2 is rearranged and removes the PFR reflexivity example, which remains in Appendix A.5. Numerous appendix proof images are resized and repaginated without changing their contents; Table 4 gains metric-direction arrows.

R1.justification: V7 adds the TheoremLlama reference and removes the ProofNet and PutnamBench references alongside their exclusion rationale. Added discussion positions LeanAgent relative to TheoremLlama, DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5, and Aesop, emphasizing lifelong learning and limits on direct comparisons. The broader related-work account remains intact.

The displayed proof scripts, complexity measure, EWC objective, and TPPS formula otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V7 substantially improves the credibility of the empirical claims by withdrawing the weighted '11 times' headline, separating seven exploits from the claimed proof total, explaining evaluation limitations, and adding a held-out MiniF2F comparison. These changes address central weaknesses in v1's evidence and interpretation. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 2 includes two acknowledged exploits and contradicts Appendix A.5 about Coxeter's learning-stage timing, but these issues do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LeanAgent, with matching methods, repositories, and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including the added Appendix A.7 in v7.

after.justification: V7 retains these original experiments and additionally reports a Lean4 MiniF2F test-set evaluation of LeanAgent and ReProver in Appendix A.5.

before.justification: V1 reports original theorem-proving experiments across 23 Lean repositories, lifelong-learning measurements, seven-variant ablations, and generated proof examples.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the central claims that representation alignment improves diffusion-transformer training and generation, including the greater-than-17.5× speedup and FID 1.42 headline results. Appendix J adds a four-metric superiority interpretation, although Table 11 shows tied precision at 100 epochs and worse sFID and precision at 200 epochs.

Figure 11 extends the training-convergence analysis to CFG. These supplement the retained ablations without replacing their central questions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

P1.justification: v2 shortens Section 5, relocates part of its discussion to Appendix I, adds appendix sections and cross-references, and makes localized caption and prose edits. Figure 10's mistaken SiT identification is corrected to DiT. Most of the main narrative remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with encoder-provenance and new benchmark tables, a CFG convergence plot, higher-resolution samples, paired text-to-image examples and PCA maps (Tables 6, 11–12; Figures 11, 36–38). Table 2 and Figure 5 gain SigLIP entries. Existing appendix image galleries are preserved and renumbered.

R1.justification: References are added for SigLIP, MS-COCO and the new text-to-image comparators. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical generality beyond v1's single-resolution, class-conditioned ImageNet setting, especially through matched MMDiT comparisons on MS-COCO. Higher-resolution validation, repaired configuration inconsistencies and explicit applicability limits also improve the paper. Appendix J's overbroad four-metric claim is a reporting weakness, but it does not outweigh the substantial gain in validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REPA work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including retained material that is relocated or renumbered.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds results for SigLIP alignment, ImageNet 512×512, MS-COCO text-to-image generation and feature-map analysis.

results.title: Representation Alignment for Generation: Training Diffusion Transformers Is Easier Than You Think

C1.justification: The central claims of jointly trained JPEG quantization, classification gains up to 20.9% and improved adversarial robustness remain. V2 narrows the contribution by removing claims about reducing input-image file sizes from the introduction and conclusion and removing data compression from the contribution list.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations connecting alternative-quantizer results and layer replacement to nonlinear expressiveness, and chroma-subsampling results to DNN reliance on color information. It also discusses learning-rate sensitivity and acknowledges the computational burden of full-space quantization while motivating masking. V1's interpretation that hard quantization preserves accuracy while enabling compression is removed; its foreground/background explanations remain.

D1.justification: The appendix substantially expands implementation information: alternative-baseline optimizer and initialization details, feature-layer quantization configuration, five-point masked-softmax computation, and inference measurement on a single NVIDIA RTX A5000. Masking is newly documented without establishing whether the retained benchmark runs changed implementation. The abstract also changes the stated code repository owner from JpegInspiredDl to AhmedHussKhalifa.

E1.justification: The same six classification datasets and CIFAR-100 adversarial scenarios remain. V2 removes the auxiliary image-compression evaluation reported in v1 Section 5 and Table 4. The new appendix experiments use retained datasets rather than introducing additional dataset or domain coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 6 adds evaluated quantization alternatives from Ballé et al. (2016), Shin and Song (2017), and Esser et al. (2019). Table 8 adds random-quality JPEG augmentation, Gaussian denoising, histogram equalization and Tu et al.'s learnable resizing. These substantially broaden comparison beyond standard training. The standalone hard-quantizer comparison in v1 Table 4 is removed.

E3.justification: Retained benchmark settings remain unchanged, but substantial new evaluation designs are added. These include layer replacement with learning rate 0.001, alpha 2 and b 6; three JPEG quality-factor ranges; three chroma formats; and a 0.003-versus-0.005 learning-rate comparison. Appendix A.12 adds full-versus-masked inference timing and throughput evaluation on ImageNet ResNet-18. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of activation replacement, chroma subsampling, learning-rate sensitivity and masked-quantizer approximation error and computational cost in Appendices A.7–A.9 and A.12. It removes v1's soft-versus-hard quantization/compression ablation. Existing adversarial tests, sensitivity plots, learned quantization tables and feature-map examples are retained, including those moved to A.10–A.11.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over three runs for the main CIFAR-100 and fine-grained results, and explicitly mention different random seeds for EfficientFormer-L1. V2's added accuracy tables follow the same practice. No changed run counts, new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the matched EfficientFormer-L1 results are unchanged. V2 adds extensive results in Tables 6–11, including 72.10% Flowers accuracy for the new layer-replacement configuration and inference times of 5.46, 7.43 and 18.86 milliseconds for baseline, masked and full-space inference, respectively. These are newly reported conditions, not improvements to matched v1 runs. V1 Table 4's hard-quantizer accuracies and compression rates are removed.

M1.justification: The principal input-layer JPEG-DL algorithm, soft quantizer and training objective remain unchanged. Appendix A.7 adds a localized architectural extension: replacing the first ResNet-18 ReLU with feature-space JPEG quantization, without color conversion and with a separate 8×8 quantization table for each output channel.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are retained. V2 locally rewrites the architecture description and gradient explanations, separates the classification-results discussion, removes the compression discussion and adds appendix subsections with updated cross-references. These are focused editorial and organizational changes alongside the scientific additions, rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show the unified architecture and input layer. V2 adds six tables and Figure 13, including a large color-grouped comparison table, while removing v1 Table 4. Existing feature-map and GradCAM displays are enlarged or rearranged, notably Figure 12. V1 Tables 5–6 are retained as v2 Tables 4–5, not newly added results.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the principal positioning against prior JPEG-based learning remain essentially unchanged. Focused appendix additions discuss Ballé et al., Bengio et al., Shin and Song, Tu et al., and Yun et al.; the already-cited Esser et al. additionally becomes an evaluated comparator. These extend the local discussion of quantization alternatives and preprocessing without replacing the paper's overall research positioning.

T1.justification: The original quantizer definitions, objectives and derivative derivations in Equations (1)–(13) remain unchanged. Appendix A.12 newly defines a five-level reconstruction set centered on the uniform-quantizer output and argues for approximating the full distribution by restricting support to this set. This is a limited mathematical addition, without a general approximation-error theorem.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparison against alternative ways to make JPEG differentiable or preprocess images through Tables 6 and 8. The added sensitivity studies and explicit inference-cost measurements also make the method's benefits and practical costs more assessable. Removing the compression study sacrifices an ancillary result, but the corresponding claims are withdrawn. Although the masking justification remains limited, the stronger comparative evidence and computational transparency provide a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JPEG Inspired Deep Learning by the same authors. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original classification and adversarial results and adds experiments on alternative methods, layer replacement, chroma subsampling, learning rates and inference cost in its appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original JPEG-DL classification experiments, adversarial evaluations, compression measurements and visual analyses, including Tables 1–4 and the transformer results in Appendix A.5.

results.title: JPEG Inspired Deep Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction refine the contribution's scope from generic long-range interactions to atomic-range density compression and molecular-range message passing, with an explicit contrast to earlier fixed descriptors. The headline energy-only training, accuracy, and data-efficiency claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of individual component contributions, MD17 interpolation versus extrapolation, and complementarity with Δ-learning. It also explicitly identifies the need for spin information in open-shell systems and qualifies the benefits of physical constraints using the inconclusive Appendix O comparison. These substantially expand the mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code access link, the explicit multi-iteration energy loss, SiLU activation and differentiation details, expanded quadrature/Fock implementation explanations, and disclosure of summation truncation. Appendix N supplies timing hardware and implementation details, including a single NVIDIA A100 and density fitting for hybrid exchange. Existing hyperparameter values are retained.

E1.justification: MD17, 3BPA, and QM9 coverage is retained. Appendix N adds cumulene chains CNH4, with the stated N ranging from 2 to 38, for runtime scaling; the other new analyses reuse existing coverage.

E2.justification: The original comparisons remain, while Table 8 adds SchNet, PaiNN, and NequIP Δ-learning combinations based on learned Dick and EG-XC functionals. Figure 7 adds runtime comparisons against LDA, SCAN, B3LYP, and ωB97X. Table 9 separately introduces an evaluated Dick-versus-Nagai comparison of physical constraints.

E3.justification: Existing accuracy benchmarks retain their splits, metrics, and stated hyperparameters. New protocols include fixed-budget runtime measurements using 15 SCF cycles and 6-31G(d), plus component-removal controls, including replacement of message passing with a node-wise equivariant MLP.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled removal of the mGGA, graph readout, and GNN in Table 3. Appendices L, N, and O additionally investigate complementarity with Δ-learning, runtime scaling, and whether physical constraints improve extrapolation. These address architectural and explanatory questions absent from v1's analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix N newly reports ten repetitions per timing calculation and uses their minimum. This is a new timing aggregation practice, not evidence of increased training runs. Neither version reports seed-based uncertainty or confidence intervals for the accuracy results.

E6.justification: The retained benchmark tables and QM9 heatmap preserve their numerical results. Substantial new outcomes include 300K relative MAE of 7.00 mEh without mGGA versus 0.42 for full EG-XC in Table 3, 0.29 for EG-XC-based Δ-PaiNN in Table 8, mixed Dick/Nagai rankings in Table 9, and the runtime curves in Figure 7.

M1.justification: The four-component EG-XC architecture, readouts, and differentiable SCF training remain unchanged. The explicit loss, activation, and truncation descriptions add implementation information. Appendix L evaluates the Δ-learning combination already suggested in v1 Appendix I.

P1.justification: The abstract and introductory method explanation are rewritten, terminology is refined, and loss and interpretation paragraphs are added. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact; Appendices L–O extend the document without reorganizing its established narrative.

P2.justification: New Tables 3, 8, and 9 and runtime Figure 7 substantially expand the displayed evidence. Existing Figures 1–6 retain their content but are repositioned or resized within the conference layout. The new ablation table incorrectly labels all three dihedral columns β = 120°, obscuring their individual identities.

R1.justification: Section 3 remains essentially unchanged, while the abstract sharpens positioning against semi-local functionals and fixed descriptors. Hendrycks and Gimpel is newly cited; the Gasteiger et al. (2022) reference disappears, leaving unresolved citation markers in Section 4. Nagai et al. (2020) was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Appendix M adds stage-by-stage asymptotic cost analysis with explicit truncation and omitted-precomputation assumptions. Appendix A inserts a missing factor of one-half in the Hartree integral expansion, and Section 5 states the twice-differentiability requirement. The underlying equivariance and SCF mathematical framework is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1: Table 3 tests which architectural components matter, and Appendices M–N substantiate computational-efficiency claims with cost analysis and measurements. Expanded implementation documentation and code access improve reproducibility, while the open-shell limitation and physical-constraints analysis better qualify applicability. These gains substantially strengthen the paper despite localized new defects, especially the repeated dihedral headers and unresolved method citations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EG-XC work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite layout changes and added appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds component ablations, learned-functional Δ-learning experiments, runtime measurements, and a physical-constraints comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of EG-XC and comparison methods on MD17, 3BPA, and QM9, including additional experiments in Appendices H–K.

results.title: Learning Equivariant Non-Local Electron Density Functionals

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: Mamba-based model-based RL, competitive Atari100k performance with a small world model, Mamba-2 advantages, and DFS mitigation of imperfect-model learning. The conclusion also retains its qualification that Drama does not decisively dominate Atari100k.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of applicability and failure. Its DFS discussion attributes advantages to later-stage dynamics and opponent exploitation while acknowledging weaknesses in Breakout and KungFuMaster. Appendix A.7 connects Breakout failures to omitted balls and visual complexity, qualifying the autoencoder explanation as needing further investigation. Appendix A.8 adds the qualification that Mamba-2's training advantage depends on sequence length.

D1.justification: v2 adds training pseudocode, grid-world construction and error-calculation details, implementation attribution, and timing information specifying an NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada Mobile GPU and Transformer KV caching. Existing architecture hyperparameters and losses are retained. The repository URL's capitalization change does not establish a change in resource availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds a synthetic 5-by-5 grid-world trajectory-prediction task requiring geometrically and dynamically consistent token generation (Section 4.2.3). This substantially extends evaluation beyond Atari reinforcement learning. The 26-game Atari100k coverage remains unchanged; expanding its sampling ablation does not itself add a dataset.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's direct Mamba-1 versus Mamba-2 ablation, v2 evaluates standalone GRU and Transformer controls in the grid-world comparison and adds a Transformer control to timing experiments. These broaden the direct backbone comparisons substantially. Table 1 retains its original comparator membership.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 12M-parameter DreamerV3 comparison while retaining the original 200M comparison. New protocols evaluate grid-world sequences of 208 and 1664 tokens using reconstruction error, memory usage, and per-step training time, plus timing sweeps over training and imagination lengths. Existing Atari interaction budgets and documented Drama hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The DFS ablation expands from four games to all 26 Atari100k games. v2 also adds sequence-length comparisons, computational scaling analyses, and reconstructed-frame case studies investigating Breakout failures and differences from Pong. The existing model-size analysis is retained in Appendix A.3, rather than removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report five Atari seeds and use min-max learning-curve bands. v2 additionally reports grid-world errors as mean plus/minus standard deviation in Table 2 and explicitly identifies standard-deviation intervals in Figure 10. It does not establish an increase in repeated runs or specify their count for these new measurements.

E6.justification: Table 1 scores remain unchanged. New comparisons report normalized means of 105 versus 37 for Drama versus DreamerV3XS, and 105 versus 80 for DFS versus uniform sampling; the latter medians are 27 versus 28. Table 2 adds prediction, memory, and timing results, including Transformer out-of-memory at 1664 tokens. The Freeway sampling finding changes from a clear DFS advantage in v1 Figure 2 to scores of 15 for both methods in v2 Table 4. Backbone learning curves and qualitative reconstruction findings also add or revise reported results.

M1.justification: The Mamba-2 dynamics model, discrete VAE, actor-critic procedure, DFS sampling probabilities, and training losses remain unchanged. Clarified notation, explanations of parallel training, and Appendix A.5 pseudocode document the existing procedure rather than introduce a new method.

P1.justification: Most foundational prose remains intact. v2 corrects terminology and notation, clarifies dynamics-model targets, rewrites the experimental overview and sampling discussion, and relocates the model-size subsection to Appendix A.3. It also introduces an editorial defect by duplicating the Experiments heading and introductory paragraph as Sections 3 and 4.

P2.justification: v2 adds grid-world illustrations and results, comparative learning-curve displays, reconstruction montages, and timing plots. The four-game DFS display becomes a full-benchmark appendix figure and table, while existing ablation plots are reformatted or relocated. Figure 6 introduces an incorrect Mamba-1/Mamba-2 legend despite its retained S-versus-XS caption and analysis.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Long Range Arena, DITTO, mamba.py, and Recall to Imagine, including a short discussion of the latter's SSM-based model-based RL. It also corrects the placement of the TWM-style sampling attribution. The broader related-work organization and first-Mamba-agent positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.6 introduces mathematical constraints defining valid grid-world geometry and definitions of geometric and logical prediction errors, whose average forms the new evaluation metric. The existing SSM derivations, DFS formula, and loss equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a similar-size DreamerV3 control and direct measurements supporting computational-efficiency claims. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence through the smaller-model comparison, sequence-length experiments, and timing measurements. Full-benchmark DFS evaluation and reconstruction case studies also improve assessment of effectiveness and failure conditions. Limited setup details for new tests, the unexplained Freeway revision, duplicated Experiments text, and Figure 6's incorrect legend weaken reporting, but the added controls and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Drama research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original Atari100k results and adds smaller-model comparisons, expanded sampling experiments, grid-world prediction results, timing measurements, and reconstruction examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Atari100k results for Drama, learning curves, and ablations of sampling, Mamba backbones, and model size.

results.title: Drama: Mamba-Enabled Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Is Sample and Parameter Efficient

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the online-planning claim from superior FAS to comparable FAS. The introduction adds an explicit claim of outperforming GPM. The central contributions—sequence generation at low decision frequencies, model-based training with model-free control, and FAS—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations for SAC's Swimmer advantage and GPM's weak sequence generalization, plus discussion of delay handling and hardware constraints in Section 2 and Appendix A.3. Future work qualifies infinite-horizon control as near-infinite control in noiseless settings with corrections. Existing modeling-error limitations and latent-space interpretations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an official SRL repository link, and the new comparisons document plan-length choices and selected TempoRL maximum sequence lengths. Existing network sizes, optimization parameters, hardware specifications and environment-budget tables are retained. The PDFs establish the new access information, not the repository's availability or contents.

E1.justification: V3 adds Pendulum-v1, expanding the benchmark suite from ten to eleven continuous-control environments. This is distinct from the InvertedPendulum and InvertedDoublePendulum environments already evaluated in v1. The stochastic-timestep scenario and latent Walker2d evaluation were already present.

E2.justification: V3 adds GPM as a direct comparator in four environments (Figure 4) and randomized SAC, SAC-R, in Appendix A.10. TempoRL, already compared with latent SRL on Walker2d in v1, receives a broader seven-environment evaluation in Table 7. The latter reports rewards and sequence lengths rather than a matched FAS comparison.

E3.justification: V3 trains SAC at J = 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, enabling comparisons beyond v1's baseline trained at the default timestep. It also introduces randomized frame-skipping during SAC training, specifies GPM plan-length choices and adds TempoRL maximum-length tuning. The original SRL update schedule, common hyperparameters and stochastic-timestep evaluation procedure remain.

E4.justification: The SAC timestep sweep and randomized frame-skipping analysis test whether adapting baseline training closes the frequency-robustness gap. These add substantial controls absent from v1. Existing stochastic-timestep correlations and latent-space analyses are retained; the additional matched-J learning-curve figures primarily redisplay the expanded comparisons.

E5.justification: The main FAS tables retain five-trial means and standard deviations, and frequency plots retain standard-error reporting. V3 Table 7 newly specifies averaging TempoRL results over ten seeds. This adds experiment-specific seed information without establishing an increase in runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Numerous retained FAS entries change: Hopper SRL-16 changes from 0.44 ± 0.04 in v1 Table 2 to 0.57 ± 0.02 in v3 Table 3, while Lunar Lander SRL-16 changes from 0.89 ± 0.05 to 0.84 ± 0.03. New comparator results substantially expand the evidence and reveal stronger SAC performance on Swimmer. These are reported revisions, not verified improvements under identical experimental conditions.

M1.justification: Equation 5 corrects the documented actor-loss summation endpoint from J to J−1, matching the stated J-action sequence. The GRU actor, dynamics model, critics, Algorithm 1 and latent-space extension otherwise remain unchanged. This correction does not establish that the implementation changed.

P1.justification: V3 revises the motivation, delay discussion, experimental narrative and future-work prose, merges the macro-action and action-repetition subsections, and adds appendix headings. The main section order and much of the method, neuroscience and existing appendix exposition remain intact; these are targeted revisions rather than a wholesale narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, the combined FAS table becomes separate SAC and SRL tables, and learning and frequency plots are separated and expanded. V3 adds GPM and randomized-SAC displays and matched-J curve panels, while relocating existing illustrations and appendix material. Presentation changes are substantial, although several appendix pages become sparse and some comparison panels are very small.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning around temporally correlated exploration, including GPM, TLA and related exploration methods. It connects the evaluation to Dulac-Arnold's real-world RL challenges and discusses hardware acceleration and software optimization alternatives. The MPC distinction also shifts from requiring an already accurate model to requiring model access during deployment.

T1.justification: Equation 5 removes an extra terminal loss term by changing the summation endpoint from J to J−1; the accompanying sequence range is corrected accordingly. This resolves a mathematical inconsistency with the stated sequence length. Other substantive equations, including the latent temporal-consistency objective, are retained; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses an important weakness in v1: the main SAC baseline was trained at the default timestep. SAC-J and SAC-R controls test whether training adaptation explains SRL's advantage, while GPM supplies a close sequence-generating comparator. The Swimmer exception and moderated online-planning claim make the conclusions more informative. Unexplained FAS revisions and inconsistently updated illustrations, such as the Hopper curves in v3 Figures 2 and 9, remain drawbacks, but the stronger comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SRL work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments involving GPM, multiple SAC training timesteps, randomized frame-skipping and broader TempoRL evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original continuous-control experiments, FAS comparisons, stochastic-timestep evaluations and a latent-space Walker2d experiment in its appendix.

results.title: Overcoming Slow Decision Frequencies in Continuous Control: Model-Based Sequence Reinforcement Learning for Model-Free Control

C1.justification: The introduction retains the same three contributions: sharing unaggregated prompts, personalized attention-based prompt mixtures, and empirical superiority across nine datasets. Although the abstract and conclusion are shortened, the central novelty, applicability, and comparative-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds explanations linking prompt provenance and KNN selection to privacy risk, local gating to noise tolerance, gate aggregation to reduced personalization, additional experts to diminishing returns, and large feature dimensions to overparameterization. It also interprets attention weights as expert contributions and claims every expert is indispensable, an inference stronger than the visualization alone establishes.

D1.justification: Table 5 newly documents dataset training/test sizes and class counts; the appendix supplies configurations, gate sizes, and attention-averaging procedures for its added studies. v3 also provides a repository link and states code availability, replacing v1's promised public release upon acceptance. Existing backbone, optimizer, learning-rate, and epoch details are retained; repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five CLIP classification datasets, CIFAR10/100, DomainNet, and Office-Caltech10 with the same label- and feature-shift coverage. The added privacy and architectural studies vary procedures and configurations within these retained tasks and datasets.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the original benchmark tables remain unchanged. Appendix Table 7 newly evaluates linear-projection gating with three and ten experts and an aggregated attention gate against the proposed local attention gate. The additional related-work citations do not introduce evaluated benchmark baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds privacy experiments with epsilon 25/50 and delta 0.05, gate-aggregation controls, expert-count sweeps on DomainNet and CIFAR10, and pooled feature dimensions from 32 to 1024. Separately, Section 5.1 corrects CIFAR's stated client count from 10 to 100, agreeing with v1's existing caption and discussion; this does not establish rerunning the original experiments.

E4.justification: v1 analyzes shot count and the local-logit coefficient. v3 retains those analyses and adds privacy-noise robustness, attention versus linear gating, local versus aggregated gating, sensitivity to expert count and feature dimension, and attention-contribution visualizations. These substantially expand tests of architectural choices and operating conditions.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 in both versions specifies means and standard deviations over three runs with different seeds. The added tables continue this reporting practice without announcing additional runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original benchmark values and Figures 3–4 are retained, including the renumbered CIFAR and DomainNet tables. Appendix A adds substantial results: Table 7 reports Flowers102 accuracy of 69.64±4.57 for ten-expert linear gating versus 98.41±0.04 for local attention gating; Table 6 reports 98.36±0.12 for private pFedMoAP at epsilon 25. Further results cover expert count, feature dimension, and attention contributions.

M1.justification: The core pFedMoAP architecture, objectives, expert selection, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix A.2 adds an evaluated differential-privacy adaptation that clips prompt gradients and adds noise to uploaded prompts, introducing limited training and communication operations.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are condensed, several related-work and evaluation passages are edited, and Appendix A introduces four organized subsections. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose, including the method exposition, remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–9, an expert-count curve in Figure 5, and six contribution charts in Figure 6. The original figures remain; the CIFAR and DomainNet tables exchange numbering, DomainNet moves beside Office-Caltech10, and best-score bolding and associated caption statements are removed from the original tables.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Cai et al., Deng et al., FedTP, and Pan et al. in its research context, plus Collins et al. and Dwork for appendix discussions. These modestly broaden coverage of personalization, prompt-learning theory, and privacy while preserving the original positioning around unaggregated prompt sharing.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, and derivations in Equations 1–11 remain unchanged. The added privacy experiments and citation to a theoretical federated-learning framework introduce no new formal definition, theorem, proof, or mathematical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v1's central arguments for attention-based and locally maintained gating lacked direct experimental controls. v3's Table 7 tests both choices, while Tables 8–9 examine dependence on expert count and feature dimension, substantially strengthening validation of the design. Dataset statistics and stated code access also improve reproducibility. Privacy guarantees remain under-specified, and attention weights do not prove expert indispensability, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence supporting the central architecture.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pFedMoAP research. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 ends after the references; v3 adds a readable Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds measured privacy, gating-network, expert-count, feature-dimension, and attention-contribution results in Appendix A.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original experiments across nine datasets, including comparative accuracies in Tables 1–4 and ablations in Figures 3–4.

results.title: Mixture of Experts Made Personalized: Federated Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: Both versions claim input-driven surrogate modeling with automatically reduced latent dimensionality, continuous propagation of variational parameters, stochastic stabilization, and Koopman approximation. The expanded benchmark examples and condensed conclusion change supporting evidence and emphasis without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v1's discussion emphasizes real-data inference requirements, unresolved uncertainty-quantification applications, and numerical stability. v3 replaces this with comparative accuracy, automation, speed, and applicability arguments, and removes explicit dynamic-variance training caveats from Section 3.4. It also adds interpretations connecting fewer function evaluations to speed and masking results to persistent dimensionality reduction.

D1.justification: A.5.6–A.5.10 add dataset construction settings, MuJoCo filtering, PyKoopman implementation information, DMD rank searches, and radial-basis-function tuning. Small Grid and Water Hammer models or datasets are stated to be available on request. A.5.4 newly documents final-stage dopri5 training and adaptive batch step-size control; the main code-access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds controlled robot dynamics from MuJoCo Ant, pressure-wave dynamics from Water Hammer, and three-dimensional airflow from Small Grid (Sections 4.3, 5.3, and A.5.6–A.5.8). These substantially broaden the evaluated domains beyond the retained thermal examples and analytic Koopman system.

E2.justification: Table 2 introduces evaluated eDMDc and DMDc comparisons for linear surrogates. Table 1 adds zero-β B-NODE controls and changes comparator membership on retained tasks, including SS-NODE on heat flow and input-conditioned Latent NODE on the power plant. These extend v1's heat-flow TBR/Latent ODE and power-plant SS-NODE comparisons.

E3.justification: New benchmark protocols specify variance-normalized RMSE, with power-plant outputs evaluated in the nonlinear benchmark and states in the linear benchmark (A.5.9–A.5.10); retained plots use mean normalization. Added experiments introduce MuJoCo sequence/feature filtering, DMD rank and observable searches, and masking/retraining and sensitivity controls. These are new evaluation designs, not demonstrated changes to existing accuracy experiments.

E4.justification: A.6.1 newly tests masking low-KL channels in linear and nonlinear B-NODEs, followed by training with β set to zero. This differs from the retained static VAE masking analysis in A.3.3. A.6.2 adds sensitivity tests covering network depth and width, activations, decoder controls, latent capacity, solver tolerances, and β.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The existing latent-distribution variability visualization remains, while the added benchmark and sensitivity tables report point estimates without run-level uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2, Table 4, and Figure A.10 add substantial results. For example, Table 2 reports power-plant RMSE 0.20 for both B-NODE β=0.01 with 25 states and eDMDc with 45 states. Figure 6b replaces B-NODE CPU timing of 4.1 seconds with 0.5 seconds and SS-NODE GPU timing of 15.5 seconds with 68 seconds; the expanded solver and batch descriptions prevent treating these as established same-setting performance comparisons.

M1.justification: The encoders, Gaussian latent distributions, continuous propagation of variational parameters, stochastic training, ELBO objective, and linear Koopman variants remain unchanged. The new masking and architectural variations are supplementary experiments, rather than revisions to the proposed core procedure.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites expand the motivation and KL-channel explanation, standardize SS-NODE terminology, replace the discussion/future-work text, and condense the conclusion. Benchmark subsections are added, but the overall background–method–applications progression and most existing method and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds four tables and Figures A.8–A.10. Figure 6b is redesigned with an additional CPU comparison, speedup factors, and ODE-evaluation counts. Several retained figures are relocated or resized, and plot annotations are revised. This substantially expands and reorganizes the presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting PyKoopman, Gymnasium/Minari, and the Water Hammer example, while removing the Koopman VAE discussion and citation and the hybrid-modeling reference to Thummerer and Mikelsons. The broader positioning relative to Neural ODEs, DVAEs, model reduction, and Koopman theory remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The probabilistic factorizations, ELBO derivations, KL decomposition, and Koopman equations are retained. The Gaussian KL formula newly displayed in Section 2.2 already appears in v1 Appendix A.3.1. Expanded explanations of independence and fixed priors do not establish a substantive change to the existing mathematical formulation.

improvement.justification: Table 2 supplies the DMD comparisons explicitly left for future work in v1, while Table 1 broadens comparative validation across distinct dynamics. The new B-NODE masking and sensitivity experiments directly strengthen evidence for the central dimensionality-reduction claim. Removing useful stability and real-data caveats weakens qualification, and timing comparisons require care, but the improved comparative and diagnostic evidence substantially strengthens the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Balanced Neural ODE research, retaining matching methods, case studies, and appendix derivations. Text extraction and visual inspection covered both complete documents, including figures, tables, and appendices, without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds nonlinear and linear surrogate benchmarks, B-NODE masking experiments, and hyperparameter sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original VAE and B-NODE experiments, including heat-flow reconstruction and generalization, power-plant accuracy and runtime, Koopman approximation, and appendix latent-channel analyses.

results.title: Balanced Neural ODEs: nonlinear model order reduction and Koopman operator approximations

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion replace the convex-GM headline bound O(L0R²/ε+L1²R²) with O(L0R²/ε+L1R ln(F0/ε)); normalized-gradient and Polyak guarantees retain the former order. The acceleration headline now explicitly includes the line-search oracle factor m, which v1 discussed only in the detailed analysis.

C2.justification: V2 explains when bounded initial residuals make the finer GM bound advantageous and describes normalized gradient's guarantee as generally worse than that bound. It explicitly acknowledges the need for f* to stop the first acceleration stage, expands the sublevel-set explanation, and qualifies empirical advantages through best-iterate behavior and the new good-initialization results.

D1.justification: V2 explains the distinct normalization rules of STM and STM-Max and more explicitly documents acceleration inputs and stopping requirements. However, it removes v1's explicit R=10 specification for Figure 7.1, and its listed distance estimates omit the plotted 0.1R case. Neither version provides code-access or hardware information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate minimization of f(x)=||x||^p/p with p=4,6,8. The added initialization and parameter-sensitivity experiments vary settings within this retained function family and optimization task.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods: the gradient stepsize variants, normalized gradient, Polyak and AccGD in Figure 7.1, and gradient descent, AccGD, STM and STM-Max in Figure 7.3. Additional normalized-gradient curves vary a parameter. NAG receives theoretical analysis but no empirical comparison.

E3.justification: Figure 7.3 changes initial distances from {5,100,500} to {10,100,1000}, extends the plotted horizon from 2500 to 5000 iterations, and changes the reported acceleration parameter from 4L0 to 3L0. Figure 7.1 expands distance-estimate settings, while Figure 7.4 introduces initialization satisfying F0≤L0/(5L1²), bypassing the first stage.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained smoothness-parameter and initial-distance studies, v2 tests normalized-gradient sensitivity to the estimated initial distance in Figure 7.1. New Figure 7.4 isolates the accelerated stage through good initialization. These additions test two central practical assumptions that v1 did not systematically examine.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests for its deterministic numerical comparisons.

E6.justification: Figure 7.1 adds normalized-gradient curves labeled 0.1-NGD, 0.5-NGD and 10-NGD alongside the retained 2R setting. Figure 7.4 adds the finding that STM and STM-Max outperform AccGD for p=6,8 under good initialization, while the accelerated methods are reported as comparable for p=4. Figure 7.3 also replaces convergence curves under revised settings, rather than establishing a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The basic gradient, normalized-gradient, Polyak and AGMsDR updates are retained. The two-stage procedure now also permits the existing clipped rule (3.6), and Section 6 changes its prescribed acceleration constant from 3L0 to 5L0/(2a), with a depending on the stepsize rule.

P1.justification: Section 2 moves examples and closure operations before the first-order characterizations. Section 6 substantially rewrites the acceleration explanation and presents AGMsDR before the two-stage procedure. Appendix C is reorganized into general, constant-stepsize and decreasing-stepsize analyses, alongside terminology and prose revisions throughout.

P2.justification: V2 expands Figure 7.1's legend, redraws convergence displays, extends Figure 7.3's iteration axis and adds the three-panel Figure 7.4. Figures and algorithm boxes are rearranged, while the overall document and plotting styles remain similar.

R1.justification: V2 changes its comparison with Gorbunov et al. from matching the convex-GM complexity to obtaining a potentially sharper bound. It replaces the previously quoted NAG rate with the rescaled bound derived in Appendix F, substantially revising the theoretical comparison with Li et al. It also adds Rodomanov's thesis as a supporting reference.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.2 introduces the finer O(L0R²/ε+L1R ln(F0/ε)) bound with a new distance-monotonicity lemma and integral proof. Appendix A.6 supplies previously absent supporting proofs, Appendix C develops the existing decreasing-stepsize discussion into an explicit complexity theorem, and new Appendix F derives a rescaled-NAG bound. Several convergence constants and iteration-count formulas are also revised.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's coarser convex bound and brief decreasing-stepsize analysis, v2 supplies a finer Theorem 3.2 with a new proof and a detailed Theorem C.2. Appendix F makes the NAG comparison inspectable, while explicit oracle costs, stopping requirements and good-initialization results better qualify the acceleration contribution. These substantially strengthen this theory-centered paper despite minor experimental reporting inconsistencies.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same optimization problem, algorithms and research contributions. Their main text, equations, numerical figures and complete appendices support comparison, including the new Appendix F in v2.

after.justification: Section 7 and Figures 7.1–7.4 report original numerical results, including expanded normalized-gradient comparisons and a new good-starting-point experiment.

before.justification: Section 7 and Figures 7.1–7.3 report original numerical comparisons of gradient methods on power-function minimization problems.

results.title: Optimizing $(L_0, L_1)$-Smooth Functions by Gradient Methods

C1.justification: The contributions and conclusion replace the two-stage O(m sqrt(L0 R²/ε)+(L1 R)²) acceleration claim with a direct AGMsDR bound of νO(sqrt(L0 R²/ε)+ceil((L1 R)^(2/3)) ceil(ln(F0/ε))). The abstract also qualifies the parameter-agnostic methods' guarantees from 'the same' to 'nearly the same,' and the introduction stops calling NGM and PS-GM new methods.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the explanation based on first entering a region of uniformly small gradients with an explanation based on observed progress and control of average gradient norms. The old accelerator's need for f* to terminate its preliminary stage disappears. The conclusion replaces the question of improving first-stage complexity with the question of whether the new second complexity term is optimal; eliminating line search remains open.

D1.justification: Section 7 removes the explicit L=3L0 setting and the initial-distance/warm-start specifications accompanying v2's accelerated experiments. The replacement comparison does not provide an explicit starting-distance specification. V3 also retains 10R in the NGM setup text although its curve is absent. Neither version supplies code, software, or hardware information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same objective family, f(x)=||x||^p/p, with p=4, 6, and 8. Changes concern initialization, parameters, and iteration horizons within this retained optimization task; no dataset or domain is added.

E2.justification: The comparator algorithms remain GM with the three stepsize rules, NGM, and PS-GM in Figure 7.1, and GM, STM, and STM-Max in the accelerated comparisons. Removed NGM radius choices are parameter configurations. AccGD's replacement by AGMsDR changes the proposed accelerator rather than introducing a new baseline.

E3.justification: V2 reports accelerated comparisons over 5,000 iterations, varying R=10, 100, 1000 at p=6 and separately testing warm starts. V3 replaces these with a 500-iteration comparison at p=4, 6, 8 using the revised accelerator. Figure 7.1 also reduces the displayed NGM radius configurations from 0.1R, 0.5R, 2R, and 10R to 0.5R and 2R.

E4.justification: The explicit initialization-distance sensitivity study and the good-starting-point study in v2 Figures 7.3 and 7.4 are removed. NGM initialization-estimate sensitivity is also narrowed in Figure 7.1. The smoothness-parameter sensitivity analysis in Figure 7.2 is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or empirical uncertainty bars. Both present individual convergence curves.

E6.justification: V2's findings about AccGD outperforming STM-Max at large initial distances and underperforming STM variants for warm starts at p=6 and 8 are removed with their experiments. V3 Figure 7.3 instead shows rapid early AGMsDR convergence at smaller p, while STM variants perform better at p=8. Figure 7.1 also contains revised trajectories and fewer entries. These are changed results under changed methods/settings, not matched-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V3 replaces v2's two-stage acceleration procedure with direct AGMsDR. Algorithm 6.1 replaces the fixed L in its acceleration-weight equation with an iteration-dependent quantity computed from the gradient norm and achieved objective decrease. The preliminary gradient-descent stage and its stopping condition requiring f* disappear; the basic GM, NGM, and Polyak updates remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory discussion, contribution statements, related-work paragraphs, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Section 6 changes from an extended two-stage motivation to a more direct algorithm-and-analysis narrative, and Appendix E is reorganized around the new proof. The overall main-section and appendix structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 7.1 is redrawn with fewer curves and revised legends; the accelerated comparisons are replaced by a new Figure 7.3 with different panel labels and iteration axes, and Figure 7.4 is removed. Algorithm 6.1's display is revised and Algorithm 6.2 is deleted. Figure 7.2 is retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V3 adds Lobanov et al.'s 'Linear convergence rate in convex setup is possible!' and acknowledges in Section 3.2 that it independently derives the same bound as Theorem 3.2. The principal prior-work comparisons and Appendix F's NAG analysis remain.

T1.justification: Theorem 6.1 replaces the fixed-L sufficient-decrease assumption and rate with a general strictly decreasing update and a bound involving the sum of inverse square roots of the observed per-step quantities. Theorem 6.2 receives a different complexity bound and proof, supported by new Lemmas E.1–E.3. Smaller corrections include the admissible accuracy range in Theorem 3.2 and L0 replacing L0 squared in Section 4's optimized NGM bound.

improvement.justification: Section 6 and Appendix E resolve an important limitation of v2: acceleration no longer needs a preparatory stage whose termination requires f*. The revised method receives a more general convergence analysis and a lower-power dependence on L1R, with an added logarithmic factor and retained line-search costs. These substantial methodological and theoretical gains outweigh the narrower initialization studies and reduced experimental detail.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 7 and Figures 7.1–7.3 report original numerical convergence results, including experiments with the revised accelerated method.

before.justification: Section 7 and Figures 7.1–7.4 report original numerical comparisons of gradient methods on polynomial objectives.

results.title: Optimizing $(L_0, L_1)$-Smooth Functions by Gradient Methods

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a generalized iterative preference framework, overconfident labeling as a source of rewarding bias, and cross-iteration consistency regularization to improve self-rewarding. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: New discussion explains label smoothing versus loss scaling, the rarity of near-zero consistency, model-level uncertainty, and averaging as variance reduction. Appendices A and C.6 explicitly discuss computational costs and the need for initial alignment. Longer-term stability and ensemble comparisons receive substantive interpretations. The arena discussion also newly mentions GPT-4o as an opponent, although Figure 3 still shows it only as judge.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies five sampled responses per prompt, comparator hyperparameter grids, ensemble learning rates and weighted-DPO checkpoint selection. Conversely, it removes the NVIDIA A6000 hardware statement and explicit GPT-4o provenance of curated preference labels. The code link and principal optimizer, learning-rate and epoch disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use OpenAssistant, ARC-Easy/Challenge, OpenBookQA, SIQA and GSM8K, plus curated preference-ranking data and RewardBench. The added larger and initially unaligned models are configurations evaluated on retained tasks, without new datasets, domains or input scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands evaluated comparators. Table 1 adds SRLM + KL and CREAM w/o RC; Tables 6, 8 and 12 add weighted-DPO SRLM, Ensemble-Worst, Ensemble-Mean, Distilled DPO and P-CREAM comparisons. Original SRLM, Oracle and P-SRLM comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols extend training from M3 through M6, evaluate Llama-2-13B and non-chat Llama-3-8B, and introduce regularization grids and three-model ensembles trained with different learning rates. Appendix C.2 also specifies checkpoint selection for weighted-DPO experiments. The original benchmark settings remain; newly specifying five responses per prompt is disclosure, not evidence of a changed sampling budget.

E4.justification: v3 adds targeted tests of adaptive versus fixed consistency, simple loss weighting, ensemble rewards, thresholded versus per-example regularization, and prompt-based regularization. It also examines M4–M6 stability, consistency distributions, model size and initial alignment. The original date-arithmetic case study in Section 4.3.4 and Table 5 is removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: The existing plus/minus reporting in Table 2 is unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. New consistency-score distributions in Table 7 describe an additional analysis, without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores and Figures 3–5 are retained, and v1 Table 6 reappears as v3 Table 13. Extensive new results include CREAM's average peaking at 83.65 at M4 and declining to 82.73 at M6, versus SRLM's 68.59 at M6 (Table 5). New M3 comparisons report 57.46 versus 49.33 on Llama-2-13B and 42.67 versus 35.55 with initially unaligned Llama-3. These are added settings, not improvements to the original scores.

M1.justification: The default algorithm, intrinsic rewards and consistency-weighted normal/reversed DPO objective remain unchanged. Appendix C adds limited procedural variants: threshold-dependent regularization, per-example consistency weights and prompt-rewarding P-CREAM. The corrected worst-response selection formula agrees with v1's existing best/worst-response description.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental discussion are edited and condensed, the case-study subsection is removed, and appendices are reorganized into Limitations, Proofs and subdivided Additional Results. The main five-section narrative and method exposition remain largely intact. The publication header changes from Preprint to ICLR 2025.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains comparator rows and an Average column and is substantially resized. Eight new appendix tables appear as Tables 5–12; the original case-study table is removed, while v1 Table 6 becomes Table 13. Existing figures are retained, but experiment-page table placement, sizing and text flow are substantially rearranged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix C.4 substantially expand positioning against reward hacking, reward-model ensembles and robust preference optimization, including Coste, Eisenstein, Rame, Zhang and Fisch. New distillation references support that discussion. Two peripheral vision-language references are removed. The revision develops substantive distinctions about preference regularization, conservatism and ensemble costs.

T1.justification: The original theorems, lemmas and proofs are retained, with Appendix A becoming B. Equations 3.11–3.12 correct worst-response selection from argmin to argmax. Appendices C.2 and C.4 add gradient/equal-ratio analysis, a zero-loss self-distillation minimizer argument and mathematical comparisons of regularization objectives; these supplement the existing theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: Table 1 and Appendix C substantially strengthen validation by testing adaptive consistency against simpler regularization and weighting alternatives, examining later-iteration degradation, and probing model-size and initial-alignment dependence. These address important gaps in v1, while explicit limitations clarify applicability. Lost hardware and label-provenance details and unsupported GPT-4o-opponent wording are drawbacks; run-based uncertainty also remains unreported. The targeted validation gains outweigh these narrower weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CREAM research, with matching authors, core algorithm and original experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and can be matched across the expanded and reorganized material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds comparator, longer-training, model-configuration and regularization experiments in Section 4 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama-2/Llama-3 benchmark experiments, preference-ranking evaluations, consistency analyses and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: CREAM: Consistency Regularized Self-Rewarding Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract expands its claim of consistent superiority over DPO from three publicly available LLMs to five, retaining four math datasets. The stated contributions and conclusion are otherwise unchanged, so this is a limited expansion of claimed empirical scope.

C2.justification: V2 interprets BBH improvements as transferred long-chain reasoning and stable MMLU performance as preserved knowledge. Appendix C adds explanations involving chosen-response likelihood decline, absolute ranking positions, semantic similarity versus token overlap, and the beta/forgetting trade-off. These substantially extend interpretation while retaining the original forgetting and reward-imbalance limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies exact BBH and MMLU prompts, while Appendix C specifies the new DPO pair constructions and TPO beta settings. Existing data-generation prompts, hardware, optimizer, learning rate and code-access information remain. This is a limited expansion of reproducibility documentation.
