E1.justification: V2 adds BBH multi-step reasoning and MMLU multiple-choice evaluations to the retained four math and two coding datasets (Section 4.1, Table 2). This substantially broadens out-of-distribution task coverage. The mathematical preference-training corpus remains unchanged.

E2.justification: SFT becomes an evaluated comparator in Tables 1-2. Appendix C.2/Table 5 adds custom DPO* and DPO+ baselines constructed from top-versus-other and adjacent ranked preferences, respectively. Table 6 additionally compares Pointwise SoftMax, Pairwise Logistic and Listwise MLE against LambdaLoss. These are substantive additions to the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 backbones, BBH step-by-step and MMLU multiple-choice prompting, preference-pair construction controls, and a beta sweep over 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01. These expand the evaluation design; the original pass@1 metric and stated one-epoch training recipe are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds analyses of preference-data use, alternative ranking losses, statistical validation of Adaptive Step Reward, two reward-margin case studies and beta sensitivity. Conversely, v1's MATH difficulty and problem-type breakdowns in Appendix A.2 are removed. The original component ablations and preference-list analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix C.4/Table 7 newly reports 20 independent experiments for each TPO/without-Adaptive-Step-Reward condition, performance means with standard errors, independent t-tests, exact p-values and significance markers. V1 reports variability in reward distributions but no corresponding repeated-run uncertainty or significance analysis of model performance.

E6.justification: Original numerical results in Tables 1-3 and Figure 3 are retained, but substantial new results cover SFT, additional backbones, BBH/MMLU, DPO variants, ranking losses, repeated-run estimates and beta settings. For example, new BBH results give Qwen2-7B TPO 69.62 versus DPO 65.58. These are added comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains. The earlier MATH subgroup results are removed.

M1.justification: Equation (10) changes the stated reward calculation: the semantic-similarity weight now multiplies the entire difference between step log-ratios, whereas v1 weights only the first term. This is a limited correction within Adaptive Step Reward; the other components and Algorithm 1 remain. The PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the section sequence remain. V2 removes two introductory method-summary paragraphs, moves Algorithm 1 to Appendix A, reorganizes the appendix into algorithms, prompts, experiments and related literature, updates affiliations and conference headers, and adds acknowledgments. The retained narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: Tables 1-2 gain SFT rows, and Table 2 gains grouped reasoning columns. V2 adds six appendix tables, a four-panel reward-margin Figure 4 and two case-study boxes, while removing v1's two MATH breakdown tables and relocating Algorithm 1. Figures 1-3 remain unchanged. This substantially changes the presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: New Appendix D and Table 9 explicitly position TPO against S-DPO, Rose-DPO and ODPO through their objectives and treatment of negative preferences, ranking positions and weighting. Additional ranking-loss, LambdaLoss and preference-optimization literature supports the expanded discussion. These related methods are not reported as direct empirical baselines.

T1.justification: Equation (10)'s revised weighting makes identical shared steps contribute zero, resolving the inconsistency between v1's printed formula and its stated cancellation property. V2 also explicitly explains that cancellation. The other core mathematical definitions and derivations remain, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The stronger preference-data controls, alternative-loss and beta comparisons, and 20-run significance tests substantially strengthen validation of TPO's central components, especially the previously unquantified small Adaptive Step Reward gains. Additional backbones and reasoning tasks improve assessment of generality, and Equation (10) is corrected. These benefits outweigh the loss of MATH subgroup detail and a flawed new Case 1, whose supposedly correct responses incorrectly calculate (5+3i)(5-3i) as 16.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TPO research and are readable throughout, including equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be reliably matched despite appendix restructuring.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C retain original evaluations and add reasoning benchmarks, model backbones, comparison methods, sensitivity experiments and repeated-run statistical results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A.2 report original math and coding evaluations, component ablations, preference-list analyses and detailed MATH results.

results.title: TPO: Aligning Large Language Models with Multi-branch & Multi-step Preference Trees

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the broad contributions in object binding, reasoning, robustness, and calibration. Novelty positioning changes locally: Section 3 stops calling the symmetry-breaking term novel, while Section 5 explicitly claims the first standalone scaling of a synchrony-based model to natural images.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations and applicability boundaries: it diagnoses underfitting at N=2, discusses degradation at large dimensions and under symmetric constraints, and identifies failures on overlapping Shapes objects. It also interprets energy voting as energy-based-model behavior despite task-only training. Conversely, Figure 28 removes v1 Figure 18's qualification that all sampled predictions fail on approximately 30% of boards. The fixed-norm memory limitation remains.

D1.justification: Existing training recipes and repository access largely remain. v2 adds Shapes construction and hyperparameters, implementation details for the CIFAR10 ItrConv comparator, runtime measurements and their measurement definitions, and a project-page link. The existing up-tiling code receives partial variable corrections, although its malformed final reshape statement remains.

E1.justification: v2 adds the authors' Shapes dataset to object discovery: images containing two to four potentially overlapping objects drawn from four basic shapes. The existing synthetic and natural-image datasets, Sudoku distributions, and CIFAR10 scenarios remain. This is a limited expansion within an existing task.

E2.justification: v2 adds Energy Transformer and symmetrized AKOrN to Sudoku comparisons, Gaussian-noise-trained ResNets to robustness comparisons, and ItrConv to the extended CIFAR10 table. Table 18 additionally compares Rotating Features on PascalVOC and NSI on COCO2017. These substantially broaden the alternatives evaluated across the paper's principal tasks.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes Sudoku energy voting from 100 to 4,096 samples at 128 steps. However, v2 Table 19 assigns the same 89.5% result to 1,000 samples and 512 steps, leaving its exact protocol unresolved. New dimensionality, depth, component-control, and runtime experiments substantially expand evaluation design. Figure 11 also revises the stated baseline MLP width from four to two times the channel size, without establishing whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing positional-encoding, up-tiling, noise, and natural-frequency analyses, v2 Appendix A adds projection removal, replacement with residual updates, dimensionality sweeps, training-loss analyses, bias/readout-norm ablations, and runtime comparisons. Appendix D.4 adds symmetry controls, while Table 16 and Figures 26 and 31 add depth comparisons and overlapping-object failure cases.

E5.justification: Synthetic object-discovery results previously reported as point estimates now include means and standard deviations, with Tables 14, 15, and 17 specifying three weight-initialization seeds. Uncertainty is also added to cited baseline entries where available. Sudoku's five-seed reporting remains; Table 19 newly discloses exclusion of one failed symmetrized-AKOrN run. These are reporting changes, not evidence of an explicit increase in run counts.

E6.justification: Many synthetic-object scores change: Tetrominoes FG-ARI changes from 86.19 versus 86.81 for AKOrNattn and ItrSA to 88.6 versus 85.8, reversing their ordering. Headline Sudoku OOD accuracy changes from 61.1±14.7 to 89.5±2.5 under revised, inconsistently documented conditions, so this is not a controlled same-setting gain. Shapes, ablation, baseline, and runtime results add substantial evidence; the main natural-image and CIFAR10 Table 4 scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core Kuramoto updates, connectivity mechanisms, and training objectives remain. However, v2 Table 19 introduces prediction selection using summed energies across timesteps, extending v1's final-state energy voting. Appendix C.2 also changes the reported Sudoku readout from Batch Normalization, ReLU, and linear layers to ReLU and linear layers; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects rerunning experiments or correcting documentation.

P1.justification: Most main-text organization and wording remain. v2 fixes the malformed Section 6.3 heading and opening, clarifies layer indexing, expands metric and up-tiling explanations, and rewrites related-work passages. Earlier physics and robustness discussions become Appendix B.1/B.2, and the rotating-dimension discussion moves from the conclusion into the appendices. The additions do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the network diagram and adds projection, sensitivity, loss, runtime, corruption-example, and failure-case displays. Figure 3 gains Shapes and error bars; Figure 7 expands its sampling axis and removes the majority-voting curve. Tables gain uncertainty displays and new comparison structures. Many earlier cluster visualizations are retained and renumbered rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially broadens coverage of historical oscillatory networks, learned Kuramoto synchronization, graph-based oscillator models, and spiking synchrony. It develops a more specific comparison with Energy Transformer. Section 3 adds generalized-Kuramoto predecessors, and Figure 2 acknowledges related recurrent architectures. These changes expand and refine research positioning beyond bibliographic date corrections.

T1.justification: Equation (3) gains a factor of one-half on the pairwise interaction term. Section 3 narrows its example Lyapunov conditions from general symmetric coupling blocks to scalar multiples of the identity. New Appendices F and G supply a derivation and propositions involving commutator and normality conditions for non-increasing energy. These materially revise the mathematical justification.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper through controlled tests of its central architectural choices, uncertainty reporting for previously single-valued object-discovery results, and expanded formal support for the energy argument. These address important gaps in v1's evidential and mathematical foundation. The conflicting Sudoku budgets in Tables 3 and 19 weaken reproducibility of the headline result, but the broader gains remain substantial; the higher reported accuracy alone does not establish improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AKOrN research work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, experiments, tables, and figures can be matched across revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Shapes experiments, architectural ablations, sensitivity analyses, runtime measurements, and further baseline comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original object-discovery, Sudoku-solving, and CIFAR10 robustness and calibration experiments, including additional results and analyses in the appendices.

results.title: Artificial Kuramoto Oscillatory Neurons

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction/discussion claims remain: a scalable influence-function framework unifying earlier approaches, improved attribution performance, and limitations in predicting numerical counterfactual changes. Explicitly foregrounding EK-FAC does not introduce a contribution absent from v3.

C2.justification: The overall caution about numerical attribution remains. Observation 3 shifts from ELBO stability to marginal-density stability, with a more explicit training-size threshold interpretation. Appendix C.3 adds rank-related explanations for the ablation results while acknowledging that Hessian approximation quality was not directly measured. The trajectory-specific failure explanation is removed.

D1.justification: V4 fills substantial documentation gaps for existing ArtBench experiments: image resolution, latent diffusion architecture, frozen Stable Diffusion 2 autoencoder, sampling, training iterations, optimiser, learning rate, warm-up, clipping, and EMA settings. It also adds a project source-code link and autodifferentiation guidance. These disclosures do not establish that the underlying ArtBench method changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate image attribution using CIFAR-2, CIFAR-10, and ArtBench. ArtBench's expanded description is not a new dataset addition. Uniform dequantisation, alternative measurements, and training-set-size sweeps change preprocessing and evaluation settings within the retained coverage.

E2.justification: TRAK, D-TRAK, CLIP similarity, and exact retraining remain. Figure 2a drops the separate ordinary K-FAC row while retaining EK-FAC under the renamed K-FAC Influence label. New Appendix C.3 comparisons evaluate additional combinations of empirical/model Fisher, expand/reduce, and eigenvalue correction.

E3.justification: V4 introduces marginal-density evaluation on uniformly dequantised CIFAR and training-size sweeps from 10 to 25,000 examples. New Hessian ablations specify matched computation budgets, including 125 samples each for EK-FAC eigenbasis and eigenvalues. ArtBench's stated LDS design changes from v3's universal 100-subset specification to 50 subsets; this establishes a reporting revision, not necessarily rerunning.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds a controlled ablation of Fisher choice, expand/reduce approximation, and eigenvalue correction. V4 also expands distribution-stability analysis across training-set sizes and adds likelihood damping sensitivity. V3's gradient-sample-count sweep is removed. Compression and timestep/downweighting analyses remain, although several results are updated.

E5.justification: V3 Appendix K.5 reports 500 retrained models for every LDS benchmark. V4 Appendix J.6 specifies 250 for ArtBench, arising from 50 subsets with five seeds each. This revises reported retraining counts; five-seed averaging and standard-error reporting otherwise remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Matching the EK-FAC variant, Figure 2 loss LDS changes from 27.4%/23.2% to 26.7%/22.6% on CIFAR-2/10. New Figure 21 reports marginal-density LDS of 21.6% for K-FAC Influence using loss versus 14.9% for D-TRAK; these replace a different trajectory-probability evaluation. Ablation, timestep, and removal results also change. In v4 Figure 3, CIFAR-10 with 2% removal gives 0.00067 for K-FAC Influence versus 0.00079 for D-TRAK.

M1.justification: The influence-function pipeline, curvature approximations, query batching, and gradient quantisation remain. EK-FAC was already introduced and evaluated in v3; v4 foregrounds it and calls it K-FAC Influence. The expanded derivations and evaluations of existing design options do not establish a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Evaluation definitions move from v3 Appendix D into Section 4. Appendix C is subdivided into background, derivation, and ablation sections, and sampling receives a separate subsection. Terminology and several paragraphs are edited, but most of the main narrative and appendix structure remain recognisable.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially revised: new Hessian-ablation and likelihood-sensitivity figures appear; v3's correlation matrices are replaced by a multipanel size-sweep display with generated images; and trajectory-result plots are replaced by marginal-density plots. Figure 2's row structure changes, and main figures are relocated. The runtime and memory tables remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds references to Dangel et al. (2025), Liao et al. (2022), and Rombach et al. (2022). Related work adds emphasis on damping's contribution to earlier D-TRAK results and condenses the separate K-FAC/EK-FAC history. The overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Equations (8) and (11) correct the empirical-Fisher decomposition from log/exp(loss) to negative-log/exp(negative loss). Appendix B replaces the score-based derivation with a random-vector second-moment derivation. Appendix C revises the weight-sharing formulation and adds explicit diffusion-specific expand/reduce derivations, substantially extending the mathematical treatment.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens support for its central design choices through controlled Hessian ablations and explicit weight-sharing derivations, corrects the empirical-Fisher sign error, and fills important ArtBench reproducibility gaps. Marginal-density experiments provide more direct evidence for the attribution question. The retained claim of consistently superior removal results is now overstated by Figure 3, but this limited inconsistency does not outweigh the substantial gains in justification and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and corresponding material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V4 retains original attribution experiments and reports additional Hessian-approximation ablations and marginal-density evaluations, including Figures 5, 19, and 21.

before.justification: V3 reports original LDS evaluations, counterfactual retraining results, and attribution analyses on CIFAR-2, CIFAR-10, and ArtBench, including Figures 2–3 and the appendices.

results.title: Influence Functions for Scalable Data Attribution in Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract expands the robotics claim from training manipulation policies in simulation to transferring those policies to a real robotic system. The principal actor-critic, multimodal articulation and 75% benchmark claims, together with the introduction's contribution list, remain essentially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking matched-modality advantages to foundation-model common sense and planning, identifies small parts and irregular motion as difficult cases, and suggests camera zoom as a possible remedy. Appendix A.8 also explains why task-conditioned segmentation is needed to avoid under- or over-segmentation. The original retrieval limitation and critic-overconfidence discussion remain.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies placement-API alignment and collision checking, documents the generation/segmentation workflow, and identifies robotic action outputs, randomization and LiDAR reference capture. However, Appendix A.3 removes v1's policy observation descriptions, network architecture, end-effector camera specification and manual reward-design disclosure. Code-access information is substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 extends the simulation-only robotics application to physical Franka deployment and adds evaluation of human asset-annotation labor. PartNet-Mobility and the existing in-the-wild reconstruction examples remain; additional mesh-quality measurements on those objects do not themselves constitute new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The main URDFormer and Real2Code comparator sets are retained. Section 6 adds human-expert asset annotation using RialTo as a comparator, while Figure 24 qualitatively compares the selected Rodin frontend with Instant Mesh and Stable-Fast-3D. The new matched-modality experiment reuses existing baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds matched-modality comparisons on the baselines' seen classes, actor-only prompt-count and VLM sweeps, and physical robot evaluation with stated physics, scale and pose randomization. New Chamfer evaluations use LiDAR reference meshes and exclude the evaluated object from retrieval candidates. The original articulation thresholds remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 adds sensitivity to prompting examples and VLM choice; Appendix A.5 adds matched-modality controls; Appendix A.6 adds error-distribution and category-based failure analyses. These substantially broaden scrutiny beyond v1's modality and critic-refinement studies. Conversely, v1's RGB-D versus depth-only robot-learning curves are removed.

E5.justification: v2 extends uncertainty reporting to the central benchmark: Figure 5 adds 95% confidence intervals, Table 1 adds confidence intervals for joint-type errors and standard deviations for continuous errors, and Table 3 reports standard deviations. The three-seed robotics statement is retained, but the earlier shaded-standard-deviation learning curves are removed. No increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: The main 75.0% articulation success result remains unchanged. v2 adds matched-modality results of 40.3% for text and 48.5% for images, prompt/VLM and category results, Chamfer scores, and reported 100% real-robot success with 40.58 minutes of human annotation labor per task. The old RL curves disappear. Table 1 also changes Real2Code Oracle's all-class type error from 0.538 to 0.537 and URDFormer Oracle's OOD origin error from 0.514 to 0.513.

M1.justification: The core actor-critic articulation procedure remains intact, but Appendix A.8 adds a substantial alternative to mesh retrieval: Rodin mesh generation followed by video-conditioned Grounded SAM segmentation, multiview projection and transfer of part labels to dense meshes. v1 only proposed upstream mesh reconstruction as future work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include a rewritten robotics paragraph, local explanatory and cross-reference edits, relocation of baseline details, and new Section 5.4 and Appendices A.5–A.8. The additions do not amount to extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands and reorganizes the displays: Table 1 moves to the appendix and gains uncertainty entries; new ablation, annotation-time, distribution and category plots and two reconstruction tables appear. The reconstruction montage gains a generation row, robotics illustrations show transfer to reality, and the old RL learning-curve figure is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Rodin, Grounded SAM, RialTo and Instant Mesh for the new generation and robotics experiments. Stable-Fast-3D was already cited in v1. The related-work section and central positioning against URDFormer and Real2Code remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, losses and assumptions in Section 3 and the error definitions in Appendix A.1 remain unchanged, including Equations 1–11. The added reconstruction procedure and experiments introduce no new formal results or proofs.

improvement.justification: Matched-modality controls, prompt/VLM ablations, and uncertainty and category-level reporting substantially strengthen evidence for the method and address important comparison and robustness gaps in v1. Physical robot demonstrations also extend the earlier simulation-only application. These gains outweigh the loss of RL curves and implementation details, although real-robot trial counts remain unspecified. A new reporting flaw needs correction: Table 2 claims retrieval superiority despite displaying average Chamfer distances of 0.1102 for retrieval versus 0.1085 for Real2Code.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Articulate-Anything, with matching core methods and traceable retained experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables and all appendices support comparison, including v2's added Appendices A.5–A.8.

after.justification: v2 retains original articulation experiments and adds prompt/VLM ablations, mesh-reconstruction measurements, real-robot outcomes and human annotation-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original PartNet-Mobility evaluations, modality and iterative-refinement experiments, in-the-wild reconstructions, and simulated robot-learning results.

results.title: Articulate-Anything:  Automatic Modeling of Articulated Objects via a Vision-Language Foundation Model

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about dynamic hierarchical memory, efficient online updates, and performance relative to online and offline methods. The added experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning traversal-induced search restrictions and redundancy, applicability with smaller models, threshold robustness, compression tradeoffs, and alignment with human judgments. Appendix C newly distinguishes failures caused by insufficient retrieval from failures where relevant evidence is buried in lengthy context, providing more concrete applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2.1 newly specifies insertion without chunking for dialogue rounds and non-overlapping chunks of 512 tokens for QuALITY and 1024 tokens for MultiHop RAG. New studies also document their configurations and sampling controls. These improve reproducibility disclosure; the original algorithm, prompts, retrieval budgets, and promise of code release upon acceptance remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The four original QA datasets and their coverage are retained. Appendix A.3.8 adds a human semantic-similarity judgment task using sampled tree nodes, extending evaluation beyond question answering without introducing a new document domain.

E2.justification: The main QA comparator sets remain unchanged. Appendix A.3.5 newly evaluates traversal retrieval with k = 1, 3, 5, and 10 against MemTree's collapsed retrieval. LLMLingua is applied to both MemTree and MemoryStream rather than evaluated as a standalone competing memory system.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce retrieval-width comparisons, smaller LLM and embedding configurations, a nine-setting threshold sweep, compression-rate sweeps, and LLM-call efficiency measurements. The human study adds 500 questions, five annotators, controlled descendant/non-descendant alternatives, and randomized option ordering. These substantially expand evaluation design; the original benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices A.3.4-A.3.9 add efficiency analysis, collapsed-versus-traversal retrieval ablation, model-size robustness, threshold sensitivity, human assessment of hierarchy quality, and prompt-compression analysis. Appendix C additionally supplies retrieval examples and two explicit failure analyses, substantially extending v1's benchmark breakdowns and illustrative tree analysis.

E5.justification: The existing MSC-E standard-deviation reporting is retained. New measurements include dispersion and error bars, but extend the existing reporting convention without specifying new seed counts, repeated-run procedures, confidence-interval methods, or statistical tests. The new statement about statistical insignificance in A.3.7 does not identify a testing procedure.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1-5 are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative evidence. Examples include 3.27 ± 2.38 LLM calls per insertion, smaller-model accuracies of 78.4% and 78.1%, human-alignment results, and retrieval, threshold, and compression curves. These are additional conditions and outcomes, not improved original benchmark scores. Figure A.4's approximately 79% collapsed-retrieval accuracy differs from Table 4's retained 80.5%, without an explained setting difference.

M1.justification: Section 3, Algorithm 1, and Appendix A.1 retain the same insertion, aggregation, adaptive-threshold, and collapsed-retrieval procedures. Traversal retrieval and prompt compression are evaluated as experimental alternatives rather than adopted changes to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v2 shortens table captions, rewrites the efficiency discussion, corrects node-content notation, groups experimental details under A.2, and moves the theory into Appendix B. These are limited editorial and organizational changes rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures A.4-A.9 and Tables A.2-A.9, including sensitivity plots, a heatmap, human-evaluation plots, and detailed retrieval/failure tables. Figure 5 is revised to visibly include GraphRAG runtime lines, while existing tables and appendix plots are also repositioned. The visual evidence is substantially expanded.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to LongLoRA and Focused Transformer in the long-context background, and LLMLingua for the compression experiment. The related-work discussion and positioning of MemTree against static structured retrieval and flat memory systems otherwise remain stable.

T1.justification: The Moseley-Wang revenue definition, beta-separation assumption, approximation theorem, and threshold derivation are retained, moving from Appendix A.7 to Appendix B. The node-content symbol correction in Section 3 matches its existing explanation and does not change the mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny of the central method: v1 lacked direct retrieval and threshold ablations, smaller-model robustness checks, human validation of the hierarchy, and explicit failure analyses. The additions address these gaps and clarify preprocessing. Reporting weaknesses remain, especially the Figure A.4/Table 4 discrepancy and unspecified significance testing, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same MemTree research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated theoretical material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds retrieval and parameter ablations, smaller-model experiments, human evaluation, compression experiments, and qualitative results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MemTree and baseline experiments on MSC, MSC-E, QuALITY, and MultiHop RAG, alongside memory-structure and runtime results.

results.title: From Isolated Conversations to Hierarchical Schemas: Dynamic Tree Memory Representation for LLMs

C1.justification: v3 extends the central performance claim from low-resolution EDM distillation to guidance-free, single-step ImageNet 512x512 generation across six EDM2 sizes. It specifically claims that an EDM2-S student can outperform the guided EDM2-XXL teacher and presents adapting SiD to EDM2 as an additional contribution.

C2.justification: The imperfect-teacher motivation remains. v3 adds qualifications about unavoidable approximate-score bias despite alternative stop-gradient interpretations, explicitly discusses iteration overhead, and explains normalization-related backpropagation failures. It also revises the GDD-I feature-leakage discussion and identifies guidance and post-hoc EMA techniques omitted from its EDM2 experiments.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's EDM pseudocode and settings table, v3 supplies EDM2-specific hyperparameters, hardware, timing, and memory measurements (Table 6), model-specific normalization choices, and original/modified MPConv code listings. Appendices A–B also document loss balancing and checkpoint selection. The code-integration statement remains a future promise.

E1.justification: v3 adds label-conditioned ImageNet 512x512 generation, substantially extending the resolution and complexity of the evaluated task. CIFAR-10, ImageNet 64x64, FFHQ 64x64, and AFHQ-v2 64x64 remain covered; relocated face-generation results are retained.

E2.justification: The original benchmark comparator sets remain. v3 adds comparisons with sCT and sCD in Table 4 and a substantially broader high-resolution comparison set in Table 9, including MaskGIT, MAGVIT-v2, MAR, and VAR. These include results attributed to prior work, rather than necessarily new baseline implementations.

E3.justification: New EDM2 experiments cover six model sizes from 125M to 1.5B parameters, with batch size 2048 and learning rate 5e-5. v3 adds FDDINOv2 evaluation and a controlled 5%-versus-100% real-training-data comparison. The documented settings of the retained EDM benchmarks are otherwise preserved.

E4.justification: The existing alpha ablations remain. v3 adds a targeted data-availability test (Figure 7), qualitative comparisons of normalization and learned loss-weighting choices (Appendix B.2), and fixed-noise training-progression visualizations (Figures 8–10). The normalization comparisons lack detailed numerical ablation tables.

E5.justification: v1 already reports results with plus/minus values but does not explain the repetition count. v3 Appendix A explicitly describes ten independent re-evaluations of selected generators. This newly documents evaluation repetition; it does not establish an increase in runs or ten independent training seeds.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values remain unchanged, including v1 Tables 4–5 relocated to v3 Tables 7–8. New ImageNet 512x512 results include SiD2A FIDs of 1.669 for S and 1.366 for XXL (Table 4). Table 10 adds FDDINOv2 results with different rankings: XXL SiD2A scores 44.52 versus 33.09 for the guided teacher. New convergence and subsampling findings are also reported.

M1.justification: The core shared-discriminator SiDA procedure remains. v3 adds EDM2-specific adaptations: optional learned log-variance loss weighting, modified or disabled forced weight normalization, and a separately weighted discriminator loss (Algorithm 2 and Appendix B.2). Equation (7) also changes the stated generator adversarial term from D to ln D; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative and appendices are substantially reorganized: setup moves from the main text into Appendix A, algorithms move into an expanded Appendix B, and supplementary results collect in Appendix C. Benchmarking splits into EDM and EDM2 subsections, while the abstract and conclusion are revised around the expanded scope. Much introductory and foundational prose remains.

P2.justification: v3 adds an algorithm schematic, model-size comparison tables, a six-panel convergence figure, a subsampling plot, training snapshots, and high-resolution image galleries. Existing plots are resized and wrapped alongside text; CIFAR and ImageNet convergence panels are regrouped, while FFHQ/AFHQ tables and curves move to the appendix. These are substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against EDM2, concurrent sCD, and the high-resolution generative-model landscape. It adds discussion of Luo et al. (2024)'s alternative SiD justification and distinguishes OSGAN's terminology. The account of GDD-I changes from an LPIPS discriminator to Projected-GAN-style VGG16-BN and EfficientNet-lite0 features.

T1.justification: Equation (7) substantively revises the mathematical definition of the adversarial generator loss by introducing logarithms. Algorithm 2 additionally formalizes the optional log-variance-weighted objective. The underlying Fisher-divergence and score-identity mathematics remain, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens scalability evidence beyond v1's 32x32 and 64x64 experiments through six-size ImageNet 512x512 evaluation, targeted robustness checks, and detailed adaptation code and resource reporting. It also clarifies evaluation repetition and adds an alternative feature-space metric. A material limitation remains: the broad superiority narrative insufficiently discusses Table 10, where guided teachers outperform the students on FDDINOv2. Nevertheless, the gains in empirical scope and reproducibility support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SiDA research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching experiments and algorithms relocated in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original ImageNet 512x512 distillation results, model-size comparisons, and a real-data subsampling experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original SiDA and SiD2A generation results on CIFAR-10, ImageNet 64x64, FFHQ, and AFHQ-v2, including quantitative comparisons and alpha ablations.

C1.justification: v1 only conjectures applicability to reasoning. v2 adds an abstract and introduction contribution claiming approximately 70% faster asynchronous GSM8k training with matching accuracy. Its conclusion also explicitly qualifies competitiveness by acknowledging that optimized synchronous libraries likely outperform the presented implementation.

C2.justification: v2 adds proposed explanations for PPO's optimization and computational disadvantages, reasoning-task efficiency without a reward model, and synchronous backend memory, integration, and maintenance costs. It newly acknowledges stronger optimized synchronous implementations and VinePPO's higher GSM8k accuracy at greater cost. The original GIL and communication discussion is relocated, rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: v2 supplies GSM8k hyperparameters and hardware details, additional runtime measurements, explicit RLOO implementation mathematics, and asynchronous pseudocode in Appendix D. A new reproducibility statement reports released baseline checkpoints and training datasets and integration into open-instruct. The code link and original experiment hyperparameter tables were already present in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds GSM8k mathematical reasoning alongside the retained TLDR summarization and No Robots instruction-following tasks. Generating reasoning traces and obtaining exact-answer correctness rewards substantially extends coverage beyond preference-based evaluation.

E2.justification: The No Robots comparison expands from synchronous/asynchronous Online DPO to include synchronous/asynchronous PPO (Table 9). Appendix B adds an evaluated CoPG-style RLOO comparator against Proximal RLOO. These change comparator membership within experiments, even though PPO already appeared in v1's TLDR comparisons.

E3.justification: The added GSM8k experiments introduce Rho-1B, binary correctness rewards, greedy pass@1 evaluation, four sampled completions per prompt, and a 4-L40s setup (Section 5.2; Table 10). Added chatbot PPO experiments use a KL coefficient of 0.01. The retained TLDR and chatbot Online DPO hyperparameter tables are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds the CoPG/Proximal RLOO staleness comparison in Figure 13, qualitative GSM8k checks of completion counts and selection, and a detailed generation/training overhead analysis in Appendix A.3. Figure 14 adds backend timing comparisons across model scales. The original off-policy, scaling, and compute-allocation analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated training runs or seeds, or reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The added figures and tables continue reporting results without error bars.

E6.justification: New GSM8k results report synchronous/asynchronous Online DPO at 52.2%/52.6% pass@1 and 218/129 minutes (Table 2). New PPO chatbot and CoPG robustness results also substantially expand the findings. Original Figures 1-9 and the 57.2% chatbot win rates are retained. Added chatbot runtimes conflict: Table 1 gives 230/142, whereas Table 9 gives 213.04/154.03 for synchronous/asynchronous Online DPO.

M1.justification: The asynchronous pipeline, Online DPO objective, and best/worst-of-K selection are retained. Appendix B newly specifies Proximal RLOO with importance weighting and PPO clipping. However, v1 underspecifies its RLOO implementation and Figure 4 is unchanged, leaving uncertainty about whether this changes the procedure or documents a variant already used.

P1.justification: Most existing background, TLDR, and optimization prose remains substantially unchanged. Local revisions reshape the abstract, contribution list, scaling section, and conclusion; move the practical-runtime subsection into Appendix A.2; and add a reproducibility statement and appendix organization. The expanded scientific content does not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 10-14, new comparison and hyperparameter tables, and Algorithm 1. Figure 9 moves to Appendix A.2, while main-text Table 1 redisplays existing chatbot scores with a runtime column. All nine original figure images are retained unchanged, but the added displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against CoPG's off-policy formulation and detailed discussion of NeMo-Aligner, TensorRT-LLM, and DeepSpeed-Chat. GSM8k, Rho-1, and VinePPO references establish a new reasoning comparison context, while Tulu 3 is cited as subsequent adoption. These extend the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a focused mathematical comparison of RLOO and CoPG gradients, derives the importance-weighted RLOO gradient, and defines the clipped objective in Equation 1. v1 contains no corresponding derivation; the existing RLHF and Online DPO mathematics remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's speculative reasoning extension into a tested GSM8k result and verifies asynchronous training with PPO at 8B scale, substantially strengthening evidence beyond preference rewards and Online DPO. Added protocols, pseudocode, and implementation information improve reproducibility, while the conclusion better qualifies competitiveness. Conflicting chatbot runtimes in Tables 1 and 9 and Figure 10's speedup caption weaken numerical consistency, but the broader empirical support and technical transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same asynchronous RLHF work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds original GSM8k, asynchronous PPO, and RLOO robustness results.

before.justification: v1 reports original TLDR experiments on off-policy robustness, scaling, and computational efficiency, plus LLaMA 3.1 8B instruction-following experiments.
