C1.justification: The headline empirical claims expand from beating GPT-2 on four benchmarks to beating it on six and matching TinyLlama's training budget while winning four benchmarks. v2 adds competitive GSM8K performance against Llama-2-7B using less than 5% of its pretraining FLOPs. Conversely, the conclusion narrows its broad comparable-or-superior performance claim and explicitly acknowledges scaling and generation gaps.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking chain-rule evaluation to stepwise reasoning and Monte Carlo evaluation to contextual understanding. Appendix C.4 explains T5's BLEU/exact-match discrepancy and attributes weaker reverse-direction MDM performance to greater train-test divergence. It also expands the training-objective explanation of reversal performance and removes v1's speculation about complementary ARM/MDM strengths.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds GSM8K training and sampling parameters, T5 learning-rate search details, and explicit documentation of which pretrained MDM serves each experiment. Table 7 adds model-checkpoint and mathematical-dataset links. Most existing reproducibility information remains, although v1's explicit 24-GPU pretraining count is dropped.

E1.justification: v2 adds augmented mathematical-reasoning training data and GSM8K evaluation, extending coverage to supervised multi-step mathematical reasoning. The eight existing language-understanding benchmarks, ShareGPT/MT-Bench, reversal dataset, and FineWeb scenarios remain. ARC-e and Obqa are shortened names for retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds evaluated TinyLlama-1.1B and Llama-2-7B comparators to language understanding while retaining GPT-2. The 220M ARM comparisons in v1 Table 2 are removed rather than relocated. v2 Table 5 additionally evaluates T5-3B on reversal, alongside the retained GPT-3 and Llama-2-13B comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendices B.2–B.3 explicitly replace the language-understanding MDM trained for 1.6×10^21 FLOPs plus variable-length fine-tuning with one pretrained for 3.3×10^21 FLOPs using 1% variable-length data; batch size changes from 384 to 1024. New protocols include 40-epoch GSM8K fine-tuning and compute-matched CFG evaluation. Generation and reversal retain the earlier MDM.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.3/Table 13 tests whether CFG remains beneficial at equal sampling computation, comparing 128/256 guided steps with 256/512 unguided steps. Existing length-handling and likelihood-estimation ablations, scaling analysis, temporal tests, reversal CFG ablation, and generated examples are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 128 Monte Carlo samples for validation-loss estimation and 1024 for the likelihood-method comparison. Neither reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests; v2 introduces no new statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: The principal language-understanding results are replaced under changed training conditions: for example, MDM LAMBADA accuracy is 44.71 in v1 Table 3 and 52.73 in v2 Table 2. New results include GSM8K accuracy of 58.5 against a cited Llama-2 result of 58.6, T5 reversal scores, and an unguided 512-step MT-Bench score of 1.35. These additions do not establish same-setting improvements; existing scaling plots and generation/temporal results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The MDM architecture, masking and denoising processes, training objective, unsupervised CFG formulation, and Appendix A sampling algorithm remain unchanged. The replacement checkpoint and GSM8K experiments use existing methods with different training and evaluation settings.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the abstract, introduction, language-understanding discussion, and conclusion. Section 5 loses the zero-shot qualifier, Appendix C gains a related-work subsection, and terminology and typographical errors are corrected. The overall section order and most explanatory text remain.

P2.justification: The two main language-understanding tables are replaced by one expanded table; the reversal table gains T5, and a new appendix ablation table is added. Resource and benchmark-example tables expand, with associated caption and placement changes. All six figures retain their substantive visual content.

R1.justification: Section 3 now distinguishes its scaling-law study from Ye et al.'s earlier XLM-RoBERTa adaptation work. New Appendix C.1 positions unsupervised CFG relative to Zhao et al. and Holtzman et al.; mathematical-reasoning, T5, and reversal-explanation references are also added. These clarify positioning while retaining the central novelty claims.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(8), the scaling-law fitting formulation, and the conditional-distribution reasoning are unchanged. No mathematical definitions, formal assumptions, proofs, or derivations are substantively added or revised.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of central claims: Table 2 supplies a same-size, same-data, compute-matched TinyLlama comparison missing at the 1.1B scale in v1, and Table 13 addresses the extra-computation confound in CFG evaluation. GSM8K and T5 broaden capability testing, while clearer budget disclosures and a qualified conclusion improve interpretation. Removing the 220M comparison loses useful evidence, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the stronger controls and comparisons provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. Corresponding material can be reliably matched despite revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of a more extensively trained MDM, GSM8K fine-tuning, T5 reversal experiments, and an additional guidance control.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training and IsoFLOP experiments, language-understanding evaluations, conditional-generation results, reversal experiments, and temporal-shift tests.

results.title: Scaling up Masked Diffusion Models on Text

C1.justification: The central claims about finite-library hybrid screening, pruning difficult examples, and reducing acquisition costs remain. v2's expanded Section 5 adds a broader concluding claim that heuristic acquisition orderings can be highly suboptimal and introduce biases that undermine performance estimation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting heuristic failures to chemical-element coverage and selection bias, and explains why least-confidence selection permits conservative performance estimation. It also explicitly identifies perfectly accurate, deterministic observed labels as a limitation for noisy biological experiments. The earlier limitation concerning low predictive power on RxRx3 is retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds grid-search guidance for computing the confidence bound, specifies regression stopping parameters, and describes diversity selection through Tanimoto distance. Most preprocessing and architectural details are retained or relocated, alongside the reported QM9 batch-size revision. Code remains promised upon publication, and the proprietary dataset remains unavailable.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same MNIST variants, QM9 classification, Molecules3D HOMO-LUMO-gap and energy regression, RxRx3, and proprietary phenomics task. Molecules3D moves into Appendix E.1; the new diagnostic analyses use retained datasets and task conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds BALD, diversity sampling, and SA-score ordering to the QM9 and biological classification comparisons, substantially expanding v1's random and limited ordering baselines. Molecules3D additionally compares SA-score and large-to-small ordering against the retained QBC, random, and small-to-large methods. These methods appear in the reported curves, not merely citations.

E3.justification: The reported QM9 acquisition batch changes from 50 to 250 between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2. v2 introduces regression stopping evaluations with patience 10 and MSE thresholds of 0.1 and 100 eV^2, plus a separate stopping-validation protocol using delta = 0.05 and dataset-specific accuracy targets. Existing dataset splits and network sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of weak calibration throughout acquisition, empirical checks of accuracy at stopping, and an analysis of chemical-element coverage explaining failures of large-to-small molecular acquisition (Figures 9, 11, 13, and 14). The earlier MNIST corruption analyses and QM9 difficult-example tracking are retained, with the latter extended to more acquisition methods.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed benchmark experiments. v2 explicitly identifies curve shading as standard error and stopping-time intervals as minimum-to-maximum ranges. Its separate stopping-validation study uses 100 seeds for MNIST variants and QM9 and 50 for phenomics, reporting empirical failure frequencies; this is not a blanket increase in repetitions for all existing experiments.

E6.justification: v2 substantially expands comparator and diagnostic outcomes. QM9 active/LC and random savings are replaced from 54.6%/23.2% in v1 Figure 6 to 53.6%/16.6% in v2 Figure 5 under changed batch settings. New regression stopping results report QBC savings of 21.3% and 20.2%. Figure 14 reports no LC stopping failures and random-agent failure rates of 1% on MNIST and 6% on QM9.

M1.justification: The core hybrid-screening procedure, least-confidence/QBC acquisition, and KL-based classification stopping remain. v2 Appendix E.1 adds a regression-specific stopping procedure requiring acquired-batch MSE below a threshold for a patience period. Algorithm 1 also corrects label acquisition and explicitly removes acquired examples, aligning its pseudocode with operations already described in v1.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the stopping-criterion exposition and reorganizes supporting material: theory becomes the first appendix, preprocessing is consolidated, and Molecules3D results move out of the main text. It adds Section 4.4 and expands the former conclusion into a discussion. These structural changes accompany wording and terminology revisions throughout.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the introductory schematic and reworks benchmark plots with additional method curves, expanded legends, revised axes, and stopping-time intervals. It adds calibration panels, a chemical-element coverage plot, and stopping-accuracy violin plots. The Molecules3D display moves to the appendix, while both existing tables are retained and reordered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chernoff (1952) and Guo et al. (2017) on calibration, and removes Yang and Loog (2018). The substantive positioning relative to active learning, Bayesian optimization, and core-set selection in Section 3 remains essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 reformulates weak calibration using multiclass top-prediction confidence and replaces v1's short, internally inconsistent proof with an explicit ordered-confidence argument in Appendix A.1. This corrects the inequality direction used in v1 Appendix D. Appendix A.2 additionally derives the Chernoff/KL confidence bound instead of only citing a concentration result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central stopping rule. Compared with v1's inconsistent calibration statement, sketch proof, and untested calibration assumption, it provides a clearer formal treatment, calibration diagnostics, and extensive repeated-trial stopping evaluations. Broader evaluated baselines and an explicit perfect-label limitation also improve the credibility and scope of interpretation. These gains address central evidential gaps, although code access remains promised and the proprietary data remain unavailable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same inference-set-design study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical studies and reports additional comparator results, calibration analyses, chemical-element coverage analysis, and repeated-trial evaluations of stopping accuracy.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on MNIST variants, QM9, Molecules3D, RxRx3, and a proprietary phenomics dataset, including acquisition curves and analyses of difficult examples.

results.title: Efficient Biological Data Acquisition through Inference Set Design

C1.justification: The central unification, generator characterization, Bregman training and model-combination claims remain. The introduction's experimental contribution changes from protein structure generation to multimodal protein generation, while Section 9 replaces FrameFlow-focused improvement claims with state-of-the-art claims for MultiFlow jump variants. This expands the empirical claim without redefining the framework.

C2.justification: Appendix E adds substantive interpretations connecting transport versus jumps to probability-path suitability and explaining discretization sensitivity through large Lipschitz constants and repeated small movements. Appendix A further explains the regularity restrictions and why matching marginals can suffice without full time reversal. Appendix I interprets alternative losses as improving training stability.

D1.justification: Appendix G.4 changes the implementation/checkpoint source from FrameFlow to MultiFlow and newly specifies model size, NFE usage and reliance on default configurations. Appendix I documents loss-mixture weights and its sampler. Most image implementation details remain in Appendix F, although the explicit joint-model output-channel count is omitted from the revised main text.

E1.justification: Protein evaluation expands from structure generation to joint structure–sequence generation, alongside a retained structure-only task. This directly tests multimodal generation. CIFAR-10, ImageNet32 and the checkerboard distribution were already evaluated in v1; their additional analyses do not constitute new datasets.

E2.justification: The protein comparison changes from FrameDiff and FrameFlow to FrameFlow, RFdiffusion, FoldFlow, Protpardelle, ProteinGenerator and MultiFlow; FrameDiff disappears from the reported comparison. The expanded checkerboard comparison also adds flow under the mixture path. The image benchmark comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix G.4 changes protein evaluation from 690 samples across lengths 60–128 to 400 samples at lengths 70, 100, 200 and 300, and changes rotation discretization from 1024 to 2056 bins. V2 adds designability reporting and separate multimodal/unimodal comparisons. New experiments introduce 5–500 NFE sweeps and flow-only loss comparisons using dopri5. Protein sampling remains at 100 steps.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's trajectory illustrations and image-sampler comparison, Appendix E systematically examines probability-path/process combinations and sensitivity to sampling NFEs, including mixture-path flow failures. Appendix I adds CIFAR-10 ablations of Bregman loss choices and their training dynamics. These substantially expand analysis of design choices and numerical sensitivity.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional generated-sample counts and training curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Image FIDs are unchanged between v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 2. The protein results are replaced under different models and protocols, with new multimodal and designability entries; v2 reports multimodal diversity of 0.48 for jumps versus 0.38 for MultiFlow. Appendix I newly reports flow-only FID 2.62 for MSE versus 2.54 for a modified Bregman loss. These are new comparisons, not direct v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The general GM recipe remains, but its concrete models expand substantially. Section 9 replaces the FrameFlow-based structure model with a MultiFlow-based joint structure–sequence model. Appendix E introduces a mixture-path flow and a three-component superposition; Appendix I implements cosh- and exponential-based Bregman training losses.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. V2 standardizes capitalization and measure notation, clarifies explanations, reorders image/protein experiments, reorganizes Appendix E and removes the acknowledgments. Much of the appendix expansion comprises new scientific content rather than rewriting existing exposition.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the protein montage, expands the protein comparison into multimodal/unimodal columns, and adds the systematic model table, full protein table, checkerboard comparison/NFE panels and loss-training plot. Some checkerboard displays expand existing Figure 2 material. The original manifold illustration is retained as Figure 9 rather than newly added.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against prior jump-based generation through a new Appendix H.7 covering piecewise-deterministic models, Lévy-process models and trans-dimensional jump diffusion. It also adds a substantive Blackout Diffusion discussion and citations supporting new theoretical and protein comparisons. MultiFlow was already discussed in v1; its empirical comparator role is new.

T1.justification: V2 adds formal strong/weak time-reversal definitions and a general KFE criterion in Appendix A.4. Appendix E adds several path-specific derivations and an impossibility argument for a zero-drift diffusion generating the CondOT path. It also restores missing B-function terms in the Bregman sufficiency proof. These changes extend mathematical substance beyond the retained core propositions and revised notation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the framework's distinctive multimodal and loss-flexibility claims through actual co-design experiments and loss ablations. Its systematic path/process study explains practical failure conditions, while expanded prior-work discussion improves positioning. The gains concern evidential and explanatory quality, not comparable cross-version score improvements. Limitations remain: uncertainty is unreported, and Table 5 shows lower designability for jump variants despite higher diversity, making the blanket claim of best results in all categories too strong.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Generator Matching research, retaining the core framework, propositions and image experiments. Their full texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports image and protein experiments, expanded checkerboard analyses in Appendix E, and original CIFAR-10 loss-function experiments in Appendix I.

before.justification: V1 reports original image and protein generation experiments in Section 9, Tables 2–3, and checkerboard simulations in Figure 2.

results.title: Generator Matching: Generative modeling with arbitrary Markov processes

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of increasing algorithm-dependent margins and directional convergence to KKT points for arbitrary norms, together with connections to Adam and Shampoo. The proof changes support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 now explicitly distinguishes arbitrary-norm asymptotic stationarity from finite-time approximate-KKT guarantees requiring smooth squared norms. It also clarifies that normalized limit points are proportional to KKT points. The empirical interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix D preserves the implementation framework, hyperparameters, sampling details, initialization rules, early stopping, and plotting conventions. The normalization explanation in Appendix C.1 restates the existing sign-gradient relationship rather than disclosing a different implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate sparse Gaussian teacher–student classification and MNIST digit-pair classification, including the appendix experiment on digits 2 and 7. No dataset, task, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: GD, CD, and SD in teacher–student experiments; GD, SD, and Adam variants in the Adam experiments; and GD, Adam, and Shampoo in the spectral-margin comparison.

E3.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D retain the same sample counts, architectures, learning rates, initialization scales, losses, training budgets, and stopping procedures. Moving experimental details and figures does not alter the protocols.

E4.justification: The initialization-scale analysis, switching from GD to CD or SD after separation, Adam precision/momentum comparisons, and additional digit-pair experiment are retained. No empirical ablation or supplementary analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 seeds for the teacher–student experiment and three seeds for Figure 2, with unchanged averaging, plotted uncertainty, and descriptions of seed-dependent sampling and initialization.

E6.justification: The empirical plots and reported findings are unchanged. Figures 1–3 match across versions, and v2 Figures 5–6 correspond to v3 Figures 4–5 with the same results; the removed v2 Figure 4 is a conceptual illustration.

M1.justification: The steepest-descent/flow procedures, network models, and losses are unchanged. Describing sign gradient descent as normalized steepest descent clarifies the existing relationship without establishing an algorithm or implementation change.

P1.justification: Targeted rewriting updates the proof overview, reorganizes parts of Appendices A and B, clarifies normalization terminology, and changes author and acknowledgment text. The main section order and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2's conceptual Bregman-proximity illustration, Figure 4, is removed. The retained appendix plots are renumbered, and the additional MNIST plot moves to a separate page. Main empirical figures retain their visual design.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged, but Section 3.2 revises the technical positioning: it explicitly contrasts the direct limit-point proof with the approximate-KKT sequence approach of Lyu and Li and the earlier ICLR version.

T1.justification: Theorem A.16 receives a substantially different proof: v2's approximate-iterate argument is replaced by a direct limit-point construction using convergent loss subgradients and bounded multipliers. Appendix B retains the Bregman bound, incorporates the existing complementarity estimate, and adds Proposition B.7, Corollary B.8, and Remark B.9 on finite-time guarantees for smooth squared norms. The general proximity-measure optimization in v2 Appendix B.1 is removed.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses a central proof gap: v2 Equation (61) assumes convergence of selected norm subgradients from membership in the limiting subdifferential, which is insufficient for nonsmooth norms. The revised Theorem A.16 instead uses closed-graph subsequence arguments and bounded multipliers, substantially strengthening support for the paper's arbitrary-norm claim. The finite-time limitations are also clearer. New Equation (79) appears to omit a square in its strong-convexity bound, but this local auxiliary defect does not outweigh the repair to the central proof.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Flavors of Margin. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and Appendices A–D are readable and support a complete comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their empirical results in Section 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 reports original teacher–student and MNIST experiments measuring margins, losses, and generalization under several optimizers, including additional appendix results.

results.title: Flavors of Margin: Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent in Homogeneous Neural Networks

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement substantially narrow the convergence claims: the large-batch O(1/T) guarantee is removed, and PL convergence is explicitly to a neighborhood of the optimum. The method's central flexibility claim remains. Abstract CIFAR-100 advantages change from 21.4%/12.2% to 18.2%/7.4%, reflecting stronger comparators rather than changed LASER-VFL scores.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking Combinatorial's behavior to training-data scarcity for larger feature subsets, discusses task-sampling variance growing with client count, and explicitly states the MCAR boundary. Appendix A.2 argues that adjusted representation models preserve aggregation expressivity. These substantially expand interpretation beyond the retained dropout-like regularization explanation.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-availability link. Appendix D newly identifies the MLP, LSTM, and ResNet18 model choices, explains PlugVFL's zero-filled missing representations and per-party dropout adaptation, and reports runtimes. These improve documentation, although detailed training hyperparameters and hardware remain unspecified.

E1.justification: All five datasets and prediction tasks are retained. Appendix E adds a CIFAR-10 scenario with heterogeneous, Beta-distributed missingness probabilities across feature blocks, including independently sampled training and inference probabilities. This is a limited extension of input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Combinatorial and an adapted PlugVFL across all five datasets, substantially strengthening the comparator set. Combinatorial was previously only a conceptual alternative, while the work underlying PlugVFL was cited but not evaluated. Existing baselines retain their dataset participation.

E3.justification: The primary four-client missingness grid and metrics remain unchanged. Added protocols measure accuracy and runtime across two to eight clients at missingness probability 0.1, and compare Beta(2,2) block probabilities against a fixed 0.5 control. Combinatorial is omitted at eight clients because of resource constraints.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's missingness grid, v2 adds dedicated scalability and runtime analysis in Figure 2 and nonuniform-missingness robustness tests in Appendix E. These provide substantial new examinations of the method's efficiency and sensitivity to heterogeneous feature availability.

E5.justification: Both versions report Table 1 means and standard deviations over five seeds. The new Table 3 follows the same practice. No changed run count, confidence-interval procedure, or significance-testing method is stated.

E6.justification: All retained Table 1 scores are unchanged, but new comparator results alter rankings: with complete HAPT training data and inference missingness 0.5, PlugVFL scores 90.3 ± 1.3 versus LASER-VFL's retained 87.0 ± 1.2. Figure 2, Appendix D runtimes, and Table 3 add substantial scaling, cost, and nonuniform-missingness findings.

M1.justification: The shared representation and fusion models, averaging aggregation, weighted objective, task-sampling procedure, and training/inference algorithms remain equivalent. Revised notation and the aggregation explanation in Appendix A.2 do not establish a changed architecture or procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the objective and task-sampling exposition, revise notation and terminology, and expand and reorganize the appendices. The main section sequence and much of the introductory and concluding prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the two-panel scalability/runtime Figure 2, the LASER-VFL forward-pass diagram in Figure 3, and the nonuniform-missingness Table 3. Table 1 gains comparator rows and revised best-score emphasis. Figure 1 is relocated and its preview explicitly labeled MIMIC-IV.

R1.justification: V2 adds Ganguli et al. and supporting references for missingness mechanisms and model architectures, fixes the unresolved FedSVD citation, and expands closest-work comparisons in Appendix A.1. The central research positioning remains. Sun's updated PlugVFL reference corresponds to work already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Section 4 and the proofs replace the single variance bound sigma^2/B with separate mini-batch and task-sampling bounds, producing sigma_b^2 + K sigma_s^2 terms in both theorems. Large-batch O(1/T) and full-batch exact-convergence statements disappear. V2 also explicitly assumes missingness completely at random and adds an aggregation-equivalence derivation in Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for effectiveness and efficiency through relevant additional baselines, measured scaling, and heterogeneous-missingness tests that v1 lacked. Separate task-sampling variance accounting and narrower convergence claims improve theoretical qualification; implementation disclosures improve transparency. Some Section 5 wording overstates Combinatorial's dominance relative to Table 1, and training details remain limited, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LASER-VFL work. Their text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison; retained appendix content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds baseline evaluations, client-count/runtime experiments, and nonuniform-missingness experiments in Figure 2 and Appendix E.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on HAPT, Credit, MIMIC-IV, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, including Table 1 results across training and inference missingness conditions.

results.title: Vertical Federated Learning with Missing Features During Training and Inference

C1.justification: The principal claims about reasons without recourse, responsive feature highlighting, and flagging potentially fixed predictions remain. v2 adds an explicit contribution concerning information missing from explanations and strengthens the conclusion that explainability mandates need clearer requirements for explanation content and construction.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds a substantive distinction between a feature admitting recourse and an explanation providing enough information to attain it. It explains failures caused by nonmonotonic responses and counterintuitive directions, and discusses supplying thresholds or imposing model constraints. v2 also introduces potential applications in content moderation and criminal justice; the earlier individual-feasibility and causal-assumption limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds algorithm pseudocode, detailed optimization and sampling routines, the enumeration setting epsilon_min=0.5, preprocessing explanations, feature-partition mappings, and continuous-case actionability specifications. Code links change from responsiveness-public to reachml. Conversely, v1's illustrative enumeration cost of roughly one hour and 18.8 GB is removed.

E1.justification: Empirical coverage remains loan repayment and recourse on heloc, german, and givemecredit. The continuous-feature givemecredit case uses the existing population and task; its changed representation and diagnostic criteria constitute protocol and supplementary-analysis changes rather than additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain LIME, SHAP, their action-aware variants, and RESP across the same classifier families. The actionable-feature columns in v1 Table 9 already represent the variants explicitly named LIME-AW and SHAP-AW in v2 Table 12. The new case study uses existing methods LIME and SHAP.

E3.justification: Section 5 introduces a substantial additional evaluation protocol: an 11-feature mixed continuous/discrete givemecredit representation, an XGBoost model, sampled reachable sets for 23,459 adversely predicted individuals, and checks of monotonicity and intuitive direction. The original experiments retain their 80/20 split, classifier families, and primary evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: The new Section 5 and Table 5 investigate whether feature lists omit necessary information about the direction and amount of change. Cases include disjoint responsive intervals for credit utilization and approval requiring decreased income. This substantive failure analysis is absent from v1; the existing feature-ranking analyses remain in the supplement.

E5.justification: v1 already provides a corrected binomial confidence interval in Proposition 2. v2 Appendix A.2 identifies the Agresti-Coull construction and adds sample-size calibration for shortest and widest intervals, with Tables 6–7. The new case specifies N=500 and alpha=0.01; neither version reports repeated-run variability or seed-based uncertainty.

E6.justification: Numerous existing results are revised. For heloc/LR, Table 3's no-recourse rate changes from 19.1% to 22.2%, while Table 4's wholly unresponsive LIME explanations change from 82.0% to 92.7%. RF results also change. New Table 5 reports that fewer than 7% of explanations contain any feature satisfying responsiveness, monotonicity, and intuitive direction together. Original classifier AUCs remain unchanged; the PDFs do not explain all benchmark revisions.

M1.justification: The central responsiveness score is retained. Whereas v1 describes enumerating general reachable sets and selecting single-feature actions, v2 Algorithm 2 directly enumerates consequences of fixed single-feature interventions. Section 3.1 also adds a cost-weighted extension and replaces the earlier robust-score variant with a worst-case score over bounded perturbations.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the introduction, problem statement, methods, and results prose are substantially rewritten. Actionability moves into the method section, the results narrative is reordered, and a dedicated Discussion section is introduced. The supplement is reorganized into method details, experiment details, results, and case-study details, with a contents page.

P2.justification: v2 revises Figure 1 and the reachable-set illustration, adds the conceptual comparison in Figure 2, introduces two algorithm panels and several new tables, and expands constraint-table columns. Existing ranking plots are resized and repacked, and the RF table is relocated. The conference template also substantially changes page composition.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning binomial intervals, explanation disagreement, legal rights, reason codes, and fairness tools, including Agresti and Coull, Krishna et al., and Kaminski. It removes citations including Fokkema et al. and Anchors. The positioning among feature attribution and algorithmic recourse remains, with a clearer comparison to nearest-action recourse methods.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the action/downstream-set formulation with explicit interventions and downstream effects, resolving v1 Definition 3's conflicting restrictions on the intervened feature. Appendix A adds mixed-integer formulations and a proof of confidence-interval width extrema in Fact 3. Cost-weighted and worst-case robust score definitions also add or revise substantive mathematics; the existing confidence interval is relocated and expanded.

improvement.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and Appendix A substantially improve the self-contained technical specification, while Section 5 supplies important evidence about when responsive feature lists still need direction and threshold information. These address significant documentation and applicability gaps in v1. Reporting weaknesses remain: benchmark revisions are unexplained, and Appendix A.2's formula gives an upper bound of about 0.0158 for N=500, alpha=0.01, and zero successes, contradicting Section 5's claimed 0.01 bound. These issues qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same feature-responsiveness framework and consumer-finance study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark study with revised results and adds an original continuous-feature case study in Section 5, supported by Tables 5 and 14.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original experiments evaluating recourse feasibility and explanation responsiveness for logistic regression, XGBoost, and random forests on three lending datasets.

results.title: Feature Responsiveness Scores: Model-Agnostic Explanations for Recourse

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: comprehensive Mamba PEFT exploration, Mamba-specific methods, hybrid search, and greater PEFT benefits for Mamba than Transformers. The conclusion reorganizes the existing findings and adds evidence pointers without materially changing these headline claims.

C2.justification: Appendix A.5 qualifies the data-size interpretation by explaining that the preferred method becomes task-dependent with more data. A.6–A.7 add a possible limited-data adaptation barrier for larger vision Mamba models and discuss performance saturation. B.2 expands the rationale for preserving pre-trained behavior during hybrid search. These are focused additions to the existing interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 newly states that evaluation uses final-epoch weights, clarifies shared-task hyperparameter selection, and separates Mamba and Pythia learning-rate configurations. It reports relative training times and refines the stated A100 search-trial duration from 20–30 minutes to around 20 minutes. Code remains promised after publication in both versions.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same 19 VTAB image-classification tasks and eight commonsense-reasoning tasks, with unchanged pre-training dataset coverage. The additions vary sample counts, splits, and model configurations within this coverage rather than introducing new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds SPT-LoRA for ViT-S, ViT-B, and ViT-tiny, and adds Adapter+ to the ViT-B/DeiT/ImageNet-1K and ViT-tiny comparisons in Table 4. Tables 1 and 8 add combined-LoRA comparators; Table 3 adds LoRA(in_proj) at every Mamba size. Table 6 newly compares DoRA_p(X) with LoRA_p(X), substantially broadening the evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix A.5 introduces training-size sweeps using exchanged official VTAB training/test roles. Other additions evaluate Vim-B and VMamba-S/B configurations. Table 1 adds a relative training-time metric and changes the stated parameter-count basis from CIFAR-100 to an average across tasks. Appendix B.1 changes the reported Pythia-1.4B full-fine-tuning learning rate from 5e-5 to 5e-6.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether training-data quantity explains the vision/language differences (A.5, Figure 7), examine model-size saturation (A.6–A.7), test DoRA substitution (A.8), and vary combined LoRA placements and ranks (B.2, Table 8). These substantially extend the retained initialization, token-placement, rank, and learning-rate ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages across tasks without seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises projected Prompt-tuning from 54.76 to 62.54 and unprojected Affix-tuning from 54.30 to 65.04. Table 4 changes several aggregates despite unchanged task scores, including ViT-B/ImageNet-21K LoRA from 74.5 to 72.3. Pythia full-fine-tuning rows change; the 1.4B average rises from 44.8 to 50.5 alongside its revised learning rate, so this is not a matched-setting gain. Numerous new configuration and analysis results are also reported.

M1.justification: Appendix A.8 introduces the limited DoRA_p(X) variant by replacing LoRA with DoRA at the same partial projection. The original Affix-tuning, Additional-scan, Partial-tuning objectives, and two-stage hybrid search remain unchanged; Algorithm 1 and its search settings are retained.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section ordering remain intact. v2 expands the SSM/Vim explanation, reformats the conclusion into numbered findings with cross-references, adds Appendix A.5–A.8, and expands and rearranges the hybrid-search explanation. The language and structural revisions are localized.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evidence displays: Table 1 gains a timing column, Tables 3 and 4 gain comparison rows and model blocks, and Figure 7 adds three data-size panels. New Tables 5, 6, and 8 display VMamba, DoRA, and combined-LoRA results. The learning-rate table is restructured and relocated; Figures 1–6 and the existing algorithm are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds He et al. (2023) on sensitivity-aware tuning, Lian et al. (2022) on scaling and shifting features, and Zhang et al. (2024c) on gradient-based parameter selection. Related-work discussion modestly expands, while Appendix A.8 further positions the exploration as guidance for subsequent tuning methods. The overall novelty positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Section 2.1, Equation 2 replaces the bilinear discretization formula with an exponential zero-order-hold formula. Appendix B.2 adds mathematical search-space size calculations for simultaneous versus staged optimization. These are localized mathematical changes; the Additional-scan derivation remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens this benchmarking paper by directly testing the earlier data-size hypothesis within vision, checking another Mamba architecture and larger models, and adding controls for partial and combined LoRA. It also corrects Equation 2 and several inconsistent benchmark aggregates, improving mathematical and reporting reliability. The added analyses expose practical scaling limits instead of merely reporting higher scores. Some inconsistencies remain, such as differing Vim-S full-fine-tuning averages in Tables 1 and 4, and run-to-run uncertainty is still unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MambaPEFT with matching authors, core methods, and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A and B support reliable comparison, including relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for larger vision models, VMamba, training-data-size variation, DoRA substitution, and LoRA combinations.

before.justification: v1 reports original VTAB-1k and commonsense-reasoning experiments, hyperparameter ablations, and hybrid PEFT search results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: MambaPEFT: Exploring Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mamba

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about episodic-memory limitations, PEM, memory-guided exploration, and improved task solving. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine those main contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 replaces the untested LLM-integration limitation with the narrower limitation that high-level planners cannot access PEM. New discussion explains task-relevant exploration and the storage-efficiency versus task-success tradeoff of retaining cluster centers. Existing terrain and positional-information limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly specifies the existing DP-Means penalty as delta = 1 and explains initialization. New appendices document Qwen2.5-72B, heuristic crafting actions, exploration prompts, spatial smoothing, and compressed-memory handling. These extend reproducibility information; the original hardware, training details, and code-release statements are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix M extends evaluation from resource collection and navigation to multi-step crafting and planning. Table 10 evaluates eleven tasks with ground-truth plans, while Table 9 evaluates four with an LLM-based DEPS planner. These introduce task requirements absent from v1.

E2.justification: Appendix P adds the center-embedding-only memory variant to the ABA-Sparse comparison, and Appendix N compares task-conditioned and task-free exploration. Existing external baselines remain; STEVE-FM/EM/PM becoming MrSteve-FM/EM/PM are renamings. Applying the retained Steve-1 comparator to planning tasks does not itself add a baseline.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include LLM-generated versus ground-truth plans, task-specific 3,000/6,000-step budgets, and memory capacities from 100 to 12,000 frames. Appendix N additionally measures exploration-mode duration and pasture visitation over time. The settings documented for the retained experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing navigation and memory-hyperparameter ablations, v3 tests whether semantic task conditioning improves exploration, whether memory performance survives capacity restrictions, and whether retaining only cluster centers reduces redundancy without sacrificing success. Ground-truth-plan controls also examine controller performance without LLM planning errors.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2.1 retains 100 episodes with different seeds and five runs for the original long-horizon tasks. Standard-error reporting was already present in v1. The additions use that reporting practice without documenting increased repetitions or new statistical procedures; planning success rates have no accompanying uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Substantial new results appear in Tables 9–11 and Figures 16–18. For bed, newly reported success rates are 50% versus 27% with DEPS and 60% versus 37% with ground-truth plans, favoring MrSteve; ground-truth sign instead favors Steve-1, 70% versus 67%. Table 11 reports shorter exploration durations, including 1202.64 versus 1512.00 steps for Beef-Log-Beef. These are added comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1 results.

M1.justification: The original controller remains, but v3 adds two substantive implemented alternatives. Appendix N introduces task-conditioned exploration using semantic relevance maps and spatial smoothing. Appendix P introduces PEM that discards individual frame embeddings after clustering and retains cluster centers, changing storage and retrieval.

P1.justification: v3 standardizes agent and variant names, changes observation notation, expands MineCLIP and DP-Means explanations, and revises the limitations paragraph. Appendices M–P are appended without substantial reorganization of the existing narrative. The conclusion also acquires a duplicated opening clause.

P2.justification: Tables 8–11 and Figures 16–18 substantially expand the visual presentation with planning comparisons, exploration trajectories, memory-capacity curves, and compression results. Existing plots also receive revised legends, fonts, and colors. Earlier tables and figures remain identifiable despite pagination changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to GPT-4, CLIP, and Qwen2.5, including repairing the unresolved introduction citation. The main positioning against planner-oriented memory systems remains unchanged. Updated bibliographic details for already cited works do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix M adds formal plan/subgoal notation and the horizon-prediction-based selection distribution in Equation 3. Existing memory-complexity reasoning and navigator equations remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly left LLM-planner integration untested despite motivating the work through hierarchical-controller bottlenecks. Appendix M addresses this gap with DEPS comparisons and ground-truth-plan controls, while Appendices O–P strengthen evidence about memory capacity and efficiency tradeoffs. Together these substantially improve support for the paper's central rationale. Planning results still lack uncertainty estimates, and compressed memory has notable task-specific losses, limiting broader claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MrSteve research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching renamed methods and relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds planning-task evaluations, task-conditioned exploration experiments, memory-capacity sweeps, and memory-compression comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original Minecraft exploration, sequential-task, memory-constrained navigation, and long-horizon experiments, alongside appendix ablations and computational measurements.

results.title: MrSteve: Instruction-Following Agents in Minecraft with What-Where-When Memory

C1.justification: The central claims about generating conditional counterfactuals and exposing intervention side effects remain. v3's introduction adds an explicit qualification that the Gumbel causal parameterization is not unique and motivates its selection through the Thurstone model, refining the scope of the contribution.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly discusses non-identifiability, dependence on the chosen causal mechanism, counterfactual stability, and alternative sampling mechanisms. Its Louvre discussion changes from substantial semantic deviation to generally similar but nonminimal counterfactuals. Revised instruction-tuning examples acknowledge factual corrections and alternative correct facts, while the gender-stereotype mechanism discussion is removed.

D1.justification: v3 removes the project repository link advertised below v1's abstract; this establishes loss of an access pointer, not repository unavailability. Appendix D.2 supplies five additional explicit Louvre prompts. Appendix D.1 retains the intervention hyperparameters, model-access references, eight RTX-4096 GPUs, and 32-bit precision.

E1.justification: Wikipedia and Bios remain represented, including retained GPT2-XL gender examples in Appendix E.2. v3 adds targeted koala-habitat prompts and counterfactuals in Section 4.2/Figure 5; v1 evaluated the koala edit only on neutral Wikipedia prompts.

E2.justification: Figure 2 retains the same six intervention conditions: GPT2-XL gender steering and two MEMIT edits, plus LLaMA3 gender steering, Honest steering, and instruction tuning. Neither version evaluates an alternative counterfactual generator against the proposed procedure. v3's inverse-CDF comparison is attributed to cited work.

E3.justification: The principal evaluation replaces normalized longest-common-prefix length and E5 cosine similarity with normalized character edit distance. Appendix D.2 expands the reported Louvre prompt list from eight to thirteen while retaining 75 filtered sentences. The Wikipedia protocol retains 500 sentences, five-word prompts, and a maximum 25-token original continuation.

E4.justification: v1's 500-biography LLaMA3 gender study, including pronoun outcomes and word-probability-ratio analysis, is removed rather than relocated. Its LLaMA3 appendix examples also disappear, although GPT2-XL Bios examples remain. v3 expands the targeted knowledge-editing case studies with Louvre and koala examples in Figures 4–5.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both show distributions across generated sentences; the changed histograms do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: v3 replaces the prefix-length and cosine-similarity results with edit-distance results and removes the quantitative gender outcomes and word rankings. Louvre outcomes change from 60.0% Rome/40.0% Paris to 54.6%/45.4%. The expanded prompt list and revised stated sampler prevent treating this as a same-setting performance decline. New MEMIT examples and changed GPT2-XL steering outputs also alter the reported qualitative evidence.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Proposition 3.1 change the stated posterior sampler: v1 draws the observed token's noise from a standard Gumbel; v3 samples the perturbed maximum using the log-sum-exp location, samples truncated competitors, and subtracts logits to recover noise. Generation also changes from a fixed token count to stopping at EOS, with fresh noise beyond the observed length. These alter the procedure, independently of the formalism's renaming.

P1.justification: Sections 2–3 receive extensive rewriting around ASEM/WSEM terminology and a reorganized mathematical exposition. Section 4.2 loses its separate gender and Louvre subsections and becomes a MEMIT-focused discussion. Appendices B/C are reorganized into identifiability and proofs, and the title adds 'Gumbel.'

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn from two causal diagrams into a single language-process diagram. Figure 2 changes axes, legend ordering, and plotted distributions. The gender example figure is removed, two MEMIT example figures are introduced, and Figure 3 is reformatted with smaller text and without the earlier colored difference highlighting. Algorithm 1 is also reformatted.

R1.justification: Appendix A replaces its earlier assertion that this formulation had not been explored in language modeling with a substantial comparison to concurrent Chatzi et al. work, distinguishing intervention scope and inference for observed sentences. The introduction and Appendix B substantially expand positioning through choice theory, Thurstone models, and alternative counterfactual mechanisms.

T1.justification: Section 2 replaces the general GSEM formulation with explicit acyclic and well-founded SEM definitions, ordering assumptions, and an LM construction. New Appendix B discusses identifiability and states a Thurstone/Gumbel characterization theorem. Proposition 3.1 is substantively revised, and Appendix C.2 supplies a detailed posterior-sampling derivation in place of v1's brief argument.

improvement.justification: v3 corrects an important defect in the stated posterior sampler: the observed token's unconditional Gumbel draw is replaced by the conditional maximum construction, supported by Appendix C.2's derivation. The explicit identifiability discussion also substantially improves the interpretation of the central contribution. These gains outweigh the loss of the quantitative gender analysis, semantic-similarity measurements, and project link. The improvement concerns the documented method and reasoning; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were recomputed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Gumbel-based counterfactual generation work. Their text, equations, algorithms, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original edit-distance distributions, knowledge-editing outcomes, and generated counterfactual examples in Section 4 and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments, similarity measurements, gender-steering outcomes, and knowledge-editing results in Section 4 and Appendix E.

results.title: Gumbel Counterfactual Generation From Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution statement, and discussion retain the same central claims: a generative explanation of conditional and label shifts, limitations of recentering under label shifts, and parameter-efficient SPDIM adaptation. Expanded supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds a specific limitation: noise and outliers can make IM estimate a bias in the wrong direction and increase variability. Section 4.3 additionally interprets domainwise centering as harmful relative to global centering under label shifts and introduces a limited qualification concerning TSMNet+STMA.

D1.justification: v4 newly specifies full-target gradient estimation and 50 adaptation epochs, and Appendix A7 documents TSMNet layers, filter counts, eigenvalue rectification, model selection, and sleep-baseline implementation and training choices. These materially expand reproducibility information. Existing source-training optimizer settings, batch sizes, and hardware descriptions are retained or relocated.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four motor-imagery datasets, CAP, Dreem, HMC, ISRUC, and synthetic binary classification. Cross-session/cross-subject transfer and balanced/shifted conditions already occur in v1. The added simulation sweeps vary configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated EA and STMA comparisons, DeepSleepNet and AttnSleep for sleep staging, and EEGNet v4, EEG-Conformer, ATCNet, and EEGInceptionMI for motor imagery (Tables A2, A4–A5). This substantially broadens external benchmarking. The former TSMNet+RCT rows match TSMNet+SPDDSBN and are not new comparators.

E3.justification: The simulation design expands to controlled sweeps of source-domain counts, 100–800 samples per domain, covariance dimensions 2/4/8, and 1–3 informative dimensions. Appendix A6 also specifies two informative dimensions where v1 Section 4.1 specified one; this is a reported setting revision without establishing reruns. Existing real-EEG preprocessing and cross-validation protocols are retained.

E4.justification: New Figures A1–A4 test sensitivity to source-domain count, sample availability, covariance dimensionality, and informative dimensions, substantially extending the original separability/label-ratio analysis. These reveal conditions where adaptation becomes less reliable. The sleep-staging ablation scores in v4 Table A3 were already present in v1 Table A2 and are reorganized rather than new.

E5.justification: Figure 3 newly identifies error bars as 95% confidence intervals; v1's caption referred to standard deviations in brackets. Reported multiple-testing families change, including 4 to 14 tests in Table 1 and 7 to 14 for shifted motor imagery. The permutation/t-max framework remains, and neither version supplies repeat-run counts or seeds. v4's sleep-table captions inconsistently state 14 versus 10 tests.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive baseline scores and simulation sensitivity results, while retaining original SPDIM scores, including 73.5%/69.9% for healthy/patient sleep groups and 77.5%/68.5% for shifted cross-session/cross-subject motor imagery. New comparisons qualify superiority: Table A2 reports AttnSleep+STMA at 74.6% on ISRUC patients versus SPDIM's 71.6%. These are expanded findings, not an improvement in SPDIM's retained scores.

M1.justification: The operational SPDIM method remains unchanged: domain recentering, the SPD bias and geodesic parameterizations, information-maximization loss, and adaptation with the feature extractor and classifier fixed. Expanded architecture and optimization descriptions do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: Most prose and the overall section sequence remain. v4 reorganizes training/adaptation descriptions, moves implementation material into expanded appendices, rewrites portions of the experimental discussion, and standardizes terminology and class-prior notation. These are localized editorial and structural revisions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is comprehensively redesigned around generation, source training, and target adaptation. Table 2 becomes a component-based ablation display; appendix comparisons are expanded and separated into dedicated tables. Four sensitivity figures are added, Figure 2 gains separability annotations, and Figure 3 is relocated and relabeled.

R1.justification: v4 adds alignment references including Collas et al. (2024), Ju and Guan (2022), and Gnassounou et al. (2024), plus architecture and sleep-model references. These broaden the surrounding context and support the added comparisons without substantially changing the paper's novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 newly assumes that B is sparse and structured so label information occupies the first D-dimensional block of log(E). This narrows the formal generative specification. Propositions 1–2 and their appendix proofs remain substantively unchanged; other mathematical edits mainly simplify notation.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's narrow external benchmarking and limited sensitivity evidence through Tables A2/A4–A5 and Figures A1–A4. Added implementation details and an explicit failure mechanism also make the work easier to reproduce and assess. These gains outweigh reporting shortcomings: Section 4.3 still overstates significant superiority despite unmarked comparisons in Table A2, and the sleep-table captions disagree on testing-family size. The improvement comes from stronger scrutiny and documentation, not higher retained scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPDIM research, with matching central methods, datasets, and retained results. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and reports additional baseline comparisons and simulation sensitivity experiments in Tables A2–A5 and Figures A1–A4.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations and motor-imagery and sleep-staging experiments in Sections 4.1–4.3, with results in Figures 2–3, Tables 1–2, and the appendix.

results.title: SPDIM: Source-Free Unsupervised Conditional and Label Shift Adaptation in EEG

C1.justification: The Alignment Hypothesis, IP/OOP framework and central claim of dependence on pretraining remain. v3 drops the conclusion's explicit prediction of similar findings for single-source finetuning and changes the contribution statement from a promised split release to a stated release.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning forgetting of initially correct IP predictions, task-irrelevant pretraining captions, competing image context and object size, including the TerraIncognita exception. It motivates raw alignment through cross-dataset score comparability and clarifies that the analysis does not assume how alignment arose. These extend v2's primarily alignment-based interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 provides a stated Hugging Face dataset-release location and documents VisDiff sampling, selection thresholds and OWLv2 use. It removes v2 Appendix A.1's statement that code is zipped in the supplement. The original optimizer settings, method hyperparameters and GPU information remain unchanged; actual external resource availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate multi-source image classification on DomainNet, OfficeHome, PACS, TerraIncognita and VLCS, with LAION-400M used for pretraining/retrieval. New analyses reuse this coverage. OpenAI CLIP and DINOv2 backbone evaluations already appear in v2 Appendix B.4.

E2.justification: v3 adds OpenCLIP ZS throughout the aggregate and per-domain IP/OOP/All comparisons, supplying a direct reference without source finetuning that v2 lacks. Appendix B.6 also compares confidence-based and averaged scores against AlignmentScore. The existing fine-tuned comparators and oracle remain.

E3.justification: The original training and target-domain evaluation protocol is retained. New experimental designs include a perceptual-similarity split at 0.86, ResNet-50 training from scratch with MPA, paired zero-shot/CLIPood correctness analysis, and VisDiff sampling with AUC filtering plus OWLv2 object-size measurements. These supplement rather than replace existing settings.

E4.justification: New Appendices B.5–B.9 test alternative split criteria, confidence-based and combined scores, similarity to source images, learning without pretraining, and prediction changes after finetuning. Sections C.4–C.5 add contextual-distractor and object-size analyses. The earlier backbone, labeling-noise and distribution analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new softmax-confidence diagnostic in Appendix B.6 is an alternative predictive score, not uncertainty reporting for experimental estimates.

E6.justification: All matched fine-tuned benchmark scores remain unchanged. v3 adds zero-shot averages of 79.0 on IP, 48.1 on OOP and 71.5 on All, alongside scratch-training, alternative-score, prediction-transition and image-characterization results. It also corrects the prose claim of beating the IP oracle on three datasets to two, although a subsequent sentence still says three.

M1.justification: The principal procedure retains cosine AlignmentScore, filtering below 0.15 and above 0.4, and the 0.21 IP/OOP threshold. Algorithm 1 formalizes the previously described retrieval-and-binning workflow. Alternative scores are evaluated as diagnostic comparisons without replacing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v3 introduces an explicit Discussion section and pseudocode explanation, converts algorithm descriptions from bullets to prose, condenses protocol and results passages, and updates publication and affiliation formatting. The main section sequence and much of the original exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds diagnostic figures, comparison tables, confusion matrices and a multi-page VisDiff table, while expanding benchmark tables with zero-shot rows. Figure 2's panels are exchanged, dataset-statistics displays move to the appendix, and many retained plots are reproduced at substantially higher resolution.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations and discussion concerning domain contamination, subpopulation shifts and evaluation leakage, including Mayilvahanan et al. (2025), Dehdashtian et al. (2024) and Yu et al. (2024). ADDA, VisDiff and OWLv2 references are also added. These broaden context without substantially redefining the central research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix B.6 newly defines Calibrated AlignmentScore using the true-class softmax probability p(c), and considers averaging AlignmentScore with PerceptualSimilarityScore. These are limited diagnostic definitions; the original cosine definitions and DG assumptions remain unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important validation gap by adding same-backbone zero-shot comparisons and paired prediction counts, making the gains and forgetting from source finetuning directly assessable (Table 1; Tables 5–6). Alternative-score controls substantially strengthen the benchmarking rationale, while sharper figures and a stated dataset-release location improve inspectability and reuse. The scratch comparison also changes architecture, uncertainty remains unreported, and the code-supplement statement disappears. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidence addressing the paper's central question.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Alignment Hypothesis and DomainBed-IP/OOP study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained equations, experiments, tables and figures can be matched despite expansion and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original zero-shot comparisons, scratch-training results, prediction-transition counts and image-content analyses (Tables 1, 3–6 and 9; Figure 10).

before.justification: v2 reports original five-dataset DG experiments, alignment and perceptual-similarity analyses, and additional backbone evaluations (Table 2, Figure 2 and Appendix B).

results.title: Is Large-scale Pretraining the Secret to Good Domain Generalization?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the central claims of symmetry-preserving generation, information sharing across space groups, structural diversity, competitive stability and computational efficiency. The additional experiments support these existing contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the earlier novelty-filtering advantage interpretation with a more qualified stability comparison. It acknowledges weaker structural validity, suggests limited access to interatomic distances as a cause, and discusses seed variability. The new DFT interpretation includes strong fidelity claims alongside substantive caveats about lax thresholds and roughly 60% nonconvergence. Existing composition-conditioning and polycrystal limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive CP2K configuration details, including the functional, basis, pseudopotential, optimization settings and convergence thresholds. It also documents MPTS-52 splits and training duration, baseline retraining, and proxy evaluation on 1,000 valid crystals using a pretrained DimeNet++ energy predictor. These expand reproducibility information; the original model hyperparameters and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on MPTS-52 alongside MP-20 (Section 5.6 and Appendix F.1). This extends coverage to crystals with up to 52 rather than 20 atoms per primitive cell and broader chemistry, including materials containing radioactive elements.

E2.justification: The evaluated generation baselines remain CDVAE, DiffCSP, DiffCSP++ and FlowMM. The new DFT comparison reuses this set, while MPTS-52 reports SymmCD alone. The original representation and property-prediction comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Stability evaluation expands from a random 1,000-crystal subset in v1 to all 10,000 generated crystals per method in v2. New protocols include CP2K relaxation of 100 structures per model and MPTS-52 training for 1,500 epochs with chronological train/validation/test splits. The original MP-20 split and preprocessing remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix F.6 add substantial physical-fidelity diagnostics through DFT relaxation displacements, residual gradients and nonconvergence analysis. Appendix F.2 extends atom-count distribution validation to MPTS-52. The original site-symmetry property-prediction ablation and six crystal examples are retained.

E5.justification: v2 first reports five seeded model trainings per method, with 10,000 generated samples per seed, and adds +/- variability to the main proxy-results table. v1 reports point values without run counts or uncertainty. This establishes expanded statistical reporting, although v1's run count and the precise meaning of v2's +/- statistic are unspecified.

E6.justification: Proxy scores are replaced by five-seed summaries, and stability results change under expanded sampling. v1 Table 3 reports 10-SG SymmCD S.U.N. yield of 9.9% versus DiffCSP's 9.7%; v2 Table 2 reports 7.59% versus 8.92% on 10,000 samples. These are revised evaluation summaries, not demonstrated same-setting performance changes. MPTS-52 and DFT results are added; original template, efficiency and regression-ablation values are retained.

M1.justification: The symmetry representation, joint diffusion processes, losses, denoising network, projection and replication procedures remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 and Appendices A–E describe the same method; the added dataset experiments do not introduce a new component.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative places stability before proxy metrics, moves detailed proxy definitions into Appendix F.5 and reorganizes Appendix F around the extensions. Elsewhere, revisions mainly shorten wording, standardize terminology and rename algorithm headings. The main exposition and method structure remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds MPTS-52 distribution plots and result tables, DFT displacement and gradient plots, and configuration and gradient-summary tables. It also uses denser formatting for the proxy-results table and relocates several displays. The original atom-count histogram, property ablation and crystal examples remain identifiable despite renumbering and presentation changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MPTS-52, CP2K, PBE and EGNN, and notes the absence of reported de novo MPTS-52 results for its baselines. The central positioning against template-based DiffCSP++ and Wyckoff-label approaches remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The crystallographic definitions, replication construction, lattice constraints and diffusion equations remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof or formal derivation is introduced; the new DFT quantities serve as empirical diagnostics.

improvement.justification: Five-seed proxy comparisons and the larger stability evaluation substantially strengthen empirical reliability and temper the earlier S.U.N. superiority interpretation. MPTS-52 supplies direct evidence for larger-crystal applicability, with expanded reproducibility documentation. These gains outweigh weaknesses in the new DFT superiority evidence: most relaxations fail to converge, and Table 10's reported mean gradients appear inconsistent with Figure 10's distribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SymmCD research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds repeated-seed evaluations, MPTS-52 generation experiments and DFT relaxation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MP-20 generation experiments, computational-efficiency measurements and a formation-energy prediction ablation.
